questions.question: Rates are close to zero and a desk needs a short-rate model to price interest rate options across a wide range of strikes. One modeller proposes switching from a normal model to a lognormal model to remove negative rates; a colleague proposes keeping the normal model and flooring negative rates at zero. Which assessment is most appropriate?

options.text: The lognormal switch is preferable, because it rules out negative rates without changing the model’s volatility at any level of rates.
Flooring is preferable here, because its effect is localised around zero, whereas changing the distribution alters rate dynamics, including volatilities, across all rates.
Neither is needed, because adding time steps to the normal tree makes the terminal distribution continuous and so removes the negative rates.
The two are equivalent, because any distribution that rules out negative rates has the same volatility structure as a floored normal model.

questions.solution:
**Step 1 – Cost of the lognormal switch**

Building the model around a distribution that rules out negative rates “may result in volatilities that are unacceptable for the purpose at hand”, and it changes dynamics across the entire range of rates, which matters when pricing options at many strikes.

**Step 2 – Cost of the floor**

Only rates near and below zero change.

⇒ With rates close to zero, the floor is the less disruptive fix; Vardeez notes it is preferred in very low-rate environments.

**Interpretation**

The choice depends on purpose. Here the desk prices options across strikes, so it should avoid a fix that distorts volatility at every rate level.

**LO:** MR-14 c: Describe methods for addressing the possibility of negative short-term rates in term structure models.

- **Reference:** Tuckman and Serrat, Ch.9 (GARP MR Ch.14); Vardeez notes MR-14 c

**Source:** Written new for the Market Risk P1–P3 workbook (question MR-14 c.7), built from GARP MR Ch.14, 14.2 and Vardeez.

a.reason: Absolute claim: a lognormal model does change volatility behaviour (basis-point volatility proportional to $r$).

c.reason: A finer normal tree still has mass below zero.

d.reason: The two methods have different volatility structures; that is the whole trade-off.

questions.loText: Estimate VaR using a historical simulation approach.
questions.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.topic: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.source: High quality paper MR-1 a Q1
questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a German Landesbank is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts that explains, in one sentence, how the historical simulation (HS) approach estimates VaR and how it differs from parametric approaches. Which of the following sentences best describes the HS approach?

*Conventions for this paper:* “HS” means historical simulation. L/P data record losses as positive values and profits as negative values; P/L data record profits as positive values.

options.text: HS estimates VaR from the ordered loss observations themselves, so no statistical distribution has to be specified for the data from which the observations are drawn.
HS fits a curve through the loss observations and reads the VaR off the fitted curve, so the observations serve only to pin down the parameters of that curve.
HS orders the loss observations and takes the VaR as the average of the losses in the tail, so the estimate reflects every loss beyond the confidence level.
HS estimates VaR from actual observed losses, so the estimate is guaranteed to equal the true quantile of the loss distribution at the chosen confidence level.

questions.solution:
**What historical simulation does**

Stem in one line: which sentence best describes how HS estimates VaR and how it differs from parametric approaches?

**Concept and theory**

VaR at confidence level $\alpha$ is the loss that separates the worst (1 $- \alpha$) of outcomes (the tail) from the rest (the body). There are two broad ways to locate that point.

|  | Historical simulation (HS) | Parametric approaches |
|---|---|---|
| What is assumed | Nothing about the distribution: the observed losses are the distribution | A specific distribution (normal, lognormal, . . . ) must be specified explicitly |
| How VaR is found | Order the loss observations and read off the one that separates tail from body | Fit a curve through the data (estimate its parameters) and read the VaR off the fitted curve |
| Typical tool | Large(Loss\_data,k) or a sorted array | $\mu$, $\sigma$ and a standard normal variate $z_{\alpha}$ |

GARP §1.2: “The simplest way to estimate VaR is by means of historical simulation (HS). The HS approach estimates VaR by means of ordered loss observations.” GARP §1.3: parametric approaches have the distinguishing feature that “they require us to explicitly specify the statistical distribution from which our data observations are drawn” and can be thought of as “fitting curves through the data and then reading off the VaR from the fitted curve.” Why HS exists: it is the most direct estimator; Schweser calls it “by far the simplest and most straightforward VaR method.”

**Applying it to this question**

The slide must capture both halves: how (ordered loss observations) and the difference (no distribution has to be specified). Option A contains both. Each other option either imports a parametric or ES feature, or overclaims.

**Fragile fact.** HS = ordered observations, no distribution; parametric = specified distribution, fitted curve. VaR is one observation, not an average.

**Reference**

LO 1.a: “Estimate VaR using a historical simulation approach.” GARP Ch. 1, §1.2 Estimating Historical Simulation VaR; §1.3 Estimating Parametric VaR (opening paragraph). Schweser Reading 1, Module 1.1, “Historical Simulation Approach” and “Parametric Estimation Approaches”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-1 a, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: It restates GARP §1.2 (“by means of ordered loss observations”) and the GARP §1.3 contrast (the parametric approach’s distinguishing feature is the explicitly specified distribution, which HS does not need).

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap. “Fitting curves through the data and then reading off the VaR from the fitted curve” is GARP’s description of the parametric approach (§1.3). B would be correct if the slide were describing parametric VaR.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap with LO 1.c. Averaging the tail losses produces an expected shortfall estimate, not a VaR. HS VaR is a single ordered observation, the one just outside the tail. C would be correct if the slide described HS expected shortfall.

d.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. HS gives an estimate. GARP’s own Figure 1.2 shows 1,000 draws from a standard normal giving an HS 95% VaR of 1.704 against a true 1.645. D would be correct only with “guaranteed to equal” replaced by “an estimate of”.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Swiss private bank is estimating the one-day 99% VaR of an equity book by historical simulation. She has 500 daily L/P observations (CHF thousands, losses positive). The sample mean of the L/P series is −35 (an average daily profit) and its standard deviation is 160. The ten largest losses in the sample, in no particular order, are:

Ten largest losses (CHF thousands)

|  |  |  |  |  |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 412 | 655 | 389 | 527 | 701 |
| 468 | 590 | 445 | 372 | 498 |

Convention: with $n$ observations and confidence level $\alpha$, the HS VaR is the $($(1 $- \alpha$)$n$ + 1$)$th highest loss (GARP/Dowd notation; Schweser writes the same rank as $\alpha n$ + 1 with $\alpha$ the significance level). Which of the following is closest to the 99% HS VaR?

*Conventions for this paper:* “HS” means historical simulation. L/P data record losses as positive values and profits as negative values; P/L data record profits as positive values.

options.text: CHF 498 thousand
CHF 594.2 thousand
CHF 483 thousand
CHF 468 thousand

questions.solution:
**The rank rule on unordered L/P data**

Stem in one line: 500 daily L/P observations (CHF thousands), ten largest losses given unordered; find the 99% HS VaR.

**Concept and theory**

With $n$ equally likely observations, a tail of probability 1 $- \alpha$ holds (1 $- \alpha$)$n$ observations. The VaR is the first observation outside the tail, the one that separates tail from body:

$k$ = (1 $- \alpha$) $n$ + 1$, \text{VaR}_{\alpha}$ = $L_{\text{(}k\text{)}}$

where $\alpha$ is the confidence level (GARP notation), $n$ is the number of observations, and $L_{\text{(}k\text{)}}$ is the $k$th highest loss. GARP: with 1,000 observations at 95%, “there are 50 observations in the tail, and we can take the VaR to be the 51st highest loss observation.”

|  | GARP (Dowd) | Schweser |
|---|---|---|
| Symbol $\alpha$ means | confidence level (e.g. 0.95) | significance level (e.g. 0.05) |
| Rank of VaR observation | (1 $- \alpha$)$n$ + 1 | $\alpha n$ + 1 |
| 1,000 obs at 95% | 0.05(1000) + 1 = 51 | 0.05(1000) + 1 = 51 |

HS does not use the mean or standard deviation of the sample: those are inputs to parametric VaR.

**Applying it to this question**

$k$ = (1 $- \alpha$)$n$ + 1 = (1 − 0.99)(500) + 1 = 5 + 1 = 6

Ordered losses : 701, 655, 590, 527, 498, **468**, 445, 412, 389, 372

Tail = {701, 655, 590, 527, 498} (5 observations)

$\text{VaR}_{\text{99\%}}$ = $L_{\text{(6)}}$ = 468

Meaning: on 1% of days (5 of 500) the book lost more than CHF 468 thousand; CHF 468 thousand is the boundary loss. The mean of −35 and standard deviation of 160 are irrelevant to HS.

**Fragile fact.** Tail = (1 $- \alpha$)$n$ observations; VaR = the next one, (1 $- \alpha$)$n$ + 1. Sort first: the losses were given unordered.

**Reference**

LO 1.a (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 1, §1.2 Estimating Historical Simulation VaR. Schweser Reading 1, Module 1.1, “Historical Simulation Approach” and Example “Identifying the VaR limit”. Difference: notation only ($\alpha$ = confidence in GARP, significance in Schweser); same rank.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-1 a, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: dropped term (the +1). (1 $- \alpha$)$n$ = 5 picks the 5th highest loss, 498: this is the ($\alpha n$) convention Schweser says past exams have used. Correct if the stem had specified the ($\alpha n$)th observation.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap with LO 1.c. Averaging the five tail losses, (701 + 655 + 590 + 527 + 498)/5 = 2971/5 = 594.2, is an expected shortfall estimate, not VaR. Correct if the question asked for the 99% HS ES on these data.

c.reason: Error type: scope error (the stated convention ignored). Averaging the 5th and 6th observations, (498 + 468)/2 = 483, is the “combination” GARP mentions as possible in principle. Correct only if the stem had told you to interpolate between the 50th-equivalent and 51st-equivalent observations.

d.reason: The 1% tail holds 5 observations; the 6th highest loss, CHF 468 thousand, is the observation the stated GARP rule selects.

questions.question:
The treasurer of an Australian regional bank receives 400 daily P/L observations for the bank’s rates book (AUD thousands, profits positive, losses negative). The table shows the 12 lowest and the 12 highest P/L values, ranked from the extreme inwards.

| Rank | Lowest P/L | Highest P/L |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | −842 | 905 |
| 2 | −731 | 788 |
| 3 | −655 | 702 |
| 4 | −610 | 640 |
| 5 | −574 | 597 |
| 6 | −538 | 561 |
| 7 | −502 | 533 |
| 8 | −489 | 514 |
| 9 | −463 | 495 |
| 10 | −441 | 480 |
| 11 | −427 | 466 |
| 12 | −409 | 451 |

Convention: with $n$ observations and confidence level $\alpha$, the HS VaR is the $($(1 $- \alpha$)$n$ + 1$)$th highest loss (GARP/Dowd notation; Schweser writes the same rank as $\alpha n$ + 1 with $\alpha$ the significance level). Which of the following is the 97.5% HS VaR, expressed as a loss?

*Conventions for this paper:* “HS” means historical simulation. L/P data record losses as positive values and profits as negative values; P/L data record profits as positive values.

options.text: AUD 441 thousand
AUD 466 thousand
AUD 427 thousand
AUD 584.5 thousand

questions.solution:
**HS VaR from P/L data**

Stem in one line: 400 daily P/L observations (AUD thousands, profits positive); 12 lowest and 12 highest given; find 97.5% HS VaR as a loss.

**Concept and theory**

Data can arrive as P/L (profits positive) or L/P (losses positive). GARP §1.1: “L/P data are a simple transformation of P/L data”,

$L/P_{t}$ = $-P/L_{t},$

and L/P is “sometimes more convenient” for risk measurement “because the risk measures are themselves denominated in loss terms.” The HS rule is stated for losses: VaR is the $($(1 $- \alpha$)$n$ + 1$)$th highest loss. On P/L data the highest losses are the lowest (most negative) P/L values, so:

$\text{VaR}_{\alpha}$ = $- P/L^{\text{low}}_{\text{(}k\text{)}}, k$ = (1 $- \alpha$)$n$ + 1,

where $P/L^{\text{low}}_{\text{(}k\text{)}}$ is the $k$th lowest P/L value. GARP makes the same point for P/L in Figure 1.4: “the VaR is indicated by the negative of the cut off point between the lower 5% and the upper 95% of P/L observations.”

**Applying it to this question**

$k$ = (1 − 0.975)(400) + 1 = 10 + 1 = 11

11th lowest P/L = −427

$\text{VaR}_{97.\text{5\%}}$ = −(−427) = 427

Meaning: the 10 worst days (2.5% of 400) lost more than AUD 427 thousand; the 97.5% VaR is a loss of AUD 427 thousand. The right-hand column (highest P/L) is irrelevant: it is the profit tail.

**Fragile fact.** On P/L data the VaR sits in the lower tail and is reported as the negative of the cut-off P/L, i.e., as a positive loss.

**Reference**

LO 1.a (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 1, §1.1 Data (Loss/Profit Data, Eq. (1.4)); §1.2 Estimating Historical Simulation VaR; Figure 1.4 note on P/L form (§1.3). Schweser Reading 1, “Estimating Returns” (losses quoted as positive values) and Module 1.1. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-1 a, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: dropped term (the +1). (1 $- \alpha$)$n$ = 10 gives the 10th lowest P/L, −441. Correct if the stem had specified the ($\alpha n$)th observation.

b.reason: Error type: sign error (wrong tail). Treating the P/L data as if they were L/P and taking the 11th highest value picks a profit of 466. Correct if the data had been L/P (losses positive) and the right-hand column were losses.

c.reason: Convert P/L to losses, take the 11th highest loss: −(−427) = 427 (GARP §1.1 and §1.2).

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap with LO 1.c. The average of the 10 tail losses, (842 + 731 + 655 + 610 + 574 + 538 + 502 + 489 + 463 + 441)/10 = 5845/10 = 584.5, is an ES estimate. Correct if the question asked for the 97.5% HS ES.

questions.source: High quality paper MR-1 a Q4
questions.question:
A risk consultant at a Japanese trust bank is reviewing a methodology note on how HS VaR is read from ordered data. The note uses 1,000 daily loss observations and a 95% confidence level and contains four statements:

I. The 5% tail contains 50 observations, and the reading takes the VaR to be the 51st highest loss observation.

II. Taking the 50th highest loss, or a combination of the 50th and 51st, would also be defensible; the reading treats the choice as an issue of approximation that arises with finite samples.

III. Because VaR is defined as a quantile, only the 51st highest loss is a correct estimate, and any other choice of observation produces a biased VaR.

IV. The rule places the VaR observation inside the tail, so with 1,000 observations at 95% the tail consists of the 51 highest losses.

Which of the statements are accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* “HS” means historical simulation. L/P data record losses as positive values and profits as negative values; P/L data record profits as positive values.

options.text: I only
I and II only
I, II and III only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
**Why 50th versus 51st is an approximation issue**

Stem in one line: methodology note on reading HS VaR from 1,000 losses at 95%; which of four statements are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

In theory VaR is a quantile: the point with exactly (1 $- \alpha$) of probability above it. With a finite sample the empirical distribution moves in jumps of 1$/n$, so no observation sits exactly on that point. With 1,000 observations at 95%, 50 observations form the 5% tail; the 50th highest loss is the last observation in the tail and the 51st is the first observation outside it. The true quantile lies somewhere between them.

GARP footnote 2: “with finite samples there is a certain level of arbitrariness in how the ordered observations relate to the VaR itself; that is, do we take the VaR to be the 50th observation, the 51st observation, or some combination of them? However, this is just an issue of approximation, and taking the VaR to be the 51st highest observation is not unreasonable.” Schweser repeats this and adds that “on past FRM exams, VaR using the historical simulation method has been calculated as just: ($\alpha\times n$)”, the 50th observation. This is why every stem in this paper states the convention.

**Applying it to this question**

I: 5% of 1,000 = 50 in the tail; VaR = 51st. True. II: matches footnote 2 (50th, 51st or a combination; “an issue of approximation”). True. III: “only . . . correct” and “biased” contradict footnote 2. False. IV: the 51st is the first observation outside the tail; the tail has 50, not 51. False. Answer: I and II only.

questions.solution:
**Implementing HS VaR in a spreadsheet**

Stem in one line: 750 L/P observations; cell uses PERCENTILE(Loss\_data,0.98); which recommendation is most appropriate?

**Concept and theory**

GARP describes the practical recipe. Order the data and read off the $k$th largest loss, or use Excel’s Large directly: “if our data are an array called ‘Loss\_data’, then our VaR is given by the Excel command ‘Large(Loss\_data,51)’.” In general, with $n$ observations and confidence level $\alpha$, the command is Large(Loss\_data,(1-alpha)\*n+1).

Why not a percentile function? GARP footnote 3: “We can also estimate HS VaR using percentile functions such as the ‘Percentile’ function in Excel or the ‘prctile’ function in MATLAB. However, such functions are less transparent (i.e., it is not obvious to the reader how the percentiles are calculated), and the Excel percentile function can be unreliable.” A validator wants a calculation that a reader can trace to one named observation.

Rank direction matters. LARGE counts down from the largest value. The empirical cumulative frequency (Q6) counts up from the smallest value: the observation at ascending position $i$ has cumulative frequency $i/n$. The two positions are linked by $k$ = $n - i$ + 1.

**Applying it to this question**

$k$ = (1 $- \alpha$)$n$ + 1 = (1 − 0.98)(750) + 1 = 15 + 1 = 16

Formula = LARGE(Loss\_data,16)

Check (ascending) : $i$ = $n - k$ + 1 = 750 − 16 + 1 = 735$, i/n$ = 735/750 = 0.98

The recommended cell returns the 16th largest loss, a single traceable observation.

**Fragile fact.** LARGE counts from the top: $k$ = (1 $- \alpha$)$n$ + 1. Cumulative frequency counts from the bottom: $i$ = $\alpha n$. Do not mix the two.

**Reference**

LO 1.a (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 1, §1.2 Estimating Historical Simulation VaR and footnote 3 (GARP-only; Schweser does not discuss spreadsheet functions). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-1 a, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: It gives the correct rank (GARP rule) and GARP’s stated reason (footnote 3) for preferring an ordered observation to a percentile function.

b.reason: Error type: dropped term (the +1). (1 $- \alpha$)$n$ = 15 returns the last observation inside the tail. Correct if the stem had specified the ($\alpha n$)th observation.

c.reason: **Keep PERCENTILE.** Error type: polarity flip. GARP says percentile functions are less transparent and the Excel one can be unreliable. Correct only if the reason were reversed in the source, which it is not.

d.reason: Error type: wrong input twin (ascending position used in a descending function). 735 is the ascending position whose cumulative frequency is 0.98; LARGE(Loss\_data,735) returns the 735th largest value, i.e., the 16th smallest, which is a large profit. Correct if the function counted from the smallest value upwards.

questions.solution:
**Reading HS VaR from the empirical cumulative frequency function**

Stem in one line: 120 L/P observations ordered from largest profit to largest loss; cumulative frequency $i/n$; find 95% HS VaR.

**Concept and theory**

GARP §1.2: “it is often helpful to obtain HS VaR estimates from a cumulative histogram, or empirical cumulative frequency function. This is a plot of the ordered loss observations against their empirical cumulative frequency (e.g., so if there are $n$ observations in total, the empirical cumulative frequency of the $i$th such ordered observation is $i/n$).” To read the VaR: “move up the cumulative frequency axis to where the cumulative frequency equals our confidence level, draw a horizontal line along to the curve, and then draw a vertical line down to the x-axis.”

Algebraically, with observations sorted in ascending order of loss:

$\frac{i}{n}$ = $\alpha\Rightarrow i$ = $\alpha n, k$ = $n - i$ + 1 = (1 $- \alpha$)$n$ + 1,

where $i$ is the ascending position and $k$ the rank counted from the largest loss. So the cumulative-frequency reading and the “(1 $- \alpha$)$n$ + 1th highest loss” rule pick the same observation.

**Applying it to this question**

$i$ = $\alpha n$ = 0.95 × 120 = 114 ($i/n$ = 114/120 = 0.95)

L/P at $i$ = 114 = 1.79

Cross-check: $k$ = (1 − 0.95)(120) + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7 = 120 − 114 + 1

Ranks 120 down to 115 are the six tail losses (5% of 120). The 95% VaR is SGD 1.79 million. The left-hand block (the profit end) is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Read the cumulative frequency at the confidence level (0.95), not at the tail probability (0.05); with $i/n$ counting from the profit end, the VaR is at $i$ = $\alpha n$.

**Reference**

LO 1.a (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 1, §1.2 Estimating Historical Simulation VaR, Figure 1.3 “Historical simulation via an empirical cumulative frequency function” (GARP-only; the figure is absent from Schweser). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-1 a, where it is Q6 of 12.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap with LO 1.c. The mean of the six tail losses, (1.88 + 1.96 + 2.09 + 2.27 + 2.58 + 3.15)/6 = 13.93/6 = 2.3217, is an ES estimate. Correct if the question asked for the 95% HS ES.

c.reason: Cumulative frequency 114/120 = 0.95 equals the confidence level (GARP §1.2, Figure 1.3), and the same observation is the 7th highest loss under the stated rule.

questions.solution:
**HS VaR at two confidence levels**

Stem in one line: 600-day window (was 500); 15 largest losses unordered; find 99% HS VaR minus 98% HS VaR.

**Concept and theory**

Under HS every VaR is just an order statistic, and the rank depends on both the confidence level and the number of observations:

$k$($\alpha, n$) = (1 $- \alpha$)$n$ + 1.

A higher confidence level shrinks the tail, so $k$ falls and the VaR moves to a larger loss. GARP’s general statement: “if we have $n$ observations, and our confidence level is $\alpha$, we would want the (1 $- \alpha$) $\cdot n$ + 1th highest observation.” The window size $n$ in the rule must be the window actually used for the losses being ranked.

**Applying it to this question**

Ordered losses : 2940, 2615, 2388, 2201, 2067, 1954, **1872**, 1790,

1733, 1688, 1641, 1602, **1566**, 1530, 1497

$k_{\text{99\%}}$ = (1 − 0.99)(600) + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7 $\Rightarrow\text{VaR}_{\text{99\%}}$ = 1872

$k_{\text{98\%}}$ = (1 − 0.98)(600) + 1 = 12 + 1 = 13 $\Rightarrow\text{VaR}_{\text{98\%}}$ = 1566

$\text{VaR}_{\text{99\%}} - \text{VaR}_{\text{98\%}}$ = 1872 − 1566 = 306

Meaning: moving from 98% to 99% adds CNY 306 thousand of VaR; the difference is positive because the higher confidence level reaches further into the tail.

**Fragile fact.** Higher confidence ⇒ smaller rank $k \Rightarrow$ larger loss. Use the $n$ of the window the losses came from.

**Reference**

LO 1.a (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 1, §1.2 Estimating Historical Simulation VaR. Schweser Reading 1, Module 1.1, “Historical Simulation Approach”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-1 a, where it is Q7 of 12.

**Extending the HS window**

Stem in one line: 99% HS VaR on 200 days (reported 990) extended to 400 days by adding the preceding stressed 200; find new VaR.

**Concept and theory**

An HS VaR is determined entirely by the observations in the sample: change the sample and you change both the rank (through $n$) and the set of losses being ranked. Two steps are therefore needed whenever the window changes:

1. recompute $k$ = (1 $- \alpha$)$n$ + 1 with the new $n$;
2. merge and re-order all observations in the new window before counting down to rank $k$.

GARP §1.2: HS “estimates VaR by means of ordered loss observations”; Schweser: “order return observations from largest to smallest. The observation that follows the threshold loss level denotes the VaR limit.”

**Applying it to this question**

Old rank : $k$ = (1 − 0.99)(200) + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3 ⇒ 990 (matches the reported VaR)

New rank : $k$ = (1 − 0.99)(400) + 1 = 4 + 1 = 5

Merged ordered losses : 1615, 1380, 1240, 1105, **1020**, 990, 955, 948, . . .

$\text{VaR}^{\text{new}}_{\text{99\%}}$ = $L_{\text{(5)}}$ = 1020

Meaning: adding the stressed block raises the 99% VaR from GBP 990 thousand to GBP 1,020 thousand. The four tail losses (1% of 400) are 1,615, 1,380, 1,240 and 1,105.

**Fragile fact.** When the window changes, update both $n$ (the rank) and the observation set (merge and re-sort).

**Reference**

LO 1.a (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 1, §1.2 Estimating Historical Simulation VaR. Schweser Reading 1, Module 1.1, “Historical Simulation Approach”. No conflict. The window-extension set-up is an application of the rank rule; window design itself is not discussed in this reading.

II. Because HS makes no distributional assumption, the gap between 2.71 and 2.326 proves that a normal distribution is wrong for this portfolio.

III. Even data drawn from a normal distribution can give an HS VaR away from the normal quantile: in the reading, 1,000 standard normal draws give a 95% HS VaR of 1.704 rather than 1.645.

*Conventions for this paper:* “HS” means historical simulation. L/P data record losses as positive values and profits as negative values; P/L data record profits as positive values.

I and II only
III and IV only

questions.solution:
**Interpreting an HS VaR against the normal quantile**

Stem in one line: standardized data, HS 99% VaR 2.71 versus normal 2.326; which memo statements are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

When L/P data are standardized (mean 0, standard deviation 1), a normal distribution would put the 99% VaR at $z_{0.99}$ = 2.326 (GARP §1.3). Comparing the HS VaR with that benchmark says something about the empirical tail:

| HS VaR versus normal quantile | Losses beyond the cut-off are | Most likely tail |
|---|---|---|
| HS VaR > normal quantile | further out than normal | fatter than normal |
| HS VaR \< normal quantile | closer in than normal | thinner than normal |

Schweser Module Quiz 1.1: an HS 95% VaR of 1.56 against 1.65 means “the historical simulation has thinner tails than a standard normal distribution.”

But HS gives an estimate from a finite sample. GARP Figure 1.2 is built from “1000 random numbers drawn from a standard normal L/P distribution”, and the HS 95% VaR is 1.704, not 1.645. A gap between the HS VaR and the normal quantile is therefore evidence, not proof. (How large such sampling gaps can be is LO 1.e.)

**Applying it to this question**

I: 2.71 > 2.326, so a fatter-than-normal tail is the most likely reading. True (Schweser logic). II: “proves” overstates; a normal sample can miss the normal quantile (GARP Figure 1.2). False. III: restates GARP Figure 1.2 exactly. True. IV: 2.10 \< 2.326 points to a thinner tail. False. Answer: I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** HS VaR above the normal quantile ⇒ fatter tail (most likely); below ⇒ thinner. “Most likely”, never “proves”.

**Reference**

LO 1.a (verbatim above). Schweser Reading 1, Module Quiz 1.1 Q1 and answer (Schweser-only, condensed source). GARP Ch. 1, §1.2, Figure 1.2 “Historical simulation VaR” (95% VaR = 1.704 from 1,000 standard normal draws); §1.3 for $z_{0.99}$ = 2.326. No conflict; the two sources make complementary points.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-1 a, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: **I only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement. Rejecting III means doubting that a normal sample can give an HS VaR away from 1.645, which GARP shows directly. A would be correct if III had misquoted the figure (for example, “1.704 rather than 1.960”).

b.reason: **I and II only.** Error type: absolute-claim trap in II. “Proves” converts a sample estimate into certainty. B would be correct if II said “is consistent with a non-normal distribution.”

c.reason: **III and IV only.** Error type: polarity flip in IV (and rejecting the true I). An HS VaR below the normal quantile means thinner tails. C would be correct if IV said “thinner” and I were false.

d.reason: Statement I follows the Schweser comparison; statement III is GARP’s own illustration; II and IV each contain one error.

A member of the risk committee of a Brazilian bank is reviewing the BRL desk’s HS VaR, which is estimated from the 500 most recent daily L/P observations. Two weeks ago the central bank made an abrupt policy change, and the volatility of the desk’s daily P/L has risen sharply since then. Which of the following statements about the desk’s HS VaR is least likely to be accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* “HS” means historical simulation. L/P data record losses as positive values and profits as negative values; P/L data record profits as positive values.

options.text: HS is sensible only if future P/L follows the same return-generating process as the observations in the window, which the policy change calls into question.
HS adjusts to the new regime as soon as it begins, because the estimate is read directly from actual observations rather than from fitted parameters.
HS cannot adjust for abrupt shifts in parameter values such as the jump in volatility, since the estimate is still drawn from the ordered losses of the full window.
HS does not require a statistical distribution to be specified, so the policy change does not force the desk to choose a new distribution for its data.

questions.solution:
**When HS is (and is not) sensible**

Stem in one line: 500-day HS VaR after an abrupt policy change that raised volatility; which statement is least likely accurate?

**Concept and theory**

HS assumes nothing about the shape of the distribution, but it assumes something stronger about time: that the past sample is representative of the future. Schweser LO 1.a: “the historical simulation approach is sensible only if you expect future performance to follow the same return-generating process as in the past. Furthermore, this approach is unable to adjust for changing economic conditions or abrupt shifts in parameter values.”

Why: the VaR is one ordered observation from the full window. After a regime change, almost all of the 500 observations still come from the old regime, so the ordered tail, and the VaR, barely move until enough new-regime observations accumulate. Freedom from a distributional assumption (GARP §1.2 to §1.3) does not remove this dependence on the past.

**Applying it to this question**

Ten trading days of high volatility sit among 500 observations; 490 are from before the change. A, C and D are all accurate descriptions. B claims instant adjustment, the opposite of Schweser’s statement.

**Fragile fact.** No distributional assumption ̸= no assumption: HS needs the future to follow the past return-generating process, and it cannot adjust to abrupt shifts.

**Reference**

LO 1.a (verbatim above). Schweser Reading 1, Module 1.1, “Historical Simulation Approach” (final paragraph). Schweser-only (condensed source): GARP’s LO 1.a section does not state these limitations. GARP Ch. 1, §1.3 opening for the parametric contrast in D.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-1 a, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: Accurate: restates the “same return-generating process” condition (Schweser). It would be the answer if it said HS is sensible “whatever the return-generating process”.

b.reason: B contradicts “unable to adjust for changing economic conditions or abrupt shifts in parameter values.” Reading VaR from actual observations is exactly why HS is slow to adjust: the window is dominated by old observations.

c.reason: Accurate: restates “unable to adjust . . . abrupt shifts in parameter values” (Schweser). It would be the answer under a polarity flip (“can adjust immediately”).

d.reason: Accurate: HS requires no distribution to be specified; that is the parametric approaches’ distinguishing feature (GARP §1.3). It would be the answer if it said “HS requires a normal distribution to be re-fitted” (sibling swap with LO 1.b).

**Concept and theory**

HS can be run on returns rather than on currency P/L. The rank rule picks the cut-off return; the loss in currency follows from the definition of the arithmetic return. GARP Eq. (1.12): a return is the P/L over the period divided by the asset value at the start of the period, so

$\text{Loss}_{t}$ = $- r_{t} P_{t-1}, \text{VaR}_{\alpha}$ = $- r_{\text{(}k\text{)}} \times V_{\text{current}},$

where $r_{\text{(}k\text{)}}$ is the $k$th worst return, $k$ = (1 $- \alpha$)$n$ + 1, and $V_{\text{current}}$ is the value of the holding at the start of the VaR horizon (today’s value; the stem states this convention). The purchase cost and the mean return play no part in HS.

**Applying it to this question**

$k$ = (1 − 0.99)(300) + 1 = 3 + 1 = 4

Ordered returns (%) : −6.20, −5.05, −4.85, −**3**.**62**, −3.48, −3.27, −3.10, −2.95

$r_{\text{(4)}}$ = −3.62%

$\text{VaR}_{\text{99\%}}$ = 0.0362 × 25,000,000 = 905,000

Meaning: on 1% of days (3 of 300) the holding lost more than 3.62%; on today’s CAD 25.0 million that is a one-day 99% VaR of CAD 905,000.

**Fragile fact.** Cut-off return times current value. Mean return and purchase price are distractors in HS.

**Reference**

LO 1.a (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 1, §1.2 Estimating Historical Simulation VaR; §1.1 Arithmetic Return Data and Eq. (1.12) in §1.3 for the return-to-loss relation. Schweser Reading 1, Module 1.1 (1,000 monthly returns example: −15.5% × \$1,000,000 = \$155,000). Applying the cut-off return to the current value is stated in the stem and is confirmed by the question bank’s LO 1.a worked solutions (bank Q5 and Q7). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-1 a, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: dropped term (the +1). The 3rd worst return, 4.85%, gives 0.0485 × 25,000,000 = 1,212,500. Correct under the ($\alpha n$) convention.

b.reason: Error type: wrong input twin (cost basis for current value). 0.0362 × 20,000,000 = 724,000. Correct if the holding were still worth CAD 20.0 million today.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap with LO 1.c. The average of the three tail returns, (6.20 + 5.05 + 4.85)/3 = 5.3667%, times 25.0 million gives an ES of 1,341,667. Correct if the question asked for the 99% HS ES.

d.reason: The 4th worst return applied to the current value, as the stem specifies (GARP §1.2 rank rule with the Eq. (1.12) return-to-loss relation).

questions.question:
A supervisor at a euro area national competent authority is examining a bank’s HS VaR engine. The engine uses a window of 1,500 daily L/P observations (EUR, losses positive) and reports the 31st highest loss as its VaR. The largest loss in the window is EUR 41.2 million. The confidence parameter is set in a configuration file the supervisor cannot open. Convention: with $n$ observations and confidence level $\alpha$, the HS VaR is the $($(1 $- \alpha$)$n$ + 1$)$th highest loss (GARP/Dowd notation; Schweser writes the same rank as $\alpha n$ + 1 with $\alpha$ the significance level). Which confidence level is the engine implicitly using?

*Conventions for this paper:* “HS” means historical simulation. L/P data record losses as positive values and profits as negative values; P/L data record profits as positive values.
questions.solution:
**Inferring the confidence level from the rank**

Stem in one line: 1,500 observations, engine reports the 31st highest loss; which confidence level is implied?

**Concept and theory**

The rank rule can be run backwards. If the engine reports the $k$th highest loss from $n$ observations, then

$k$ = (1 $- \alpha$)$n$ + 1 ⇒ 1 $- \alpha$ = $\frac{k - 1}{n} \Rightarrow\alpha$ = 1 $- \frac{k - 1}{n} ,$

where $\alpha$ is the confidence level (GARP notation) and $k -$ 1 is the number of observations in the tail. VaR is one-tailed: the whole 1 $- \alpha$ sits in the loss tail (Schweser: “since VaR is a one-tailed test, the entire significance level . . . is in the left tail”).

**Applying it to this question**

Tail observations = $k -$ 1 = 31 − 1 = 30

1 $- \alpha$ = 30/1500 = 0.02

$\alpha$ = 0.98 = 98.0%

Meaning: the engine is producing a 98% VaR, with 30 losses (2% of 1,500) in the tail. The EUR 41.2 million largest loss is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** $\alpha$ = 1 − ($k -$ 1)$/n$ in GARP notation; the same number is 1 $- \alpha$ in Schweser notation. VaR is one-tailed.

**Reference**

LO 1.a (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 1, §1.2 Estimating Historical Simulation VaR. Schweser Reading 1, Module 1.1 (rank ($\alpha n$) + 1 and “VaR is a one-tailed test”). Difference: notation only; GARP’s $\alpha$ (confidence) and Schweser’s $\alpha$ (significance) give the same rank.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-1 a, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: Inverting GARP’s $($(1 $- \alpha$)$n$ + 1$)$ rule gives $\alpha$ = 98.0%.

b.reason: Error type: dropped term (the −1, i.e., the ($\alpha n$) convention). 1 − 31/1500 = 1 − 0.02067 = 97.93%. Correct if the engine followed the ($\alpha n$)th-observation convention.

c.reason: Error type: wrong input twin (significance reported as confidence). 30/1500 = 2.0% is the tail probability, Schweser’s $\alpha$. Correct if the question asked for the significance level.

d.reason: Error type: one-tailed versus two-tailed confusion. Splitting the 2% across two tails, 1 − 30/(2 × 1500) = 99.0%, treats VaR like a two-tailed confidence interval. Correct only for a two-tailed interval, which VaR is not.

questions.question:
A model validator at a German Landesbank is reviewing the methodology note for a new parametric VaR engine that will run on the bank’s EUR trading book. Which of the following statements in the note is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* VaR figures are reported as positive numbers for losses. Use the following one-tailed standard normal quantiles, where $z_{p}$ is the value with probability $p$ to its left:

options.text: A parametric approach estimates VaR by ordering the loss observations and reading off the $($(1 $- \alpha$)$n$ + 1$)$th highest one, so the VaR does not depend on any assumed distribution.
A parametric approach requires the distribution of the data to be specified explicitly, and the VaR formula depends on both that distribution and the type of data (P/L, L/P or returns) it applies to.
A parametric approach requires the distribution of the data to be specified explicitly, but once that distribution is normal the same VaR formula applies unchanged to P/L, L/P and return data.
A parametric approach requires the distribution of the data to be specified explicitly, and because it works with the true mean and standard deviation of P/L, its VaR is free of estimation error.

questions.solution:
**What makes an approach parametric**

Stem in one line: which statement in a methodology note on a parametric VaR engine is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

There are two broad ways to get a VaR from data. Historical simulation (LO 1.a) lets the data speak for themselves: order the losses and read off the quantile. A parametric approach instead assumes a statistical distribution for the data, estimates its parameters, and reads the VaR off that fitted distribution. GARP: the distinguishing feature of parametric approaches is “that they require us to explicitly specify the statistical distribution from which our data observations are drawn. We can also think of parametric approaches as fitting curves through the data and then reading off the VaR from the fitted curve.”

GARP then adds the point this question turns on: “In making use of a parametric approach, we therefore need to take account of both the statistical distribution and the type of data to which it applies.” The same normal assumption produces a different formula depending on the data:

| Data assumed normal | VaR at confidence $\alpha$ | GARP equation |
|---|---|---|
| P/L (profits positive) | $-\mu_{P/L}$ + $\sigma_{P/L} z_{\alpha}$ | 1.8 |
| L/P (losses positive) | $\mu_{L/P}$ + $\sigma_{L/P} z_{\alpha}$ | 1.10a |
| Arithmetic returns $r_{t}$ | ($-\mu_{r}$ + $\sigma_{r}z_{\alpha}$) $P_{t-1}$ | 1.14 |
| Geometric returns $R_{t}$ (lognormal price) | $P_{t-1}($1 − exp\[$\mu_{R} - \sigma_{R}z_{\alpha}$\]$)$ | 1.16 |

Here $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are the mean and standard deviation of the series named in the subscript, $z_{\alpha}$ is the standard normal value with probability $\alpha$ to its left, and $P_{t-1}$ is the asset value at the end of the previous period. In practice $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are unknown, so GARP’s Equation 1.9 replaces them with sample estimates $m$ and $s$, giving an estimate of VaR.

**Applying it to this question**

Options B, C and D all start correctly (explicit distribution). They differ in the second clause. B adds that the formula depends on the data type, which is GARP’s own sentence. C says the formula is unchanged across data types, which the table above contradicts. D claims the parameters are known, which GARP says they are not. A describes a different method altogether.

**Fragile fact.** Parametric = distribution and data type both chosen explicitly; the parameters are estimated ($m$, $s$), not known.

**Reference**

LO 1.b (Schweser, verbatim in the Source note). GARP Ch. 1, §1.3 Estimating Parametric VaR (opening paragraphs and Eq. 1.9). Schweser Reading 1, “Parametric Estimation Approaches” (“explicitly assumes a distribution for the underlying observations”; “the researcher will use the sample mean and standard deviation”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-1 b, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap (LO 1.a property attributed to the parametric approach). Ordering losses and taking the $($(1 $- \alpha$)$n$ + 1$)$th highest is GARP’s historical simulation rule. It would be correct if the stem asked about historical simulation VaR.

b.reason: GARP §1.3: parametric approaches “require us to explicitly specify the statistical distribution” and “we therefore need to take account of both the statistical distribution and the type of data to which it applies.”

c.reason: Error type: scope or condition error (the data-type condition is dropped). With L/P data the mean enters with a plus sign; with return data the result must be scaled by $P_{t-1}$; with geometric returns the exponential appears. It would be correct only for the narrow claim that the P/L and L/P versions give the same number once $\mu_{L/P}$ = $-\mu_{P/L}$ is substituted.

d.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. GARP: “In practice, $\mu_{P/L}$ and $\sigma_{P/L}$ would be unknown, and we would have to estimate VaR based on estimates of these parameters.” The output is an estimate with sampling error. It would be correct as “its VaR depends on the accuracy of the estimated mean and standard deviation.”

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at an Australian superannuation fund is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts on parametric VaR for the fund’s currency overlay desk. The desk’s annual P/L is normally distributed with a mean of AUD 24 million and a standard deviation of AUD 11 million. The draft slide contains four statements:

I. In Dowd’s notation, $z_{\alpha}$ is the standard normal value with probability mass $\alpha$ to its left, so at a 95% confidence level $z_{\alpha}$ = $z_{0.95}$ = 1.645.

II. Because the data are in P/L form, the 95% VaR is the negative of the cut-off point between the lower 5% and the upper 95% of P/L outcomes.

III. The desk’s 95% VaR is about −AUD 5.9 million, which means that the 5% quantile of its annual P/L is a profit of about AUD 5.9 million.

IV. The desk’s 99% VaR is lower than its 95% VaR, because the expected profit offsets a larger share of the tail at the higher confidence level.

Which of the statements are correct?

*Conventions for this paper:* VaR figures are reported as positive numbers for losses. Use the following one-tailed standard normal quantiles, where $z_{p}$ is the value with probability $p$ to its left:

options.text: I and III only
II and III only
I, II and III only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
**Normal P/L VaR: notation, sign and confidence**

Stem in one line: P/L normal with mean AUD 24m and s.d. AUD 11m; which of four slide statements are correct?

**Concept and theory**

For normally distributed P/L, GARP Equation 1.8 gives

$\alpha$VaR = $-\mu_{P/L}$ + $\sigma_{P/L} z_{\alpha}$

where $\alpha$ is the confidence level, $\mu_{P/L}$ and $\sigma_{P/L}$ are the mean and standard deviation of P/L, and $z_{\alpha}$ is “the value of the standard normal variate such that $\alpha$ of the probability density mass lies to its left, and 1 $- \alpha$ of the probability density mass lies to its right.” At 95%, $z_{0.95}$ = 1.645; at 99%, $z_{0.99}$ = 2.326.

Where the formula comes from. The VaR cut-off sits in the left (loss) tail of P/L at $\mu_{P/L} - \sigma_{P/L}z_{\alpha}$. Since the data are in P/L form, GARP says the VaR “is indicated by the negative of the cut off point between the lower 5% and the upper 95% of P/L observations”, which gives −($\mu_{P/L} - \sigma_{P/L}z_{\alpha}$) = $-\mu_{P/L}$ + $\sigma_{P/L}z_{\alpha}$.

Negative VaR. If the expected profit is large relative to $\sigma_{P/L}z_{\alpha}$, the cut-off itself is a profit and the VaR is negative. Schweser: “the calculated value at risk is negative, but is typically reported as a positive value since the negative amount is implied”; a genuinely negative result means even the bad tail is profitable.

Notation warning. Schweser writes $\alpha$ for the significance level (5%), GARP for the confidence level (95%). The slide says “in Dowd’s notation”, so GARP’s convention applies.

**Applying it to this question**

95% cut-off of P/L = 24 − 11(1.645) = 24 − 18.095 = 5.905 (a profit)

95% VaR = −24 + 11(1.645) = −5.905 ≈ −AUD 5.9 million

99% VaR = −24 + 11(2.326) = −24 + 25.586 = 1.586 million

Statement I matches GARP’s definition of $z_{\alpha}$: true. Statement II is GARP’s sentence on reading VaR from P/L: true. Statement III: the 5% quantile of P/L is +5.905, a profit, so the VaR is −5.9: true. Statement IV: the 99% VaR (1.586) is higher than the 95% VaR (−5.905): false. Meaning: in 95% of years the desk earns at least AUD 5.9 million, but at 99% the tail reaches into a loss of about AUD 1.6 million.

**Fragile fact.** Dowd: $\alpha$ = confidence level; Schweser: $\alpha$ = significance level. VaR always rises with confidence, and a negative VaR means the quantile of P/L is a profit.

**Reference**

LO 1.b. GARP Ch. 1, §1.3 “Estimating VaR with Normally Distributed Profits/Losses”, Eq. 1.8 and Figure 1.4. Schweser Reading 1, “Normal VaR” (XYZ example). Difference: notation for $\alpha$ as above; Schweser rounds $z$ to 1.65 and 2.33. Eq. 1.8 is lost in the GARP scan; reconstructed from GARP Example 1.2 (−10 + 20 × 1.645 = 22.9) and confirmed by the question bank’s worked solutions.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-1 b, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: **I and III only.** Error type: sign error (rejecting II). A candidate who thinks the VaR is the cut-off point, not its negative, rejects II. With P/L data the cut-off is a P/L value (negative when it is a loss), so the VaR is its negative. A would be correct if II referred to L/P data, where the VaR is the cut-off itself.

b.reason: **II and III only.** Error type: notation sibling swap (rejecting I). A candidate using Schweser’s convention reads $\alpha$ as the significance level and rejects “$z_{\alpha}$ = $z_{0.95}$”. B would be correct if I had said “in Schweser’s notation”.

c.reason: I, II and III follow from GARP §1.3 (definition of $z_{\alpha}$; “the negative of the cut off point”; Eq. 1.8). IV contradicts Schweser: “the VaR (at 99% confidence) is greater than the VaR (at 95% confidence) as follows from the definition of value at risk.”

d.reason: **I, II, III and IV.** Error type: polarity flip (accepting IV). The mean is fixed at AUD 24 million while the tail term grows from 18.1 to 25.6 as confidence rises, so VaR must rise. D would be correct only if IV said “higher”.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Swiss private bank is estimating the quarterly VaR of the bank’s structured products desk. Preliminary data analysis shows that quarterly P/L is close to normal, and the analyst uses the following sample estimates:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Sample mean of quarterly P/L (a profit) | CHF 1.8 million |
| Sample standard deviation of quarterly P/L | CHF 7.5 million |
| Gross notional of the desk’s positions | CHF 640 million |

Which of the following is closest to the desk’s 99% quarterly VaR?

*Conventions for this paper:* VaR figures are reported as positive numbers for losses. Use the following one-tailed standard normal quantiles, where $z_{p}$ is the value with probability $p$ to its left:

options.text: CHF 10.54 million
CHF 15.65 million
CHF 17.45 million
CHF 19.25 million

questions.solution:
**Normal VaR from P/L data**

Stem in one line: quarterly P/L normal, sample mean +CHF 1.8m, sample s.d. CHF 7.5m, notional CHF 640m; find 99% VaR.

**Concept and theory**

Normal P/L VaR uses GARP Equation 1.8 with the unknown parameters replaced by sample estimates (Equation 1.9):

$\alpha\widehat{\text{VaR}}$ = $-m_{P/L}$ + $s_{P/L} z_{\alpha}$

where $m_{P/L}$ is the sample mean of P/L, $s_{P/L}$ the sample standard deviation, and $z_{\alpha}$ the standard normal value with probability $\alpha$ to its left. The horizon of the VaR is the horizon of the P/L data: quarterly P/L gives a quarterly VaR. Intuition: $s_{P/L}z_{\alpha}$ is how far the bad tail lies below the mean; an expected profit $m_{P/L} >$ 0 cushions it, so it is subtracted.

**Applying it to this question**

$z_{0.99}$ = 2.326

$s_{P/L} z_{0.99}$ = 7.5 × 2.326 = 17.445

99% VaR = −1.8 + 17.445 = 15.645 ≈ CHF 15.65 million

Meaning: with 99% confidence the desk will not lose more than about CHF 15.65 million in a quarter; equivalently, the 1% quantile of quarterly P/L is 1.8 − 17.445 = −15.645. The gross notional (CHF 640 million) is irrelevant: a P/L-based VaR needs only the P/L distribution.

**Fragile fact.** With P/L data a positive mean is subtracted; $z_{0.99}$ = 2.326 (one-tailed), not 1.645 or 2.576.

**Reference**

LO 1.b. GARP Ch. 1, §1.3 “Estimating VaR with Normally Distributed Profits/Losses”, Eq. 1.8 and 1.9, Example 1.2. Schweser Reading 1, “Normal VaR”. No conflict (Schweser rounds $z$ to 2.33; with 2.33 the answer is 15.68, still closest to B).

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-1 b, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: wrong percentile. Using $z_{0.95}$ = 1.645: −1.8 + 7.5 × 1.645 = 10.54. Correct if the stem asked for the 95% VaR.

b.reason: GARP Eq. 1.8 and 1.9 with $z_{0.99}$ = 2.326 give CHF 15.65 million (same structure as GARP Example 1.2).

c.reason: Error type: dropped term (mean ignored). 7.5 × 2.326 = 17.445 omits the expected profit. Correct if the mean quarterly P/L were zero.

d.reason: Error type: sign error. +1.8+17.445 = 19.245 treats the expected profit as an expected loss. Correct if the mean quarterly P/L were −CHF 1.8 million, or if the data were L/P with mean +1.8.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Japanese trust bank is estimating the monthly VaR of a legacy structured-note book that is being run off. The bank’s risk system stores the book’s results in loss/profit (L/P) form, so losses are positive numbers and profits negative. Monthly L/P is normally distributed:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean of monthly L/P | +JPY 0.36 billion |
| Standard deviation of monthly L/P | JPY 1.75 billion |
| Remaining notional of the book | JPY 48 billion |

Which of the following is closest to the book’s 99% monthly VaR?

*Conventions for this paper:* VaR figures are reported as positive numbers for losses. Use the following one-tailed standard normal quantiles, where $z_{p}$ is the value with probability $p$ to its left:

options.text: JPY 3.24 billion
JPY 3.71 billion
JPY 4.07 billion
JPY 4.43 billion

questions.solution:
**Normal VaR from L/P data**

Stem in one line: run-off book, monthly L/P normal with mean +JPY 0.36bn (an expected loss) and s.d. JPY 1.75bn; find 99% VaR.

**Concept and theory**

Loss/profit (L/P) data are P/L with the sign reversed: losses positive, profits negative. GARP prefers them for risk work “because the risk measures are themselves denominated in loss terms.” The mapping is

$\mu_{L/P}$ = $-\mu_{P/L}, \sigma_{L/P}$ = $\sigma_{P/L}$

so substituting into Equation 1.8 gives Equation 1.10a:

$\alpha$VaR = $\mu_{L/P}$ + $\sigma_{L/P} z_{\alpha}$

where $\mu_{L/P}$ and $\sigma_{L/P}$ are the mean and standard deviation of L/P. In L/P form the VaR is simply the point that cuts off the top 1 $- \alpha$ of the loss distribution (GARP Figure 1.5), so it is read off directly, with no change of sign.

| Data form | Mean enters as | Expected loss of 0.36 gives |
|---|---|---|
| P/L | $-\mu_{P/L}$ | $\mu_{P/L}$ = −0.36, so $-\mu_{P/L}$ = +0.36 |
| L/P | +$\mu_{L/P}$ | $\mu_{L/P}$ = +0.36, so +$\mu_{L/P}$ = +0.36 |

Both routes add the expected loss to the tail term; only the bookkeeping sign differs.

**Applying it to this question**

$\sigma_{L/P} z_{0.99}$ = 1.75 × 2.326 = 4.0705

99% VaR = $\mu_{L/P}$ + $\sigma_{L/P} z_{0.99}$ = 0.36 + 4.0705 = 4.4305 ≈ JPY 4.43 billion

Meaning: a run-off book bleeds an expected JPY 0.36 billion a month, and that expected loss adds to the tail, so the 99% monthly VaR is JPY 4.43 billion. The remaining notional is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** P/L: VaR = $-\mu_{P/L}$ + $\sigma z_{\alpha}$. L/P: VaR = +$\mu_{L/P}$ + $\sigma z_{\alpha}$. Check what a positive mean means in each before choosing the sign.

**Reference**

LO 1.b. GARP Ch. 1, §1.1 “Loss/Profit Data” and §1.3, Eq. 1.10a/b and Figure 1.5. The equation image is lost in the GARP scan; reconstructed from GARP’s stated mapping ($\mu_{L/P}$ = $-\mu_{P/L}$, $\sigma_{L/P}$ = $\sigma_{P/L}$) and Figure 1.5 (VaR 1.645 with $\mu_{L/P}$ = 0, $\sigma_{L/P}$ = 1), and confirmed by the question bank’s worked solutions. GARP-only: Schweser does not present L/P data.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-1 b, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: wrong percentile. 0.36 + 1.75 × 1.645 = 3.239. Correct for the 95% VaR.

b.reason: Error type: sign error (P/L formula applied to L/P data). −0.36 + 4.0705 = 3.7105 treats the expected loss as an expected profit. Correct if the data were P/L with mean +0.36.

c.reason: Error type: dropped term (mean ignored). 1.75 × 2.326 = 4.0705. Correct if the mean L/P were zero.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a UK pension scheme is estimating the one-year VaR of a multi-asset portfolio. One-year arithmetic returns are assumed to be normally distributed, and income is not reinvested. The manager has the following data:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Current portfolio value | GBP 250 million |
| Mean of one-year arithmetic return | 7.2% |
| Standard deviation of one-year arithmetic return | 14.0% |
| Consensus forecast of year-end portfolio value | GBP 268 million |

Which of the following is closest to the portfolio’s 95% one-year VaR?

*Conventions for this paper:* VaR figures are reported as positive numbers for losses. Use the following one-tailed standard normal quantiles, where $z_{p}$ is the value with probability $p$ to its left:

options.text: GBP 39.58 million
GBP 42.42 million
GBP 57.58 million
GBP 75.58 million

questions.solution:
**Normal VaR from arithmetic returns**

Stem in one line: GBP 250m portfolio, one-year arithmetic return normal with mean 7.2% and s.d. 14%, consensus year-end value GBP 268m; find 95% VaR.

**Concept and theory**

When the normal assumption is placed on arithmetic returns $r_{t}$ instead of P/L, GARP works in three steps.

1. Find the critical return $r^{*}$, defined so that the probability that $r_{t}$ exceeds $r^{*}$ is the confidence level $\alpha$ (Eq. 1.11):

$r^{*}$ = $\mu_{r} - \sigma_{r}z_{\alpha}$

2\. Link returns to losses. The arithmetic return is the P/L divided by the asset value at the end of the previous period, $P_{t-1}$, so a loss equal to the VaR corresponds to $r^{*}$ = $-\alpha\text{VaR}/P_{t-1}$ (Eq. 1.12 and 1.13).

3\. Combine (Eq. 1.14):

$\alpha$VaR = $( - \mu_{r}$ + $\sigma_{r}z_{\alpha}) P_{t-1}$

where $\mu_{r}$ and $\sigma_{r}$ are the mean and standard deviation of the arithmetic return over the horizon and $P_{t-1}$ is today’s value. GARP Example 1.3 applies this with a portfolio worth 1. Arithmetic returns assume interim payments earn no return of their own, which matches the stem (income not reinvested).

**Applying it to this question**

$\sigma_{r}z_{0.95}$ = 0.14 × 1.645 = 0.2303

$-\mu_{r}$ + $\sigma_{r}z_{0.95}$ = −0.072 + 0.2303 = 0.1583 (VaR as a fraction of value)

95% VaR = 0.1583 × 250 = 39.575 ≈ GBP 39.58 million

Meaning: with 95% confidence the one-year loss will not exceed about 15.8% of today’s value, GBP 39.58 million. The consensus year-end value, GBP 268 million = 250 × 1.072, is the expected end-of-period value; it is not the base for the VaR.

**Fragile fact.** The base is $P_{t-1}$ (today’s value), and a positive expected return is subtracted from $\sigma_{r}z_{\alpha}$.

**Reference**

LO 1.b. GARP Ch. 1, §1.3 “Estimating VaR with Normally Distributed Arithmetic Returns”, Eq. 1.11 to 1.14, Example 1.3. Schweser Reading 1, “Normal VaR” (arithmetic return example, \$100 portfolio). Eq. 1.11 to 1.14 are lost in the GARP scan and Schweser’s formula image is missing; the form is reconstructed from GARP’s text and Example 1.3 and confirmed by the question bank’s worked solutions. Erratum noted: GARP Example 1.3 prints 0.331 for −0.1 + 0.25 × 1.645, which is 0.311.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-1 b, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: GARP Eq. 1.14 scales the return quantile by $P_{t-1}$, the value at the start of the horizon (GBP 250 million).

b.reason: Error type: wrong input twin (end-of-period value used as the base). 0.1583 × 268 = 42.42. The return is defined on $P_{t-1}$, not on an expected $P_{t}$. Correct if today’s value were GBP 268 million.

c.reason: Error type: dropped term (mean ignored). 0.2303 × 250 = 57.575. Correct if the expected return were zero.

d.reason: Error type: sign error. (0.072 + 0.2303) × 250 = 75.575 treats the expected return as an expected loss. Correct if the mean arithmetic return were −7.2%.

questions.question:
A model validator at an Indian bank is reviewing the documentation of a VaR engine that assumes arithmetic returns $r_{t}$ are normally distributed with mean $\mu_{r}$ and standard deviation $\sigma_{r}$, where $\alpha$ is the confidence level and $P_{t-1}$ is the asset value at the end of period $t -$ 1. The documentation contains four statements:

I. The critical return $r^{*}$ is chosen so that the probability that $r_{t}$ exceeds $r^{*}$ equals $\alpha$, which gives $r^{*}$ = $\mu_{r} - \sigma_{r}z_{\alpha}$.

II. Because the arithmetic return equals the P/L divided by the asset value at the end of period $t$, the VaR equals $-r^{*}P_{t}$.

III. With $\alpha$ = 0.95, $\mu_{r}$ = 0, $\sigma_{r}$ = 1 and $P_{t-1}$ = 1, the engine gives a VaR of 1.645, the same as a normal P/L or L/P approach with mean 0 and standard deviation 1.

IV. Like the normal P/L approach, this approach assigns a positive probability to the asset value becoming negative.

Which of the statements are correct?

*Conventions for this paper:* VaR figures are reported as positive numbers for losses. Use the following one-tailed standard normal quantiles, where $z_{p}$ is the value with probability $p$ to its left:

options.text: I and III only
I, II, III and IV
I, III and IV only
III and IV only

questions.solution:
**Deriving normal VaR from arithmetic returns**

Stem in one line: which of four documentation statements about the arithmetic-return normal VaR engine are correct?

**Concept and theory**

The derivation has three links, each a possible trap:

| Link | Correct statement (GARP) | Typical corruption |
|---|---|---|
| Critical return | Pr($r_{t} > r^{*}$) = $\alpha$, so $r^{*}$ = $\mu_{r} - \sigma_{r}z_{\alpha}$ | sign of $\sigma_{r}z_{\alpha}$ flipped |
| Return to loss | $r_{t}$ is P/L divided by $P_{t-1}$, so VaR = $-r^{*}P_{t-1}$ | dividing by $P_{t}$ |
| Consistency | with $\alpha$ = 0.95, $\mu_{r}$ = 0, $\sigma_{r}$ = 1, $P_{t-1}$ = 1, VaR = 1.645 | believing the approaches differ |

GARP on the third link: “the three approaches give the same results, because all three sets of underlying assumptions are equivalent.” GARP then opens the lognormal subsection with the weakness common to all three: “Each of the previous approaches assigns a positive probability of the asset value, $P_{t}$, becoming negative.” A normal return has no lower bound, so $r_{t} < -$1 (a loss of more than the whole position) has positive probability.

**Applying it to this question**

I: matches Eq. 1.11 and its definition. True. II: the divisor is the asset value at the end of $t -$ 1, not $t$; and VaR is $-r^{*}P_{t-1}$. False. III: (−0 + 1 × 1.645) × 1 = 1.645, equal to −0 + 1 × 1.645 (P/L) and 0 + 1 × 1.645 (L/P). True. IV: GARP’s own sentence. True. So I, III and IV only.

**Fragile fact.** $r^{*}$ is exceeded with probability $\alpha$ (it is in the left tail), the base is $P_{t-1}$, and every normal approach allows a negative asset value.

**Reference**

LO 1.b. GARP Ch. 1, §1.3 “Estimating VaR with Normally Distributed Arithmetic Returns” and first paragraph of “Estimating Lognormal VaR”. Schweser Reading 1, “Normal VaR”. GARP-only: the derivation through $r^{*}$ and the equivalence check are not in Schweser.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-1 b, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: **I and III only.** Error type: polarity flip (rejecting IV). A candidate who thinks normal returns already keep the asset value positive rejects IV; that property belongs to geometric returns and the lognormal model. Correct if IV were written about the lognormal approach and claimed a positive probability of a negative value.

b.reason: **I, II, III and IV.** Error type: wrong input twin (accepting II). Dividing by $P_{t}$ instead of $P_{t-1}$ changes the base of the return. Correct if II read “the asset value at the end of period $t -$ 1” and “$-r^{*}P_{t-1}$”.

c.reason: GARP §1.3: Eq. 1.11 to 1.14; “aVaR is 1.645: the three approaches give the same results”; “Each of the previous approaches assigns a positive probability of the asset value, $P_{t}$, becoming negative.”

d.reason: **III and IV only.** Error type: sign error (rejecting I). A candidate who believes $r^{*}$ = $\mu_{r}$ +$\sigma_{r}z_{\alpha}$ places the critical return in the right tail. Since Pr($r_{t} > r^{*}$) = $\alpha$ = 95%, $r^{*}$ must sit in the left tail. Correct if I were wrongly written with a plus sign.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is presenting to the risk committee of a Chinese asset manager that has adopted lognormal VaR for its CNY equity funds, on the assumption that geometric returns are normally distributed and interim income is reinvested. The slide contains four statements, in which $\mu$ and $\sigma$ denote the mean and standard deviation of ln $X$:

I. The fund value $P_{t}$ is lognormally distributed, so its density is defined only for positive values and is skewed to the right.

II. The skewness of a lognormal distribution is always positive, which confirms its long right-hand tail.

III. The median of a lognormal variable $X$ is exp($\mu$) and its mean is exp($\mu$) exp($\sigma^{2}/$2), so its mean lies above its median.

IV. Because $P_{t-1}$ is known, the lognormal VaR is normally distributed even though $P_{t}$ itself is lognormal.

Which of the statements are correct?

*Conventions for this paper:* VaR figures are reported as positive numbers for losses. Use the following one-tailed standard normal quantiles, where $z_{p}$ is the value with probability $p$ to its left:

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
I, II, III and IV
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
**Properties of the lognormal distribution**

Stem in one line: which of four committee-slide statements about lognormal prices and lognormal VaR are correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP Box 1.1: a random variable $X$ is lognormal if ln $X$ is normal. With $\mu$ and $\sigma$ the mean and standard deviation of ln $X$:

| Property | Box 1.1 |
|---|---|
| Support | pdf defined only for $x >$ 0 |
| Median | $m$ = exp($\mu$) |
| Mean | $m$ exp($\sigma^{2}/$2), above the median |
| Variance | $m^{2}w$($w -$ 1), with $w$ = exp($\sigma^{2}$) |
| Skewness | ($w$ + 2)($w -$ $\text{1)}^{1/2}$, “always positive”: long right-hand tail |

Why this matters for VaR. If geometric returns are normal (and interim payments are zero or reinvested), ln $P_{t}$ is normal, so $P_{t}$ is lognormal. GARP: “Since the VaR is a loss, and since the loss is the difference between $P_{t}$ (which is random) and $P_{t-1}$ (which we can take here as given), then the VaR itself has the same distribution as $P_{t}$. Normally distributed geometric returns imply that the VaR is lognormally distributed.” Figure 1.7 shows the L/P distribution as “a reflection of the distribution of $P_{t}$”.

**Applying it to this question**

I: support and right skew are in Box 1.1 and Figure 1.6. True. II: Box 1.1 says the skewness “is always positive”; the absolute word is correct here. True. III: median exp($\mu$), mean exp($\mu$) exp($\sigma^{2}/$2) > exp($\mu$) since $\sigma^{2} >$ 0. True. IV: subtracting a random lognormal $P_{t}$ from a known $P_{t-1}$ does not make the loss normal; it is a (reflected) lognormal. False.

**Fragile fact.** Median = exp($\mu$); mean = exp($\mu$ + $\sigma^{2}/$2). Normal geometric returns make the price and the VaR lognormal, not normal.

**Reference**

LO 1.b. GARP Ch. 1, Box 1.1 “The Lognormal Distribution”, §1.3 “Estimating Lognormal VaR”, Figures 1.6 and 1.7. Schweser Reading 1, “Lognormal VaR” (“right-skewed with positive outliers and bounded below by zero”). GARP-only: Box 1.1 moments and the distribution of VaR. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-1 b, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: **I and II only.** Error type: sibling swap (rejecting III). A candidate who swaps mean and median (thinking the mean is exp($\mu$)) rejects III. Correct if III had said the mean is exp($\mu$).

b.reason: **I and III only.** Error type: absolute-claim reflex (rejecting II). Here “always” is the source’s own word: for any $\sigma>$ 0, $w >$ 1 and the skewness is positive. Correct only if II had said “can be negative for small $\sigma$”.

c.reason: **I, II, III and IV.** Error type: sibling swap (accepting IV). It transfers the normality of $R_{t}$ to the loss. Correct for the arithmetic-return model, where the VaR (a linear function of a normal $r_{t}$) is normal.

d.reason: I to III restate Box 1.1; IV contradicts “Normally distributed geometric returns imply that the VaR is lognormally distributed.”

questions.question:
The treasurer of a Singapore family office is estimating the one-year VaR of an equity fund. Annual geometric returns are normally distributed, and dividends are reinvested in the fund. The treasurer has the following data:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Current fund value | SGD 80 million |
| Mean of annual geometric return | 9.0% |
| Standard deviation of annual geometric return | 26.0% |
| Dividend yield (reinvested) | 2.1% |

Which of the following is closest to the fund’s 99% one-year lognormal VaR?

*Conventions for this paper:* VaR figures are reported as positive numbers for losses. Use the following one-tailed standard normal quantiles, where $z_{p}$ is the value with probability $p$ to its left:

options.text: SGD 32.19 million
SGD 36.30 million
SGD 41.18 million
SGD 47.81 million

questions.solution:
**Lognormal VaR**

Stem in one line: SGD 80m fund, annual geometric return normal with mean 9% and s.d. 26%, dividends reinvested; find 99% lognormal VaR.

**Concept and theory**

The lognormal VaR follows the same three-step logic as the arithmetic case, with the exponential in place of the linear link.

1. Critical geometric return, exceeded with probability $\alpha$ (Eq. 1.15):

$R^{*}$ = $\mu_{R} - \sigma_{R}z_{\alpha}$

2\. Unravel the price. Since $R^{*}$ = ln($P^{*}/P_{t-1}$), the critical (worst-case) value is

$P^{*}$ = $P_{t-1}$ exp($R^{*}$) = $P_{t-1} \text{exp} \left[\mu_{R} - \sigma_{R}z_{\alpha}\right]$

3\. The VaR is the fall from today’s value to $P^{*}$ (Eq. 1.16):

$\alpha$VaR = $P_{t-1} - P^{*}$ = $P_{t-1}($1 $- \text{exp} \left[\mu_{R} - \sigma_{R}z_{\alpha}\right])$

Symbols: $\mu_{R}$ and $\sigma_{R}$ are the mean and standard deviation of the geometric return over the horizon, $z_{\alpha}$ the standard normal quantile, $P_{t-1}$ today’s value, $P^{*}$ the (1 $- \alpha$) quantile of the end-of-period value. Because exp(·) > 0, the VaR is always below $P_{t-1}$. GARP Example 1.4 applies this with $P_{t-1}$ = 1.

**Applying it to this question**

$R^{*}$ = 0.09 − 0.26 × 2.326 = 0.09 − 0.60476 = −0.51476

exp($R^{*}$) = 0.59764

$P^{*}$ = 80 × 0.59764 = 47.81 (1% quantile of the year-end fund value)

99% VaR = 80 × (1 − 0.59764) = 80 × 0.40236 = 32.19 ≈ SGD 32.19 million

Meaning: with 99% confidence the fund will not end the year below about SGD 47.81 million, so the loss will not exceed SGD 32.19 million. The dividend yield matters only qualitatively: reinvestment is the condition that makes $P_{t}$ lognormal; it is already inside the geometric return.

**Fragile fact.** Lognormal VaR = $P_{t-1}$(1 $- e^{\mu_{R}-\sigma_{R}z_{\alpha}}$ ): the mean is added inside the exponent, and the answer is the loss, not $P^{*}$.

**Reference**

LO 1.b. GARP Ch. 1, §1.3 “Estimating Lognormal VaR”, Eq. 1.15 and 1.16 (1.16 legible in the scan), Example 1.4, Figure 1.7. Schweser Reading 1, “Lognormal VaR” (formula image missing). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-1 b, where it is Q8 of 12.

b.reason: Error type: dropped term (mean ignored). 80(1 $- e^{-0.60476}$) = 80 × 0.45379 = 36.30. Correct if $\mu_{R}$ were zero.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap (normal arithmetic-return formula applied to geometric parameters). 80(−0.09 + 0.60476) = 41.18. Correct if 9% and 26% described normally distributed arithmetic returns.

d.reason: Error type: intermediate result. $P^{*}$ = 47.81 is the critical fund value, not the loss $P_{t-1} - P^{*}$. Correct if the stem asked for the 1% quantile of the year-end fund value.

questions.question:
An investment risk analyst at a US life insurer is asked by the investment committee why the insurer’s long-horizon VaR model for a USD balanced fund was switched from normally distributed arithmetic returns to normally distributed geometric returns. Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* VaR figures are reported as positive numbers for losses. Use the following one-tailed standard normal quantiles, where $z_{p}$ is the value with probability $p$ to its left:

options.text: Normal geometric returns imply that the fund value itself is normally distributed, so the VaR can be read directly from a normal distribution of fund values.
Normal geometric returns imply that the log of the fund value is normal whether interim payments are paid out or reinvested, so payout policy does not affect the model.
If interim payments are zero or continually reinvested, normal geometric returns imply that the log of the fund value is normal, so the fund value is lognormal and cannot become negative.
If interim payments are zero or continually reinvested, normal geometric returns imply that the log of the fund value is normal, so the fund value is lognormal with a long left-hand tail.

questions.solution:
**Why normal geometric returns give a lognormal price**

Stem in one line: most accurate explanation for switching a long-horizon VaR model from normal arithmetic to normal geometric returns.

**Concept and theory**

The motivation is a defect of every normal approach: GARP, “Each of the previous approaches assigns a positive probability of the asset value, $P_{t}$, becoming negative, but we can avoid this drawback by working with geometric returns.”

The chain, with its condition:

| Step | GARP |
|---|---|
| Assumption | Geometric returns $R_{t}$ are normal with mean $\mu_{R}$, s.d. $\sigma_{R}$ |
| Condition | “If $D_{t}$ is zero or reinvested continually in the asset itself (e.g., as with profits reinvested in a mutual fund)” |
| Consequence | “the natural logarithm of $P_{t}$ is normally distributed, or $P_{t}$ itself is lognormally distributed” |
| Shape | “the price is always non-negative, and its distribution is skewed with a long right-hand tail” |

Why the condition is needed: the geometric return is $R_{t}$ = ln $($($P_{t}$ + $D_{t}$)$/P_{t-1})$. Only if $D_{t}$ is zero or folded back into the asset does ln $P_{t}$ = ln $P_{t-1}$ + $R_{t}$ hold, so that normality of $R_{t}$ passes to ln $P_{t}$. Since $P_{t}$ = $P_{t-1}e^{R_{t}} >$ 0 for any $R_{t}$, the price cannot go negative. This matters most at long horizons, where large negative returns are more plausible.

**Applying it to this question**

The committee wants the reason and the conditions. C states the condition (zero or reinvested interim payments), the consequence (log price normal, price lognormal) and the payoff (no negative fund value).

**Fragile fact.** Normal returns (geometric) give a lognormal price, only if interim payments are zero or reinvested; the long tail is on the right.

**Reference**

LO 1.b. GARP Ch. 1, §1.3 “Estimating Lognormal VaR” and Figure 1.6; §1.1 “Geometric Return Data” (Eq. 1.6) for the definition. Schweser Reading 1, “Lognormal VaR”. Difference: Schweser states the implication without the $D_{t}$ condition; GARP’s condition is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-1 b, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap (return and price confused). Normal geometric returns make the log of the price normal, so the price is lognormal. A would be correct for normal P/L, where the end-of-period value is normal.

b.reason: Error type: scope or condition error (the reinvestment condition dropped). GARP makes the result conditional on $D_{t}$ being zero or continually reinvested. Correct only for a fund that pays no interim income.

c.reason: GARP §1.3 “Estimating Lognormal VaR”, quoted above; Schweser: the lognormal “is commonly used to counter the possibility of negative asset prices”.

d.reason: Error type: polarity flip (right tail becomes left tail). The lognormal price has a long right-hand tail and is bounded below by zero. Correct if it read “long right-hand tail”.
