questions.question:
A treasurer at a Canadian bank runs filtered historical simulation for a CAD 200 million single-asset position. Five days from the sample used to fit the asymmetric GARCH model are shown below, with each day’s realised return and the model’s volatility forecast for that day. The mean return is negligible, the model’s asymmetry parameter $\gamma$ is 0.08, and the forecast of tomorrow’s volatility is 1.5%.

| Day | Realised return (%) | Volatility forecast for that day (%) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | −3.6 | 2.4 |
| 2 | −2.1 | 0.7 |
| 3 | +1.8 | 1.2 |
| 4 | −1.0 | 0.8 |
| 5 | −2.8 | 1.6 |

The first eight bootstrap draws (with replacement) select days 3, 1, 5, 1, 4, 2, 3 and 5. What is the largest one-day loss among these eight simulated outcomes?

options.text: CAD 4.50 million
CAD 6.00 million
CAD 7.20 million
CAD 9.00 million

questions.solution:
**FHS: rescaling standardised returns**

Stem in one line: CAD 200m, five days of returns and forecasts, tomorrow’s forecast 1.5%, eight draws; largest simulated loss?

**Concept and theory**

In FHS each historical return is standardised by its own day’s volatility forecast, $z_{t}$ = $r_{t}/\sigma_{t}$, and each bootstrapped draw is rescaled by the forecast of tomorrow’s volatility, $\tilde{r}$ = $z \sigma_{T \text{+1}}$ (mean neglected). A modest loss in a very calm period has a large standardised value, and today’s volatility can turn it into a loss bigger than anything in the raw history. This is attraction (iii): FHS “allows us to get VaR and ES estimates that can exceed the maximum historical loss in our data set.”

**Applying it to this question**

| Day | $r_{t}$ (%) | $\sigma_{t}$ (%) | $z_{t}$ = $r_{t}/\sigma_{t}$ | $z_{t} \times$ 1.5% |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | −3.6 | 2.4 | −1.50 | −2.250% |
| 2 | −2.1 | 0.7 | −3.00 | −4.500% |
| 3 | +1.8 | 1.2 | +1.50 | +2.250% |
| 4 | −1.0 | 0.8 | −1.25 | −1.875% |
| 5 | −2.8 | 1.6 | −1.75 | −2.625% |

The draws are days 3, 1, 5, 1, 4, 2, 3, 5, so day 2 is drawn once.

Worst simulated return = −3.00 × 1.5% = −4.50%

Loss = 0.045 × 200,000,000 = CAD 9,000,000

This exceeds the largest raw loss in the data (3.6%, CAD 7.2 million). The asymmetry parameter $\gamma$ = 0.08 is irrelevant once the forecasts are given.

**Fragile fact.** Rank by standardised return, not raw return. A small loss in a calm period can become the worst FHS loss.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 2, §2.4, “Filtered Historical Simulation” (steps and attraction iii). Schweser Reading 2, “Filtered Historical Simulation” (“can predict losses outside the historical range”). Difference: Schweser’s standardisation wording is inverted (see Q10); GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-2 c, where it is Q12 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: wrong input twin (raw loss used to rank instead of standardised loss). Picking day 1 because it has the largest raw loss gives −1.50 × 1.5% = −2.25%, or CAD 4.5 million. Correct only if all days had the same $\sigma_{t}$, so ranks were unchanged.

b.reason: Error type: intermediate result. Treating $z$ = −3.00 as a 3.00% return, without rescaling by tomorrow’s 1.5% forecast, gives CAD 6.0 million. Correct only if tomorrow’s forecast were 1.0%.

c.reason: Error type: dropped step (no filtering). Taking the raw maximum loss of 3.6% gives CAD 7.2 million, the answer bootstrapped HS would allow at most. Correct if the question asked for the largest historical loss.

d.reason: It applies GARP’s FHS steps: divide each return by its day’s forecast, bootstrap, multiply by tomorrow’s forecast.

questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee at a French bank is reviewing a EUR market risk paper that summarises the attractions and limitations of filtered historical simulation (FHS):

I. FHS is fast, even for large portfolios.

II. FHS maintains the correlation structure in the return data without relying on knowledge of the variance-covariance matrix.

III. Pritsker’s simulation study suggests that FHS VaR may not pay enough attention to extreme observations or to time-varying correlations.

IV. Because every simulated return is a resampled historical observation, FHS cannot produce a VaR larger than the maximum historical loss.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and IV only
II and III only
I, II and III only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
**FHS: attractions and problems**

Stem in one line: which of four statements about the attractions and limitations of FHS are correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP lists seven attractions of FHS: (i) it combines the non-parametric attractions of HS with a sophisticated (e.g., GARCH) treatment of volatility; (ii) it is fast, even for large portfolios; (iii) it can produce VaR and ES estimates above the maximum historical loss; (iv) it maintains the correlation structure without relying on the variance-covariance matrix or the conditional distribution of asset returns; (v) it can be modified for autocorrelation or past cross-correlations; (vi) it can be combined with OS or bootstrap methods to give confidence intervals; (vii) there is evidence that it works well. The problems (footnote 15): Pritsker’s simulation study tentatively concludes that FHS VaR “might not pay enough attention to extreme observations or time-varying correlations”; he also finds FHS VaR may understate true 10-day VaR by about 10%, which conflicts with results from real data. The evidence is therefore mixed.

**Applying it to this question**

I is attraction (ii): true. II is attraction (iv): true. III is Pritsker’s conclusion: true. IV contradicts attraction (iii): the bootstrapped standardised returns are rescaled by tomorrow’s volatility, so simulated losses can exceed the historical maximum. False. Hence I, II and III only.

**Fragile fact.** FHS bootstraps, yet it can exceed the historical maximum loss, because the draws are rescaled by current volatility.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 2, §2.4, “Filtered Historical Simulation” (attractions i to vii, footnote 15). Schweser Reading 2, “Filtered Historical Simulation” (“computationally ... very reasonable even for large portfolios”; Pritsker’s reservations are GARP-only). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-2 c, where it is Q13 of 15.

a.reason: **I and IV.** Error type: polarity flip in IV, plus rejection of true II and III. Would be correct only if FHS resampled raw returns without rescaling, which is bootstrapped HS.

b.reason: **II and III.** Error type: rejects true I. GARP explicitly says FHS “is fast, even for large portfolios.” Would be correct only if speed were not among the listed attractions.

c.reason: GARP §2.4 lists (ii), (iii) and (iv) as attractions and reports Pritsker’s reservations in footnote 15.

d.reason: **All four.** Error type: absolute claim accepted in IV. The resampled quantity is a standardised return; its rescaled value is new. Correct only if IV were true, which GARP’s attraction (iii) rules out.

questions.question:
The head of market risk at a Japanese bank is preparing a JPY risk committee paper that compares the four weighted historical simulation approaches. The draft contains four statements:

I. Age-weighting changes the probability weights attached to the historical P/L observations but not their values, whereas volatility-weighting changes the values but keeps equal weights.

II. Volatility-weighted historical simulation and FHS can both produce VaR estimates above the largest loss in the historical data set, whereas age-weighted historical simulation cannot.

III. Correlation-weighted historical simulation is a generalisation of age-weighted historical simulation, because it adjusts the probability weights for correlations as well as for age.

IV. FHS filters returns through a conditional volatility model, whereas volatility-weighted historical simulation uses no volatility model at all.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I only
I and II only
I, II and III only
II and IV only

questions.solution:
**Comparing the four approaches**

Stem in one line: which comparison statements about the four weighted HS approaches are correct?

**Concept and theory**

The four approaches modify traditional HS in different places. GARP groups them as “weighted historical simulation” and calls them semi-parametric, because they add parametric elements (decay rates, GARCH forecasts, correlation matrices) to the HS framework.

| Approach | What changes | Parametric add- on | Above his- torical maximum? | Builds on |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Age-weighted | Probability weights | Decay $\lambda$ | No | Equal-weighted HS ($\lambda\to$ 1) |
| Volatility- | Return values, equal | GARCH/EWMA | Yes | Equal-weighted |
| weighted | weights kept | forecasts |  | HS |
| Correlation-weighted | Return values (via $\bar{A}A^{-1}$) | Correlation matrices | Not stated in GARP | HW (generalises it) |
| Filtered HS | Standardised returns, bootstrapped | (A)GARCH | Yes | HS plus bootstrap |

**Applying it to this question**

I: true, the core contrast between BRW and HW. II: true; GARP states it for HW and FHS, and age-weighted VaR is always one of the observed losses (or an interpolation between two). III: false, correlation weighting generalises HW, not BRW, and it adjusts returns, not probability weights. IV: false, HW uses GARCH or EWMA volatility forecasts. Hence I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** BRW changes weights; HW, correlation weighting and FHS change returns. Correlation weighting generalises HW.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 2, §2.4 (all four subsections). Schweser Reading 2, LO 2.c Key Concepts. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-2 c, where it is Q14 of 15.

a.reason: **I only.** Error type: rejects true II. Choosing A means believing either that HW or FHS cannot exceed the historical maximum, or that age-weighting can. Correct only if II were false.

b.reason: GARP §2.4: under age-weighting “we merely replace the old equal weights 1$/n$ with the age-dependent weights”; under HW we “estimate HS VaRs or ESs in the traditional way (i.e., with equal weights, etc.)”; HW and FHS both allow estimates that “exceed the maximum loss in our historical data set”.

c.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: sibling swap in III (BRW put where HW belongs). Correct if III read “a generalisation of volatility-weighted HS, because it adjusts returns for correlations as well as volatilities”.

d.reason: **II and IV.** Error type: rejects true I and accepts the polarity error in IV. HW explicitly relies on “the historical GARCH (or EWMA) forecast of the volatility”. Correct only if HW used no volatility forecasts.

questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a USD hedge fund asks the risk team how a one-day equity market crash would affect the next day’s 95% VaR under the methods the fund is considering. The window holds 500 daily observations, and the fund’s GARCH model raises its volatility forecast sharply after the crash. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Equal-weighted historical simulation VaR will rise sharply the next day, because the crash loss enters the window with the same weight 1$/n$ as every other observation.
Age-weighted historical simulation VaR will be largely unaffected the next day, because the newest observation receives the smallest probability weight in the window.
Volatility-weighted historical simulation VaR will rise only through the crash observation itself, because the new volatility forecast is applied only to the crash-day return.
Volatility-weighted historical simulation VaR will tend to rise beyond the effect of the crash observation itself, because the higher current forecast scales up every historical return.

questions.solution:
**How each approach responds to a crash**

Stem in one line: after a one-day equity crash, how does the next day’s 95% VaR respond under each method?

**Concept and theory**

GARP uses a crash to show why equal weighting is a problem: “a stock market crash might have no effect on VaRs except at a very high confidence level”, so risk can rise sharply while HS VaR barely moves; the increase shows up only if the market keeps falling. Age-weighting helps because “a large loss event will receive a higher weight than under traditional HS, and the resulting next-day VaR would be higher than it would otherwise have been.” Volatility weighting helps more directly: the conditional volatility model reacts to the large surprise (in the AGARCH equation, last period’s surprise drives this period’s variance), the current forecast $\sigma_{T}$ jumps, and every historical return is multiplied by $\sigma_{T} /\sigma_{t}$.

**Applying it to this question**

With 500 observations, the 95% tail holds 25 losses. Under equal weighting the crash adds one loss to that tail and shifts the quantile by one rank: little change. Under age-weighting the newest observation has the largest weight. Under HW, the jump in $\sigma_{T}$ scales the whole adjusted P/L series, so the VaR rises well beyond the effect of one extra observation.

**Fragile fact.** HS: a crash may barely move VaR. BRW: newest observation, biggest weight. HW: the new $\sigma_{T}$ rescales the whole window.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 2, §2.4 introduction (crash example), “Age-weighted Historical Simulation” (second attraction), “Volatility-weighted Historical Simulation” and “Filtered Historical Simulation” (equation 2.6b). Schweser Reading 2, LO 2.c. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-2 c, where it is Q15 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: absolute claim. A single crash observation with weight 1$/n$ moves the 95% quantile by at most one rank. GARP’s point is that HS VaR may hardly respond. Correct only at a confidence level so high that the crash itself sets the VaR.

b.reason: Error type: polarity flip. Under BRW the newest observation has the largest weight, $w$(1). Correct only if weights increased with age.

c.reason: Error type: scope error. $\sigma_{T}$ enters the adjustment of every historical return, not only the crash day’s. Correct only if the volatility forecast did not change after the crash.

d.reason: GARP §2.4: HW “produces risk estimates that are appropriately sensitive to current volatility estimates”; returns are “increased (or decreased), depending on whether the current forecast of volatility is greater (or less than) the estimated volatility for period $t$.”

questions.source: High quality paper MR-2 d Q1
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at an Indian asset manager is choosing a VaR and ES method for an INR corporate bond fund. Two years of daily fund returns show pronounced negative skewness and excess kurtosis, and a colleague proposes historical simulation (HS) instead of a normal-based approach. Which of the following best describes the advantage of the non-parametric approach in this setting?

options.text: Because the inputs are actual historical outcomes, the HS estimates will be more accurate than any parametric estimate, whatever sample period is used.
Because no assumption is made about the P/L distribution, the skewness and fat tails present in the data pass directly into the VaR and ES estimates.
Because the data are first transformed towards normality, the skewness and excess kurtosis are removed before the VaR and ES are estimated.
Because the empirical distribution keeps the fat tails, the VaR and ES estimates can extrapolate to losses larger than any loss in the sample.

questions.solution:
**Fat tails and skewness: the distribution-free advantage**

Stem in one line: INR bond fund with negative skew and excess kurtosis; what is the advantage of HS here?

**Concept and theory**

Parametric approaches start by assuming a form for the P/L or return distribution (normal, $t$, lognormal and so on), estimate its parameters, and read VaR and ES off the fitted distribution. If the assumed shape is wrong, the risk estimate inherits the error: a normal fit to a negatively skewed, fat-tailed series understates the left tail.

Non-parametric approaches reverse the logic. GARP opens the chapter by saying they try to “let the P/L data speak for themselves”, using the recent empirical distribution of P/L rather than an assumed theoretical one. Whatever shape the data have, the estimate uses that shape.

|  | Parametric (e.g., normal) |  | Non-parametric (e.g., HS) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Distribution | Assumed, then fitted |  | Empirical; none assumed |
| Skew and fat tails | Lost unless the model them | allows | Carried into VaR and ES automatically |
| Losses beyond sample maximum | Possible by extrapolation |  | Not possible in basic HS |

GARP §2.5 lists as an advantage that, since they do not depend on parametric assumptions about P/L, non-parametric approaches can accommodate fat tails, skewness and any other non-normal features that cause problems for parametric approaches. Schweser: “Not hindered by parametric violations of skewness, fat tails, etc.”

**Applying it to this question**

The stem flags negative skewness and excess kurtosis, the exact features a normal model mishandles. The deciding fact is the mechanism: no distributional assumption is imposed, so the empirical skew and tail thickness feed straight into the estimates.

**Fragile fact.** Distribution-free means the tails in the data are captured, not that losses beyond the data can be produced.

**Reference**

LO 2.d: “Identify advantages and disadvantages of non-parametric estimation methods.” GARP Ch. 2, §2.5 Advantages and Disadvantages of Non-Parametric Methods (Advantages, second bullet; Disadvantages, largest-loss bullet); chapter introduction. Schweser Reading 2, “Advantages and Disadvantages of Nonparametric Methods”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-2 d, where it is Q1 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. Real data do not guarantee accuracy: GARP’s biggest disadvantage is that results depend (in most cases completely) on the historical sample, so a quiet or turbulent window biases them. “More accurate than any parametric estimate, whatever sample period” overstates. A softened version would be acceptable: GARP’s Conclusions say non-parametric methods are often superior to parametric approaches based on simplistic assumptions such as normality.

b.reason: B states both the cause (no assumption about the P/L distribution) and the effect (skewness and fat tails pass directly into VaR and ES), matching GARP §2.5 and Schweser’s LO 2.d list.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap. Transforming data towards normality is a parametric-style fix; it is the opposite of letting the data speak. Would describe a parametric approach that first normalises the data, not HS.

d.reason: Error type: scope or condition error. Keeping the fat tails that are in the sample is not the same as extrapolating beyond it. GARP: in simpler HS “we cannot extrapolate from the largest historical loss to anything larger”. Would be correct for a parametric fat-tailed model (for example a fitted $t$), which can extrapolate.

questions.question: The CRO of a Canadian bank reviews the bank’s HS VaR and ES, which use the most recent 500 daily observations of CAD rates and credit P/L. The last two years were unusually calm, but the bank’s economists expect the coming months to be considerably more turbulent. Which statement best describes the likely bias in the bank’s non-parametric risk estimates?

options.text: VaR and ES will tend to be too high, because a quiet sample period overstates the risks the bank is actually facing.
VaR and ES will tend to be about right, because a method free of distributional assumptions adjusts to new conditions.
VaR and ES will tend to be too low, because the estimates depend on a sample period quieter than the risks now faced.
VaR and ES will tend to be too low only above 99% confidence, because a quiet sample period affects the extreme tail alone.

questions.solution:
**Quiet sample period: direction of the bias**

Stem in one line: 500-day HS window drawn from an unusually calm period; turbulence expected; direction of bias?

**Concept and theory**

Because a non-parametric estimate is built entirely from the sample, it can only be as representative as that sample. GARP calls this the biggest potential weakness: results are very (and in most cases completely) dependent on the historical data set. The first related problem GARP lists is directional:

| Sample period | Non-parametric VaR and ES | Relative to risks faced | actually |
|---|---|---|---|
| Unusually quiet | Built from small losses | Often too **low** |  |
| Unusually volatile | Built from large losses | Often too **high** |  |

The underlying assumption of every non-parametric approach (GARP introduction) is that the near future will be sufficiently like the recent past; when it is not, the bias follows the sample, not the future.

**Applying it to this question**

The window covers an unusually calm period, and the stem says the future is expected to be more turbulent. The estimates are built from calm-period losses, so they will tend to understate the risk the bank is about to face. Both VaR and ES are affected, at the usual confidence levels.

**Fragile fact.** Quiet sample, too low; volatile sample, too high. The bias follows the sample.

**Reference**

LO 2.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 2, §2.5, Disadvantages (first related problem); chapter introduction (“near future will be sufficiently like the recent past”). Schweser Reading 2, LO 2.d disadvantages list. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-2 d, where it is Q2 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip. Quiet periods give estimates that are too low; “too high” belongs to unusually volatile periods. Correct if the stem described an unusually volatile sample followed by calmer conditions.

b.reason: Error type: scope or condition error. Being free of distributional assumptions (an advantage) is confused with being responsive to new conditions. The estimate adjusts only as new observations enter the window. Would be correct only if market conditions stayed the same as in the sample, the case in which GARP says these methods work fairly well.

c.reason: GARP §2.5: if the data period was unusually quiet, non-parametric methods will often produce VaR or ES estimates that are too low for the risks actually faced. Schweser: “Quiet data periods lead to VaR and ES estimates that are too low.”

d.reason: Error type: scope or condition error. GARP’s statement applies to VaR and ES in general, not only to extreme confidence levels; the whole sample distribution is calm. Would be correct only for a claim restricted, by assumption, to the far tail.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Swiss private bank is preparing a training slide on the advantages of non-parametric estimation methods. The draft contains four statements:

I. They are, in varying degrees, fairly easy to implement on a spreadsheet.

II. Their results are easy to report and communicate to senior managers and to outsiders such as bank supervisors and rating agencies.

III. Formal empirical evidence conclusively shows that historical simulation outperforms parametric approaches.

IV. Confidence intervals for non-parametric VaR and ES are hard to produce, so the estimates are normally reported as point estimates only.

Which of the statements should be kept on the slide?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
II and IV only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
**Practical advantages: spreadsheets, reporting, confidence intervals, evidence**

Stem in one line: which of four slide statements on non-parametric advantages should be kept?

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s list of advantages (§2.5) contains several practical points that Schweser compresses into “intuitive and often computationally simple (even on a spreadsheet)”:

| GARP advantage | Exact strength of the claim |
|---|---|
| Intuitive and conceptually simple | Stated without qualification |
| Easy to implement on a spreadsheet | “in varying degrees, fairly” easy |
| Easy to report and communicate | To senior managers and outsiders (supervisors, rating agencies) |
| Easy to produce confidence intervals | For non-parametric VaR and ES (order statistics, bootstrap) |
| Perceived to work well empirically | A widespread perception among practitioners; formal evidence “inevitably mixed” |

The last row is the trap: GARP is careful to separate practitioner perception from formal evidence.

**Applying it to this question**

I matches the spreadsheet advantage, including the hedge “in varying degrees, fairly”. Keep. II matches the communication advantage and names the right audiences. Keep. III converts a perception with mixed evidence into conclusive proof. Drop. IV reverses the confidence-interval advantage. Drop. Answer: I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Practitioners perceive that HS works well; the formal evidence is mixed. Confidence intervals are easy to produce.

**Reference**

LO 2.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 2, §2.5, Advantages. Schweser Reading 2, LO 2.d (“Intuitive and often computationally simple (even on a spreadsheet)”). Difference: reporting, confidence intervals and practitioner perception are GARP-only; Schweser does not list them. No contradiction.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-2 d, where it is Q3 of 15.

a.reason: GARP §2.5 lists spreadsheet implementation and ease of reporting to senior managers and outsiders (e.g., bank supervisors or rating agencies) as advantages; it also lists ease of producing confidence intervals and says the formal empirical evidence on HS is mixed, which rules out III and IV.

b.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: absolute-claim trap in III. GARP: “a widespread perception among risk practitioners that HS works quite well empirically, although formal empirical evidence on this issue is inevitably mixed.” III would be acceptable as “practitioners widely perceive that HS works quite well empirically”.

c.reason: **II and IV.** Error type: polarity flip in IV (“easy” becomes “hard”), together with rejecting the true statement I. GARP: “It is easy to produce confidence intervals for non-parametric VaR and ES” (§2.3 shows the order-statistics and bootstrap routes). IV would describe a method without such tools.

d.reason: **I, III and IV.** Error type: combines the absolute claim (III) and the polarity flip (IV), and drops the true statement II. Would be correct only if GARP had listed communicability as a weakness, which it does not.

questions.question: A model validator at a Brazilian bank reviews an equity desk that uses basic HS on 750 daily observations. The largest loss in the sample is BRL 41 million. The desk head argues: “Our 99.9% ES can never exceed BRL 41 million, but if we switch to volatility-weighted HS the largest-loss problem goes away and we are on the same footing as a parametric model.” Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.text: The largest-loss constraint binds parametric and non-parametric estimates equally, so switching to volatility weighting changes nothing.
Volatility-weighted HS removes the largest-loss constraint entirely, so its estimates are on the same footing as parametric estimates.
The largest-loss constraint matters mainly in large samples; in small or medium samples the largest loss is extreme enough to make it irrelevant.
Volatility-weighted HS can relax the constraint, but its estimates stay constrained by the largest loss in a way parametric estimates are not.

questions.solution:
**The largest-loss constraint and more sophisticated HS**

Stem in one line: basic HS, worst loss BRL 41m; does volatility-weighted HS remove the largest-loss constraint?

**Concept and theory**

In basic HS every VaR or ES is computed from losses that actually occurred in the sample, so no estimate can exceed the largest of them. GARP §2.5 states three graded claims:

1. In the simpler versions of HS we cannot extrapolate from the largest historical loss to anything larger that might occur.
2. More sophisticated versions of HS can relax this constraint (volatility weighting scales past returns up when current volatility is high, so adjusted losses can exceed actual ones; GARP §2.4 lists this as a major advantage of the HW approach).
3. Even so, non-parametric estimates remain constrained by the largest loss in a way that parametric estimates are not, so these methods are not well suited to handling extremes, particularly with small or medium-sized samples.

Schweser’s version: difficult to estimate losses significantly larger than the maximum loss (“historical simulation cannot; volatility-weighting can, to some degree”).

**Applying it to this question**

The desk head is right about basic HS but overstates the cure. Volatility weighting can push estimates above BRL 41 million (if today’s volatility exceeds the volatility on the worst days), but the adjusted series is still a rescaled version of the same 750 observations, so the estimates are still tied to the sample’s extremes. Only D gives all three graded claims.

**Fragile fact.** Relax, not remove. Small and medium samples make the constraint more damaging.

**Reference**

LO 2.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 2, §2.5, Disadvantages (largest-loss bullet); §2.4 Volatility-weighted Historical Simulation (HW advantages, as background). Schweser Reading 2, LO 2.d disadvantages list. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-2 d, where it is Q4 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap. It attributes the non-parametric limitation to parametric methods too. A parametric model extrapolates from the fitted distribution and is not tied to the sample’s worst loss. Would be correct only if both methods were restricted to observed outcomes.

b.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. “Removes entirely” and “same footing” overstate “can relax”. Correct if “removes entirely” read “relaxes to some degree”.

c.reason: Error type: polarity flip. GARP says the methods are not well suited to extremes particularly with small- or medium-sized samples; small samples make the constraint worse, not irrelevant. Would be correct with “large” and “small or medium” swapped.

d.reason: GARP §2.5: sophisticated HS “can relax this constraint, but even so ... non-parametric estimates of VaR or ES are still constrained by the largest loss in a way that parametric estimates are not.”

questions.question: A risk consultant is advising a Japanese securities firm whose JPY trading book is exposed to about 3,000 risk factors and includes a large book of exotic options. The board is choosing between a parametric variance-covariance approach and historical simulation. Which statement most accurately identifies an advantage of the non-parametric approach here?

options.text: It needs a covariance matrix only for the option positions, which keeps the dimension of the estimation problem manageable.
It needs no covariance matrix and avoids the curse of dimensionality, and it can in theory accommodate any position, including the options.
It avoids the curse of dimensionality, but it can accommodate only linear positions, so the options must first be mapped to their deltas.
It needs no covariance matrix, but this advantage is lost once the number of risk factors exceeds the number of historical observations.

questions.solution:
**High dimensions and any type of position**

Stem in one line: 3,000 risk factors plus exotic options; advantage of HS over variance-covariance?

**Concept and theory**

A variance-covariance (parametric) approach needs a covariance matrix of all risk factors. With $m$ factors there are $m$($m$ + 1)/2 distinct variances and covariances to estimate; with $m$ = 3,000 that is about 4.5 million, and the matrix must also be positive definite. GARP calls these the operational problems of parametric methods in high-dimensional problems (“curses of dimensionality”).

HS sidesteps them. GARP §2.1: because multiple positions collapse into a single HS P/L series (the current portfolio revalued under each past day’s returns), it is very easy for non-parametric methods to accommodate high dimensions, and they will often be the most natural choice for such problems. Because each historical scenario revalues the actual positions, GARP §2.5 adds that non-parametric approaches can in theory accommodate any type of position, including derivatives.

**Applying it to this question**

Two features of the stem matter: very many risk factors (dimension) and exotic options (non-linear positions). B is the only option that states both advantages without a false condition.

**Fragile fact.** The dimension problem belongs to parametric methods; HS collapses every position into one P/L series.

**Reference**

LO 2.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 2, §2.5 Advantages (high-dimensional and derivatives bullets); §2.1 Compiling Historical Simulation Data. Schweser Reading 2, LO 2.d advantages list. Difference: the derivatives point is GARP-only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-2 d, where it is Q5 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: scope or condition error. HS needs no covariance matrix for any position, including options. Would describe a hybrid in which only part of the book is modelled parametrically.

b.reason: GARP §2.5 Advantages: “free of the operational problems ... applied to high-dimensional problems: no need for covariance matrices, no curses of dimensionality” and “can in theory accommodate any type of position, including derivatives positions.” Schweser: “Avoids complex variance-covariance matrices and dimension problems.”

c.reason: Error type: polarity flip (“any type” becomes “only linear”). GARP says non-parametric approaches can in theory accommodate any position, including derivatives. Would be correct for a delta-normal (parametric) approach.

d.reason: Error type: scope or condition error (invented condition). Since the HS P/L collapses into one series, the number of risk factors relative to observations does not reintroduce a covariance problem. Would be a fair concern for a sample covariance matrix, which becomes singular when factors exceed observations: a parametric issue.

questions.question: The treasurer of an Australian bank is reviewing a memo on whether to lengthen the HS window for the bank’s AUD trading book from two years to eight years of daily data. Which statement in the memo is most accurate?

options.text: Lengthening the window eliminates ghost effects, because with more observations no single loss can have any influence on the VaR.
About 250 daily observations are generally regarded as enough for acceptable precision, so there is no case for using more than one year of data.
Lengthening the window improves precision, but the news in current market observations is more likely to be drowned out by older observations.
Lengthening the window reduces data-collection problems, because long runs of history are easiest to find for new and emerging market instruments.

questions.solution:
**Window length: precision against responsiveness**

Stem in one line: lengthen the AUD HS window from two to eight years; which memo statement is accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Window length is a trade-off. Too short and the estimates are imprecise: GARP’s rule of thumb is that most experts believe we usually need at least a couple of years of daily observations (about 500, at 250 trading days a year), and often more. Too long and four problems grow (GARP §2.5): 1. greater problems with aged data;

2. a longer period over which results are distorted by unlikely-to-recur past events, and a longer wait for ghost effects to disappear;
3. the news in current market observations is more likely to be drowned out by older observations, so estimates respond less to current conditions;
4. greater potential for data-collection problems, particularly for new or emerging market instruments, where long runs of data do not exist and are not easy to proxy.

**Applying it to this question**

Moving from two to eight years helps precision but triggers all four costs. C states the trade-off exactly: precision up, responsiveness down.

**Fragile fact.** Rule of thumb: about 500 daily observations, often more. Longer window: more precision, less responsiveness, longer wait for ghost effects.

**Reference**

LO 2.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 2, §2.5, paragraph on the length of the sample window. Schweser Reading 2, LO 2.d (“Need sufficient data, which may not be possible for new instruments or markets”). Difference: the 500-observation rule of thumb and the four costs of a long window are GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-2 d, where it is Q6 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap, and the direction is also wrong. A longer window does not eliminate ghost effects; GARP says we have to wait longer for them to disappear. Would be closer to correct for age-weighting with a growing sample, which GARP says can effectively eliminate remaining ghost effects.

b.reason: Error type: scope or condition error (rule of thumb halved). The benchmark is at least a couple of years, about 500 observations, and often more. Would be correct if “250” read “500” and “one year” read “two years”.

c.reason: GARP §2.5: a reasonably long window is needed for acceptable precision, but the longer the window, “the more the news in current market observations is likely to be drowned out by older observations”.

d.reason: Error type: polarity flip. Long histories are hardest to obtain for new or emerging market instruments. Correct with “easiest” replaced by “hardest” and “reduces” by “increases”.

questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a UK asset manager is reviewing a proposal to extend HS VaR to a new GBP-reported fund that will hold local-currency bonds from several emerging markets. The data team writes that “data are never a constraint for non-parametric methods.” Which statement best describes the position in the reading?

options.text: Data are always readily available from public sources, so data availability is never a binding constraint for non-parametric methods.
Data are often readily available, publicly or in-house from marking to market, but time series on all current positions may be missing, as in emerging markets.
Data are rarely available from public sources, so non-parametric methods must rely on in-house data collected for regulatory reporting.
Data are often readily available, and once collected they need no checks for reliability, compatibility or timely delivery to the risk system.

questions.solution:
**Data availability: advantage with caveats**

Stem in one line: emerging market bond fund; data team says data are never a constraint; best description?

**Concept and theory**

GARP lists data availability as an advantage, carefully hedged: non-parametric methods use data that are (often) readily available, either from public sources (e.g., Bloomberg) or from in-house data sets (e.g., collected as a by-product of marking positions to market). Footnote 16 then adds the caveat: there can also be problems getting the data set. We need time series data on all current positions, and such data are not always available (e.g., if the positions are in emerging markets). We also have to ensure that the data are reliable, compatible and delivered to the risk estimation system on a timely basis.

Schweser condenses this to: “Data is often readily available and does not require adjustments (e.g., financial statement adjustments).” Schweser’s “no adjustments” refers to accounting-type adjustments; it does not say that data quality need not be checked.

**Applying it to this question**

The fund will hold emerging market local-currency bonds: exactly GARP’s example of positions whose time series may be unavailable. The data team’s “never” is wrong; the accurate view is “often available, but not always”.

**Fragile fact.** Data are often readily available; emerging market positions are GARP’s named exception.

**Reference**

LO 2.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 2, §2.5, Advantages (data bullet) and footnote 16. Schweser Reading 2, LO 2.d advantages list. Difference: Schweser-only phrase “does not require adjustments (e.g., financial statement adjustments)”; GARP-only data-quality caveat in footnote 16. GARP used; the two are about different things and are not a version conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-2 d, where it is Q7 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. “Always” and “never” replace GARP’s “often”. Would be correct only for markets with complete, long public histories on every position.

b.reason: B gives the advantage with GARP’s hedge (“often”), both sources (public and in-house mark-to-market by-product), and the footnote 16 caveat on emerging markets.

c.reason: Error type: polarity flip. GARP says data are often readily available, including from public sources. Would be correct if the sentence described a disadvantage of a data-poor setting.

d.reason: Error type: scope or condition error (a stated condition dropped). Footnote 16 says we must ensure the data are reliable, compatible and delivered on a timely basis. Would be correct only if data checks were unnecessary, which GARP never says. Do not confuse with Schweser’s “no financial statement adjustments”.

questions.source: High quality paper MR-2 d Q8
questions.question: A bank examiner at a central bank is reviewing a CNY foreign exchange desk. Six weeks ago the authorities permanently widened the currency’s trading band, which all parties agree has permanently increased exchange rate risk. The desk’s HS VaR, based on 500 daily observations, has barely moved. Which of the following best explains this?

options.text: Non-parametric methods have difficulty handling shifts during the sample period, so it usually takes time for HS VaR to reflect the new exchange rate risk.
Non-parametric methods pick up permanent shifts quickly and are slow only for temporary shocks, so the band change is unlikely to be the cause.
Non-parametric methods cannot accommodate the skewness that a regime change introduces, so the new exchange rate risk is excluded from HS VaR.
Non-parametric methods are slow here only because the window is short; a longer window would let HS VaR reflect the new risk more quickly.

questions.solution:
**Shifts during the sample period**

Stem in one line: permanent widening of the CNY band six weeks ago; 500-day HS VaR has barely moved; why?

**Concept and theory**

In an equal-weighted HS window of $n$ observations, a new day’s return carries weight 1$/n$. After a permanent change in the risk environment, only the few post-change observations reflect the new risk; the other $n$ minus a few still describe the old regime. The estimate catches up only as old observations roll out. GARP §2.5: non-parametric approaches can have difficulty handling shifts that take place during the sample period; if there is a permanent change in exchange rate risk, it will usually take time for the HS VaR or ES estimates to reflect it; similarly, such approaches are sometimes slow to reflect major events, such as the increases in risk associated with sudden market turbulence. Schweser: “Difficult to detect structural shifts/regime changes in the data.”

**Applying it to this question**

Six weeks is about 30 trading days out of 500, roughly 6% of the window. The VaR is still dominated by pre-change observations, so it has barely moved. This is GARP’s own example, a permanent change in exchange rate risk.

**Fragile fact.** Permanent shifts are reflected slowly; a longer window makes this worse.

**Reference**

LO 2.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 2, §2.5, Disadvantages (shifts bullet). Schweser Reading 2, LO 2.d disadvantages; Key Concepts (“slow to respond to changing market conditions”). Difference: Schweser says “detect”; GARP says “handle” and gives the exchange rate example. Same substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-2 d, where it is Q8 of 15.

a.reason: It names the disadvantage (difficulty handling shifts in the sample period) and its consequence (it takes time for HS VaR to reflect the new exchange rate risk), as in GARP §2.5.

b.reason: Error type: polarity flip. GARP says it takes time for HS to reflect a permanent change; B claims the reverse. Would be correct only for a method that reweights recent data heavily (not equal-weighted HS).

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap. Inability to accommodate skewness is a limitation of parametric methods; non-parametric methods accommodate skewness (an advantage). Would be correct for a normal-based VaR.

d.reason: Error type: scope or condition error (direction of the window effect reversed). A longer window makes estimates less responsive, because current news is drowned out by older observations (GARP §2.5). Correct with “short” and “longer” swapped: a shorter window would reflect the new risk more quickly.

questions.source: High quality paper MR-2 d Q9
questions.question:
A risk analyst at a German bank is showing the board which HS variants can report a loss larger than the worst loss in the data. The bank holds a EUR 40 million single-stock position and uses 600 daily returns. The three largest losses in the sample are:

| Day | Loss (%) | Volatility forecast for that day (%) |
|---|---|---|
| a | 4.20 | 2.80 |
| b | 3.10 | 1.40 |
| c | 2.60 | 1.05 |

Every other day has a loss below 2.00% and a volatility forecast of at least 1.40%. Today’s volatility forecast is 2.10%. The age-weighted variant uses a decay parameter $\lambda$ = 0.98, and the volatility-weighted variant scales each historical return by the ratio of today’s volatility forecast to that day’s forecast. What is the largest daily loss that basic HS, age-weighted HS and volatility-weighted HS, respectively, could report as a VaR at any confidence level?
questions.solution:
**Which HS variants can exceed the worst sample loss**

Stem in one line: worst losses 4.20% (vol 2.80%), 3.10% (1.40%), 2.60% (1.05%); today’s vol 2.10%; maximum reportable loss for basic, age-weighted and volatility-weighted HS?

**Concept and theory**

The LO 2.d point (GARP §2.5; Schweser) is that basic HS cannot report a loss larger than the largest loss in the sample, while more sophisticated versions can relax this constraint, volatility weighting “to some degree”. The mechanism differs by variant:

| Variant | What changes | Maximum reportable loss |
|---|---|---|
| Basic HS | Nothing; equal weights 1$/n$ | Largest actual loss |
| Age-weighted HS | Probability weights only | Largest actual loss |
| Volatility-weighted HS | The return values are rescaled | Largest adjusted loss |

Volatility weighting (the LO 2.c mechanism, used here only to show the effect) replaces each historical return by

$r^{*}_{t}$ = $r_{t} \frac{\sigma_{T}}{\sigma_{t}}$

where $r_{t}$ is the historical return on day $t$, $\sigma_{t}$ the volatility forecast for day $t$, $\sigma_{T}$ today’s forecast and $r^{*}_{t}$ the volatility-adjusted return.

**Applying it to this question**

Basic and age-weighted HS: both use the actual loss values, so the maximum is the largest actual loss.

Max loss (basic HS) = max(4.20, 3.10, 2.60) = 4.20%

Max loss (age-weighted HS) = 4.20% ($\lambda$ = 0.98 changes weights, not values)

Volatility-weighted HS: rescale each candidate by $\sigma_{T} /\sigma_{t}$ with $\sigma_{T}$ = 2.10.

Day a: 4.20 $\times\frac{2.10}{2.80}$ = 4.20 × 0.75 = 3.15%

Day b: 3.10 $\times\frac{2.10}{1.40}$ = 3.10 × 1.50 = 4.65%

Day c: 2.60 $\times\frac{2.10}{1.05}$ = 2.60 × 2.00 = 5.20%

Bound on all other days: 2.00 $\times\frac{2.10}{1.40}$ = 3.00%

Max loss (volatility-weighted HS) = 5.20%

Meaning: the volatility-weighted model can report a loss 1.00 percentage point above the worst loss ever observed, because day c happened in a calm period and today is twice as volatile. It is still capped by the largest adjusted loss, which is why GARP says such methods only “relax” the constraint. The EUR 40 million position size, the 600-day sample and $\lambda$ = 0.98 are irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Reweighting (age) never creates new loss values; rescaling (volatility) does. Today’s volatility goes in the numerator.

**Reference**

LO 2.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 2, §2.5, Disadvantages (largest-loss bullet); §2.4 Volatility-weighted Historical Simulation, Equation (2.3), used as mechanism only (formula garbled in the OCR text and absent from Schweser; notation confirmed from GARP’s prose “actual returns ... increased (or decreased), depending on whether the current forecast of volatility is greater (or less than) the estimated volatility for period $t$” and Schweser’s quiz answer “multiplied by (current volatility estimate / volatility estimate at time t)”). Schweser Reading 2, LO 2.d. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-2 d, where it is Q9 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: wrong input twin. Only the largest raw loss is rescaled: 4.20 × 2.10/2.80 = 3.15. After rescaling, the ranking changes, so the maximum must be taken over the adjusted series. Would be correct if day a were the only loss in the sample.

b.reason: 4.20%, 4.20%, 5.20%: basic and age-weighted HS cannot exceed the largest actual loss (GARP §2.5, simpler versions cannot extrapolate), while volatility weighting can (Schweser: “volatility-weighting can, to some degree”; GARP §2.4: HW estimates “can exceed the maximum loss in our historical data set”).

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap. Age-weighting is treated as if it rescaled returns like volatility weighting. Age-weighting changes only probability weights, so its maximum stays at 4.20%. Would be correct only if the age-weighted variant also volatility-adjusted the returns (a combination GARP says is possible, but not the one described).

d.reason: Error type: unit or ratio slip (ratio inverted). Using $\sigma_{t}/\sigma_{T}$ : 4.20 × 2.80/2.10 = 5.60, 3.10 × 1.40/2.10 = 2.07, 2.60 × 1.05/2.10 = 1.30; the maximum is 5.60. Would be correct only if the stem defined the scaling as that day’s forecast divided by today’s forecast, which is the reverse of the adjustment described.

questions.question: A risk committee member at a Singapore bank asks how the bank’s SGD historical simulation model could be improved without abandoning the HS framework. Which response by the senior risk analyst is most accurate?

options.text: Parametric add-ons such as age-weighting (BRW), volatility-weighting (HW and FHS) and correlation-weighting remove all dependence on the historical data.
Parametric add-ons such as age-weighting (HW), volatility-weighting (BRW and FHS) and correlation-weighting turn the methods into semi-parametric ones.
Parametric add-ons such as age-weighting (BRW), volatility-weighting (HW and FHS) and correlation-weighting turn the methods into semi-parametric ones.
Parametric add-ons such as age-weighting (BRW), volatility-weighting (HW and FHS) and correlation-weighting can only be used one at a time, never combined.

questions.solution:
**Refinement into semi-parametric methods**

Stem in one line: how can HS be improved without abandoning the HS framework?

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s last listed advantage is that non-parametric approaches are capable of considerable refinement and potential improvement if combined with parametric “add-ons”, which make them semi-parametric. GARP names three:

| Refinement | Associated with | What it adds |
|---|---|---|
| Age-weighting | BRW (Boudoukh, Richardson, Whitelaw) | Recent observations weighted more |
| Volatility-weighting | HW (Hull and White) and FHS | Returns rescaled to current volatility |
| Correlation-weighting | (Duffie and Pan, in §2.4) | Returns adjusted to current correlations |

They keep the broad HS framework while bringing in parametric elements (such as GARCH volatility forecasts), which is why GARP calls the result semi-parametric. The refinements can be combined: Schweser’s advantage is that the methods “can accommodate more complex analysis (e.g., by incorporating age-weighting with volatility-weighting)”, and GARP §2.4 notes that HW can be combined with age-weighting.

**Applying it to this question**

The committee member wants improvement within the HS framework, which is exactly the semi-parametric route. The options share the same structure; the discrimination lies in the author attributions, the label “semi-parametric”, and the claims about dependence and combination.

**Fragile fact.** BRW = age; HW and FHS = volatility. Adding parametric pieces makes the method semi-parametric, not parametric.

**Reference**

LO 2.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 2, §2.5, Advantages (last bullet); §2.4 Weighted Historical Simulation (for attributions). Schweser Reading 2, LO 2.d (“Can accommodate more complex analysis”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-2 d, where it is Q10 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. The refinements ameliorate problems but the estimates are still built from historical data (GARP: “we can often ameliorate these problems”). Correct if “remove all dependence on” read “reduce some weaknesses of”.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (attributions exchanged). Age-weighting is BRW; volatility-weighting is HW and FHS. Correct with the author labels swapped back.

c.reason: Correct attributions (BRW age-weighting; HW and FHS volatility-weighting; correlation-weighting) and the correct consequence (semi-parametric), as in GARP §2.5.

d.reason: Error type: scope or condition error (a false restriction). The add-ons can be combined (Schweser LO 2.d; GARP §2.4 on HW plus age-weighting; FHS combines bootstrapping with GARCH). Correct only for a system that, by design, allowed one adjustment at a time.

questions.source: High quality paper MR-2 d Q11
questions.question: An internal auditor at a US bank reviews an equal-weighted HS model with a 500-day window. The window contains a single extreme USD loss from a one-off operational failure that management agrees is very unlikely to recur. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Because the event is unlikely to recur, the equal-weighted model automatically gives that loss a lower weight than the other observations.
The loss can dominate the estimate while it is in the window, but its removal after 500 days will leave the VaR unchanged, so no ghost effect arises.
Ghost effects arise only when observations are age-weighted, so the equal-weighted model is free of them, whatever losses its window contains.
The loss can dominate the risk estimate although it is not expected to recur, and its later exit from the window can produce a ghost effect.

questions.solution:
**Unlikely-to-recur losses and ghost effects**

Stem in one line: equal-weighted 500-day HS window contains one extreme, non-recurring loss; most accurate statement?

**Concept and theory**

Two disadvantages from GARP §2.5 apply:

- If the data set incorporates extreme losses that are unlikely to recur, these losses can dominate non-parametric risk estimates even though we do not expect them to recur.
- Most (if not all) non-parametric methods are subject, to a greater or lesser extent, to ghost or shadow effects.

A ghost effect (defined in GARP §2.4) works like this: under equal weights, an extreme loss keeps the VaR unduly high for as long as it is in the window; after about $n$ days it drops out and the VaR falls abruptly. That fall reflects no change in risk; it is an artefact of the weighting structure and the window length. Remedy (GARP §2.5): age-weight the data and allow the sample size to rise over time.

**Applying it to this question**

The loss is extreme and non-recurring, so it can dominate the estimate (first bullet). In an equal-weighted window it keeps full weight 1/500 until day 500, then vanishes, producing the ghost effect (second bullet). D states both.

**Fragile fact.** Ghost effects are worst under equal weights; age-weighting reduces them, and age-weighting plus a growing sample can effectively eliminate them.

**Reference**

LO 2.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 2, §2.5, Disadvantages (unlikely-to-recur and ghost-effect bullets) and closing paragraph; §2.4 for the definition. Schweser Reading 2: ghost effects discussed under LO 2.c only. Difference: these two disadvantages are GARP-only in the LO 2.d list.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-2 d, where it is Q11 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap. Down-weighting by age is a property of age-weighted HS (BRW), not of equal-weighted HS, and even age-weighting reduces weight by age, not by how likely an event is to recur. Would be closer to correct for an age-weighted model as the loss ages.

b.reason: Error type: polarity flip (the drop-out effect denied). The sudden fall when the loss leaves the window is the ghost effect. Correct only if the loss were not among the observations that determine the VaR.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap. Age-weighting is the remedy that reduces ghost effects; GARP says most, if not all, non-parametric methods suffer from them. Correct with “age-weighted” and “equal-weighted” swapped (and “only” removed).

d.reason: GARP §2.5 lists both disadvantages in these terms.

questions.question: The CRO of a Swiss bank presents HS VaR and ES for the bank’s CHF portfolio, based on data from 2019 to 2025. A board member asks how the figures capture a plausible scenario in which a pegged currency to which the bank is exposed suddenly devalues by 25% against CHF, an event that never occurred in the sample period. Which response is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: The estimates make no allowance for plausible events absent from the sample, so they should be supplemented with stress tests of such “what if” events.
The estimates allow for the event through the fat tails of the empirical distribution, so supplementing them with stress tests adds little.
The estimates allow for the event once the sample is bootstrapped, because resampling generates outcomes more extreme than those observed.
The estimates make no allowance for the event, so they should be replaced by stress tests, which removes the need for VaR and ES altogether.

questions.solution:
**Plausible events absent from the sample**

Stem in one line: 25% devaluation never observed in the 2019 to 2025 sample; how do HS figures capture it?

**Concept and theory**

A non-parametric estimate can only reflect what is in its sample. GARP §2.5: non-parametric estimates of VaR or ES make no allowance for plausible events that might occur but did not actually occur in the sample period. Schweser: “Cannot accommodate plausible large impact events if they did not occur within the sample period.”

GARP’s Conclusions give the response: non-parametric methods work fairly well if market conditions remain reasonably stable, but have limitations, so it is often a good idea to supplement them with other approaches, in particular stress testing to gauge vulnerability to “what if” events. GARP: “We should never rely on non-parametric methods alone.” The word is supplement, not replace.

**Applying it to this question**

The devaluation is plausible but absent from the sample, so it has no influence on the HS figures. The right response is to run a stress test alongside the VaR and ES.

**Fragile fact.** Supplement with stress testing; do not replace. Bootstrapping cannot create unseen events.

**Reference**

LO 2.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 2, §2.5, Disadvantages (plausible-events bullet); Conclusions. Schweser Reading 2, LO 2.d disadvantages list. Difference: the stress-testing recommendation is GARP-only (Conclusions).

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-2 d, where it is Q12 of 15.

a.reason: It identifies the disadvantage (no allowance for unobserved plausible events) and GARP’s prescribed supplement (stress testing of “what if” events).

b.reason: Error type: scope or condition error. Fat tails are captured only to the extent they appear in the sample; an event that never occurred contributes nothing. Correct only if a comparable devaluation were in the sample.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap with LO 2.a. Bootstrapping resamples the observed data with replacement; it cannot create outcomes more extreme than those observed. Would describe a parametric Monte Carlo simulation from a fitted fat-tailed distribution.

d.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. GARP says supplement, never rely on non-parametric methods alone; it does not say discard VaR and ES. Correct if “replaced by” read “supplemented with” and the final clause were removed.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at an Indian bank is assessing a proposal to lengthen the HS window for the INR rates book from two years to six years of daily data (250 trading days per year, 5 trading days per week) to improve precision. A stress episode of 8 consecutive trading days, with losses averaging INR 310 million a day, began 30 weeks ago and still drives the current 99% VaR of INR 420 million. Assume an observation leaves the window exactly $n$ trading days after it occurred, where $n$ is the window length in trading days. Under the proposed window, how long from today will it be before the first observation of the episode leaves the window and the ghost effect begins?

options.text: 1,000 trading days (4.0 years)
1,500 trading days (6.0 years)
350 trading days (1.4 years)
1,350 trading days (5.4 years)

questions.solution:
**Longer window, longer wait for the ghost effect**

Stem in one line: window from two to six years; stress episode began 30 weeks ago; when does its first observation leave the proposed window?

**Concept and theory**

GARP §2.5 says the longer the window, the longer the period over which results are distorted by unlikely-to-recur past events, and the longer we have to wait for ghost effects to disappear. With an equal-weighted window of $n$ trading days, an observation that occurred $j$ trading days ago leaves the window after a further

wait = $n - j$

trading days (using the stem’s convention that an observation leaves exactly $n$ days after it occurred), where $n$ is the window length in trading days and $j$ the observation’s current age in trading days.

**Applying it to this question**

$n_{\text{proposed}}$ = 6 years × 250 = 1,500 trading days

$j$ = 30 weeks × 5 = 150 trading days

wait = 1,500 − 150 = 1,350 trading days

in years = 1,350/250 = 5.4 years

Cross-check with the current window: 500 − 150 = 350 trading days (1.4 years). Lengthening the window therefore extends the distortion by 1,350 − 350 = 1,000 trading days (4 years). Meaning: the precision gain is bought with five more years of a VaR propped up by an episode that may not recur. The 8-day length, the INR 310 million average loss and the INR 420 million VaR are irrelevant to the timing of the first exit.

**Fragile fact.** Wait = $n -$ age. A longer window delays, it does not prevent, the ghost effect.

**Reference**

LO 2.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 2, §2.5, paragraph on window length (rule of thumb of about 500 observations; longer wait for ghost effects); §2.4 for the drop-out mechanism. Schweser Reading 2, LO 2.d (sufficient data). Difference: window-length detail is GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-2 d, where it is Q13 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: intermediate result. 1,500 − 500 = 1,000 is the extra wait caused by lengthening the window, not the total wait from today. Correct if the question asked how much longer the ghost effect is delayed relative to the current window.

b.reason: Error type: dropped term. The 150 trading days already elapsed are ignored, as if the episode had just occurred. Correct if the episode began today.

c.reason: Error type: wrong input twin. Uses the current two-year window (500 − 150) instead of the proposed six-year window. Correct if the question asked about the current window.

d.reason: 1,500 − 150 = 1,350 trading days, or 5.4 years, illustrating GARP’s point that a longer window means a longer wait for ghost effects to disappear.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at a Canadian pension fund is reviewing a consultant’s report on why the fund’s CAD non-parametric risk estimates are only as good as the historical data behind them. Which of the following statements in the report is NOT correct?

options.text: If the data period was unusually volatile, the VaR and ES will often be too high for the risks the fund is actually facing.
Time series data are needed on all current positions, and such data are not always available, for example for emerging market positions.
Skewness and fat tails in the P/L data must be removed before estimation, because otherwise the non-parametric VaR and ES are biased.
Plausible large-impact events that did not occur in the sample period receive no allowance in the non-parametric VaR and ES.

questions.solution:
**Consequences of dependence on the historical data set**

Stem in one line: which statement about the effects of relying on historical data is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP §2.5 names dependence on the historical data set as the biggest potential weakness of nonparametric methods, then lists the related problems. Sorting the chapter’s statements:

| Statement | Status in GARP §2.5 |
|---|---|
| Volatile sample period gives VaR and ES too | Disadvantage (related problem) |
| high |  |
| Time series needed on all current positions; not | Disadvantage (footnote 16) |
| always available (EM) |  |
| No allowance for plausible events absent from | Disadvantage |
| the sample |  |
| Skewness and fat tails are accommodated, no parametric assumption | **Advantage** |

**Applying it to this question**

A, B and D are listed consequences of relying on the sample. C claims that skewness and fat tails must be removed, but non-parametric methods are valued precisely because they keep these features. C is the statement that is not correct.

**Fragile fact.** Skew and fat tails are an advantage of non-parametric methods; dependence on the sample is the weakness.

**Reference**

LO 2.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 2, §2.5 Advantages and Disadvantages; footnote 16. Schweser Reading 2, LO 2.d lists. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-2 d, where it is Q14 of 15.

a.reason: A true statement (GARP §2.5: unusually volatile data period, VaR or ES too high). It would be the answer only if it said “too low” (polarity flip).

b.reason: A true statement (GARP footnote 16). It would be the answer only if it said such data are always available (absolute claim).

c.reason: GARP §2.5 Advantages: since they do not depend on parametric assumptions about P/L, nonparametric approaches can accommodate fat tails, skewness and other non-normal features. Removing them would discard the very information HS is designed to use.

d.reason:
A true statement (GARP §2.5 and Schweser LO 2.d). It would be the answer only if it claimed the estimates do allow for such events, for example “through bootstrapping” (sibling swap).

Corruption in C: polarity flip of the distribution-free advantage (“accommodate” becomes “must be removed”), plus a sibling swap that imports a parametric-style correction.

questions.question:
The CRO of a UK bank proposes remedies for weaknesses in its basic GBP historical simulation model:

I. Ghost effects: age-weight the data and allow the sample size to rise over time.

II. Failure to reflect current volatility and market turbulence: apply semi-parametric adjustments such as volatility weighting.

III. Inability to report losses larger than the largest loss in the sample: switch from basic HS to bootstrapped HS.

IV. Historical correlations that differ from current correlations: adjust the historical returns by correlation weighting.

Which of the proposed remedies are consistent with the reading?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
II, III and IV only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
**Which refinement ameliorates which weakness**

Stem in one line: four proposed remedies for basic HS weaknesses; which are consistent with the reading?

**Concept and theory**

After listing the disadvantages, GARP §2.5 says we can often ameliorate these problems by suitable refinements:

| Weakness | Remedy named in GARP §2.5 |
|---|---|
| Volatility, market turbulence, correlation and other problems | Semi-parametric adjustments (volatility weighting as in HW and FHS; correlation weighting) |
| Ghost effects | Age-weighting the data and allowing the sample size to rise over time |
| Plausible “what if” events not in the sample | Supplement with stress testing (Conclusions) |
| Largest-loss constraint | More sophisticated HS (volatility weighting) can relax it; basic HS cannot |

Bootstrapping is not on the list: it resamples the observed data with replacement (LO 2.a), so every resampled loss is a loss already in the sample.

**Applying it to this question**

I: ghost effects by age-weighting plus a growing sample. Consistent. II: volatility and turbulence by semi-parametric (volatility) adjustment. Consistent. III: bootstrapping cannot produce losses beyond the largest observed loss. Not consistent. IV: correlation problems by correlation weighting, a semi-parametric adjustment. Consistent. Answer: I, II and IV only.

**Fragile fact.** Ghost effects: age-weight and let the sample grow. Bootstrap never creates a loss larger than the worst observation.

**Reference**

LO 2.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 2, §2.5, closing paragraph of Disadvantages; Conclusions. Schweser Reading 2, LO 2.d (“Can accommodate more complex analysis”). Difference: the remedy-to-weakness mapping is GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-2 d, where it is Q15 of 15.

a.reason: **I and II only.** Error type: rejects a true remedy. IV is a named semi-parametric adjustment for correlation problems. Would be correct if IV proposed an unrelated fix.

b.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: sibling swap in III. The ability to exceed the sample maximum belongs to volatility weighting, not to the bootstrap, which only recombines observed losses. Would be correct if III read “switch to volatility-weighted HS”.

c.reason: **II, III and IV.** Error type: accepts the sibling swap in III and rejects the true remedy I. Would be correct only if age-weighting did not affect ghost effects, which contradicts GARP.

d.reason: GARP §2.5: “we can ameliorate volatility, market turbulence, correlation and other problems by semi-parametric adjustments, and we can ameliorate ghost effects by age-weighting our data and allowing our sample size to rise over time.”

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee at an Indian bank asks why the risk function spends INR budget and staff time on events to which its own models assign a probability of well under 1% a year. Which of the following best explains why such events matter to risk management?

options.text: They occur often enough that their losses dominate the centre of the loss distribution, so they matter most when estimating typical outcomes.
They are low-probability, high-impact events, such as large market falls, failures of major institutions, financial crises and natural catastrophes.
They arise only from large market falls, so failures of major institutions, financial crises and natural catastrophes lie outside extreme risk estimation.
Their probabilities can be estimated precisely from historical data, so extreme risk measures are the most reliable figures a risk manager can report.

questions.solution:
**Why extreme events matter**

Stem in one line: a board member asks why the risk function spends resources on events with a probability well under 1% a year.

**Concept and theory**

A risk manager cares about an event in proportion to both its likelihood and its cost. Dowd opens the chapter by pointing to a class of events where the first is tiny and the second is huge: events “that are unlikely to occur, but can be very costly when they do.” He calls them low-probability, high-impact events and gives four examples: large market falls, the failures of major institutions, the outbreak of financial crises, and natural catastrophes. His conclusion: “Given the importance of such events, the estimation of extreme risk measures is a key concern for risk managers.”

| Feature | Central outcomes | Extreme outcomes |
|---|---|---|
| Probability | High | Low |
| Impact when they occur | Small to moderate | Very large (can be catastrophic) |
| Data available | Plentiful | Sparse |

Schweser makes the same point: extreme events are rare, but “it is crucial to identify these extreme events for risk management since they can prove to be very costly.”

**Applying it to this question**

The board member’s premise (a tiny probability) is correct but incomplete. The deciding fact is the second dimension, impact. Only B combines low probability with high impact and names Dowd’s four examples.

**Fragile fact.** Importance comes from impact, not frequency: low probability, high impact. The reliability of extreme estimates is the challenge, not the reason they matter.

**Reference**

LO 3.a (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 3, chapter introduction (before §3.1 Generalised Extreme-Value Theory). Schweser Reading 3, “Managing Extreme Values”. Difference: Schweser’s list adds “political crises”; GARP lists financial crises. Not material here; GARP’s list is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 a, where it is Q1 of 9.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip on frequency. Extreme events are rare, not frequent, and they sit in the tail, not the centre. A would describe ordinary, central outcomes rather than extremes.

b.reason: GARP chapter introduction: extreme events “are often referred to as low-probability, high-impact events, and they include large market falls, the failures of major institutions, the outbreak of financial crises and natural catastrophes.”

c.reason: Error type: scope error (the list is narrowed). Dowd’s list explicitly includes failures of major institutions, financial crises and natural catastrophes alongside market falls. C would be right only if the stem asked which single example of extreme events is purely a market-price event.

d.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. Dowd says the opposite: because extreme observations are few, “estimates of extreme risks must therefore be very uncertain.” D would be right for central quantiles estimated from plentiful data, not for extremes.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Japanese life insurer is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts on why extreme values are hard to estimate for the insurer’s JPY bond and equity portfolios. The draft slide contains four statements:

I. Extreme events are rare by definition, so there are relatively few extreme observations and estimates of extreme risks must be very uncertain.

II. The uncertainty is less pronounced for events more extreme than any in the historical data set, because such estimates draw on the full sample rather than on a few tail points.

III. The difficulty of estimating the risks of low-frequency events from limited data increases as the events concerned become rarer.

IV. Some extreme values that could occur lie in ranges that have not yet been observed in the data.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I, III and IV only
I and III only
I, II and III only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
**Why extremes are hard to estimate**

Stem in one line: which statements on the scarcity of extreme data and the resulting uncertainty are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

The challenge follows in a chain from the definition of an extreme:

1. Extreme events are rare by definition.
2. So any sample contains relatively few extreme observations.
3. So estimates of extreme risks “must therefore be very uncertain”.
4. The uncertainty is “especially pronounced” when we care about risks beyond the range of observed data, for example “an unprecedented stock market fall”.
5. The difficulties “increase as the events concerned become rarer”.

Schweser adds the complementary point that “there are ranges of extreme values that have yet to occur”, so some possible extremes have no observations at all.

**Applying it to this question**

I restates links 1 to 3: true. II reverses link 4: events beyond any in the data are the most uncertain, not the least. False. III restates link 5: true. IV is Schweser’s “ranges of extreme values that have yet to occur”: true. So I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: the further beyond the observed data, and the rarer the event, the greater the uncertainty.

**Reference**

LO 3.a. GARP Ch. 3, chapter introduction, paras. 2 and 4. Schweser Reading 3, “Managing Extreme Values”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 a, where it is Q2 of 9.

a.reason: GARP chapter introduction (rarity, few observations, very uncertain estimates; difficulties increase with rarity) and Schweser “Managing Extreme Values” (ranges of extreme values yet to occur).

b.reason: **I and III only.** Error type: scope error (a true condition dropped). It rejects IV, missing that Schweser names unobserved ranges as part of the challenge. B would be right if IV claimed that all possible extremes had already been observed.

c.reason: **I, II and III only.** Error type: polarity flip accepted in II and IV rejected. Accepting II means believing extrapolation reduces uncertainty, when GARP says uncertainty is “especially pronounced” beyond the data. II would be right if it said “more pronounced”.

d.reason:
**II, III and IV only.** Error type: polarity flip accepted in II, plus rejecting the core statement

I. Rejecting I denies the root cause of the whole challenge. D would be right only if I said extreme observations were plentiful.
