questions.question:
A treasury analyst at an Australian superannuation fund is asked to estimate one-week loss quantiles for the fund’s balanced portfolio at the 99%, 99.5% and 99.9% confidence levels, using the data below. Treat a quantile as lying within the range of the observed data only if at least one observation is expected to exceed it, that is, if $n$(1 $- \alpha$) ≥ 1, where $n$ is the number of observations used and $\alpha$ is the confidence level.

| Data item | Value |
|---|---|
| Sample period | 6 years |
| Returns used | Weekly, 52 per year |
| Average weekly return | 0.15% |
| Portfolio value | AUD 850 million |
| Trading days per year (daily reporting convention) | 250 |

Which of the following is most accurate?

options.text: None of the three quantiles lies beyond the observed data, since at least one loss is expected to exceed each of them.
Only the 99.9% quantile lies beyond the observed data, but fitting a distribution to all 312 returns makes it as reliable as the others.
Only the 99.9% quantile lies beyond the observed data, and its estimate is the most uncertain of the three.
The 99.5% and 99.9% quantiles lie beyond the observed data, and both estimates are more uncertain than the 99% one.

questions.solution:
**Within versus beyond the range of the observed data**

Stem in one line: 6 years of weekly returns; which of the 99%, 99.5% and 99.9% loss quantiles lie beyond the observed data?

**Concept and theory**

An extreme quantile within the data rests on few observations; one beyond the data, a loss more extreme than any in the sample, is harder still. GARP: the uncertainty “is especially pronounced if we are interested in extreme risks not only within the range of observed data, but well beyond it.” To locate a quantile, count the observations expected to exceed it:

$E$\[number of exceedances\] = $n$(1 $- \alpha$)

where $n$ is the number of observations and $\alpha$ the confidence level. If $n$(1 $- \alpha$) \< 1, not even one observation is expected beyond the quantile, so the estimate must extrapolate beyond the data.

**Applying it to this question**

Use the frequency of the data actually used (weekly):

$n$ = 6 × 52 = 312

$\alpha$ = 99% : $n$(1 $- \alpha$) = 312 × 0.010 = 3.12 ≥ 1 ⇒ within

$\alpha$ = 99.5% : $n$(1 $- \alpha$) = 312 × 0.005 = 1.56 ≥ 1 ⇒ within

$\alpha$ = 99.9% : $n$(1 $- \alpha$) = 312 × 0.001 = 0.312 \< 1 ⇒ beyond

The average weekly return (0.15%), the portfolio value (AUD 850 million) and the 250-day convention are irrelevant. Meaning: the 99.9% weekly quantile is a loss larger than the sample is expected to contain, so its estimate is an extrapolation and is the most uncertain of the three.

**Fragile fact.** Use the frequency of the data actually used ($n$ = 312 weekly, not 1,500 daily). Beyond the data means more uncertain, never less.

**Reference**

LO 3.a. GARP Ch. 3, chapter introduction, para. 2. Schweser Reading 3, “Managing Extreme Values”. The convention $n$(1 $- \alpha$) ≥ 1 is stated in the stem (arithmetic, not a source formula). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 a, where it is Q3 of 9.

a.reason: Error type: unit or time-conversion slip. Treating the weekly sample as daily data gives $n$ = 6 × 250 = 1,500, so the counts become 15, 7.5 and 1.5, all at least 1, and no quantile looks out of range. A would be right if the analyst had six years of daily returns.

b.reason: Error type: polarity flip on reliability (the count is right, the conclusion reversed). Fitting a distribution to all 312 returns makes the fit follow the many central observations, which does nothing for a quantile beyond the data (GARP intro, para. 3). B would be right only for a central quantile.

c.reason: Only the 99.9% quantile has $n$(1 $- \alpha$) \< 1; GARP says uncertainty is especially pronounced beyond the observed data.

d.reason: Error type: condition error (cut-off misapplied). D uses a cut-off of 2, but the stem’s cut-off is 1 and the 99.5% count of 1.56 meets it. D would be right if the sample were shorter than 1/0.005 = 200 weeks.

questions.question: A model validator at a Canadian bank is reviewing a model that estimates the 99.9% one-day VaR of a CAD trading desk. The developer selected a single parametric distribution, fitted it directly to all 2,000 observations of the desk’s aggregate daily P&L, and reports that a goodness-of-fit test over the full sample is passed comfortably. Which of the following is the most accurate concern for the validator to raise?

options.text: The extreme observations, being the largest in size, dominate the fit, so the model is more likely to misdescribe the centre of the distribution than its tail.
With 2,000 observations and a passed full-sample test, the tail is validated as well, so the 99.9% VaR can be relied on without further work.
The desk P&L combines several risk factors, so the main concern is that correlations cannot describe how the extremes of those factors depend on each other.
The fit must accommodate the many central observations rather than the sparse extremes, so a good overall fit says little about the 99.9% quantile.

questions.solution:
**A good overall fit is not a good tail fit**

Stem in one line: one distribution fitted to all 2,000 daily P&L observations passes a full-sample test; what should the validator worry about?

**Concept and theory**

Faced with scarce extreme data, “practitioners can only respond by relying on assumptions to make up for lack of data”, and those assumptions “are often questionable”. Dowd describes the usual practice and why it fails:

- A distribution is selected arbitrarily and fitted to the whole data set.
- The fit therefore accommodates the more central observations, “because there are so many of them”, rather than the extreme observations, “which are much sparser”.
- So the approach is often good for the central part of the distribution but “ill-suited to handling extremes”.

Schweser’s version: the assumed distribution will probably not be identical to the true one, so some error is present, and distributions chosen on central tendency miss the extremes.

**Applying it to this question**

A goodness-of-fit test over the full sample is driven by the bulk of the 2,000 observations; at the 99.9% level only about 2,000 × 0.001 = 2 observations lie in the relevant tail. Passing the test says the centre is well described; it says little about the 99.9% quantile. That is D.

**Fragile fact.** Many central points dominate a whole-sample fit; sparse extremes do not. A good fit in the body is not evidence of a good fit in the tail.

**Reference**

LO 3.a. GARP Ch. 3, chapter introduction, para. 3. Schweser Reading 3, “Managing Extreme Values”. Difference: Schweser says researchers “choose distributions based on measures of central tendency”; GARP says the distribution is chosen arbitrarily and the fit to the whole data set is dominated by central observations. Same idea; GARP’s mechanism is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 a, where it is Q4 of 9.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip. Extremes are large but few; the many central observations dominate the fit. A would be right if the question concerned a fit made only to the largest losses (an approach tailored to the tail).

b.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. A full-sample test cannot validate the extreme tail, which rests on very few points. B would be right for a central quantile such as the median.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap with LO 3.f (multivariate EVT). The model is fitted directly to the desk’s aggregate P&L, a single variable, so dependence between factor extremes is not the issue raised by this model. C would be the right concern for a model that combines separate factor tails using correlations.

d.reason: GARP chapter introduction, para. 3: a distribution fitted to the whole data set “will tend to accommodate the more central observations” and is “ill-suited to handling extremes”.

questions.question: A risk consultant is reviewing a case at a Swiss private bank. The bank estimated the 99.9% one-day VaR of a single CHF equity index position by fitting a normal distribution to 15 years of daily index returns; no threshold or tail index was estimated. The fitted curve matched the body of the return distribution closely. During a market crash, the position lost more than three times the estimated VaR, a loss larger than any in the sample. Which lesson best fits Dowd’s diagnosis of this case?

options.text: The normal was chosen without regard to the tail and fitted to all 15 years of returns, so it accommodated the many central observations and was ill-suited to the extremes.
The threshold for the peaks-over-threshold model was set so high that too few exceedances remained to estimate the generalized Pareto parameters reliably.
Extremes in the bank’s different risk factors were jointly dependent, and correlations alone cannot describe the dependence among extremes.
The Hill estimate of the tail index failed to settle as the tail size $k$ changed, so the tail index that was used was effectively arbitrary.

questions.solution:
**Case: a normal fitted to all returns fails in a crash**

Stem in one line: a normal fitted to 15 years of daily returns on one index position; a crash loss of three times VaR, larger than any in the sample.

**Concept and theory**

This is the practice criticised in Q4, seen after the event. Dowd’s diagnosis has two layers:

- Mechanism (introduction): a distribution chosen arbitrarily and fitted to the whole data set accommodates the many central observations, so it is good for the centre but ill-suited to extremes.
- Lesson (§3.4): EVT is important for what it tells us not to do, and “the most important point is not to use distributions justified by central limit theory, most particularly, the normal or Gaussian distribution, for extreme-value estimation.”

In a case-based question, the wrong options are usually true lessons from other cases. The task is to match the lesson to the facts of this case.

**Applying it to this question**

The facts: one index position (so no multi-factor dependence), a normal fitted to all returns (so no threshold and no tail index), a close fit in the body, and a loss beyond anything in the sample. Every fact points to the central-observation mechanism; each of the other lessons needs a feature this case lacks.

**Fragile fact.** A close fit in the body is exactly what a whole-sample fit produces, and it is not evidence about the tail.

**Reference**

LO 3.a. GARP Ch. 3, chapter introduction, para. 3; §3.4 Conclusions (the warning against the normal is GARP-only). Schweser Reading 3, “Managing Extreme Values”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 a, where it is Q5 of 9.

a.reason: GARP chapter introduction, para. 3, and §3.4 Conclusions (do not use the normal for extreme-value estimation).

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (a true lesson of another case, LO 3.e). The threshold trade-off is real for a POT model, but this bank estimated no threshold. B would be the lesson if the bank had fitted a generalized Pareto distribution to a handful of exceedances over a very high threshold.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap (LO 3.f). The point about dependence among extremes is true, but the case concerns a single index position. C would be the lesson for a multi-asset portfolio modelled with correlations.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap (LO 3.b). The Hill horror plot is a real hazard when estimating a tail index, but no tail index was estimated here. D would be the lesson if the bank had used a Fréchet model with a Hill estimate.

questions.question: A risk consultant is briefing the risk committee of a German reinsurer on why its EUR catastrophe and market risk teams use methods first worked out for flood defences. Which of the following best describes the parallel with hydrology that Dowd draws?

options.text: Hydrologists had far more data than financial risk practitioners, so the flood levels they needed could usually be read directly from their samples.
Hydrologists had even less data than financial risk practitioners, and the flood levels they needed typically lay well outside their sample data.
Hydrologists had about as much data as financial risk practitioners, and the flood levels they needed typically lay inside the range of past floods.
Hydrologists adopted EVT after risk managers had developed it, and the flood levels they needed typically lay well outside their sample data.

questions.solution:
**The hydrology parallel**

Stem in one line: what parallel does Dowd draw between risk management and flood engineering?

**Concept and theory**

Dowd uses hydrology to show that the problem of extremes is not unique to finance and that it needs an approach tailored to it. The basic problem is that “the estimation of the risks associated with low-frequency events with limited data is inevitably problematic”. Engineers deciding how high dikes, sea walls and similar barriers must be faced the same problem in a harsher form:

| Dimension | Financial risk managers | Hydrologists |
|---|---|---|
| Data available | Limited | Even less |
| Quantiles needed | Often beyond the sample | Typically well out of the sample range |
| Stakes | High | Potentially much higher |

GARP: “The result of their efforts is extreme-value theory (EVT)”, a branch of applied statistics tailor-made to these problems. Schweser’s version is a dam that must be built above the flood levels observed to date.

**Applying it to this question**

Three slots discriminate: the amount of data (even less), where the needed quantile lies (well outside the sample) and who developed EVT (hydrologists, through their efforts). Only B gets the first two right without a wrong attribution.

**Fragile fact.** Actor and direction: hydrology produced EVT; finance borrowed it. Hydrologists had even less data and potentially more at stake.

**Reference**

LO 3.a. GARP Ch. 3, chapter introduction, paras. 4 and 5. Schweser Reading 3, “Managing Extreme Values” (flood-control and dam example). Difference: Schweser uses a dam and omits the “even less data” and “EVT resulted from their efforts” points; GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 a, where it is Q6 of 9.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip on data. Hydrologists had less data, not more, and their quantiles were outside the sample. A would describe a field with abundant, in-sample data, which is the opposite of Dowd’s point.

b.reason: GARP chapter introduction, para. 4: hydrologists “have had to do so with even less data than financial risk practitioners usually have, and their quantile estimates . . . were also typically well out of the range of their sample data.”

c.reason: Error type: scope error (the beyond-sample condition is dropped). If the needed flood levels lay inside past floods, there would be no extrapolation problem. C would be right for a routine within-sample design question.

d.reason: Error type: role misassignment. The second clause is right, but the direction of borrowing is reversed: EVT was the result of the hydrologists’ efforts, and finance adopted it. D would be right if it said “risk managers adopted EVT after hydrologists had developed it”.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Singapore bank is reviewing the limitations section of the documentation for an extreme value (EV) model used to set SGD tail-risk limits. The section contains four statements:

I. EV estimates carry relatively wide confidence intervals; this is not a fault of EVT as such but an inevitable consequence of having few extreme observations.

II. EV results are often very sensitive to the precise assumptions made, but those assumptions are easy to verify with a goodness-of-fit test on the full sample.

III. Because data are scarce and the theory is mostly asymptotic, EV estimates can be very sensitive to small-sample effects, biases and non-linearities.

IV. Ancillary decisions such as threshold values follow objectively from the theory, so applying EV methods involves little subjective judgment.

Which of the statements are consistent with Dowd’s assessment of the limitations of EV approaches?

options.text: I only
I, II and III only
I, III and IV only
I and III only

questions.solution:
**Limitations of EV estimates**

Stem in one line: which statements in an EV model’s limitations section match Dowd’s assessment?

**Concept and theory**

In his conclusions Dowd praises EVT as the tailor-made way to estimate extreme risks, then lists limitations that “stand out”:

| Limitation | What GARP says |
|---|---|
| Intrinsic difficulty | Few extreme observations, so EV estimates are very uncertain with relatively wide confidence intervals. This “is not a fault of EVT as such, but an inevitable consequence of our paucity of data.” |
| Model risk | Results are often very sensitive to the precise assumptions made, and those assumptions can be difficult to verify; estimates often depend on assumptions that are “effectively unverifiable”. |
| Judgment | Ancillary decisions about threshold values and the like have no easy answers; applying EV methods involves a lot of subjective judgment. |
| Small samples | With little data and mostly asymptotic theory, estimates can be very sensitive to small-sample effects, biases and non-linearities. |

**Applying it to this question**

I is the first row, including the attribution to data rather than to EVT: true. II says the assumptions are easy to verify; GARP says effectively unverifiable: false. III is the last row: true. IV says threshold decisions are objective; GARP says they involve a lot of subjective judgment: false. So I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Attribution: wide confidence intervals are caused by scarce data, not by a flaw in EVT. Assumptions are hard to verify; thresholds need judgment.

**Reference**

LO 3.a. GARP Ch. 3, §3.4 Conclusions (GARP-only; Schweser’s LO 3.a Key Concepts say only that extremes are difficult to model). Boundary call: treated as LO 3.a “challenges”; the question bank tags these points to LO 3.a.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 a, where it is Q7 of 9.

a.reason: **I only.** Error type: scope error (a true statement rejected). It discards III, the small-sample point. A would be right if III claimed EV theory was exact in finite samples.

b.reason: **I, II and III only.** Error type: polarity flip accepted in II (“easy to verify” for “difficult to verify”). B would be right if II said the assumptions are difficult, often effectively impossible, to verify.

c.reason: **I, III and IV only.** Error type: polarity flip accepted in IV (“little subjective judgment” for “a lot of subjective judgment”). C would be right if IV said threshold choices have no easy answers and require judgment.

d.reason: GARP §3.4 Conclusions, limitations bullets.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Brazilian bank asks two teams to estimate the 99.9% one-day VaR of the same BRL rates book from the same 1,250 daily observations. Both teams use EV methods but make different, individually reasonable modelling assumptions and threshold choices. Team 1 reports BRL 41 million and Team 2 reports BRL 63 million. Which of the following best explains the gap?

options.text: One team must have made an error, because for a given data set EVT yields a unique tail estimate that does not depend on the analyst’s judgment.
The sample is too long, and using only a smaller, more recent sample would reduce the uncertainty and make the two estimates converge.
EV estimates carry considerable model risk: results are very sensitive to assumptions that are hard to verify and to judgment calls such as thresholds.
EVT relies on the central limit theorem, which converges slowly in the tails, so any two EV estimates of a high quantile are bound to differ.

questions.solution:
**Two reasonable EV models, two different answers**

Stem in one line: two teams, same 1,250 observations, different reasonable assumptions; 99.9% VaR of BRL 41 million versus BRL 63 million.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s second limitation is model risk. To produce any extreme-value estimate we “have to make various assumptions”, and “our results will often be very sensitive to the precise assumptions we make”. These assumptions are hard to check, so estimates are “often critically dependent on assumptions that are effectively unverifiable”. EVT also requires “ancillary decisions about threshold values and the like” for which there are no easy rules, so applying it involves “a lot of subjective judgment”.

Implication: two competent teams can legitimately produce materially different extreme quantiles from identical data. The spread itself is information about the uncertainty.

**Applying it to this question**

The data are identical, the methods are both EV, and both teams’ choices are described as reasonable. What differs is assumptions and thresholds, exactly the channel GARP identifies. A gap of BRL 22 million (about 54% of the lower figure) at the 99.9% level is the kind of sensitivity GARP warns about. That is C.

**Fragile fact.** Divergent EV estimates from the same data are a symptom of model risk and judgment, not proof of an error.

**Reference**

LO 3.a. GARP Ch. 3, §3.4 Conclusions (GARP-only). Distractor D uses LO 3.b material (GARP chapter introduction on central limit theorems). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 a, where it is Q8 of 9.

a.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. EVT does not deliver a unique, judgment-free estimate; GARP stresses the opposite. A would be right only if both teams had used identical assumptions and thresholds and still disagreed.

b.reason: Error type: polarity flip on data. Fewer observations increase uncertainty; GARP’s whole challenge is the paucity of extreme data, and estimates are sensitive to small-sample effects. B would be right if it said a longer sample would tend to narrow the uncertainty.

c.reason: GARP §3.4 Conclusions: EV estimates “are subject to considerable model risk”; results are very sensitive to assumptions that are difficult to verify; ancillary decisions require subjective judgment.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap with LO 3.b. Central limit theorems do not apply to extremes; extremes are governed by extreme-value theorems. D would be right as a criticism of using a normal approximation for the tail, not of EVT.

questions.question: The CRO of a UK bank must present an EV-based 99.9% expected shortfall for a GBP credit trading book to the board, after the model validator noted that the estimate has a wide confidence interval. Which of the following approaches is most consistent with Dowd’s guidance?

options.text: Replace the EV estimate with a normal distribution fitted to the full history, since using all observations makes the tail estimate more reliable.
Keep the EV estimate, report its confidence interval and subject it to stress testing, while stating that scarce data limit its reliability.
Keep the EV estimate and report it as a precise figure, since EVT is a tailor-made theory and its confidence interval adds nothing.
Withhold the EV estimate until enough data have accumulated to remove its uncertainty, and report no extreme risk measure meanwhile.

questions.solution:
**What to do about the uncertainty**

Stem in one line: how should the CRO present an EV-based 99.9% ES that has a wide confidence interval?

**Concept and theory**

Dowd does not conclude that EVT should be abandoned. His responses to the limitations are:

- “It is especially important with extremes to estimate confidence intervals for our estimated risk measures and to subject the latter to stress testing.”
- Acknowledge that “the paucity of our data inevitably limits the reliability of our results”.
- Keep using EVT: quoting McNeil, if we wish to quantify rare events “we are better off using the theoretically supported methods of EVT than other ad hoc approaches.”
- Do not overreach: quoting Diebold et al., “we shouldn’t ask more of the theory than it can deliver.”

**Applying it to this question**

The wide confidence interval is expected, not a reason to drop the measure. The approach consistent with GARP keeps the EV estimate, shows its interval, stress tests it and states its limits. That is B.

**Fragile fact.** Respond to EV uncertainty by quantifying it (confidence intervals) and testing it (stress tests), not by switching to the normal or by hiding it.

**Reference**

LO 3.a. GARP Ch. 3, §3.4 Conclusions (GARP-only, including the McNeil and Diebold et al. quotations). Schweser Reading 3 does not cover these responses. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 a, where it is Q9 of 9.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip. GARP says the most important thing EVT tells us not to do is use the normal for extreme-value estimation, and a fit to the whole history is dominated by central observations. A would be right for estimating a central quantile.

b.reason: GARP §3.4 Conclusions: confidence intervals and stress testing, plus acknowledging that data paucity limits reliability.

c.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. EV estimates are inherently uncertain; reporting them as precise asks more of the theory than it can deliver. C would be right only if the estimate rested on abundant tail data, which extremes never do.

d.reason: Error type: scope or condition error. The uncertainty is an inevitable consequence of scarce extreme data, so it cannot be removed by waiting, and GARP still prefers EVT to having no estimate or an ad hoc one. D would be right only if the uncertainty were a temporary data-collection problem.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Canadian pension fund is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts that introduces extreme value theory (EVT) for its CAD equity portfolio. The draft slide contains four statements:

I. Central tendency statistics are governed by central limit theorems, but these do not apply to extremes, which are governed instead by extreme-value theorems.

II. EVT fits a chosen distribution to the whole data set, so that the many central observations anchor the estimate of the tail.

III. The distributions used in EVT differ from the familiar central tendency distributions, their parameters are different, and those parameters are more difficult to estimate.

IV. Results derived for maxima can be applied to extremes that are minima by multiplying the data by −1.

Which of the statements are accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, $X$ denotes a loss (losses are positive), the generalised extreme value (GEV) parameters are location $\mu$, scale $\sigma$ and tail index $\xi$, and $n$ is the number of observations from which each maximum is drawn.

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
I, III and IV only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
**What EVT is**

Stem in one line: which of four slide statements introducing EVT are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Most of statistics is about the middle of a distribution: sample means, variances, regressions. Its workhorse is the central limit theorem (CLT), which says that averages of many observations tend to a normal distribution. Risk management, however, cares about the worst outcomes: large market falls, failures of major institutions, crises. GARP: EVT is “a branch of applied statistics that is tailor-made” for these problems, and it “is quite different from the more familiar ‘central tendency’ statistics”. The reason: “central tendency statistics are governed by central limit theorems, but central limit theorems do not apply to extremes. Instead, extremes are governed, appropriately enough, by extreme-value theorems.”

|  | Central tendency statistics | EVT |
|---|---|---|
| Governing theorem | Central limit theorem | Extreme-value theorems (Fisher-Tippett; GPBdH) |
| Typical distribution | Normal (elliptical) | GEV (Fréchet, Gumbel, Weibull); GP |
| Parameters | Mean, standard deviation | Location, scale, tail index; harder to estimate |
| Data used | The whole sample | Extremes only (maxima or exceedances) |

EVT uses these theorems “to tell us what distributions we should (and should not!) fit to our extremes data” and guides parameter estimation. GARP footnote 2: the theory also works for minima; “we simply apply the maxima extremes results but multiply our data by −1.”

**Applying it to this question**

I restates GARP’s CLT versus extreme-value-theorem contrast: true. II describes exactly what EVT replaces: GARP says the common practice of fitting an arbitrary distribution to the whole data set lets the fitted distribution “accommodate the more central observations, because there are so many of them”, which makes it “ill-suited to handling extremes”. False. III: GARP, “These EV distributions are quite different . . . Their parameters are also different, and the estimation of these parameters is more difficult.” True. IV is footnote 2: true. Accurate set: I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** CLT governs averages, extreme-value theorems govern extremes. EVT fits the tail, not the whole data set.

**Reference**

LO 3.b: “Describe extreme value theory (EVT) and its use in risk management.” GARP Ch. 3, introduction and footnote 2. Schweser Reading 3, “Extreme Value Theory”. No conflict (the minima rule, footnote 2, is GARP-only).

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 b, where it is Q1 of 16.

a.reason: **I and III only.** Error type: scope error (a true statement rejected). It drops IV, probably because the minima rule sits in a footnote. Correct only if IV said minima need a different limiting theory altogether.

b.reason: **I, II and III only.** Error type: sibling swap. Statement II attributes to EVT the whole-sample fitting of the conventional approach that EVT is designed to avoid. B would be right if II read “Conventional approaches fit a distribution to the whole data set . . . ” and IV were false.

c.reason: Statements I, III and IV are near-verbatim GARP statements (Ch. 3 introduction and footnote 2); II contradicts GARP.

d.reason: **II, III and IV only.** Error type: polarity flip on I plus acceptance of II. Rejecting I means believing the CLT governs extremes. Correct only in a world where extremes were normal, which is exactly what EVT denies.

A model validator at a German bank is reviewing the documentation of a block maxima VaR model for its EUR equity book. The documentation must state the theorem on which the model rests. Which of the following best describes the Fisher-Tippett theorem?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, $X$ denotes a loss (losses are positive), the generalised extreme value (GEV) parameters are location $\mu$, scale $\sigma$ and tail index $\xi$, and $n$ is the number of observations from which each maximum is drawn.

options.text: As a threshold $u$ rises, the distribution of losses in excess of $u$ converges to a generalised Pareto distribution, whatever the parent distribution.
As the sample size $n$ gets large, the distribution of the sample maximum converges to a normal distribution, which justifies a normal VaR for extreme losses.
As the sample size $n$ gets large, the distribution of the sample maximum converges to a GEV distribution, provided the parent distribution is known to be normal or lognormal.
As the sample size $n$ gets large, the distribution of the sample maximum of iid losses converges to a GEV distribution, even though the parent distribution is unknown.

questions.solution:
**The Fisher-Tippett theorem**

Stem in one line: which description of the Fisher-Tippett theorem belongs in a block maxima model document?

**Concept and theory**

Let $X$ be an iid random loss with unknown distribution $F$ ($x$) = Pr($X \le x$). We want extreme risks of $X$, but we do not know $F$ . Draw a sample of size $n$ and let $M_{n}$ be its maximum. GARP §3.1: “Under relatively general conditions, the celebrated Fisher-Tippett theorem (1928) then tells us that as $n$ gets large, the distribution of extremes (i.e., $M_{n}$) converges to the following generalised extreme-value (GEV) distribution”:

$$H_{\xi,\mu,\sigma}(x) = \begin{cases} \exp\left[-\left(1 + \xi\,\dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\right)^{-1/\xi}\right] & \xi \ne 0 \\ \exp\left[-\exp\left(-\dfrac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\right)\right] & \xi = 0 \end{cases} \qquad \text{with } 1 + \xi(x - \mu)/\sigma > 0,$$

where $\mu$ is the location parameter, $\sigma$ the scale parameter and $\xi$ the tail index. The theorem is the extremes counterpart of the CLT: it gives a universal limiting family without requiring us to know $F$ . That is “where EVT comes to our rescue”.

**Applying it to this question**

Three ingredients must all be right: the object (the sample maximum), the limit (GEV) and the condition (the parent may be unknown). Only D has all three.

**Fragile fact.** Fisher-Tippett: block maxima → GEV. GPBdH: threshold exceedances → GP. Neither needs the parent to be known.

**Reference**

LO 3.b (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 3, §3.1 “Theory”, eq. (3.1). Schweser Reading 3, “Extreme Value Theory”. GEV formula garbled in the GARP OCR and absent from Schweser; notation confirmed from question bank Q143 (LO 3.b). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 b, where it is Q2 of 16.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap. This is the Gnedenko-Pickands-Balkema-deHaan theorem behind the POT approach (LO 3.c and 3.e), which concerns exceedances over a threshold. Correct if the stem asked for the theorem underlying the peaks-over-threshold approach.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap with the CLT. The normal is the limit for averages, and EVT’s central message is that it should not be used for extremes. Correct only if “maximum” read “mean” and the conclusion were dropped.

c.reason: Error type: scope or condition error. The theorem holds under relatively general conditions for an unknown parent; normal or lognormal parents merely lead to one case (Gumbel). Correct if the condition were deleted.

d.reason: It matches GARP §3.1 and Schweser LO 3.b (“as the sample size $n$ gets large, the distribution of extremes, denoted $M_{n}$, converges to . . . the generalized extreme value (GEV) distribution”). GARP stresses that $F$ ($x$) is unknown.

The treasurer of an Australian general insurer is reading a risk report on its AUD investment portfolio. The report fits a GEV distribution to the maxima of daily losses and states estimates of $\mu$, $\sigma$ and $\xi$. Which of the following best describes these three parameters?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, $X$ denotes a loss (losses are positive), the generalised extreme value (GEV) parameters are location $\mu$, scale $\sigma$ and tail index $\xi$, and $n$ is the number of observations from which each maximum is drawn.

options.text: $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are the mean and standard deviation of the parent daily loss distribution, and $\xi$ indicates the shape or heaviness of the tail of the limiting distribution.

$\mu$ and $\sigma$ measure the central tendency and dispersion of the maximum $M_{n}$ and are related to, but distinct from, its mean and standard deviation; $\xi$ indicates the shape or heaviness of the tail.
$\mu$ measures the central tendency of the maximum $M_{n}$, $\xi$ measures the dispersion of $M_{n}$, and $\sigma$ indicates the shape or heaviness of the tail of the limiting distribution.

$\mu$ and $\sigma$ measure the central tendency and dispersion of the maximum $M_{n}$ and are related to, but distinct from, its mean and standard deviation; $\xi$ scales with the square root of the holding period.

questions.solution:
**Meaning of the GEV parameters**

Stem in one line: which description of $\mu$, $\sigma$ and $\xi$ in the insurer’s GEV report is best?

**Concept and theory**

The GEV has three parameters, and all three describe the distribution of the extreme $M_{n}$, not of the parent loss $X$. GARP §3.1: “The first two are $\mu$, the location parameter of the limiting distribution, which is a measure of the central tendency of $M_{n}$, and $\sigma$, the scale parameter of the limiting distribution, which is a measure of the dispersion of $M_{n}$. These are related to, but distinct from, the more familiar mean and standard deviation . . . The third parameter, $\xi$, the tail index, gives an indication of the shape (or heaviness) of the tail of the limiting distribution.”

| Symbol | Name | What it measures |
|---|---|---|
| $\mu$ | Location | Central tendency of $M_{n}$ (not the mean of $X$) |
| $\sigma$ | Scale | Dispersion of $M_{n}$ (not the standard deviation of $X$) |
| $\xi$ | Tail index (shape) | Heaviness of the tail; sign fixes Fréchet, Gumbel or Weibull |

GARP footnote 5 adds how they behave with the holding period $h$: the mean scales with $h$, the standard deviation with $\sqrt{h}$, and “(subject to certain conditions) the tail index does not scale at all”.

**Applying it to this question**

Check each option on two points: what $\mu$ and $\sigma$ describe ($M_{n}$, and only approximately its mean and dispersion), and what $\xi$ does (shape). B gets both right.

**Fragile fact.** $\mu$ and $\sigma$ describe the maximum $M_{n}$, are only related to its mean and dispersion, and $\xi$ does not scale with the horizon.

**Reference**

LO 3.b (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 3, §3.1 “Theory” and footnote 5. Schweser Reading 3, “Extreme Value Theory”. Difference: Schweser says $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are “related to the mean and variance”; GARP says “mean and standard deviation” and adds that they measure the central tendency and dispersion of $M_{n}$. Wording only; GARP used. Scaling of $\xi$ is GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 b, where it is Q3 of 16.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap (parent moments for limiting-distribution parameters). $\mu$ and $\sigma$ describe $M_{n}$, and even then are not exactly its mean and standard deviation. Correct only if the stem described a normal fitted to the parent losses.

b.reason: It reproduces GARP §3.1 and Schweser (“The parameters $\mu$ and $\sigma$ are the location parameter and scale parameter . . . Although related to the mean and variance, they are not the same. The symbol $\xi$ is the tail index and indicates the shape (or heaviness) of the tail”).

c.reason: Error type: role misassignment. It gives $\xi$ the job of $\sigma$ (dispersion) and $\sigma$ the job of $\xi$ (tail shape). Correct with the roles of $\xi$ and $\sigma$ swapped back.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap on scaling. Square-root scaling belongs to the standard deviation; GARP says the tail index does not scale with the horizon. Correct if “$\xi$” read “the standard deviation”.

A senior risk analyst at an Indian bank is presenting to newly hired analysts. Three INR desks have each fitted a parent distribution to their daily losses:

| Desk | Business | Parent distribution fitted to daily losses |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | FX options | Student’s $t$ with 4 degrees of freedom |
| 2 | Commodities | Lognormal |
| 3 | Catastrophe reinsurance | Pareto |

As the block size $n$ gets large, the maxima of each desk’s losses fall in the domain of attraction of which GEV case?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, $X$ denotes a loss (losses are positive), the generalised extreme value (GEV) parameters are location $\mu$, scale $\sigma$ and tail index $\xi$, and $n$ is the number of observations from which each maximum is drawn.

options.text: Desk 1: Gumbel; Desk 2: Gumbel; Desk 3: Fréchet
Desk 1: Fréchet; Desk 2: Fréchet; Desk 3: Fréchet
Desk 1: Fréchet; Desk 2: Gumbel; Desk 3: Fréchet
Desk 1: Fréchet; Desk 2: Weibull; Desk 3: Fréchet

questions.solution:
**Domains of attraction**

Stem in one line: Student’s $t$, lognormal and Pareto parents; into which GEV case do their maxima fall?

**Concept and theory**

The sign of $\xi$ splits the GEV into three cases, and each parent distribution’s extremes are “attracted” to exactly one (GARP footnote 4: “Extremes drawn from Levy or $t$-distributions fall in the domain of attraction of the Fréchet . . . ; extremes drawn from normal and lognormal distributions fall in the domain of attraction of the Gumbel”).

| Tail index | GEV case | Parent tail | Example parents |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\xi>$ 0 | Fréchet | Power function, heavy | Lévy, Student’s $t$, Pareto |
| $\xi$ = 0 | Gumbel | Exponential, relatively light | Normal, lognormal |
| $\xi<$ 0 | Weibull | Lighter than normal | Rare in finance |

The key intuition is tail decay: a power-law tail ($x^{-1/\xi}$) dies slowly, an exponential tail dies fast. Skewness of the parent (lognormal) is not the same thing as a power-law tail.

**Applying it to this question**

Desk 1, Student’s $t$: power-law tail, Fréchet. Desk 2, lognormal: exponential-type tail, Gumbel. Desk 3, Pareto: power law, Fréchet. Hence Fréchet; Gumbel; Fréchet. The degrees of freedom and the business lines do not change the case.

**Fragile fact.** Lognormal → Gumbel (not Fréchet). Student’s $t \to$ Fréchet (not Gumbel).

**Reference**

LO 3.b (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 3, §3.1 “Theory” and footnote 4. Schweser Reading 3, “Extreme Value Theory” (three cases). No conflict (domain-of-attraction wording is GARP-only).

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 b, where it is Q4 of 16.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap ($t$ treated like the normal). A symmetric, bell-shaped $t$ looks normal near the centre, but its tail is a power law. Correct only if Desk 1 had fitted a normal.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (skewness mistaken for heavy tail). The lognormal is right-skewed but its tail is in the Gumbel domain. Correct if Desk 2 had fitted, say, a Lévy distribution.

c.reason: GARP §3.1: Fréchet “applies where the tail of $F$ ($x$) obeys a power function and is therefore heavy (e.g., . . . a Levy distribution, a $t$-distribution, a Pareto distribution)”; Gumbel corresponds to “relatively light tails such as those we would get with normal or lognormal distributions”.

d.reason: Error type: polarity flip on tail weight. Weibull is for tails lighter than normal; the lognormal is not lighter than normal. Correct only if Desk 2’s distribution had a bounded or lighter-than-normal tail.

questions.question:
A risk analyst at a Chinese bank fits a GEV distribution to the maxima of daily losses on a CNY bond portfolio. Each maximum is the largest loss in a block of 50 trading days.

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Trading days per block, $n$ | 50 |
| Number of blocks in the sample | 36 |
| Fitted location $\mu$ / scale $\sigma$ / tail index $\xi$ | 1.80% / 0.55% / 0.22 |
| Required VaR confidence level for daily losses, $\alpha$ | 99.5% |

To obtain the daily 99.5% VaR from the GEV quantile formula, which cumulative probability $p$ of the distribution of block maxima should she use?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, $X$ denotes a loss (losses are positive), the generalised extreme value (GEV) parameters are location $\mu$, scale $\sigma$ and tail index $\xi$, and $n$ is the number of observations from which each maximum is drawn.
questions.solution:
**From the parent confidence level to the extremes probability**

Stem in one line: blocks of 50 days; which cumulative probability of the block-maximum distribution gives the 99.5% daily VaR?

**Concept and theory**

GARP warns that the probabilities in the GEV quantile formulas “refer to the probabilities associated with the extreme loss distribution, not to those associated with the distribution of the ‘parent’ loss distribution”. A 5th percentile of the extremes distribution is a small extreme loss (left side of the extremes distribution) yet lies in the right tail of the parent.

The bridge is independence. Let $M^{*}_{n}$ be a threshold. The maximum of $n$ iid losses lies below $M^{*}_{n}$ only if every one of the $n$ losses does:

Pr \[$M_{n} < M^{*}_{n}$\] = $p$ = {Pr \[$X < M^{*}_{n}$\]$\}^{n}$ = $\alpha^{n}$ (GARP eq. 3.4)

where $\alpha$ is the VaR confidence level for the parent loss and $p$ the cumulative probability for the extremes distribution. To get the $\alpha$ VaR we put $p$ = $\alpha^{n}$ into the GEV quantile formula; this is how $-n$ ln $\alpha$ enters the VaR formulas, because $- \text{ln} p$ = $-n$ ln $\alpha$.

**Applying it to this question**

$n$ = 50 (trading days per block)$, \alpha$ = 0.995

$p$ = $\alpha^{n}$ = $\text{0.995}^{50}$

ln $p$ = 50 × ln(0.995) = 50 × (−0.0050125) = −0.250627

$p$ = $e^{-0.250627}$ = 0.7783

Meaning: the daily 99.5% VaR is the 77.8th percentile of the distribution of 50-day maxima. Many 50-day blocks contain a loss bigger than the daily 99.5% VaR (about 22% of them), which is exactly what one would expect: 50 draws give the 0.5% tail 50 chances. The number of blocks (36) and the GEV parameters are irrelevant to $p$.

**Fragile fact.** Parent $\alpha\to$ extremes $p$ = $\alpha^{n}$, which is lower than $\alpha$. Hence $- \text{ln} p$ = $-n$ ln $\alpha$ in every GEV VaR formula.

**Reference**

LO 3.b (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 3, §3.1 “Theory”, eqs (3.3) to (3.5) and the discussion of extreme versus parent percentiles. GARP-only (Schweser omits the VaR derivation).

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 b, where it is Q5 of 16.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (parent probability used for the extremes distribution). This is the precise mistake GARP warns against. Correct if the block size were $n$ = 1, so that each “maximum” is a single daily loss.

c.reason: Error type: polarity flip (complement taken). 1 − 0.7783 = 0.2217 is the probability that a block maximum exceeds the VaR. Correct if the question asked for the exceedance probability of a 50-day block.

d.reason: Error type: inverted exponent (unit or scaling slip). $\text{0.995}^{1/50}$ = 0.99990 treats the block as a fraction of a day. Correct only if $\alpha$ were the block-level probability and the question asked for the implied daily level.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Brazilian asset manager estimates an extreme-value VaR for a BRL equity fund. A Fréchet GEV has been fitted to block maxima of daily losses (in %), and the VaR at confidence level $\alpha$ is

VaR = $\mu_{n} - \frac{\sigma_{n}}{\xi_{n}} [$1 − ($-n$ ln $\alpha$)$^{-\xi}n ] .$

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Location $\mu_{n}$ | 3.10% |
| Scale $\sigma_{n}$ | 0.90% |
| Tail index $\xi_{n}$ | 0.25 |
| Block size $n$ (trading days per block) | 60 |
| Standard deviation of all daily returns in the sample | 1.35% |
| Confidence level $\alpha$ | 99.8% |

Which of the following is closest to the 99.8% VaR?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, $X$ denotes a loss (losses are positive), the generalised extreme value (GEV) parameters are location $\mu$, scale $\sigma$ and tail index $\xi$, and $n$ is the number of observations from which each maximum is drawn.
questions.solution:
**Fréchet VaR**

Stem in one line: $\mu_{n}$ = 3.10%, $\sigma_{n}$ = 0.90%, $\xi_{n}$ = 0.25, $n$ = 60, $\alpha$ = 99.8%; find the VaR.

**Concept and theory**

Setting the GEV CDF equal to $p$ and solving for $x$ gives the quantiles (GARP eqs 3.3a, 3.3b):

$x_{p}$ = $\mu- \frac{\sigma}{\xi} [$1 − ($- \text{ln} p$)$^{-\xi}]$ (Fréchet)$, x_{p}$ = $\mu- \sigma$ ln\[$- \text{ln} p$\] (Gumbel).

Substituting $p$ = $\alpha^{n}$ (Q5) gives the VaR (eqs 3.5a, 3.5b):

VaR = $\mu_{n} - \frac{\sigma_{n}}{\xi_{n}} [$1 − ($-n$ ln $\alpha$)$^{-\xi}n ]$ (Fréchet), VaR = $\mu_{n} - \sigma_{n}$ ln\[$-n$ ln $\alpha$\] (Gumbel),

where $\mu_{n}$, $\sigma_{n}$, $\xi_{n}$ are the GEV parameters for maxima of blocks of $n$ observations and $\alpha$ is the VaR confidence level. At high confidence $-n$ ln $\alpha$ is small, so ($-n$ ln $\alpha$)$^{-\xi}$ exceeds 1, the bracket is negative and VaR lies above $\mu_{n}$.

**Applying it to this question**

1 − 1.69862 = −0.69862

Meaning: on a given day the fund can be 99.8% confident of not losing more than about 5.62% of its value. The 1.35% standard deviation of all daily returns is irrelevant: EVT uses the parameters of the extremes, not the parent’s moments.

questions.question:
The CRO of a Singapore private bank is reviewing a draft board paper on the shape of the tail in its SGD trading book’s GEV model. The paper contains four statements:

I. If $\xi<$ 0, the GEV becomes the Weibull, which corresponds to lighter than normal tails and is not particularly useful for modelling financial returns.

II. The standardised Fréchet is more skewed to the right than the standardised Gumbel and has a noticeably longer right-hand tail.

III. Estimates of $\xi$ for financial return data are often found to be positive but less than 0.35.

IV. If $\xi$ = 0, the GEV becomes the Gumbel, which corresponds to a parent whose tail obeys a power function.

Which of the statements are correct?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, $X$ denotes a loss (losses are positive), the generalised extreme value (GEV) parameters are location $\mu$, scale $\sigma$ and tail index $\xi$, and $n$ is the number of observations from which each maximum is drawn.

options.text: I and II only
II, III and IV only
I, III and IV only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
**Tail shape: Weibull, Fréchet and Gumbel**

Stem in one line: which of four board-paper statements on GEV tail shape are correct?

**Concept and theory**

The tail index decides how fast the tail of the parent dies away and therefore which GEV case applies (Q4). Three facts from GARP §3.1 are frequently tested:

- Weibull ($\xi<$ 0): “lighter than normal tails”; “not particularly useful for modelling financial returns, because few empirical financial returns series are so light-tailed”.
- Fréchet versus Gumbel (Fig. 3.1): “Both are skewed to the right, but the Fréchet is more skewed than the Gumbel and has a noticeably longer right-hand tail”, so it has “considerably higher probabilities of producing very large X-values”.
- Size of $\xi$ in practice: “estimates of $\xi$ for financial return data are positive but less than 0.35”.

The Gumbel ($\xi$ = 0) corresponds to exponential tails; it is the Fréchet that corresponds to a power function.

**Applying it to this question**

I: true (Weibull, lighter than normal, not useful). II: true (Fig. 3.1 commentary). III: true. IV: false; “power function” belongs to the Fréchet. Correct set: I, II and III.

**Fragile fact.** Power function ⇒ Fréchet ($\xi>$ 0); exponential ⇒ Gumbel ($\xi$ = 0); lighter than normal ⇒ Weibull ($\xi<$ 0).

**Reference**

LO 3.b (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 3, §3.1 “Theory” and Figure 3.1. Schweser Reading 3, “Extreme Value Theory”. Difference: Schweser describes the Gumbel tails as “light” and the Weibull as “lighter than a normal”; GARP says “exponential tails” and gives the 0.35 and skewness facts (GARP-only).

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 b, where it is Q7 of 16.

a.reason: **I and II only.** Error type: scope error (a true statement rejected). It rejects III, perhaps because “less than 0.35” looks too precise. Correct only if III claimed $\xi$ exceeded 0.35 or were negative.

b.reason: **II, III and IV only.** Error type: polarity flip on I and acceptance of the sibling swap in IV. Correct only if Weibull were heavy-tailed and the Gumbel had a power-law tail.

c.reason: **I, III and IV only.** Error type: sibling swap. It accepts IV (Fréchet’s power function attributed to the Gumbel) and rejects II. Correct if IV said “exponential tails” and II reversed the skew comparison.

d.reason: Statements I to III restate GARP §3.1; IV swaps the tail description of the Fréchet into the Gumbel.

questions.question:
The head of market risk at a Japanese bank reviews how three analysts chose between the Gumbel and the Fréchet for their JPY desks:

- Analyst X is confident that daily losses follow a Student’s $t$ and chooses the Fréchet.
- Analyst Y tests the tail index, cannot reject $\xi$ = 0 at the 5% level, and chooses the Gumbel.
- Analyst Z chooses the Fréchet regardless of the data, citing model risk.

Which of the following assessments is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, $X$ denotes a loss (losses are positive), the generalised extreme value (GEV) parameters are location $\mu$, scale $\sigma$ and tail index $\xi$, and $n$ is the number of observations from which each maximum is drawn.

options.text: All three follow approaches described in the reading, but Y’s choice leaves the desk open to underestimating extreme risk if $\xi$ has been wrongly concluded to be zero.
X should have chosen the Gumbel, because extremes drawn from a Student’s $t$ fall in the domain of attraction of the Gumbel.
Y’s choice is fully reliable, because failing to reject the hypothesis establishes that the tail index is exactly zero.
Z’s choice is the least conservative of the three, because estimated extreme risk measures fall as the tail index rises.

questions.solution:
**Choosing between the Gumbel and the Fréchet**

Stem in one line: three analysts choose Fréchet (parent is $t$), Gumbel (cannot reject $\xi$ = 0), Fréchet (model risk); assess.

**Concept and theory**

Because financial returns are rarely Weibull, the practical choice is between $\xi$ = 0 (Gumbel) and $\xi>$ 0 (Fréchet). GARP §3.1 gives three ways to choose:

1. Identify the parent. If confident of the parent, choose the EV distribution in whose domain of attraction it resides; a $t$ parent implies the Fréchet.
2. Test the tail index. Choose the Gumbel if $\xi$ is insignificant and the Fréchet otherwise. “However, this leaves us open to the danger that we might incorrectly conclude that $\xi$ is 0, and this could lead us to underestimate our extreme risk measures.”
3. Always choose the Fréchet. “Given the dangers of model risk and bearing in mind that the estimated risk measure increases with the tail index, a safer option is always to choose the Fréchet.”

The logic: risk measures rise with $\xi$ (Examples 3.2, 3.4 and 3.5), so a mistaken $\xi$ = 0 errs on the side of too little capital.

**Applying it to this question**

X uses method 1 correctly ($t \to$ Fréchet). Y uses method 2, legitimate but exposed to a type II error: failing to reject $\xi$ = 0 does not prove $\xi$ = 0. Z uses method 3, the conservative choice. A captures all of this.

**Fragile fact.** Risk measures rise with $\xi$. Wrongly assuming $\xi$ = 0 understates risk; always choosing the Fréchet is the conservative choice.

**Reference**

LO 3.b (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 3, §3.1, “How do we choose between the Gumbel and the Fréchet?”. Schweser Reading 3, “Extreme Value Theory” (three ways). Difference: Schweser presents the test route neutrally (“cannot reject the hypothesis $\xi$ = 0 . . . uses the assumption $\xi$ = 0”); GARP adds the underestimation danger. GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 b, where it is Q8 of 16.

a.reason: All three are methods listed by GARP and Schweser; GARP explicitly attaches the underestimation danger to the testing route.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap. Student’s $t$ extremes lie in the Fréchet domain; the Gumbel domain holds the normal and lognormal. Correct if X’s parent were normal.

c.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. A non-rejection is not proof that $\xi$ is exactly zero; that is precisely GARP’s warning. Correct only as “Y’s choice is one of the accepted methods”.

d.reason: Error type: polarity flip. Estimated risk measures increase with the tail index, which is why always choosing the Fréchet is the safer, more conservative option. Correct if “least” read “most” and “fall” read “rise”.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is reviewing a UK bank’s GBP trading book model. A GEV has been fitted to block maxima of daily losses (in %). The estimated tail index is not significantly different from zero, and the consultant wants to show the bank how much the choice of distribution matters. The VaR formulas are

$\text{VaR}_{\text{Fréchet}}$ = $\mu_{n} - \frac{\sigma_{n}}{\xi_{n}} [$1 − ($-n$ ln $\alpha$)$^{-\xi}n ] , \text{VaR}_{\text{Gumbel}}$ = $\mu_{n} - \sigma_{n}$ ln \[$-n$ ln $\alpha$\] .

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Trading days per block, $n$ | 40 |
| Number of blocks in the sample, $m$ | 25 |
| Location $\mu_{n}$ / scale $\sigma_{n}$ | 2.40% / 0.65% |
| Tail index $\xi_{n}$ (Fréchet only) | 0.20 |
| Confidence level $\alpha$ | 99.9% |

Which pair gives the 99.9% Gumbel VaR and the 99.9% Fréchet VaR, respectively?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, $X$ denotes a loss (losses are positive), the generalised extreme value (GEV) parameters are location $\mu$, scale $\sigma$ and tail index $\xi$, and $n$ is the number of observations from which each maximum is drawn.
questions.solution:
**Gumbel versus Fréchet VaR, and $n$ versus $m$**

Stem in one line: $n$ = 40, $m$ = 25, $\mu_{n}$ = 2.40%, $\sigma_{n}$ = 0.65%, $\xi_{n}$ = 0.20; 99.9% Gumbel and Fréchet VaR.

**Concept and theory**

The VaR formulas are those of Q6. Two interpretive points matter here. First, $n$ is the number of observations from which each maximum is drawn (the block size); GARP subscripts the parameters with $n$ “to make explicit that in practice these would refer to the parameters associated with maxima drawn from samples of size $n$”. The number of maxima $m$ (blocks) is the sample used for estimation (GARP’s regression and ML sections) and does not enter the VaR. Second, EV VaRs “are sensitive to the value of the tail index” (GARP Examples 3.4 and 3.5): with the same $\mu$ and $\sigma$, the Gumbel VaR is lower than the Fréchet VaR. This is why “we should use the Gumbel only if we think $\xi$ is insignificantly different from zero”.

**Applying it to this question**

$-n$ ln $\alpha$ = 40 × (− ln 0.999) = 40 × 0.0010005 = 0.040020

ln(0.040020) = −3.21838

$\text{VaR}_{\text{Gumbel}}$ = 2.40 − 0.65 × (−3.21838) = 2.40 + 2.09194 = 4.492%

$\text{(0.040020)}^{-0.20}$ = $e^{0.20\times3.21838}$ = 1.90352

$\sigma_{n}/\xi_{n}$ = 0.65/0.20 = 3.25

$\text{VaR}_{\text{Fréchet}}$ = 2.40 − 3.25 × (1 − 1.90352) = 2.40 + 2.93644 = 5.336%

Meaning: the Gumbel VaR (4.49%) is about 0.84 percentage points, or 16%, below the Fréchet VaR (5.34%). If $\xi$ is truly 0.20, choosing the Gumbel on the strength of an insignificant test understates the 99.9% risk.

**Fragile fact.** $n$ = observations per block, not number of blocks. With the same $\mu$, $\sigma$, the Gumbel VaR is below the Fréchet VaR.

**Reference**

LO 3.b (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 3, §3.1 “Theory”, eqs (3.5a), (3.5b), Examples 3.3 to 3.5 (Gumbel Example 3.3 recomputed: − ln\[−100 ln 0.995\] = 0.6906). GARP-only (formulas dropped in Schweser).

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 b, where it is Q9 of 16.

a.reason: Error type: unit or scaling slip ($n$ omitted). Using $- \text{ln} \alpha$ = 0.0010005: Gumbel 2.40 − 0.65 ln(0.0010005) = 6.890; Fréchet 2.40 + 3.25 × $\text{(0.0010005}^{-0.2} -$ 1) = 12.087. Correct only if each block were one day.

b.reason: Error type: wrong input twin (number of blocks $m$ = 25 used for $n$). −25 ln 0.999 = 0.025013; Gumbel 2.40+0.65×3.68836 = 4.797; Fréchet 2.40+3.25×(2.09107−1) = 5.946. Correct if the blocks were 25 days long.

c.reason: Error type: dropped term (Fréchet $\sigma_{n}$ not divided by $\xi_{n}$). 2.40 + 0.65 × 0.90352 = 2.987. The Gumbel is right. A Fréchet VaR below the Gumbel VaR contradicts the fact that risk measures rise with $\xi$. Correct only if $\xi_{n}$ were 1.

d.reason: Both formulas evaluated with block size $n$ = 40 (GARP eqs 3.5a, 3.5b).

A treasury analyst at a Swiss bank has estimated a one-day 99% extreme-value VaR of CHF 4.2 million for a CHF bond book, from a Fréchet GEV with tail index $\xi$ = 0.28. She needs a 10-day figure and assumes that the EV VaR scales with the holding period $h$ as VaR($h$) = VaR(1) $h^{\kappa}$, with $\kappa$ = 0.45. Which of the following is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, $X$ denotes a loss (losses are positive), the generalised extreme value (GEV) parameters are location $\mu$, scale $\sigma$ and tail index $\xi$, and $n$ is the number of observations from which each maximum is drawn.

options.text: The 10-day VaR is CHF 8.00 million; the tail index $\xi$ is the appropriate scaling exponent for EV distributions.
The 10-day VaR is CHF 11.84 million; square-root-of-time scaling would overstate it.
The 10-day VaR is CHF 11.84 million; square-root-of-time scaling would understate it.
The 10-day VaR is CHF 13.28 million; square-root-of-time scaling is appropriate for EV distributions.

questions.solution:
**Scaling EV VaR to a longer holding period**

Stem in one line: one-day EV VaR CHF 4.2m, $\kappa$ = 0.45, $\xi$ = 0.28; 10-day VaR and comparison with $\sqrt{h}$.

**Concept and theory**

GARP footnote 5: “We can obtain estimates of EV VaR over longer time periods by using appropriately scaled parameters, bearing in mind that the mean scales proportionately with the holding period $h$, the standard deviation scales with the square root of $h$, and (subject to certain conditions) the tail index does not scale at all. In general, we find that the VaR scales with a parameter $\kappa$ (i.e., so VaR($h$) = VaR(1)($h$)$^{\kappa}$ . . . ), and empirical evidence reported by Hauksson et al. (2001, p. 93) suggests an average value for $\kappa$ of about 0.45. The square-root scaling rule (i.e., $\kappa$ = 0.5) is therefore usually inappropriate for EV distributions.”

VaR($h$) = VaR(1) $h^{\kappa},$

where $h$ is the holding period in days and $\kappa$ the scaling exponent. Because $\kappa<$ 0.5 and $h >$ 1, $h^{\kappa} < \sqrt{h}$: square-root scaling overstates the long-horizon EV VaR.

**Applying it to this question**

$h^{\kappa}$ = $\text{10}^{0.45}$ = 2.81838

VaR(10) = 4.2 × 2.81838 = 11.837 ≈ CHF 11.84 million

$\sqrt{10}$ = 3.16228 ⇒ 4.2 × 3.16228 = 13.282 (overstates by CHF 1.44 million)

The tail index (0.28) is an irrelevant input: it does not set the scaling exponent and itself does not scale.

**Fragile fact.** EV VaR scales with $h^{\kappa}$, $\kappa\approx$ 0.45, so $\sqrt{h}$ overstates; the tail index does not scale.

**Reference**

LO 3.b (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 3, §3.1 “Theory”, footnote 5. GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 b, where it is Q10 of 16.

a.reason: Error type: wrong input twin ($\xi$ used as the exponent): 4.2 × $\text{10}^{0.28}$ = 8.003. Correct only if the stem had said VaR scales with $h^{\xi}$, which GARP does not.

b.reason: $\kappa$ = 0.45 gives CHF 11.84 million, below the square-root figure of CHF 13.28 million, so square-root scaling would overstate the 10-day EV VaR (GARP footnote 5).

c.reason: Error type: polarity flip. The number is right but $\text{10}^{0.45} <$ $\text{10}^{0.5}$, so square-root scaling gives a larger figure. Correct if $\kappa$ were above 0.5.

d.reason: Error type: time-conversion slip (square-root-of-time applied): 4.2 $\times\sqrt{10}$ = 13.28. Correct for a normal (iid) VaR, not for EV distributions per GARP.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a US hedge fund uses the short-cut EV method. If $\xi>$ 0 the loss tail follows a power law, and the out-of-sample quantile is

$x_{\text{out-of-sample}}$ = $x_{\text{in-sample}} \left( \frac{n p_{\text{out-of-sample}}}{t} \right)^{-\xi} ,$

where $n$ is the sample size and $t$ the number of observations higher than $x_{\text{in-sample}}$.

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Daily losses in the sample, $n$ | 2,500 |
| Chosen in-sample quantile, $x_{\text{in-sample}}$ | 2.60% |
| Daily losses larger than 2.60% | 50 |
| Hill estimate of the tail index, $\xi$ | 0.30 |
| Average daily loss | 0.02% |

Which of the following is closest to the 99.9% daily VaR?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, $X$ denotes a loss (losses are positive), the generalised extreme value (GEV) parameters are location $\mu$, scale $\sigma$ and tail index $\xi$, and $n$ is the number of observations from which each maximum is drawn.
questions.solution:
**The short-cut EV method**

Stem in one line: $n$ = 2,500, 50 losses above 2.60%, $\xi$ = 0.30; short-cut 99.9% VaR.

**Concept and theory**

If $\xi>$ 0, the tail of the loss distribution follows a power law times a slowly varying function: Pr($X > x$) = $k$($x$)$x^{-1/\xi}$ (GARP eq. 3.6). Treating $k$ as constant, Pr($X > x$) = $kx^{-1/\xi}$ (eq. 3.7). Write this at two points: an in-sample quantile $x_{\text{in}}$ with tail probability $p_{\text{in}}$, and an out-of-sample quantile $x_{\text{out}}$ with smaller tail probability $p_{\text{out}}$. Dividing removes $k$:

$$\frac{p_{\text{in}}}{p_{\text{out}}} = \left(\frac{x_{\text{in}}}{x_{\text{out}}}\right)^{-1/\xi} \Rightarrow x_{\text{out}} = x_{\text{in}} \left(\frac{p_{\text{in}}}{p_{\text{out}}}\right)^{\xi}.$$

Proxy $p_{\text{in}}$ by its empirical value $t/n$, where $t$ is the number of observations above $x_{\text{in}}$ (eq. 3.10):

$x_{\text{out}}$ = $x_{\text{in}} \left( \frac{n p_{\text{out}}}{t} \right)^{-\xi} .$

All inputs are readily available: the VaR confidence level gives $p_{\text{out}}$ = 1 $- \alpha$, and $\xi$ comes from a tail index estimator such as the Hill. The method lets us extrapolate beyond the data.

**Applying it to this question**

$p_{\text{out}}$ = 1 − 0.999 = 0.001

$n p_{\text{out}}/t$ = 2,500 × 0.001/50 = 2.5/50 = 0.05

$\text{(0.05)}^{-0.30}$ = $e^{0.30\times2.99573}$ = 2.45646

$x_{\text{out}}$ = 2.60 × 2.45646 = 6.387% ≈ 6.39%

Meaning: the 99.9% daily VaR is about 2.5 times the in-sample 98th percentile (2.60%, exceeded by 50/2,500 = 2% of days). The average daily loss is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Both probabilities are tail probabilities ($t/n$ and 1 $- \alpha$); exponent $-\xi$ on $np_{\text{out}}/t$ (equivalently +$\xi$ on $p_{\text{in}}/p_{\text{out}}$).

**Reference**

LO 3.b (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 3, §3.1 “A Short-Cut EV Method”, eqs (3.6) to (3.10). GARP-only. Power-law form consistent with question bank Q139 and Q149 (LO 3.b).

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 b, where it is Q11 of 16.

a.reason: Error type: wrong percentile (99% used): $np_{\text{out}}/t$ = 25/50 = 0.5; $\text{0.5}^{-0.3}$ = 1.23114; 2.60 × 1.23114 = 3.201. Correct for a 99% VaR.

b.reason: Error type: sign error in the exponent (+$\xi$): $\text{0.05}^{0.3}$ = 0.40709; 2.60 × 0.40709 = 1.058. A 99.9% VaR below the 98% in-sample quantile is impossible. Never correct.

c.reason: Direct application of GARP eq. (3.10) with $p_{\text{out}}$ = 0.001 and $t/n$ = 0.02.

d.reason: Error type: wrong input twin (cumulative probability 1 $- t/n$ = 0.98 used instead of the tail probability $t/n$ = 0.02): $\text{(0.98/0.001)}^{0.3}$ = $\text{980}^{0.3}$ = 7.8953; 2.60 × 7.8953 = 20.53. Correct only if the power law were written in cumulative rather than tail probabilities, which it is not.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a French bank is reviewing the methodology note for estimating the GEV parameters of its EUR credit trading book. The note makes four statements:

I. Maximum likelihood (ML) estimators are consistent and asymptotically normal provided $\xi>$ −1/2, and hypotheses about the parameters can be tested with likelihood ratio statistics.

II. ML has closed-form solutions for the GEV parameters, so no numerical solution method is needed.

III. The regression method orders the $m$ sample maxima from lowest to highest, uses $i/$(1 + $m$) as the cumulative probability of the $i$th, and fits the parameters by least squares; it is easier to apply than ML.

IV. The Hill estimator of the tail index is applied to the ordered block maxima rather than to the parent loss observations.

Which of the statements are correct?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, $X$ denotes a loss (losses are positive), the generalised extreme value (GEV) parameters are location $\mu$, scale $\sigma$ and tail index $\xi$, and $n$ is the number of observations from which each maximum is drawn.

options.text: I, III and IV only
I, II and III only
III and IV only
I and III only

questions.solution:
**Estimation methods: ML, regression and Hill**

Stem in one line: which of four methodology-note statements on GEV parameter estimation are correct?

**Concept and theory**

To compute EV risk measures we must estimate $\mu$, $\sigma$ and (for the Fréchet) $\xi$. GARP and Schweser list three families.

| Method | How it works | Strengths and weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| Maximum | Maximise the (log-)likelihood of | Statistically well grounded; |
| likelihood | the $m$ observed maxima, subject | consistent and asymptotically |
|  | to 1 + $\xi$($M^{i}_{n} - \mu$)$/\sigma>$ 0 | normal if $\xi> -$1/2; likelihood ratio tests. No closed form, needs numerical methods and software; may not be robust; small-sample problems because the theory is asymptotic |
| Regression | Order the maxima lowest to | Easier to apply than ML |
| (Gumbel 1958) | highest, $M^{1}_{n} \le\cdot\cdot\cdot\le M^{m}_{n}$; set $E$\[$H$($M^{i}_{n}$)\] = $i/$(1 + $m$); regress log\[− log($i/$(1 + $m$))\] on the GEV transform and get least squares estimates |  |
| Semi- | Applied directly to the ordered | Consistent, asymptotically |
| parametric | parent losses; estimates $\xi$ | normal; finite-sample properties |
| (Hill) |  | poorly understood; sensitive to $k$ |

Here $m$ is the number of observed maxima and $H$ the GEV CDF. For the Gumbel, the regression form is log\[− log($i/$(1 + $m$))\] = −($M^{i}_{n} - \mu_{n}$)$/\sigma_{n}$ (GARP eq. 3.16).

**Applying it to this question**

I: GARP’s list of ML properties. True. II: GARP says ML “lacks closed-form solutions for the parameters, so the ML approach requires the use of an appropriate numerical solution method”. False. III: GARP eq. (3.13) and Schweser (“easier to apply than ML and consists of ordering extreme values from lowest to highest”). True. IV: GARP, the Hill estimator “is directly applied to the ordered parent loss observations”. False. Correct set: I and III.

**Fragile fact.** ML: good asymptotics ($\xi> -$1/2) but no closed form. Regression: orders maxima lowest to highest, easier. Hill: parent losses ordered highest to lowest.

**Reference**

LO 3.b (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 3, §3.1 “Estimation of EV Parameters”: ML Estimation Methods, Regression Methods (eqs 3.13 to 3.16), Semi-Parametric Estimation Methods. Schweser Reading 3, “Extreme Value Theory”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 b, where it is Q12 of 16.

questions.question:
A risk analyst at a Canadian bank estimates the tail index of daily losses on a CAD equity book with the Hill estimator

$\hat{\xi}^{\text{Hill}}_{n,k}$ = $\frac{1}{k} \sum_{i\text{=1}}^{k}$ ln $X_{i} - \text{ln} X_{k\text{+1}},$

where $X_{1} \ge X_{2} \ge. . .$ are the parent losses ordered from highest to lowest. The seven largest daily losses (in %) are:

| Rank $i$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Loss $X_{i}$ (%) | 8.4 | 6.3 | 5.5 | 4.8 | 4.4 | 4.0 | 3.6 |

Using $k$ = 5, which of the following is closest to the Hill estimate of $\xi$?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, $X$ denotes a loss (losses are positive), the generalised extreme value (GEV) parameters are location $\mu$, scale $\sigma$ and tail index $\xi$, and $n$ is the number of observations from which each maximum is drawn.
questions.solution:
**Computing the Hill estimator**

Stem in one line: losses 8.4, 6.3, 5.5, 4.8, 4.4, 4.0, 3.6 (%); Hill estimate of $\xi$ with $k$ = 5.

**Concept and theory**

The Hill estimator is the most popular semi-parametric estimator of the tail index. Order the parent losses from highest to lowest, $X_{1} \ge X_{2} \ge\cdot\cdot\cdot\ge X_{n}$, and choose the tail threshold $k$ (the number of tail observations used):

$\hat{\xi}^{\text{Hill}}_{n,k}$ = $\frac{1}{k} \sum_{i\text{=1}}^{k}$ ln $X_{i} - \text{ln} X_{k\text{+1}},$

where $X_{k\text{+1}}$ is the first observation outside the tail. GARP’s verbal summary: “the average of the $k$ most extreme (i.e., tail) observations, minus the $k$ + 1th observation, or the one next to the tail”, where both are taken in logs. The estimate is of $\xi$, not of the power-law exponent 1$/\xi$.

**Applying it to this question**

ln 8.4 = 2.12823, ln 6.3 = 1.84055, ln 5.5 = 1.70475

ln 4.8 = 1.56862, ln 4.4 = 1.48160

$\sum^{5}_{i\text{=1}}$ ln $X_{i}$ = 8.72375

$\frac{1}{5} \sum^{5}_{i\text{=1}}$ ln $X_{i}$ = 1.74475

ln $X_{6}$ = ln 4.0 = 1.38629

$\hat{\xi}^{\text{Hill}}$ = 1.74475 − 1.38629 = 0.35846 ≈ 0.358

Meaning: a positive tail index of about 0.36, a heavy (Fréchet-type) tail, slightly above the range GARP reports as typical for financial returns (positive but below 0.35), a reminder that a small $k$ gives a noisy estimate. $X_{7}$ = 3.6 is irrelevant with $k$ = 5.

**Fragile fact.** Logs, top $k$ averaged, minus the log of the ($k$ + 1)th; the result is $\xi$, not 1$/\xi$.

**Reference**

LO 3.b (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 3, §3.1 “Semi-Parametric Estimation Methods”, eq. (3.17). Schweser Reading 3, “Extreme Value Theory” (Hill estimator named, no formula). Eq. (3.17) is garbled in the GARP OCR; the log form is confirmed by question bank Q153 (LO 3.b: “averages log-exceedances of the top $k$ observations”). Difference: GARP’s verbal gloss omits the logs; the formula is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 b, where it is Q13 of 16.

a.reason: Error type: wrong input twin ($X_{k}$ used instead of $X_{k\text{+1}}$): 1.74475 − ln 4.4 = 1.74475 − 1.48160 = 0.263. Correct if the formula subtracted the smallest tail observation.

b.reason: GARP eq. (3.17) evaluated with $k$ = 5 and $X_{k\text{+1}}$ = $X_{6}$ = 4.0.

c.reason: Error type: dropped term (logs omitted, a literal reading of GARP’s verbal summary): (8.4 + 6.3 + 5.5 + 4.8 + 4.4)/5 − 4.0 = 5.88 − 4.0 = 1.880. Correct only for the mean excess in % over $X_{6}$, which is not the tail index.

d.reason: Error type: wrong output twin (power-law exponent 1$/\xi$ reported): 1/0.35846 = 2.790. Correct if the question asked for the tail exponent $\alpha$ = 1$/\xi$ in Pr($X > x$) $\approx kx^{-\alpha}$.

questions.question:
A model validator at a Singapore bank reviews the Hill tail index estimate for an SGD rates book based on 900 daily losses. The modeller proposes (i) raising the tail threshold $k$ from 30 to 90 to make the estimate more precise, and (ii) choosing $k$ by the Danielsson and de Vries subsample bootstrap. Which assessment is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, $X$ denotes a loss (losses are positive), the generalised extreme value (GEV) parameters are location $\mu$, scale $\sigma$ and tail index $\xi$, and $n$ is the number of observations from which each maximum is drawn.

options.text: Raising $k$ lowers variance but raises bias, because more weight falls on observations nearer the centre; the bootstrap is impractical because it needs at least 1,500 observations.
Raising $k$ lowers bias but raises variance, because the estimate moves further out into the tail; the bootstrap is impractical because it needs at least 1,500 observations.
Raising $k$ lowers variance but raises bias, because more weight falls on observations nearer the centre; the bootstrap is appropriate because it works at any sample size.
Raising $k$ lowers both variance and bias, because more data always improve the estimate; the bootstrap is impractical because it needs at least 1,500 observations.

questions.solution:
**Choosing $k$: bias versus variance**

Stem in one line: 900 losses; raise $k$ from 30 to 90 and use the Danielsson-de Vries bootstrap?

**Concept and theory**

Schweser: for the Hill estimator, “The most challenging aspect of this method is selecting how many observations to include in the tail.” GARP explains the trade-off behind the Danielsson and de Vries procedure: “If we increase $k$, we get more data and so move to the centre of the distribution. This increases the precision of our estimator (and therefore reduces its variance), but also increases the bias of the tail estimator by placing relatively more weight on observations closer to the centre of our distribution. Alternatively, if we decrease $k$ and move further out along the tail, we decrease bias but have fewer data to work with and get a higher variance.”

| Change in $k$ | Data used | Variance | Bias |
|---|---|---|---|
| Increase $k$ | More, nearer the centre | Lower | Higher |
| Decrease $k$ | Fewer, further into the tail | Higher | Lower |

Danielsson and de Vries choose $k$ to minimise a mean-squared-error loss (bias and variance traded off optimally) via a subsample bootstrap. But “this approach requires a large sample size, at least 1500 observations, and is therefore impractical with small sample sizes”, and automatic procedures “tend to ignore other, softer, but nonetheless often very useful, information”.

**Applying it to this question**

Proposal (i): raising $k$ to 90 does make the estimate more precise (lower variance) but at the cost of more bias. Proposal (ii): with 900 observations the bootstrap is below the 1,500 minimum. A states both.

**Fragile fact.** Higher $k$: lower variance, higher bias. Danielsson-de Vries needs at least 1,500 observations.

**Reference**

LO 3.b (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 3, §3.1 “Semi-Parametric Estimation Methods”. Schweser Reading 3, “Extreme Value Theory” (only that choosing $k$ is the hardest part). GARP-only for the trade-off and the procedure. Note that the same high-versus-low trade-off reappears for the POT threshold (LO 3.e); here it is applied to $k$.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-3 b, where it is Q14 of 16.

a.reason: Direction of the trade-off and the 1,500-observation requirement are both as stated in GARP §3.1 “Semi-Parametric Estimation Methods”.

b.reason: Error type: polarity flip. Raising $k$ moves towards the centre, not further out, so bias rises and variance falls. Correct if the proposal were to lower $k$.

c.reason: Error type: scope or condition error (the large-sample condition dropped). The bias-variance part is right, but the bootstrap needs at least 1,500 observations. Correct if the sample had, say, 2,000 observations.

d.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. More data reduce variance but not bias here, because the extra data come from nearer the centre. Correct only if every added observation were genuinely from the tail.
