options.text: Extending the sample to $T$ = 1,000 observations with a cutoff of 14 exceptions gives a Type 1 error rate of 13.4% and a Type 2 error rate of about 0.03%.
The lack of power of the framework is due to the high 99% VaR confidence level, which generates too few exceptions for a reliable test.
Raising the VaR confidence level to 99.9% would increase the power of the test, because each exception would then be a more extreme and so more informative event.
A longer backtesting period may be less practical, because the nature of markets, portfolios and risk changes over time.

questions.solution:
**Remedy 2: more observations, and the limits of each remedy**

Stem in one line: least accurate statement on improving the Basel backtest’s ability to catch faulty models.

**Concept and theory**

Power is low because a 99% VaR over 250 days generates only about 2.5 exceptions, too few to distinguish a 1% from a 3% exception rate reliably. GARP offers two remedies (§4.4 Conclusions: “The current framework could be improved by choosing a lower VaR confidence level or by increasing the number of data observations”):

1. Lower the VaR confidence level (Q10).
2. Increase $T$ . “With $T$ = 1000, for instance, we would choose a cutoff of 14 exceptions, for a type 1 error rate of 13.4 percent and a type 2 error rate of 0.03 percent, which is now very small. Increasing the number of observations drastically improves the test.”

Python check: $P$ ($N \ge$ 14 $| p$ = 0.01$, T$ = 1000) = 13.4%; $P$ ($N <$ 14 $| p$ = 0.03$, T$ = 1000) = 0.035%. The practical limit on remedy 2 is structural change. GARP §4.4: “Trading portfolios do change over the horizon. Models do evolve over time . . . All this may cause further structural instability.” Schweser: a longer backtesting period “may not be as practical because the nature of markets, portfolios, and risk changes over time.” GARP also advises that “the confidence level should not be too high because this decreases the effectiveness, or power, of the statistical tests”.

**Applying it to this question**

A matches GARP’s $T$ = 1,000 numbers. B is GARP’s diagnosis of the lack of power. D is Schweser’s (and GARP’s §4.4) caveat on longer samples. C claims a higher confidence level raises power. A 99.9% VaR over 250 days gives only 0.001 × 250 = 0.25 expected exceptions, so the count carries even less information. C is the false statement.

**Fragile fact.** Power rises with a lower VaR confidence level or a larger $T$ ; a higher confidence level makes exceptions rarer and the test weaker.

**Reference**

LO 4.f (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 4, §4.2 “The Basel Rules” and §4.4 Conclusions. Schweser Reading 4, “Basel Committee Rules for Backtesting”. Note: $T$ = 1,000 figures GARP-only; the longer-window caveat is explicit in Schweser and general in GARP §4.4. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-4 f, where it is Q11 of 11.

a.reason: Accurate: GARP’s $T$ = 1,000 example, cutoff 14, Type 1 13.4%, Type 2 0.03%. It would be the inaccurate statement if it claimed that a longer sample cuts both error rates below the Basel levels; in fact Type 1 rises slightly (13.4% versus 10.8%) while Type 2 collapses.

b.reason: Accurate: GARP’s own diagnosis of why the framework lacks power. It would be inaccurate if it blamed the 250-day window alone, since GARP attributes the problem to the high VaR confidence level.

c.reason: GARP: the confidence level “should not be too high because this decreases the effectiveness, or power, of the statistical tests”. Raising it to 99.9% moves in the wrong direction.

d.reason: Accurate: the practical caveat on longer windows (Schweser LO 4.f; GARP §4.4 on structural instability). It would be inaccurate if it said a longer window has no practical drawback.

questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a German mortgage bank is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts on how the bank’s EUR covered-bond portfolio is mapped onto risk factors using principal, duration or cash-flow mapping. Which of the following statements best describes the requirement that the reading sets for mapping fixed-income positions onto risk factors?

options.text: Mapping should preserve the market value of the position and, ideally, it should also preserve its market risk.
Mapping should preserve the face value of the principal and, ideally, it should also preserve its market risk.
Mapping should preserve the market risk of the position and, ideally, it should also preserve its market value.
Mapping must preserve both the market value and the market risk exactly, whichever of the three methods is used.

questions.solution:
**What every fixed-income mapping must preserve**

Stem in one line: which statement best describes the reading’s requirement for mapping fixed-income positions onto risk factors?

**Concept and theory**

Mapping replaces each position by exposures on a small set of primitive risk factors; for bonds, these are zero-coupon bonds (or yields) at a set of standard maturities called vertices. Once the risk factors have been selected, GARP asks how to map the positions onto them and names three systems: principal, duration and cash flows. It then states the rule that applies to all three: “Mapping should preserve the market value of the position. Ideally, it also should preserve its market risk.”

Why the two halves have different strength: the market value is a hard constraint, because the VaR is a percentage risk applied to a value; if the mapped exposures do not add up to the current value, the VaR is scaled on the wrong base from the start. Preserving market risk is the aim, and the three methods meet it with increasing success:

|  | Principal | Duration | Cash flow |
|---|---|---|---|
| Value mapped | Full market value | Full market value | PV of each payment |
| Placed at | Average maturity | Portfolio duration | Each payment’s vertex |
| Risk factors | One | One (interpolated) | One per vertex |
| Correlations used | None | None | Full matrix $R$ |
| Precision | Lowest; overstates | Next step | Most precise, most complex |
| GARP example VaR | USD 2.97m | USD 2.70m | USD 2.63m undiv.; 2.57m div. |

All three preserve the USD 200 million market value in GARP Table 5.2; only cash-flow mapping comes close to preserving the market risk.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding fact is the ranking of the two properties: market value is required (“should preserve”), market risk is the ideal (“ideally”). Only A has both the right object (market value, not face value) and the right priority.

**Fragile fact.** Market value: must. Market risk: ideally. The methods differ in how well they meet the ideal, not in whether they meet the requirement.

**Reference**

LO 5.c (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 5, §5.2 Mapping Fixed-Income Portfolios, “Mapping Approaches” and Table 5.2. Schweser Reading 5, Module 5.2, LO 5.c. GARP-only: Schweser does not state the market-value requirement. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 c, where it is Q1 of 10.

a.reason: GARP §5.2, Mapping Approaches: “Mapping should preserve the market value of the position. Ideally, it also should preserve its market risk.”

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap. Face value of principal is the quantity that matters for when principal mapping places the value (redemption timing), not the quantity that must be preserved. In GARP Table 5.2 every method maps the USD 200 million market value. Correct only if the bonds traded at par and the stem asked what principal mapping keys on for timing.

c.reason: Error type: polarity flip (priority reversed). Market risk is the ideal and market value the requirement, not the other way round. Correct if the reading said “preserve market risk; ideally also market value”, which it does not.

d.reason: Error type: absolute claim. Principal and duration mapping do not preserve market risk exactly: GARP shows principal mapping overstating risk and duration mapping giving USD 2.70 million against 2.57 million from cash flows. Correct only for a portfolio of a single zero-coupon bond sitting on a vertex, where the three methods coincide.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Chinese commercial bank is drafting training notes on the principal mapping of the bank’s CNY government bond portfolio. The draft contains four statements about principal mapping:

I. It considers the timing of redemption payments only.

II. It chooses one risk factor, corresponding to the average maturity of the portfolio.

III. It maps each bond’s redemption payment to the vertex matching that bond’s own maturity, so a portfolio of two bonds is mapped on two risk factors.

IV. It needs the correlation matrix of the zero-coupon vertices to turn the undiversified VaR into a diversified VaR.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I, II and III only
I, II and IV only
I only
I and II only

questions.solution:
**What principal mapping does**

Stem in one line: which four statements about principal mapping are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Principal mapping is the crudest of the three methods. GARP: “With principal mapping, one risk factor is chosen that corresponds to the average portfolio maturity” and “Principal mapping considers the timing of redemption payments only.” Schweser: the method “includes only the risk of repayment of principal amounts”, and “VaR is calculated using the risk level from the zero-coupon bond that equals the average maturity of the portfolio. This method is the simplest of the three approaches.”

How it works, in three steps:

1. Take the redemption dates of the bonds and weight them by position size to get the average maturity $\bar{M}$ = $\sum_{i} w_{i}M_{i}$, where $w_{i}$ is the weight of bond $i$ and $M_{i}$ its maturity (GARP example: 0.5 × 1 + 0.5 × 5 = 3 years).
2. Place the whole portfolio value on the single zero-coupon risk factor at $\bar{M}$ .
3. Apply that zero’s risk to the full value.

Coupons play no part in the timing, and only one risk factor is used, so no correlations are involved. GARP’s verdict: “The only positive aspect of this method is its simplicity.”

**Applying it to this question**

I matches GARP word for word. True.

II matches GARP’s definition (one factor, average portfolio maturity). True.

III maps each redemption at its own maturity, giving two risk factors. That is not principal mapping: principal mapping collapses all redemptions to one point at the average. False.

IV puts a correlation matrix into principal mapping. With one factor there is nothing to correlate; the matrix $R$ and the diversified/undiversified distinction belong to cash-flow mapping. False.

So I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Principal mapping: one factor, at the average maturity, redemption timing only, no correlations.

**Reference**

LO 5.c. GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, “Mapping Approaches”. Schweser Reading 5, Module 5.2, LO 5.c (“Principal mapping”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 c, where it is Q2 of 10.

a.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: scope error accepted in III. It drops the averaging step: redemptions are not mapped at their own dates. III would describe a (crude) cash-flow map of principal only; it would be right if the stem asked how a cash-flow map that ignored coupons would look.

b.reason: **I, II and IV.** Error type: sibling swap accepted in IV. The undiversified-to-diversified step with $R$ is the cash-flow method’s aggregation (GARP Eq. 5.7). IV would be right if it began “Cash-flow mapping needs . . . ”.

c.reason: **I only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement. A candidate who believes principal mapping uses the duration, or several factors, rejects II. Correct only if II had said “corresponding to the portfolio duration”, which is the duration method.

d.reason: GARP §5.2: one risk factor at the average portfolio maturity; timing of redemption payments only.

questions.question: A member of the risk committee of a Canadian life insurer reviews a report on a CAD 600 million portfolio of fixed-coupon government bonds. The monthly 95% VaR is CAD 4.6 million under principal mapping and CAD 4.2 million under duration mapping, with the same zero-coupon vertex risks used in both runs. She asks why principal mapping gives the higher figure. Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

options.text: Principal mapping maps the face value of the bonds rather than their market value, so the exposure placed on the risk factor exceeds the portfolio’s value.
Principal mapping ignores the intervening coupons, which moves the mapped value to a shorter maturity, where zero-coupon risk is higher.
Principal mapping ignores the intervening coupons, so the whole value sits at the average maturity, later than the duration, where zero-coupon risk is higher.
Principal mapping adds the VaRs of the separate redemption payments as if they were perfectly correlated, so it reports an undiversified figure.

questions.solution:
**Why principal mapping overstates risk**

Stem in one line: CAD bond portfolio; principal-mapped VaR 4.6m above duration-mapped 4.2m; why?

**Concept and theory**

For a coupon bond, part of the value arrives before maturity as coupons. The value-weighted timing of all cash flows is the duration; the timing of redemptions alone is the maturity. Hence, for coupon-bearing portfolios:

duration \< average maturity of redemptions.

GARP’s example: average maturity 3 years, duration 2.733 years.

Zero-coupon risk rises with maturity. GARP Table 5.3 lists monthly 95% VaRs of 0.4696%, 0.9868%, 1.4841%, 1.9714% and 2.4261% for 1 to 5 years. Placing the whole value at a later maturity therefore assigns it a higher risk percentage. GARP: principal mapping “overstates the true risk because it ignores intervening coupon payments.” In the example, principal mapping gives USD 2.97 million against USD 2.70 million under duration mapping and USD 2.57 million under cash-flow mapping.

**Applying it to this question**

Both runs use the same vertex risks and the same CAD 600 million value, so the only difference is where the value is placed. Principal mapping places it at the average maturity, which is later than the duration because coupons are ignored; the zero at that later point is riskier. Mechanism: coupons ignored ⇒ later mapping point ⇒ higher risk percentage ⇒ higher VaR.

**Fragile fact.** Principal mapping overstates (not understates) risk, because ignoring coupons pushes the value to a later maturity.

**Reference**

LO 5.c. GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, “Mapping Approaches” and Tables 5.2, 5.3. Schweser Reading 5, LO 5.c and LO 5.d (“it ignores all coupon payments”). GARP-only: the word “overstates”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 c, where it is Q3 of 10.

a.reason: Error type: scope error (face value for market value). Principal mapping maps the portfolio’s value at the average maturity; in GARP Table 5.2 the principal column holds the USD 200 million market value. The method differs in timing, not in the amount mapped. Would be right only for a method that mapped undiscounted face amounts of bonds trading below par.

b.reason: Error type: polarity flip (direction of the shift). Ignoring coupons moves the mapped value later, not earlier, and the later point is the riskier one. Would be right if the stem asked how the mapping point of principal mapping compares with that of a method placing value at the first coupon date.

c.reason: GARP §5.2: principal mapping “overstates the true risk because it ignores intervening coupon payments”; the average maturity (3 years) exceeds the duration (2.733 years), and the risk of the zero rises with maturity (Table 5.3).

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap. Summing individual VaRs as if perfectly correlated is the undiversified VaR of cash-flow mapping. Principal mapping uses one factor, so there is nothing to sum. Would be right if the stem compared cash-flow undiversified VaR with cash-flow diversified VaR.

questions.question: A model validator at a Swiss private bank is reviewing the documentation of the duration-mapping option in the bank’s VaR system for its CHF bond book. The system holds zero-coupon risk factors only at the 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7 and 10-year vertices. Which of the following descriptions of duration mapping should the validator expect to find?

options.text: The portfolio is replaced by a single zero-coupon bond whose maturity equals the portfolio duration, and the risk at that maturity is found by linear interpolation between the adjacent vertices.

The portfolio is replaced by a single zero-coupon bond whose maturity equals the average portfolio maturity, and the risk at that maturity is found by linear interpolation between the adjacent vertices.
The portfolio is replaced by a single zero-coupon bond whose maturity equals the portfolio duration, and the risk at that maturity is read from the nearest vertex without any interpolation.
The portfolio is replaced by a single zero-coupon bond whose maturity equals the portfolio duration, and because duration is matched the resulting VaR equals the cash-flow-mapped VaR exactly.

questions.solution:
**What duration mapping does**

Stem in one line: which description of duration mapping should a validator expect in the CHF system documentation?

**Concept and theory**

Duration mapping keeps the single-factor simplicity of principal mapping but moves the mapping point to where the value of all cash flows (coupons included) is centred. GARP: “With duration mapping, one risk factor is chosen that corresponds to the portfolio duration” and “We replace the portfolio by a zero-coupon bond with maturity equal to the duration of the portfolio.”

The duration seldom falls on a vertex, so the risk at that maturity has to be built from the neighbouring vertices by linear interpolation:

$V_{D}$ = $V_{a}$ + ($V_{b} - V_{a}$) $\times\frac{D - a}{b - a}$

where $D$ is the portfolio duration, $a$ and $b$ are the vertices either side of $D$, and $V_{a}$, $V_{b}$ are the zero-coupon VaR percentages at those vertices. GARP example: $D$ = 2.733, so $V_{D}$ = 0.987 + (1.484 − 0.987)(2.733 − 2) = 1.351%. Schweser adds that “it may be difficult to calculate the risk level that exactly matches the duration of the portfolio”, which is why interpolation is needed.

**Applying it to this question**

Three slots discriminate: (1) maturity of the replacing zero (duration, not average maturity); (2) how the risk is obtained (interpolation, not rounding); (3) no claim of exact equality with cash-flow mapping. Only A gets all three right.

**Fragile fact.** Duration mapping places the value at the duration and interpolates the risk there; the average maturity belongs to principal mapping.

**Reference**

LO 5.c. GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, “Mapping Approaches”. Schweser Reading 5, LO 5.c (“Duration mapping”). Schweser-only (condensed source): the remark that matching the risk level to the duration exactly may be difficult. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 c, where it is Q4 of 10.

a.reason: GARP §5.2: zero-coupon bond with maturity equal to the duration; “Using a linear interpolation, we find a risk of . . . 1.351 percent”.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap. Average portfolio maturity is the principal-mapping point. Would be right for principal mapping when the average maturity fell between vertices.

c.reason: Error type: scope error (interpolation step dropped). The reading interpolates between adjacent vertices; snapping to the nearest vertex moves the mapping point and changes the risk. Would be right only if the duration happened to fall exactly on a vertex.

d.reason: Error type: absolute claim. Matching duration does not reproduce the cash-flow VaR: GARP gives USD 2.70 million versus USD 2.57 million because risk is not linear in maturity and correlations are below one. Would be right only for a single zero-coupon bond maturing on a vertex.

questions.question: The CRO of an Indian bank is choosing among the three fixed-income mapping methods for the bank’s INR 85 billion bond portfolio and asks a consultant to position duration mapping against the other two. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Duration mapping is more precise than cash-flow mapping, because it uses the portfolio’s exact duration rather than a fixed set of vertices.
Duration mapping is the simplest of the three methods, because it needs only one risk factor and a single mapping point.
Duration mapping is the next step in precision after principal mapping, but it still uses one risk factor and so ignores imperfect correlation along the curve.
Duration mapping gives the same VaR as principal mapping, because both methods place the whole portfolio value on one risk factor.

questions.solution:
**Duration mapping in the precision ranking**

Stem in one line: which statement positions duration mapping correctly against principal and cash-flow mapping?

**Concept and theory**

The three methods form a ladder of precision and complexity:

| Method | What it captures | What it misses |
|---|---|---|
| Principal | Timing of redemptions | Coupons (so it overstates risk); shape of the curve; correlations |
| Duration | Timing of all cash flows, summarised in one number | Non-linearity of risk in maturity; imperfect correlation along the curve |
| Cash flow | Amount and timing of every payment, vertex risks, correlation matrix | Little; the cost is complexity |

GARP calls duration mapping “the next step in precision”. Schweser: principal mapping is “the simplest of the three approaches”; cash-flow mapping “is the most precise method” but “also the most complex”. Because duration mapping uses one risk factor, it has no correlation inputs. GARP attributes part of the gap between duration and cash-flow VaR to the fact that “correlations are below unity, which reduces risk even further”; a single-factor method cannot see that.

**Applying it to this question**

Three positioning facts: better than principal, worse than cash flow, single factor. C states all three.

**Fragile fact.** Simplest = principal; most precise and most complex = cash flow; duration sits in between and is still single-factor.

**Reference**

LO 5.c. GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, “Mapping Approaches”. Schweser Reading 5, LO 5.c and LO 5.d (“cash flow mapping is the most precise method, but it is also the most complex”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 c, where it is Q5 of 10.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip (ranking reversed). Cash-flow mapping, not duration mapping, is the most precise. Would be right if “cash-flow mapping” read “principal mapping”.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap. “Simplest” is the label both sources give principal mapping. Its single factor does not make it simpler than principal mapping, which also uses one factor and needs no duration calculation or interpolation. Would be right for principal mapping.

c.reason: GARP §5.2: “The next step in precision is duration mapping”; one risk factor at the duration; the cash-flow result is lower partly because “correlations are below unity”.

d.reason: Error type: absolute claim. Using one factor does not make the two equal: they use different maturities (average maturity versus duration). GARP: USD 2.97 million versus USD 2.70 million. Would be right only for a portfolio of zero-coupon bonds, where there are no coupons and the two mapping points coincide.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at a Brazilian pension fund is implementing cash-flow mapping for a BRL portfolio of fixed-coupon bonds. Every coupon and principal date in the portfolio falls exactly on one of the vertices for which the fund’s system provides volatilities. Which of the following implementations is consistent with cash-flow mapping?

options.text: Each coupon and principal payment is assigned, at its undiscounted amount, to the vertex at its date, so the total mapped equals the sum of all promised payments.
Each coupon and principal payment is assigned, at its present value using the zero-coupon rate for its date, to the vertex at its date, so the total mapped equals the market value.
Each coupon and principal payment is assigned, at its present value using its own bond’s yield to maturity, to the vertex at its date, so the total mapped equals the market value.
Each coupon payment is assigned, at its present value using the zero-coupon rate for its date, to its vertex, while principal is mapped at the average maturity of the portfolio.

questions.solution:
**How cash-flow mapping places each payment**

Stem in one line: BRL portfolio, every payment date on a vertex; which implementation is cash-flow mapping?

**Concept and theory**

Cash-flow mapping drops the single-factor shortcut. GARP: “the cash-flow mapping method consists of grouping all cash flows on term-structure ‘vertices’ that correspond to maturities for which volatilities are provided. Each cash flow is represented by the present value of the cash payment, discounted at the appropriate zero-coupon rate.” Schweser: “we map the present value of the cash flows (i.e., face amount discounted at the spot rate for a given maturity) onto the risk factors for zeros of the same maturities”.

For the payment $CF_{t}$ due at vertex $t$, the mapped exposure is

$x_{t}$ = $\frac{CF_{t}}{\text{(1 +} z_{t}\text{)}^{t}}$

where $z_{t}$ is the zero-coupon (spot) rate for maturity $t$, and payments from different bonds falling at the same vertex are added together. Because the bond price itself equals the sum of its cash flows discounted at the zero rates, $\sum_{t} x_{t}$ equals the portfolio’s market value: GARP notes that “the current value of USD 200 million is fully allocated to the five risk factors.”

**Applying it to this question**

Two slots discriminate: the amount mapped (PV, not face) and the discount rate (zero-coupon rate for each date, not each bond’s yield). Option B is the only one that gets both right and also maps principal like any other payment.

**Fragile fact.** Present value, at the zero-coupon rate for that date, at the vertex of that date; the total equals market value.

**Reference**

LO 5.c. GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, “Mapping Approaches” and Tables 5.2, 5.4. Schweser Reading 5, LO 5.c (“Cash flow mapping”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 c, where it is Q6 of 10.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap (face amount for present value). Undiscounted payments sum to more than the market value, breaking the requirement that mapping preserve market value, and overweight distant flows. Would be right if the question asked for the cash-flow schedule fed into the mapping, before discounting.

b.reason: GARP §5.2: each cash flow is represented by its present value discounted at the appropriate zero-coupon rate, and the whole current value is allocated to the vertices.

c.reason: Error type: scope error (wrong discount rate). Both sources specify the zero-coupon (spot) rate for each maturity, the same rate the risk factor represents. A yield to maturity is a single average rate for all of one bond’s payments. Would be right only on a flat curve, where every zero rate equals every yield.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap (principal-mapping step imported). Placing principal at the average maturity is the principal method; cash-flow mapping treats a redemption like any other payment at its own vertex. Would be right for a hybrid that the reading does not describe; no source supports it.

questions.question: A risk consultant is drafting a note for a Singapore asset manager on how cash-flow mapping turns its SGD bond positions into a portfolio VaR. Here $x$ is the vector of present values mapped to the vertices, $V$ is the vector of VaRs of the zero-coupon bond returns at those vertices, and $R$ is the correlation matrix of the vertices. Which of the following statements in the draft is least accurate?

options.text: The diversified VaR is $\sqrt{\text{(}x \times V \text{)}^{'}R \text{(}x \times V \text{)}}$, so it requires the correlation matrix of the vertices in addition to the mapped present values and vertex risks.
The undiversified VaR is the sum of the individual vertex VaRs, $\sum_{i} |x_{i}|V_{i}$, and it is the VaR that would apply if every correlation between vertices were one.
Because each payment is mapped at its present value discounted at the appropriate zero-coupon rate, the full current value of the portfolio is allocated across the vertices.
Because the correlations between vertices are below one, the diversified VaR exceeds the undiversified VaR, as spreading value over more vertices adds more risk factors.

questions.solution:
**How cash-flow mapping aggregates vertex risks**

Stem in one line: which statement about diversified and undiversified VaR under cash-flow mapping is least accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Cash-flow mapping is the only one of the three methods that produces several exposures, so it is the only one that needs to know how the vertices move together. GARP Eq. (5.7):

VaR = $\sqrt{\text{(}x \times V \text{)}^{'} R \text{(}x \times V \text{)}}$

where $x$ is the vector of present values mapped to the vertices, $V$ is the vector of VaRs (in %) of the zero-coupon bond returns at those vertices, $x \times V$ is the element-by-element product giving the individual VaR at each vertex, and $R$ is the correlation matrix of the vertices. With perfect correlation,

Undiversified VaR = $\sum_{i\text{=1}}^{N} |x_{i}| V_{i}$

In GARP’s example: undiversified USD 2.63 million, diversified USD 2.57 million. Since every correlation is at most one, the diversified VaR can never exceed the undiversified VaR; it equals it only when all correlations are one.

**Applying it to this question**

A: GARP Eq. (5.7). True.

B: GARP: “With perfect correlation across all zeros, the VaR of the portfolio is” the sum of individual VaRs. True.

C: GARP: “the current value of USD 200 million is fully allocated to the five risk factors.” True.

D: Reverses the effect of correlation. Correlations below one reduce risk (GARP: “correlations are below unity, which reduces risk even further”). False. The question asks for the least accurate statement, so D.

**Fragile fact.** Diversified ≤ undiversified; equality only when all correlations are one. More vertices with imperfect correlation lower risk.

**Reference**

LO 5.c. GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, “Mapping Approaches”, Eq. (5.7) and Table 5.4. Schweser Reading 5, LO 5.d (diversified VaR by matrix algebra). Note: GARP’s Eq. (5.7) is garbled in the OCR text; the symbols ($x$ = present values, $V$ = vertex VaRs of zero-coupon returns, $R$ = correlation matrix) are confirmed by Schweser’s verbal definition. Schweser places the formulas under LO 5.d; GARP presents them as part of the cash-flow method. No conflict of substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 c, where it is Q7 of 10.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Japanese trust bank compares two VaR runs on a JPY 120 billion bond portfolio. The monthly 95% VaR is JPY 1.84 billion under duration mapping and JPY 1.71 billion under cash-flow mapping with the full correlation matrix. The vertex risks used in both runs are:

| Vertex (years) | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Zero-coupon VaR (%) | 0.52 | 1.06 | 1.55 | 2.01 | 2.44 |

Which of the following best explains why the cash-flow-mapped VaR is lower?

options.text: Duration mapping ignores the intervening coupons, so it places the portfolio’s value at a later maturity than its cash flows justify.
Vertex risk is not linear in maturity, so the interpolated risk at the duration differs from the vertex risks, and correlations below one reduce risk further.
Cash-flow mapping discounts every payment, so the total value it maps to the vertices is smaller than the market value used in duration mapping.
Correlations below one between the vertices explain the entire difference; the choice of a single maturity has no effect once the duration is matched.

questions.solution:
**Why the duration-mapped VaR exceeds the cash-flow VaR**

Stem in one line: JPY portfolio, duration VaR 1.84bn, cash-flow diversified VaR 1.71bn; best explanation?

**Concept and theory**

Moving from duration mapping to cash-flow mapping changes two things at once:

1. Shape of risk across maturities. Duration mapping uses the risk interpolated at one point. Cash-flow mapping uses the actual vertex risks of each payment. Because “risk measures are not perfectly linear with maturity”, the PV-weighted vertex risks (the undiversified cash-flow VaR) do not equal the risk at the duration.
2. Correlations. Cash-flow mapping applies the correlation matrix; correlations “below unity . . . reduce risk even further”. This is the step from undiversified to diversified.

GARP decomposes its USD 130,000 gap (2.70 to 2.57): USD 70,000 due to differences in yield volatility across maturities (2.70 to 2.63) and USD 60,000 due to imperfect correlations (2.63 to 2.57).

**Applying it to this question**

The vertex table shows risk rising by 0.54, 0.49, 0.46 and 0.43 per year: not linear in maturity, so the first effect is present. The cash-flow run uses the full correlation matrix, so the second effect is present. B names both.

**Fragile fact.** Duration minus undiversified cash flow = non-linearity. Undiversified minus diversified = correlation. Coupons ignored = principal mapping, not duration mapping.

**Reference**

LO 5.c. GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, “Mapping Approaches” (paragraph after Eq. 5.7). Schweser does not give the decomposition (GARP-only). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 c, where it is Q8 of 10.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap. Ignoring intervening coupons is the flaw of principal mapping; duration already reflects coupon timing. Would be right if the comparison were principal-mapped VaR against duration-mapped VaR.

b.reason: GARP §5.2: the difference “is due to two factors. First, risk measures are not perfectly linear with maturity . . . Second, correlations are below unity, which reduces risk even further.”

c.reason: Error type: scope error (market-value requirement ignored). Discounting at zero rates makes the mapped PVs add up to the market value; nothing is lost. Would be right only if payments were discounted at rates above the zero curve, which no source describes.

d.reason: Error type: absolute claim. Correlation explains only part of the gap; the rest comes from risk not being linear in maturity, which the table shows. Would be right if vertex risk were exactly proportional to maturity (for example a flat curve with the same yield volatility at all maturities), which removes the non-linearity effect.

|---|---|
| Principal mapping | 7.384 |
| Duration mapping | 6.712 |
| Cash-flow mapping, undiversified | 6.493 |
| Cash-flow mapping, diversified | 6.351 |

She must split the difference between the duration-mapped VaR and the diversified cash-flow-mapped VaR into the part due to risk not being linear in maturity and the part due to imperfect correlations. Which of the following gives the correct split?

options.text: Non-linearity AUD 219,000; imperfect correlations AUD 142,000
Non-linearity AUD 142,000; imperfect correlations AUD 219,000
Non-linearity AUD 891,000; imperfect correlations AUD 142,000
Non-linearity AUD 361,000; imperfect correlations AUD 142,000

questions.solution:
**Splitting the duration versus cash-flow gap**

Stem in one line: AUD 420m portfolio; principal 7.384, duration 6.712, CF undiversified 6.493, CF diversified 6.351; split duration minus CF diversified into non-linearity and correlation parts.

**Concept and theory**

Order the four VaRs from the crudest method to the most refined (arrows show the direction of refinement):

$\text{VaR}_{\text{principal}} \to\text{VaR}_{\text{duration}} \to\text{VaR}_{\text{CF, undiv}} \to\text{VaR}_{\text{CF, div}}$

Each step isolates one difference between methods. Duration to undiversified cash flow keeps perfect correlation but replaces the single interpolated risk with the actual vertex risks: this step measures the effect of risk not being linear in maturity. Undiversified to diversified cash flow keeps the vertex risks but introduces the correlation matrix: this step measures imperfect correlations. GARP does exactly this split: of USD 130,000, “USD 70,000 is due to differences in yield volatility, and USD 60,000 is due to imperfect correlations.”

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first:

Non-linearity effect = $\text{VaR}_{\text{duration}} - \text{VaR}_{\text{CF, undiv}}$

Correlation effect = $\text{VaR}_{\text{CF, undiv}} - \text{VaR}_{\text{CF, div}}$

Step by step (AUD million):

Non-linearity effect = 6.712 − 6.493 = 0.219

Correlation effect = 6.493 − 6.351 = 0.142

Check: total gap = 6.712 − 6.351 = 0.361 = 0.219 + 0.142

Meaning: of the AUD 361,000 by which duration mapping overstates the cash-flow VaR, AUD 219,000 comes from placing all value at one interpolated maturity, and AUD 142,000 from ignoring diversification along the curve. The principal-mapped VaR and the 4.0-year average maturity are irrelevant to this split.

**Fragile fact.** Non-linearity is measured against the undiversified cash-flow VaR; correlation is undiversified minus diversified.

**Reference**

LO 5.c. GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, “Mapping Approaches” (decomposition of the USD 130,000 difference). GARP-only. Numbers recomputed in calc.py. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 c, where it is Q9 of 10.

a.reason: It applies GARP’s decomposition in the right order: AUD 219,000 non-linearity, AUD 142,000 correlation.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap of the two effects. The two numbers are right but attached to the wrong causes. Correct if the stem had asked for the correlation effect first.

c.reason: Error type: wrong input twin. Uses the principal-mapped VaR in place of the duration-mapped VaR: 7.384 − 6.493 = 0.891. That mixes in the coupon effect of principal mapping. Correct if the stem asked for the gap between principal mapping and undiversified cash-flow mapping.

d.reason: Error type: wrong base (intermediate result). Measures non-linearity from the diversified figure, 6.712−6.351 = 0.361, which is the total gap and double-counts the correlation effect (the two parts then sum to 503,000, more than the gap). Correct if the stem asked for the total difference between duration and diversified cash-flow VaR.

| Maturity (years) | Run 1 | Run 2 | Run 3 | Run 4 | Run 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | – | – | 6.94 | – | 7.15 |
| 2 | – | – | 146.97 | 150.00 | 157.15 |
| 2.83 | 200.00 | – | – | – | – |
| 3 | – | 200.00 | 1.84 | – | 2.05 |
| 4 | – | – | 1.76 | – | 2.05 |
| 5 | – | – | 1.68 | – | 2.05 |
| 6 | – | – | 40.81 | 50.00 | 52.05 |
| Total | 200.00 | 200.00 | 200.00 | 200.00 | 222.50 |

Which of the following correctly identifies the runs produced by principal, duration and cash-flow mapping, in that order?

options.text: Run 1, Run 2 and Run 3
Run 2, Run 1 and Run 3
Run 2, Run 1 and Run 5
Run 4, Run 1 and Run 3

questions.solution:
**Recognising each method from its mapped exposures**

Stem in one line: GBP 150m 2-year 3.40% and GBP 50m 6-year 4.10% par bonds; five runs; identify principal, duration and cash-flow runs.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Table 5.2 shows the same portfolio mapped three ways side by side. The signatures are:

| Method | Where the value goes | Total mapped |
|---|---|---|
| Principal | All of it at one point: average redemption maturity | Market value |
| Duration | All of it at one point: portfolio duration (earlier than the average maturity for coupon bonds) | Market value |
| Cash flow | PV of each payment at its own vertex | Market value (PVs at zero rates) |

Two shortcuts do not belong to any method: mapping each redemption at its own date (no averaging, coupons ignored), and mapping undiscounted payments (total above market value).

**Applying it to this question**

Average redemption maturity (weights 150/200 and 50/200; both bonds at par, so face weights equal value weights):

$\bar{M}$ = 0.75 × 2 + 0.25 × 6 = 3.00 years ⇒ Run 2 is principal mapping.

Run 1 places all value at 2.83 years, a single point earlier than 3.00: the duration. (Check from Run 3’s PVs: $D$ = (1 × 6.94 + 2 × 146.97 + 3 × 1.84 + 4 × 1.76 + 5 × 1.68 + 6 × 40.81)/200 = 2.83.) Run 3 spreads PVs over every payment date and totals GBP 200.00 million: cash-flow mapping.

Run 4 maps the two redemptions at their own dates (no averaging, no coupons): not one of the three methods.

Run 5 maps undiscounted payments, total GBP 222.50 million, above market value: breaks the market-value requirement.

Answer: Run 2, Run 1, Run 3.

**Fragile fact.** For coupon bonds the duration point is earlier than the principal (average-maturity) point; every valid map totals the market value.

**Reference**

LO 5.c. GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, “Mapping Approaches” and Table 5.2 (columns Principal, Duration, Cash Flow). Schweser Reading 5, LO 5.c and LO 5.d (average life with market-value weights). Numbers built in calc.py from par yields 3.10%, 3.40%, 3.65%, 3.85%, 4.00%, 4.10% (1 to 6 years), bootstrapped to zero rates. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 c, where it is Q10 of 10.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap of the two single-point methods. It labels the earlier point (duration) as principal. Would be right if principal mapping used the duration and duration mapping the average maturity, i.e. the definitions reversed.

b.reason: Principal mapping = one factor at the average maturity (3 years); duration mapping = one factor at the duration (2.83 years); cash-flow mapping = PVs at zero-coupon rates on the vertices, preserving the GBP 200 million value (GARP §5.2 and Table 5.2).

c.reason: Error type: wrong input twin (face amounts for present values). Run 5 maps promised payments undiscounted; its GBP 222.50 million total violates “Mapping should preserve the market value”. Would be right if the question asked which run shows the cash-flow schedule before discounting.

d.reason: Error type: scope error (averaging step dropped). Run 4 places each redemption at its own maturity, using two risk factors; principal mapping uses one factor at the average maturity. Would be right only if the portfolio held a single bond, where the average maturity is that bond’s maturity.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Canadian public pension plan is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts. The slide summarizes how the plan’s risk system maps its CAD government bond portfolio into positions on standard instruments, namely zero-coupon bonds at the vertices from 1 to 10 years, and then turns those positions into a portfolio VaR. Which sequence of steps is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question says otherwise, VaR figures are monthly at the 95% confidence level, “vertex VaR” means the VaR of a zero-coupon bond return at that maturity, expressed as a percentage of value, and a vertex is a maturity for which the risk system provides volatilities and correlations.

options.text: Lay out every bond’s cash flows by payment date and group them on the vertices; discount each vertex’s cash flow at the yield to maturity of the bond that pays it; multiply each present value by the vertex VaR; combine the products using the vertex correlation matrix.

Lay out every bond’s cash flows by payment date and group them on the vertices; discount each vertex’s cash flow at that vertex’s zero-coupon rate; multiply each present value by the vertex VaR; add the products to obtain the diversified VaR.

Compute the duration of the portfolio and place its full market value on one zero-coupon bond of that maturity; read that zero’s VaR by interpolating between the two adjacent vertices; multiply the market value by the interpolated VaR.

Lay out every bond’s cash flows by payment date and group them on the vertices; discount each vertex’s cash flow at that vertex’s zero-coupon rate; multiply each present value by the vertex VaR; combine the products using the vertex correlation matrix.

questions.solution:
**The mapping procedure in order**

Stem in one line: which sequence correctly summarizes how a bond portfolio is mapped onto zero-coupon vertices and turned into VaR?

**Concept and theory**

A bond cannot be risk-measured from its own price history, because its maturity shortens every day. The risk system therefore keeps a fixed set of standard instruments: zero-coupon bonds at chosen maturities (the vertices) for which it holds volatilities and correlations. Mapping replaces each bond by positions in those zeros. GARP §5.2: “the cash-flow mapping method consists of grouping all cash flows on term-structure ‘vertices’ that correspond to maturities for which volatilities are provided. Each cash flow is represented by the present value of the cash payment, discounted at the appropriate zero-coupon rate.”

The procedure, in the order GARP and Schweser apply it to the two-bond example:

| Step | Action | Output |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | List every cash flow by date; group flows on the same date onto one vertex | Cash flows by vertex (GARP Table 5.2) |
| 2 | Discount each vertex’s cash flow at that vertex’s zero rate | PV position $x_{i}$ (sums to market value) |
| 3 | Multiply by the vertex VaR $V_{i}$ | Individual VaRs $x_{i}V_{i}$ |
| 4a | Add the individual VaRs (absolute values) | Undiversified VaR |
| 4b | Pre- and post-multiply $R$ by the vector $x \times V$ , take the square root | Diversified VaR (Eq. 5.7) |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem asks for positions at the vertices and a portfolio VaR. Three options share the first step (group by date on vertices). Then check the discount rate (must be the vertex zero rate) and the aggregation (correlation matrix gives the diversified figure; a plain sum gives the undiversified one). Only D gets both right.

**Fragile fact.** Discount at the vertex zero rate, not the bond’s yield; a plain sum is undiversified, the matrix product is diversified.

**Reference**

LO 5.d: “Summarize how to map a fixed-income portfolio into positions of standard instruments.” GARP Ch. 5, §5.2 Mapping Fixed-Income Portfolios, “Mapping Approaches”. Schweser Reading 5, LO 5.d (cash flow mapping, Figure 5.5). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 d, where it is Q1 of 10.

a.reason: Error type: wrong input twin (yield to maturity for zero rate). Once flows from several bonds sit on one vertex, there is no single “bond that pays it”, and GARP specifies the zero-coupon rate for that maturity. A would be right only on a flat curve where every yield equals every zero rate.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap of labels. Adding $x_{i}V_{i}$ gives the undiversified VaR (perfect correlation), not the diversified one. B would be correct if its last words were “to obtain the undiversified VaR”.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap with duration mapping (LO 5.c). It maps the whole portfolio to one hypothetical zero, not to positions at the vertices, and ignores correlations. It would be correct if the stem asked for duration mapping.

d.reason: It follows GARP §5.2 exactly: group on vertices, PV at the appropriate zero-coupon rate, $x \times V$ as individual VaRs, then “premultiply and postmultiply the matrix by the dollar amounts ($xV$ ) at each vertex” and take the square root.

| Bond | Face (GBP million) | Coupon | Maturity (years) |
|---|---|---|---|

questions.solution:
**PV position at the 2-year vertex**

Stem in one line: three GBP bonds; find the PV mapped onto the 2-year vertex from annually compounded zero rates.

**Concept and theory**

The position on a vertex is the present value of all cash flows, from every instrument, that fall on that date. GARP Table 5.2 shows this: the 1-year vertex holds USD 110, the USD 104 redemption of the 1-year bond plus the USD 6 coupon of the 5-year bond, and its PV is USD 110/1.04 = 105.77. In general, for vertex $t$:

$x_{t}$ = $\frac{CF_{t}}{\text{(1 +} s_{t}\text{)}^{t}} , CF_{t}$ = $\sum_{\text{bonds} j} CF_{j,t}$

where $CF_{j,t}$ is bond $j$’s cash flow at time $t$, $s_{t}$ is the annually compounded zero (spot) rate for maturity $t$, and $x_{t}$ is the mapped PV position.

**Applying it to this question**

Bond X coupon at year 2 = 60 × 4.50% = 2.70

Bond Y coupon plus principal at year 2 = 40 × 1.03 = 41.20

$CF_{2}$ = 2.70 + 41.20 = 43.90

(1 + $s_{2}$)$^{2}$ = $\text{1.039}^{2}$ = 1.079521

$x_{2}$ = 43.90/1.079521 = 40.666 ≈ GBP 40.67 million

Bond Z pays nothing until year 4, and the 1-, 3- and 4-year rates do not enter: they are irrelevant inputs for this vertex. The figure is the amount of a 2-year zero the risk system will treat the portfolio as holding.

**Fragile fact.** A vertex position aggregates every instrument’s flow on that date, and it is a present value at that vertex’s zero rate.

**Reference**

LO 5.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 5, §5.2 “Mapping Approaches”, Table 5.2 (cash-flow mapping column). Schweser Reading 5, LO 5.d (“face amount discounted at the spot rate for a given maturity”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 d, where it is Q2 of 10.

a.reason: Error type: dropped term. Only Bond Y’s 41.20 is discounted: 41.20/1.079521 = 38.17. Bond X’s year-2 coupon is forgotten. Correct only if X paid no coupon at year 2 (for example, a zero-coupon bond).

b.reason: GARP §5.2: each cash flow is grouped on its vertex and “represented by the present value of the cash payment, discounted at the appropriate zero-coupon rate”.

c.reason: Error type: time-conversion slip (one period instead of two). 43.90/1.039 = 42.25. Correct only for a cash flow at year 1 discounted at 3.90%.

d.reason: Error type: wrong input twin (1-year rate for 2-year rate). $\text{43.90/1.034}^{2}$ = 41.06. Correct only if the 2-year zero rate were 3.40%.

A risk consultant reviewing the VaR engine of a Swiss private bank reads four statements in the vendor’s documentation on how the bank’s CHF bond positions are mapped onto zero-coupon vertices:

I. The mapping should preserve the market value of the positions and, ideally, their market risk.

II. Each cash flow is represented by its present value, discounted at the zero-coupon rate for the vertex on which it falls.

III. Because the mapping preserves market risk exactly, the VaR of the mapped positions always equals the VaR that would be obtained by fully repricing every bond.

IV. After mapping, the positions across all vertices sum to the current market value of the portfolio. Which of the statements are accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question says otherwise, VaR figures are monthly at the 95% confidence level, “vertex VaR” means the VaR of a zero-coupon bond return at that maturity, expressed as a percentage of value, and a vertex is a maturity for which the risk system provides volatilities and correlations.

options.text: I and IV only
I, II, III and IV
II and IV only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
**Principles of the mapping**

Stem in one line: which of four documentation statements on mapping CHF bonds onto zero-coupon vertices are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

GARP sets out what a mapping must achieve before it describes the methods: “Mapping should preserve the market value of the position. Ideally, it also should preserve its market risk.” The hierarchy matters: market value is a requirement; market risk is an aspiration, because grouping cash flows on a finite set of vertices and using linear exposures is an approximation. Cash-flow mapping meets the value requirement by mapping present values: in GARP Table 5.4, “the current value of USD 200 million is fully allocated to the five risk factors”.

| Property | Status in GARP |
|---|---|
| Preserve market value | Required; PVs sum to the portfolio value |
| Preserve market risk | “Ideally”; not guaranteed |
| Amount mapped | PV of each cash flow at the vertex zero rate, not face |

**Applying it to this question**

I restates GARP’s principle, including the word “ideally”. True. II restates the PV rule. True. III upgrades “ideally” to “exactly” and “always”. False. IV is the full-allocation property shown in Table 5.4. True. Hence I, II and IV only.

**Fragile fact.** Value: must. Risk: ideally. Positions are PVs, and they add up to the current market value.

**Reference**

LO 5.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 5, §5.2 “Mapping Approaches” (preservation sentence; Table 5.4 text). GARP-only for the value/risk preservation sentence; Schweser LO 5.d covers the PV rule only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 d, where it is Q3 of 10.

a.reason: **I and IV only.** Error type: wrong input twin, rejecting a true statement. A candidate who thinks flows are discounted at each bond’s yield to maturity, or mapped at face, rejects II. Correct only if II said “at the yield to maturity of the bond”.

b.reason: **All four.** Error type: absolute-claim trap (accepting III). Mapping is an approximation of risk; GARP only says it should “ideally” preserve risk. Correct only if III read “should ideally approximate the risk of the bonds”.

c.reason: **II and IV only.** Error type: polarity flip on the requirement (rejecting I). A candidate who believes mapping must preserve risk and need not preserve value rejects I. It would be right only if I reversed the two, which GARP never does.

d.reason: GARP §5.2: value must be preserved, risk ideally; each flow is its PV at the appropriate zero rate; the current value is fully allocated to the vertices.

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question says otherwise, VaR figures are monthly at the 95% confidence level, “vertex VaR” means the VaR of a zero-coupon bond return at that maturity, expressed as a percentage of value, and a vertex is a maturity for which the risk system provides volatilities and correlations.

questions.solution:
**Undiversified VaR of a mapped two-bond portfolio**

Stem in one line: AUD 50m 3-year 5% and AUD 70m 1-year 3.5% bonds; map to 1Y to 3Y vertices and find the undiversified VaR.

**Concept and theory**

Once each PV $x_{i}$ sits on its vertex, the individual VaR of that position is $x_{i}V_{i}$, where $V_{i}$ is the VaR of the zero-coupon return at vertex $i$. If all zeros were perfectly correlated, the worst moves would happen together and the portfolio VaR would be the plain sum. GARP §5.2:

Undiversified VaR = $\sum_{i\text{=1}}^{N} |x_{i}| V_{i}$

where $N$ is the number of vertices, $x_{i}$ the PV mapped to vertex $i$ (absolute value) and $V_{i}$ the vertex VaR as a fraction. In GARP’s example this gives USD 2.63 million. The correlation matrix plays no role in this number.

**Applying it to this question**

Step 1, cash flows by vertex:

$CF_{1}$ = 50 × 5% + 70 × 1.035 = 2.50 + 72.45 = 74.95

$CF_{2}$ = 2.50$, CF_{3}$ = 50 × 1.05 = 52.50

Step 2, PV at each vertex zero rate:

$x_{1}$ = 74.95/1.036 = 72.3456

$x_{2}$ = $\text{2.50/1.04}^{2}$ = 2.3114

A senior risk analyst at a Japanese trust bank has already mapped a JGB portfolio, whose total face value is JPY 168 billion, onto three vertices. The risk system reports the monthly volatility $\sigma$ of zero-coupon bond returns at each vertex, and the bank computes 95% VaR with $\alpha$ = 1.645.

| Vertex | Mapped PV (JPY bn) | $\sigma$ (monthly) | $\frac{\text{Correlation with}}{\text{1Y 3Y 5Y}}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1Y | 45 | 0.29% | 1 |
| 3Y | 80 | 0.90% | 0.89 1 |
| 5Y | 35 | 1.47% | 0.85 0.99 1 |

What is the diversified monthly 95% VaR of the portfolio?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question says otherwise, VaR figures are monthly at the 95% confidence level, “vertex VaR” means the VaR of a zero-coupon bond return at that maturity, expressed as a percentage of value, and a vertex is a maturity for which the risk system provides volatilities and correlations.

options.text: JPY 1.347 billion
JPY 2.216 billion
JPY 2.245 billion
JPY 1.471 billion

questions.solution:
**Diversified VaR with $V$ = $\alpha\sigma$**

Stem in one line: JPY positions 45, 80, 35 bn at 1Y, 3Y, 5Y with monthly $\sigma$ and correlations; find the 95% diversified VaR.

**Concept and theory**

Correlations between vertices are below one, so the worst moves at different maturities do not all occur together. GARP Equation 5.7 gives the diversified VaR:

VaR = $\alpha\sqrt{x^{'}\Sigma x}$ = $\sqrt{\text{(}x \times V \text{)}^{'} R \text{(}x \times V \text{)}}$

where $x$ is the vector of PV positions at the vertices, Σ the covariance matrix of zero-coupon returns, $R$ their correlation matrix, $\alpha$ the standard normal deviate for the confidence level, and $V$ = $\alpha\sigma$ the vector of vertex VaRs (“the vector of VaR for zero-coupon bond returns”). The product $x \times V$ is element by element: the individual VaRs.

**Applying it to this question**

Step 1, vertex VaRs $V_{i}$ = 1.645 $\sigma_{i}$: 0.4771%, 1.4805%, 2.4182%.

Step 2, individual VaRs $x_{i}V_{i}$:

45 × 0.4771% = 0.2147, 80 × 1.4805% = 1.1844, 35 × 2.4182% = 0.8464

Step 3, $R$($x \times V$ ), row by row:

1Y : 0.2147 + 0.89(1.1844) + 0.85(0.8464) = 1.9882

3Y : 0.89(0.2147) + 1.1844 + 0.99(0.8464) = 2.2133

5Y : 0.85(0.2147) + 0.99(1.1844) + 0.8464 = 2.2014

Step 4, quadratic form and square root:

($x \times V$ $\text{)}^{'}R$($x \times V$ ) = 0.2147(1.9882) + 1.1844(2.2133) + 0.8464(2.2014)

= 0.4268 + 2.6215 + 1.8631 = 4.9114

Diversified VaR = $\sqrt{4.9114}$ = 2.216 JPY billion

Meaning: the bank expects a monthly loss above JPY 2.216 billion only once in 20 months. The JPY 168 billion face value is irrelevant: mapping uses PVs.

**Fragile fact.** $V$ in Equation 5.7 is already a VaR ($\alpha\sigma$); if the table gives $\sigma$, multiply by $\alpha$ first.

**Reference**

LO 5.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 5, §5.2 “Mapping Approaches”, Equation 5.7 and Table 5.4. Schweser Reading 5, LO 5.d, Figure 5.5 (“$x$ is the present value of cash flows vector, $V$ is the vector of VaR for zero-coupon bond returns and $R$ is the correlation matrix”). Equation 5.7 is garbled in the GARP extract and missing in Schweser; reconstructed from GARP’s wording and confirmed against the question bank’s LO 5.d solutions. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 d, where it is Q5 of 10.

An internal auditor at an Indian bank is checking a validation memo on the cash-flow mapping of the bank’s INR government bond portfolio. Every mapped position is long, and all correlations between vertices are positive and below one. Which of the following statements in the memo is NOT correct?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question says otherwise, VaR figures are monthly at the 95% confidence level, “vertex VaR” means the VaR of a zero-coupon bond return at that maturity, expressed as a percentage of value, and a vertex is a maturity for which the risk system provides volatilities and correlations.

options.text: The diversified VaR cannot exceed the undiversified VaR, and the two would coincide only if every pair of vertices were perfectly correlated.
The diversified VaR is the square root of the vector of rupee VaRs $x\times V$ pre- and post-multiplied by the correlation matrix, where $V$ = $\alpha\sigma$ holds the VaRs of zero-coupon returns.
If the correlations between the 1-year vertex and the longer vertices fell, with positions and vertex VaRs unchanged, the diversified VaR would rise toward the undiversified VaR.
The undiversified VaR is the sum of the individual VaRs $x_{i}V_{i}$, which is the portfolio VaR that would apply if all zero-coupon bonds were perfectly correlated.

questions.solution:
**Diversified versus undiversified VaR: properties**

Stem in one line: long-only INR mapped portfolio, correlations positive and below one; which memo statement is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

Write the individual VaRs as $a_{i}$ = $x_{i}V_{i} \ge$ 0 (all positions long). Then

Diversified $\text{VaR}^{2}$ = $\sum_{i} a^{2}_{i}$ + 2 $\sum_{i<j} \rho_{ij} a_{i}a_{j} , \text{Undiversified VaR}^{2}$ = $\left( \sum_{i} a_{i}\right)^{2}$ = $\sum_{i} a^{2}_{i}$ + 2 $\sum_{i<j} a_{i}a_{j}$

where $\rho_{ij}$ is the correlation between vertices $i$ and $j$. Each cross term is weighted by $\rho_{ij} \le$ 1, so the diversified VaR is at most the undiversified VaR, with equality only when every $\rho_{ij}$ = 1. Lower correlations shrink the cross terms and lower the diversified VaR. GARP: correlations “below unity” reduce risk; “with perfect correlation across all zeros” the VaR is the undiversified sum.

**Applying it to this question**

A states the bound and the equality condition: true. B restates Equation 5.7 with $V$ = $\alpha\sigma$: true. D restates the undiversified formula and its perfect-correlation meaning: true. C says that lower correlations would raise the diversified VaR toward the undiversified figure. With long positions, lower correlations move it away, downward. C is the incorrect statement.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: correlation down, diversified VaR down (long-only); correlation one, diversified equals undiversified.

**Reference**

LO 5.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 5, §5.2 “Mapping Approaches” (undiversified formula, Equation 5.7, the “below unity” sentence). Schweser Reading 5, LO 5.d. Formula notation confirmed as in Q5. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 d, where it is Q6 of 10.

a.reason: True. The “only if” clause relies on the long-only condition in the stem: with a short leg, the cross term 2$\rho_{ij} a_{i}a_{j}$ is negative and equality with $\sum|a_{i}|$ would need a correlation of −1 between the opposite legs. It would be false (absolute-claim trap) if it said equality held at any correlation.

b.reason: True. GARP: “we premultiply and postmultiply the matrix by the dollar amounts ($xV$ ) at each vertex. Taking the square root. . . ”. It would be false if it used face amounts or omitted the square root.

c.reason: GARP §5.2: “correlations are below unity, which reduces risk”. Reducing $\rho_{1j}$ reduces every cross term involving the 1-year vertex.

d.reason: True. GARP: “With perfect correlation across all zeros, the VaR of the portfolio is” $\sum|x_{i}|V_{i}$. It would be false if it called this sum the diversified VaR.

The 1-year zero rate is 4.00% (annual compounding). Vertex VaRs are 0.47% (1-year) and 2.43% (5-year), and the correlation between the two vertices is 0.85. Which pair of figures correctly states the undiversified and the diversified VaR of the position?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question says otherwise, VaR figures are monthly at the 95% confidence level, “vertex VaR” means the VaR of a zero-coupon bond return at that maturity, expressed as a percentage of value, and a vertex is a maturity for which the risk system provides volatilities and correlations.

options.text: Undiversified EUR 1.77 million; diversified EUR 1.42 million
Undiversified EUR 1.39 million; diversified EUR 1.42 million
Undiversified EUR 1.77 million; diversified EUR 1.74 million
Undiversified EUR 1.77 million; diversified EUR 1.59 million

questions.solution:
**Signed positions: a long zero financed by a short note**

Stem in one line: long EUR 65m 5-year zero, short 1-year note repaying EUR 41.6m; find undiversified and diversified VaR.

**Concept and theory**

A liability that repays a fixed amount is a short position in the zero of that maturity, so it maps to a negative PV. The two aggregations treat the sign differently:

| Measure | Formula | Sign treatment |
|---|---|---|
| Undiversified | $\sum_{i} \|x_{i}\| V_{i}$ | Absolute values: individual VaRs simply add |
| Diversified | $\sqrt{\text{(}x \times V \text{)}^{'}R\text{(}x \times V \text{)}}$ | Signed $x$: a short leg hedges a correlated long leg |

GARP writes the undiversified sum with $|x_{i}|$, and its forward-contract table (Table 5.7) labels the individual VaR column “$|x| V$ ”.

**Applying it to this question**

$x_{1}$ = −41.6/1.04 = −40.00 $x_{5}$ = +65.00

$x_{1}V_{1}$ = −40.00 × 0.47% = −0.1880 $x_{5}V_{5}$ = 65.00 × 2.43% = 1.5795

Undiversified = \|−0.1880\| + 1.5795 = 1.7675 ≈ 1.77

$\text{Diversified}^{2}$ = $\text{0.1880}^{2}$ + $\text{1.5795}^{2}$ + 2(0.85)(−0.1880)(1.5795)

= 0.0353 + 2.4948 − 0.5048 = 2.0254

Diversified = $\sqrt{2.0254}$ = 1.4232 ≈ 1.42

Meaning: the correlated short note offsets part of the 5-year risk.

**Fragile fact.** Short position: negative $x$; absolute value only in the undiversified sum; the sign stays in the matrix product.

**Reference**

LO 5.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 5, §5.2 “Mapping Approaches” (undiversified formula with $|x_{i}|$, Eq. 5.7); column label $|x| V$ from Table 5.7 (LO 5.g). Bank LO 5.d Q284 maps a short bond to negative PVs. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 d, where it is Q7 of 10.

a.reason: Undiversified VaR adds absolute individual VaRs (GARP formula); diversified VaR keeps the sign of each position inside Equation 5.7.

b.reason: Error type: sign error in the undiversified sum. Netting −0.1880+1.5795 = 1.3915 ignores the absolute value. Correct only if the undiversified VaR were defined on signed positions, which GARP’s $|x_{i}|$ rules out.

c.reason: Error type: sign error in the diversified VaR. Treating the short as long makes the cross term +0.5048: $\sqrt{3.0350}$ = 1.742. Correct if both positions were long.

d.reason: Error type: correlation misuse (cross term dropped). $\sqrt{0.\text{0353 + 2}.4948}$ = 1.591. Correct only if the 1-year and 5-year zeros were uncorrelated.

questions.question:
A model validator at a Singapore bank compares VaR figures for a SGD 150 million bond portfolio. The portfolio’s duration is 3.40 years and the average maturity of its principal repayments is 4.0 years. The 3-year and 4-year vertex VaRs are 1.46% and 1.94%. Cash-flow mapping gives an undiversified VaR of SGD 2.38 million and a diversified VaR of SGD 2.29 million. Taking the duration-mapped VaR (linear interpolation between vertices) as the comparison, how much of its gap to the diversified cash-flow VaR is due to risk not being linear in maturity, and how much to correlations below one?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question says otherwise, VaR figures are monthly at the 95% confidence level, “vertex VaR” means the VaR of a zero-coupon bond return at that maturity, expressed as a percentage of value, and a vertex is a maturity for which the risk system provides volatilities and correlations.

options.text: Non-linearity SGD 90,000; correlations SGD 98,000
Non-linearity SGD 530,000; correlations SGD 90,000
Non-linearity SGD 98,000; correlations SGD 90,000
Non-linearity SGD 242,000; correlations SGD 90,000

questions.solution:
**Reading the result against duration mapping**

Stem in one line: SGD 150m, duration 3.40, vertex VaRs 1.46% and 1.94%, cash-flow VaRs 2.38 and 2.29; split the gap.

**Concept and theory**

GARP compares its cash-flow result with the duration-mapped VaR: the diversified VaR of USD 2.57 million “is slightly less than the duration VaR of USD 2.70 million. This difference is due to two factors. First, risk measures are not perfectly linear with maturity. . . Second, correlations are below unity, which reduces risk even further.” The bridge has two legs:

$$\begin{aligned}\underbrace{\text{Duration VaR} - \text{Diversified VaR}}_{\text{total gap}} &= \underbrace{(\text{Duration VaR} - \text{Undiversified VaR})}_{\text{non-linearity of risk in maturity}} \\ &\quad + \underbrace{(\text{Undiversified VaR} - \text{Diversified VaR})}_{\text{correlations below one}}\end{aligned}$$

The first leg compares two figures that both assume perfect correlation, so it isolates the effect of interpolating risk at one maturity instead of using each vertex’s own risk. The second leg isolates diversification. Duration VaR uses linear interpolation: $V$ ($D$) = $V_{a}$ + ($V_{b} - V_{a}$)($D - a$) for vertices $a < D < b$ one year apart.

**Applying it to this question**

$V$ (3.40) = 1.46% + (1.94% − 1.46%)(3.40 − 3) = 1.46% + 0.192% = 1.652%

Duration VaR = 150 × 1.652% = 2.478

Non-linearity = 2.478 − 2.38 = 0.098 = SGD 98,000

Correlations = 2.38 − 2.29 = 0.090 = SGD 90,000

Total gap = 2.478 − 2.29 = 0.188 = SGD 188,000

The 4.0-year average principal maturity belongs to principal mapping and is irrelevant here.

**Fragile fact.** Non-linearity = duration minus undiversified; correlations = undiversified minus diversified. Both cash-flow figures sit below the duration figure here.

**Reference**

LO 5.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 5, §5.2 “Mapping Approaches” (comparison paragraph after Table 5.4; duration interpolation 0.987 + (1.484 − 0.987) × (2.733 − 2) = 1.351%). GARP quirk: the printed sentence places “(USD 2.70 − USD 2.63 million)” next to the USD 60,000 correlation figure; the arithmetic (2.70−2.63 = 0.07; 2.63−2.57 = 0.06) shows USD 70,000 is non-linearity (“differences in yield volatility”) and USD 60,000 correlations, and the arithmetic is used. Schweser LO 5.d gives duration (2.768) and cash-flow figures from its own example but not the split. Boundary: the attribution is also tested under LO 5.c; here it is used to read the cash-flow mapping output.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 d, where it is Q8 of 10.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap of the two legs. The two correct amounts are attached to the wrong causes. Correct only if the cash-flow undiversified VaR were SGD 2.388 million, so that the duration-to-undiversified leg were 90,000 and the correlation leg 98,000.

b.reason: Error type: wrong input twin (principal mapping for duration mapping). 150 × 1.94% = 2.91 and 2.91 − 2.38 = 0.53. Correct if the comparison were principal mapping at the 4-year average maturity.

c.reason: It follows GARP’s two-factor split: non-linearity is duration VaR minus undiversified VaR, correlations is undiversified minus diversified (GARP’s USD 70,000 and USD 60,000).

d.reason: Error type: interpolation weight reversed. 1.46% + 0.48% × 0.60 = 1.748%, so 150 × 1.748% = 2.622 and 2.622 − 2.38 = 0.242. Correct only if the duration were 3.60 years.

questions.solution:
**Reading the cash-flow mapping output table**

Stem in one line: BRL table of PVs, individual VaRs and component VaRs at 1Y, 3Y, 5Y; which commentary statement is right?

**Concept and theory**

GARP Table 5.4 has the layout of this output. The “Individual VaR” column is $x_{i}\times V_{i}$; its total is the undiversified VaR. The last column is the component VaR (labelled $x$∆VaR in GARP, computed “as explained earlier” in the readings on VaR decomposition). Component VaRs add up to the diversified VaR: in Table 5.4 they are 0.45, 0.05, 0.08, 0.09 and 1.90, totalling USD 2.57 million; in the swap example (Table 5.10) the component VaR column “adds up to a total diversified VaR”.

| Column | Sum equals | Correlation assumption |
|---|---|---|
| Individual VaR $x_{i}V_{i}$ | Undiversified VaR | All correlations one |
| Component VaR | Diversified VaR | Actual correlation matrix |

**Applying it to this question**

Undiversified VaR = 0.744 + 0.740 + 2.790 = 4.274

Diversified VaR = 0.649 + 0.730 + 2.764 = 4.142

Diversification benefit = 4.274 − 4.142 = 0.132

Shares of diversified VaR: 1Y 0.649/4.142 = 15.7%, 3Y 17.6%, 5Y 66.7%, although the 1Y vertex carries 120/250 = 48% of the PV.

**Fragile fact.** Individual VaRs add to undiversified; component VaRs add to diversified. Large PV does not mean large risk at a short vertex.

LO 5.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, Table 5.4 (individual and component VaR columns); §5.3 Table 5.10 text for component additivity (LO 5.g section, used only for the statement). The component VaR formula itself comes from an earlier reading and is not needed; the column is given. Schweser LO 5.d does not show component VaR (GARP-only). No conflict.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap (component for individual). 4.142 is the diversified figure; the undiversified VaR is 4.274. Correct if it said “sum of the individual VaRs, BRL 4.274 million”.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (individual for component) with a false reason. Individual VaRs ignore correlations entirely; their sum is undiversified. Correct if “diversified” read “undiversified” and the reason were dropped.

c.reason: Error type: scope error (PV size taken as risk). Risk per unit of PV rises with maturity (0.62% at 1Y against 3.10% at 5Y), so the 5Y vertex dominates with 66.7%. Correct only if all vertex VaRs were equal.

d.reason: Component VaRs sum to the diversified VaR (GARP Table 5.4), and the gap to the sum of individual VaRs is the reduction from correlations “below unity”.

| Instrument | Position | Face (USD m) | Annual coupon | Maturity |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bond M | Long | 20 | 5.0% | 1 year |
| Bond K | Long | 10 | 6.0% | 1.5 years |
| Note N | Short | 5 | zero-coupon | 1 year |

What is the net position mapped onto the 12-month vertex?

options.text: USD 14.496 million
USD 15.127 million
USD 15.893 million

questions.solution:
**Net position at the 12-month vertex, semiannual convention**

Stem in one line: long M (1y, 5% semiannual), long K (1.5y, 6% semiannual), short N (1y zero); find the PV mapped to 12 months.

**Concept and theory**

Mapping sums every instrument’s cash flow on a date, long flows positive and short flows negative, then discounts the net flow at that vertex’s zero rate under the stated compounding convention. GARP’s swap example works with “PV of net cash flows” at each vertex, and the question bank’s LO 5.d item decomposes a semiannual bond into 6- and 12-month zeros with the rate halved per period. With annualized rates $s_{t}$ compounded semiannually:

$x_{t}$ = $\frac{\sum_{j} CF_{j,t}}{\text{(1 +} s_{t}/\text{2)}^{2t}}$

where $t$ is in years, $CF_{j,t}$ is instrument $j$’s signed cash flow at $t$, and 2$t$ is the number of half-year periods.

**Applying it to this question**

M at 12 months = 20 × (1 + 0.05/2) = 20.50

K at 12 months (coupon only) = 10 × 0.06/2 = 0.30

N at 12 months (short) = −5.00

Net $CF_{1}$ = 20.50 + 0.30 − 5.00 = 15.80

(1 + $\text{0.044/2)}^{2}$ = $\text{1.022}^{2}$ = 1.044484

$x_{1}$ = 15.80/1.044484 = 15.127 USD million

The 6- and 18-month rates are not needed for this vertex.

**Fragile fact.** Shorts net against longs on the same vertex; semiannual means $s/$2 per period and 2$t$ periods. (Annual compounding gives 15.134, close to but not equal to the answer.)
