questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Swiss private bank is preparing a training note for newly hired analysts on how the bank measures the risk of a CHF bond mandate relative to its benchmark index. Let $x$ be the vector of the portfolio’s positions on the term-structure vertices, $x_{0}$ the vector of the index’s positions on the same vertices, Σ the covariance matrix of vertex returns and $\alpha$ the standard normal deviate for the chosen confidence level. Which of the following statements should the note include?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, positions are market values mapped onto zero-coupon vertices, and VaR figures are monthly at the 95% confidence level.

options.text: Tracking error VaR equals $\alpha\sqrt{\text{(}x - x_{0}\text{)}^{'}\Sigma \text{(}x - x_{0}\text{)}}$, the VaR of the deviation between the portfolio’s and the index’s vertex positions.
Tracking error VaR equals $\alpha\sqrt{x^{'}\Sigma x} - \alpha\sqrt{x^{'}_{0}\Sigma x_{0}}$, the portfolio’s absolute VaR minus the index’s absolute VaR.
Tracking error VaR equals $\alpha\sqrt{x^{'}\Sigma x \text{+} x^{'}_{0}\Sigma x_{0}}$, combining the portfolio’s and the index’s variances on the vertices.
Tracking error VaR equals the index’s absolute VaR scaled by the ratio of the portfolio’s duration to the index’s duration.

questions.solution:
**What tracking error VaR measures**

Stem in one line: which formula and description of tracking error VaR belong in the training note?

**Concept and theory**

Many portfolios are not judged on their absolute gain or loss but on how they do relative to a benchmark index. A bond fund that loses 3% in a month when its index loses 3.2% has done well. The risk that matters for such a mandate is the risk of the difference between the portfolio and the index. GARP: “we provide a practical fixed-income example where we compute VaR in relative terms, that is, relative to a performance benchmark.”

VaR mapping makes this easy. Map the portfolio onto the term-structure vertices to get a position vector $x$; map the index onto the same vertices to get $x_{0}$. The difference $x - x_{0}$ is itself a portfolio (long where the fund is overweight, short where it is underweight). Its VaR is the tracking error VaR (GARP Eq. 5.8):

TE-VaR = $\alpha\sqrt{\text{(}x - x_{0}\text{)}^{'} \Sigma \text{ (}x - x_{0}\text{)}}$

where $x$ = portfolio positions (market values) at each vertex, $x_{0}$ = index positions at the same vertices, Σ = covariance matrix of vertex returns over the horizon, and $\alpha$ = standard normal deviate for the confidence level (about 1.65 at 95%).

|  | Absolute VaR | Tracking error VaR |
|---|---|---|
| Position vector | $x$ | $x - x_{0}$ |
| Question answered | How much can the portfolio lose? | How far can it fall behind the index? |
| Index itself | USD 1.99m (GARP Table 5.5) | USD 0.00 |

**Applying it to this question**

The note must say two things: the vector inside the quadratic form is the difference of positions, and the result is the VaR of that deviation. Only A has both.

**Fragile fact.** TE-VaR is the VaR of the difference in positions, never the difference of two VaRs.

**Reference**

LO 5.f: “Explain how VaR can be calculated and used relative to a performance benchmark.” GARP Ch. 5, §5.2 Mapping Fixed-Income Portfolios, “Benchmarking”, Eq. 5.8 (garbled in the extract; notation confirmed from the question bank’s LO 5.f solutions). Schweser Reading 5, “Benchmarking a Portfolio”. Difference: Schweser also calls TE-VaR “the difference between the VaR of the target portfolio and the benchmark portfolio”; GARP’s definition (VaR of the deviation) is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 f, where it is Q1 of 11.

a.reason: GARP §5.2 Benchmarking: “Define the new vector of positions for this portfolio as $x$ and for the index as $x_{0}$. The VaR of the deviation relative to the benchmark is Tracking Error VaR = $\alpha\sqrt{\text{(}x - x_{0}\text{)}^{'}\Sigma \text{(}x - x_{0}\text{)}}$.” Schweser: “The VaR of the deviation between the two portfolios is referred to as a tracking error VaR.”

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (difference of VaRs for VaR of the difference). VaR is not additive: a portfolio can have the same absolute VaR as the index but a completely different maturity profile and so a large tracking error. GARP Table 5.5 shows it: portfolio 5 has absolute VaR USD 1.71m versus USD 1.99m (a gap of 0.28) but TE-VaR USD 0.81m. Schweser’s loose phrase “the difference between the VaR of the target portfolio and the benchmark portfolio” invites this error. B would be correct only for a stem asking how much lower or higher the portfolio’s absolute risk is than the index’s.

c.reason: Error type: dropped term (and wrong sign). Expanding the correct form gives $x^{'}$Σ$x$ + $x^{'}_{0}$Σ$x_{0} -$ 2$x^{'}$Σ$x_{0}$. C drops the covariance term, which is exactly what makes a well-matched portfolio’s TE-VaR small. C would be correct only if portfolio and index returns were uncorrelated and the sum of their variances were wanted.

d.reason: Error type: scope error (single duration factor). Scaling by durations treats all yield moves as parallel, the very thing benchmarking at the vertex level is designed to go beyond; a duration-matched portfolio would get TE-VaR zero. D would describe a crude duration-based relative risk estimate, not TE-VaR.

A portfolio manager at an Australian superannuation fund is starting a benchmarking exercise by building a two-bond tracking portfolio for an AUD government bond index. The tracking portfolio must have the same market value and the same duration as the index, using only a 3-year zero and an 8-year zero. Index data:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Market value of the index | AUD 150 million |
| Face value of the index | AUD 160 million |
| Duration of the index | 5.40 years |
| Average maturity of the index | 6.20 years |

Which of the following is closest to the market values to be held in the two zeros?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, positions are market values mapped onto zero-coupon vertices, and VaR figures are monthly at the 95% confidence level.

options.text: 3-year zero AUD 72.0 million; 8-year zero AUD 78.0 million
3-year zero AUD 78.0 million; 8-year zero AUD 72.0 million
3-year zero AUD 54.0 million; 8-year zero AUD 96.0 million
3-year zero AUD 83.2 million; 8-year zero AUD 76.8 million

questions.solution:
**Building the duration-matched tracking portfolio**

Stem in one line: AUD 150m index (face 160m), duration 5.40, average maturity 6.20; match with 3-year and 8-year zeros.

**Concept and theory**

Benchmarking starts by building a simple portfolio that matches the index on the first-order risk. Schweser: “The first step in the benchmarking process is to match the duration with two zero-coupon bonds.” GARP: “The rightmost columns in the table display the positions of two-bond portfolios with duration matched to that of the index. Since no zero-coupon has a maturity of exactly 4.62 years, the closest portfolio consists of two positions, each in a 4- and a 5-year zero.” Two conditions fix two unknowns:

Market value: $x_{1}$ + $x_{2}$ = $W$

Duration: $\frac{x_{1}T_{1} \text{+} x_{2}T_{2}}{W}$ = $D$

where $W$ = market value of the index, $D$ = its duration, $T_{1} < D < T_{2}$ = maturities of the two zeros (a zero’s duration equals its maturity), and $x_{1}, x_{2}$ = market values held in each zero. Solving:

$w_{1}$ = $\frac{x_{1}}{W}$ = $\frac{T_{2} - D}{T_{2} - T_{1}} , w_{2}$ = 1 $- w_{1}$

The zero closer to $D$ gets the larger weight. Mapping preserves market value, so $W$ is the market value, not the face value.

**Applying it to this question**

$w_{3Y}$ = $\frac{8 - 5.40}{8 - 3}$ = $\frac{2.60}{5}$ = 0.52

$x_{3Y}$ = 0.52 × 150 = AUD 78.0 million

$x_{8Y}$ = 150 − 78.0 = AUD 72.0 million

Check: $D$ = $\frac{78.\text{0(3) + 72}.\text{0(8)}}{150}$ = $\frac{\text{234 + 576}}{150}$ = 5.40

The fund holds AUD 78.0m in the 3-year zero and AUD 72.0m in the 8-year zero: same value and duration as the index, ready for the tracking error VaR to be measured.

**Fragile fact.** The weight on the short zero is ($T_{2} - D$)/($T_{2} - T_{1}$): distance from the far end. Use market value and duration, never face value or average maturity.

**Reference**

LO 5.f (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, “Benchmarking” (Table 5.5, portfolio 1). Schweser Reading 5, “Benchmarking a Portfolio” (Figures 5.7 and 5.8, missing in the extract; text describes the 23%/77% 4-year/5-year split). Difference: Schweser’s example uses duration 4.77 and 23%/77%; GARP uses 4.62 and USD 38m/62m. Version difference; method identical.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 f, where it is Q2 of 11.

b.reason: It is the unique split that preserves market value and matches the index duration, as in GARP’s 4-year/5-year portfolio (USD 38m/62m for duration 4.62).

c.reason: Error type: wrong input twin (average maturity for duration). (8−6.20)/5 = 0.36, 0.36 × 150 = 54.0. Average maturity is what principal mapping uses (LO 5.c), not the duration match. C would be correct if the index duration were 6.20 years.

d.reason: Error type: wrong input twin (face value for market value). 0.52 × 160 = 83.2, total 160. Mapping must preserve market value. D would be correct if the index’s market value were AUD 160 million.

questions.question:
The CIO of a Singapore insurer’s investment arm reviews a quarterly risk pack for an SGD bond portfolio that is managed against an SGD bond index. The pack reports, at the monthly 95% level: index absolute VaR SGD 2.05 million; portfolio absolute VaR SGD 1.80 million; tracking error VaR SGD 0.52 million. The CIO’s draft commentary contains four statements:

I. Under normal market conditions, the portfolio’s monthly shortfall relative to the index should exceed SGD 0.52 million in only about 5% of months.

II. Because the portfolio’s absolute VaR is SGD 0.25 million below the index’s, the portfolio cannot fall behind the index by more than SGD 0.25 million.

III. If the portfolio held exactly the index’s position at every vertex, its tracking error VaR would be zero while its absolute VaR would still be SGD 2.05 million.

IV. The SGD 0.52 million figure bounds the deviation from the index in stressed markets as well as in normal markets.

Which of the statements are accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, positions are market values mapped onto zero-coupon vertices, and VaR figures are monthly at the 95% confidence level.

options.text: I only
I and IV only
I and III only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
**Reading a tracking error VaR in a risk pack**

Stem in one line: index VaR 2.05, portfolio VaR 1.80, TE-VaR 0.52 (SGD m); which commentary statements are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

TE-VaR is a VaR, so it inherits VaR’s meaning, applied to the relative P&L (portfolio minus index). At 95% over a month, it is the relative shortfall that should be exceeded only 5% of the time. GARP, interpreting its USD 0.43m figure: “the maximum deviation between the index and the portfolio is at most USD 0.43 million under normal market conditions. This potential shortfall is much less than the USD 1.99 million absolute risk of the index.” Three features follow:

| Feature | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Quantile, not a cap | Exceeded with probability 1− confidence (5% here) |
| Normal market conditions | Built on the normal covariance matrix; not a stress bound |
| Depends on $x - x_{0}$ only | Holding the index gives TE-VaR 0, absolute VaR unchanged |

**Applying it to this question**

I: correct reading of a 95% monthly quantile of relative shortfall under normal markets. True.

II: uses the gap between two absolute VaRs (2.05 − 1.80 = 0.25) as a bound on relative loss. False. III: with $x$ = $x_{0}$, ($x - x_{0}$) = 0 so TE-VaR is zero, while absolute VaR is the index’s 2.05. GARP Table 5.5 shows exactly this in its index column (absolute VaR USD 1.99m, TE-VaR USD 0.00). True.

IV: extends the bound to stressed markets. False.

So I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** “At most X under normal market conditions” at the stated confidence: a quantile of relative shortfall, not a guaranteed cap and not a stress figure.

**Reference**

LO 5.f (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, “Benchmarking” (interpretation of USD 0.43m; Table 5.5 index column). Schweser Reading 5, “Benchmarking a Portfolio”. No conflict on interpretation.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 f, where it is Q3 of 11.

a.reason: **I only.** Error type: scope error (rejecting III by confusing relative and absolute risk). A candidate who thinks holding the index “still has risk” rejects III; it does, but only absolute risk. A would be correct if III said the absolute VaR would also be zero.

b.reason: **I and IV.** Error type: scope or condition error (“normal market conditions” dropped). TE-VaR is built from the normal-period covariance matrix and is exceeded 5% of the time even then; in stress, correlations along the curve can break down. B would be correct if IV said “in normal markets”.

c.reason: Statements I and III follow from GARP’s interpretation (“at most . . . under normal market conditions”) and from Table 5.5’s zero TE-VaR for the index itself.

d.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: sibling swap (difference of VaRs for VaR of the difference). The portfolio can trail the index by much more than 0.25; the reported TE-VaR is 0.52. D would be correct if relative risk were the difference of absolute VaRs, which GARP Table 5.5 disproves.

| Vertex | VaR (%) | $\frac{\text{Position (CAD million)}}{\text{Index Portfolio}}$ | $\frac{\text{Correlation}}{\text{3Y 7Y 15Y}}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| 3Y | 1.40 | 90.0 100.0 | 1.00 |
| 7Y | 3.05 | 60.0 70.0 | 0.94 1.00 |
| 15Y | 5.60 | 50.0 30.0 | 0.86 0.97 1.00 |
| Total |  | 200.0 200.0 |  |

Which of the following is closest to the monthly 95% tracking error VaR of the portfolio?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, positions are market values mapped onto zero-coupon vertices, and VaR figures are monthly at the 95% confidence level.

options.text: CAD 0.51 million
CAD 0.66 million
CAD 1.54 million
CAD 0.72 million

questions.solution:
**Computing tracking error VaR on three vertices**

Stem in one line: CAD index 90/60/50 and portfolio 100/70/30 on 3Y/7Y/15Y, with vertex VaR (%) and correlations; find the monthly 95% TE-VaR.

**Concept and theory**

Tracking error VaR is the VaR of a portfolio of differences. Once both the portfolio and the index are mapped onto the same vertices, subtract them vertex by vertex to get $d$ = $x-x_{0}$: positive where the fund is overweight, negative where it is underweight. Then apply the ordinary delta-normal VaR machinery to $d$ (GARP Eq. 5.8):

TE-VaR = $\alpha\sqrt{\text{(}x - x_{0}\text{)}^{'} \Sigma \text{ (}x - x_{0}\text{)}}$

In GARP’s tables each vertex comes with a “VaR (%)” figure, $V_{i}$ = $\alpha\sigma_{i}$, which already contains the normal deviate and the vertex volatility. Writing Σ in terms of volatilities and the correlation matrix $R$, the same quantity becomes

TE-VaR = $\sqrt{\text{(}d ◦ V \text{)}^{'} R \text{(}d ◦ V \text{)}},$ ($d ◦ V$ $\text{)}_{i}$ = $d_{i}V_{i}$

which is exactly how GARP computes a diversified VaR: “we premultiply and postmultiply the matrix by the dollar amounts ($xV$ ) at each vertex. Taking the square root, we find a diversified VaR measure.” Symbols: $x_{i}$ = portfolio market value at vertex $i$; $x_{0,i}$ = index market value at vertex $i$; $d_{i}$ = $x_{i} - x_{0,i}$; $V_{i}$ = monthly 95% VaR of the vertex zero as a fraction of value; $R$ = correlation matrix of vertex returns. Because $V_{i}$ already embeds $\alpha$, no further 1.65 multiplier is applied. Signs matter: an underweight is a short position in the difference portfolio, so cross-terms between an overweight and an underweight on highly correlated vertices are negative and offset each other.

**Applying it to this question**

$d$ = $x - x_{0}$ = (100 − 90, 70 − 60, 30 − 50) = (+10, +10, −20) CAD m

$d ◦ V$ = (10 × 0.0140, 10 × 0.0305, −20 × 0.0560) = (0.140, 0.305, −1.120)

Own terms = $\text{0.140}^{2}$ + $\text{0.305}^{2}$ + $\text{1.120}^{2}$ = 0.019600 + 0.093025 + 1.254400 = 1.367025

3Y–7Y = 2(0.94)(0.140)(0.305) = +0.080276

3Y–15Y = 2(0.86)(0.140)(−1.120) = −0.269696

7Y–15Y = 2(0.97)(0.305)(−1.120) = −0.662704

($d ◦ V$ $\text{)}^{'}R$($d ◦ V$ ) = 1.367025 + 0.080276 − 0.269696 − 0.662704 = 0.514901

TE-VaR = $\sqrt{0.514901}$ = 0.7176 ≈ CAD 0.72 million

The “Total” row (both CAD 200m) is irrelevant to the answer: equal market values do not make the tracking error small. Meaning: under normal market conditions the portfolio should trail the index by more than CAD 0.72 million in only about one month in twenty. For comparison, the absolute VaRs are CAD 5.76m (index) and CAD 5.10m (portfolio).

**Fragile fact.** Keep the minus sign on underweights, and do not multiply by 1.65 again: the vertex VaR (%) already contains $\alpha$.

**Reference**

LO 5.f (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, “Benchmarking”, Eq. 5.8; computational device (premultiply and postmultiply $R$ by $xV$ ) from the same section’s cash-flow-mapping VaR table (USD 200 million portfolio). Equation 5.8 is garbled in the GARP extract and Schweser’s formula image is missing; notation confirmed from the question bank’s LO 5.f worked solutions. No conflict on method.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 f, where it is Q4 of 11.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (difference of VaRs for VaR of the difference). Portfolio absolute VaR $\sqrt{\text{(}x ◦ V \text{)}^{'}R\text{(}x ◦ V \text{)}}$ = 5.0955; index absolute VaR 5.7550; \|5.0955 − 5.7550\| = 0.6595 ≈ 0.66. VaR is not additive, so this gap is not the risk of the deviation. It would be correct for a stem asking by how much the portfolio’s absolute VaR is lower than the index’s.

It would be correct if the portfolio were overweight by CAD 10m, 10m and 20m at the three vertices (a portfolio of CAD 240m).

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, positions are market values mapped onto zero-coupon vertices, and VaR figures are monthly at the 95% confidence level.

questions.solution:
**Why a duration-matched portfolio still has tracking error**

Stem in one line: a GBP fund claims its value- and duration-matched two-zero portfolio has zero TE-VaR; the system disagrees.

**Concept and theory**

Duration is one number. Matching it equalises the portfolio’s and the index’s sensitivity to a parallel shift of the curve. But the term structure also twists and bends. An index spread across many maturities and a tracking portfolio concentrated on two vertices respond differently to those nonparallel moves, so their returns still differ. GARP’s verdict after Table 5.5: “The remaining tracking error is due to nonparallel moves in the term structure.” And the lesson: “This example demonstrates that duration hedging only provides a first approximation to interest-rate risk management. If the goal is to minimize tracking error relative to an index, it is essential to use a fine decomposition of the index by maturity.”

| Yield-curve move | Duration-matched portfolio | Cash-flow-matched portfolio |
|---|---|---|
| Parallel shift | Hedged | Hedged |
| Slope or curvature change | Not hedged | Largely hedged |

**Applying it to this question**

The manager matched market value and duration, which removes only parallel-shift exposure. A positive TE-VaR is exactly what GARP expects (USD 0.43m for its first duration-matched portfolio). The fix is to bring the portfolio’s cash flows closer to the index’s, maturity by maturity.

**Fragile fact.** Duration hedges parallel shifts; TE-VaR left after duration matching comes from nonparallel shifts.

**Reference**

LO 5.f (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, “Benchmarking” (closing paragraphs). Schweser Reading 5, “Benchmarking a Portfolio” (“due to nonparallel shifts in the term structure of interest rates”). No conflict. The “fine decomposition by maturity” wording is GARP’s.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 f, where it is Q5 of 11.

a.reason: Error type: absolute claim. It promises that duration and value matching eliminate tracking error; GARP Table 5.5 shows five duration-matched portfolios with TE-VaR from USD 0.16m to 0.81m. It would be correct only if yield curves moved in parallel.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (specific risk from LO 5.b). The vertices are zero-coupon government risk factors; GARP attributes the residual to nonparallel term-structure moves, not issue-specific risk, and more bonds at the same duration can still sit far from the index’s cash flows (the barbell has the highest TE-VaR). It would be correct for a question about the residual of a portfolio of individual credits mapped onto a general factor.

c.reason: C names the right residual source (nonparallel moves) and GARP’s remedy (fine decomposition by maturity, matching cash flows).

d.reason: Error type: polarity flip. It reverses which move duration hedges (parallel, not nonparallel) and so names the wrong residual; GARP’s remedy is a maturity decomposition, not a further single summary statistic. It would be correct only with “parallel” and “nonparallel” swapped back.

questions.solution:
**Choosing the tracking portfolio with the lowest TE-VaR**

Stem in one line: EUR 200m index heavy at 1Y and 10Y; four duration-matched two-zero candidates; which has the lowest TE-VaR?

**Concept and theory**

All duration-matched candidates hedge parallel shifts equally. What separates them is how much of the index’s cash-flow profile they replicate, because the residual comes from nonparallel moves that hit different maturities differently. GARP: portfolio 3 “comes the closest to approximating the cash-flow positions in the index, which has the greatest weight on the 2-year vertex. The TE-VaR is reduced further to USD 0.16 million.” Schweser Key Concepts: “The tracking error VaR is smallest for portfolios most closely matched based on cash flows.” Absolute VaR is a separate quantity and is not the selection criterion here.

**Applying it to this question**

Where is the index? EUR 60m at 1Y and EUR 66m at 10Y: 63% of its value sits on two vertices. A rough gauge of mismatch is the gross deviation $\sum_{i} |x_{i} - x_{0,i}|$ (not the TE-VaR itself, but it shows how far each candidate’s cash flows sit from the index’s):

| Candidate | Where it puts its value | Gross deviation (EUR m) |
|---|---|---|
| W | 1Y 94.2; 10Y 105.8 (the index’s two heaviest vertices) | 148.0 |
| X | 1m 162.0; 30Y 38.0 (no index cash flows there) | 400.0 |
| Y | 5Y 124.0; 7Y 76.0 | 348.0 |
| Z | 5Y 169.6; 10Y 30.4 | 315.2 |

W: deviations −10 (6m), +34.2 (1Y), −16, −12, −12, −14 (2Y to 7Y), +39.8 (10Y), −10 (20Y), total 148.0. Only W holds the 1Y and 10Y vertices together, so its cash flows best approximate the index’s and its TE-VaR should be lowest. The absolute VaR column is a trap: it points to X.

**Fragile fact.** With duration fixed, the lowest TE-VaR goes to the pair that sits on the index’s largest cash flows, not the pair nearest the duration and not the pair with the lowest absolute VaR.

**Reference**

LO 5.f (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, “Benchmarking” (portfolios 2 to 5, Table 5.5). Schweser Reading 5, “Benchmarking a Portfolio” and Key Concepts LO 5.f. No conflict. The gross-deviation column is a teaching gauge only, not a source measure.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 f, where it is Q6 of 11.

a.reason: W is the candidate whose cash flows sit on the index’s heaviest vertices, which is GARP’s and Schweser’s stated criterion for the lowest tracking error.

b.reason: **X, barbell.** Error type: sibling swap (minimum absolute VaR for minimum TE-VaR). X has the lowest absolute VaR (EUR 4.22m) because correlations fall between distant maturities, but its cash flows sit where the index has none. GARP: “minimizing absolute market risk is not the same as minimizing relative market risk.” It would be correct if the question asked for the lowest absolute VaR.

c.reason: Error type: scope error (bracketing the duration as tightly as possible). The two zeros nearest 5.76 years replicate duration with the least spread, but the index’s value is at 1Y and 10Y, not at 5Y to 7Y; Y leaves the 1Y and 10Y exposure entirely unmatched. It would be correct for an index whose cash flows were concentrated around 5 to 7 years.

d.reason: Error type: scope error (matching one heavy vertex is not matching the profile). Z touches the 10Y vertex but, to hit the duration, it must put EUR 169.6m at 5Y where the index holds 12 and only 30.4 at 10Y against 66, and nothing at 1Y. It would be correct if the index were concentrated at 5Y and 10Y.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Brazilian pension fund compares duration-matched tracking portfolios for a BRL bond index. A barbell of 1-month bills and 30-year zeros shows the lowest absolute VaR of all candidates but also the highest tracking error VaR. Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, positions are market values mapped onto zero-coupon vertices, and VaR figures are monthly at the 95% confidence level.

options.text: The barbell has a shorter duration than the other candidates, which lowers its absolute VaR, and that duration gap to the index raises its tracking error VaR.
Correlations decline between distant maturities, which lowers the barbell’s absolute VaR, but its cash flows sit far from the index’s, so nonparallel moves cause large deviations.
Correlations rise between distant maturities, which lowers the barbell’s absolute VaR, but its 30-year zero has the largest VaR percentage, which raises its tracking error VaR.
Correlations decline between distant maturities, which lowers the barbell’s absolute VaR, and its high tracking error VaR means it will underperform the index in most months.

questions.solution:
**Lowest absolute VaR, highest tracking error: the barbell**

Stem in one line: why does a duration-matched barbell of 1-month bills and 30-year zeros have the lowest absolute VaR but the highest TE-VaR?

**Concept and theory**

Two different questions, two different answers. Absolute risk of a duration-matched pair falls as the two legs move further apart, because the correlation between their returns falls: the legs diversify each other. GARP: “As correlations decrease for more distant maturities, we should expect that a duration-matched portfolio should have the lowest absolute risk for the combination of most distant maturities, such as a barbell portfolio of cash and a 30-year zero.” Relative risk depends on how far the portfolio’s cash flows sit from the index’s. The barbell’s sit at the two extremes, where the index holds almost nothing, so nonparallel moves open a wide gap. GARP Table 5.5: portfolio 5 has absolute VaR USD 1.71m (lowest) and TE-VaR USD 0.81m (highest). “However, minimizing absolute market risk is not the same as minimizing relative market risk.”

|  | Driver | Barbell outcome |
|---|---|---|
| Absolute VaR | Correlation between the two legs | Low (distant legs, low correlation) |
| TE-VaR | Distance from the index’s cash flows | High (cash flows at the extremes) |

**Applying it to this question**

The explanation needs both halves with the right direction: correlations decline with distance (low absolute VaR), and the cash flows sit far from the index’s (high TE-VaR under nonparallel moves). Only B has both.

**Fragile fact.** Correlations decrease for more distant maturities: that lowers the barbell’s absolute VaR, not its TE-VaR.

**Reference**

LO 5.f (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, “Benchmarking” (portfolio 5 and the paragraph after Table 5.5). Schweser Reading 5, “Benchmarking a Portfolio” (Portfolio E). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 f, where it is Q7 of 11.

a.reason: Error type: scope or condition error. Every candidate is duration-matched, so the barbell has the same duration as the index; there is no duration gap to explain either number. It would be correct only if the barbell had not been duration-matched.

b.reason: It restates GARP’s two reasons: falling correlations for distant maturities and the mismatch of cash flows relative to the index.

c.reason: Error type: polarity flip. Correlations fall, not rise, between distant maturities; rising correlation would remove the diversification that lowers absolute VaR. The second half (largest VaR (%) at 30 years) is true but is not why TE-VaR is high. It would be correct with “decline” in place of “rise” and a cash-flow-mismatch reason.

d.reason: Error type: scope error (a tail quantile read as a forecast of direction). The first half is right, but TE-VaR measures how large a deviation can be at the stated confidence, not that the portfolio will lag in most months; deviations can go either way. It would be correct if it said the barbell’s potential deviation from the index is the largest.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Japanese asset manager selects a duration-matched tracking portfolio for a JPY bond index whose monthly 95% absolute VaR is JPY 2.40 billion. The mandate is to minimize tracking error. Candidates (index duration 6.1 years):

| Candidate | Zeros held | Tracking error VaR (JPY bn) |
|---|---|---|
| P1 | 4-year and 8-year | 0.62 |
| P2 | 2-year and 10-year | 0.38 |
| P3 | 3-month bills and 30-year | 0.88 |

P3 has the lowest absolute VaR of the three. Which of the following is closest to the variance improvement, relative to the index, of the candidate the manager should select?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, positions are market values mapped onto zero-coupon vertices, and VaR figures are monthly at the 95% confidence level.
questions.solution:
**Variance improvement of the selected tracking portfolio**

Stem in one line: JPY index VaR 2.40bn; TE-VaRs 0.62, 0.38, 0.88 for P1, P2, P3; mandate minimises tracking error.

**Concept and theory**

Once a tracking portfolio is chosen, how much of the index’s risk has it neutralised? GARP: “Relative to the original index, the tracking error can be measured in terms of variance reduction, similar to an $R^{2}$ in a regression.” Because VaR is proportional to standard deviation, a ratio of VaRs squared is a ratio of variances:

Variance improvement = 1 $- \left( \frac{\text{TE-VaR}}{\text{VaR}_{\text{index}}} \right)^{2}$

where TE-VaR = VaR of the deviation $x - x_{0} \text{and VaR}_{\text{index}}$ = absolute VaR of the index at the same confidence and horizon. (TE-VaR$/\text{VaR}_{\text{index}}$)$^{2}$ is the share of index variance left unexplained. GARP’s example: 1 − $\text{(0.43/1.99)}^{2}$, printed as 95.4% (95.3% from the rounded inputs).

**Applying it to this question**

The mandate is to minimise tracking error, so select P2 (lowest TE-VaR, JPY 0.38bn). P3’s lowest absolute VaR and the index duration are irrelevant.

$\frac{\text{TE-VaR}}{\text{VaR}_{\text{index}}}$ = $\frac{0.38}{2.40}$ = 0.158333

$\text{(0.158333)}^{2}$ = 0.025069

Variance improvement = 1 − 0.025069 = 0.974931 ≈ 97.5%

P2 removes about 97.5% of the index’s variance; about 2.5% remains as tracking risk from nonparallel moves.

**Fragile fact.** Square the ratio, and pick the candidate by the mandate (lowest TE-VaR), not by the lowest absolute VaR.

**Reference**

LO 5.f (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, “Benchmarking” (variance improvement, 95.4%). Schweser Reading 5, “Benchmarking a Portfolio” (formula image missing; confirmed from the question bank’s LO 5.f solutions). Difference: GARP prints 95.4%; its rounded inputs give 95.3%. Not material.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 f, where it is Q8 of 11.

a.reason: Error type: dropped term (the square). 1 − 0.38/2.40 = 1 − 0.158333 = 0.841667. It would be correct only if the measure were defined on VaR (standard deviation) rather than variance.

b.reason: Error type: wrong input twin (lowest absolute VaR candidate for lowest TE-VaR candidate). Using P3: 0.88/2.40 = 0.366667, squared 0.134444, 1 − 0.134444 = 0.865556. It would be correct if the mandate were to minimise absolute risk and P3 were chosen.

c.reason: It applies GARP’s squared variance-improvement formula to the portfolio chosen under the mandate, the one with the lowest tracking error.

d.reason: Error type: intermediate result. 0.025069 is the squared ratio, the variance not explained. It would be correct for a stem asking what share of the index variance remains as tracking risk.

questions.question:
A risk committee member at a UK asset manager must approve tracking portfolios for two clients that share the same gilt index as reference. Fund X has an absolute VaR budget and wants the lowest absolute risk. Fund Y is an index-tracking mandate and wants the lowest risk relative to the index. All candidates are duration-matched to the index (monthly 95% VaR, GBP million):

| Candidate | Zeros held | Yield (%) | Absolute VaR | Tracking error VaR |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| P1 | 4-year and 6-year | 4.15 | 3.10 | 0.52 |
| P2 | 2-year and 10-year | 4.08 | 2.95 | 0.24 |
| P3 | 1-year and 15-year | 4.02 | 2.80 | 0.37 |
| P4 | 1-month and 30-year | 4.30 | 2.42 | 1.05 |

Which pairing of fund and candidate is most appropriate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, positions are market values mapped onto zero-coupon vertices, and VaR figures are monthly at the 95% confidence level.

options.text: Fund X: P4; Fund Y: P2
Fund X: P2; Fund Y: P4
Fund X: P4; Fund Y: P4
Fund X: P2; Fund Y: P2

questions.solution:
**Matching the tracking portfolio to the mandate**

Stem in one line: Fund X wants the lowest absolute risk, Fund Y the lowest risk relative to the gilt index; four duration-matched candidates.

**Concept and theory**

Benchmarking gives every candidate two risk numbers, and the right one depends on the mandate. An investor judged on total P&L (an absolute VaR budget) cares about absolute VaR, $\alpha\sqrt{x^{'}\Sigma x}$. An index-tracking investor is judged on the deviation from the index and cares about TE-VaR, $\alpha\sqrt{\text{(}x - x_{0}\text{)}^{'}\Sigma \text{(}x - x_{0}\text{)}}$. GARP stresses that the two rankings differ: the barbell has the lowest absolute risk but the highest tracking error, so “minimizing absolute market risk is not the same as minimizing relative market risk.”

**Applying it to this question**

Fund X (absolute budget): lowest absolute VaR is P4, GBP 2.42m. Fund Y (index tracker): lowest TE-VaR is P2, GBP 0.24m. P4 is the 1-month/30-year barbell, consistent with GARP: lowest absolute, highest relative risk (1.05). The yield column is irrelevant to either mandate.

**Fragile fact.** Absolute mandate: lowest $\sqrt{x^{'}\Sigma x}$. Index mandate: lowest $\sqrt{\text{(}x - x_{0}\text{)}^{'}\Sigma \text{(}x - x_{0}\text{)}}$. The barbell wins the first and loses the second.

**Reference**

LO 5.f (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, “Benchmarking” (absolute versus relative risk). Schweser Reading 5, “Benchmarking a Portfolio” (“minimizing the absolute VaR . . . is not the same as minimizing the tracking error”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 f, where it is Q9 of 11.

a.reason: Each fund gets the portfolio that minimises the risk measure its mandate is judged on, as GARP distinguishes absolute from relative risk.

b.reason: Error type: role misassignment. Both selections are right portfolios but given to the wrong funds: P2 is the tracker’s choice and P4 the absolute-risk choice. It would be correct if Fund X were the index tracker and Fund Y had the absolute budget.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap (minimum absolute VaR for minimum TE-VaR). It assumes the lowest absolute VaR also minimises tracking error; P4 in fact has the highest TE-VaR. It would be correct if minimising absolute risk did minimise relative risk.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap in the other direction (minimum TE-VaR for minimum absolute VaR). P2’s absolute VaR (2.95) is higher than P3’s and P4’s. It would be correct if Fund X’s budget were set relative to the gilt index.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at an Indian bank is reviewing a validation report on how the treasury benchmarks an INR bond portfolio against an index using the variance improvement measure. The report contains four statements:

I. The variance improvement measures the share of the index’s variance removed by the tracking portfolio, in the same way as an $R^{2}$ in a regression.

II. For a duration-matched portfolio, a variance improvement of about 95% is in line with the explanatory power of the first factor in the variance decomposition of the term structure, the remainder reflecting nonparallel moves.

III. The variance improvement is computed as one minus the ratio of tracking error VaR to the index’s absolute VaR; squaring is unnecessary because both figures are already VaRs.

IV. The variance improvement is maximized by choosing, among duration-matched portfolios, the one with the lowest absolute VaR.

Which of the statements are correct?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, positions are market values mapped onto zero-coupon vertices, and VaR figures are monthly at the 95% confidence level.

options.text: I only
I and II only
I, II and III only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
**Variance improvement: meaning and computation**

Stem in one line: which statements in a validation report on the variance improvement measure are correct?

**Concept and theory**

The variance improvement converts a TE-VaR into a share of index risk removed:

2

1 $- \left( \frac{\text{TE-VaR}}{\text{VaR}_{\text{index}}} \right)$

GARP: “the tracking error can be measured in terms of variance reduction, similar to an $R^{2}$ in a regression.” Squaring is required because VaR scales with standard deviation, so the squared VaR ratio is the variance ratio. GARP then reads its 95.4% figure as “in line with the explanatory power of the first factor in the variance decomposition”, and attributes what is left to the term structure’s shape: “the remaining tracking error is due to nonparallel moves in the term structure.”

**Applying it to this question**

I: share of index variance removed, like $R^{2}$. True.

II: about 95% for a duration-matched portfolio, in line with the first factor; the rest from nonparallel moves. True (GARP).

III: no square needed. False: VaRs are standard-deviation units.

IV: maximised by the lowest absolute VaR. False: it is maximised by the lowest TE-VaR, and the lowest absolute VaR (barbell) usually has the highest TE-VaR.

So I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Square the ratio of TE-VaR to the index’s VaR; the result is the variance explained, not the variance left.

**Reference**

LO 5.f (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, “Benchmarking”. Schweser Reading 5, “Benchmarking a Portfolio” (R-squared analogy; formula image missing). Statement II’s first-factor reading is GARP-only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 f, where it is Q10 of 11.

a.reason: **I only.** Error type: definition gap (rejecting II). A candidate who knows only the formula may doubt the first-factor reading, but GARP states it explicitly. It would be correct if II had tied 95% to the second factor or to specific risk.

b.reason: I and II restate GARP’s $R^{2}$ analogy and its first-factor interpretation; III and IV each contain one error.

c.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: dropped term (the square). With GARP’s numbers, 1 − 0.43/1.99 = 78.4% instead of 1 − $\text{(0.43/1.99)}^{2}$ = 95.3%. It would be correct if the measure were defined on standard deviations.

d.reason: **I, II and IV.** Error type: sibling swap (absolute VaR for TE-VaR). For a fixed index VaR the measure depends only on TE-VaR; in GARP Table 5.5 the lowest absolute VaR (portfolio 5, 1.71) gives the lowest variance improvement, 1 − $\text{(0.81/1.99)}^{2}$ = 83.4%. It would be correct if IV said “lowest tracking error VaR”.

questions.question:
A model validator at a US asset manager is reviewing the benchmarking module of a USD fixed-income risk system. The module maps both the index and each portfolio onto a single duration factor and, as a result, reports a tracking error VaR close to zero for every duration-matched portfolio, whatever its maturity profile. Which recommendation is the validator most likely to make?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, positions are market values mapped onto zero-coupon vertices, and VaR figures are monthly at the 95% confidence level.

options.text: Replace duration mapping of the index with principal mapping at the index’s average maturity, which captures the timing of redemption payments.
Compute each absolute VaR on the full vertex grid and report the difference between the portfolio’s and the index’s absolute VaR as the tracking error VaR.
Assume perfect correlation across all vertices, as when each zero is shocked by its own VaR, so that the reported tracking error VaR is conservative.
Map the index and the portfolio onto the full set of vertices and compute the VaR of the vertex-by-vertex position differences using the vertex covariance matrix.

questions.solution:
**Fixing a benchmarking module that maps onto one duration factor**

Stem in one line: a USD risk system maps index and portfolios onto a single duration factor and reports near-zero TE-VaR for every duration-matched portfolio.

**Concept and theory**

If the index and the portfolio are each reduced to one duration number, the only risk the system can see is a parallel shift, and any duration-matched portfolio looks perfectly hedged. GARP’s Table 5.5 shows why that is wrong: five portfolios with the same duration of 4.62 years have TE-VaRs from USD 0.16m to 0.81m. The cure is to map both onto the full set of vertices and take the VaR of the deviation vector (Eq. 5.8), $\alpha\sqrt{\text{(}x - x_{0}\text{)}^{'}\Sigma \text{(}x - x_{0}\text{)}}$, with the full vertex covariance matrix. GARP: “duration hedging only provides a first approximation . . . If the goal is to minimize tracking error relative to an index, it is essential to use a fine decomposition of the index by maturity.”

**Applying it to this question**

The symptom (TE-VaR near zero whatever the maturity profile) is the signature of a single-factor mapping. The recommendation must (1) add maturity detail and (2) compute the VaR of the position differences with correlations below one. Only D does both.

**Fragile fact.** Same duration does not mean same risk relative to the index: TE-VaR needs the vertex-by-vertex differences and correlations below one.

**Reference**

LO 5.f (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 5, §5.2, “Benchmarking” (Eq. 5.8, Table 5.5, closing paragraph). Schweser Reading 5, “Benchmarking a Portfolio”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-5 f, where it is Q11 of 11.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap (principal mapping from LO 5.c). Principal mapping puts all value at the average maturity: still one point on the curve, even cruder than duration mapping, so it would still miss nonparallel moves. It would be correct for a question on the simplest of the three fixed-income mapping methods.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (difference of VaRs for VaR of the difference). Even with full-grid absolute VaRs, subtracting them ignores the covariance between portfolio and index; a portfolio with nearly the index’s absolute VaR can have a large TE-VaR (GARP portfolio 4: absolute VaR 1.94 against the index’s 1.99, a gap of 0.05, yet TE-VaR 0.20). It would be correct for reporting the gap in absolute risk.

c.reason: Error type: scope error (stress-testing assumption from LO 5.e). Shocking each zero by its VaR reproduces the undiversified VaR, valid only under perfect correlation. Perfect correlation along the curve is the same as allowing only parallel moves, so it would not reveal the nonparallel tracking error. It would be correct for a question on how mapping supports stress testing.

d.reason: It implements GARP Eq. 5.8 on a fine maturity decomposition, which is what captures nonparallel moves.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Singapore insurer is preparing an induction slide on financial correlation risk for newly hired analysts. The draft contains four statements:

I. Financial correlation risk is the risk of financial loss due to adverse movements in correlation between two or more variables.

II. The variables involved need not be financial; correlation risk can involve economic or political events.

III. Correlation risk arises only when correlations rise; a fall in correlation between two variables cannot by itself cause a loss.

IV. In a severe systemic crisis correlations typically fall, which is why portfolios of low or negatively correlated assets suffered unexpected losses in 2007 to 2009.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
I, II and IV only
I only

questions.solution:
**Defining financial correlation risk**

Stem in one line: which induction-slide statements about the definition of financial correlation risk are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

A correlation measures how two variables move together. A position whose value depends on that co-movement carries a hidden exposure: if the co-movement changes, the value changes even if each variable’s own behaviour does not. GARP §8.3 defines financial correlation risk as the risk of financial loss due to adverse movements in correlation between two or more variables. Three features of this definition matter for the exam:

| Feature | What the reading says |
|---|---|
| Direction | The word is adverse, not increasing. Whether a rise or a fall hurts depends on the position; the CDS spread is even non-monotonic in correlation (Q8). |
| Variables | Any financial variables, and also nonfinancial ones such as economic or political events (exporters and the euro in 2012; airlines and Middle East tension). |
| Crisis behaviour | An increase in correlation is typical in a severe, systemic crisis; in 2007 to 2009 assets that had been negatively or lowly correlated declined together. |

GARP’s chapter summary repeats that correlation risk is the risk of loss from adverse movements in correlation between two or more variables, which can be financial (correlated defaults of two debtors) or nonfinancial (political tension and an exchange rate).

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I is the GARP definition. True. Statement II matches GARP §8.3 and Schweser (“between financial or nonfinancial assets”). True. Statement III turns “adverse” into “increasing”. The definition is direction-neutral, and the reading’s CDS example shows that over strongly negative correlations a further fall in correlation lowers the CDS spread, which lowers the value of protection already bought. False. Statement IV reverses the crisis behaviour: correlations rise in a systemic crisis (“Suddenly everything was highly correlated”). False. So I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Adverse movement, not upward movement; variables can be nonfinancial; correlations rise in systemic crises.

**Reference**

LO 8.a (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 8, §8.3 What is Financial Correlation Risk? and Summary. Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.1. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 a, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: GARP §8.3: correlation risk is the risk of financial loss due to adverse movements in correlation between two or more variables, and it can also involve nonfinancial variables such as economic or political events. Schweser LO 8.a gives the same definition (“financial or nonfinancial assets”).

b.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: absolute-claim trap. Statement III promises that only rising correlation can hurt. That is true for some positions (a long CDS hedge in the positive-correlation region) but not as a definition. III would be acceptable if it read “for a CDS buyer facing a positively correlated counterparty, rising correlation causes a loss”.

c.reason: **I, II and IV.** Error type: polarity flip, “rise” becomes “fall”. GARP: during 2007 to 2009 financial assets and markets worldwide became highly correlated. IV would be right if it said correlations typically increase in a systemic crisis.

d.reason: **I only.** Error type: scope error, the definition narrowed to financial variables. Rejecting II means believing correlation risk excludes economic or political variables. D would be correct only for a definition restricted to “financial variables”, which neither source uses.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Canadian asset manager is reviewing three CAD-reported client losses that a training note uses as illustrations of financial correlation risk:

- Case 1: an investor in Mexican government bonds lost money in 2012 when Greek bond prices fell during the Greek crisis.
- Case 2: an investor in commodities lost money when interest rates rose.
- Case 3: an investor in an insured bond lost money because the bond issuer and the bond insurer ran into difficulty together.

Which of the following correctly states the sign of the correlation that produced the loss in Cases 1, 2 and 3, respectively?

options.text: Negative; negative; positive
Positive; negative; positive
Positive; positive; positive
Positive; negative; negative

questions.solution:
**Sign of the correlation in the reading’s examples**

Stem in one line: Mexican bonds and Greek prices; commodities and rising rates; issuer and insurer: what sign of correlation produced each loss?

**Concept and theory**

A Pearson correlation $\rho$ lies between −1 and +1. Positive means the variables tend to move in the same direction; negative means opposite directions. A correlation produces a loss when the variable you do not hold moves in a way that, through the correlation, drags the variable you do hold against you. GARP §8.3 gives three financial-variable illustrations:

| Example | Sign | Loss channel |
|---|---|---|
| Mexican and Greek bonds (2012) | Positive | Greek bond prices fall; Mexican bond prices fall with them. |
| Commodity prices and interest rates | Negative | Rates rise; commodity prices fall; commodity investors lose. |
| Bond issuer and bond insurer | Positive | Issuer and insurer deteriorate together; the insurance fails when needed (the CDS example). |

**Applying it to this question**

Case 1: the trigger was a fall in Greek prices and the loss was a fall in Mexican prices: same direction, positive. Case 2: the trigger was a rise in rates and the loss came from a fall in commodity prices: opposite directions, negative. Case 3: issuer and insurer in difficulty together: positive default correlation, the wrong-way risk structure of GARP Figure 8.1.

**Fragile fact.** Mexican/Greek: positive. Commodities/rates: negative. Issuer/insurer: positive (wrong-way risk). Read the trigger and the loss direction before assigning the sign.

**Reference**

LO 8.a. GARP Ch. 8, §8.3 What is Financial Correlation Risk? Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.1 (Schweser gives the Mexican/Greek and commodity/rate examples but not the issuer/insurer example; that one is GARP-only, illustrated by the CDS in Figure 8.1). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 a, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: **Negative; negative; positive.** Error type: polarity flip on Case 1. A negative correlation would have made Mexican bonds rise as Greek bonds fell, a gain. A would be right if Case 1 described a Mexican investor who lost when Greek prices rose.

b.reason: GARP §8.3: the positive correlation between Mexican and Greek bonds can hurt Mexican bond investors if Greek prices decrease; the negative correlation between commodity prices and interest rates can hurt commodity investors if rates rise; the correlation between a bond issuer and a bond insurer can hurt the bond investor, and with a positive default correlation the investor has wrong-way risk.

c.reason: **Positive; positive; positive.** Error type: polarity flip on Case 2, usually from the belief that correlation risk always means positive correlation. With a positive correlation, rising rates would lift commodity prices. C would be right if the investor had lost when rates fell.

d.reason: **Positive; negative; negative.** Error type: polarity flip on Case 3. A negative issuer/insurer correlation would make it likely that only one of the two fails, so the insurance would usually pay. D would describe an investor who lost because the insurer failed while the issuer survived (the repurchase scenario of Q8), not a joint failure.

questions.question: A risk consultant engaged by the INR treasury of an Indian conglomerate is classifying the group’s exposures. She separates correlation risk that involves only financial variables from correlation risk that involves nonfinancial variables such as economic or political events. Which of the following exposures is least likely to be classified, in line with the reading, as correlation risk involving a nonfinancial variable?

options.text: The group’s export arm is hurt when rising sovereign debt in its main export market coincides with a weakening of that market’s currency.
The group’s airline subsidiary is hurt when geopolitical tension in the Middle East drives up the oil price.
The group’s commodity trading book is hurt when interest rates rise, given the negative correlation between commodity prices and interest rates.
The group’s manufacturing exports are hurt when GDP growth slows in the United States, because economies and markets are correlated worldwide.

questions.solution:
**Correlation risk with nonfinancial variables**

Stem in one line: which group exposure is least likely to count as correlation risk involving a nonfinancial variable?

**Concept and theory**

GARP §8.3 builds the definition in two steps. First, the variables “can comprise any financial variables”, illustrated by bond prices across countries and by commodity prices against interest rates. Second, correlation risk “can also involve variables that are non-financial as economic or political events”. The three nonfinancial illustrations are:

| Nonfinancial driver | Who is hurt and how |
|---|---|
| Rising sovereign debt and currency value | Exporters: in Europe in 2012 a decreasing euro hurt US exporters. |
| Geopolitical tension (Middle East) | Airlines, through an increasing oil price. |
| Slowing US GDP | Asian and European exporters and investors, since economies and markets are correlated worldwide. |

**Applying it to this question**

Options A, B and D map one-for-one onto the three nonfinancial illustrations (sovereign debt and currency; geopolitical tension and oil; US GDP). Option C is the commodity/interest-rate example, which both sources present as a financial correlation risk: an interest rate and a commodity price are both financial variables, even though rates feel “economic”.

**Fragile fact.** Interest rates and commodity prices are financial variables in this reading; sovereign debt, GDP and geopolitical events are the nonfinancial ones.

**Reference**

LO 8.a. GARP Ch. 8, §8.3 What is Financial Correlation Risk? Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.1. Schweser phrases the nonfinancial examples as affecting “nonfinancial assets”; GARP speaks of nonfinancial variables. Same substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 a, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: This is GARP’s sovereign debt and currency example (Europe 2012, US exporters), explicitly nonfinancial. Error that would lead a candidate to choose it: sibling swap, treating a currency value as purely financial and overlooking that the driver is the economic variable, sovereign debt. A would be the answer if the stem asked for a financial-only exposure such as two bond prices.

b.reason: GARP’s political example: Middle East tension raises the oil price and hurts airlines. Error that leads to it: treating the oil price as the driver rather than the political event. B would be the answer only if the stem had asked which exposure involves a commodity price.

c.reason: Schweser LO 8.a: “An example of financial correlation risk is the negative correlation between interest rates and commodity prices.” GARP §8.3 lists it among the financial-variable examples, before turning to nonfinancial variables.

d.reason: GARP’s macroeconomic example: a slowing US GDP hurts Asian and European exporters. Error that leads to it: assuming GDP is a market variable. D would be the answer if the stem asked which example is about worldwide market linkage between financial assets only.

questions.question:
A model validator at a German bank is building an inventory of the EUR-denominated correlation measures in use across the bank and must label each one as a static or a dynamic financial correlation:

I. A value-at-risk model that answers the question of the maximum loss of correlated assets in a portfolio with a certain probability for a given time period.

II. The copula approach for CDOs, measuring the default correlations between all the assets in the CDO, typically 125, for a certain time period.

III. The Heston (1993) model, which correlates the Brownian motions $dz_{1}$ and $dz_{2}$ of two assets through a correlation parameter $\rho$.

IV. The binomial default correlation model of Lucas (1995), which measures the probability of two assets defaulting together within a short time period.

V. A pairs-trading strategy run by the bank’s equity desk.

Which of the measures should the validator label as static financial correlations?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and IV only
I, II, III and IV only
I, II, IV and V only

questions.solution:
**Static versus dynamic financial correlations**

Stem in one line: VaR, CDO copula, Heston, Lucas binomial, pairs trading: which are static?

**Concept and theory**

GARP §8.2 gives a heuristic (non-mathematical) split of financial correlations:

| Type | Definition | Examples in the reading |
|---|---|---|
| Static | How two or more financial assets are associated at a certain point in time or within a certain time period. | Bond prices and their yields at a point in time; classic VaR; copula approach for CDOs (default correlations of all assets, typically 125, for a certain period); Lucas (1995) binomial default correlation model (probability of two assets defaulting together within a short period; a special case of the Pearson model). |
| Dynamic | How two or more financial assets move together in time. | Pairs trading; deterministic correlation approaches such as the Heston (1993) model; stochastic correlation processes. |

The test is not whether a model contains a fixed parameter but whether it describes association over one window or co-movement through time.

**Applying it to this question**

I (VaR): static. II (CDO copula for a certain time period): static. III (Heston): dynamic, a deterministic correlation approach that correlates Brownian motions in time. IV (Lucas binomial, defaulting together within a short period): static. V (pairs trading): dynamic. Static set: I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Static = association over a period (VaR, CDO copula, Lucas binomial). Dynamic = co-movement in time (pairs trading, Heston, stochastic correlation).

**Reference**

LO 8.a. GARP Ch. 8, §8.2 What are Financial Correlations? Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.1. GARP adds a fourth static example (bond prices and yields at a point in time) that Schweser omits; not used here. No conflict on the items tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 a, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: **I and II only.** Error type: scope error on IV. “Within a short time period” is still a single window, so the Lucas model is static. A would be correct if IV described a model of how default correlation evolves through time.

b.reason: GARP §8.2 lists exactly VaR, the CDO copula approach and the binomial default correlation model of Lucas (1995) as static examples, and pairs trading and the Heston model as dynamic. Schweser agrees (static: VaR, CDO copula correlations, binomial default correlation model; dynamic: pairs trading, deterministic approaches, stochastic processes).

c.reason: **I, II, III and IV.** Error type: sibling swap. Heston has a constant parameter $\rho$, which tempts candidates to call it static, but it correlates the Brownian motions in time; GARP files it under deterministic, dynamic approaches. C would be correct if III described a one-period correlation estimate.

d.reason: **I, II, IV and V.** Error type: sibling swap on V. Pairs trading uses a historical relationship but trades on how the pair moves through time, so it is dynamic (Schweser Module Quiz 8.1 makes the same point). D would be correct if V were a one-off correlation estimate used to set a static hedge ratio.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Swiss hedge fund is explaining dynamic financial correlations to a new analyst on the CHF equity desk. She writes four statements:

I. If the returns of assets X and Y have moved highly correlated in time and X now performs poorly relative to Y, a pairs trader buys X and sells Y, expecting the gap to narrow.

II. In the Heston model the Brownian motions are linked by $dz_{1}$($t$) = $\rho dz_{2}$($t$) + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dz_{3}$($t$), so that $dz_{1}$ and $dz_{2}$ are correlated in time with parameter $\rho$.

III. Stochastic correlation processes are time-dependent by construction, and they suit correlations that behave randomly and unpredictably.

IV. Because correlations behave randomly and unpredictably, the reading recommends modelling them as deterministic functions of time rather than as stochastic processes.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and III only
II and III only
I, II, III and IV
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
**How dynamic correlations work**

Stem in one line: pairs trading direction, the Heston equation, stochastic correlation and a “deterministic” recommendation: which are correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP §8.2 gives three dynamic examples, each describing co-movement through time:

1. Pairs trading: assume returns $x$ and $y$ have moved highly correlated in time. If $X$ now performs poorly with respect to $Y$ , $X$ is bought and $Y$ is sold, in the expectation that the gap will narrow.
2. Deterministic correlation approaches, for example the Heston (1993) model, which correlates the Brownian motions of the two assets:

$dz_{1}$($t$) = $\rho dz_{2}$($t$) + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dz_{3}$($t$)

where $dz_{1}$ and $dz_{2}$ are the Brownian increments of assets 1 and 2, $dz_{3}$ is an independent Brownian increment, and $\rho$ is the correlation parameter. The weight $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}$ keeps the variance of $dz_{1}$ equal to that of a standard Brownian increment.

3. Stochastic correlation processes: correlations behave randomly and unpredictably, so it is a good idea to model them as a stochastic process. Such processes are time-dependent by construction and can replicate correlation properties well.

**Applying it to this question**

I matches the pairs-trading description (buy the laggard, sell the leader, bet on convergence). True. II is the Heston equation with the square root correctly placed. True. III matches the stochastic correlation description. True. IV reverses the conclusion: randomness and unpredictability are GARP’s reason for stochastic, not deterministic, modelling. False. Correct set: I, II and III.

**Fragile fact.** Pairs trading buys the underperformer and sells the outperformer. Heston uses $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}$. Randomness motivates stochastic correlation.

**Reference**

LO 8.a. GARP Ch. 8, §8.2 What are Financial Correlations? (dynamic examples 1 to 3). Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.1 lists the three dynamic examples without detail, so the pairs-trade direction and the Heston equation are GARP-only. The Heston equation is garbled in the GARP OCR (“$V$ (1 $- p$2)”); it is reconstructed as $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}$, consistent with GARP’s statement that $dz_{1}$ and $dz_{2}$ are correlated with parameter $\rho$.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 a, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: **I and III only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement (notation doubt). Candidates who expect $\sqrt{\rho}$ or a (1 $- \rho^{2}$) term without the root reject II. A would be correct if II had written the second coefficient as (1 $- \rho^{2}$) without the square root.

b.reason: **II and III only.** Error type: polarity flip on the pairs trade. A candidate who believes you buy the outperformer and sell the laggard rejects I. B would be correct if I read “buys $Y$ and sells $X$”, which bets on divergence, not convergence.

c.reason: **I, II, III and IV.** Error type: sibling swap, deterministic for stochastic. IV would be correct if it read “as stochastic processes”.

d.reason: GARP §8.2, dynamic financial correlations, items 1 to 3, as summarised above.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at an Australian superannuation fund holds the AUD equivalent of 50 million of bonds issued by a eurozone sovereign. To hedge, the fund has bought a five-year CDS on the sovereign from a large bank headquartered in the same country, at a fixed spread of 120 basis points. Assume recovery and accrued interest are zero. Over the next quarter, the default correlation between the sovereign and the bank rises from 0.2 to 0.6, while the sovereign’s own default probability is unchanged. Which of the following best describes the effect on the fund?

options.text: The present value of the CDS to the fund falls and the fund suffers a paper loss, because a joint default of the sovereign and the bank has become more likely.
The present value of the CDS to the fund rises and the fund gains, because a higher correlation raises the probability that the protection will be triggered.
The present value of the CDS to the fund is unchanged, because the CDS spread is determined only by the default probability of the reference entity.
The present value of the CDS to the fund falls, but the wrong-way risk created by the higher correlation is borne by the bank as CDS seller, not by the fund.

questions.solution:
**CDS hedge when reference/counterparty correlation rises**

Stem in one line: AUD fund hedges sovereign bonds with a CDS bought from a same-country bank; correlation rises from 0.2 to 0.6. Effect?

**Concept and theory**

A credit default swap transfers credit risk from the investor (CDS buyer) to a counterparty (CDS seller). The buyer pays a fixed spread $s$; if the reference entity $r$ defaults, the seller $c$ pays the notional (with zero recovery and accrued interest, the full amount invested). GARP §8.3 explains what determines $s$:

- mainly the default probability of the reference entity $r$;
- but also the joint default correlation of $r$ and $c$.

The protection pays only if $r$ defaults and $c$ survives. If the correlation between $r$ and $c$ increases, the present value of the CDS for the investor decreases and the investor suffers a paper loss. The worst case is the joint default of $r$ and $c$, in which the investor loses the entire bond investment. Over correlations from about −0.3 upward, GARP’s Figure 8.2 shows that the higher the correlation, the lower the CDS spread.

**Applying it to this question**

The move from 0.2 to 0.6 lies in the region where the spread falls as correlation rises. The sovereign’s own default probability is unchanged, so the only change is a higher probability that the bank fails alongside the sovereign. Protection bought at the old (higher) fair spread is now worth less: a paper loss for the fund. The 120 bp contract spread and the five-year tenor are not needed to sign the effect.

**Fragile fact.** Rising $\rho$($r, c$) (positive region): CDS spread down, CDS value to the buyer down, paper loss for the buyer. The buyer, not the seller, has wrong-way risk.

**Reference**

LO 8.a. GARP Ch. 8, §8.3 What is Financial Correlation Risk? and Figure 8.2. Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.1 (“A paper loss occurs if the correlation risk ... increases because the value of the CDS will decrease”). GARP’s example uses Spain and BNP Paribas, Schweser’s France and Deutsche Bank: version difference, same mechanism.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 a, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: GARP §8.3: if the correlation between the reference entity and the CDS seller increases, the present value of the CDS for the investor decreases and the investor suffers a paper loss, because an increasing $\rho$ means a higher probability of the reference asset and the counterparty defaulting together.

b.reason: Error type: polarity flip. Higher correlation does not change the sovereign’s own default probability, so it does not make the protection more likely to be triggered; it makes it more likely to be worthless when triggered. B would be correct if the stem said the sovereign’s default probability had risen with correlation unchanged.

c.reason: Error type: scope error, the second determinant dropped. GARP: the spread is “mainly” determined by the reference entity’s default probability, but “also” by the joint default correlation. C would be correct only for a CDS with a default-free seller (or fully collateralised protection).

d.reason: Error type: role misassignment. The direction (value falls) is right, but wrong-way risk is borne by the protection buyer, whose exposure to $r$ grows just as $c$ becomes less able to pay. D would be correct if it named the fund rather than the bank.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a Japanese bank is reviewing a memo from the credit desk, which holds JPY bonds of a reference entity $r$ and has hedged them by buying CDS protection from a counterparty $c$. The default correlation between $r$ and $c$ is positive. Which of the following statements in the memo is NOT correct?

options.text: If the default probabilities of $r$ and $c$ both increase, the desk’s credit exposure to $r$ increases while the likelihood that $c$ can pay the protection falls.
If the default correlation between $r$ and $c$ rose to +1, the CDS would be worth most to the desk, because the protection would then be certain to be triggered.
The CDS spread is the premium the protection buyer pays; it is approximately the yield of the risky bond minus the yield of a riskless bond.
The desk’s worst-case scenario is the joint default of $r$ and $c$, in which case it loses its entire investment in the bonds of $r$.

questions.solution:
**Wrong-way risk in a CDS hedge**

Stem in one line: credit desk hedges bonds of $r$ with CDS bought from $c$, positive correlation: which memo statement is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP §8.3 defines wrong-way correlation risk (wrong-way risk, WWR) through the CDS example: when the default correlation between the reference entity $r$ and the counterparty $c$ is positive, deterioration in $r$ tends to come with deterioration in $c$. Two things then happen at once:

| Effect | Why |
|---|---|
| Credit exposure to $r$ rises | The CDS has a higher present value to the buyer as $r$’s default probability rises. |
| Credit risk to $c$ rises | It becomes more unlikely that $c$ can pay the default insurance. |

At the extreme of perfect correlation, $\rho$ = +1, the CDS is worthless: if $r$ defaults, so does $c$. The worst case for the buyer is joint default, when the whole investment is lost. Footnote 1 of GARP defines the CDS spread $s$ as the premium or fee the buyer pays for protection, called a spread because it is approximately the yield of the risky bond minus the yield of a riskless bond.

**Applying it to this question**

A restates the two simultaneous effects. True. B claims that at $\rho$ = +1 the CDS is worth most. At $\rho$ = +1 the two default together, so the protection never pays when needed: the CDS is worthless. False, and therefore the answer. C restates footnote 1. True. D restates the worst case. True.

**Fragile fact.** $\rho$($r, c$) = +1 makes the CDS worthless, not most valuable. WWR sits with the protection buyer.

**Reference**

LO 8.a. GARP Ch. 8, §8.3 What is Financial Correlation Risk? and footnote 1. Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.1 (WWR and worst-case joint default). The $\rho$ = +1 worthlessness and the spread definition in footnote 1 are GARP-only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 a, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: True statement (GARP §8.3, WWR paragraph). It would become the answer under a role misassignment, for example if it said the seller’s exposure to $r$ increases.

b.reason: GARP §8.3: in the extreme case of a perfect correlation of 1, the CDS is worthless, because if the reference entity defaults, so will the insurance seller.

c.reason: True statement (GARP footnote 1). It would become the answer under a sibling swap, for example “approximately the yield of the riskless bond minus the yield of the risky bond” or “the premium paid by the protection seller”.

d.reason: True statement (GARP §8.3: worst case is joint default, losing the entire investment). It would become the answer under an absolute claim, for example “the worst case is limited to the premium already paid”.

questions.question: A risk consultant is presenting to the CRO of a UK insurer a chart of the fair CDS spread of a hedged GBP bond purchase plotted against the default correlation between the reference entity and the CDS seller, for correlations from −1 to +1. The CRO asks what happens to the spread as the correlation becomes more strongly negative, below roughly −0.3. Which of the following best describes the behaviour and its cause?

options.text: The spread keeps rising as correlation falls, so it is monotonic over the whole range, because joint default becomes ever less likely.
The spread increases slightly as correlation falls, because a more negative correlation lowers the probability that both parties default together.
The spread decreases slightly as correlation falls, because a more negative correlation raises the probability that both parties default together.
The spread decreases slightly as correlation falls, because one of the two is then more likely to default alone, and a seller default forces costly repurchase.

questions.solution:
**Non-monotonic CDS spread in the negative-correlation region**

Stem in one line: as reference/seller correlation falls below about −0.3, what does the CDS spread do and why?

**Concept and theory**

A relationship is monotonic if the output always moves the same way as the input rises. GARP §8.3 uses Figure 8.2 to show that the CDS spread is non-monotonic in the default correlation $\rho$ between reference entity $r$ and counterparty $c$:

| Correlation region | Spread as $\rho$ rises | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| About −0.3 to +1 | Falls | Joint default of $r$ and $c$ becomes more likely; at +1 the CDS is worthless. |
| About −1 to −0.3 | Rises slightly (equivalently, falls slightly as $\rho$ moves towards −1) | A more negative $\rho$ makes it more likely that either $r$ or $c$ defaults, not both. |

In the negative region there are two scenarios: (a) $r$ defaults and $c$ survives, so the buyer is compensated; (b) $c$ defaults and $r$ survives, so the buyer loses the protection and must repurchase it, possibly at a higher cost if $r$’s credit quality has deteriorated (GARP’s illustration: an original spread of 3% that has risen to 6%). Combined, the scenarios produce a slight decrease of the spread as correlation becomes more negative.

**Applying it to this question**

The CRO asks about correlation falling below about −0.3. In that region the spread decreases slightly as $\rho$ falls. The cause is not joint default (which is unlikely when $\rho$ is negative) but single default, and specifically the cost of replacing protection after a seller default.

**Fragile fact.** Below about −0.3: as $\rho$ falls, spread falls slightly; cause = single default and costly repurchase after a seller default. Above −0.3: as $\rho$ rises, spread falls; cause = joint default.

**Reference**

LO 8.a. GARP Ch. 8, §8.3 What is Financial Correlation Risk?, Figure 8.2. Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.1. Difference: GARP places the turning point at about −0.3 and words the effect as a slight decrease as correlation moves from −0.3 to −1; Schweser places it at −0.4 and words it as a slight increase from −1 to −0.4. Read in the same direction they agree; the turning point differs, likely a version difference. GARP used, and the stem says “roughly −0.3”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 a, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: scope error (the non-monotonic region dropped). A extends the falling-joint-default logic across the whole range. It would be correct for a chart that was monotonic, which GARP explicitly says Figure 8.2 is not.

b.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the direction. The reason given (joint default less likely) is true, but it is not the dominant effect; the spread decreases slightly as $\rho$ falls. B would be correct read in the opposite direction: as correlation rises from −1 to about −0.3, the spread increases slightly (Schweser’s wording).

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap of mechanisms. Higher joint default probability is the mechanism of the positive region. A more negative correlation lowers, not raises, the chance of joint default. C would describe the region above −0.3 if “falls” read “rises”.

d.reason: GARP §8.3: for a correlation from about −0.3 to −1 the CDS spread decreases slightly, because an increase in the negative correlation means a higher probability of either party defaulting; if the seller defaults the buyer loses the insurance and may have to repurchase it at a higher cost.
