questions.question: A member of the board risk committee at a US bank is reviewing a USD training paper that maps the areas of finance in which correlations play an important role. Which of the following statements in the paper is least accurate?

options.text: Regulation: the Basel accords have legal authority in every member country, so banks are bound to apply the correlation approaches they contain.
Trading: correlation desks at major investment banks and hedge funds try to forecast changes in correlation and to gain financially from them.
Risk management: an increase in the correlation of asset returns increases the risk of financial loss, which is often measured by VaR.
Investments: high diversification is related to low correlation, and an increase in diversification increases the return/risk ratio.

questions.solution:
**The areas of finance in which correlations appear**

Stem in one line: which area-by-area statement in a training paper is least accurate?

**Concept and theory**

GARP §8.4 (“correlations and correlation risk are everywhere in finance”) names five areas, and an entity exposed to correlation in any of them has correlation risk, the risk of a change in the correlation:

| Area | Role of correlation (area level) |
|---|---|
| Investments | Markowitz (1952) and Sharpe (1964): more diversification raises the return/risk ratio; high diversification is related to low correlation. |
| Trading | Correlation desks at major investment banks and hedge funds forecast changes in correlation and try to gain from them (every risk is also an opportunity). |
| Risk management | An increase in the correlation of asset returns increases the risk of financial loss, often measured by VaR. |
| Global financial crisis | Correlations rose sharply in 2007 to 2009 (Schweser labels this area “global markets”). |
| Regulation | Correlations are critical inputs in the Basel accords, especially for market and credit risk. None of the accords has legal authority; most countries (about 100 for Basel II) have legislated to enforce them. |

**Applying it to this question**

B, C and D restate the trading, risk-management and investment rows. A asserts that the Basel accords have legal authority in every member country. GARP says the opposite: the accords have no legal authority; national legislation enforces them. A is the least accurate statement.

**Fragile fact.** Five areas: investments, trading, risk management, the global financial crisis (Schweser: global markets), regulation. The Basel accords have no legal authority of their own.

**Reference**

LO 8.a. GARP Ch. 8, §8.3 (risk management sentence), §8.4 Motivation and Investments and Correlation, §8.5 Trading and Correlation, and the Regulation and Correlation subsection. Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.1 lists the five areas only. The regulation detail (no legal authority, about 100 countries) is GARP-only. Difference: fourth area named “the global financial crisis” (GARP) versus “global markets” (Schweser); not tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 a, where it is Q9 of 12.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Brazilian pension fund is preparing a BRL investment committee note showing how correlation affects risk-adjusted return. The proposed two-asset portfolio is:

| Asset | Weight | Average return | Volatility |
|---|---|---|---|
| X (equity fund) | 40% | 11.0% | 28.0% |
| Y (bond fund) | 60% | 6.0% | 14.0% |

The correlation between the returns of X and Y is −0.45, and the fund’s cash benchmark rate is 2.5%. Which of the following is closest to the portfolio’s return/risk ratio, defined as the portfolio average return divided by the portfolio volatility?
questions.solution:
**Return/risk ratio of a two-asset portfolio**

Stem in one line: 40% X ($\mu$ 11%, $\sigma$ 28%), 60% Y ($\mu$ 6%, $\sigma$ 14%), $\rho$ = −0.45, cash rate 2.5%: find $\mu_{P} /\sigma_{P}$ .

**Concept and theory**

Markowitz showed that correlation is the lever through which diversification reduces risk. For a portfolio of assets $X$ and $Y$ (GARP equations 8.1, 8.3 to 8.5):

$\mu_{P}$ = $w_{X} \mu_{X}$ + $w_{Y} \mu_{Y} , w_{X}$ + $w_{Y}$ = 1

$\text{COV}_{XY}$ = $\rho_{XY} \sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$

$\sigma_{P}$ = $\sqrt{w^{2}_{X} \sigma^{2}_{X} \text{+} w^{2}_{Y} \sigma^{2}_{Y} \text{+ 2}w_{X} w_{Y} \text{COV}_{XY}}$

where $w_{X} , w_{Y}$ are portfolio weights, $\mu_{X} , \mu_{Y}$ average returns, $\sigma_{X} , \sigma_{Y}$ volatilities (standard deviations of returns), $\rho_{XY}$ the Pearson correlation and $\text{COV}_{XY}$ the covariance. The reading’s risk-adjusted performance measure is the return/risk ratio $\mu_{P} /\sigma_{P}$ . Correlation does not appear in $\mu_{P}$ but does appear in $\sigma_{P}$ , so lowering $\rho$ raises the ratio (GARP Figure 8.3).

**Applying it to this question**

Formula: ratio = $\mu_{P} /\sigma_{P}$ .

$\mu_{P}$ = 0.40(11.0%) + 0.60(6.0%) = 4.40% + 3.60% = 8.00%

$\text{COV}_{XY}$ = −0.45 × 0.28 × 0.14 = −0.017640

$w^{2}_{X} \sigma^{2}_{X}$ = 0.16 × 0.0784 = 0.012544

$w^{2}_{Y} \sigma^{2}_{Y}$ = 0.36 × 0.0196 = 0.007056

2$w_{X} w_{Y} \text{COV}_{XY}$ = 2(0.40)(0.60)(−0.017640) = −0.008467

$\sigma^{2}_{P}$ = 0.012544 + 0.007056 − 0.008467 = 0.011133

$\sigma_{P}$ = $\sqrt{0.011133}$ = 10.55%

$\mu_{P} /\sigma_{P}$ = 8.00%/10.55% = 0.758

Meaning: each unit of portfolio volatility earns about 0.76 units of average return. With $\rho$ = +1 (no diversification) the same assets would give only 0.41 (option A), so the negative correlation almost doubles the risk-adjusted return. The 2.5% cash rate plays no part in the reading’s ratio.

**Fragile fact.** $\mu_{P}$ is independent of $\rho$; $\sigma_{P}$ carries 2$w_{X} w_{Y} \rho\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$ . The reading’s ratio is $\mu_{P} /\sigma_{P}$ with no risk-free deduction.

**Reference**

LO 8.a. GARP Ch. 8, §8.4 Investments and Correlation, equations 8.1 to 8.5 and Figure 8.3. Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.1, “Correlations in Financial Investments” (formula images missing in the Schweser extract; GARP equations 8.1 and 8.5 used, legible in the GARP text). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 a, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: dropped term (correlation ignored). Using the weighted-average volatility 0.40(28%) + 0.60(14%) = 19.60% gives 8.00%/19.60% = 0.408. This is the ratio for $\rho$ = +1; it would be correct if the assets were perfectly positively correlated.

b.reason: Error type: wrong input (irrelevant cash rate used). (8.00% − 2.50%)/10.55% = 0.521 is a Sharpe ratio, not the reading’s return/risk ratio. Correct if the stem had asked for the excess return per unit of volatility.

c.reason: It applies GARP equations 8.1 and 8.5 and the return/risk ratio $\mu_{P} /\sigma_{P}$ exactly as defined in the stem.

d.reason: Error type: dropped term (the factor 2 on the covariance term). $\sigma^{2}_{P}$ = 0.012544 + 0.007056 − 0.004234 = 0.015366, $\sigma_{P}$ = 12.40%, ratio 8.00/12.40 = 0.645. Correct only if the covariance term entered once, which happens for no portfolio.

questions.question:
A junior analyst at a Chinese asset manager is checking a correlation input. The year-end prices (CNY) of two assets are:

| Year-end | 2021 | 2022 | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Asset A | 100 | 95 | 120 | 135 | 120 |
| Asset B | 50 | 60 | 58 | 60 | 62 |

Returns are percentage changes, ($S_{t} -S_{t-1}$)$/S_{t-1}$, and sample statistics divide by $n-$1. A colleague has already computed the sample standard deviations of the four annual returns as 17.01% for A and 9.94% for B. Which of the following is closest to the Pearson correlation coefficient between the annual returns of A and B?
questions.solution:
**Pearson correlation from a price series**

Stem in one line: five CNY year-end prices for A and B, sample SDs 17.01% and 9.94% given: find the correlation of annual returns.

**Concept and theory**

Correlation must be computed on returns, not prices. GARP defines the return as the percentage change ($S_{t} - S_{t-1}$)$/S_{t-1}$, the sample covariance (equation 8.3) and the Pearson coefficient (equation 8.4):

$\text{COV}_{XY}$ = $\frac{1}{n - 1} \sum_{t\text{=1}}^{n}$($x_{t} - \mu_{X}$ )($y_{t} - \mu_{Y}$ )

$\rho_{XY}$ = $\frac{\text{COV}_{XY}}{\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}}$

where $x_{t}, y_{t}$ are the returns at time $t$, $\mu_{X} , \mu_{Y}$ their means, $n$ the number of returns and $\sigma_{X} , \sigma_{Y}$ the sample standard deviations (equation 8.2, also with $n -$ 1). The covariance ranges from −∞ to +∞ and is hard to interpret; dividing by $\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$ standardises it to the range −1 to +1. Numerator and denominator must use the same divisor.

**Applying it to this question**

Step 1, returns ($n$ = 4):

| Year | $r_{A}$ | $r_{B}$ | $r_{A} - \mu_{A}$ | $r_{B} - \mu_{B}$ | Product |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 2022 | −5.000% | 20.000% | −0.10676 | 0.14138 | −0.015094 |
| 2023 | 26.316% | −3.333% | 0.20640 | −0.09195 | −0.018979 |
| 2024 | 12.500% | 3.448% | 0.06824 | −0.02414 | −0.001647 |
| 2025 | −11.111% | 3.333% | −0.16787 | −0.02529 | 0.004245 |
| Mean / sum | 5.676% | 5.862% |  |  | −0.031475 |

$\text{COV}_{AB}$ = −0.031475/(4 − 1) = −0.010492

$\sigma_{A}\sigma_{B}$ = 0.1701 × 0.0994 = 0.016908

$\rho_{AB}$ = −0.010492/0.016908 = −0.621

Meaning: the annual returns of A and B are fairly strongly negatively correlated, so combining them would diversify, even though the price levels of both drifted upward together.

**Fragile fact.** Returns, not prices; covariance and standard deviations on the same ($n -$ 1) basis; covariance is unbounded, correlation is in \[−1, +1\].

**Reference**

LO 8.a. GARP Ch. 8, §8.4 Investments and Correlation, equations 8.2 to 8.4 and Table 8.1. Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.1, “Correlations in Financial Investments” (Figures 8.2 and 8.3; same $n -$ 1 convention). Difference: the worked example numbers differ between GARP (Table 8.1: $\rho$ = −0.7403) and Schweser ($\rho$ = −0.7501); version difference, method identical.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 a, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: **(+0.46).** Error type: wrong input twin (prices for returns). Correlating the five price levels gives +0.456, because both prices trend upward. Correct only if the stem had asked for the correlation of price levels, which the reading never uses.

b.reason:
**(−0.47).** Error type: divisor mismatch. Dividing the sum of products by $n$ = 4 gives a population covariance of −0.007869. Dividing that by the sample standard deviations gives

−0.007869/0.016908 = −0.465.

Correct only if the given standard deviations had also been population values.

c.reason: **(−0.01).** Error type: intermediate result. −0.0105 is the covariance, not the correlation; the standardising division by $\sigma_{A}\sigma_{B}$ is skipped.

d.reason: GARP equations 8.3 and 8.4 applied to percentage returns with the $n -$ 1 convention used for the given standard deviations.

questions.question:
The treasurer of a Singapore corporate is reviewing an SGD investment committee paper on why correlation matters for a two-asset portfolio. The paper contains four statements:

I. The portfolio average return is the weighted average of the asset returns and does not depend on the correlation, so a lower correlation raises the return/risk ratio only through a lower portfolio volatility.

II. Standard deviation is an imperfect measure of risk, because a high standard deviation may also reflect high upside potential, so it penalises possible profits.

III. In the reading’s example, a high positive correlation gives a return/risk ratio of close to 250%, whereas a high negative correlation gives a ratio of about 50%.

IV. Covariance is easy to interpret because, like the Pearson coefficient, it is bounded between −1 and +1.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I only
I, II and IV only
I and II only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
**Correlation, diversification and the return/risk ratio**

Stem in one line: which statements about $\mu_{P}$ , standard deviation as risk, the reading’s 250%/50% result and covariance are correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP calls the link between low correlation and a higher return/risk ratio one of the few “free lunches” in finance: the lower (preferably negative) the correlation of the assets, the higher $\mu_{P} /\sigma_{P}$ . It is free because $\mu_{P}$ = $w_{X} \mu_{X}$ + $w_{Y} \mu_{Y}$ contains no correlation term, while $\sigma_{P}$ does, so risk falls with no sacrifice of return. GARP’s Figure 8.3, built on Table 8.1, shows a high negative correlation giving a ratio of close to 250% and a high positive correlation giving about 50%.

Two interpretive points in GARP §8.4:

- Standard deviation as risk: “not great, but one of the best there are”. A high standard deviation may mean high upside potential, so it penalises possible profits; it also means high downside risk, which risk-averse investors dislike.
- Covariance versus correlation: covariance measures the strength of the linear relationship but takes values from −∞ to +∞, so it is hard to interpret; the Pearson coefficient is a standardised covariance between −1 and +1.

**Applying it to this question**

I: $\mu_{P}$ is a weighted average independent of $\rho$, so the ratio rises with falling $\rho$ only through $\sigma_{P}$ . True. II: GARP’s caveat on standard deviation. True. III: the extremes are reversed; 250% belongs to high negative correlation. False. IV: the bounds belong to correlation, not covariance. False. Correct set: I and II.

**Fragile fact.** Low (negative) $\rho\Rightarrow$ high $\mu_{P} /\sigma_{P}$ (close to 250% at high negative $\rho$; about 50% at high positive $\rho$). Covariance is unbounded; correlation is bounded.

**Reference**

LO 8.a. GARP Ch. 8, §8.4 Investments and Correlation, equations 8.1 to 8.5 and Figure 8.3. Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.1, “Correlations in Financial Investments” (Figure 8.4). The caveat on standard deviation (statement II) and the unbounded covariance (statement IV) are GARP-only. Difference: GARP says a high negative correlation gives a ratio of close to 250%; Schweser says a correlation of −0.9 gives a ratio greater than 250%. Minor version difference; the direction is the same.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 a, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: **I only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement (scope error). Candidates who treat standard deviation as a pure downside measure reject II. A would be correct if II claimed standard deviation captures only downside risk.

b.reason: **I, II and IV.** Error type: sibling swap, covariance given the correlation coefficient’s bounds. IV would be true with “covariance” replaced by “the Pearson correlation coefficient”.

c.reason: GARP §8.4, Investments and Correlation: equations 8.1 and 8.5, the discussion of standard deviation as risk, and Figure 8.3.

d.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: polarity flip on Figure 8.3. III would be true with “positive” and “negative” swapped.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Canadian pension fund is preparing a CAD-denominated training slide for newly hired analysts on the main reasons that Meissner gives for the 2007 to 2009 global financial crisis. The draft slide lists four candidate reasons:

I. An extremely benign economic and risk environment from 2003 to 2006, with record low credit spreads, low volatility and low interest rates.

II. A moral hazard of rating agencies, which were paid by the same companies whose assets they rated, so that many structured products received AAA ratings.

III. Growing risk aversion among traders and investors in the calm years from 2003 to 2006, which drained speculative capital from the housing and mortgage markets.

IV. A new copula correlation model, trusted naively by many investors, which could presumably correlate the $n$($n -$ 1)/2 assets in a structured product.

Which of the statements should be kept on the slide?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and IV only
I, III and IV only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
**Main reasons for the crisis**

Stem in one line: which of four candidate reasons for the 2007 to 2009 crisis are among Meissner’s main reasons?

**Concept and theory**

Meissner stresses that a crisis that brought the world financial system to a standstill “is naturally not mono-causal”. He lists six main reasons, and only after that narrows down to the correlation aspect:

|  | Main reason (GARP list) |
|---|---|
| (a) (b) (c) | An extremely benign economic and risk environment from 2003 to 2006: record low credit spreads, low volatility, low interest rates. Increasing risk-taking and speculation of traders and investors in these presumably calm times, producing a bubble in housing, mortgages (especially subprime), stocks and commodities; in 2007 US investors had borrowed 470% of US national income to invest and speculate. A new class of structured products: CDOs, CDO squared, CPDOs, CPPI, options on CDSs, credit indices. |
| (d) (e) (f) | The new copula correlation model, trusted naively, which could presumably correlate the $n$($n-$ 1)/2 assets in a structured product. A moral hazard of rating agencies, paid by the companies whose assets they rated; AAA ratings gave the illusion of low price and default risk. Risk managers and regulators who lowered their standards in light of the greed and profit frenzy. |

The logic is a chain: calm conditions encourage risk-taking; risk-taking is channelled through new products; the products are valued with a correlation model that is trusted too much; and the gatekeepers (rating agencies, risk managers, regulators) fail to stop it.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I is reason (a), almost word for word. Statement II is reason (e). Statement IV is reason (d). Statement III reverses reason (b): the calm years encouraged more risk-taking and speculation, and GARP says that around 2003 “the risk appetite of the financial markets increased” and investors speculated “especially in the real-estate market”. So I, II and IV are kept.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: calm conditions led to more risk-taking, not less. Schweser’s line that investors became “more risk-averse shortly after the internet bubble” refers to the period just after 2000, before risk appetite rose again from around 2003.

**Reference**

LO 8.b (Schweser): “Explain how correlation contributed to the global financial crisis of 2007– 2009.” GARP Ch. 8, §8.5, “The Global Financial Crises 2007 to 2009 and Correlation”, list (a) to (f). Schweser Reading 8, “Correlations During the Global Financial Crisis”. Difference: Schweser says investors became more risk-averse shortly after the internet bubble; GARP says risk appetite increased around 2003. GARP is used; this looks like Schweser compressing two time periods, not a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 b, where it is Q1 of 16.

a.reason: **I and II only.** Error type: scope error, a true reason dropped. Rejecting IV means missing that the naive trust in the copula model is itself on the list; it is the bridge to the correlation story. A would be correct only if IV said the copula model was distrusted by investors.

b.reason: GARP, “The Global Financial Crises 2007 to 2009 and Correlation”, reasons (a), (d) and (e). Schweser agrees that “the economic environment, risk attitude, new derivative products, and new copula correlation models all contributed”.

c.reason: **I, III and IV only.** Error type: polarity flip accepted (III) and a true actor reason rejected (II). III turns “increasing risk-taking” into “growing risk aversion”. C would be correct if III read “growing risk-taking and speculation” and II were false.

d.reason: **II, III and IV only.** Error type: polarity flip accepted (III) plus a true reason rejected (I). The benign 2003 to 2006 environment is the first item on GARP’s list. D would be correct only if conditions had been turbulent and investors had retreated, which is the opposite of the reading.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a Swiss private bank is reviewing a CHF credit-risk training note that attributes pre-crisis failures to specific actors. Which of the following attributions is most accurate according to the reading?

options.text: Rating agencies were paid by the investors who bought the structured products they rated, so the AAA ratings mainly reflected investor demand for assets that looked safe.
Regulators were paid by the institutions they supervised, so they approved overinvestment, and the AAA ratings that followed gave the illusion of low price and default risk.
Rating agencies were paid by the same companies whose assets they rated, so many structured products received AAA ratings and gave the illusion of low price and default risk.
Rating agencies were paid by the same companies whose assets they rated, but the AAA ratings stayed accurate because the structured products were protected by lower tranches.

questions.solution:
**Actor attribution: the rating-agency moral hazard**

Stem in one line: which attribution of a pre-crisis failure to an actor is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

A moral hazard exists when the party taking a decision does not bear its consequences, or is paid by someone who benefits from a particular outcome. Meissner’s reason (e): rating agencies were “paid by the same companies whose assets they rated. As a consequence, many structured products received AAA ratings and gave the illusion of low price and default risk.” The incentive problem sits with the issuer-pays model: the agency’s customer is the company whose product it judges.

The other gatekeepers fail differently. Reason (f): “risk managers and regulators who lowered their standards in light of the greed and profit frenzy.” Schweser: “rating agencies, risk managers, and regulators overlooked the amount of leverage individuals and financial institutions were taking on.” In the blame discussion GARP adds that “the moral hazard of the rating agencies, being paid by the same companies whose assets they rate, needs to also be addressed.”

| Actor | Failure in the reading |
|---|---|
| Rating agencies | Moral hazard: paid by the issuers whose assets they rated; AAA ratings gave an illusion of low risk |
| Risk managers, regulators | Lowered their standards; turned a blind eye; overlooked leverage |

**Applying it to this question**

Three things must be right together: the actor (rating agencies), who paid them (the issuers), and the effect (an illusion of low price and default risk). Only C has all three.

**Fragile fact.** Actor: rating agencies. Payer: the issuer. Effect: the illusion, not the reality, of low risk.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.5, “The Global Financial Crises 2007 to 2009 and Correlation”, reasons (e) and (f), and the blame paragraph. Schweser Reading 8, “Correlations During the Global Financial Crisis”. Difference: Schweser does not mention the issuer-pays moral hazard; it says rating agencies, risk managers and regulators overlooked leverage. GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 b, where it is Q2 of 16.

a.reason: Error type: role misassignment of the payer. Investors are not the agencies’ paymasters in the reading; the issuers are. A would be correct for an investor-pays rating model, which the reading does not describe.

b.reason: Error type: role misassignment of the actor. The moral hazard of being paid by the rated entity is the rating agencies’ problem; regulators “lowered their standards” and “approved the overinvestments”, but the reading never says they were paid by the institutions they supervised. B would be correct if “Regulators” read “Rating agencies” and the approval clause were removed.

c.reason: It restates reason (e) of GARP’s list exactly.

d.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the consequence. GARP says the AAA ratings gave the illusion of low price and default risk; super-senior AAA tranches later lost up to 20% of their value. D would be correct only if the ratings had proved reliable through the crisis.

questions.question:
A model validator at a Singapore bank is reviewing the copula model behind a SGD 2.0 billion synthetic CDO whose equity tranche attaches at 0% and detaches at 3%. The reference pool is being expanded from 125 to 150 assets, and the validator must state how many asset correlation pairs the copula must now quantify and manage, and how many more than before.

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Assets in the current reference pool | 125 |
| Assets in the expanded reference pool | 150 |
| Pool notional (SGD) | 2.0 billion |
| Equity tranche | 0% to 3% |

Which of the following states both figures accurately?

options.text: 11,175 pairs in total; 300 more than before
22,350 pairs in total; 6,850 more than before
11,325 pairs in total; 3,450 more than before
11,175 pairs in total; 3,425 more than before

questions.solution:
**Copula correlation pairs when the pool grows**

Stem in one line: a CDO pool grows from 125 to 150 assets; how many asset correlation pairs in total, and how many more?

**Concept and theory**

A copula model of a CDO needs a correlation for every distinct pair of assets. With $n$ assets, each asset can be paired with $n -$ 1 others, giving $n$($n -$ 1) ordered pairs; but the pair ($i, j$) is the same as ($j, i$), so each is counted twice. Diagonal terms ($i, i$) are always 1 and need no estimation.

Number of correlation pairs = $\frac{n\text{(}n - \text{1)}}{2}$

where $n$ is the number of assets in the structured product. GARP reason (d): the copula model “could presumably correlate the $n$($n -$ 1)/2 assets in a structured product. Most CDOs contained 125 assets. Hence there are 125(125 − 1)/2 = 7,750 asset correlation pairs to be quantified and managed.” The count grows roughly with $n^{2}$.

**Applying it to this question**

Original pairs = $\frac{125 \times124}{2}$ = 7,750

Expanded pairs = $\frac{150 \times149}{2}$ = 11,175

Increase = 11,175 − 7,750 = 3,425

Check by counting the new pairs directly: each of the 25 new assets pairs with the 125 existing ones (25 × 125 = 3,125), and the 25 new assets pair among themselves (25 × 24/2 = 300); 3,125 + 300 = 3,425. The SGD notional and the 0% to 3% equity tranche are irrelevant. Meaning: 20% more assets, about 44% more correlations.

**Fragile fact.** Pairs = $n$($n -$ 1)/2; 125 assets give 7,750. Do not include the diagonal and do not double-count.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.5, reason (d). Schweser Reading 8, “Correlations During the Global Financial Crisis” (“risk managers of CDOs needed to estimate and manage 7,750 correlations”). Difference: Schweser: CDOs contain “up to 125 assets”; GARP: “most” contained 125. Not material.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 b, where it is Q3 of 16.

a.reason: Error type: dropped term. The total is right, but the increase counts only pairs among the 25 new assets (25 × 24/2 = 300) and drops the 3,125 cross pairs between new and existing assets. A would be correct if the question asked how many correlations exist within the added group alone.

b.reason: Error type: dropped division by 2 (ordered pairs counted twice): 150 × 149 = 22,350 and 125 × 124 = 15,500, difference 6,850. B would be correct for the number of off-diagonal entries in the full correlation matrix.

c.reason: Error type: diagonal included, $n$($n$ + 1)/2: 150 × 151/2 = 11,325 and 125 × 126/2 = 7,875, difference 3,450. C would be correct for the number of distinct entries in the upper triangle including the diagonal of 1s, which need no estimation.

d.reason: It applies GARP’s $n$($n -$ 1)/2 count to both pools and differences them.

questions.question: The treasurer of a German Landesbank is drafting a EUR board paper on the role that correlation modelling played before the crisis. Which of the following statements about the copula correlation model is most accurate according to the reading?

options.text: It was derived by Abe Sklar in 1959 and transferred to finance by David Li in 2000, and many investors trusted it naively to manage the default correlations in CDOs.
It was derived by David Li in 1959 and transferred to finance by Abe Sklar in 2000, and many investors trusted it naively to manage the default correlations in CDOs.
It was introduced only after the crisis as part of the Basel III proposals, so it played no part in the valuation of the CDOs sold between 2003 and 2006.
It modelled the dynamic correlation of mortgage defaults through time, so its outputs updated automatically when housing prices started to level off in 2006.

questions.solution:
**The copula correlation model: origin and naive trust**

Stem in one line: most accurate statement about the copula correlation model’s role before the crisis.

**Concept and theory**

A copula joins individual (marginal) default distributions into a joint distribution, so it can express how likely assets are to default together. That is exactly what a CDO tranche price needs: whether losses reach the 3%, 7% or higher attachment points depends on how many assets default in the same scenarios. GARP: “The new copula correlation model, derived by Abe Sklar in 1959 and transferred to finance by David Li in 2000, could presumably manage the default correlations in the CDOs.” In reason (d) it is “trusted naively by many investors”. GARP’s taxonomy (LO 8.a) classifies the copula approach for CDOs as a static correlation measure: it measures default correlations between all assets in the CDO “for a certain time period”.

The words “presumably” and “naively” carry Meissner’s point: the model existed and was used before the crisis; the problem was trusting it to manage thousands of correlation pairs.

**Applying it to this question**

The discriminating facts are the attribution (Sklar derived it; Li transferred it to finance), the dates (1959, 2000) and the timing of use (before the crisis). Only A has all three.

**Fragile fact.** Sklar 1959 derived it; Li 2000 brought it to finance. It was used before the crisis; Basel III proposals later name the Gaussian copula for correlated defaults.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.5, reason (d) and the paragraph on CDO tranches; §8.2 (static correlations). Schweser Reading 8, “Correlations During the Global Financial Crisis”. GARP-only: the Sklar and Li attribution. Difference: Schweser lists the Gaussian copula among new post-crisis models; GARP shows the copula was used pre-crisis. GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 b, where it is Q4 of 16.

a.reason: It combines GARP’s attribution sentence with reason (d)’s “trusted naively”.

b.reason: Error type: role misassignment. Sklar and Li are swapped. B would be correct only with the names reversed.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap with the Basel III paragraph. GARP says that among the proposed new correlation models, “correlated defaults in a multi-asset portfolio \[are\] quantified with the Gaussian copula”, and Schweser lists the Gaussian copula among models “being developed and implemented”. But the copula model was already used to value pre-crisis CDOs (reason (d)). C would be correct for a question about which models regulators proposed after the crisis, and even then not with “played no part”.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap (static versus dynamic, LO 8.a) plus absolute claim. The copula approach for CDOs is a static correlation measure over a time period, and nothing in the reading says it updated “automatically”. D would be correct for a stochastic correlation process, which GARP lists as a dynamic approach.

questions.question:
A risk analyst at a US multi-strategy hedge fund is reconstructing a 2005-style CDO trade for a USD case study. The fund is long the equity tranche and short the mezzanine tranche of the same CDO, believing that each leg hedges the other. Notional is USD 50 million on each leg. Shortly after General Motors and Ford are downgraded to junk status, market spreads move as follows:

| Tranche | Contract spread (bps) | Market spread after downgrade (bps) |
|---|---|---|
| Equity (0% to 3%), fund long | 1,800 | 2,450 |
| Mezzanine (3% to 7%), fund short | 260 | 185 |

Which of the following best describes the mark-to-market of each leg, in running-spread terms, and the change in correlation between the assets in the CDO that is consistent with the mezzanine move?

options.text: Equity leg: 650 bps loss; mezzanine leg: 75 bps gain; consistent with a rise in correlation
Equity leg: 650 bps loss; mezzanine leg: 75 bps loss; consistent with a fall in correlation
Equity leg: 650 bps gain; mezzanine leg: 75 bps loss; consistent with a fall in correlation
Equity leg: 650 bps loss; mezzanine leg: 75 bps loss; consistent with a rise in correlation

questions.solution:
**Long equity, short mezzanine: the paper-loss mechanics**

Stem in one line: equity spread 1,800 to 2,450 bps (fund long), mezzanine 260 to 185 bps (fund short); mark-to-market of each leg and the consistent correlation move.

**Concept and theory**

A CDO is cut into tranches with different degrees of default risk. GARP: “The equity tranche holder is exposed to the first 3% of mortgage defaults, the mezzanine tranche holder is exposed to the 3 to 7% of defaults and so on.”

Position conventions (GARP footnotes 10 to 12):

|  | Long equity tranche | Short mezzanine tranche |
|---|---|---|
| Credit view | “Assuming credit risk”: hurt by credit deterioration | “Short credit”: benefits from credit deterioration |
| Spread Paper loss when | Receives the high equity contract spread Market spread rises above the spread received | Pays the fairly low mezzanine contract spread Market spread falls below the spread paid |

How correlation moves the spreads (GARP, Figure 8.7 discussion): if default correlation increases, the equity tranche spread decreases; “a lower correlation lowers the mezzanine tranche spread”. In May 2005 the bonds in the CDOs became less correlated, so the equity spread rose and the mezzanine spread fell, which is the worst combination for long equity plus short mezzanine.

**Applying it to this question**

Equity: market − received = 2,450 − 1,800 = 650 bps ⇒ receiving 650 bps below market: loss Mezzanine: paid − market = 260 − 185 = 75 bps ⇒ paying 75 bps above market: loss

A fall in the mezzanine spread is what GARP links to lower correlation. The USD 50 million notional is irrelevant to the direction. Meaning: the “hedge” lost on both legs at once.

**Fragile fact.** Long equity receives spread and loses when spreads widen; short mezzanine pays spread and loses when spreads tighten. Lower correlation: equity spread up, mezzanine spread down.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.5, Figure 8.7 discussion and footnotes 10 to 12. Schweser Reading 8, “Correlations During the Global Financial Crisis”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 b, where it is Q5 of 16.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the short leg and on correlation (the hedging assumption). A short mezzanine position gains only if the mezzanine spread rises above the spread paid, which GARP links to higher correlation. A would be correct if the mezzanine market spread had risen from 260 to 335 bps.

b.reason: GARP: the equity spread increased sharply, so “the spread that the hedge fund received in the original transaction was now significantly lower than the current market spread, resulting in a paper loss”; and the funds “lost on their short mezzanine tranche position, since a lower correlation lowers the mezzanine tranche spread”.

c.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the long leg. A wider market spread does not raise the fund’s income: its contract spread is fixed at 1,800 bps, so it is now under-compensated. C would be correct if the fund were short the equity tranche.

d.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the correlation link. Both leg results are right, but a falling mezzanine spread goes with lower correlation in GARP. D would be correct if the mezzanine market spread had risen rather than fallen, since a rise in correlation raises the mezzanine spread.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Japanese bank is preparing a JPY case note on the May 2005 correlation crisis, when General Motors was downgraded to BB and Ford to BB+. Which of the following best explains why the correlation between the bonds in the affected CDOs decreased?

options.text: The junk downgrades forced mutual funds and pension funds to sell GM and Ford bonds, which pushed the prices of all bonds in the CDOs down together.
Bonds of the same credit quality are typically lower correlated, and after the downgrades the CDOs held bonds of a single, uniformly lower credit quality.
Default correlations between the residential mortgages in the CDOs fell as housing prices levelled off, which reduced the correlation of the whole pool.
The CDOs originally held only investment-grade bonds, and bonds of different credit qualities are typically lower correlated, so the downgrades lowered pool correlation.

questions.solution:
**May 2005: why the correlation in the CDOs fell**

Stem in one line: after GM (BB) and Ford (BB+) were downgraded, why did the correlation of bonds in the CDOs decrease?

**Concept and theory**

GARP calls May 2005 “a first correlation-related crisis, which was a forerunner of the major one to come”. General Motors was downgraded to BB and Ford to BB+, “so both companies were now in junk status”. A downgrade to junk typically leads to a sharp bond price decline, “since many mutual funds and pension funds are not allowed to hold junk bonds”.

The correlation effect: “the correlation of the bonds in CDOs (which originally were only investment-grade bonds) decreased, since bonds of different credit qualities are typically lower-correlated.” Schweser states the same rule from both sides: “Bonds within specific credit quality levels typically are more highly correlated. Bonds across credit quality levels typically have lower correlations.”

| Pair of bonds | Typical correlation |
|---|---|
| Same credit quality | Higher |
| Different credit qualities | Lower |

So a pool that was homogeneous (all investment grade) became mixed (investment grade plus junk), and its average correlation fell.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding fact is the composition change: an investment-grade-only pool now contains junk names, and cross-quality pairs are lower correlated. That is D.

**Fragile fact.** Same credit quality: higher correlation. Different credit qualities: lower correlation. In May 2005 CDO correlation fell; in 2007 to 2009 default correlation rose.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.5, paragraph on the May 2005 crisis. Schweser Reading 8, “Correlations During the Global Financial Crisis”. No conflict. GARP-only: the BB and BB+ ratings.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 b, where it is Q6 of 16.

a.reason: Error type: scope error. Forced selling by mutual and pension funds explains the sharp price fall of the downgraded bonds, not a fall in correlation; and “all bonds down together” would describe rising correlation. A would be correct as an explanation of why junk downgrades cause sharp bond price declines.

b.reason: Error type: polarity flip of the credit-quality rule. Bonds of the same quality are more highly correlated. B would be correct if “same” read “different” and the pool had become mixed, not uniform.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap with the 2007 to 2009 episode. The 2005 CDOs referenced corporate bonds, and when mortgage default correlations moved in 2007 to 2009 they increased. C would be correct for neither episode as written.

d.reason: It reproduces GARP’s sentence, including the parenthesis on the original investment-grade composition.

questions.question: A member of the board risk committee at a UK insurer asks for a GBP briefing on why hedge funds such as Marin Capital, Aman Capital and Baily Coates Cromwell filed for bankruptcy after May 2005. Which of the following best describes what happened and the lesson Meissner draws?

options.text: The equity tranche spread fell while higher correlation raised the mezzanine spread, so both legs lost; the losses came from a lack of understanding of tranche correlation properties.
The equity and mezzanine spreads both rose, so the short mezzanine gain offset most of the long equity loss; the failures came from leverage rather than from correlation.
The equity tranche spread rose while lower correlation lowered the mezzanine spread, so both legs lost; the losses came from a lack of understanding of tranche correlation properties.
The equity tranche spread rose while lower correlation lowered the mezzanine spread, so both legs lost; the CDOs themselves were toxic because their correlation properties could not be understood.

questions.solution:
**May 2005: what happened to the hedge funds and the lesson**

Stem in one line: why did Marin Capital, Aman Capital and Baily Coates Cromwell fail after May 2005, and what lesson does Meissner draw?

**Concept and theory**

The trade: hedge funds went long the equity tranche (0% to 3%) “to collect the high equity tranche spread” and “presumably hedged the risk by going short the mezzanine tranche” (3% to 7%). “However, as we can see from Figure 8.7, this ‘hedge’ is flawed. When the correlations between the assets in the CDO decreased, the hedge funds lost on both positions.”

1. The equity tranche spread increased sharply: paper loss on the long equity leg.
2. A lower correlation lowered the mezzanine tranche spread: paper loss on the short mezzanine leg.

The lesson: “It is important to point out that the losses resulted from a lack of understanding of the correlation properties of the tranches in the CDO. The CDOs themselves can hardly be blamed or called toxic for their correlation properties.” The hedge rested on the belief that the two tranches move together; their response to a correlation change differs, so a single correlation shock can hurt both legs.

**Applying it to this question**

You need the right spread directions (equity up, mezzanine down), the right correlation direction (down), the right outcome (both legs lost) and the right lesson (misunderstanding, not toxic products). Only C has all four.

**Fragile fact.** Equity spread up, mezzanine spread down, correlation down, both legs lose. The fault is a misunderstanding, not the product.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.5, Figure 8.7 discussion. Schweser Reading 8, “Correlations During the Global Financial Crisis” and Key Concepts LO 8.b. No conflict. GARP-only: the hedge fund names.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 b, where it is Q7 of 16.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip on both spreads and on correlation. A falling equity spread would have helped the long equity leg, and a rising mezzanine spread would have helped the short mezzanine leg. A would be right only for the opposite positions.

b.reason: Error type: scope error, the hedging assumption that failed. If both spreads had risen together, the short mezzanine leg would have gained. GARP attributes the failures to the correlation properties of the tranches. B would be correct if the tranches had moved together, which was precisely the funds’ mistaken belief.

c.reason: It restates GARP points 1 and 2 and the lesson sentence. Schweser Key Concepts LO 8.b: “Both positions resulted in paper losses when equity tranche spreads increased and mezzanine tranche spreads decreased.”

d.reason: Error type: absolute claim (blame shifted to the product). GARP explicitly says the CDOs “can hardly be blamed or called toxic for their correlation properties”. D would be correct only under the “toxic asset” view that Meissner calls absurd.

questions.question:
A risk consultant advising a Brazilian bank is reviewing a BRL training note on how CDO tranche positions respond to correlation, as discussed in the reading. The note contains four statements:

I. All else equal, if the default correlation between the assets in a CDO increases, the equity tranche spread decreases and the value of the equity tranche increases.

II. Going long the equity tranche means being short credit, that is, benefiting from a credit deterioration of the assets in the CDO.

III. All else equal, a lower correlation between the assets in a CDO lowers the mezzanine tranche spread.

IV. Going short the mezzanine tranche means being short credit and paying the fairly low mezzanine tranche contract spread.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
II, III and IV only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
**Tranche spreads and correlation; position conventions**

Stem in one line: which of four statements about tranche spreads, correlation and position conventions are correct?

**Concept and theory**

Why do tranches respond to correlation in opposite ways? Total expected default loss on the pool does not depend on correlation; correlation decides how that loss is spread across scenarios.

- Low correlation: defaults are scattered, so in most scenarios a few assets default, which eats into the first-loss equity tranche but rarely reaches higher tranches.
- High correlation: assets tend to survive together or default together. More scenarios with almost no defaults (good for equity), and some scenarios with many defaults (bad for higher tranches).

Hence GARP: “If default correlations between the assets in the CDO increase, the equity tranche spread decreases, leading to an increase in the value of the equity tranche”; and “a lower correlation lowers the mezzanine tranche spread”. Conventions (GARP footnotes 10 and 12): long equity means “assuming credit risk” and receiving the high equity spread; short mezzanine means “short credit”, benefiting from a credit deterioration, and “paying the (fairly low) mezzanine tranche contract spread”.

**Applying it to this question**

I: true (GARP sentence). II: false; long equity is long credit (assuming credit risk), hurt by a credit deterioration. III: true. IV: true (footnote 12). So I, III and IV only.

**Fragile fact.** Correlation up: equity spread down, equity value up. Correlation down: mezzanine spread down. Long equity is long credit; short mezzanine is short credit.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.5, Figure 8.7 discussion and footnotes 10 to 12. Schweser Reading 8 (“The CDO equity tranche spread typically decreases when default correlations increase”). No conflict. The scenario intuition in part a is a reading of GARP Figure 8.7 and the stated directions; the reading does not give a formal derivation.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 b, where it is Q8 of 16.

a.reason: **I and III only.** Error type: scope error, a true statement rejected. IV is footnote 12 almost verbatim. A would be correct if IV said the short mezzanine position receives the spread.

b.reason: **I, II and III only.** Error type: sibling swap accepted (II) and true statement rejected (IV). II gives the long equity position the short mezzanine position’s credit view. B would be correct if II read “Going short the mezzanine tranche”.

c.reason: **II, III and IV only.** Error type: sibling swap accepted (II) and polarity doubt on I. Rejecting I means believing higher correlation raises the equity spread, the trap in Q9. C would be correct only if both I and II were reversed.

d.reason: GARP Figure 8.7 discussion and footnotes 10 and 12 support I, III and IV; footnote 10 contradicts II.

questions.question: The CRO of an Australian asset manager is reviewing AUD losses on CDO equity tranches held through 2007. From 2007 to 2009, default correlations between the mortgages in the CDOs increased, and a portfolio manager argues that this should have helped the equity tranche. Which of the following is most accurate?

options.text: The argument is wrong, because an increase in default correlation between the mortgages raises the equity tranche spread, so rising correlation itself caused the loss.
The argument is wrong, because default correlations between the mortgages actually fell from 2007 to 2009, which raised the equity tranche spread.
The argument is right as far as it goes, but the gain was overcompensated by a strong rise in the mortgages’ default probability, so the tranche spreads increased sharply.
The argument is right as far as it goes, but the gain was offset because equity tranche investors had typically leveraged their positions 10 or 20 times.

questions.solution:
**2007: rising default correlation and the equity tranche**

Stem in one line: default correlation between mortgages rose from 2007 to 2009; should that have helped equity tranche holders?

**Concept and theory**

Two forces act on a tranche spread at once: the default probability of the underlying assets and the default correlation between them. GARP: “From 2007 to 2009, default correlations between the mortgages in the CDOs increased. This actually helped equity tranche investors, as we can see from Figure 8.7. If default correlations between the assets in the CDO increase, the equity tranche spread decreases, leading to an increase in the value of the equity tranche. However, this increase was overcompensated by a strong increase in default probability of the mortgages; as a consequence, tranche spreads increased sharply, resulting in a huge loss of the equity tranche investors as well investors in the other tranches.”

| Force (2007 to 2009) | Effect on equity tranche spread | Effect on equity value |
|---|---|---|
| Default correlation up | Down | Up (helps) |
| Default probability up strongly | Up | Down (hurts) |
| Net | Up sharply | Large loss |

**Applying it to this question**

The manager’s argument isolates the correlation effect and is correct on its own terms. The deciding fact is that the default-probability effect was larger. That is C.

**Fragile fact.** Correlation up helps equity; default probability up hurts all tranches; in 2007 the probability effect won.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.5, paragraph after Figure 8.8 caption (“In a systemic crash like this. . . ”). Schweser Reading 8: “The CDO equity tranche spread typically decreases when default correlations increase. . . Unfortunately, the probability of default in the subprime market increased so dramatically in 2007 that it lowered the value of all CDO tranches.” No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 b, where it is Q9 of 16.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the correlation effect. Higher default correlation lowers the equity spread. A would be correct for the mezzanine or senior side, where higher correlation is harmful, not for equity.

b.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the fact. Default correlations between the mortgages increased from 2007 to 2009. B would describe May 2005 (corporate bond CDO correlation fell), a sibling episode.

c.reason: It is GARP’s “overcompensated by a strong increase in default probability” sentence.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap. Leverage of 10 or 20 times belongs to leveraged super-senior (LSS) tranches, not equity tranches. D would be correct for super-senior investors’ amplified losses.

questions.question: A treasury analyst at an Indian bank is building an INR training timeline of how the mortgage CDO crisis unfolded. To fuel CDO issuance, more and more questionable subprime mortgages, nicknamed NINJA loans (“no income, no job or assets”), were granted. Which of the following timelines is most accurate?

options.text: 2003 to 2006: the CDO market, mainly referencing residential mortgages, grows from about USD 8 trillion to almost USD 60 trillion. 2006: housing prices level off and the first mortgages default. 2007: defaults mount, the real-estate market collapses and the CDO market collapses with it.

2003 to 2006: the CDO market, mainly referencing residential mortgages, grows from USD 64 billion to USD 455 billion. 2006: the CDO market collapses first. 2007: the CDO collapse triggers the first mortgage defaults and the real-estate market collapses.

2003 to 2006: the CDO market, mainly referencing investment-grade corporate bonds, grows from USD 64 billion to USD 455 billion. 2006: housing prices level off and the first mortgages default. 2007: defaults mount, the real-estate market collapses and the CDO market collapses with it.

2003 to 2006: the CDO market, mainly referencing residential mortgages, grows from USD 64 billion to USD 455 billion. 2006: housing prices level off and the first mortgages default. 2007: defaults mount, the real-estate market collapses and the CDO market collapses with it.

questions.solution:
**The 2003 to 2007 sequence in the mortgage CDO market**

Stem in one line: which timeline of CDO growth and the 2006 to 2007 collapse is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

GARP: “From 2003 to 2006 the CDO market, mainly referencing residential mortgages, had exploded and increased from USD 64 billion to USD 455 billion. To fuel the CDOs, more and more questionable subprime mortgages were given, named NINJA loans. . . When housing prices started levelling off in 2006, the first mortgages started to default. In 2007 more and more mortgages defaulted, finally leading to a real-estate market collapse. With it the huge CDO market collapsed, leading to the stock market and commodity market crash and a freeze in the credit markets.”

The causal arrow runs from the underlying (mortgages) to the derivative (CDOs), then to other markets:

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 2003 to 2006 | CDO market (mainly residential mortgages) grows from USD 64bn to USD 455bn; NINJA loans |
| 2006 | Housing prices level off; first mortgage defaults |
| 2007 | Defaults mount; real-estate collapse; CDO market collapses with it |
| Then | Stock and commodity crash; credit markets freeze; global “great recession” |

A different market grew in parallel: the CDS market, from about USD 8 trillion in 2004 to almost USD 60 trillion in 2007.

**Applying it to this question**

Check three slots in each option: the CDO market size, its collateral, and the causal order. Only D is right on all three.

**Fragile fact.** CDO: USD 64bn to USD 455bn (2003 to 2006). CDS: USD 8tn to almost USD 60tn (2004 to 2007). Mortgages default first; the CDO market follows.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.5, paragraph beginning “From 2003 to 2006 the CDO market”. Schweser Reading 8, “Correlations During the Global Financial Crisis”. No conflict. GARP-only: the NINJA label and the credit-market freeze.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 b, where it is Q10 of 16.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap of figures. USD 8 trillion to almost USD 60 trillion is the CDS market (2004 to 2007). A would be correct if “CDO market” read “CDS market” with dates 2004 to 2007.

b.reason: Error type: polarity flip of causation. Mortgage defaults came first and the CDO market collapsed with the real-estate market, not before it. B would be correct only if the CDO collapse had caused the defaults.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap with the 2005 episode. Investment-grade corporate bonds were the collateral of the CDOs hit in May 2005; the 2003 to 2006 boom was mainly in residential mortgage CDOs. C would describe the wrong collateral.

d.reason: It matches GARP’s paragraph and Schweser’s “The CDO market, composed primarily of residential mortgages, increased from \$64 billion in 2003 to \$455 billion in 2006.”

questions.question: A banking regulator at a euro-area supervisor is writing a EUR thematic review of why investors in super-senior CDO tranches, previously regarded as extremely safe, were hurt during the crisis. Which of the following best explains the losses according to the reading?

options.text: Correlations between the tranches of the CDOs increased and the credit market deteriorated, so AAA ratings and subordination no longer made the tranches safe; they lost up to 20% of their value.
Correlations between the tranches of the CDOs decreased, so the super-senior tranches no longer moved with the protecting lower tranches; they lost up to 20% of their value.
Correlations between the tranches of the CDOs increased, which lowered super-senior spreads just as higher default correlation lowers the equity spread, so losses came from leverage alone.
The super-senior tranches lost value only because CDS sellers such as AIG failed to pay, since their AAA ratings and the lower tranches kept the tranches themselves free of credit risk.

questions.solution:
**Why super-senior tranches were hurt**

Stem in one line: why did investors in supposedly safe super-senior tranches lose?

**Concept and theory**

A super-senior tranche sits at the top of the capital structure: it loses only after all lower tranches have been wiped out. In normal times it looked doubly safe. GARP: “Correlations between the tranches of the CDOs also increased during the crisis. This had a devastating effect on the super-senior tranches. In normal times, these tranches were considered extremely safe since (a) they were AAA-rated and (b) they were protected by the lower tranches. But, with the increased tranche correlation and the generally deteriorating credit market, these super-senior tranches were suddenly considered risky and lost up to 20% of their value.”

Intuition: subordination protects only if losses stay contained in the lower tranches. When correlation rises, defaults cluster; a clustered wave of defaults blows through the equity and mezzanine tranches and reaches the top. Schweser: AAA tranches “were no longer protected from the lower tranches”.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are the direction (tranche correlation increased), the companion cause (deteriorating credit market), the broken protection (AAA plus subordination) and the size (up to 20%). Only A has all of them.

**Fragile fact.** Tranche correlation up hurts super-senior. Loss: up to 20% (GARP); Schweser writes “lost 20%”.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.5, paragraph “Correlations between the tranches of the CDOs also increased”. Schweser Reading 8, “Correlations During the Global Financial Crisis”. Difference: GARP “lost up to 20%”; Schweser “lost 20%”. GARP used; looks like Schweser compression rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 b, where it is Q11 of 16.

a.reason: It restates GARP’s paragraph.

b.reason: Error type: polarity flip. Tranche correlations increased. B would be correct only if rising losses in lower tranches had stayed separate from the senior tranche, which is the opposite of what happened.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap. The property “higher correlation lowers the spread” belongs to the equity tranche. For the super-senior tranche, rising correlation was devastating. C would be correct if “super-senior” read “equity” and the default-probability effect were ignored.

d.reason: Error type: absolute claim. The tranches themselves were “suddenly considered risky and lost up to 20%”; the reading does not attribute their loss to CDS seller default. D would be correct only if the tranches carried no credit risk, which subordination never guarantees.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Chinese asset manager is reviewing a pre-crisis CNY investment in a leveraged super-senior (LSS) tranche. The fund paid CNY 40 million for the LSS position, which carried leverage of 20 times. During the crisis the super-senior tranche lost 12% of its value.

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Cash paid for the LSS position | CNY 40 million |
| Leverage | 20 times |
| Fall in value of the super-senior tranche | 12% |
| LSS running spread received | 45 bps per annum |
| Tranche attachment and detachment points | 15% to 30% |

Which of the following is closest to the fund’s loss, and the loss as a multiple of the cash paid?

options.text: CNY 4.8 million; 0.12 times the cash paid
CNY 91.2 million; 2.28 times the cash paid
CNY 96.0 million; 2.40 times the cash paid
CNY 800.0 million; 20.00 times the cash paid

questions.solution:
**Leveraged super-senior (LSS) loss**

Stem in one line: CNY 40m paid for an LSS with 20 times leverage; the tranche loses 12%; loss and loss multiple?

**Concept and theory**

GARP: “To make things worse, many investors had leveraged the super-senior tranches, termed LSS (leveraged super-senior tranche) to receive a higher spread. This leverage was typically 10 or 20 times, meaning an investor paid USD 10,000,000 but had risk exposure of USD 100,000,000 or USD 200,000,000.” Schweser: “The leverage in the CDO market caused risk exposures for investors to be 10 to 20 times higher than the investments.”

So the economic exposure, not the cash paid, is what loses value:

Exposure = $L \times C,$ Loss = $d \times L \times C, \frac{\text{Loss}}{C}$ = $d \times L$

where $C$ is the cash paid, $L$ the leverage multiple, and $d$ the percentage fall in the tranche’s value. GARP adds a feedback loop: LSSs “came with an option for the investors to unwind the super-senior tranche if the spread had widened (increased). So many investors started to sell the LSS at low prices, realising a loss and increasing the LSS tranche spread even further.”

**Applying it to this question**

Exposure = 20 × CNY 40m = CNY 800m

Loss = 12% × CNY 800m = CNY 96.0m

Loss/cash paid = 96.0/40 = 2.40 times

The 45 bps spread and the 15% to 30% attachment points are irrelevant. Meaning: a 12% fall in a tranche that was “extremely safe” destroys the cash paid more than twice over.

**Fragile fact.** Leverage of 10 or 20 times means exposure 10 or 20 times the cash paid. The unwind option made things worse: forced sales widened the LSS spread further.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.5, paragraph “To make things worse, many investors had leveraged the super-senior tranches”. Schweser Reading 8 (“10 to 20 times higher than the investments”). No conflict. GARP-only: the term LSS and the unwind option.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 b, where it is Q12 of 16.

a.reason: Error type: dropped term (leverage ignored): 12% × 40 = 4.8. A would be correct for an unleveraged super-senior holding of CNY 40m.

b.reason: Error type: wrong input twin, the borrowed amount used in place of the total exposure: 12% × (800 − 40) = 91.2, so 91.2/40 = 2.28. The whole CNY 800m exposure is at risk, including the part funded by the cash paid. B would be correct only if the stem asked for the loss on the leveraged increment alone.

c.reason: It applies GARP’s definition of LSS leverage (exposure equals leverage times cash paid) to the stated fall in value.

d.reason: Error type: intermediate result. CNY 800m is the exposure, the first step of the calculation, not the loss. D would be correct only for a 100% fall in value.

questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a Canadian life insurer is reviewing a CAD proposal to sell credit default swap protection as an income strategy, and asks what the reading says about the CDS market in the crisis. Which of the following is most accurate?

options.text: CDSs are toxic in themselves, since insurance against default concentrates rather than spreads risk; AIG’s London unit sold close to USD 500 billion of CDSs without much reinsurance.
CDSs used as insurance spread risk, but a seller can speculate by keeping the spread as income, as AIG’s London unit tried with close to USD 500 billion sold.
CDSs used as insurance spread risk, but they can also be speculative, as AIG’s London unit showed by buying close to USD 500 billion of protection on debt it did not own.
CDSs used as insurance spread risk, and as the market grew from USD 8 trillion to almost USD 60 trillion, no single seller, even AIG’s London unit, faced concentrated exposure.

questions.solution:
**The CDS market and AIG**

Stem in one line: what does the reading say about CDSs and AIG in the crisis?

**Concept and theory**

GARP: “In addition to the overinvestment in CDOs, the CDS market also exploded from its beginnings in the mid-1990s from about USD 8 trillion in 2004 to almost USD 60 trillion in 2007. CDSs are typically used as insurance to protect against default of a debtor. . . No one will argue that an insurance contract is toxic. On the contrary, it is the principle of insurance to spread the risk to a wider audience and hence reduce individual risk.”

But a CDS can also be speculative, on both sides:

| Side | Speculative use (GARP) |
|---|---|
| CDS seller | “Hopes that the insured event (eg, default or credit deterioration of the company) will not occur. In this case, the CDS seller keeps the CDS spread (ie, the insurance premium), as income as AIG tried to do in the crisis.” |
| CDS buyer without the underlying | “Speculates on the credit deterioration of the underlying asset, just like a naked put option holder.” |

AIG: “the London unit of the insurance company AIG had sold close to USD 500 billion in CDSs without much reinsurance!” Schweser: “The CDS seller must be financially stable enough to protect against losses.”

**Applying it to this question**

Each option has two parts: the nature of a CDS and the AIG fact. B is the only option correct on both: insurance spreads risk, seller-side speculation exists, AIG was a seller of close to USD 500bn without much reinsurance.

**Fragile fact.** AIG sold close to USD 500bn of CDSs, with little reinsurance. The CDS market grew from USD 8tn (2004) to almost USD 60tn (2007).

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.5, paragraphs on the CDS market and the blame paragraph (AIG). Schweser Reading 8, “Correlations During the Global Financial Crisis”. No conflict; speculation detail GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 b, where it is Q13 of 16.

a.reason: Error type: absolute claim (product blamed). GARP: “No one will argue that an insurance contract is toxic”; insurance spreads risk. The AIG half is right. A would be correct if its first half read “CDSs used speculatively can concentrate risk in an overextended seller”.

b.reason: It combines GARP’s insurance principle, the seller-side speculation sentence and the AIG sentence.

c.reason: Error type: role misassignment. AIG’s London unit sold protection. The naked-buyer form of speculation exists, but it was not AIG’s. C would be correct if “buying” read “selling” and “on debt it did not own” were removed.

d.reason: Error type: scope error (insurance principle over-extended). Market growth did not disperse AIG’s risk: it sold close to USD 500bn “without much reinsurance”. The growth figures are correct. D would be correct for an idealised insurance market in which no seller is overextended.

questions.question:
A junior credit analyst at a Swiss bank is comparing a broker-dealer’s year-end balance sheet with the Lehman Brothers case in the reading. The analyst measures leverage the way the reading reports Lehman’s figure.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Total assets | CHF 540 billion |
| Total liabilities | CHF 522 billion |
| Stockholders’ equity | CHF 18 billion |
| Derivatives transactions on the books | 1.2 million |
| Number of derivatives counterparties | 6,500 |

Which of the following best states the broker-dealer’s reported leverage and, if it used materially misleading repo transactions as Lehman did, how its true leverage compares?

options.text: 30.0 times; true leverage is higher, because the misleading repo transactions hide part of the leverage
29.0 times; true leverage is higher, because the misleading repo transactions hide part of the leverage
30.0 times; true leverage is lower, because 1.2 million derivatives with 6,500 counterparties diversify it
30.0 times; true leverage is the same, because a repo is a short-term collateralised loan on the balance sheet

questions.solution:
**Leverage: the Lehman benchmark**

Stem in one line: assets CHF 540bn, liabilities CHF 522bn, equity CHF 18bn; reported leverage and how true leverage compares with misleading repos.

**Concept and theory**

The reading measures Lehman’s leverage as assets over stockholders’ equity: Lehman “reported a leverage of 30.7, ie, USD 691 billion in assets and only USD 22 billion in stockholders’ equity. The true leverage was even higher, since Lehman tried to hide their leverage with materially misleading repo transactions. In addition, Lehman had 1.5 million derivatives transactions with 8,000 different counterparties on their books.” (A repo is defined in GARP’s footnote as a short-term collateralised loan.)

Leverage = $\frac{\text{Total assets}}{\text{Stockholders’ equity}}$

Leverage is how correlation shocks turn into failures: Schweser Key Concepts LO 8.b says the troubles of AIG and Lehman “revealed the impact of increasing default correlations with tremendous leverage”.

**Applying it to this question**

Reported leverage = $\frac{540}{18}$ = 30.0 times

Check: 540 − 522 = 18 (equity consistent)

The number of derivatives transactions and counterparties does not enter the ratio. Interpretation: if part of the leverage is hidden through misleading repo transactions, the true leverage is higher than 30.0.

**Fragile fact.** Leverage = assets / equity (30.7 for Lehman). True leverage was higher.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.5, blame paragraph (Lehman) and footnote 13. Schweser Reading 8, “Correlations During the Global Financial Crisis”. Difference: GARP attributes the higher true leverage to misleading repo transactions; Schweser to the large number of derivatives transactions with 8,000 counterparties. GARP used. Source note: GARP’s own figures give 691/22 ≈ 31.4 against the stated 30.7, so the equity figure appears rounded in the source; not used in this question.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 b, where it is Q14 of 16.

a.reason: It uses the reading’s assets-to-equity measure and its statement that true leverage was even higher because of misleading repo transactions.

b.reason: Error type: wrong input twin, liabilities used for assets: 522/18 = 29.0. That is a debt-to-equity ratio. B would be correct if the question asked for liabilities over equity.

c.reason: **Lower.** Error type: polarity flip. The reading presents the derivatives book as an addition to Lehman’s exposure (“in addition”), not as diversification that reduces leverage. C would be correct only if the derivatives were offsetting hedges that reduced risk, which the reading does not say.

d.reason: **Same.** Error type: scope error. A repo is indeed a short-term collateralised loan, but GARP says Lehman’s repos were materially misleading and were used to hide leverage. D would be correct for ordinary, fully disclosed repo financing.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a US bank is preparing a lessons-learned report on who was to blame for the 2007 to 2009 crisis. Which of the following is most consistent with Meissner’s assessment?

options.text: Mainly the quants who created CDSs and CDOs and the models to value them, because the products themselves were toxic and caused the losses.
All of them: quants, upper management and traders, rating agencies, regulators and risk managers; at root it was greed, and humans, not products, are toxic.
All of them except risk managers and regulators, who could not see the leverage being built up and so bear no part of the blame.
All of them, but chiefly the complexity of the products, since most traders did not understand the risks they were taking.

questions.solution:
**Who was to blame**

Stem in one line: which statement is most consistent with Meissner’s view of who was to blame?

**Concept and theory**

Meissner asks: the quants who created CDSs and CDOs and the models to value them? Upper management and traders who authorised and conducted the overinvesting? Rating agencies? Regulators? Risk managers? “The answer is: All of them. The whole global financial crisis can be summed up in one word: greed!”

He rejects the “toxic asset” explanation: it is “like a murderer saying: ‘I did not shoot that person, it was my gun!’ Toxic are not the financial products, but humans and their greed.” Two further points: “Most traders were well aware of the risks that they were taking. In the few cases where traders did not understand the risks, the asset itself cannot be blamed, rather the incompetence of the trader”; and “risk managers and regulators have to take part of the blame to allow the irresponsible risk taking.”

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts: blame is shared by all five groups, the root cause is greed, and the products are not toxic. Only B states all three.

**Fragile fact.** All of them; greed; most traders knew the risks; products are not toxic, people are.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.5, paragraphs beginning “So who can we blame for the 2007-09 global financial crises?”. GARP-only: Schweser’s LO 8.b section does not cover the blame discussion; included because it sits inside GARP’s crisis section and explains Meissner’s view of the role of correlation products.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 b, where it is Q15 of 16.

a.reason: Error type: scope error (one actor) plus the toxic-asset myth. The quants are one of five groups, and Meissner calls the toxic-asset idea absurd. A would describe the “myth” that GARP says management and traders created.

b.reason: It restates GARP’s “All of them”, “greed” and “Toxic are not the financial products, but humans”.

c.reason: Error type: polarity flip on two actors. GARP: risk managers and regulators “have to take part of the blame”. C would be correct only if they had been unaware, which the reading denies (“turned a blind eye”).

d.reason: Error type: polarity flip on trader awareness. “Most traders were well aware of the risks”; where they were not, the trader, not the asset, is at fault. D would be correct if “most” read “a few” and the blame went to trader incompetence rather than product complexity.

questions.question: A member of the risk committee at a Japanese bank asks how regulation has responded to the correlation lessons of the crisis, as described in the reading. Which of the following statements is NOT correct?

options.text: Among the new correlation approaches, CVA is proposed for correlated defaults in a multi-asset portfolio and the Gaussian copula for correlations in derivatives transactions.
Basel III addresses deficiencies of the banking system revealed by the crisis and introduces many new ratios to ensure liquidity and adequate leverage of banks.
New correlation models are implemented that deal with double defaults in insured risk transactions, such as a bond position hedged with a CDS.
Correlations in what is called wrong-way risk (WWR) are among the new correlation approaches that have been proposed.

questions.solution:
**Regulatory response: Basel III and new correlation models**

Stem in one line: which statement about the regulatory response to the crisis’s correlation lessons is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP, “Regulation and Correlation”: “Basel III addresses the deficiencies of the banking system during the financial crisis 2007 to 2009. Basel III introduces many new ratios to ensure liquidity and adequate leverage of banks. In addition, new correlation models are implemented that deal with double defaults in insured risk transactions as displayed in Figure 8.1. Correlated defaults in a multi-asset portfolio quantified with the Gaussian copula, correlations in derivatives transactions termed credit value adjustment (CVA) and correlations in what is called ‘wrong-way risk’ (WWR) have been proposed.”

| Correlation problem | Model or approach named |
|---|---|
| Double default (bond plus CDS) | New models implemented |
| Correlated defaults in a multi-asset portfolio | Gaussian copula |
| Correlations in derivatives transactions | CVA |
| Wrong-way correlation | WWR |

**Applying it to this question**

B, C and D each restate part of the paragraph. A swaps the two applications: the Gaussian copula is for correlated defaults in a multi-asset portfolio, and CVA is for correlations in derivatives transactions.

**Fragile fact.** Gaussian copula: correlated defaults in a multi-asset portfolio. CVA: derivatives transactions. WWR: the third named approach.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.5, “Regulation and Correlation” (“Why Basel I, II and III?”). Schweser Reading 8, “Correlations During the Global Financial Crisis”, final paragraph. Boundary call: Schweser places this paragraph under LO 8.b; GARP places it under “Regulation and Correlation”. Included because Schweser decides scope. Difference: Schweser: “being developed and implemented”; GARP: “have been proposed”. GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 b, where it is Q16 of 16.

a.reason: GARP pairs “correlated defaults in a multi-asset portfolio” with the Gaussian copula and “correlations in derivatives transactions” with CVA; A reverses the pairing (sibling swap).

b.reason: True: GARP says Basel III addresses the crisis deficiencies and “introduces many new ratios to ensure liquidity and adequate leverage”. Schweser: “New standards for liquidity and leverage ratios”. It would be the false statement only if it claimed Basel III dropped leverage limits.

c.reason: True: “new correlation models are implemented that deal with double defaults in insured risk transactions as displayed in Figure 8.1” (the bond hedged with a CDS). It would be false if it said the models ignored the counterparty’s default.

d.reason: True: WWR correlations “have been proposed”; Schweser lists WWR correlation among the new models. It would be false if it attributed WWR to multi-asset portfolio defaults.
