questions.question:
A junior analyst at a Canadian credit union is reviewing two commercial loans, to Debtor P (CAD 12 million, 5-year term) and Debtor Q (CAD 3 million, 5-year term). A rating agency supplies the following default term structures; each entry is the probability that the debtor defaults in that year:

| Year | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Debtor P | 0.03% | 0.06% | 0.10% | 0.13% | 0.16% |
| Debtor Q | 18.50% | 12.40% | 8.90% | 6.30% | 4.80% |

Which of the following best interprets the two term structures?

options.text: P’s rising profile is typical of a distressed debtor, because for a weak company the probability of default keeps rising as adverse events accumulate over time.
P’s rising profile is typical of investment-grade debt, as a longer horizon allows more adverse internal or external events; Q’s falling profile is typical of a distressed debtor.
Q’s falling profile is typical of investment-grade debt, because a sound company faces fewer adverse internal or external events as the horizon lengthens.
Because the two term structures slope in opposite directions, the default correlation between P and Q must be zero, so the credit union carries no default correlation risk.

questions.solution:
**Default term structures: investment grade versus distressed**

Stem in one line: P’s yearly default probabilities rise from 0.03% to 0.16%, Q’s fall from 18.50% to 4.80%; interpret.

**Concept and theory**

A single default probability compresses time. A default term structure shows, for each future year, the probability that the debtor defaults in that year (GARP Table 8.4: “an A-rated bond has a 0.15% probability to default in year 5”). GARP explains the two typical shapes:

| Debtor | Shape | Reason (GARP §8.6) |
|---|---|---|
| Investment grade (A-rated in Table 8.4) | Rising with time | “The longer the time horizon, the higher the probability of adverse internal events as mismanagement, or external events as increased competition or a recession.” |
| Distressed (CC-rated in Table 8.4) | Inverse (falling) | “For a distressed company, the immediate future is critical. If the company survives the coming problematic years, the probability of default decreases.” |

**Applying it to this question**

P: 0.03% to 0.16%, low and rising: the investment-grade shape. Q: 18.50% to 4.80%, very high and falling: the distressed shape. Loan sizes and terms are not needed.

**Fragile fact.** Investment grade: default term structure rises. Distressed: inverse, because the immediate future is critical.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.6, “Correlation Risk and Credit Risk”, Table 8.4 (Moody’s, 2002). Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.3, Figure 8.8 (figure missing in the text extract). No conflict: Schweser says the investment-grade curve “increases slightly” and the non-investment-grade default probability “is higher in the immediate time horizon”.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 f, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap. It gives the investment-grade reason (adverse events accumulate) to a distressed debtor. For a distressed debtor the near term is the danger, so the curve falls. A would be correct with “investment-grade” in place of “distressed”.

b.reason: It matches each shape to the right type of debtor and gives GARP’s reason for the rising curve.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap in the opposite direction. A falling curve that starts at 18.50% is the distressed profile, not investment grade. C would be correct if the curve described were low and rising.

d.reason: Error type: scope error. The slope of each marginal term structure says nothing about how the two debtors’ defaults move together; GARP models that separately, by correlating the term structures with a copula (Q10). D would be correct only if the stem had stated that the two defaults are independent, and even then “no default correlation risk” would overstate it.

questions.question:
The CRO of a UK general insurer is preparing a GBP risk committee paper on why the default correlation of debtors matters for credit risk. The draft contains four statements:

I. Default correlation is the degree to which the defaults of debtors occur together.

II. Default correlation is critical for lenders such as commercial banks, credit unions, mortgage lenders and trusts, which give many types of loans to companies and individuals.

III. Default correlation is also critical for insurance companies, which are exposed to the credit risk of numerous debtors.

IV. A creditor benefits from a high default correlation among its debtors, because defaults that occur together are easier to provision for.

Which of the statements should the CRO keep?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and IV only
I, II and III only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
**Default correlation: what it is and who it matters to**

Stem in one line: which of four risk committee statements on default correlation should the CRO keep?

**Concept and theory**

GARP §8.6 defines default correlation as “the degree to which defaults occur together”. It matters to any institution that holds credit exposure to many debtors:

- “financial lenders such as commercial banks, credit unions, mortgage lenders and trusts, which give many types of loans to companies and individuals”;
- “insurance companies, which are exposed to credit risk of numerous debtors”.

The desired direction is stated twice: “a low default correlation of debtors is desired to diversify the credit risk” and “a creditor will benefit from a low default correlation of their debtors, which spreads the default correlation risk”. Intuition: if defaults are nearly independent, a bad year brings a few defaults; if they are highly correlated, many debtors fail in the same year.

**Applying it to this question**

I is the definition: keep. II lists GARP’s lenders: keep. III adds insurers, which GARP names explicitly: keep. IV reverses the desired direction: drop.

**Fragile fact.** Creditors want low default correlation among debtors. Insurers count as well as lenders.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.6, “Correlation Risk and Credit Risk”. Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.3: “A lower default correlation is associated with greater diversification of credit risk.” GARP-only: insurance companies, credit unions and trusts (Schweser names “mortgage companies and banks”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 f, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: **I and II only.** Error type: scope error (a true condition dropped). It leaves out insurers, which GARP names. A would be correct if III had said that insurers have no credit exposure to debtors.

b.reason: **I, II and IV only.** Error type: polarity flip, plus the loss of a true statement. Keeping IV means believing that clustered defaults help a creditor; GARP says the reverse. B would be correct only if IV said “low” and III were false.

c.reason: GARP §8.6 supports I, II and III directly and contradicts IV.

d.reason: **I, II, III and IV.** Error type: polarity flip in IV. Defaults that occur together produce large, concentrated losses; predictability does not make them smaller. D would be correct if IV read “low default correlation”.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Chinese commercial bank models two borrowers’ defaults as binomial events (1 if default, 0 otherwise), with the joint default probability linked to the default correlation through the binomial correlation model in the reading. The data are:

|  | Borrower X | Borrower Y |
|---|---|---|
| Loan amount (CNY million) | 600 | 400 |
| One-year default probability | 4.0% | 9.0% |

The credit committee revises the default correlation between X and Y from 0.10 to 0.40. By how much does the joint probability that both X and Y default increase?

options.text: 1.80 percentage points
1.68 percentage points
2.60 percentage points
2.24 percentage points

questions.solution:
**Change in default correlation and the joint default probability**

Stem in one line: $P_{X}$ = 4%, $P_{Y}$ = 9%; default correlation revised from 0.10 to 0.40; find the increase in the joint default probability.

**Concept and theory**

A default is a binomial event: the indicator equals 1 on default and 0 otherwise. For a binomial variable with default probability $P$ , the standard deviation is $\sqrt{P \text{(1} - P \text{)}}$ (GARP eq. 8.12). The joint probability that both debtors default is (GARP eq. 8.11):

$P$ ($X \cap Y$ ) = $\rho_{XY} \sqrt{P_{X} \text{(1} - P_{X} \text{)}}\sqrt{P_{Y} \text{(1} - P_{Y} \text{)}}$ + $P_{X} P_{Y}$

where $P_{X}$ , $P_{Y}$ are the individual default probabilities, $\rho_{XY}$ is the default correlation, $P_{X} P_{Y}$ is the joint default probability under independence, and the first term is the covariance of the two indicators. Because $P$ ($X \cap Y$ ) is linear in $\rho_{XY}$ , a change in correlation changes the joint default probability by

∆$P$ ($X \cap Y$ ) = ∆$\rho_{XY} \sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y} .$

This makes GARP’s statement concrete: the higher the default correlation, the more often debtors default together, which is why creditors want it low (Q7).

**Applying it to this question**

$\sigma_{X}$ = $\sqrt{0.04 \times0.96}$ = $\sqrt{0.0384}$ = 0.195959

$\sigma_{Y}$ = $\sqrt{0.09 \times0.91}$ = $\sqrt{0.0819}$ = 0.286182

$\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$ = 0.195959 × 0.286182 = 0.056080

$P_{X} P_{Y}$ = 0.04 × 0.09 = 0.003600

$P$ ($X \cap Y$ )$||_{\rho\text{=0}.10}$ = 0.10 × 0.056080 + 0.003600 = 0.009208 = 0.92%

$P$ ($X \cap Y$ )$||_{\rho\text{=0}.40}$ = 0.40 × 0.056080 + 0.003600 = 0.026032 = 2.60%

∆$P$ ($X \cap Y$ ) = 0.026032 − 0.009208 = 0.016824 = 1.68 percentage points

Check: ∆$\rho\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$ = 0.30 × 0.056080 = 0.016824. The loan amounts (CNY 600 million and CNY 400 million) are not needed for a probability.

Meaning: raising the default correlation from 0.10 to 0.40 nearly triples the chance that both borrowers default in the same year (0.92% to 2.60%), with no change in either borrower’s own default probability.

**Fragile fact.** The binomial standard deviation is $\sqrt{P \text{(1} - P \text{)}}$, not $\sqrt{P}$; and “increase” means new level minus old level.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.6, “Correlation Risk and Credit Risk” (default correlation as the degree to which defaults occur together); formula from §8.8, eqs. (8.11) and (8.12). The formula is garbled in the GARP OCR and missing from the Schweser text; its notation is confirmed from the question bank’s worked solutions for Reading 8 (Q452, Q454). Boundary call: formula shared with LO 8.g, used here without any concentration ratio. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 f, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: wrong input twin. It uses $\sqrt{P_{X} P_{Y}}$ = $\sqrt{0.0036}$ = 0.06 in place of $\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$ , dropping the (1 $- P$ ) terms: 0.30 × 0.06 = 0.0180. Correct only if the standard deviation of a binomial variable were $\sqrt{P}$.

b.reason: It is the difference between the joint default probabilities at the new and the old correlation, computed with GARP eq. 8.11.

c.reason: Error type: intermediate result. 2.60% is the new level of the joint default probability at $\rho$ = 0.40, not the increase. Correct if the stem asked “what is the joint default probability after the revision?”

d.reason: Error type: dropped term (wrong base). 0.40 × 0.056080 = 0.022432 is the increase measured from independence ($\rho$ = 0), ignoring the starting correlation of 0.10. Correct if the correlation had been revised from 0 to 0.40.

questions.question: A member of the credit committee at a German regional bank notes that 70% of its EUR loan book is lent to car manufacturers and their suppliers. The head of corporate lending argues: “If one large carmaker defaults, our other auto borrowers gain market share, so the auto concentration hedges itself.” Which response is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: The argument holds, because intra-sector default correlations are typically lower than intersector ones, so a rival’s default tends to benefit the surviving firms.
The argument fails only for investment-grade borrowers; for non-investment-grade borrowers a rival’s default typically benefits the surviving firms.
The argument fails: intra-sector default correlations exceed inter-sector ones, as systematic factors dominate, so the bank should diversify its loan book across sectors.
The argument fails, and the remedy is to add more borrowers within the auto sector, since a larger number of auto borrowers removes the default correlation risk.

questions.solution:
**Why a lender diversifies across sectors**

Stem in one line: 70% of a EUR loan book is in autos; the lending head says a rival’s default helps the survivors.

**Concept and theory**

Two forces act when a firm defaults. An idiosyncratic view says rivals gain market share. A systematic view says the forces that sank one firm (a recession, the structural decline of a sector) hit its rivals too. GARP’s data (Table 8.3, Q5) settle it: default correlations are higher within sectors than between them, so “systematic factors . . . impact on defaults more than idiosyncratic factors. Hence if General Motors defaults, it is more likely that Ford defaults, rather than Ford benefiting from the default of its rival GM.” The policy conclusion: “Since the intra-sector default correlations are higher than inter-sector default correlations, a lender is advised to have a sector-diversified loan portfolio to reduce default correlation risk.”

**Applying it to this question**

The lending head’s argument is the idiosyncratic view GARP rejects with the GM and Ford example. The fix is to spread lending across sectors, which lowers the default correlation among the bank’s debtors.

**Fragile fact.** GM defaults ⇒ Ford more likely to default. The remedy is diversification across sectors.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.6, “Correlation Risk and Credit Risk”. Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.3 (Chrysler, Ford and GM example; “creditors benefit by diversifying exposure across industries”). No conflict; Schweser adds Chrysler to the example.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 f, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip. Intra-sector correlations are higher, not lower. A would be correct if the table showed near-zero within-sector entries and higher cross-sector entries.

b.reason: Error type: scope error (an invented condition). GARP’s Table 8.3 is built from non-investment-grade bonds and still shows high within-sector correlation; nothing in the reading exempts weaker borrowers. B would be correct only if the data showed negative within-sector correlation for that group.

c.reason: It states the empirical fact (intra > inter), its cause (systematic factors) and GARP’s policy (sector diversification).

d.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. Adding auto borrowers leaves the book exposed to the same systematic auto factor; it cannot “remove” default correlation risk, and GARP’s remedy is across sectors. D would be correct if it said “lend to more borrowers in different sectors, which reduces default correlation risk”.

questions.question: A risk consultant is training credit analysts at an Indian non-bank lender on default modelling for an INR loan book. Which of the following statements made in the training is NOT correct?

options.text: Defaults are binomial events, either default or no default, so a simple binomial model is often applied to model them.
For most investment-grade bonds the default term structure rises over time, since a longer horizon raises the probability of mismanagement, increased competition or a recession.
By correlating two debtors’ default term structures with a copula model, a lender can estimate the joint probability that Debtor 1 defaults in Year 3 and Debtor 2 defaults in Year 5.
Because defaults are binomial events, a default term structure adds no information beyond a single one-year default probability for each debtor in the loan book.

questions.solution:
**Binomial default modelling, term structures and the copula**

Stem in one line: which training statement on default modelling is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP §8.6 builds the credit risk toolkit in three steps:

1. “Defaults are binomial events: either default or no default. Therefore, to model defaults, often a simple binomial model is applied.”
2. “However, we can also analyse defaults in more detail and look at term structure of defaults”: the probability of default year by year, rising for investment-grade debt and inverse for distressed debt (Q6).
3. The term structures of two debtors can be correlated “with the famous (now infamous) copula model”, which answers questions such as “What is the joint probability of Debtor 1 defaulting in Year 3 and Debtor 2 defaulting in Year 5?”

So the term structure adds timing information to the one-period binomial picture, and the copula carries correlation into that timing.

**Applying it to this question**

A restates step 1, B the investment-grade reason, C step 3. D says the term structure adds nothing, which contradicts step 2 and the A-rated versus CC-rated contrast.

**Fragile fact.** Binomial model: one period, default or not. Term structure: when. Copula: correlate the term structures to get joint defaults in different years.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.6, “Correlation Risk and Credit Risk”, Table 8.4. Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.3 (term structure only). GARP-only: the binomial-model remark and the copula. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 f, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: True statement (GARP §8.6, quoted above). It would be the answer only if defaults were continuous outcomes, which the reading rules out.

b.reason: True statement: GARP’s reason for the rising investment-grade curve. It would be the answer only if it described a distressed debtor, where the curve is inverse (Q6, option A trap).

c.reason: True statement: GARP’s copula example, almost verbatim. It would be the answer if it named a model the reading does not use for term structures, such as a correlation swap.

d.reason: GARP presents the term structure as the way to analyse defaults “in more detail”. Two debtors with the same one-year default probability can have very different year-by-year profiles.

questions.question: A board risk committee member at a Singapore bank asks how correlation risk fits into the bank’s SGD risk taxonomy alongside market risk and credit risk. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Correlation risk can be a category of its own, but correlation parameters are critical inputs, so it is also part of market and credit risk; higher correlation raises VaR for market risk and credit VaR for default risk.
Correlation risk is a stand-alone category that sits outside market and credit risk, so it is captured by correlation desks rather than by the bank’s VaR or credit VaR measures.
Correlation risk is part of market and credit risk, but in credit risk it enters only through migration risk, because default risk depends on each debtor’s default probability alone.
Correlation risk is part of market and credit risk; higher correlation raises VaR for market risk but lowers credit VaR, because correlated defaults reduce the number of separate loss events.

questions.solution:
**Correlation risk in the risk taxonomy; VaR and credit VaR**

Stem in one line: most accurate statement on how correlation risk fits with market risk and credit risk.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s Summary answers the taxonomy question directly: “Correlation risk can be categorised as its own type of risk. However, correlation parameters and correlation matrices are critical inputs and hence a part of market risk and credit risk. Market risk and credit risk are highly sensitive to changing correlations.”

The two measures run in parallel (GARP §8.8, closing paragraph):

|  | VaR | Credit VaR (CVaR) |
|---|---|---|
| Risk measured | Correlated market risk | Correlated default risk |
| Definition | Maximum loss of a portfolio for a given probability and time frame | “Maximum loss of a portfolio of correlated debt with a certain probability for a certain timeframe” |
| Correlation effect | Higher asset-return correlation, higher VaR (long portfolio; §8.3, §8.5) | “A higher (copula) correlation between assets results in a higher credit value-at-risk” |

**Applying it to this question**

The member needs three things: correlation risk is both its own category and part of market and credit risk; it acts through VaR and through credit VaR; and in both, higher correlation means more risk. Only A gives all three.

**Fragile fact.** Higher correlation raises both VaR (correlated market risk) and credit VaR (correlated default risk). In GARP, CVaR means credit VaR, not conditional VaR.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, Summary; §8.8 closing paragraph; §8.3 (“An increase in the correlation of asset returns increases the risk of financial loss, which is often measured by the VaR concept”). GARP-only: the taxonomy sentence and credit VaR are not in Schweser’s LO 8.f text. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 f, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: GARP Summary (taxonomy) and §8.8 (“CVaR measures correlated default risk and is analogous to the VaR concept for correlated market risk”; higher correlation, higher CVaR).

b.reason: Error type: scope error. GARP allows correlation risk to be a separate category but says it is “hence a part of market risk and credit risk” because the correlation inputs sit inside VaR and credit risk models. B would be correct only for a bank whose risk measures used no correlation inputs.

c.reason: Error type: scope error (default risk dropped). Default correlation, the degree to which defaults occur together, is at the centre of credit risk (Q7 to Q9); credit VaR measures correlated default risk. C would be correct if it said “through both migration risk and default risk”.

d.reason: Error type: polarity flip for credit VaR. Correlated defaults cluster losses, raising credit VaR. D would be correct with “raises credit VaR” in place of “lowers”.

questions.question: A model validator at a Brazilian bank reviews the market risk model of a trading book that holds only long positions in Brazilian equities, BRL-denominated bonds and commodity futures. VaR and ES are computed with a covariance matrix estimated over a period in which correlations between these assets were low. Since the estimation window ended, the correlations between the assets have risen sharply. Which statement in the validation report is most accurate?

options.text: This is correlation risk within credit risk, because rising correlations change the issuers’ default correlation; the VaR and ES of the book are unaffected.
This is correlation risk within market risk, but it affects only VaR; ES measures the tail beyond VaR, where correlations between returns are not an input.
This is correlation risk within market risk; for a long-only book, higher correlations reduce VaR and ES because gains and losses offset more often.
This is correlation risk within market risk: the correlations in the covariance matrix behind VaR and ES have changed, so both measures now understate the book’s risk.

questions.solution:
**Changing correlations in the covariance matrix behind VaR and ES**

Stem in one line: long-only book; VaR and ES use a low-correlation covariance matrix; correlations have since risen sharply.

**Concept and theory**

VaR and ES both take the covariance matrix of the assets as an input (GARP §8.6). Schweser puts the concern this way: “Given that correlation risk refers to the risk that the correlation between assets changes over time, the concern is how the covariance matrix used for calculating VaR or ES changes over time.”

Direction for a long portfolio: in $\sigma^{2}_{P}$ = $\sum_{i} \sum_{j} w_{i}w_{j} \rho_{ij} \sigma_{i}\sigma_{j}$ (with dollar amounts $w_{i} >$ 0), every cross term rises with $\rho_{ij}$ , so $\sigma_{P}$ and VaR rise. GARP §8.3: “An increase in the correlation of asset returns increases the risk of financial loss, which is often measured by the VaR concept.” A model that still uses the old low correlations reports too low a figure.

**Applying it to this question**

Equities, BRL bonds and commodities are market risk positions (equity, interest-rate and commodity risk). The change is in the correlations between their returns, the inputs to VaR and ES. All positions are long, so higher correlation means less offsetting and more risk. The model’s VaR and ES are therefore too low.

**Fragile fact.** Long-only book: correlation up ⇒ VaR and ES up. A stale low-correlation matrix understates risk.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 8, §8.6, “Correlation Risk and Market Risk”; §8.3. Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.3 (covariance matrix for VaR or ES changing over time). No conflict. The size of the VaR change for given correlations is LO 8.e and is not tested here; the crisis-period rise in correlations is LO 8.g.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 f, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap (credit channel substituted for market channel). The correlations that changed are between asset returns, inputs to VaR and ES. Default correlation is a different quantity. A would be correct for a loan book where the default correlation among borrowers had risen.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap between VaR and ES (scope error on ES’s inputs). GARP: “A rigorous valuation of expected shortfall naturally includes the correlation between the asset returns in the portfolio, as VaR does.” B would be correct if ES were computed position by position and simply added.

c.reason: Error type: polarity flip. For long positions, higher correlation means the assets fall together more often, so there is less offsetting, not more. C would be correct if correlations had fallen, or for a book with offsetting long and short positions.

d.reason: It classifies the risk correctly (correlation risk within market risk), names the channel (the covariance matrix behind VaR and ES) and gives the right direction for a long-only book.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Singapore bank is preparing a training slide on systemic risk for newly hired analysts. The draft slide contains four statements:

I. Systemic risk is the risk that a financial market or an entire financial system collapses.

II. When Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy in September 2008, the credit markets were virtually frozen, but lending resumed quickly once the Federal Reserve guaranteed interbank loans.

III. Systemic financial failures such as the one from 2007 to 2009 typically spread to the economy through a decreasing GDP, increasing unemployment and a lower standard of living.

IV. The fall of the Dow from October 2007 to March 2009 counts as a systemic collapse because the losses were confined to financial stocks while most other Dow components rose.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
I, III and IV only
I only

questions.solution:
**What systemic risk is and what it looked like in 2007 to 2009**

Stem in one line: which of four training-slide statements on systemic risk (definition, 2008 credit freeze, spread to the economy, Dow collapse) are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Most risks in finance are risks to a position or a firm. Systemic risk is the risk to the system itself: GARP defines it as the risk that a financial market or an entire financial system collapses (Schweser: the potential collapse of the entire financial system). GARP gives two examples from the 2007 to 2009 crisis.

| Example | What the reading says |
|---|---|
| Credit market, 2008 | At the height of the crisis, when Lehman Brothers filed for bankruptcy in September 2008, credit markets were virtually frozen with essentially no lending. Even with the Federal Reserve guaranteeing interbank loans, lending resumed only very gradually and slowly. |
| Stock market, 2007 to | The Dow fell from 14,093 (October 2007) by 53.54% to 6,547 (March |
| 2009 | 2009). All but one of the Dow 30 stocks declined; 489 of the S&P 500 stocks declined. |
| Real economy | Systemic failures typically spread to the economy: decreasing GDP, increasing unemployment and so a lower standard of living. |

The link to correlation risk (developed in Q2) is that a systemic collapse is, by definition, a collapse of almost everything at once: co-movement is the defining feature.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I is GARP’s definition. True. Statement II has the right first half (frozen credit markets after Lehman) but reverses the recovery: lending resumed only very gradually, even with the Fed guarantee. False. Statement III restates GARP’s point on the spread to GDP, unemployment and the standard of living. True. Statement IV inverts the breadth of the Dow decline: all but one of the 30 Dow stocks fell, which is exactly why it counts as systemic. False. Answer: I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** After Lehman, lending resumed slowly even with the Fed guarantee; the Dow collapse was market-wide (29 of 30 fell), not sector-specific.

**Reference**

LO 8.g (Schweser, verbatim): “Explain how correlation risk relates to systemic and concentration risk.” GARP Ch. 8, §8.7 Correlation Risk and Systemic Risk. Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.3. Difference: GARP gives the Dow fall as 53.54%; Schweser says “over 50%”. Schweser does not mention the Fed guarantee or the credit-market freeze (GARP-only); not material to the answer.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 g, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: GARP 8.7 defines systemic risk as the collapse of a financial market or an entire financial system and states that systemic failures spread to the economy through lower GDP, higher unemployment and a lower standard of living. Statements II and IV each contradict a stated fact.

b.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: polarity flip in statement II (“very gradually and slowly” becomes “quickly”). Accepting II means believing a central-bank guarantee immediately unfroze the market. B would be correct if II read “lending resumed only very gradually, even with the Federal Reserve guarantee”.

c.reason: **I, III and IV.** Error type: scope error in statement IV. A collapse confined to one sector is the opposite of systemic; the reading says all but one Dow stock declined (Walmart was the exception). C would be correct if IV said “all but one of the Dow 30 stocks declined”.

d.reason: **I only.** Error type: scope error in the other direction, rejecting a true statement. A candidate who thinks systemic risk stays inside the financial system rejects III. D would be correct only if the reading treated the real-economy effects as outside systemic risk, which it does not.

questions.question: The CRO of a Canadian pension plan is reviewing why a CAD 4 billion equity portfolio, judged well diversified using pairwise correlations estimated over 2004 to 2006, lost far more than the risk model predicted between August 2008 and March 2009. Which explanation is most consistent with the reading?

options.text: In a systemic decline, the average correlation between stocks fell as investors rotated into defensive names, so the offsetting benefit of low-correlation pairs disappeared.
The average correlation between stocks stayed near its pre-crisis level of about 27%, so the losses came from higher volatility alone and diversification worked as designed.
A systemic decline involves almost the entire market, so the average correlation between stocks rose sharply from about 27% to over 50%, and diversification failed when it was most needed.
The correlation between every pair of stocks moved to 1 throughout the period, so no diversification benefit of any kind remained at any point between August 2008 and March 2009.

questions.solution:
**Why diversification failed in the systemic decline**

Stem in one line: a portfolio diversified on 2004 to 2006 correlations lost far more than predicted in August 2008 to March 2009; which explanation fits the reading?

**Concept and theory**

Diversification works because assets that are not perfectly correlated do not all fall at the same time. The benefit is therefore only as reliable as the correlation estimate. GARP’s central claim in §8.7 is that systemic risk and correlation risk are highly dependent: a systemic decline in stocks involves almost the entire stock market, so the correlations between stocks increase sharply. The evidence:

| Measure (stocks in the Dow) | Value |
|---|---|
| Average correlation before the severe decline (non-crisis level) | about 27% |
| Average correlation, August 2008 to March 2009 | over 50% |
| Peak monthly correlation, February 2009 (GARP Ch. 9 cross-reference) | 96.97% |

The consequence, in GARP’s words in substance: portfolios considered well diversified in benign times experienced a sharp increase in correlation and therefore unexpected losses, because many stocks declined together. GARP §8.3 makes the same point (assets that were negatively or lowly correlated suddenly declined together), and the chapter Summary says correlations typically increase in a systemic crisis and can lead to high unexpected losses. Schweser adds (Schweser-only) that the problem is worse once the higher correlations of US equities with bonds and international equities are considered.

The mechanism to remember: correlation risk is the risk that the correlation you rely on changes. Systemic crises are when it changes most, and always in the direction that hurts a diversified long investor.

**Applying it to this question**

The portfolio’s correlations came from a calm window (2004 to 2006, when GARP reports a stable correlation). The loss window is exactly the August 2008 to March 2009 decline, when the reading reports the jump from about 27% to over 50%. The model therefore overstated diversification at the worst possible time.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: in a systemic crisis correlations go up (about 27% to over 50%), so diversification shrinks exactly when it is needed.

**Reference**

LO 8.g (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 8, §8.7 Correlation Risk and Systemic Risk; §8.3 What is Financial Correlation Risk?; Summary. Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.3 and Key Concepts LO 8.g. Difference: Schweser adds the higher correlations of US equities with bonds and international equities (Schweser-only, condensed source); GARP gives the 96.97% February 2009 peak by reference to Chapter 9 (GARP-only). No conflict on the 27% to over 50% evidence.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 g, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip. Correlations rose, not fell. A would describe a world in which crisis rotation lowers co-movement; the reading says the opposite.

b.reason: Error type: scope error (the correlation change is dropped). It keeps the 27% figure but treats it as constant, attributing the loss to volatility alone. B would be correct only if correlations had stayed at their non-crisis level, which contradicts Figure 8.8.

c.reason: It names the cause (a systemic decline involves almost the whole market), the direction and size (about 27% to over 50%) and the consequence (diversification fails when needed), all from GARP §8.7.

d.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. Correlation rose to over 50% on average and peaked at 96.97% in February 2009; it did not equal 1 for every pair throughout. D would be correct only for perfect co-movement of every pair over the whole window.

questions.question: A model validator at a UK asset manager is checking a consultant’s replication of the reading’s evidence on the correlation between the stocks in the Dow before and during the 2007 to 2009 crisis (GARP Figure 8.8). Which of the following statements in the consultant’s report is NOT correct?

options.text: From January 2007 to February 2008, correlation in the Dow fell while the Dow increased more strongly, showing that correlation rises only once prices are falling.
Monthly 30 by 30 Pearson correlation matrices of the Dow stocks were averaged, and the resulting series was smoothed with a one-year moving average.
Correlation was somewhat stable from 2004 to 2006, a period in which the Dow increased moderately.
During the severe decline of the Dow from August 2008 to March 2009, the average correlation rose sharply from about 27% to over 50%.

questions.solution:
**The evidence behind “correlations rise in a systemic crisis”**

Stem in one line: which statement about the GARP Figure 8.8 replication (Dow correlation, 2004 to 2009) is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP supports the systemic-correlation link with its own calculation (Figure 8.8):

- Data and method. Daily closing prices of all 30 Dow stocks, put into monthly bins; a 30 × 30 Pearson correlation matrix for each month; the matrices averaged; the series smoothed with a one-year moving average. The chart shows the Dow level against this average correlation.
- Phase 1, 2004 to 2006. Correlation somewhat stable while the Dow increased moderately.
- Phase 2, January 2007 to February 2008. Correlation in the Dow increased when the Dow increased more strongly.
- Phase 3, August 2008 to March 2009. During the severe decline, a sharp increase from non-crisis levels of an average 27% to over 50%.

Phase 2 is the subtle one: it shows that correlation can also rise in a strong up-move. The systemic point is about the scale of the rise in Phase 3, not a claim that correlation rises only in declines.

**Applying it to this question**

B, C and D restate the method, Phase 1 and Phase 3 correctly. A reverses Phase 2 (correlation fell instead of rose) and then draws an “only in declines” conclusion that the reading does not make. A is the incorrect statement.

**Fragile fact.** Phase 2 (Jan 2007 to Feb 2008): correlation rose with a strongly rising Dow. Do not memorise “correlation rises only when markets fall”.

**Reference**

LO 8.g (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 8, §8.7 Correlation Risk and Systemic Risk, Figure 8.8. GARP-only: Schweser omits Figure 8.8’s method and phases and reports only the 27% to over 50% rise. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 g, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: GARP §8.7 states that from January 2007 to February 2008 the correlation in the Dow increases when the Dow increases more strongly. Statement A says the opposite.

b.reason: A true statement of the method (monthly bins, 30 × 30 Pearson matrices, averaged, one-year moving average). It would be the incorrect statement if it said, for example, Spearman matrices or no smoothing.

c.reason: A true statement of Phase 1. It would be incorrect if it placed the sharp rise in 2004 to 2006.

d.reason: A true statement of Phase 3 and the key number of the LO. It would be incorrect if the direction or the 27% to over 50% figures were reversed.

questions.question: An equity strategist at an Australian superannuation fund is reviewing how individual stocks behaved during the systemic stock market collapse from October 2007 to March 2009, as described in the reading. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Walmart was the only Dow stock that declined over the period, while 489 of the S&P 500 stocks declined and 11 rose.
Of the S&P 500 stocks, 489 declined; the 11 that rose included consumer staples, which provide basic necessities, and educational firms, which benefit as many unemployed seek further education.
Of the S&P 500 stocks, 489 declined; the 11 that rose were mainly banks and insurers, which benefited directly from the Federal Reserve’s guarantee of interbank loans.
Of the S&P 500 stocks, 489 declined; educational firms were among the weakest, because rising unemployment cut household spending on further education.

questions.solution:
**Which stocks rose in the systemic collapse, and why**

Stem in one line: which statement about stock behaviour from October 2007 to March 2009 is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

A systemic collapse is broad, but not literally universal. GARP reports that all but one of the Dow 30 stocks declined (Walmart was the lone riser) and that 489 of the S&P 500 stocks declined, leaving 11 risers: Apollo Group and DeVry (education), AutoZone (auto replacement parts), CF Industries (fertiliser), Edwards Lifesciences and Gilead (pharmaceuticals), Family Dollar, Ross Stores and Walmart (consumer staples), Netflix (entertainment) and Southwestern Energy (energy). GARP draws two lessons:

| Sector | Why it held up (GARP) |
|---|---|
| Consumer staples | Provide basic necessities such as food and basic household items, so demand holds in a crisis. |
| Education | Typically thrives in a crisis, since many unemployed seek to further their education. |

For correlation risk the message is that even when correlations jump, a few sectors with low or negative sensitivity to the systemic factor survive; Schweser also calls pharmaceuticals recession resistant (Schweser-only).

**Applying it to this question**

The option must get the count (489 down, 11 up), the sectors and the reasons right. B does all three.

**Fragile fact.** Walmart: the only Dow stock up. S&P 500: 489 down, 11 up. Education thrives in a crisis.

**Reference**

LO 8.g (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 8, §8.7 Correlation Risk and Systemic Risk. Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.3. Difference: Schweser groups the 11 risers by sector and calls pharmaceuticals recession resistant as well (Schweser-only); GARP singles out only staples and education. Not material here.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 g, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip on Walmart. Walmart was the only Dow stock that rose. A would be correct if “declined” read “rose”.

b.reason: It matches GARP §8.7: 489 of the S&P 500 declined, consumer staples fared well because they provide necessities, and the educational sector thrives as unemployed people seek education.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap of sectors. The risers were staples, education, pharmaceuticals and a few others; financial firms were at the centre of the collapse. The Fed guarantee belongs to the credit-market example and did not even restore lending quickly. C would be correct only for a list of risers drawn from financials, which the reading does not give.

d.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the mechanism. Unemployment raises demand for further education in the reading’s account. D would be correct only under the reverse behavioural assumption.

questions.question: The chief compliance officer of a German Landesbank is reviewing a draft EUR credit policy that defines concentration risk and the concentration ratio. Which of the following definitions in the draft is most accurate?

options.text: Concentration risk is the risk that a financial market or an entire financial system collapses; it is measured by the concentration ratio, which is 1$/n$ for $n$ loans of equal size.

Concentration risk is the risk of loss from a concentrated exposure to a specific group of counterparties; a lower concentration ratio means more diversified default risk, whatever the default correlation.

Concentration risk is the risk of loss from a concentrated exposure to a specific group of counterparties; a lower concentration ratio means more diversified default risk, provided the default correlation is below 1.

Concentration risk is the risk of loss from a concentrated exposure to a specific group of counterparties; a higher concentration ratio means more diversified default risk, provided the default correlation is below 1.

questions.solution:
**Defining concentration risk and the condition on the concentration ratio**

Stem in one line: which draft definition of concentration risk and the concentration ratio is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

GARP calls concentration risk a fairly new risk category that is not yet uniquely defined, and offers a sensible definition: the risk of financial loss due to a concentrated exposure to a specific group of counterparties. It is quantified with the concentration ratio. For $n$ loans of equal size to $n$ different counterparties:

Concentration ratio = $\frac{1}{n}$

so 10 equal loans give 0.1 and a single loan gives 1. The lower the ratio, the more diversified the creditor’s default risk, assuming the default correlation between the counterparties is smaller than 1.

Why the condition? Diversification works only if the borrowers can default separately. With a default correlation of 1, they default together or survive together, so splitting the money among them changes nothing (GARP: for any model, a default correlation of 1 leaves no benefit from the lower concentration ratio). This is where concentration risk and correlation risk meet: the benefit of a low ratio is a correlation benefit.

|  | Low concentration ratio | High concentration ratio |
|---|---|---|
| Number of equal loans | many | few |
| Default risk diversified? | more (if $\rho<$ 1) | less |

**Applying it to this question**

Three options share the right definition, so the decision sits in the direction and the condition. Lower ratio, more diversified, provided $\rho<$ 1: only C has all of these.

**Fragile fact.** Ratio = 1$/n$; lower is better; the benefit exists only while default correlation is below 1.

**Reference**

LO 8.g (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 8, §8.8 Correlation Risk and Concentration Risk. Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.3. Difference: Schweser defines concentration risk as loss from the exposure of multiple counterparties to a specific group and states the lower-ratio rule without the $\rho<$ 1 condition; GARP states the condition explicitly and is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 g, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap. It gives the definition of systemic risk (§8.7) to concentration risk. A would be correct if it began “Systemic risk is. . . ” and dropped the ratio.

b.reason: Error type: absolute claim (the $\rho<$ 1 condition is dropped). At $\rho$ = 1 a lower ratio gives no benefit. B would be correct with “provided the default correlation is below 1”.

c.reason: GARP §8.8: concentration risk is loss from a concentrated exposure to a specific group of counterparties; the lower the concentration ratio, the more diversified the default risk, assuming the default correlation is smaller than 1.

d.reason: Error type: polarity flip. A higher ratio means fewer, larger exposures, so less diversification. D would be correct with “lower” in place of “higher”.

questions.question:
A credit risk analyst at a Swiss private bank is summarising its CHF corporate loan book for the risk committee:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Number of loans | 20 |
| Size of each loan | CHF 15 million |
| Number of different counterparties | 20 |
| Number of sectors (5 loans per sector) | 4 |
| Average one-year default probability | 2.5% |

Which of the following correctly states the bank’s concentration ratio and the effect of spreading the same loans across more sectors?

options.text: 0.05; more sectors raise sector diversification and reduce default risk, because defaults within a sector are more highly correlated than defaults across sectors.
0.25; more sectors raise sector diversification and reduce default risk, because defaults within a sector are more highly correlated than defaults across sectors.
0.05; more sectors lower sector diversification and raise default risk, because defaults across sectors are more highly correlated than defaults within a sector.
0.20; more sectors raise sector diversification and reduce default risk, because defaults within a sector are more highly correlated than defaults across sectors.

questions.solution:
**Concentration ratio and sector concentration**

Stem in one line: 20 equal CHF 15m loans to 20 counterparties in 4 sectors; give the concentration ratio and the effect of using more sectors.

**Concept and theory**

The concentration ratio counts counterparties, not sectors or currency amounts:

Concentration ratio = $\frac{1}{n} , n$ = number of equal-size loans to different counterparties.

GARP then adds a second layer: counterparties can be grouped, for example into sectors, to analyse sector concentration risk. The more sectors a creditor lends to, the higher its sector diversification, and high sector diversification reduces default risk because defaults within a sector are more highly correlated than defaults of counterparties in different sectors. Again the underlying driver is correlation: moving exposure across sectors lowers the default correlation between debtors.

**Applying it to this question**

$n$ = 20 loans of equal size (CHF 15 million each) to 20 counterparties

Concentration ratio = 1/20 = 0.05

The 4 sectors, the 5 loans per sector and the 2.5% average default probability do not enter the ratio. On sectors, the reading’s direction is: more sectors, more sector diversification, lower default risk, because intra-sector default correlation is higher.

**Fragile fact.** The ratio uses the number of equal loans to different counterparties; the sector rule rests on intrasector default correlation being the higher one.

**Reference**

LO 8.g (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 8, §8.8 Correlation Risk and Concentration Risk (GARP-only for the sector-concentration sentence). Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.3 (“Loans can be further analyzed by grouping them into different sectors”). Boundary note: the industry default-correlation table and the GM/Ford example are LO 8.f content and are not tested. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 g, where it is Q6 of 12.

a.reason: It combines the correct ratio (0.05) with GARP §8.8’s sector-concentration rationale.

b.reason: Error type: wrong input twin. 1/4 uses the number of sectors instead of the number of loans. Would be correct if the bank had made 4 equal loans (one per sector).

c.reason: Error type: polarity flip on correlation. It claims cross-sector defaults are more correlated than intra-sector defaults, and hence that more sectors raise risk. Would be correct only in a world where defaults cluster across sectors rather than within them.

d.reason: Error type: wrong input twin. 1/5 uses loans per sector. Would be correct for a creditor with 5 equal loans in total.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a UK building society is quantifying the worst-case scenario for two commercial loans. Default of each borrower is modelled as a binomial event (1 if default, 0 otherwise).

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Loan to Company X | GBP 6 million |
| Loan to Company Y | GBP 6 million |
| One-year default probability, X and Y (each) | 8% |
| Default correlation between X and Y | 0.35 |
| Loss given default | 100% |
| Annual coupon on each loan | 6.75% |

Which of the following is closest to the expected loss under the worst-case scenario in which both X and Y default?
questions.solution:
**Worst-case expected loss on two correlated loans**

Stem in one line: GBP 6m to each of X and Y, PD 8% each, default correlation 0.35, LGD 100%; expected loss when both default.

**Concept and theory**

GARP models each default as a binomial (Bernoulli) variable: 1 if in default, 0 otherwise. For such a variable with default probability $P$ :

$\sigma$ = $\sqrt{P \text{(1} - P \text{)}}$ (GARP eq. 8.12)

The joint probability that both $X$ and $Y$ default is (GARP eq. 8.11):

$P$ ($X \cap Y$ ) = $\rho_{XY} \sqrt{P_{X} \text{(1} - P_{X} \text{)}} \sqrt{P_{Y} \text{(1} - P_{Y} \text{)}}$ + $P_{X} P_{Y}$

where $P_{X}$ , $P_{Y}$ are the individual default probabilities and $\rho_{XY}$ is the default correlation. Read it as two pieces: $P_{X} P_{Y}$ is the joint default probability if defaults were independent ($\rho$ = 0), and $\rho\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$ is the extra (or reduced) joint probability caused by correlation, which is the covariance of the two default indicators. The worst-case scenario for a creditor is that every debtor defaults; with LGD of 100% its expected loss is

$\text{EL}_{\text{worst}}$ = (total exposure) $\times P$ ($X \cap Y$ ).

**Applying it to this question**

$\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$ = 0.08 × 0.92 = 0.0736 ($\sigma$ = 0.2713 each)

$\rho\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$ = 0.35 × 0.0736 = 0.02576

$P_{X} P_{Y}$ = 0.08 × 0.08 = 0.0064

$P$ ($X \cap Y$ ) = 0.02576 + 0.0064 = 0.03216

Total exposure = 6 + 6 = GBP 12 million

$\text{EL}_{\text{worst}}$ = 12,000,000 × 0.03216 = GBP 385,920

Meaning: correlation of 0.35 makes the joint default five times more likely than independence would (3.216% versus 0.64%). The 6.75% coupon is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** $\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$ = $\sqrt{P_{X} \text{(1} - P_{X} \text{)}}\sqrt{P_{Y} \text{(1} - P_{Y} \text{)}}$; with equal PDs it is simply $P$ (1 $- P$ ), not its square root. Then add $P_{X} P_{Y}$ and multiply by the total exposure.

**Reference**

LO 8.g (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 8, §8.8, eq. (8.11) and (8.12), Example 8.3. Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.3 (Bank Y example; formula image missing). Eq. (8.11) is garbled in the GARP text and missing in Schweser; notation confirmed from question bank Q454 and Q456 worked solutions. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 g, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: correlation ignored. 12,000,000 × 0.0064 = 76,800 is the independence case, $\rho$ = 0. Correct if the default correlation were 0.

b.reason: Error type: dropped term (exposure). 6,000,000 × 0.03216 = 192,960 uses one loan’s exposure; when both default, both loans are lost. Correct if the question asked for the worst-case loss on one loan only.

c.reason: Error type: dropped term ($P_{X} P_{Y}$ ). 12,000,000 × 0.02576 = 309,120 uses only the correlation (covariance) term. Correct only if the independence term were zero, which never happens with positive default probabilities.

d.reason: It applies eq. (8.11) with both terms and multiplies by the full GBP 12 million that is lost when both default, as in GARP Example 8.3 and Schweser’s Bank Y example.

questions.question:
A senior risk consultant is validating a bank’s methodology note on how default correlation affects the benefit of a lower concentration ratio. Default of each borrower is modelled as a binomial event. The note states:

I. If the default correlation between two borrowers is 1, they can only default together or survive together, so splitting one loan between them gives no reduction in the worst-case expected loss.

II. If the default correlation between two borrowers is 0, their joint default probability equals the product of their individual default probabilities.

III. If the default correlation between two borrowers is negative, their joint default probability is always zero.

IV. If the default correlation lies between 0 and 1, the exact joint default probability is the same under every correlation model, so the model choice does not matter.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I only
I and II only
I, II and III only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
**What the level of default correlation does to the joint default probability**

Stem in one line: which methodology statements about $\rho$ = 1, $\rho$ = 0, negative $\rho$ and model choice are correct?

**Concept and theory**

Using eq. (8.11), $P$ ($X \cap Y$ ) = $\rho\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$ + $P_{X} P_{Y}$ , GARP walks through the correlation range for its Example 8.3 ($P_{X}$ = $P_{Y}$ = 10%, $\sigma$ = 0.3):

| $\rho_{XY}$ | $P$ ($X \cap Y$ ) | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10.0% | Default or survive together; same as one loan, no benefit from the lower ratio |
| 0.5 | 5.5% | Partial benefit |
| 0 | 1.0% | Independence: $P_{X} P_{Y}$ |
| −0.1 | 0.1% | Still positive despite negative correlation |

Two further points from §8.8: (1) the exact joint default probability depends on the correlation model and its parameter values; the binomial formula is one model; (2) for any model, a default correlation of 1 removes the benefit of a lower concentration ratio. GARP notes that a slightly negative correlation can still give a positive joint default probability.

**Applying it to this question**

I: GARP’s own description of $\rho$ = 1 (default together or survive together; no benefit). True. II: set $\rho$ = 0 in eq. (8.11). True. III: contradicted by the −0.1 ⇒ 0.1% example. False. IV: GARP says the exact joint probability depends on the model and parameter values. False. Answer: I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Model-free: $\rho$ = 1 means no benefit. Model-dependent: the exact joint probability for 0 $< \rho<$ 1. Negative $\rho$ does not mean zero joint default.

**Reference**

LO 8.g (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 8, §8.8 Correlation Risk and Concentration Risk, Example 8.3 and eq. (8.11). Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.3 (gives the $\rho$ = 1 and $\rho$ = 0 cases only; the model-dependence and negative-correlation points are GARP-only). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 g, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: **I only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement (definition gap on the independence case). Correct only if eq. (8.11) did not reduce to $P_{X} P_{Y}$ at $\rho$ = 0.

b.reason: Statements I and II follow directly from GARP §8.8 and eq. (8.11); III and IV are each contradicted by a specific sentence of the same section.

c.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: absolute-claim trap in III. A negative correlation lowers the joint probability below $P_{X} P_{Y}$ but need not reach zero (see Q10). III would be true only for a sufficiently negative correlation, $\rho\le-P_{X} P_{Y} /$($\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$ ).

d.reason: **I, II and IV.** Error type: scope error in IV, overextending the model-free statement. Only the $\rho$ = 1 conclusion holds “for any model”; the exact joint probability is model dependent. IV would be true if it read “if the default correlation is 1”.

questions.question:
A credit risk manager at a Japanese regional bank compares two ways of lending a total of JPY 2 billion. Default of each borrower is modelled as a binomial event and loss given default is 100%.

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Plan 1: single loan to Company W | JPY 2 billion |
| Plan 2: loans to Companies X and Y | JPY 1 billion each |
| One-year default probability of W, X and Y (each) | 6% |
| Default correlation between X and Y | 0.40 |

By how much does Plan 2 reduce the expected loss under the worst-case scenario (all borrowers default) relative to Plan 1?

options.text: JPY 41.46 million
JPY 52.32 million
JPY 60.00 million
JPY 67.68 million

questions.solution:
**The benefit of a lower concentration ratio, in yen**

Stem in one line: JPY 2bn as one loan to W versus JPY 1bn each to X and Y (PD 6%, $\rho$ = 0.40); reduction in worst-case expected loss.

**Concept and theory**

GARP Example 8.3 is built exactly this way. Case (a): one loan, concentration ratio 1, worst case is the default of the single borrower, so EL = exposure $\times P$ . Case (b): the same money split into two loans, ratio 1/2; the worst case is now the joint default, whose probability is given by eq. (8.11):

$P$ ($X \cap Y$ ) = $\rho_{XY} \sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$ + $P_{X} P_{Y} , \sigma$ = $\sqrt{P \text{(1} - P \text{)}}.$

If 0 $< \rho<$ 1 the joint probability lies between $P_{X} P_{Y}$ and $P$ , so the worst-case loss falls. If $\rho$ = 1 the joint probability equals $P$ and nothing is gained. So “both a lower concentration ratio and a lower correlation coefficient reduce the worst-case scenario”, but the size of the gain from the lower ratio is set by the correlation.

**Applying it to this question**

Plan 1: $\text{EL}_{\text{worst}}$ = 2,000 × 0.06 = JPY 120.00 million

$\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$ = 0.06 × 0.94 = 0.0564

$\rho\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$ = 0.40 × 0.0564 = 0.02256

$P_{X} P_{Y}$ = $\text{0.06}^{2}$ = 0.0036

$P$ ($X \cap Y$ ) = 0.02256 + 0.0036 = 0.02616

Plan 2: $\text{EL}_{\text{worst}}$ = 2,000 × 0.02616 = JPY 52.32 million

Reduction = 120.00 − 52.32 = JPY 67.68 million

Meaning: halving the concentration ratio cut the worst-case expected loss by about 56%, more than half, because the correlation of 0.40 is well below 1.

**Fragile fact.** Single loan: worst case uses $P$ . Two loans: worst case uses $P$ ($X \cap Y$ ) and the same total exposure. The gain comes from $\rho<$ 1, not from the ratio alone.

**Reference**

LO 8.g (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 8, §8.8, Example 8.3 cases (a) and (b), eq. (8.11) and (8.12). Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.3 (Bank X and Bank Y examples). Eq. (8.11) notation confirmed from question bank Q454 and Q456. Difference: GARP’s example uses USD 10 million and $P$ = 10%; Schweser’s uses USD 5 million and $P$ = 5% (version difference, not reused).

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 g, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: correlation misuse ($\sqrt{\rho}$ for $\rho$). $\sqrt{0.40}$ = 0.6325; 0.6325 × 0.0564 + 0.0036 = 0.03927; Plan 2 EL = 78.54; reduction = 120 − 78.54 = 41.46. Correct only if the true default correlation were $\text{0.40}^{2}$ = 0.16 and the stem had quoted its square root.

b.reason: Error type: intermediate result. 52.32 is Plan 2’s worst-case EL, not the reduction. Correct if the question asked for Plan 2’s worst-case expected loss.

c.reason: Error type: scaling by the concentration ratio. It assumes the worst-case EL falls in proportion to the ratio (120 × 0.5 = 60, so a reduction of 60). That ignores correlation entirely. It would be correct only in the special case where $\rho$ happens to give $P$ ($X \cap Y$ ) = $P/$2, which needs $\rho$ = (0.03 − 0.0036)/0.0564 = 0.468.

d.reason: It compares the single-loan worst case (exposure $\times P$ ) with the two-loan worst case (exposure × $P$ ($X \cap Y$ ) from eq. 8.11), as in GARP Example 8.3 cases (a) and (b).

questions.question: A risk analyst at a Chinese bank models loans of CNY 250 million each to two companies in unrelated industries. Default of each company is a binomial event with a one-year default probability of 15%, and the estimated default correlation between the two companies is −0.12. Which of the following is closest to their joint probability of default?
questions.solution:
**Negative default correlation, positive joint default probability**

Stem in one line: two loans, PD 15% each, default correlation −0.12; joint default probability.

**Concept and theory**

In eq. (8.11), $P$ ($X \cap Y$ ) = $\rho\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$ + $P_{X} P_{Y}$ , a negative $\rho$ makes the correlation term negative and so pulls the joint probability below the independence value $P_{X} P_{Y}$ . But $P_{X} P_{Y}$ is always positive, so a mildly negative correlation only partly offsets it. GARP’s example: $P$ = 10%, $\sigma$ = 0.3, $\rho$ = −0.1 gives −0.1 × 0.09 + 0.01 = 0.1%, still positive. The joint probability reaches zero only when

$\rho\le- \frac{P_{X} P_{Y}}{\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}} .$

**Applying it to this question**

$\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$ = 0.15 × 0.85 = 0.1275

$\rho\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$ = −0.12 × 0.1275 = −0.0153

$P_{X} P_{Y}$ = $\text{0.15}^{2}$ = 0.0225

$P$ ($X \cap Y$ ) = −0.0153 + 0.0225 = 0.0072 = 0.72%

Check against the zero threshold: −0.0225/0.1275 = −0.176; since −0.12 > −0.176, the joint probability is still positive. Meaning: negative correlation cuts the joint default probability from 2.25% to 0.72%, but does not remove it. The CNY 250 million loan size is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Keep the sign of $\rho$; negative correlation lowers the joint default probability below $P_{X} P_{Y}$ but usually not to zero.

**Reference**

LO 8.g (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 8, §8.8 (negative-correlation case after eq. 8.11). GARP-only: Schweser does not discuss negative default correlation. Eq. (8.11) notation confirmed from question bank Q454 and Q455. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 g, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap (“negative correlation means no joint default”). Correct only if $\rho\le-$0.176 here.

b.reason: It applies eq. (8.11) with the negative sign kept on the correlation term, exactly as GARP does for $\rho$ = −0.1.

c.reason: Error type: correlation ignored ($\rho$ set to 0). $\text{0.15}^{2}$ = 2.25% is the independence value. Correct if the default correlation were 0.

d.reason: Error type: sign error. +0.12 × 0.1275 + 0.0225 = 0.0378. Correct if the correlation were +0.12.

questions.question:
A member of the risk committee of a Brazilian bank asks how a systemic crisis would affect the worst-case loss on two loans. Default of each borrower is modelled as a binomial event, and default probabilities are unchanged in the stress scenario.

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Loan to each of Company X and Company Y | BRL 50 million |
| One-year default probability, X and Y (each) | 4% |
| Default correlation, benign conditions | 0.05 |
| Default correlation, systemic-crisis stress scenario | 0.45 |
| Loss given default | 100% |

Which of the following is closest to the increase in the expected loss under the worst-case scenario (both X and Y default) when moving from benign conditions to the stress scenario?
questions.solution:
**How a systemic crisis erodes the benefit of a low concentration ratio**

Stem in one line: BRL 50m to each of X and Y, PD 4%; default correlation rises from 0.05 to 0.45 in a systemic stress; increase in worst-case expected loss.

**Concept and theory**

This question joins the two halves of the LO. From §8.7 and the Summary: correlations typically increase in a systemic crisis. From §8.8: the benefit of a lower concentration ratio exists only because default correlation is below 1, and a lower correlation coefficient reduces the worst-case scenario. Put together, a systemic crisis that pushes default correlations up takes back part of the protection that a low concentration ratio seemed to provide, even with unchanged default probabilities. GARP notes, in the crisis section, that default correlations between the mortgages in CDOs increased from 2007 to 2009.

With eq. (8.11), the change in the worst-case EL when only $\rho$ changes is

$\text{}\Delta \text{EL}_{\text{worst}}$ = total exposure × ($\rho_{\text{stress}} - \rho_{\text{benign}}$) $\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y} ,$

because the independence term $P_{X} P_{Y}$ is the same in both states and cancels.

**Applying it to this question**

$\sigma_{X} \sigma_{Y}$ = 0.04 × 0.96 = 0.0384$, P_{X} P_{Y}$ = 0.0016

$P$ ($X \cap Y$ $\text{)}_{\text{benign}}$ = 0.05 × 0.0384 + 0.0016 = 0.00352

$P$ ($X \cap Y$ $\text{)}_{\text{stress}}$ = 0.45 × 0.0384 + 0.0016 = 0.01888

$\text{EL}_{\text{benign}}$ = 100,000,000 × 0.00352 = BRL 352,000

$\text{EL}_{\text{stress}}$ = 100,000,000 × 0.01888 = BRL 1,888,000

∆EL = 1,888,000 − 352,000 = BRL 1,536,000

Shortcut check: 100,000,000 × 0.40 × 0.0384 = 1,536,000. Meaning: with the concentration ratio fixed at 0.5, the systemic rise in correlation multiplies the worst-case expected loss by about 5.4.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: systemic crisis means correlation up, which means worst-case loss up, even with unchanged default probabilities and an unchanged concentration ratio.

**Reference**

LO 8.g (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 8, §8.7, §8.8 (eq. 8.11) and Summary; §8.6 (correlation risk closely related to systemic and concentration risk). Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.3 and Key Concepts LO 8.g. Eq. (8.11) notation confirmed from question bank Q454 and Q456. Difference: Schweser says a decrease in the concentration ratio “results in” a decrease in default correlation; GARP says the two are closely related. GARP’s framing (two separate levers that both reduce the worst case) is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 g, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: intermediate result (the benign level). Correct if the question asked for the worst-case EL in benign conditions.

b.reason: Error type: dropped term (exposure). It uses one loan of BRL 50 million: 50,000,000 × 0.40 × 0.0384. Correct if the question asked about the increase per loan.

c.reason: It measures the change in the worst-case EL driven only by the correlation increase, using eq. (8.11) and the total BRL 100 million exposure.

d.reason:
Error type: intermediate result (the stressed level). Correct if the question asked for the worst-case EL in the stress scenario.

Note: omitting $P_{X} P_{Y}$ gives the same increase here because the term cancels; that is why it is not offered as a distractor.

questions.question: A board risk committee member at a French bank is reading a EUR credit portfolio summary on how correlation risk relates to systemic risk and concentration risk. Which of the following statements in the summary is NOT correct?

options.text: Correlation risk is closely related to systemic risk, because correlations typically increase in a systemic crisis and can lead to high unexpected losses.
Both a lower concentration ratio and a lower default correlation reduce the creditor’s worst-case scenario, the joint probability of default of its debtors.
A higher (copula) correlation between assets results in a higher credit value-at-risk, the maximum loss of a portfolio of correlated debt at a given probability and horizon.
A lower concentration ratio reduces the worst-case scenario only if default correlation is exactly zero; for any positive default correlation the benefit disappears.

questions.solution:
**The summary links: systemic risk, concentration risk and CVaR**

Stem in one line: which summary statement on correlation risk versus systemic and concentration risk is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP §8.6 places correlation risk inside the wider risk map: it is an integral part of market and credit risk (LO 8.f) and is closely related to systemic risk and concentration risk (this LO). The reading’s conclusions for this LO are:

| Link | Statement in the reading |
|---|---|
| Systemic risk | Correlations typically increase in a systemic crisis and can lead to high unexpected losses (Summary; §8.7). |
| Concentration risk | Both a lower concentration ratio and a lower correlation coefficient reduce the creditor’s worst-case scenario, the joint default probability |
| CVaR | of its debtors (§8.8 conclusion). The ratio’s benefit needs $\rho<$ 1. A higher (copula) correlation between assets results in a higher credit value-at-risk; CVaR measures the maximum loss of a portfolio of correlated debt with a certain probability over a certain timeframe, analogous to VaR for market risk (§8.8, GARP-only). |

**Applying it to this question**

A, B and C restate the three links. D claims the ratio’s benefit exists only at $\rho$ = 0 and disappears for any positive correlation. GARP’s Example 8.3 shows a benefit for any default correlation between 0 and 1 (at $\rho$ = 0.5 the joint probability is 5.5% against 10% for one loan); only at $\rho$ = 1 does it vanish. D is the incorrect statement.

**Fragile fact.** The concentration-ratio benefit disappears at $\rho$ = 1, not at $\rho>$ 0.

**Reference**

LO 8.g (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 8, §8.6 How Does Correlation Risk Fit into the Broader Picture of Risks in Finance?, §8.7, §8.8 and Summary. Schweser Reading 8, Module 8.3 and Key Concepts LO 8.g. GARP-only: the CVaR remark. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-8 g, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: A true statement (Summary and §8.7). It would be the incorrect statement if it said correlations fall in a systemic crisis.

b.reason: A true statement (§8.8 conclusion; Schweser Key Concepts LO 8.g). It would be incorrect if either lever were said to raise the worst case.

c.reason: A true statement (§8.8 closing paragraph). It would be incorrect if it said higher correlation lowers CVaR, or described CVaR as a market-risk measure.

d.reason:
GARP §8.8: if the default correlation is bigger than 0 and smaller than 1, the worst case is reduced; only at a correlation of 1 is there no benefit from the lower concentration ratio.

D is the answer: error type scope or condition error, moving the boundary of the benefit from $\rho<$ 1 to $\rho$ = 0.

questions.question:
A risk consultant at a Singapore asset manager is testing three monthly series for mean reversion. For each series she regresses the monthly change $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ on the previous month’s level $S_{t-1}$, using the standard regression $Y$ = $\alpha$ + $\beta X$. The results are:

| Series | Intercept $\alpha$ | Slope $\beta$ | $R^{2}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| SGD 5-year swap spread (bps) | 14.40 | −0.18 | 0.11 |
| Average pairwise correlation, SGD equity basket | 0.2046 | −0.66 | 0.35 |
| Commodity index (log level) | −0.13 | +0.03 | 0.01 |

Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: All three series display mean reversion, because each regression produces a slope coefficient that is different from zero.
Only the swap spread and the correlation series display mean reversion, and the correlation series is pulled back to its mean the fastest.
Only the swap spread and the correlation series display mean reversion, and the swap spread is pulled back to its mean the fastest.
Only the commodity index displays mean reversion, because its positive slope means the change rises when the prior level rises.

questions.solution:
**Recognising mean reversion from regression output**

Stem in one line: three regressions of $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ on $S_{t-1}$ with slopes −0.18, −0.66 and +0.03; which series mean revert and which reverts fastest?

**Concept and theory**

Mean reversion is the tendency of a variable to be pulled back to its long-term mean. GARP defines it statistically: mean reversion is present if there is a negative relationship between the change of a variable, $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$, and its level at $t -$ 1, $S_{t-1}$. Formally (GARP eq. 9.1)

$\frac{\partial\text{(}S_{t} - S_{t-1}\text{)}}{\partial S_{t-1}} <$ 0,

where $S_{t}$ is the value at time $t$, $S_{t-1}$ the value one period earlier, and ∂ denotes the partial derivative. In words: if $S_{t-1}$ is high, the next change tends to be low (negative), pulling the variable down; if $S_{t-1}$ is low, the next change tends to be high, pulling it up.

The size of the pull is the mean reversion rate $a$ (also called mean reversion speed or gravity). Dropping the stochastic term and setting ∆$t$ = 1, the model $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ = $a\mu_{S} - aS_{t-1}$ matches the regression $Y$ = $\alpha$ + $\beta X$ with $Y$ = $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ and $X$ = $S_{t-1}$, so $\beta$ = $-a$. A negative slope therefore signals mean reversion, and the more negative it is, the stronger the pull.

| Slope $\beta$ of $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ on $S_{t-1}$ | Implied $a$ = $-\beta$ | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| Negative | Positive | Mean reversion; larger $\|\beta\|$ means faster pull |
| Zero or positive | Zero or negative | No mean reversion |

**Applying it to this question**

Swap spread: $a$ = −(−0.18) = 0.18 ⇒ 18% of the gap closed per month

Correlation: $a$ = −(−0.66) = 0.66 ⇒ 66% of the gap closed per month

Commodity index: $a$ = −(+0.03) = −0.03 ⇒ no mean reversion (positive relation)

Only the two series with negative slopes mean revert, and the correlation series has the larger rate. The intercepts and $R^{2}$ values are not needed for this judgement. (This mirrors the source: equity correlations show very strong mean reversion.)

**Fragile fact.** Mean reversion needs a negative slope of the change on the prior level; the rate is $a$ = $-\beta$, so the more negative the slope, the faster the reversion.

**Reference**

LO 9.b (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 9, §9.2 “Do Equity Correlations Exhibit Mean Reversion?”, “How Can We Quantify Mean Reversion?”, eq. (9.1) and (9.5). Schweser Reading 9, “Mean Reversion and Autocorrelation”. Eq. (9.1) is garbled in GARP and missing in Schweser; the condition is taken from the GARP and Schweser text that states it in words. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 b, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: **All three mean revert.** Error type: scope or condition error. It drops the sign condition and treats any non-zero slope as evidence. A positive slope of +0.03 means a higher level is followed by a larger change, which is the opposite of a pull back. A would be right only if all three slopes were negative.

b.reason: GARP §9.2: “Mean reversion is present if there is a negative relationship between the change of a variable, $S_{t} -S_{t-1}$, and the variable at $t-$1” and “the regression coefficient $\beta$ is equal to the negative mean-reversion parameter $a$.” Slopes of −0.18 and −0.66 give $a$ of 18% and 66%; the correlation series reverts fastest.

c.reason: **Swap spread fastest.** Error type: polarity flip on magnitude. It reads a slope closer to zero as a stronger pull. Since $a$ = $-\beta$, the slope of −0.18 means only 18% of the gap is closed each month, against 66% for the correlation series. C would be right if the swap spread slope were, say, −0.80.

d.reason: **Only the commodity index.** Error type: polarity flip on the defining condition. A change that rises when the prior level rises is exactly what mean reversion rules out. D would be right if the definition required a positive relation, which describes a trending, not a mean-reverting, series.
