questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee of a Canadian pension fund asks a senior risk analyst to explain the discrete process used to model a mean-reverting CAD market variable:

$S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ = $a$($\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$) ∆$t$ + $\sigma_{S} \epsilon\sqrt{\Delta t}$

The analyst’s briefing note contains four statements:

I. With ∆$t$ = 1 and the stochastic term ignored, $a$ = 1 pulls a variable that is below its long-term mean all the way to $\mu_{S}$ in one time step.

II. With $a$ = 0 the first term on the right-hand side vanishes, so the process shows no mean reversion.

III. The term $\sigma_{S} \epsilon\sqrt{\Delta t}$ determines the speed of the pull towards $\mu_{S}$ , so it must be kept when the mean reversion rate is the only quantity being measured.

IV. With $a$ = 0.5, ∆$t$ = 1 and the stochastic term ignored, the variable closes half of its gap to $\mu_{S}$ in each time step and therefore reaches $\mu_{S}$ after two time steps.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I, II and IV only
I, III and IV only
II and III only
I and II only

questions.solution:
**The mean reversion rate in the discrete Vasicek process**

Stem in one line: which statements about $a$ = 1, $a$ = 0, the stochastic term and $a$ = 0.5 in $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ = $a$($\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$)∆$t$ + $\sigma_{S} \epsilon\sqrt{\Delta t}$ are correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP quantifies the degree of mean reversion with the discrete Vasicek (1987) process, which goes back to Ornstein and Uhlenbeck (1930):

$S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ = $a$($\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$) ∆$t$ + $\sigma_{S} \epsilon\sqrt{\Delta t}$ (9.2)

where $S_{t}$ is the value at $t$; $S_{t-1}$ the value at $t -$ 1; $a$ the degree of mean reversion (mean reversion rate or gravity), 0 $\le a \le$ 1; $\mu_{S}$ the long-term mean of $S$; $\sigma_{S}$ the volatility of $S$; $\epsilon$ a random drawing from a standardised normal distribution; and ∆$t$ the length of the time step.

The equation has two parts. The deterministic part $a$($\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$)∆$t$ is the pull towards the mean: it is proportional to the gap between the mean and the current level, scaled by $a$. The stochastic part $\sigma_{S} \epsilon\sqrt{\Delta t}$ adds random noise. GARP: “We are currently interested only in mean reversion, so for now we will ignore the stochastic part.” With ∆$t$ = 1 the measurement equation becomes $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ = $a$($\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$) (eq. 9.3).

GARP’s interpretation: $a$ = 1 pulls $S_{t-1}$ to $\mu_{S}$ completely at every time step; $a$ = 0.5 gives a mean reversion of 50% at each time step; $a$ = 0 gives no mean reversion.

**Applying it to this question**

I: $a$ = 1, ∆$t$ = 1: $S_{t}$ = $S_{t-1}$ + ($\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$) = $\mu_{S}$ . Correct.

II: $a$ = 0: $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ = 0 in the deterministic part, no pull. Correct.

III: the speed of the pull is $a$, which sits in the deterministic term; the stochastic term is ignored when measuring mean reversion. Incorrect.

IV: with $a$ = 0.5, each step closes half of the remaining gap:

after step 1: remaining gap = (1 − 0.5) $\times G$ = 0.5$G$

after step 2: remaining gap = (1 − 0.5) × 0.5$G$ = 0.25$G$

So 75% of the gap is closed after two steps, not 100%. Incorrect. Answer: I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** The rate $a$ acts on the remaining gap each step; only $a$ = 1 reaches the mean in one step. The stochastic term $\sigma_{S} \epsilon\sqrt{\Delta t}$ is dropped when measuring $a$.

**Reference**

LO 9.b (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 9, §9.2, “How Can We Quantify Mean Reversion?”, eq. (9.2) and (9.3). Schweser Reading 9, “Mean Reversion and Autocorrelation” (example with $a$ = 0, 0.5, 1). The bound 0 $\le a \le$ 1 is GARP-only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 b, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: **I, II and IV.** Error type: absolute-claim trap in IV. A rate of 0.5 closes 50% of the gap at each step, and each step acts on a smaller gap, so the mean is approached but not reached. IV would be right if it said “reaches $\mu_{S}$ after one step with $a$ = 1” or “closes 75% of the gap after two steps”.

b.reason: **I, III and IV.** Error type: role misassignment in III (the stochastic term is given the job of the mean reversion rate) plus the absolute claim in IV. III would be right if it said the term $\sigma_{S} \epsilon\sqrt{\Delta t}$ adds randomness and can be ignored when measuring mean reversion.

c.reason: **II and III.** Error type: role misassignment in III and rejection of the true statement I. C would suit a stem asking which statements describe a model in which the noise term drives the pull, which is not the Vasicek process.

d.reason: GARP §9.2: “a mean reversion parameter of $a$ = 1 will pull $S_{t-1}$ to the long-term mean $\mu_{S}$ completely at every time step, assuming $S_{t-1}$ was below the mean” and “a mean-reversion parameter $a$ of 0 will result in no mean reversion.” The stochastic part is set aside when quantifying mean reversion. Only I and II survive.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Brazilian bank models the spread of a BRL corporate bond index over government bonds with the discrete mean reversion process $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ = $a$($\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$)∆$t$ + $\sigma_{S} \epsilon\sqrt{\Delta t}$, in which time is measured in years. The inputs are:

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean reversion rate $a$ | 0.60 per year |
| Long-term mean spread $\mu_{S}$ | 250 bps |
| Current spread $S_{t-1}$ | 310 bps |
| Spread volatility $\sigma_{S}$ | 45 bps per year |
| Time step ∆$t$ | one month (1/12 year) |

Ignoring the stochastic term, what is the expected change in the spread over the next month?
questions.solution:
**Expected change with a monthly time step**

Stem in one line: $a$ = 0.60 per year, $\mu_{S}$ = 250 bps, $S_{t-1}$ = 310 bps, $\sigma_{S}$ = 45 bps per year, ∆$t$ = 1/12; expected one-month change?

**Concept and theory**

The discrete Vasicek process (GARP eq. 9.2) is

$S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ = $a$($\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$) ∆$t$ + $\sigma_{S} \epsilon\sqrt{\Delta t}.$

$a$ is the mean reversion rate per unit of time, $\mu_{S}$ the long-term mean, $S_{t-1}$ the current level, ∆$t$ the time step in the same units as $a$, $\sigma_{S}$ the volatility and $\epsilon$ a standard normal draw. GARP sets ∆$t$ = 1 “for ease of explanation”; when the step is shorter than the unit in which $a$ is quoted, ∆$t$ must be kept. Ignoring the stochastic part, the expected change is the deterministic drift $a$($\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$)∆$t$. Note how time enters: the drift scales with ∆$t$, and only the noise term scales with $\sqrt{\Delta t}$.

**Applying it to this question**

Gap: $\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$ = 250 − 310 = −60 bps

Annual pull: $a$($\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$) = 0.60 × (−60) = −36 bps per year

One month: − 36 $\times\frac{1}{12}$ = −3.00 bps

The spread is above its mean, so it is expected to fall, by 3 bps over the month. The volatility of 45 bps is irrelevant once the stochastic term is ignored.

**Fragile fact.** Above the mean the expected change is negative. The drift scales with ∆$t$, not $\sqrt{\Delta t}$; match the units of $a$ and ∆$t$.

**Reference**

LO 9.b (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 9, §9.2, eq. (9.2) (legible in the extract) and eq. (9.3). Schweser Reading 9, “Mean Reversion and Autocorrelation” (Schweser drops the formula image but states that the stochastic term is ignored and ∆$t$ = 1 is assumed). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 b, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: GARP eq. (9.2) with the stochastic term dropped gives an expected change of $a$($\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$)∆$t$ = 0.60 × (−60) × 1/12 = −3.00 bps.

b.reason: **(+3.00 bps).** Error type: sign error. It computes $a$($S_{t-1} - \mu_{S}$ )∆$t$, pushing the spread away from the mean. Correct only if the current spread were 250 bps below a mean of 310 bps, i.e. $S_{t-1}$ = 250, $\mu_{S}$ = 310.

c.reason: **(−10.39 bps).** Error type: time-conversion slip (square root of time on the drift). 0.60 × (−60) × $\sqrt{1/12}$ = −36 × 0.2887 = −10.39. The $\sqrt{\Delta t}$ scaling belongs to the stochastic term, not to the mean reversion term. Would be right only for a drift that, unlike eq. (9.2), scaled with $\sqrt{\Delta t}$.

d.reason: **(−36.00 bps).** Error type: unit slip (annual versus monthly ∆$t$). It sets ∆$t$ = 1, giving the change over a full year of drift. Correct if the question asked for the change over one year with a single annual step, or if $a$ = 0.60 were a monthly rate.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a German bank is reviewing the documentation of a EUR equity correlation model. The documentation explains how the mean reversion rate $a$ is estimated with a standard regression $Y$ = $\alpha$ + $\beta X$ and contains four statements:

I. The dependent variable $Y$ is the change $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ and the explanatory variable $X$ is the previous level $S_{t-1}$.

II. The slope $\beta$ equals the mean reversion rate $a$, so an estimated slope of +0.70 indicates a mean reversion rate of 70%.

III. The intercept $\alpha$ equals $a\mu_{S}$ , so the long-term mean can be recovered by dividing the intercept by the mean reversion rate.

IV. A high estimated mean reversion rate can only be obtained if the regression has an $R^{2}$ close to one, because the stochastic term is ignored.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I, II and III only
I, III and IV only
II and IV only
I and III only

questions.solution:
**Specifying the mean reversion regression**

Stem in one line: which statements about $Y$ , $X$, $\beta$, $\alpha$ and $R^{2}$ in the mean reversion regression are correct?

**Concept and theory**

Setting ∆$t$ = 1 and dropping the stochastic term, GARP rewrites the mean reversion equation by distributing $a$:

$$\underbrace{S_{t} - S_{t-1}}_{Y} = \underbrace{a\mu_{S}}_{\alpha}\ \underbrace{-a}_{\beta}\ \underbrace{S_{t-1}}_{X} \qquad (9.4),\ (9.5)$$

This has the form of a standard regression $Y$ = $\alpha$+$\beta X$, so the mean reversion rate can be estimated by ordinary regression of the change $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ on the prior level $S_{t-1}$. Matching terms:

| Regression term | Model term | Use |
|---|---|---|
| $Y$ | $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ (the change) | dependent variable |
| $X$ | $S_{t-1}$ (prior level) | explanatory variable |
| $\beta$ (slope) | $-a$ | $a$ = $-\beta$ |
| $\alpha$ (intercept) | $a\mu_{S}$ | $\mu_{S}$ = $\alpha/a$ |

In the Dow study (GARP Figure 9.4) the regression of 534 monthly average correlations gave $y$ = −0.7903$x$ + 0.256 with $R^{2}$ = 0.3948: a strong mean reversion of 79.03%, estimated with a modest $R^{2}$. Consistency check: 0.256/0.7903 = 32.39%, close to the stated long-term mean of 32.38%.

**Applying it to this question**

I matches the table: correct.

II: the slope is $-a$, not +$a$; a slope of +0.70 would mean no mean reversion. Incorrect.

III: $\alpha$ = $a\mu_{S}$ , so $\mu_{S}$ = $\alpha/a$. Correct.

IV: the regression residual absorbs the stochastic part; GARP’s own estimate of 79.03% came with $R^{2}$ = 0.3948. Incorrect.

Answer: I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** $Y$ is the change, $X$ the prior level; slope = $-a$; intercept = $a\mu_{S}$ (not $\mu_{S}$ ).

**Reference**

LO 9.b (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 9, §9.2, eq. (9.4), (9.5) and Figure 9.4. Schweser Reading 9, “Mean Reversion and Autocorrelation”. Eq. (9.5) is garbled in GARP and missing in Schweser; $\alpha$ = $a\mu_{S}$ follows from the legible eq. (9.4) and is confirmed by the question bank’s worked solution (Q476). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 b, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: polarity flip in II ($\beta$ = +$a$ instead of $-a$). Accepting II would turn every mean-reverting series into one with a negative mean reversion rate. II would be right if it said “a slope of −0.70 indicates a mean reversion rate of 70%”.

b.reason: **I, III and IV.** Error type: absolute-claim trap in IV. A high rate does not require a near-perfect fit; the noise in monthly correlations leaves most of the variance unexplained even when the pull is strong. IV would be right only if the data had no random component at all.

c.reason: **II and IV.** Error type: polarity flip (II) and absolute claim (IV), and it rejects both true statements. It would suit a stem asking which statements are incorrect.

d.reason: GARP §9.2: “we are regressing $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ with respect to $S_{t-1}$” and “the regression coefficient $\beta$ is equal to the negative mean-reversion parameter $a$”; eq. (9.4) $S_{t} -S_{t-1}$ = $a\mu_{S} -aS_{t-1}$ gives $\alpha$ = $a\mu_{S}$ . Figure 9.4 shows a 79.03% rate with $R^{2}$ = 0.3948.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Japanese life insurer estimates the mean reversion of the monthly average pairwise correlation of the JPY equities held in its portfolio. She regresses $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ on $S_{t-1}$, where $S$ is the monthly average correlation, and obtains:

| Regression output | Value |
|---|---|
| Intercept | 0.1872 |
| Slope | −0.7200 |
| Standard error of slope | 0.0480 |
| $R^{2}$ | 0.41 |
| Observations | 240 |

Which of the following correctly states the mean reversion rate $a$ and the long-term mean correlation $\mu_{S}$ implied by the regression?
questions.solution:
**Mean reversion rate and long-term mean from regression output**

Stem in one line: regression of $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ on $S_{t-1}$ gives intercept 0.1872, slope −0.72; find $a$ and $\mu_{S}$ .

**Concept and theory**

From GARP eq. (9.4), $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ = $a\mu_{S} - aS_{t-1}$, a regression $Y$ = $\alpha$ + $\beta X$ of the change on the prior level identifies both parameters of the mean reversion model:

$a$ = $-\beta, \mu_{S}$ = $\frac{\alpha}{a}$ = $- \frac{\alpha}{\beta}$

where $\alpha$ is the regression intercept, $\beta$ the slope, $a$ the mean reversion rate and $\mu_{S}$ the long-term mean. The intercept is not the mean itself: it is the mean scaled by the rate. In GARP’s Dow regression, $\alpha$ = 0.256 and $\beta$ = −0.7903 give $\mu_{S}$ = 0.256/0.7903 = 32.39%, matching the stated long-term mean of 32.38%.

**Applying it to this question**

$a$ = $-\beta$ = −(−0.7200) = 0.7200 = 72.00%

$\mu_{S}$ = $\frac{\alpha}{a}$ = $\frac{0.1872}{0.7200}$ = 0.2600 = 26.00%

Each month the average JPY equity correlation is expected to close 72% of its gap to a long-term mean of 26%. The standard error, $R^{2}$ and number of observations do not enter the calculation.

**Fragile fact.** $a$ = $-\beta$ and $\mu_{S}$ = $\alpha/a$: divide the intercept by the rate; do not read the intercept as the mean.

**Reference**

LO 9.b (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 9, §9.2, eq. (9.4), (9.5) and Figure 9.4. Schweser Reading 9, “Mean Reversion and Autocorrelation” (its examples are internally consistent with $\mu_{S}$ = $\alpha/a$, e.g. 0.273/0.78 = 35%). $\alpha$ = $a\mu_{S}$ confirmed from the question bank (Q476). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 b, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: **($\mu_{S}$ = 18.72%).** Error type: role misassignment (intercept read as the long-term mean). This forgets that the intercept is $a\mu_{S}$ . Correct only if $a$ were 1, so that $\alpha$ = $\mu_{S}$ .

b.reason: **($a$ = 28.00%, $\mu_{S}$ = 66.86%).** Error type: sibling swap (autocorrelation for mean reversion rate). 1 − 0.72 = 0.28 is the implied one-period autocorrelation, and 0.1872/0.28 = 66.86%. Would be right if the slope of the change regression were −0.28.

c.reason: GARP §9.2: the slope equals the negative mean reversion parameter, and eq. (9.4) makes the intercept $a\mu_{S}$ . Hence $a$ = 72.00% and $\mu_{S}$ = 0.1872/0.72 = 26.00%.

d.reason: **($\mu_{S}$ = 13.48%).** Error type: inverted operation (dropped division). 0.1872 × 0.72 = 0.1348. Would be right only if the question gave $\mu_{S}$ and asked for the intercept $a\mu_{S}$ for a mean of 18.72%.

questions.question:
The CRO of an Australian superannuation fund is reviewing the AUD equity book after a sharp market sell-off. A regression of the monthly change in the average pairwise correlation on the previous month’s level gives $Y$ = 0.2457 − 0.78$X$ ($R^{2}$ = 0.38). Other data:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Long-term mean correlation | 31.5% |
| Average correlation, September | 36.0% |
| Average correlation, October | 44.0% |

Ignoring the stochastic term, what is the expected average correlation for November?
questions.solution:
**Expected next-month correlation from a level above the mean**

Stem in one line: $Y$ = 0.2457 − 0.78$X$, $\mu_{S}$ = 31.5%, September 36.0%, October 44.0%; expected November correlation?

**Concept and theory**

Solving GARP eq. (9.3) for $S_{t}$ (as in GARP Example 9.1):

$S_{t}$ = $S_{t-1}$ + $a$($\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$)

where $S_{t}$ is the expected value next period, $S_{t-1}$ the latest observed value, $a$ the mean reversion rate from the regression ($a$ = $-\beta$) and $\mu_{S}$ the long-term mean. The model moves the variable a fraction $a$ of the way from where it is now towards the mean. If the variable is above the mean, the gap $\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$ is negative and the expected value falls. In GARP Example 9.1, a February 2017 correlation of 26.15%, a mean of 32.38% and $a$ = 79.03% give an expected March correlation of 31.07%.

**Applying it to this question**

$a$ = $-\beta$ = 0.78

Gap: $\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$ = 31.5% − 44.0% = −12.5%

Expected change: $a$($\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$) = 0.78 × (−12.5%) = −9.75%

$S_{t}$ = 44.0% − 9.75% = 34.25%

After the sell-off spike the correlation is expected to fall back most of the way, to 34.25%. September’s 36.0% is irrelevant because the model uses only the latest level. (The intercept is consistent with the mean: 0.2457/0.78 = 31.5%.)

**Fragile fact.** Use the latest level as $S_{t-1}$; above the mean the expected change is negative; the rate is $a$, not 1 $- a$.

**Reference**

LO 9.b (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 9, §9.2, eq. (9.3) and Example 9.1. Schweser Reading 9, “Example: Calculating expected correlation”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 b, where it is Q6 of 12.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at a Chinese asset manager is choosing the average correlation to assume for a CNY equity book in a planning exercise two months ahead. The average pairwise correlation at the end of this month is 18.0%, the long-term mean correlation is 30.0%, and a regression of monthly changes on the previous level estimates a monthly mean reversion rate of 65%. The manager applies the mean reversion model one month at a time (∆$t$ = one month) and ignores the stochastic term. What is the expected average correlation at the end of the second month from now?
questions.solution:
**Projecting the correlation two steps ahead**

Stem in one line: current 18.0%, mean 30.0%, monthly $a$ = 65%; expected correlation after two monthly steps?

**Concept and theory**

GARP: “a mean-reversion parameter $a$ of 0.5 will lead to a mean reversion of 50% at each time step.” Each step applies eq. (9.3), $S_{t}$ = $S_{t-1}$ + $a$($\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$), to the level reached at the end of the previous step. Equivalently, the gap to the mean shrinks by the factor (1 $- a$) each step:

$\mu_{S} - S_{t}$ = (1 $- a$)($\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$) $\Rightarrow\mu_{S} - S_{t\text{+1}}$ = (1 $- a$)$^{2}$($\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$)

where $a$ is the monthly mean reversion rate, $\mu_{S}$ the long-term mean and $S$ the monthly average correlation. A rate cannot simply be doubled for two steps: the second step works on a smaller gap.

**Applying it to this question**

Step 1: $S_{1}$ = 18.0% + 0.65 × (30.0% − 18.0%) = 18.0% + 7.80% = 25.80%

Step 2: $S_{2}$ = 25.80% + 0.65 × (30.0% − 25.80%) = 25.80% + 2.73% = 28.53%

Check: $S_{2}$ = 30.0% − $\text{(0.35)}^{2} \times$ 12.0% = 30.0% − 1.47% = 28.53%

After two months the correlation is expected to have closed 1 − $\text{0.35}^{2}$ = 87.75% of its original 12-point gap.

**Fragile fact.** Each step closes the fraction $a$ of the remaining gap; over $n$ steps the gap left is (1 $- a$)$^{n}$ times the original.

**Reference**

LO 9.b (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 9, §9.2, eq. (9.3) and the statement that $a$ applies “at each time step”. Schweser Reading 9, “Mean Reversion and Autocorrelation”. The two-step projection is a repeated application of eq. (9.3); the reading does not show a multi-step example. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 b, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: intermediate result. This is the expected level after the first month only. Correct if the question asked for next month.

b.reason: Error type: time-conversion slip (rate scaled linearly with the number of steps). 18.0% + 2 × 0.65 × 12.0% = 33.60%, which overshoots the mean. Correct only if the mean reversion term could be applied once to the original gap with a two-month rate of 130%, which the bound 0 $\le a \le$ 1 rules out.

c.reason: Applying GARP eq. (9.3) at each of two monthly time steps gives 28.53%.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap (autocorrelation 1 $- a$ used as the rate, twice). 18.0% + 0.35 × 12.0% = 22.20%, then 22.20% + 0.35 × 7.80% = 24.93%. Correct if the monthly mean reversion rate were 35%.

questions.question:
A risk consultant at a Swiss private bank is preparing CHF training material on the autocorrelation of correlations for newly hired analysts. The draft contains four statements:

I. Autocorrelation can be quantified with an ARCH or GARCH model, or by regressing the time series of a variable on its own past values.

II. The one-period-lag autocorrelation $AC$($\rho_{t}, \rho_{t-1}$) = $\frac{\text{cov(}\rho_{t}, \rho_{t-1}\text{)}}{\sigma\text{(}\rho_{t}\text{)} \sigma\text{(}\rho_{t-1}\text{)}}$ is algebraically identical to the Pearson correlation coefficient, with the correlation values of periods $t$ and $t -$ 1 as inputs.

III. In fund performance analysis, positive autocorrelation is termed persistence: the investor asks whether above-market performance is positively correlated with past strong performance.

IV. The one-period-lag autocorrelation is computed from the covariance between the change in correlation, $\rho_{t} - \rho_{t-1}$, and the previous level, $\rho_{t-1}$.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
II, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
**What autocorrelation is and how it is measured**

Stem in one line: which statements on ARCH/GARCH or regression, the Pearson form of $AC$, persistence and a change-on-level covariance are correct?

**Concept and theory**

Autocorrelation is the degree to which a variable is correlated with its own past values. GARP names two routes: the ARCH model of Engle (1982) or its extension GARCH by Bollerslev, or regressing the time series of a variable on its past time series values (the approach GARP takes). For a one-period lag GARP uses

$AC$($\rho_{t}, \rho_{t-1}$) = $\frac{\text{cov(}\rho_{t}, \rho_{t-1}\text{)}}{\sigma\text{(}\rho_{t}\text{)} \sigma\text{(}\rho_{t-1}\text{)}}$ (9.6)

where $\rho_{t}$ are the correlation values for period $t$ (in the study, the monthly average of the 30 × 30 Dow correlation matrix after removing the unit diagonal), $\rho_{t-1}$ the values one period earlier, cov the covariance and $\sigma$ the standard deviation. GARP’s footnote: eq. (9.6) is algebraically identical to the Pearson correlation coefficient; it simply uses the values of periods $t$ and $t -$ 1 as its two inputs. In finance, positive autocorrelation is termed persistence; in fund analysis an investor asks whether above-market performance has persisted, i.e. is positively correlated with past strong performance.

|  | Mean reversion | Autocorrelation |
|---|---|---|
| Pairs used | change $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ with level $S_{t-1}$ | level $\rho_{t}$ with level $\rho_{t-1}$ |
| Tool | regression slope ($a$ = $-\beta$) | Pearson form, ARCH/GARCH or regression |
| Measures | pull to the long-term mean | persistence towards recent values |

**Applying it to this question**

I: both routes are named in GARP §9.3. Correct.

II: GARP’s footnote states the identity with the Pearson coefficient. Correct.

III: GARP’s persistence and fund-performance example. Correct.

IV: pairing the change with the prior level is the mean reversion regression, not the autocorrelation formula, which pairs $\rho_{t}$ with $\rho_{t-1}$. Incorrect.

Answer: I, II and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Autocorrelation pairs level with lagged level; mean reversion regresses change on lagged level. Positive autocorrelation = persistence.

**Reference**

LO 9.b (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 9, §9.3 “Do Equity Correlations Exhibit Autocorrelation?”, eq. (9.6) and footnote. Schweser Reading 9, “Mean Reversion and Autocorrelation” (ARCH/GARCH or regression; “The autocorrelation equation is exactly the same as the correlation coefficient”). Eq. (9.6) is garbled in GARP and missing in Schweser; its form was confirmed from the question bank (Q477). Persistence and the fund example are GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 b, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: **I and III only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement (definition gap on eq. 9.6). A candidate who thinks autocorrelation needs a special time-series estimator would reject II. A would be right if II had claimed the formula divides by the variance rather than the product of standard deviations.

b.reason: GARP §9.3: autocorrelation “can be quantified with the Nobel prize-rewarded ARCH . . . or its extension GARCH . . . However, we can also regress the time series of a variable to its past time series values”; eq. (9.6) “is algebraically identical with the Pearson correlation coefficient”; “positive autocorrelation is also termed persistence”.

c.reason: **II, III and IV.** Error type: sibling swap in IV (mean reversion regression inputs attributed to autocorrelation) and rejection of I. IV would be right if it described how the mean reversion rate, not the autocorrelation, is estimated.

d.reason: **All four.** Error type: sibling swap in IV. Accepting IV merges the two measures; they are linked ($AC$ = 1 $- a$ for one lag) but computed from different pairs of variables.

questions.question:
A model validator at a UK bank is reviewing a junior analyst’s estimate of the mean reversion of the monthly average pairwise correlation of GBP corporate bond returns. Instead of regressing the change $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ on $S_{t-1}$, the analyst regressed the level $S_{t}$ on the previous level $S_{t-1}$ and obtained:

| Regression of $S_{t}$ on $S_{t-1}$ | Value |
|---|---|
| Intercept | 0.0864 |
| Slope | 0.7300 |
| $R^{2}$ | 0.55 |
| Observations | 180 |

The analyst reported a mean reversion rate of −73%. Using the model $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ = $a$($\mu_{S} - S_{t-1}$) without the stochastic term, which of the following correctly states the implied mean reversion rate $a$ and the implied one-period autocorrelation?

options.text: $a$ = 27.00%; autocorrelation = 73.00%
$a$ = 73.00%; autocorrelation = 27.00%
$a$ = 8.64%; autocorrelation = 91.36%
$a$ = 27.00%; autocorrelation = 32.00%

questions.solution:
**Recovering $a$ and the autocorrelation from a level regression**

Stem in one line: analyst regressed $S_{t}$ on $S_{t-1}$ (intercept 0.0864, slope 0.73) and reported $a$ = −73%; implied $a$ and one-period autocorrelation?

**Concept and theory**

The mean reversion regression (GARP eq. 9.4, 9.5) uses the change as $Y$ : $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ = $a\mu_{S} - aS_{t-1}$, slope $-a$. If the level $S_{t}$ is used as $Y$ instead, move $S_{t-1}$ to the right-hand side of eq. (9.4):

$S_{t}$ = $a\mu_{S}$ + (1 $- a$) $S_{t-1}$

so a regression of $S_{t}$ on $S_{t-1}$ has intercept $a\mu_{S}$ and slope (1 $- a$). The rule “slope = $-a$” belongs only to the change regression. GARP §9.3 then links the two properties: autocorrelation is the “opposite property” of mean reversion, and for a one-period lag the mean reversion rate and the autocorrelation add up to 1 (79.03% and 20.97% in the Dow study):

$AC_{1}$ = 1 $- a$

where $AC_{1}$ is the one-period-lag autocorrelation and $a$ the mean reversion rate.

**Applying it to this question**

Slope of $S_{t}$ on $S_{t-1}$ : 1 $- a$ = 0.7300

$a$ = 1 − 0.7300 = 0.2700 = 27.00%

$AC_{1}$ = 1 $- a$ = 1 − 0.27 = 0.7300 = 73.00%

(Long-term mean, not asked: $\mu_{S}$ = 0.0864/0.27 = 32.00%)

The bond correlation series is only weakly mean reverting (27% of the gap closed per month) and highly persistent (73%). The analyst’s −73% applied the change-regression rule to the wrong regression.

**Fragile fact.** Slope = $-a$ only when $Y$ is the change; with $Y$ the level, slope = 1 $- a$ = $AC_{1}$.

**Reference**

LO 9.b (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 9, §9.2 eq. (9.4), (9.5) and §9.3. Schweser Reading 9, “Mean Reversion and Autocorrelation” (“The sum of the mean reversion rate and the one-period autocorrelation rate will always equal one”). The level form $S_{t}$ = $a\mu_{S}$ +(1$-a$)$S_{t-1}$ is a rearrangement of GARP eq. (9.4), not printed in either source. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 b, where it is Q9 of 12.

a.reason: From GARP eq. (9.4), $S_{t}$ = $a\mu_{S}$ + (1 $- a$)$S_{t-1}$, so a slope of 0.73 means $a$ = 27%; GARP §9.3: one-period autocorrelation and mean reversion add up to 1, so $AC_{1}$ = 73%.

b.reason: **($a$ = 73%, $AC$ = 27%).** Error type: sibling swap (level regression read as the change regression, sign dropped). It takes \|slope\| = 0.73 as $a$. Correct if the analyst had regressed the change $S_{t} -S_{t-1}$ on $S_{t-1}$ and obtained a slope of −0.73.

c.reason: **($a$ = 8.64%, $AC$ = 91.36%).** Error type: role misassignment (intercept read as the rate). The intercept is $a\mu_{S}$ , not $a$. Correct only if the long-term mean were 100%, which is impossible for a correlation series of this kind.

d.reason: **($a$ = 27%, $AC$ = 32%).** Error type: wrong input twin (long-term mean reported as the autocorrelation). 0.0864/0.27 = 32% is $\mu_{S}$ . Correct if the question asked for $a$ and $\mu_{S}$ .

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at an Indian bank compares two monthly correlation series. For each series she regresses $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ on $S_{t-1}$:

| Series | Intercept $\alpha$ | Slope $\beta$ | $R^{2}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| P: average correlation, INR large-cap equities | 0.2706 | −0.82 | 0.40 |
| Q: average correlation, INR corporate bond returns | 0.1008 | −0.24 | 0.12 |

Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.text: Series P has the higher one-period autocorrelation, 82%, because a stronger pull back to the mean makes a series more persistent.
Series Q has the lower one-period autocorrelation, 24%, because its slope is the smaller of the two in absolute value.
Series P has the lower one-period autocorrelation, 18%, so its next value depends more on the long-run mean than on its current value.
Series P has the lower one-period autocorrelation, 18%, and the same 18% applies at every lag because autocorrelation equals 1 $- a$ at any lag.

questions.solution:
**Mean reversion and autocorrelation as opposite properties**

Stem in one line: equity series P slope −0.82, bond series Q slope −0.24; which statement on their one-period autocorrelations is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

GARP §9.3: autocorrelation is the “reverse property” to mean reversion: “the stronger the mean reversion, i.e. the stronger a variable is pulled back to its long-term mean, the lower is the autocorrelation, i.e. the lower is its correlation to its past values, and vice versa.” For a one-period lag the two add up to one: $AC_{1}$ = 1 $- a$, with $a$ = $-\beta$ from the regression of $S_{t} - S_{t-1}$ on $S_{t-1}$. Writing the expected next value as a blend makes the trade-off visible (from GARP eq. 9.4):

$S_{t}$ = $a \mu_{S}$ + (1 $- a$) $S_{t-1}$

The weight on the long-term mean is $a$; the weight on the current value is 1 $- a$, the one-period autocorrelation. Both sources state the identity for the one-period lag; at other lags autocorrelations differ (GARP Figure 9.5).

**Applying it to this question**

P: $a$ = 0.82$, AC_{1}$ = 1 − 0.82 = 0.18 = 18%

Q: $a$ = 0.24$, AC_{1}$ = 1 − 0.24 = 0.76 = 76%

P has the lower autocorrelation. Its expected next value puts weight 0.82 on the long-run mean and 0.18 on the current value. The intercepts and $R^{2}$ values are not needed.

**Fragile fact.** High $a$ means low autocorrelation; 1 $- a$ is the one-period autocorrelation only.

**Reference**

LO 9.b (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 9, §9.3 and Summary (e). Schweser Reading 9, “Mean Reversion and Autocorrelation”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 b, where it is Q10 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip (strong pull read as strong persistence) together with $AC$ = $a$. Correct if the stem asked which series has the higher mean reversion rate.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (mean reversion rate reported as the autocorrelation). Series Q’s 24% is its mean reversion rate; its autocorrelation is 76%. Correct if the question asked for the series with the lower mean reversion rate.

c.reason: GARP §9.3: stronger mean reversion means lower autocorrelation, and the one-period autocorrelation and mean reversion rate add up to 1. Series P: 18%, with its expected next value dominated by the mean.

d.reason: Error type: scope or condition error. The 1 $- a$ identity holds for the one-period lag; GARP Figure 9.5 shows autocorrelation varying with the lag (peak at two months, then decay). Correct if it said “at the one-month lag”.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a US bank is summarizing for the risk committee what the study of monthly average Dow stock correlations from 1972 to 2017 found about autocorrelation at lags of one to ten months. His draft contains four statements:

I. The highest autocorrelation was found at a two-month lag rather than at a one-month lag.

II. Beyond that peak, autocorrelation decayed gradually as the lag lengthened, to roughly 10% at a ten-month lag.

III. Because the one-period autocorrelation equals one minus the mean reversion rate, the roughly 26% autocorrelation at the two-month lag implies a mean reversion rate of about 74%.

IV. The decay of autocorrelation with the lag means that the correlation of ten months ago says more about today’s correlation than the correlation of two months ago.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I only
I and II only
I, II and III only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
**Autocorrelation across lags in the Dow study**

Stem in one line: which statements about the lag profile of autocorrelation of monthly Dow correlations (1972 to 2017) are correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP §9.3 computes eq. (9.6) for lags of one to ten months (Figure 9.5). Findings: the one-period autocorrelation is 20.97%, which with the mean reversion rate of 79.03% adds up to 1; the two-month lag produces the highest autocorrelation; beyond it there is “the expected decay in autocorrelation with respect to time lags of earlier periods”. Schweser gives the numbers: highest autocorrelation of 26% at the two-month lag, decreasing gradually to roughly 10% at the ten-month lag. GARP Summary (e): autocorrelation is higher for more recent time lags.

The link $AC_{1}$ = 1 $- a$ comes from the one-period structure of the regression (one step from $S_{t-1}$ to $S_{t}$), so it applies to the one-period lag only.

**Applying it to this question**

I: two-month peak. Correct.

II: decay to about 10% at ten months. Correct (Schweser figure).

III: applies 1 $- a$ to a two-month lag. The 79.03% rate is estimated from one-month changes and pairs with the 20.97% one-period autocorrelation; the 26% two-month value says nothing about $a$. Incorrect.

IV: decay means older values carry less information. Incorrect.

Answer: I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Peak at the two-month lag (not one); then decay; $AC$ = 1 $- a$ only for the one-period lag.

**Reference**

LO 9.b (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 9, §9.3, Figure 9.5 and Summary (e). Schweser Reading 9, “Mean Reversion and Autocorrelation”. The 26% and roughly 10% figures are Schweser-only (condensed source); GARP’s Figure 9.5 values are not legible in the extract, but GARP’s text confirms the two-month peak and the decay. No conflict in substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 b, where it is Q11 of 12.

a.reason: **I only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement. A candidate who remembers the peak but not the decay would stop at I. Correct if II had said autocorrelation rose with the lag.

b.reason: GARP §9.3: “2-month lag autocorrelation . . . produces the highest autocorrelation. Altogether we observe the expected decay in autocorrelation”; Schweser: highest of 26% at two months, about 10% at ten months.

c.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: scope or condition error in III (the one-period identity extended to a two-month lag). III would be right if it said “the 20.97% one-period autocorrelation implies a mean reversion rate of 79.03%”.

d.reason: **II, III and IV.** Error type: polarity flip in IV (decay read as growing information with age) plus the scope error in III, and it rejects I. IV would be right only if autocorrelation increased with the lag, which is the opposite of the finding.

A senior risk analyst at a French bank is calibrating EUR correlation models for three books and extracts the following figures from the empirical study of equity, bond and default probability correlations:

| Correlation type | Correlation level | Correlation volatility | Mean reversion rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Equity | 34.83% | 79.73% | 77.51% |
| Bond | 41.67% | 63.74% | 25.79% |
| Default probability | 30.43% | 87.74% | 29.97% |

Bond correlations have the highest implied one-period autocorrelation, about 74%, so mean reversion can be left out of the model when bond correlations are modelled.

questions.solution:
**Equity, bond and default probability correlations: implied autocorrelation**

Stem in one line: mean reversion rates 77.51% (equity), 25.79% (bond), 29.97% (default probability); which statement on implied one-period autocorrelations is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

GARP §9.6 extends the study to 7,645 bond correlations and 4,655 default probability correlations. Mean reversion was present in both, at 25.79% for bonds and 29.97% for default probabilities, “lower than the very high equity correlation mean reversion of 77.51%”. GARP Summary (d): equity correlations show very strong mean reversion, “hence, when modelling correlation, mean reversion should be included in the model”; Summary (g): bond correlations exhibit mean reversion, although lower than equity correlations. Schweser Key Concepts (LO 9.b): bond and default probability correlations show much lower mean reversion rates and higher autocorrelation rates.

With $AC_{1}$ = 1 $- a$ (GARP §9.3):

| Correlation type | Mean reversion $a$ | Implied $AC_{1}$ = 1 $- a$ |
|---|---|---|
| Equity | 77.51% | 22.49% |
| Bond | 25.79% | 74.21% |
| Default probability | 29.97% | 70.03% |

**Applying it to this question**

Bond: 1 − 0.2579 = 0.7421 ≈ 74%

Default probability: 1 − 0.2997 = 0.7003 ≈ 70%

Equity: 1 − 0.7751 = 0.2249 ≈ 22%

Ranking by implied autocorrelation: bond, then default probability, then equity. Correlation levels and correlation volatilities (LO 9.a material) are irrelevant inputs.

**Fragile fact.** Equity correlations: high mean reversion, low autocorrelation. Bond and default probability correlations: low mean reversion, high autocorrelation; bond is the most persistent.

**Reference**

LO 9.b (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 9, §9.6 “Properties of Bond Correlations and Default Probability Correlations” and Summary (d), (g); §9.3 for $AC_{1}$ = 1 $- a$. Schweser Reading 9, Key Concepts LO 9.b. Difference: GARP gives equity mean reversion as 79.03% in §9.2 and the Summary but 77.51% in §9.6 (the stem quotes the §9.6 figure); Schweser’s Key Concepts print “29%”, a typo for about 79%. Neither source reports bond or default autocorrelation figures; they are implied here through 1 $- a$, as Schweser’s Key Concepts do qualitatively. Boundary call: these rates sit in GARP §9.6, which Schweser prints under LO 9.c, but Schweser’s LO 9.b Key Concepts cite them, so they are treated as LO 9.b content.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 b, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: GARP §9.6 rates with GARP §9.3’s one-period identity give 74.21%, 70.03% and 22.49%, in that order; Schweser: bond and default correlations have lower mean reversion and higher autocorrelation than equity correlations.

d.reason: **Bond highest, so omit mean reversion.** Error type: scope or absolute-claim error. The ranking is right, but GARP finds mean reversion present in bond correlations (25.79%) and recommends including mean reversion when modelling correlation. questions.question:
A risk consultant is advising a Swiss asset manager that runs a CHF-hedged US large-cap equity fund. The quant team wants to simulate the pairwise correlations among the fund’s Dow constituents for stress testing and proposes to reuse the lognormal assumption it already applies to the stock prices themselves. Based on the empirical study, which recommendation is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, “the empirical study” refers to the study of correlations among the 30 stocks of the Dow Jones Industrial Average (Dow) from 1972 to 2017 and the accompanying studies of bond and default probability correlations.

options.text: Replace it with the Johnson SB distribution, which gave the best fit to equity correlations under the Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Anderson-Darling and chi-squared tests.
Replace it with the generalised extreme value distribution, which gave the best fit to equity correlations under the Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Anderson-Darling and chi-squared tests.
Keep the lognormal distribution, which gave the best fit to equity correlations under the Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Anderson-Darling and chi-squared tests.
Replace it with the normal distribution, which gave the best fit to equity correlations under the Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Anderson-Darling and chi-squared tests.

questions.solution:
**The best fit for equity correlations**

Stem in one line: should a fund reuse its lognormal stock-price assumption when simulating equity correlations?

**Concept and theory**

To simulate or stress a correlation matrix, risk managers must assume a distribution for the correlations themselves. GARP question 9.10 states the usual habit: “When modelling stocks, bonds, commodities, exchange rates, volatilities and other financial variables, we typically assume a normal or lognormal distribution. Can we do this for equity correlations?”

The data. Pearson correlations between the 30 Dow stocks, January 1972 to July 2017: 464,580 correlation values, 77.23% of them positive (Schweser: 77%).

The test. GARP: 61 distributions were tested with “three standard fitting tests: (a) Kolmogorov-Smirnov, (b) Anderson-Darling and (c) Chi-Squared. Not surprisingly, the versatile Johnson SB distribution . . . provided the best fit.” Normal, lognormal and beta “provided a poor fit”.

| Correlation type | Best fit | Also reported |
|---|---|---|
| Equity | Johnson SB | normal, lognormal, beta: poor fit |
| Bond | Generalised extreme value (GEV) | normal: fits quite well |
| Default probability | Johnson SB | distribution similar to equity |

**Applying it to this question**

The team carries the price-model assumption (lognormal) over to correlations. All four options cite the same three tests, so the deciding fact is only the winner’s name for equity correlations: Johnson SB.

**Fragile fact.** Equity correlations: Johnson SB. The usual normal or lognormal assumption does not carry over to them.

**Reference**

LO 9.c (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 9, §9.4 How Are Equity Correlations Distributed?, and Summary (f). Schweser Reading 9, “Best-Fit Distributions for Correlations”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 c, where it is Q1 of 9.

a.reason: GARP Summary (f): equity correlations “can be replicated well with the Johnson SB distribution”. Schweser 9.c: Johnson SB “provided the best fit for equity correlations”.

b.reason: **GEV.** Error type: sibling swap. GEV is the best fit for bond correlations, not equity correlations. B would be correct if the stem were about simulating the correlations among the bonds of a fixed income fund.

c.reason: **Lognormal.** Error type: scope error. It extends the stock price assumption to stock correlations; lognormal is a named poor fit for equity correlations. C would be correct if the question asked what is typically assumed for the stock prices themselves.

d.reason: **Normal.** Error type: sibling swap. The normal fits bond correlations “quite well” but equity correlations poorly. D would be correct if the stem asked which distribution, besides GEV, also fitted bond correlations well.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a German bank is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts, in a EUR training pack, on how the best-fit distribution for equity correlations was identified in the empirical study. The draft slide contains four statements:

I. The candidate distributions were compared using three standard fitting tests: Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Anderson-Darling and chi-squared.

II. The chi-squared distribution provided the best fit to the histogram of equity correlations.

III. Sixty-one distributions were tested for fitting the histogram of equity correlations.

IV. The input data for the fitting tests were the 534 monthly average correlations used in the mean reversion regression.

Which of the statements are accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, “the empirical study” refers to the study of correlations among the 30 stocks of the Dow Jones Industrial Average (Dow) from 1972 to 2017 and the accompanying studies of bond and default probability correlations.

options.text: I and II only
I, III and IV only
II and III only
I and III only

questions.solution:
**How the equity correlation fit was found**

Stem in one line: which statements about the fitting procedure for equity correlations are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Identifying a “best fit” has three ingredients: the data, the candidate distributions and the yardstick used to rank them.

| Ingredient | What the study used (GARP §9.4) |
|---|---|
| Data | Correlation values between all 30 Dow stocks, 1972 to 2017: 464,580 values; 77.23% positive |
| Candidates | 61 distributions (GARP-only) |
| Yardstick | Three standard goodness-of-fit tests: Kolmogorov-Smirnov, Anderson-Darling, chi-squared |
| Winner | Johnson SB (four parameters) |

Two traps: “chi-squared” names a test, not the winning distribution; and the LO 9.b mean reversion regression uses a different data set (GARP Figure 9.4: “534 monthly average Dow stock return correlations”), not the 464,580 individual values.

**Applying it to this question**

I: the three tests, as GARP lists them. True. II: turns the chi-squared test into the winning distribution. False. III: “We tested 61 distributions”. True. IV: swaps in the 534 monthly averages of the mean reversion regression. False. So I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Chi-squared appears in this LO only as a fitting test. The fitting data are the individual correlation values (464,580), not the 534 monthly averages.

**Reference**

LO 9.c (Schweser, verbatim). GARP Ch. 9, §9.4 How Are Equity Correlations Distributed? (61 distributions and the input data are GARP-only); §9.3 Figure 9.4 caption for the 534 monthly averages. Schweser Reading 9, “Best-Fit Distributions for Correlations” (tests only). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 c, where it is Q2 of 9.

a.reason: **I and II.** Error type: sibling swap, the name of a fitting test taken as the name of a distribution; it also drops the true statement III. A would be correct if II read “The chi-squared test was one of the three fitting tests” and III were false.

b.reason: **I, III and IV.** Error type: sibling swap of the data set. The 534 monthly averages are the input to the LO 9.b mean reversion regression, not to the distribution tests. B would be correct if the slide were describing the data behind the 79.03% mean reversion estimate rather than the fitting tests.

c.reason: **II and III.** Error type: sibling swap again (test read as distribution), combined with rejecting the true statement I. C would be correct only if chi-squared had been the winning distribution and not a test, which is the reverse of the source.

d.reason: GARP §9.4: “The input data of our distribution tests are daily correlation values between all 30 Dow stocks from 1972 to 2017. This resulted in 464,580 correlation values . . . We tested 61 distributions . . . applying three standard fitting tests”. Schweser 9.c confirms the three tests.

questions.question:
A model validator at an Indian bank is reviewing an INR equity stress-testing model in which the developer has chosen to sample pairwise equity correlations from a Johnson SB distribution. The developer’s documentation must describe the parameters of that distribution as used in the empirical study. Which description is consistent with the study?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, “the empirical study” refers to the study of correlations among the 30 stocks of the Dow Jones Industrial Average (Dow) from 1972 to 2017 and the accompanying studies of bond and default probability correlations.

options.text: Four parameters: two shape parameters, one location parameter and one scale parameter.
Three parameters: one location parameter, one scale parameter and one tail-index shape parameter.
Four parameters: one shape parameter, one location parameter and two scale parameters.
Two parameters: one location parameter and one scale parameter, with no shape parameter.

questions.solution:
**The parameters of the Johnson SB distribution**

Stem in one line: which parameter description of the Johnson SB matches the empirical study?

**Concept and theory**

A distribution’s parameters tell you how much flexibility it has to match a histogram. GARP calls the winner “the versatile Johnson SB distribution with four parameters”: two shape parameters, $\gamma$ and $\delta$, one location parameter, $\mu$, and one scale parameter. Schweser: “two shape parameters, one location parameter, and one scale parameter”. With two shape parameters it is flexible (GARP: “versatile”), and it ranked first among the 61 distributions tested.

Compare the GEV distribution of GARP Ch. 3 (§3.1), which is the best fit for bond correlations. It has three parameters: a location parameter $\mu$ (central tendency of the extremes), a scale parameter $\sigma$ (dispersion) and the tail index $\xi$, which “gives an indication of the shape (or heaviness) of the tail”.

| Distribution | Shape | Location | Scale |
|---|---|---|---|
| Johnson SB (equity, default correlations) | 2 ($\gamma$, $\delta$) | 1 ($\mu$) | 1 |
| GEV (bond correlations; Ch. 3) | 1 (tail index $\xi$) | 1 ($\mu$) | 1 ($\sigma$) |

**Applying it to this question**

The validator needs a count of four with the split two shape, one location, one scale. Only A gives both the count and the split.

**Fragile fact.** Johnson SB: four parameters, and the two Greek letters $\gamma$ and $\delta$ are both shape. GEV has three parameters, with a single shape parameter (the tail index).

**Reference**

LO 9.c (Schweser, verbatim). GARP Ch. 9, §9.4 How Are Equity Correlations Distributed?; GARP Ch. 3, §3.1 Generalised Extreme-Value Theory (for the GEV distractor only). Schweser Reading 9, “Best-Fit Distributions for Correlations”. No conflict. The scale symbol of the Johnson SB is illegible in the OCR extract of GARP and is therefore not named.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 c, where it is Q3 of 9.

a.reason: GARP §9.4: Johnson SB “with four parameters, $\gamma$ and $\delta$ for the shape, $\mu$ for location and \[a scale parameter\] for scale”. Schweser 9.c gives the same split.

b.reason: **Three parameters with a tail index.** Error type: sibling swap. This is the GEV parameterisation from GARP Ch. 3, i.e. the distribution that best fits bond correlations. B would be correct if the model sampled bond correlations from the GEV.

c.reason: **One shape, two scale.** Error type: role misassignment. It keeps the count of four but reassigns $\delta$ from shape to scale. C would be correct only if $\delta$ were a scale parameter; in GARP, $\gamma$ and $\delta$ are both shape parameters.

d.reason: **Location and scale only.** Error type: scope error, both shape parameters dropped. That describes a two-parameter location-scale distribution, not the four-parameter Johnson SB; it would be correct only for such a distribution.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Brazilian bank is screening candidate distributions for simulating equity correlations in a BRL equity stress model. The shortlist is:

I. Normal distribution

II. Lognormal distribution

III. Beta distribution

IV. Generalised extreme value (GEV) distribution

Which of these were explicitly reported in the empirical study as providing a poor fit to equity correlations?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, “the empirical study” refers to the study of correlations among the 30 stocks of the Dow Jones Industrial Average (Dow) from 1972 to 2017 and the accompanying studies of bond and default probability correlations.

options.text: I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
**Distributions that fit equity correlations poorly**

Stem in one line: which shortlisted distributions were reported as poor fits for equity correlations?

**Concept and theory**

The study reports both a winner and named losers. GARP §9.4: “Standard distributions such as normal distribution, lognormal distribution or beta distribution provided a poor fit.” GARP Summary (f) repeats the same three, and Schweser 9.c: “The normal, lognormal, and beta distributions provided a poor fit for equity correlations.”

The lesson is practical: the distributions most often assumed for financial variables (normal, lognormal), and the beta, are not good descriptions of how equity correlations are distributed. The GEV distribution is not named in the equity results at all; it appears only as the best fit for bond correlations.

| Distribution | Equity correlations | Bond correlations |
|---|---|---|
| Johnson SB | best fit | not reported as best |
| Normal | poor fit | fits quite well |
| Lognormal | poor fit | not reported |
| Beta | poor fit | not reported |
| GEV | not reported | best fit |

**Applying it to this question**

The qualifier is “explicitly reported . . . as providing a poor fit”. I, II and III are named in both sources. IV (GEV) is never named as a poor fit for equity correlations. So I, II and III only.

**Fragile fact.** The poor-fit trio for equity correlations is normal, lognormal and beta. Beta is the one most often forgotten.

**Reference**

LO 9.c (Schweser, verbatim). GARP Ch. 9, §9.4 How Are Equity Correlations Distributed?, and Summary (f). Schweser Reading 9, “Best-Fit Distributions for Correlations”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 c, where it is Q4 of 9.

a.reason: **I and II.** Error type: scope error, beta dropped from the list. A candidate who remembers only the “normal or lognormal” habit of GARP question 9.10 picks this. A would be correct if the stem asked which distributions are typically assumed for financial variables.

b.reason: **II and III.** Error type: sibling swap. It removes the normal because the normal fits bond correlations quite well, carrying a bond finding into the equity list. B would be correct only if the normal had been reported as a good fit for equity correlations.

c.reason: GARP §9.4 and Summary (f); Schweser 9.c: normal, lognormal and beta, and only these three, are named as poor fits for equity correlations.

d.reason: **I, II, III and IV.** Error type: absolute-claim trap, “every non-winner was named as poor”. The study names three poor fits; GEV is reported only as the best fit for bond correlations. D would be correct if GARP had listed GEV among the poor fits for equity correlations.

questions.question:
The CRO of a Japanese bank asks whether the distribution used to simulate equity correlations in the bank’s JPY stress model must switch to a different distribution family when the economy moves between expansion, normal growth and recession. The risk team cites the empirical study’s tests of the equity correlation distribution in different states of the economy. Which statement most accurately reflects that evidence?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, “the empirical study” refers to the study of correlations among the 30 stocks of the Dow Jones Industrial Average (Dow) from 1972 to 2017 and the accompanying studies of bond and default probability correlations.

options.text: The fit differed significantly across economic states, so a separate distribution family should be estimated for recessions.
The Johnson SB fit held in expansions and normal periods, but the GEV distribution gave the best fit in recessions.
The Johnson SB fit was robust across states, so correlation levels and volatilities can be held at full-sample values in every state.
Results across states were slightly but not significantly different, so the Johnson SB remains the best-fit family across the states tested.

questions.solution:
**Robustness of the equity correlation fit across economic states**

Stem in one line: must the equity correlation distribution family change between economic states?

**Concept and theory**

A best fit found on 45 years of pooled data might hide very different shapes in good and bad times. The study checked this. GARP §9.4: “We also tested the correlation distribution between the Dow stocks for different states of the economy. The results were slightly but not significantly different.” Schweser 9.c: “The Johnson SB distribution best fit was also robust with respect to testing different economic states”.

Keep two findings apart. The distribution family is robust across states (this LO). The level and the volatility of equity correlations are not: they differ by state (LO 9.a).

| State (GARP Table 9.1, LO 9.a) | Correlation level | Correlation volatility |
|---|---|---|
| Expansionary period | 27.46% | 71.17% |
| Normal economic period | 33.06% | 83.06% |
| Recession | 36.96% | 80.48% |

**Applying it to this question**

The CRO asks only about the distribution family. The evidence says the differences across states were slight and not significant, so the Johnson SB remains the best-fit family across the states tested. Nothing in the evidence says levels and volatilities can be held constant.

**Fragile fact.** Robust family, state-dependent level and volatility. Do not let one finding leak into the other.

**Reference**

LO 9.c (Schweser, verbatim). GARP Ch. 9, §9.4 How Are Equity Correlations Distributed?; §9.1 Table 9.1 for the LO 9.a figures used as distractor context. Schweser Reading 9, “Best-Fit Distributions for Correlations”. No conflict (GARP: “slightly but not significantly different”; Schweser: “robust”).

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 c, where it is Q5 of 9.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip, “not significantly” becomes “significantly”. A would be correct if the state-by-state tests had found significant differences.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap. It imports GEV, the bond correlation best fit, into an equity regime split the study never reports. B would be correct only if the recession sub-sample had been best fitted by GEV, which contradicts the robustness result.

c.reason: Error type: scope error (overextension). The robustness of the family is stretched to cover correlation levels and volatilities, which LO 9.a shows rise in worse economic states (27.46% in expansions to 36.96% in recessions). C would be correct if it stopped at “the Johnson SB fit was robust across states”.

d.reason: It restates GARP’s “slightly but not significantly different” and Schweser’s “robust with respect to testing different economic states”.

questions.question:
The treasurer of an Australian life insurer is preparing an AUD asset-liability report and must summarise the evidence on the distribution of bond correlations. Which of the following statements is NOT correct?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, “the empirical study” refers to the study of correlations among the 30 stocks of the Dow Jones Industrial Average (Dow) from 1972 to 2017 and the accompanying studies of bond and default probability correlations.

options.text: The best fit for the bond correlation distribution was the generalised extreme value distribution.
The bond correlation distribution was best fitted by the Johnson SB distribution, as default probability correlations were.
The bond correlation distribution showed a more normal shape than the equity correlation distribution.
The evidence on the distribution of bond correlations came from a study of 7,645 bond correlations.

questions.solution:
**The best fit for bond correlations**

Stem in one line: which statement about the distribution of bond correlations is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

The bond correlation study (GARP §9.6) used 7,645 bond correlations. Bond correlations share several properties with equity correlations (higher levels in bad times, mean reversion), but their distribution differs. GARP: “the bond correlation distribution shows a more normal shape and can be best fitted with the generalised extreme value distribution and quite well with the normal distribution.” Schweser 9.c: “The best-fit distribution for bond correlations was found to be the generalized extreme value (GEV) distribution. However, the normal distribution is also a good fit for bond correlations.”

By contrast, “the default probability correlation distribution is similar to equity correlation distribution . . . and can be replicated best by the Johnson SB distribution.” Of the three correlation types, bond correlations are the odd one out.

**Applying it to this question**

The qualifier is NOT correct. A, C and D each match GARP §9.6. B groups bond correlations with default probability correlations under Johnson SB, which is the reverse of the source: GARP introduces the bond result with “However” precisely to contrast it with the Johnson SB result for default probability and equity correlations.

**Fragile fact.** Bond correlations are the exception: GEV best, normal quite good. Equity and default probability correlations share the Johnson SB.

**Reference**

LO 9.c (Schweser, verbatim). GARP Ch. 9, §9.6 Properties of Bond Correlations and Default Probability Correlations (“more normal shape” is GARP-only). Schweser Reading 9, “Best-Fit Distributions for Correlations”, and Key Concepts LO 9.c. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 c, where it is Q6 of 9.

a.reason: **GEV best.** A true statement, so it is not the answer. Choosing it means confusing the bond result with the equity result (sibling swap in the candidate’s memory). A would be the answer if it read “Johnson SB”.

b.reason: B is the false statement. GARP §9.6 and Schweser 9.c: bond correlations are best fitted by GEV; Johnson SB is the best fit for equity and default probability correlations.

c.reason: **More normal shape.** A true statement (GARP-only), so it is not the answer. A candidate who knows only that equity correlations fit the normal poorly may wrongly extend that to bonds (scope error). C would be the answer if it said bond correlations showed a less normal shape.

d.reason: A true statement, so it is not the answer. Choosing it means swapping the bond and default sample sizes (7,645 and 4,655). D would be the answer if it read 4,655.

questions.question:
A senior credit risk analyst at a Singapore bank is calibrating a model of correlated default probabilities for an SGD corporate loan book. A colleague supplies the following summary statistics from the empirical studies:

| Correlation type | Average level | Correlation volatility | Mean reversion rate |
|---|---|---|---|
| Equity | 34.83% | 79.73% | 77.51% |
| Bond | 41.67% | 63.74% | 25.79% |
| Default probability | 30.43% | 87.74% | 29.97% |

The colleague argues that, because the mean reversion rate of default probability correlations is far closer to that of bond correlations than to that of equity correlations, the model should use the distribution that best fits bond correlations. Which response is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, “the empirical study” refers to the study of correlations among the 30 stocks of the Dow Jones Industrial Average (Dow) from 1972 to 2017 and the accompanying studies of bond and default probability correlations.

options.text: Agree: default probability correlations are best fitted by the generalised extreme value distribution, as bond correlations are.
Disagree: default probability correlations are best fitted by the normal distribution, reflecting their more normal shape.
Disagree: default probability correlations are best fitted by the Johnson SB distribution, as equity correlations are.
Disagree: default probability correlations are best fitted by the beta distribution, reflecting their lower average level.

questions.solution:
**The best fit for default probability correlations**

Stem in one line: should default probability correlations use the bond best fit because their mean reversion resembles bonds’?

**Concept and theory**

The default probability correlation study (GARP §9.6) used 4,655 default probability correlations. On mean reversion, default probability correlations (29.97%) sit close to bond correlations (25.79%) and far from equity correlations (77.51%). On the distribution, however, they line up with equity. Schweser makes the contrast explicit: default mean reversion of 30% is “closer to the 26% for bond correlations. However, the default probability correlation distribution was similar to equity distributions in that the Johnson SB distribution is the best fit for both”.

Similarity in mean reversion does not imply similarity in distributional shape.

**Applying it to this question**

The table is deliberately irrelevant. The colleague’s premise is numerically true: the gap to bonds is \|29.97 − 25.79\| = 4.18 percentage points, against \|29.97 − 77.51\| = 47.54 points to equities. But the conclusion does not follow, because the best fit is a finding about the shape of the distribution, and that shape resembles equity. Default probability correlations: Johnson SB.

**Fragile fact.** Mean reversion groups default with bonds; the distribution groups default with equity (Johnson SB). The Schweser sentence turns on the word “However”.

**Reference**

LO 9.c (Schweser, verbatim). GARP Ch. 9, §9.6 Properties of Bond Correlations and Default Probability Correlations (table figures from this section). Schweser Reading 9, “Best-Fit Distributions for Correlations”. Notes: Schweser rounds the figures (42%, 64%, 26%; 30%, 88%, 30%). GARP’s §9.6 equity mean reversion of 77.51% differs from the 79.03% in §9.2; an internal GARP difference, immaterial here. GARP §9.6 points to “Figure 9.4” for the equity distribution, but the equity correlation histogram is Figure 9.6 (Figure 9.4 is the mean reversion regression); a cross-reference slip in the source.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 c, where it is Q7 of 9.

a.reason: **GEV, agree.** Error type: sibling swap. GEV is the bond best fit; the colleague’s mean reversion argument tempts you to transfer it. A would be correct if the stem asked about the bond correlations in the bank’s securities portfolio.

b.reason: **Normal, more normal shape.** Error type: sibling swap. “More normal shape” and “fits quite well with the normal” are GARP’s descriptions of bond correlations, here attached to default probability correlations. B would be correct only for bond correlations, and even then the normal is the good fit rather than the best fit.

c.reason: GARP §9.6: “The default probability correlation distribution is similar to equity correlation distribution . . . and can be replicated best by the Johnson SB distribution.” Schweser 9.c and Key Concepts: equity and default probability correlation distributions are best fit with Johnson SB.

d.reason: **Beta, lower level.** Error type: scope error. Beta is a poor fit for equity correlations, the very distribution that default probability correlations resemble, and the average level (30.43%) plays no role in identifying the best fit. D would be correct only if the study had reported beta as the winner, which neither source does.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a UK bank is reviewing the documentation of the bank’s GBP correlation stress model. The documentation states that, consistent with the empirical evidence, the model draws equity correlations from a Johnson SB distribution, bond correlations from a normal distribution and default probability correlations from a Johnson SB distribution. Which assessment is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, “the empirical study” refers to the study of correlations among the 30 stocks of the Dow Jones Industrial Average (Dow) from 1972 to 2017 and the accompanying studies of bond and default probability correlations.

options.text: Inconsistent: the normal distribution was reported as a poor fit for bond correlations, so the bond assumption should be replaced with the Johnson SB distribution.
Largely consistent: the equity and default assumptions match the best fits, and for bonds the normal fitted quite well, although the GEV distribution gave the best fit.
Inconsistent: default probability correlations were best fitted by the GEV distribution, as bond correlations were, so the default assumption should be replaced.
Fully consistent: the normal distribution gave the best fit for bond correlations, with the GEV distribution a close second, so no change is needed.

questions.solution:
**Auditing a model’s correlation distribution assumptions**

Stem in one line: is a model using Johnson SB (equity), normal (bond), Johnson SB (default) consistent with the evidence?

**Concept and theory**

For each correlation type, an auditor should separate three grades of evidence: the best fit, a distribution reported as fitting well but not best, and distributions reported as poor fits.

| Correlation type | Best fit | Good fit | Poor fit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Equity | Johnson SB | none reported | normal, lognormal, beta |
| Bond | GEV | normal (“quite well”) | none reported |
| Default probability | Johnson SB | none reported | none reported |

GARP §9.6: bond correlations “can be best fitted with the generalised extreme value distribution and quite well with the normal distribution”. Schweser 9.c: “the normal distribution is also a good fit for bond correlations”. The normal is therefore a defensible but second-ranked choice for bonds.

**Applying it to this question**

Equity: Johnson SB, matches the best fit. Default: Johnson SB, matches the best fit. Bond: normal, a good fit but not the best fit, which is GEV. The documentation’s phrase “consistent with the empirical evidence” is therefore largely right, provided it does not present the normal as the best fit for bonds.

**Fragile fact.** For bonds: GEV is best, normal is good. Neither is “poor”, and the order matters.

**Reference**

LO 9.c (Schweser, verbatim). GARP Ch. 9, §9.4 and §9.6. Schweser Reading 9, “Best-Fit Distributions for Correlations”, and Key Concepts LO 9.c (“best fit with the generalized extreme value distribution, but the normal distribution is also a good fit”). No conflict: GARP’s “quite well” and Schweser’s “also a good fit” agree.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 c, where it is Q8 of 9.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the normal for bonds (“fits quite well” becomes “poor fit”), followed by a replacement with the equity winner. A would be correct if the documentation used the normal for equity correlations, where it is a reported poor fit.

b.reason: It grades each assumption correctly against GARP §9.6 and Schweser 9.c: two best fits, and for bonds a “good fit” that falls short of the GEV.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap. It assigns the bond best fit (GEV) to default probability correlations. C would be correct if the documentation had used Johnson SB for bond correlations and the stem asked about that line.

d.reason: Error type: role misassignment of rank. It makes the normal the winner and GEV the runner-up, reversing GARP’s “best fitted with the generalised extreme value distribution and quite well with the normal”. D would be correct if the ranking in the source were reversed.

questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee at a Canadian bank asks how much reliance the bank’s CAD credit and rates stress models can place on the reported best-fit distributions for bond and default probability correlations, compared with the result for equity correlations. Which response is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, “the empirical study” refers to the study of correlations among the 30 stocks of the Dow Jones Industrial Average (Dow) from 1972 to 2017 and the accompanying studies of bond and default probability correlations.

options.text: The bond and default results come from preliminary studies of 7,645 and 4,655 correlations that are still being verified with a larger sample, so they are first results rather than settled findings.
The bond and default results come from larger samples than the equity study and were shown to be robust across economic states, so they are more settled than the equity finding.
The equity result is the preliminary one, still being verified with a larger sample, whereas the bond and default results come from completed studies and are settled findings.
All three results were estimated from the same set of 464,580 correlation values, so they are equally reliable and the bond and default results are settled findings.

questions.solution:
**Weight of evidence for the bond and default findings**

Stem in one line: how much reliance can be placed on the bond and default best-fit findings relative to equity?

**Concept and theory**

The three best-fit findings rest on evidence of different maturity.

| Correlation type | Sample | Status in GARP |
|---|---|---|
| Equity | 464,580 correlation values | main study, Dow stocks 1972 to 2017 |
| Bond | 7,645 bond correlations | preliminary; being verified |
| Default probability | 4,655 default probability correlations | preliminary; being verified |

GARP §9.6 opens with “Our preliminary studies of 7,645 bond correlations and 4,655 default probability correlations” and closes with “The bond correlation and default probability results are currently being verified with a larger sample data base.” The Summary repeats the caution: items (g) and (h) begin “First results show”, and (h) adds “Studies with more data are currently being conducted.” The equity sample is roughly 61 times the bond sample and 100 times the default sample. The robustness test across economic states (Q5) is reported only for equity correlations.

**Applying it to this question**

The board member is asking about the evidence base behind the bond (GEV) and default (Johnson SB) identifications. The deciding fact is GARP’s own label: preliminary, still being verified with a larger sample. Only A states this with the correct sample sizes.

**Fragile fact.** Preliminary and “being verified” attaches to bond and default, not equity. Bond sample 7,645; default sample 4,655.

**Reference**

LO 9.c (Schweser, verbatim). GARP Ch. 9, §9.6 Properties of Bond Correlations and Default Probability Correlations, and Summary (g), (h). GARP-only: Schweser gives the sample sizes but not the preliminary status. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-9 c, where it is Q9 of 9.

a.reason: GARP §9.6 (“preliminary studies”, “currently being verified with a larger sample data base”) and Summary (g), (h) (“First results show”).

b.reason: Error type: scope error. The robustness across economic states was tested only for equity correlations, and the bond and default samples are far smaller, not larger. B would be correct only if the bond and default studies had used larger samples and been tested by economic state.

c.reason: Error type: role misassignment. It moves the “preliminary, being verified” label from the bond and default studies to the equity study. C would be correct if GARP had attached that label to the Dow study.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap of the data set. The 464,580 values are the equity correlations among the 30 Dow stocks; the bond and default studies used their own samples of 7,645 and 4,655. D would be correct only for the equity result.
