questions.question: A junior risk analyst at a Dutch pension fund is presenting to newly hired analysts. The fund holds a 25-year EUR corporate bond and hedges its interest rate risk by selling a 30-year German government bond. Over the last four months, a least-squares regression of daily changes in the corporate bond yield (bp) on daily changes in the government bond yield (bp) gives an intercept of 0.04 and a slope of 0.87. Which of the following statements about the slope is most accurate?

options.text: Over the sample, the government bond yield changed on average by 0.87 bp for each 1 bp change in the corporate bond yield.
Over the sample, 87% of the variance of daily changes in the corporate bond yield is explained by changes in the government bond yield.
On every day in the sample, the corporate bond yield changed by exactly 0.87 bp for each 1 bp change in the government bond yield.
Over the sample, the corporate bond yield changed on average by 0.87 bp for each 1 bp change in the government bond yield.

questions.solution:
**Reading the slope of the regression**

Stem in one line: EUR corporate bond hedged with a German government bond; slope 0.87; which statement about the slope is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

A DV01-neutral hedge assumes that the yield of the bond being hedged and the yield of the hedging bond change by the same number of basis points. A regression hedge replaces that assumption with the relationship observed in history. GARP §11.1 writes the model as

∆$y^{P}_{t}$ = $\alpha$ + $\beta$ ∆$y^{H}_{t}$ + $\epsilon_{t}$

where ∆$y^{P}_{t}$ is the change in yield of the position being hedged on day $t$ (here the corporate bond; JNJ in GARP), ∆$y^{H}_{t}$ is the change in yield of the hedging bond (here the government bond; the 30-year Treasury in GARP), $\alpha$ is the intercept, $\beta$ the slope and $\epsilon_{t}$ the error. The estimated slope $\hat{\beta}$ is the regression hedge adjustment factor. GARP reads its estimate of 0.842 as: “on average, the change in the yield of the JNJ bond is only 0.842 times the change in the yield of the Treasury bond.”

| Statistic | What it tells you |
|---|---|
| Slope $\hat{\beta}$ | Average bp change in the hedged yield per 1 bp change in the hedge yield |
| R-squared | Share of the variance of the dependent variable explained by the model |
| Intercept $\hat{\alpha}$ | Average change in the hedged yield when the hedge yield is unchanged; usually near zero |

**Applying it to this question**

The dependent variable is the change in the corporate yield and the independent variable is the change in the government yield. So $\hat{\beta}$ = 0.87 means that, on average over the four months, the corporate yield moved 0.87 bp for each 1 bp move in the government yield: less than one-for-one. The share of variance explained is a separate statistic (R-squared), and the word “average” matters because individual days scatter around the fitted line.

**Fragile fact.** The slope always describes the dependent variable (the bond being hedged) per 1 bp of the independent variable (the hedging bond), and only on average.

**Reference**

LO 11.c: “Calculate the regression hedge adjustment factor, beta.” GARP Ch. 11, §11.1 Single-Variable Regression Hedging (Eq. 11.1, Table 11.2 discussion). Schweser Reading 11, “Hedge Adjustment Factor”. GARP-only for the scatter-plot point in C. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-11 c, where it is Q1 of 9.

a.reason: Error type: role misassignment. It swaps the dependent and independent variables, reading the slope as the government yield’s response to the corporate yield. That is what a reverse regression slope (LO 11.g) would measure, and GARP shows that the reverse slope is a different number (0.921 versus 0.842), not the reciprocal. A would be right if the stem had regressed government yield changes on corporate yield changes.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap. It gives the slope the meaning of R-squared. The share of variance explained is measured by R-squared, which the stem does not report; a slope of 0.87 says nothing about it (GARP’s JNJ regression has a slope of 0.842 but an R-squared of 77.5%). B would be right if the stem had reported an R-squared of 87%.

c.reason: Error type: absolute claim. The slope is a least-squares average. GARP’s scatter plot shows days when the corporate yield moved by more, by less and even in the opposite direction from the Treasury yield. C would be right only if the fit were perfect, with every residual zero (R-squared of 100%).

d.reason: D attributes the slope to the right pair of variables in the right direction and uses “on average”, matching GARP’s interpretation of $\hat{\beta}$ = 0.842 in §11.1 and Schweser’s reading of 1.0198 (“over the sample period, the nominal yield increases by 1.0198 basis points for every basis point increase in real yields”).

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a US asset manager is preparing a report on a relative value trade that sells a nominal Treasury bond and buys TIPS. To set the hedge adjustment factor, she correctly specifies a least-squares regression of daily yield changes for this hedge and obtains a slope, $\hat{\beta}$, of 1.035. She must choose which statements to include in the report:

I. Over the sample, the nominal yield rose on average by 1.035 bp for each 1 bp rise in the real yield.

II. In this regression, the change in the real yield is the dependent variable and the change in the nominal yield is the independent variable.

III. A DV01-neutral hedge of the same trade implicitly assumes a beta of exactly 1, that is, equal basis-point changes in the two yields.

IV. Because $\hat{\beta}$ exceeds 1, the nominal yield must have risen by more than the real yield on every day on which the real yield rose.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.text: I only
I and III only
I, II and III only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
**Nominal-on-real beta above one**

Stem in one line: short nominal Treasury, long TIPS; regression slope 1.035; which four statements are correct?

**Concept and theory**

Schweser builds LO 11.b and 11.c around a nominal Treasury hedged with TIPS. The trader “plots a regression line, whereby the real yield is the independent variable and the nominal yield is the dependent variable.” The general rule (GARP §11.1) is that the yield of the position being hedged is the dependent variable and the yield of the hedging instrument is the independent variable. Here the nominal bond is the position being hedged and TIPS are the hedge.

The DV01-neutral hedge is the special case $\beta$ = 1. GARP: a DV01 hedge “assumes that the yields of the JNJ and Treasury bonds move up or down in parallel”, and “the risk weight of a yield-based DV01 hedge is always 100%”. Testing $\beta$ = 1 is therefore GARP’s test of the parallel-shift assumption.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I: $\hat{\beta}$ = 1.035 means the nominal yield rose on average 1.035 bp per 1 bp rise in the real yield. True. Statement II reverses the roles; the real yield is the independent variable. False. Statement III: a DV01-neutral hedge assumes equal bp changes, that is $\beta$ = 1. True. Statement IV: “every day” turns an average relationship into a certainty. False. So I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Nominal on real: nominal is the dependent variable. $\hat{\beta}$ > 1 means the nominal yield moves more than the real yield on average, not on every day.

**Reference**

LO 11.c (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 11, §11.1 Single-Variable Regression Hedging. Schweser Reading 11, “Regression Hedge” and “Hedge Adjustment Factor”. Difference: GARP’s example is a corporate bond on a Treasury ($\hat{\beta}$ = 0.842 \< 1); Schweser’s is nominal on real ($\hat{\beta}$ = 1.0198 > 1). Version difference in the example only; the method is the same.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-11 c, where it is Q2 of 9.

a.reason: **I only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement (scope error). A candidate who files the DV01 assumption under LO 11.a only, and so refuses III as “not about beta”, lands here. The DV01 hedge is exactly the $\beta$ = 1 benchmark against which $\hat{\beta}$ is read. A would be right if III said the DV01 hedge assumes a beta equal to the ratio of the DV01s.

b.reason: Statements I and III match Schweser LO 11.b and 11.c (nominal yield dependent; 1.0198 read as bp of nominal per bp of real) and GARP §11.1 (DV01 hedge assumes parallel shifts, risk weight 100%).

c.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: role misassignment in II. It makes the real yield the dependent variable, which would turn this into the reverse regression. II would be true if the trade were long nominal bonds hedging a TIPS position.

d.reason: **I, III and IV.** Error type: absolute claim in IV. $\hat{\beta}$ > 1 is an average; on individual days the nominal yield can rise by less than the real yield or even fall. IV would be true only for a perfect fit (R-squared 100%).

questions.question:
A risk analyst at an Australian superannuation fund is estimating the hedge adjustment factor for a long position in a 10-year AUD bond issued by a state government, to be hedged with a 10-year Commonwealth government bond. She collects six days of yield changes. Current yields are 4.62% on the state bond and 4.21% on the Commonwealth bond.

| Day | Change in Commonwealth yield (bp) | Change in state bond yield (bp) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | −5 | −6 |
| 2 | +5 | +4 |
| 3 | +1 | +2 |
| 4 | −3 | −3 |
| 5 | +6 | +8 |
| 6 | +2 | −1 |

Using a least-squares regression with an intercept, which of the following is closest to the regression hedge adjustment factor, beta?
questions.solution:
**Beta from six days of yield changes**

Stem in one line: six daily yield changes for a state bond (hedged) and a Commonwealth bond (hedge); compute the least-squares slope.

**Concept and theory**

Least squares chooses $\hat{\alpha}$ and $\hat{\beta}$ to minimize $\sum_{t} \hat{\epsilon}^{2}_{t}$ (GARP Eq. 11.5). For a single-variable regression with an intercept, the minimizing slope is the covariance of the two series divided by the variance of the independent variable:

$$\hat{\beta} = \frac{\text{Cov}(\Delta y^{P}, \Delta y^{H})}{\text{Var}(\Delta y^{H})} = \frac{\sum_{t}(\Delta y^{H}_{t} - \overline{\Delta y^{H}})(\Delta y^{P}_{t} - \overline{\Delta y^{P}})}{\sum_{t}(\Delta y^{H}_{t} - \overline{\Delta y^{H}})^{2}}$$

where $P$ is the bond being hedged (dependent) and $H$ the hedging bond (independent). The $n -$ 1 (or $n$) divisors cancel as long as the same one is used for both covariance and variance. The yield levels are not used: the regression is on changes.

**Applying it to this question**

Let $x$ = Commonwealth change (hedge, independent) and $y$ = state bond change (hedged, dependent).

$\bar{x}$ = (−5 + 5 + 1 − 3 + 6 + 2)/6 = 6/6 = 1.000

$\bar{y}$ = (−6 + 4 + 2 − 3 + 8 − 1)/6 = 4/6 = 0.667

$x - \bar{x}$ = −6, 4, 0, −4, 5, 1

$y - \bar{y}$ = −6.667, 3.333, 1.333, −3.667, 7.333, −1.667

∑($x - \bar{x}$)($y - \bar{y}$) = 40.000 + 13.333 + 0 + 14.667 + 36.667 − 1.667 = 103.000

∑($x - \bar{x}$)$^{2}$ = 36 + 16 + 0 + 16 + 25 + 1 = 94.000

∑($y - \bar{y}$)$^{2}$ = 127.333

Cov($x, y$) = 103.000/5 = 20.600

Var($x$) = 94.000/5 = 18.800, Var($y$) = 127.333/5 = 25.467

$\hat{\beta}$ = 20.600/18.800 = 1.0957 ≈ 1.10

Meaning: over these six days the state bond yield moved on average about 1.10 bp for each 1 bp move in the Commonwealth yield, so a regression hedge needs about 10% more DV01 in Commonwealth bonds than a DV01-neutral hedge.

**Fragile fact.** Divide by the variance of the hedging instrument’s yield change (the independent variable). Yield levels are irrelevant.

**Reference**

LO 11.c (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 11, §11.1 Single-Variable Regression Hedging (Eq. 11.1, 11.5). Schweser Reading 11, “Hedge Adjustment Factor”. The closed form Cov/Var is printed in neither GARP nor Schweser; it is confirmed from the question bank’s LO 11.c worked solutions. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-11 c, where it is Q3 of 9.

a.reason: Error type: role misassignment (reverse regression). Divides by the variance of the state bond change: 20.600/25.467 = 0.809. This is the slope of the Commonwealth yield on the state yield, the reverse regression of LO 11.g. Correct if the question asked for a hedge of Commonwealth bonds using the state bond.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (correlation for slope). $\rho$ = 20.600$/\sqrt{18.800 \times25.467}$ = 20.600/21.881 = 0.941. Correlation measures the tightness of the fit, not the size of the yield response. It would equal beta only if the two series had equal standard deviations.

c.reason: 1.10 is the least-squares slope of the hedged bond’s yield change on the hedge’s yield change, Cov/Var(∆$y^{H}$ ), which is the regression hedge adjustment factor (GARP Eq. 11.1, 11.5; Schweser LO 11.c).

d.reason: Error type: dropped term (ignores correlation). $\sigma_{P} /\sigma_{H}$ = $\sqrt{25.467/18.800}$ = 1.164. This is the slope only if $\rho$ = 1; here $\hat{\beta}$ = $\rho\sigma_{P} /\sigma_{H}$ = 0.941 × 1.164 = 1.096.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at an Indian bank is reviewing the spreadsheet used to estimate the beta for hedging an INR corporate bond with a government security. The model documentation regresses daily changes in the corporate bond yield on daily changes in the government security yield and makes four statements:

I. The intercept and slope are chosen to minimize the sum of squared residuals, where each residual is the actual change in the corporate bond yield minus the change predicted by the fitted line.

II. Squaring the residuals ensures that offsetting positive and negative errors are not treated as acceptable as zero errors, and that large errors are penalized heavily relative to small ones.

III. Each residual is measured horizontally on the scatter plot, as the gap between the actual and the predicted change in the government security yield.

IV. If the errors are independent, share the same distribution and are uncorrelated with the government yield change, the estimated beta equals the true beta in every sample.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I only
I and II only
I, II and III only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
**How least squares estimates beta**

Stem in one line: four documentation statements on how the INR beta is estimated; which are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

GARP §11.1 sets out the estimation step by step. Given estimates $\hat{\alpha}$ and $\hat{\beta}$, the predicted change in the hedged yield is $\widehat{\Delta y^{P}_{t}}$ = $\hat{\alpha}$ + $\hat{\beta}$ ∆$y^{H}_{t}$ (Eq. 11.2). The realized residual is actual minus predicted, $\hat{\epsilon}_{t}$ = ∆$y^{P}_{t} - \widehat{\Delta y^{P}_{t}}$ (Eq. 11.3, 11.4); on a scatter plot it is the vertical line from the data point to the regression line, in the units of the dependent variable. Least squares picks $\hat{\alpha}, \hat{\beta}$ to minimize $\sum_{t} \hat{\epsilon}^{2}_{t}$ (Eq. 11.5).

GARP’s illustration: with $\hat{\alpha}$ = 0, $\hat{\beta}$ = 0.84 and a Treasury change of −18.2 bp, the predicted JNJ change is −15.3 bp; an actual −11.1 bp gives a residual of +4.2 bp. Why squares: “offsetting positive and negative errors are not considered as acceptable as zero errors, and . . . large errors in absolute value are penalized heavily relative to smaller errors.” Assumptions: the model is a true description, errors share one distribution, are independent of each other and uncorrelated with the independent variable. Under these, estimates are linear, unbiased, consistent and efficient. Unbiased means the expectation of the estimator equals the true value (GARP footnote 1), not that every sample hits it.

**Applying it to this question**

I restates Eq. (11.3) to (11.5). True. II restates GARP’s reason for squaring. True. III measures the residual horizontally in the government yield; GARP drops a vertical line in units of the dependent variable. False. IV turns “unbiased” into “exact in every sample”. False. So I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Residual = actual minus predicted dependent variable, a vertical distance in bp of the hedged bond’s yield.

**Reference**

LO 11.c (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 11, §11.1 Single-Variable Regression Hedging, Eq. (11.2) to (11.5) and footnote 1. GARP-only (Schweser: “line of best fit” only). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-11 c, where it is Q4 of 9.

a.reason: **I only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement. A candidate who sees squaring as mere convenience rejects II, yet GARP gives exactly II’s two reasons. A would be right if II claimed squaring makes small errors count more than large ones.

b.reason: GARP §11.1, Eq. (11.2) to (11.5) and the paragraph after (11.5) support I and II; footnote 1 defines unbiasedness through the expectation, refuting IV.

c.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: role misassignment in III. The residual belongs to the dependent variable (the corporate yield change), measured vertically. Minimizing horizontal gaps would amount to fitting the reverse regression of LO 11.g. III would be true for a regression of government yield changes on corporate yield changes.

d.reason: **I, II and IV.** Error type: absolute claim in IV. Unbiased means correct on average across samples; any one sample has estimation error (GARP reports a standard error of 0.051 on $\hat{\beta}$ = 0.842). IV would be true with “on average across samples”.

questions.question:
The CRO of a UK insurer is validating a desk report. The desk is long a corporate bond and short a gilt, and states that the gilt short was sized as a single-variable regression hedge (corporate yield changes regressed on gilt yield changes). DV01s are per GBP 100 face.

| Position | Face (GBP million) | Yield | DV01 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Long corporate bond | 80.0 | 4.85% | 0.1850 |
| Short gilt | 92.0 | 4.42% | 0.1420 |

Which of the following is closest to the regression hedge adjustment factor, beta, implied by the desk’s hedge?
questions.solution:
**Beta implied by an existing hedge**

Stem in one line: long GBP 80m corporate (DV01 0.1850), short GBP 92m gilt (DV01 0.1420), sized as a regression hedge; what beta is implied?

**Concept and theory**

GARP §11.1 shows that a regression hedge can be described by its risk weight: the DV01 of the hedge as a fraction of the DV01 of the position being hedged. Rearranging the hedging condition gives Eq. (11.10):

risk weight = $\frac{F^{H} \times\text{DV01}^{H} /100}{F P \times\text{DV01}^{P} /100}$ = $\hat{\beta}$

where $F^{P} ,$ $\text{DV01}^{P}$ are the face amount and DV01 per 100 face of the position being hedged and $F^{H} ,$ $\text{DV01}^{H}$ those of the hedge (signs dropped; the hedge is the opposite position). GARP: “the risk weight of a regression hedge exactly equals the estimated slope coefficient”; a DV01 hedge always has a risk weight of 100%. So a reported hedge can be read backwards to recover the beta that sized it. (Sizing the face amount forwards from beta is LO 11.d.)

**Applying it to this question**

DV01 of corporate position = 80,000,000 × 0.1850/100 = GBP 148,000 per bp

DV01 of gilt position = 92,000,000 × 0.1420/100 = GBP 130,640 per bp

$\hat{\beta}$ = risk weight = 130,640/148,000 = 0.8827 ≈ 0.88

Meaning: the desk has assumed the corporate yield moves on average 0.88 bp per 1 bp move in the gilt yield, so it holds only 88% of the corporate DV01 in gilts. The yields are irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Risk weight = hedge DV01 ÷ hedged DV01 = $\hat{\beta}$. A DV01-neutral hedge has risk weight 100%.

**Reference**

LO 11.c (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 11, §11.1 Single-Variable Regression Hedging, Eq. (11.7) to (11.10). GARP-only: Schweser does not use the term risk weight for the single-variable hedge (it uses it for LO 11.e). Boundary call: the forward face-value calculation belongs to LO 11.d and is not asked. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-11 c, where it is Q5 of 9.

a.reason: Only 0.88 equals the hedge DV01 divided by the hedged DV01, which GARP Eq. (11.10) identifies with $\hat{\beta}$.

b.reason: Error type: role misassignment (inverted ratio). 148,000/130,640 = 1.133 divides the hedged DV01 by the hedge DV01. It would be the implied beta if the gilt were the position being hedged and the corporate bond the hedge.

c.reason: Error type: dropped term. 92/80 = 1.15 is the face ratio and ignores the DV01s. It would be the beta only if the two bonds had identical DV01s.

d.reason: Error type: intermediate result. 0.1850/0.1420 = 1.303 is the DV01-neutral hedge ratio (gilt face per unit of corporate face), the first factor in the LO 11.d face-value formula, not beta. It would be the face ratio of a hedge sized with $\beta$ = 1.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Japanese life insurer is reviewing the regression used to hedge a 20-year JPY corporate bond with a 20-year JGB. Daily changes in the corporate yield (bp) are regressed on daily changes in the JGB yield (bp):

| No. of observations R-squared Standard error of the regression (bp) |  | 120 81.0% 2.60 |
|---|---|---|
| Coefficient | Value | Std. error |
| Constant ($\hat{\alpha}$) | −0.110 | 0.240 |
| Change in JGB yield ($\hat{\beta}$) | 1.072 | 0.031 |

Treating each estimate plus or minus two standard errors as an approximate 95% confidence interval, which conclusion is most accurate?

options.text: $\beta$ = 1 cannot be rejected, because 1.072 ± 2 × 2.60 contains 1, so parallel yield shifts are consistent with the data.
$\beta$ = 1 cannot be rejected, because the interval for $\alpha$, (−0.590, 0.370), contains zero, so the yields move in parallel.
$\beta$ = 1 is rejected, because the interval (1.010, 1.134) excludes 1; the hypothesis $\alpha$ = 0 cannot be rejected.
$\beta$ = 1 is rejected, because the R-squared of 81.0% is below 100%, so yield changes are not one-for-one.

questions.solution:
**Is beta different from one?**

Stem in one line: JPY corporate on JGB regression, $\hat{\beta}$ = 1.072 (SE 0.031), $\hat{\alpha}$ = −0.110 (SE 0.240); which conclusion holds?

**Concept and theory**

An estimated beta has sampling error. GARP §11.1 (Table 11.2 discussion): each estimate “plus or minus two standard errors falls around the true parameter values approximately 95% of the time.” GARP’s example: 0.842 ± 2 × 0.051 = (0.740, 0.944) excludes 1, so “the hypothesis that $\beta$ = 1 can be rejected” and “the hypothesis of parallel shifts in the yields of the two bonds is rejected by the data”; meanwhile 0.060 ± 2 × 0.223 includes zero, so $\alpha$ = 0 cannot be rejected.

| Statistic | Use |
|---|---|
| SE of $\hat{\beta}$ | Confidence interval for $\beta$; test of $\beta$ = 1 (parallel shifts, DV01 hedge) |
| SE of $\hat{\alpha}$ SE of the regression (bp) | Confidence interval for $\alpha$; test of $\alpha$ = 0 Std. deviation of residuals; fit and hedged P&L risk, not a test of $\beta$ |

**Applying it to this question**

$\beta$ : 1.072 ± 2(0.031) = 1.072 ± 0.062 = (1.010, 1.134) ⇒ excludes 1: reject $\beta$ = 1

$\alpha$ : −0.110 ± 2(0.240) = −0.110 ± 0.480 = (−0.590, 0.370) ⇒ includes 0: cannot reject $\alpha$ = 0

Meaning: although 1.072 is close to 1, it is precisely estimated, so the data reject parallel shifts; the corporate yield moves more than one-for-one with the JGB yield on average.

**Fragile fact.** Test $\beta$ = 1 with the standard error of $\hat{\beta}$ (0.031), not the regression standard error (2.60 bp).

**Reference**

LO 11.c (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 11, §11.1 Single-Variable Regression Hedging, Table 11.2 discussion. GARP-only (Schweser has no coefficient standard errors). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-11 c, where it is Q6 of 9.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap (regression SE for coefficient SE). 1.072 ± 2 × 2.60 = (−4.13, 6.27) is meaningless for $\beta$: 2.60 bp is the residual standard deviation. A would be right if the standard error of $\hat{\beta}$ itself were large, say 0.10 (interval 0.872 to 1.272).

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (wrong coefficient). The interval for $\alpha$ is computed correctly but tests the intercept. Parallel shifts are a statement about the slope, $\beta$ = 1. B would be right as a statement about $\alpha$ = 0 only.

c.reason: It applies GARP’s ±2 SE rule with the standard error of $\hat{\beta}$ and states both conclusions correctly.

d.reason: Error type: scope error (wrong statistic). R-squared below 100% says the fit is imperfect (residuals exist); it says nothing about whether the average slope is 1. A regression with $\hat{\beta}$ = 1.000 exactly can still have R-squared of 81%. D would be right if the question asked whether hedging removes all interest rate risk.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Canadian pension plan hedges a 10-year CAD provincial bond with a 10-year Government of Canada bond. A regression of daily changes in the provincial yield on daily changes in the Government of Canada yield has a positive slope. The following statistics are computed over the same sample:

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---|
| Std. deviation of daily changes in the provincial yield | 4.20 bp |
| Std. deviation of daily changes in the Government of Canada yield | 5.60 bp |
| R-squared of the regression | 68.89% |
| Standard error of the regression | 2.34 bp |
| DV01 of the provincial bond (per CAD 100 face) | 0.0845 |

Which of the following is closest to the regression hedge adjustment factor, beta?
questions.solution:
**Beta from R-squared and volatilities**

Stem in one line: provincial on Government of Canada; $\sigma_{P}$ = 4.20 bp, $\sigma_{H}$ = 5.60 bp, R-squared 68.89%, positive slope; find beta.

**Concept and theory**

Writing the covariance as $\rho\sigma_{P} \sigma_{H}$ turns the least-squares slope into

$\hat{\beta}$ = $\frac{\text{Cov(}\Delta y^{P} , \Delta y^{H} \text{)}}{\sigma^{2}_{H}}$ = $\frac{\rho\sigma_{P} \sigma_{H}}{\sigma^{2}_{H}}$ = $\rho\frac{\sigma_{P}}{\sigma_{H}}$

where $\rho$ is the correlation of the two daily yield changes, $\sigma_{P}$ the standard deviation of the hedged bond’s yield change and $\sigma_{H}$ that of the hedging bond’s yield change. GARP §11.1: “In a one-variable regression, the R-squared is just the square of the correlation between the dependent and independent variables”, so $|\rho|$ = $\sqrt{R^{2}}$, with the sign of the slope.

**Applying it to this question**

$\rho$ = +$\sqrt{0.6889}$ = 0.83 (positive because the slope is positive)

$\sigma_{P} /\sigma_{H}$ = 4.20/5.60 = 0.75

$\hat{\beta}$ = 0.83 × 0.75 = 0.6225 ≈ 0.62

Meaning: the provincial yield moves on average about 0.62 bp per 1 bp move in the Government of Canada yield. The regression standard error is consistent (4.20$\sqrt{1 - 0.6889}$ = 2.34) but not needed, and the DV01 is irrelevant to beta.

**Fragile fact.** Numerator volatility belongs to the bond being hedged; take the square root of R-squared before using it.

**Reference**

LO 11.c (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 11, §11.1 Single-Variable Regression Hedging (R-squared as squared correlation). The form $\hat{\beta}$ = $\rho\sigma_{P} /\sigma_{H}$ is printed in neither GARP nor Schweser; it is confirmed from the question bank’s LO 11.c worked solutions. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-11 c, where it is Q7 of 9.

a.reason: 0.62 is $\rho\sigma_{P} /\sigma_{H}$ with $\rho$ = $\sqrt{R^{2}}$ from GARP §11.1.

b.reason: Error type: dropped term. $\sigma_{P} /\sigma_{H}$ = 0.75 omits the correlation; correct only if $\rho$ = 1 (R-squared 100%).

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap (correlation for slope). Reports $\rho$ itself. Correct only if the two yields had equal volatilities.

d.reason: Error type: role misassignment (inverted volatility ratio). 0.83×5.60/4.20 = 1.107 is the slope of the Government of Canada yield on the provincial yield, the reverse regression. Correct if the provincial bond were the hedge and the Government of Canada bond the position being hedged. A related slip, not offered as an option, multiplies by R-squared instead of $\rho$: 0.6889 × 0.75 = 0.52.

questions.question: A risk consultant is advising a Swiss private bank on how to estimate the beta used to hedge a CHF corporate bond with a Swiss Confederation bond. Which of the following recommendations is least consistent with sound practice for estimating the beta?

options.text: Avoid a very short estimation window, because too few observations may not furnish statistically reliable estimates of beta.
Consider an earlier episode, such as a past period of central bank rate rises, if it seems more relevant to the hedge horizon than the recent past.
Estimate beta over several periods and check the fitted relationship out of sample, because the hedge assumes beta is constant over time.
Use the longest history available, because adding older observations always makes the estimated beta more relevant to the hedge horizon.

questions.solution:
**Choosing the estimation window**

Stem in one line: CHF corporate hedged with a Confederation bond; which recommendation on estimating beta is least consistent with sound practice?

**Concept and theory**

The beta is only as good as the history it is estimated from. GARP §11.1 makes four points:

- Using the recent past implicitly assumes it is the most relevant period; “there are times and situations in which some earlier period seems more relevant”, for example a past episode of Federal Reserve rate rises when rises are expected.
- “Too short a window might fail to furnish statistically reliable estimates, but too long a window might include less relevant historical data.”
- Results are in-sample; relying on them assumes the future will be sufficiently like the sample. Poor out-of-sample performance “should raise questions about the stability of the regression coefficients over time”.
- Schweser (LO 11.d text): the regression hedge assumes $\beta$ is constant over time, which “is not always the case, so it is best to estimate the coefficient over different time periods and make comparisons.”

**Applying it to this question**

A, B and C each restate one of these points. D says the longest window “always” makes beta more relevant, which contradicts GARP’s warning that too long a window may include less relevant data.

**Fragile fact.** Window length is a trade-off: too short is unreliable, too long is less relevant. The hedge assumes constant beta; it does not guarantee it.

**Reference**

LO 11.c (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 11, §11.1 Single-Variable Regression Hedging (estimation window; in-sample and out-of-sample discussion). Schweser Reading 11, “Face Amount of Offsetting Position” (constant-beta caveat). Boundary call: Schweser prints the constant-beta caveat under LO 11.d; it is used here because the window choice determines the beta that is calculated. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-11 c, where it is Q8 of 9.

a.reason: Consistent with GARP: a short window may not give statistically reliable estimates. It would be the answer if it said “use as few observations as possible to keep beta current”.

b.reason: Consistent with GARP’s Fed example, generalized to any central bank: an earlier, similar episode can be more relevant than the recent past. It would be the answer if it said the most recent window is always the right one.

c.reason: Consistent with Schweser (compare periods because $\beta$ is assumed constant) and GARP (out-of-sample checks). It would be the answer if it said beta, once estimated, never needs re-examination.

d.reason:
D is the only recommendation that contradicts the source: GARP treats window length as a tradeoff, not a monotonic improvement.

**The answer.** Error type: absolute claim. “Always” overrides the trade-off between statistical reliability and relevance.

questions.question:
A bank examiner at a Singapore regulator is re-performing a bank’s beta calculation. The bank is long a 15-year SGD corporate bond and hedges it by selling a 20-year Singapore Government Security (SGS). The bank’s covariance matrix of daily yield changes (in $\text{bp}^{2}$) over the estimation window is:

|  | 15-year corporate | 10-year SGS | 20-year SGS |
|---|---|---|---|
| 15-year corporate | 9.00 | 12.00 | 10.40 |
| 10-year SGS | 12.00 | 25.00 | 18.00 |
| 20-year SGS | 10.40 | 18.00 | 16.00 |

Which of the following is closest to the regression hedge adjustment factor, beta, for this hedge?
questions.solution:
**Beta from a covariance matrix**

Stem in one line: SGD 15-year corporate hedged with 20-year SGS; pick the right entries from a 3 × 3 covariance matrix.

**Concept and theory**

The adjustment factor is the slope of the regression of the hedged bond’s yield change on the hedging bond’s yield change:

$\hat{\beta}$ = $\frac{\text{Cov(}\Delta y^{P} , \Delta y^{H} \text{)}}{\text{Var(}\Delta yH \text{)}}$

In a covariance matrix the off-diagonal entry in row $P$ , column $H$ is the covariance; the diagonal entry for $H$ is the variance of the independent variable. Two things decide the answer: which instrument is the hedge (only its column matters), and which variance goes in the denominator (the hedge’s, not the hedged bond’s).

**Applying it to this question**

$P$ = 15-year corporate, $H$ = 20-year SGS. The 10-year SGS is not part of this hedge.

Cov(∆$y^{P} ,$ ∆$y^{H}$ ) = 10.40 $\text{bp}^{2}$

Var(∆$y^{H}$ ) = 16.00 $\text{bp}^{2}$

$\hat{\beta}$ = 10.40/16.00 = 0.65

Meaning: the corporate yield moves on average 0.65 bp for each 1 bp move in the 20-year SGS yield; a regression hedge would carry only 65% of the corporate DV01 in 20-year SGS.

**Fragile fact.** Denominator = variance of the hedging instrument’s yield change. Ignore rows and columns for instruments not in the hedge.

**Reference**

LO 11.c (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 11, §11.1 Single-Variable Regression Hedging (Eq. 11.1, 11.5). Schweser Reading 11, “Hedge Adjustment Factor”. The closed form Cov/Var is printed in neither GARP nor Schweser; it is confirmed from the question bank’s LO 11.c worked solutions. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-11 c, where it is Q9 of 9.

a.reason: Error type: wrong input twin. 12.00/25.00 = 0.48 is the beta against the 10-year SGS. It would be correct if the bank hedged with the 10-year SGS.

b.reason: 0.65 is the covariance of the hedged and hedging yield changes over the variance of the hedging yield change, the least-squares slope (GARP Eq. 11.1, 11.5).

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap (correlation for slope). 10.40$/\sqrt{9.00 \times16.00}$ = 10.40/12.00 = 0.867. Correct only if the two yields had equal variances.

d.reason: Error type: role misassignment (reverse regression). 10.40/9.00 = 1.156 divides by the variance of the hedged bond, giving the slope of the 20-year SGS yield on the corporate yield (LO 11.g). Correct if the bank were hedging a 20-year SGS position with the corporate bond.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a German bank is checking the hedge for a new position on the credit trading desk. The desk has bought EUR 80 million face amount of a 15-year utility bond and will hedge its interest rate risk by selling a German government bond (Bund) in a single-variable regression hedge.

| Bond | Yield (%) | DV01 (per 100 face) |
|---|---|---|
| Utility bond | 3.412 | 0.1385 |
| Bund | 2.705 | 0.0912 |

| Regression: ∆$y$ utility on ∆$y$ Bund, 120 days |
|---|
| Coefficient Value Std. error |
| Constant ($\hat{\alpha}$) 0.041 0.198 |
| Slope ($\hat{\beta}$) 0.780 0.046 |
| R-squared 71.2% |
| Standard error (bp) 2.35 |

Which of the following is closest to the face amount of the Bund the desk should sell?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, DV01s are yield-based and quoted per 100 of face amount, yield changes are in basis points, and a regression of “∆$y$ of X on ∆$y$ of Y” has X as the dependent variable.

options.text: EUR 121.49 million
EUR 155.76 million
EUR 86.50 million
EUR 94.76 million

questions.solution:
**Face amount of a Bund regression hedge**

Stem in one line: long EUR 80 million utility bond, DV01s 0.1385 and 0.0912, regression slope 0.780; find the Bund face to sell.

**Concept and theory**

A DV01-neutral hedge matches the two DV01s, which is right only if both yields move by the same number of basis points. GARP’s JNJ example doubts this: the corporate trades at a changing spread to Treasuries. The regression hedge replaces the one-for-one assumption with the least-squares relation

∆$y^{p}_{t}$ = $\alpha$ + $\beta$ ∆$y^{h}_{t}$ + $\epsilon_{t}$ (GARP eq. 11.1)

where ∆$y^{p}_{t}$ is the yield change of the bond being hedged (dependent variable), ∆$y^{h}_{t}$ that of the hedging bond, $\alpha$ the constant, $\beta$ the slope and $\epsilon_{t}$ the error. If the hedged yield moves exactly $\hat{\beta}$ bp per bp of the hedge yield, then, writing $F_{p}, F_{h}$ for face amounts and $\text{DV01}_{p},$ $\text{DV01}_{h}$ for DV01s per 100 face, the position is hedged if

$F_{p} \frac{\text{DV01}_{p}}{100} \hat{\beta}$ + $F_{h} \frac{\text{DV01}_{h}}{100}$ = 0 (GARP eq. 11.7)

$F_{h}$ = $-F_{p} \frac{\text{DV01}_{p}}{\text{DV01}_{h}} \hat{\beta}$ (GARP eq. 11.8)

GARP: the DV01 hedge sells \$100mm × 0.2124/0.1910 = \$111.2 million; the regression hedge \$111.2mm × 0.842 = \$93.6 million.

**Applying it to this question**

DV01-neutral face = 80 × (0.1385/0.0912) = 80 × 1.51864 = EUR 121.49 million

$F_{h}$ = −80 × 1.51864 × 0.780 = −EUR 94.76 million

Negative means sell: 22% less than the DV01-neutral amount, as the utility yield has moved only 0.78 bp per bp of Bund yield. Constant, R-squared, standard errors and yields are excess data.

**Fragile fact.** Multiply by $\hat{\beta}$; the hedged bond’s DV01 is on top; $\hat{\alpha}$ and $R^{2}$ never enter.

**Reference**

LO 11.d. GARP Ch. 11, §11.1 Single-Variable Regression Hedging, eqs. (11.7) to (11.9). Schweser Reading 11, “Face Amount of Offsetting Position”. GARP equations garbled in the extract and Schweser’s formula missing; notation confirmed from bank Q539 and Q541. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-11 d, where it is Q1 of 8.

a.reason: Error type: dropped term ($\hat{\beta}$ omitted). 80 × 1.51864 = 121.49 is the DV01-neutral hedge. Correct if the stem asked for the DV01 hedge, or if $\hat{\beta}$ = 1.

b.reason: Error type: inverted adjustment (divide instead of multiply). 121.49/0.780 = 155.76. With $\hat{\beta}$ \< 1 the hedge must shrink. Correct only if the slope were 1/0.780 = 1.282.

c.reason: Error type: wrong input twin. Uses the R-squared (0.712) in place of the slope: 121.49 × 0.712 = 86.50. R-squared measures fit; it does not size the hedge. Correct only if the slope were 0.712.

d.reason: GARP eq. (11.8): the DV01-neutral face scaled by $\hat{\beta}$, as GARP’s \$111.2 million becomes \$93.6 million.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Singapore bank is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts on how the face amount of a single-variable regression hedge is set. The desk hedges long SGD corporate bond positions by selling Singapore Government Securities (SGS), using a slope $\hat{\beta}$ from regressing changes in the corporate bond yield on changes in the SGS yield. The draft slide contains four statements:

I. With $\hat{\beta}$ = 0.80, the regression hedge sells 20% less face amount of SGS than the DV01-neutral hedge of the same corporate position.

II. The regression hedge is sized so that the DV01 of the SGS position equals the DV01 of the corporate bond position.

III. For a long corporate position and a positive $\hat{\beta}$, the hedge formula gives a negative SGS face amount, which means the SGS are sold.

IV. Whenever the SGS have a larger DV01 per 100 face than the corporate bond, the regression hedge sells a smaller face amount of SGS than the corporate face amount being hedged.

Which of the statements are correct?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, DV01s are yield-based and quoted per 100 of face amount, yield changes are in basis points, and a regression of “∆$y$ of X on ∆$y$ of Y” has X as the dependent variable.

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
III only
I, III and IV only

questions.solution:
**Size and direction of a regression hedge: statement audit**

Stem in one line: which of four slide statements about the SGS regression hedge face amount are correct?

**Concept and theory**

Rewrite eq. (11.8) as

$$F_{h} = \underbrace{\left(-F_{p}\,\frac{\text{DV01}_{p}}{\text{DV01}_{h}}\right)}_{\text{DV01-neutral face}} \times \hat{\beta}.$$

eu$\overline{\text{tral face}}$

Three consequences follow, each a standard trap:

| Feature | DV01-neutral hedge | Regression hedge |
|---|---|---|
| Size | $-F_{p}$ $\text{DV01}_{p}/$DV01$_{h}$ | DV01-neutral size $\times\hat{\beta}$ |
| Hedge DV01 | = position DV01 (weight 100%) | = $\hat{\beta}$× position DV01 |
| Sign | Opposite to $F_{p}$ | Opposite to $F_{p}$ when $\hat{\beta}$ > 0 |

GARP §11.1: with $\hat{\beta}$ = 0.842, “fewer Treasury bonds need be sold”; a DV01 hedge’s risk weight “is always 100%”, a regression hedge’s “exactly equals the estimated slope coefficient”.

**Applying it to this question**

I: face = DV01-neutral face ×0.80, so 20% less. True. II: that is the DV01-neutral property; in a regression hedge the SGS DV01 is $\hat{\beta}$ times the corporate DV01 (80% in statement I’s example). False. III: $F_{p} >$ 0, $\hat{\beta}$ > 0 give $F_{h} <$ 0; GARP’s eq. (11.11) treats a negative face as a short. True. IV: the face ratio is $\text{(DV01}_{p}/$DV01$_{h}$)$\hat{\beta}$; the first factor is below 1, but if $\hat{\beta}$ > $\text{DV01}_{h}/$DV01$_{p}$ the product exceeds 1 (DV01s 0.090 and 0.100 with $\hat{\beta}$ = 1.20 give 1.08). False. So I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Regression hedge DV01 = $\hat{\beta}$× position DV01, not equal to it. The face amount depends on two factors (DV01 ratio and $\hat{\beta}$); never judge its size from one alone.

**Reference**

LO 11.d. GARP Ch. 11, §11.1, eqs. (11.8), (11.10), (11.11). Schweser Reading 11, “Face Amount of Offsetting Position”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-11 d, where it is Q2 of 8.

a.reason: GARP eqs. (11.8) and (11.10): the regression hedge is the DV01 hedge scaled by $\hat{\beta}$, has risk weight $\hat{\beta}$, and carries the opposite sign to the hedged position.

b.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: sibling swap. II gives the regression hedge the DV01-neutral hedge’s defining property. Correct for a DV01-neutral hedge, or if $\hat{\beta}$ = 1.

c.reason: **III only.** Error type: polarity flip on I. Rejecting I means believing the regression hedge divides the DV01 hedge by $\hat{\beta}$ (selling 25% more). I would be false only if the formula divided by $\hat{\beta}$; it multiplies.

d.reason: **I, III and IV.** Error type: absolute claim. IV holds when $\hat{\beta}$ ≤ $\text{DV01}_{h}/$DV01$_{p}$, not “whenever”. Correct for a DV01-neutral hedge, whose face ratio $\text{DV01}_{p}/$DV01$_{h}$ is below 1 whenever the hedge has the larger DV01.

questions.question:
A relative value trader at a London hedge fund is short GBP 120 million face amount of a nominal gilt and long an index-linked gilt, with the index-linked position sized as a DV01-neutral hedge. The fund’s risk analyst regresses daily changes in the nominal gilt yield on daily changes in the index-linked (real) gilt yield and estimates a slope of 1.064.

| Bond | Yield (%) | DV01 (per 100 face) |
|---|---|---|
| Nominal gilt | 4.215 | 0.0815 |
| Index-linked gilt | 0.842 | 0.1240 |

To convert the existing DV01-neutral hedge into a single-variable regression hedge, which trade in the index-linked gilt should the trader make?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, DV01s are yield-based and quoted per 100 of face amount, yield changes are in basis points, and a regression of “∆$y$ of X on ∆$y$ of Y” has X as the dependent variable.

options.text: Sell GBP 4.74 million of the index-linked gilt
Buy GBP 7.68 million more of the index-linked gilt
Buy GBP 5.05 million more of the index-linked gilt
Buy GBP 11.68 million more of the index-linked gilt

questions.solution:
**Adjusting a DV01-neutral index-linked hedge**

Stem in one line: short GBP 120 million nominal gilt, long DV01-neutral index-linked gilt, slope 1.064; what index-linked trade turns it into a regression hedge?

**Concept and theory**

This is Schweser’s set-up: a trader sells a nominal bond and buys an inflation-linked bond. The bond being hedged is the nominal gilt, so the regression is nominal yield changes on real yield changes, and the formula reads (Schweser notation $F_{N} , F_{R}$ for nominal and real face amounts)

$F_{R}$ = $-F_{N} \frac{\text{DV01}_{N}}{\text{DV01}_{R}} \hat{\beta}$.

With $F_{N} <$ 0 (short), $F_{R} >$ 0: the index-linked gilt is bought. Schweser notes that nominal yields empirically move by more than one basis point per basis point of real yield, so $\hat{\beta}$ > 1 and the regression hedge needs more of the real bond than the DV01-neutral hedge. Moving from one hedge to the other requires trading only the difference.

**Applying it to this question**

DV01 ratio = 0.0815/0.1240 = 0.65726

Existing DV01-neutral long = 120 × 0.65726 = GBP 78.87 million

Regression hedge long = 78.87 × 1.064 = GBP 83.92 million

Trade = 83.92 − 78.87 = +GBP 5.05 million (buy)

Each basis point of real-yield move has come with 1.064 bp of nominal move, so the short nominal leg carries more risk than the DV01 match assumes; 6.4% more index-linked gilt restores the balance. Yields are excess data.

**Fragile fact.** $\hat{\beta}$ > 1: buy more of the hedging bond; $\hat{\beta}$ \< 1: hold less. The adjustment is (DV01-neutral hedge face)×($\hat{\beta}$ − 1), not (hedged face)×($\hat{\beta}$ − 1).

**Reference**

LO 11.d. Schweser Reading 11, LO 11.b example (nominal versus TIPS) and “Face Amount of Offsetting Position”; Module Quiz Q2. GARP Ch. 11, §11.1, eq. (11.8). Difference: the nominal versus inflation-linked context and the “nominal moves more than real” observation are Schweser-only (condensed source, from an earlier edition); GARP 2026 uses a corporate versus Treasury example. Formula identical.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-11 d, where it is Q3 of 8.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip (divide by $\hat{\beta}$). 78.87/1.064 = 74.13; 74.13 − 78.87 = −4.74. Correct only if the slope were 1/1.064 = 0.940.

b.reason: Error type: scope error (adjustment applied to the wrong leg). 120 × (1.064 − 1) = 7.68 scales the nominal face, not the index-linked hedge. Correct if the two bonds had equal DV01s, so the hedge face equalled the nominal face.

c.reason: Schweser LO 11.d and Module Quiz Q2: the DV01 hedge is scaled by $\hat{\beta}$ and the difference traded; GARP eq. (11.8) gives the same formula.

d.reason: Error type: inverted DV01 ratio. 120 × (0.1240/0.0815) × 0.064 = 11.68. Correct if the nominal gilt had DV01 0.1240 and the index-linked gilt 0.0815.

questions.question:
A model validator at a Japanese life insurer is reviewing how the ALM desk sized the hedge of a JPY 5,000 million face holding of a 20-year electric utility bond, hedged by selling a 20-year Japanese government bond (JGB). Desk policy is to keep the utility bond holding fixed and choose the JGB amount that minimizes the variance of the hedged position. The validation pack shows:

| Bond | DV01 (per 100 face) |
|---|---|
| Utility bond | 0.1720 |
| 20-year JGB | 0.1810 |

|  | Regression of | Slope | $R^{2}$ | Std. error (bp) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Regression 1 | ∆$y$ utility on ∆$y$ JGB | 0.880 | 74% | 1.62 |
| Regression 2 | ∆$y$ JGB on ∆$y$ utility | 0.840 | 74% | 1.58 |

questions.solution:
**Which slope sizes the JGB hedge**

Stem in one line: JPY 5,000 million utility bond held fixed, hedged with JGB; two regressions given; find the JGB face to sell.

**Concept and theory**

Eq. (11.8) is derived from a specific regression: the yield change of the bond being hedged (dependent) on the yield change of the hedging bond (independent), GARP eq. (11.1). GARP shows that this hedge “minimizes the variance” of the P&L of the hedged position when the face amount of the bond being hedged is fixed. Running the regression the other way round gives a different slope, $\hat{\beta}^{'}$, and the two are not reciprocals unless the fit is perfect: $\hat{\beta}\hat{\beta}^{'}$ = $R^{2}$. GARP §11.4 shows that a reverse regression with slope 0.921 implies a risk weight of 1/0.921 = 108.6% for a hedge that fixes the Treasury amount, a different trade.

**Applying it to this question**

Policy fixes the utility bond holding and minimizes hedged variance, so the slope is from Regression 1 (utility on JGB), $\hat{\beta}$ = 0.880.

DV01 ratio = 0.1720/0.1810 = 0.95028

DV01-neutral face = 5,000 × 0.95028 = JPY 4,751 million

$F_{h}$ = −4,751 × 0.880 = −JPY 4,181 million

Sell JPY 4,181 million of the JGB. Check: 0.880 × 0.840 = 0.739 $\approx R^{2}$ = 74%, so the two slopes are consistent with each other. Regression 2, both $R^{2}$ figures and the standard errors are excess data.

**Fragile fact.** The bond you are hedging is the dependent variable. $\hat{\beta}$ $\times\hat{\beta}^{'}$ = $R^{2}$, not 1, so 1$/\hat{\beta}^{'} \not$= $\hat{\beta}$.

**Reference**

LO 11.d. GARP Ch. 11, §11.1, eqs. (11.1), (11.8); §11.4 Reverse Regressions (distractor source, LO 11.g). Schweser Reading 11, “Face Amount of Offsetting Position”. The consistency check $\hat{\beta}\hat{\beta}^{'}$ = $R^{2}$ is not stated in GARP or Schweser; it is taken from the question bank’s worked solutions (Q554, Q556) and is not needed to answer. No conflict. Boundary call recorded in the decomposition.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-11 d, where it is Q4 of 8.

a.reason: Error type: dropped term ($\hat{\beta}$ omitted). This is the DV01-neutral hedge. Correct if the desk’s policy were a yield-based DV01 hedge.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (reverse-regression slope). 4,751 × 0.840 = 3,991. Correct if the utility bond were the independent variable in the regression that sizes the hedge, which it is not.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap (reverse-regression risk weight). 4,751/0.840 = 5,656 uses 1$/\hat{\beta}^{'}$, the risk weight GARP attaches to a reverse-regression hedge. Correct only for a trader who fixes the JGB amount and asks how much utility bond to hold; even then that weight would size the utility leg, not the JGB leg.

d.reason: GARP §11.1, eqs. (11.1) and (11.8): the slope from regressing the hedged bond’s yield changes on the hedging bond’s yield changes, applied to the DV01-neutral face.

| Bond Yield (%) DV01 (per 100 face) |
|---|
| NSW semi-government bond 4.620 0.0745 |
| ACGB 4.310 0.0790 |
| Regression of ∆$y$ semi on ∆$y$ ACGB: slope 0.93; $R^{2}$ 88.0%; standard error 1.10 bp |

Which of the following correctly states the DV01 of the ACGB hedge position and its risk weight relative to the semi-government position?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, DV01s are yield-based and quoted per 100 of face amount, yield changes are in basis points, and a regression of “∆$y$ of X on ∆$y$ of Y” has X as the dependent variable.

options.text: AUD 111,750 per basis point; risk weight 100.0%
AUD 103,928 per basis point; risk weight 93.0%
AUD 120,161 per basis point; risk weight 107.5%
AUD 98,008 per basis point; risk weight 87.7%

questions.solution:
**DV01 and risk weight of the ACGB hedge**

Stem in one line: AUD 150 million semi-government bond hedged with ACGB, slope 0.93; find hedge DV01 and risk weight.

**Concept and theory**

The DV01 of a position in currency per basis point is face amount × DV01 per 100 face /100. Rearranging eq. (11.7) (GARP eq. 11.10):

Risk weight = $\frac{-F_{h} \text{DV01}_{h}/100}{F_{p} \text{DV01}_{p}/100}$ = $\hat{\beta}$.

In words, the left side is the DV01 of the hedge as a fraction of the DV01 of the bonds being hedged. GARP: “The risk weight of a yield-based DV01 hedge is always 100%”, while in the JNJ example “the DV01 of the Treasury bonds is only 84.2% of the DV01 of the JNJ bonds”.

**Applying it to this question**

Position DV01 = 150,000,000 × 0.0745/100 = AUD 111,750 per bp

$F_{h}$ = −150 × (0.0745/0.0790) × 0.93 = −AUD 131.55 million

Hedge DV01 = 131,553,797 × 0.0790/100 = AUD 103,928 per bp

Risk weight = 103,928/111,750 = 93.0% = $\hat{\beta}$

The hedge carries 93% of the semi-government DV01 because the semi yield has moved 0.93 bp per 1 bp of ACGB yield. Yields, $R^{2}$ and the standard error are excess data.

**Fragile fact.** Each leg’s DV01 uses its own face and its own DV01 per 100. Regression hedge risk weight = $\hat{\beta}$; DV01 hedge risk weight = 100%.

**Reference**

LO 11.d. GARP Ch. 11, §11.1, eqs. (11.7), (11.8), (11.10). Schweser Reading 11, “Face Amount of Offsetting Position”. Difference in framing: GARP derives the risk weight for the single-variable hedge in eq. (11.10); Schweser calls $\hat{\beta}$ the “hedge adjustment factor” under LO 11.d and uses “risk weight” only in its LO 11.e and 11.g sections. Same content.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-11 d, where it is Q5 of 8.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap. These are the DV01 and risk weight of the DV01-neutral hedge. Correct if the desk used a yield-based DV01 hedge.

b.reason: GARP eq. (11.10): the regression hedge’s risk weight equals $\hat{\beta}$, so its DV01 is $\hat{\beta}$ times the position DV01.

c.reason: Error type: inverted adjustment (divide by $\hat{\beta}$). 111,750/0.93 = 120,161 and 1/0.93 = 107.5%. This looks like a reverse-regression risk weight; correct only if the slope were 1.075.

d.reason: Error type: wrong input twin. Applies the semi-government DV01 to the ACGB face: 131.55m × 0.0745/100 = 98,008, ratio 87.7%. Correct only if the two bonds had the same DV01 per 100 face, in which case the answer would collapse to B anyway.

A risk consultant is reviewing a Canadian dealer’s hedge of a CAD 60 million face long position in a 30-year provincial bond. The desk sold 30-year Government of Canada (GoC) bonds in a DV01-neutral hedge, although its own regression of daily changes in the provincial yield on daily changes in the GoC yield gives a slope of 0.86 (estimated constant zero, $R^{2}$ 79%).

| Bond | DV01 (per 100 face) |
|---|---|
| Provincial bond | 0.1630 |
| GoC bond | 0.1950 |

On the review date the GoC yield rose by 8.0 basis points and the provincial yield rose by exactly the change the regression predicts (zero residual). Ignore convexity and carry. Which of the following gives the P&L of the desk’s DV01-neutral hedged position on that day, and the GoC face amount a regression hedge would have sold?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, DV01s are yield-based and quoted per 100 of face amount, yield changes are in basis points, and a regression of “∆$y$ of X on ∆$y$ of Y” has X as the dependent variable.

options.text: P&L +CAD 109,536; regression hedge sells CAD 43.13 million
P&L −CAD 109,536; regression hedge sells CAD 43.13 million
P&L +CAD 109,536; regression hedge sells CAD 58.32 million
P&L CAD 0; regression hedge sells CAD 50.15 million

questions.solution:
**What the DV01-neutral hedge left open**

Stem in one line: CAD 60 million provincial bond hedged DV01-neutral with GoC; GoC +8 bp, provincial +0.86 × 8 bp; find hedged P&L and the regression hedge face.

**Concept and theory**

GARP writes the P&L of the hedged position as

P&L = $-F_{p} \frac{\text{DV01}_{p}}{100}$ ∆$y^{p} - F_{h} \frac{\text{DV01}_{h}}{100}$ ∆$y^{h}$ (GARP eq. 11.11)

(a rise in yield lowers the value of a long position). If ∆$y^{p}$ = $\hat{\beta}$ ∆$y^{h}$ exactly, the face from eq. (11.8) makes this P&L zero: the hedge condition (11.7). A DV01-neutral hedge is flat only if both yields move equally; with $\hat{\beta}$ \< 1 it is too large, gaining when yields rise and losing when they fall.

**Applying it to this question**

∆$y^{p}$ = 0.86 × 8.0 = 6.88 bp

Position DV01 = 60,000,000 × 0.1630/100 = CAD 97,800 per bp

DV01-neutral face = 60 × 0.1630/0.1950 = CAD 50.15 million (short)

Hedge DV01 = CAD 97,800 per bp (equal by construction)

P&L long provincial = −97,800 × 6.88 = −CAD 672,864

P&L short GoC = +97,800 × 8.0 = +CAD 782,400

Net P&L = +CAD 109,536

Regression face = 50.15 × 0.86 = CAD 43.13 million (sell)

Check: CAD 43.13 million short earns 43,132,308 × 0.1950/100 × 8 = 672,864, offsetting the provincial loss exactly. The DV01-neutral hedge was over-hedged by 97,800 × 0.14 = 13,692 per bp of GoC move: a net short that paid on a sell-off.

**Fragile fact.** $\hat{\beta}$ \< 1: the DV01-neutral hedge is too big, a net short in rates. $\hat{\beta}$ > 1: it is too small, a net long.

**Reference**

LO 11.d. GARP Ch. 11, §11.1, eqs. (11.7), (11.8), (11.11) and the paragraph after (11.12) (hedged P&L is zero when the hedged yield moves $\hat{\beta}$ times the hedge yield). Schweser “Face Amount of Offsetting Position”. GARP-only: eq. (11.11).

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-11 d, where it is Q6 of 8.

a.reason: GARP eqs. (11.7), (11.8) and (11.11): the regression face makes P&L zero when yields move per the regression; the DV01-neutral face leaves (1 $- \hat{\beta}$) of the DV01 as an open short.

b.reason: **(−109,536; 43.13).** Error type: sign error. Treats the short GoC leg as losing when yields rise. Correct if yields had fallen by 8.0 bp and 6.88 bp.

c.reason: **(+109,536; 58.32).** Error type: inverted adjustment (divide by $\hat{\beta}$). 50.15/0.86 = 58.32 enlarges an oversized hedge. Correct only if the slope were 1.163.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap. Treats the DV01-neutral hedge as if it had the regression hedge’s property of zero P&L under the regression move. Correct if the slope were 1, in which case both hedges coincide.

**Assumptions behind the regression hedge face amount**

Stem in one line: which memo statement about sizing a CHF regression hedge from a six-month slope is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Eq. (11.8) uses one regression output, $\hat{\beta}$, estimated over a past window; using it going forward assumes the slope stays put. Schweser (LO 11.d): “The regression hedge approach assumes that the slope coefficient, $\beta$, is constant over time. This, of course, is not always the case, so it is best to estimate the coefficient over different time periods and make comparisons.” Schweser adds that R-squared and the standard error should be considered. GARP §11.1 makes the same point via out-of-sample tests: poor out-of-sample results “should raise questions about the stability of the regression coefficients”.

| Output | What it tells you | Role in the face amount |
|---|---|---|
| $\hat{\beta}$ | Average bp change of hedged yield per bp | Multiplies the DV01-neutral face |
| $\hat{\alpha}$ $R^{2}$ | of hedge yield Constant; usually not different from zero Share of variance of hedged yield changes | None None (judges hedge quality) |
| Standard error | explained Standard deviation of residuals, in bp | None (drives hedged P&L volatility, LO 11.b) |

**Applying it to this question**

The memo sizes the hedge from one six-month window. Only C names the assumption embedded in that face amount and the checks that follow.

**Fragile fact.** Only $\hat{\beta}$ sizes the hedge; $R^{2}$ and the standard error judge it. The slope is assumed constant, so test it across periods.

**Reference**

LO 11.d. Schweser Reading 11, “Face Amount of Offsetting Position” (constant $\beta$, R-squared and standard error: Schweser-only wording, condensed source). GARP Ch. 11, §11.1 (in-sample results, out-of-sample analysis, footnote 1 on unbiased estimators). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-11 d, where it is Q7 of 8.

a.reason: Error type: wrong input twin. $R^{2}$ does not appear in eq. (11.8); a higher $R^{2}$ means the hedge removes more risk, not that more face is needed. Would be correct if it said “a higher R-squared means the hedge removes a larger share of the variance of the corporate yield changes”.

b.reason: Error type: absolute claim. Unbiasedness means the estimator is right on average, not that the estimate equals the true value (GARP footnote 1); and even a correct historical slope may change in future. Correct as “the hedge minimizes variance in sample”.

c.reason: Schweser LO 11.d text quoted above; consistent with GARP’s out-of-sample discussion in §11.1.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap. The standard error of the regression multiplies the position DV01 to give the hedged P&L volatility (GARP eq. 11.12, LO 11.b); it does not size the hedge. Correct if the memo were estimating the daily volatility of the hedged position.

| Slope from regressing ∆$y$ corporate on ∆$y$ Treasury | 1.12 |
| R-squared of that regression | 65% |

Which of the following describes the regression hedge?

Buy USD 47.15 million face amount of the Treasury note

questions.solution:
**Hedging a short corporate position from its dollar DV01**

Stem in one line: short USD 45 million corporate, position DV01 USD 36,540 per bp, Treasury DV01 0.0868 per 100, slope 1.12; describe the hedge.

**Concept and theory**

Eq. (11.7) is a statement about dollar DV01s: the hedge’s dollar DV01 must equal $\hat{\beta}$ times the position’s dollar DV01, with the opposite sign. When the risk system gives the position’s DV01 in currency for the whole position, there is no need for the per-100 DV01 of the hedged bond:

$F_{h}$ = $- \frac{\hat{\beta} \times F_{p} \text{DV01}_{p}/100}{\text{DV01}_{h}/100} .$

Sign: a short position has $F_{p} <$ 0, so $F_{h} >$ 0 when $\hat{\beta}$ > 0. A short corporate position gains when yields rise; the hedge must lose when yields rise, so it is a long Treasury position.

**Applying it to this question**

Required hedge DV01 = 1.12 × 36,540 = USD 40,924.80 per bp

Treasury DV01 per USD 1 of face = 0.0868/100 = 0.000868

$F_{h}$ = 40,924.80/0.000868 = USD 47.15 million

$F_{p}$ = −45 million $\Rightarrow F_{h}$ = +47.15 million (buy)

Implied corporate DV01 per 100 face: 36,540/45,000,000 × 100 = 0.0812, so equivalently $F_{h}$ = 45 × (0.0812/0.0868) × 1.12 = 47.15. The corporate yield has moved 1.12 bp per bp of Treasury yield, so the hedge must carry 12% more DV01 than the position. The yield and $R^{2}$ are excess data.

**Fragile fact.** Short the bond being hedged, buy the hedge (and vice versa). Dollar DV01 = $F \times$DV01 per 100/100; do not divide by 100 twice.

**Reference**

LO 11.d. GARP Ch. 11, §11.1, eqs. (11.7), (11.8), (11.11) (sign convention: positive face is long, negative is short). Schweser Reading 11, “Face Amount of Offsetting Position” (short nominal, long TIPS example). No conflict.

c.reason: Error type: dropped term ($\hat{\beta}$ omitted). 36,540/0.000868 = 42.10 million is the DV01-neutral hedge. Correct if the slope were 1.

d.reason: Error type: inverted adjustment (divide by $\hat{\beta}$). 42.10/1.12 = 37.59. Correct only if the slope were 1/1.12 = 0.893.

I. Every six months until maturity, the swap pays $N \times$ ($y_{\text{CMT}} - K$)/2, where $y_{\text{CMT}}$ is a semiannually compounded yield of a predetermined maturity.

II. The yield $y_{\text{CMT}}$ used for each payment is the one observed six months before the payment date, so each payment is known one period in advance.

III. In practice, CMT swaps trade most commonly on the yields of the most liquid bonds, for example two-, five- and ten-year Treasury yields.

IV. When the swap is written on the six-month yield, the rates at the nodes of a six-month rate tree can be substituted directly into the payment formula, because six-month semiannually compounded yields equal six-month spot rates.

Which of the statements are accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question states otherwise, trees are recombining, dates are six months apart, the rate shown at each node is the six-month spot rate (semiannually compounded) prevailing at that node, “up” probabilities apply to every node of the stated date, and states are numbered from the bottom of each date starting at 0.

options.text: I and III only
I, II, III and IV
I, III and IV only
III and IV only

questions.solution:
**What a CMT swap pays, and when**

Stem in one line: which of four slide statements about the stylized CMT swap (payment rule, fixing date, market practice, use of tree rates) are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

A constant-maturity Treasury (CMT) swap exchanges a fixed rate (the strike $K$) for a Treasury yield of a fixed, predetermined maturity that is re-observed on every payment date. “Constant maturity” means the reference yield always has the same tenor (say, the 10-year yield), even though the swap itself is ageing. GARP’s stylized version pays, every six months until maturity,

$\text{Payment}_{t}$ = $N \times\frac{y_{\text{CMT},t} - K}{2}$

where $N$ is the notional, $K$ the strike (fixed rate), $y_{\text{CMT},t}$ the semiannually compounded yield of the predetermined maturity on the payment date $t$, and the division by 2 converts an annual rate into a six-month accrual. A positive amount is received by the party long the CMT yield; a negative amount is paid by it.

| Feature | GARP §12.5 |
|---|---|
| Payment frequency | Every six months until maturity |
| Rate exchanged | $y_{\text{CMT}}$ against the strike $K$ |
| Fixing date | $y_{\text{CMT}}$ is the yield “on the payment date” |
| Textbook example | One-year swap on the six-month yield, USD 1,000,000, $K$ = 2% |
| Market practice | Most commonly on the yields of the most liquid bonds: two-, five- and ten-year Treasuries |
| Link to the tree | Six-month semiannually compounded yields equal six-month spot rates, so tree rates go straight into the formula |

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I is equation (12.18) in words. True. Statement II moves the fixing to six months before payment; GARP fixes $y_{\text{CMT}}$ on the payment date itself, which is why the date-1 payoff uses the date-1 rate. False. Statement III is GARP’s remark on practice. True. Statement IV is GARP’s justification for substituting tree rates into (12.18). True. So I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** The CMT yield is observed on the payment date, and every payment is divided by 2 because payments are semiannual.

**Reference**

LO 12.h (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 12, §12.5 Pricing a Constant-Maturity Treasury Swap, eq. (12.18). Schweser Reading 12, “Constant-Maturity Treasury Swap”. Difference: Schweser describes a CMT swap as an agreement “to swap a floating rate for a Treasury rate such as the 10-year rate”; GARP’s stylized swap exchanges a fixed strike for the CMT yield. GARP’s framing is used; this looks like a simplification in the condensed source rather than a content conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-12 h, where it is Q1 of 8.

a.reason: **I and III only.** Error type: scope error (rejecting IV). This is the choice of a candidate who thinks a tree of six-month spot rates cannot deliver a “yield” for the payoff. For the six-month tenor the two are identical by construction. A would be right if the swap were written on, say, the ten-year yield, which a six-month rate tree does not show directly.

b.reason: **I, II, III and IV.** Error type: condition error on the fixing date (accepting II). It imports the set-in-advance, paid-in-arrears convention of a typical floating leg. B would be right only if the stem defined $y_{\text{CMT}}$ as the yield observed at the start of each accrual period.

c.reason: GARP §12.5: the swap pays $N$ ($y_{\text{CMT}} -$ 2%)/2 “every six months until it matures”, with $y_{\text{CMT}}$ “the semiannually compounded yield” of a predetermined maturity “on the payment date”; CMT swaps “trade most commonly on the yields of the most liquid bonds, for example, on two-, five- and 10-year Treasury yields”; and “because six-month semiannually compounded yields equal six-month spot rates, rates from the tree . . . can be substituted”.

d.reason: **III and IV only.** Error type: time-conversion slip (rejecting I). Rejecting I means believing each payment is $N$ ($y_{\text{CMT}} - K$) with no division by 2. D would be right for a swap paying annually on an annually compounded yield.

questions.solution:
**Node payoffs when the strike differs from today’s rate**

Stem in one line: AUD 8m CMT swap, bank receives $N$ ($y_{\text{CMT}} -$ 3.50%)/2; tree 3.40% / 3.70%, 3.10% / 4.00%, 3.40%, 2.80%; find the payoffs at date 1 state 0 and date 2 state 1.

**Concept and theory**

Before any discounting, a CMT swap tree is filled with cash flows. At every node after date 0 the payoff depends only on two things: the CMT yield at that node and the strike. With the swap written on the six-month yield, the yield at a node is simply the six-month rate shown on the tree (GARP §12.5). In GARP’s example the strike equals today’s rate (2%), so the middle node at date 2 pays exactly zero (eq. 12.22). That is a feature of the example, not a rule: the comparison is always with the strike $K$.

Payoff($t,$ state) = $N \times\frac{r\text{(}t, \text{state)} - K}{2}$

where $r$($t,$ state) is the six-month rate at that node. The sign convention is that of the party named in the stem.

**Applying it to this question**

Date 1, state 0 (rate 3.10%):

Payoff = 8,000,000 $\times\frac{3.\text{10\%} - 3.\text{50\%}}{2}$ = 8,000,000 × (−0.20%) = −16,000

Date 2, state 1 (rate 3.40%):

Payoff = 8,000,000 $\times\frac{3.\text{40\%} - 3.\text{50\%}}{2}$ = 8,000,000 × (−0.05%) = −4,000

Meaning: because the strike sits 10 bp above today’s rate, even the “unchanged” middle node costs the bank AUD 4,000. The risk-neutral probabilities are irrelevant here; they matter only when values are rolled back.

**Fragile fact.** Measure every node against the strike, not against today’s rate; the middle node pays zero only when $K$ equals the middle-node rate.

**Reference**

LO 12.h (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 12, §12.5, eqs. (12.18) to (12.23). Schweser Reading 12, “Constant-Maturity Treasury Swap” (“Fill in the missing data in the binomial tree”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-12 h, where it is Q2 of 8.

a.reason: **(−12,000 and 0).** Error type: wrong input twin (today’s rate used in place of the strike). 8,000,000 × (3.10% − 3.40%)/2 = −12,000 and 8,000,000 × (3.40% − 3.40%)/2 = 0. A would be right if the swap were struck at 3.40%, as GARP’s example is struck at the date-0 rate.

b.reason: Each payoff is notional times (node rate minus strike) divided by 2, exactly as in GARP eqs. (12.19) to (12.23), with the strike of 3.50% (not today’s 3.40%) as the reference.

c.reason: **(−32,000 and −8,000).** Error type: time-conversion slip (no division by 2). 8,000,000 × (−0.40%) = −32,000 and 8,000,000 × (−0.10%) = −8,000. C would be right for annual payments.

d.reason: **(+16,000 and +4,000).** Error type: sign error (payer’s perspective). These are the counterparty’s payoffs. D would be right if the bank paid the CMT leg and received the strike.

questions.question:
A model validator at a Japanese bank is checking one node of a valuation tree for a one-year CMT swap on the six-month yield with notional JPY 2,000,000,000 and strike 1.00%. The holder receives $N \times$ ($y_{\text{CMT}} -$ 1.00%)/2 on dates 1 and 2, where $y_{\text{CMT}}$ is the six-month rate on the payment date. The six-month rate tree is:

![Six-month rate tree: 1.00% at date 0; 1.40% or 0.60% at date 1; 1.80%, 1.00% or 0.20% at date 2](/figures/hq-mr-12h-03-rate-tree.png)

The risk-neutral up-probability is 0.70 on date 0 and 0.60 on date 1. Which of the following is closest to the value of the swap to the holder at date 1, state 1 (the up state), including the payment made on that date?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question states otherwise, trees are recombining, dates are six months apart, the rate shown at each node is the six-month spot rate (semiannually compounded) prevailing at that node, “up” probabilities apply to every node of the stated date, and states are numbered from the bottom of each date starting at 0.
questions.solution:
**Value at a date-1 node**

Stem in one line: JPY 2bn CMT swap struck at 1.00%; tree 1.00% / 1.40%, 0.60% / 1.80%, 1.00%, 0.20%; probabilities 0.70 then 0.60; value at date 1, state 1 including that date’s payment.

**Concept and theory**

A CMT swap is a contingent claim on the path of the six-month rate, so it is valued by backward induction on the risk-neutral tree (GARP §12.5). At date 2 the swap’s value is just its final payment. At a date-1 node the value has two parts:

$$V_{1,j} = \underbrace{\frac{q\,V_{2,j+1} + (1 - q)\,V_{2,j}}{1 + r_{1,j}/2}}_{\text{value of what is still to come}} + \underbrace{C_{1,j}}_{\text{payment made now}}$$

where $V_{1,j}$ is the swap value at date 1, state $j$; $q$ the risk-neutral up-probability that applies on date 1; $V_{2,j\text{+1}}, V_{2,j}$ the values (here, payments) at the two successor nodes; $r_{1,j}$ the six-month rate at the date-1 node itself, used for discounting over the next six months; and $C_{1,j}$ = $N$ ($r_{1,j} - K$)/2 the payment made at that node. GARP eq. (12.24) has exactly this structure: (.6520 × 5,000 + .3480 × 0)/(1 + .025/2) + 2,500.

**Applying it to this question**

$C_{1{,}1}$ = 2,000,000,000 $\times\frac{1.\text{40\%} - 1.\text{00\%}}{2}$ = 4,000,000

$C_{2{,}2}$ = 2,000,000,000 $\times\frac{1.\text{80\%} - 1.\text{00\%}}{2}$ = 8,000,000

$C_{2{,}1}$ = 2,000,000,000 $\times\frac{1.\text{00\%} - 1.\text{00\%}}{2}$ = 0

Expected date-2 value = 0.60 × 8,000,000 + 0.40 × 0 = 4,800,000

Discounted at 1.40%/2 = $\frac{4{,}800{,}000}{1.007}$ = 4,766,633.57

$V_{1{,}1}$ = 4,766,633.57 + 4,000,000 = 8,766,633.57

Meaning: at the up node the holder is about to receive JPY 4.0 million and holds a claim on next period’s payments worth a further JPY 4.77 million. The date-0 probability (0.70) and date-0 rate play no role at this node.

**Fragile fact.** Discount from a node at that node’s six-month rate (halved), and add the payment made at that node.

**Reference**

LO 12.h (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 12, §12.5, eq. (12.24) and Figure 12.8. Schweser Reading 12, “Constant-Maturity Treasury Swap”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-12 h, where it is Q3 of 8.

a.reason: Error type: dropped term. It is the discounted expectation of date-2 payments without the JPY 4,000,000 paid at the node. A would be right if the question asked for the value just after the date-1 payment (ex-payment value).

b.reason: Error type: time-conversion slip. Discounting by 1 + 0.014 rather than 1 + 0.014/2 gives 4,800,000/1.014 + 4,000,000 = 8,733,727.81. B would be right with annual time steps.

c.reason: Error type: wrong input twin (successor-node rate). Discounting at the date-2 up-node rate, 4,800,000/1.009 + 4,000,000 = 8,757,185.33. The rate at a date-2 node governs discounting from date 3 to date 2, not from date 2 to date 1. C would be right only if that rate were the one prevailing at date 1, state 1.

d.reason: It discounts the risk-neutral expectation over one six-month period at the up node’s own rate and adds the payment made at that node, as in GARP eq. (12.24).
