questions.question:
A risk consultant is validating a Model 1 implementation used by an Australian superannuation fund to project AUD short rates for its liability model. The terminal distribution of the short rate is normal with a mean equal to the current short rate. Model inputs are:

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Current short rate, $r_{0}$ | 3.40% |
| Annual basis-point volatility, $\sigma$ | 125 bp |
| Tree time step, $dt$ | 1/12 year |
| Projection horizon | 8 years |
| Current 10-year AUD par swap rate | 4.05% |

Which of the following is closest to the size of the negative shock, measured in standard deviations of the terminal distribution, that would push the short rate below zero at the 8-year horizon?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, “Model 1” is the short-rate process $dr$ = $\sigma dw$ with normally distributed rates and no drift, where $\sigma$ is the annual basis-point volatility and $dw$ is normal with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$.
questions.solution:
**Shock size that pushes the short rate below zero**

Stem in one line: AUD Model 1, $r_{0}$ = 3.40%, $\sigma$ = 125 bp, 8-year horizon; how many terminal standard deviations is zero below the mean?

**Concept and theory**

The size of the negative shock, in standard deviations, that would take the short rate from $r_{0}$ to zero at horizon $T$ is

$z$ = $\frac{r_{0}}{\sigma\sqrt{T}}$

where $r_{0}$ is the current short rate (the mean of the terminal distribution, since Model 1 has no drift), $\sigma$ the annual basis-point volatility and $T$ the horizon in years. GARP’s own illustration: with $r_{0}$ = 6.18% and $\sigma$ = 1.13%, the 10-year terminal standard deviation is 1.13%$\sqrt{10}$ = 3.573%, so “a random negative shock of only” 6.18%/3.573% = 1.73 standard deviations would push rates below zero. A smaller $z$ means a larger probability of negative rates.

**Applying it to this question**

$\sigma_{T}$ = $\sigma\sqrt{T}$ = 1.25% $\times\sqrt{8}$ = 1.25% × 2.8284 = 3.5355%

$z$ = $\frac{r_{0}}{\sigma_{T}}$ = $\frac{3.\text{40\%}}{3.\text{5355\%}}$ = 0.96

Meaning: a negative shock of less than one terminal standard deviation would leave the 8-year short rate below zero, so negative rates sit well inside the model’s ordinary range of outcomes (compare GARP’s 1.73 at 6.18% over 10 years). The monthly tree step and the 10-year swap rate are irrelevant: the terminal distribution depends on the horizon, not on how finely the tree is cut.

**Fragile fact.** The terminal standard deviation is $\sigma\sqrt{T}$ with $T$ the horizon; $dt$ only sets the tree’s step.

Schweser Reading 14, LO 14.c (10-year illustration whose formula image is missing from the text extract; the structure $\sigma\sqrt{T}$ is confirmed from GARP). No conflict.

b.reason: $z$ = $r_{0}/$($\sigma\sqrt{T}$) = 0.96, the same calculation GARP §14.1 uses for its 10-year example.

c.reason: Error type: dropped term ($\sqrt{T}$ omitted): 3.40%/1.25% = 2.72. This is the answer for a one-year horizon.

questions.question:
A model validator at a Brazilian development bank is reviewing a proposal to replace the normal distribution in its BRL short-rate tree with a probability distribution under which rates cannot become negative. Which of the following statements in the validation report is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, “Model 1” is the short-rate process $dr$ = $\sigma dw$ with normally distributed rates and no drift, where $\sigma$ is the annual basis-point volatility and $dw$ is normal with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$.

options.text: Lognormally distributed rates cannot become negative, and because the change is localised around zero, the model’s dynamics for rates well above zero are left as the normal model postulated.
Lognormally distributed rates cannot become negative, but they only make negative rates less likely, so a zero floor would still be needed to rule negative rates out completely.
Lognormally distributed rates cannot become negative, whereas chi-squared distributed rates can, so only the lognormal choice addresses the negative-rate problem in the tree.
Lognormally distributed rates cannot become negative, but building a model around a distribution that rules out negative rates may result in volatilities that are unacceptable for the purpose.

questions.solution:
**Method 1: changing the distribution of rates**

Stem in one line: most accurate validation statement on replacing the normal distribution with a non-negative one.

**Concept and theory**

The first remedy attacks the cause: if the normal distribution allows negative values, use a distribution that does not. GARP: “Changing the distribution of interest rates is one solution. To take but one of many examples, lognormally distributed rates . . . cannot become negative.” Schweser names lognormal or chi-squared distributions as “always non-negative”.

The cost is that the new distribution governs every rate, not just rates near zero. GARP: “building a model around a probability distribution that rules out negative rates or makes them less likely may result in volatilities that are unacceptable for the purpose at hand.” Schweser: it “may introduce other undesirable characteristics such as skewness or inappropriate volatilities.”

|  | Change the distribution | Set negative rates to zero |
|---|---|---|
| How | Use a non-negative distribution (lognormal; chi-squared) | Build the tree as desired, then replace negative rates with 0 |
| Where it changes dynamics | Across the entire range of rates | Localised around zero and negative rates |
| Main drawback | Volatilities may be unacceptable (skewness) | Observed distribution differs from the shadow one near zero |

**Applying it to this question**

All four options open with the true clause that lognormal rates cannot be negative; the discrimination is in the second clause. Only D states the drawback the sources attach to this method.

**Fragile fact.** Changing the distribution fixes negativity everywhere and changes dynamics everywhere; that global effect is its drawback.

**Reference**

LO 14.c (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 14, §14.1 (lognormal example, “volatilities that are unacceptable”). Schweser Reading 14, LO 14.c. Difference: the chi-squared example and the word “skewness” are Schweser-only (condensed source); GARP refers forward to its Chapter 15 for lognormal models and speaks only of volatilities. No content conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 c, where it is Q4 of 10.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap. “Localised around zero” is the property of the zero floor; GARP says changing the distribution “changes dynamics across the entire range of rates.” A would be correct if it described setting negative rates to zero.

b.reason: Error type: scope or condition error. GARP’s phrase “rules out negative rates or makes them less likely” describes the family of alternative distributions; the lognormal is the member that rules them out. No floor is needed. B would be correct for a distribution that only thins the left tail.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap (chi-squared misclassified with the normal). Schweser lists chi-squared alongside lognormal as distributions that are always non-negative. C would be correct if “chi-squared” were replaced by “normal”.

d.reason: GARP §14.1, quoted above: a distribution that rules out negative rates may give volatilities unacceptable for the purpose.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Swiss private bank is briefing the risk committee on a CHF short-rate tree in which the tree is first built with a normal distribution and every negative rate is then set to zero. The briefing note contains four statements:

I. Rates in the original tree are called shadow rates of interest, while rates in the adjusted tree could be called observed rates of interest.

II. When the observed rate hits zero, it can remain there for a while until the shadow rate crosses back to a positive rate.

III. The economic justification is that the shadow rate, the result of aggregate savings, investment and consumption decisions, must be non-negative because investors can invest in cash.

IV. The probability distribution of the observed rate is the same as that of the originally postulated shadow rate, because only the negative values are relabelled.

Which of the statements are correct?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, “Model 1” is the short-rate process $dr$ = $\sigma dw$ with normally distributed rates and no drift, where $\sigma$ is the annual basis-point volatility and $dw$ is normal with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$.

options.text: I only
I and II only
I, II and III only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
**Method 2: shadow rates and observed rates**

Stem in one line: which briefing statements on a zero-floored CHF tree are correct?

**Concept and theory**

The second remedy keeps the model’s distribution and edits its output. GARP: “Another popular method of ruling out negative rates is to construct rate trees with whatever distribution is desired . . . and then simply set all negative rates to zero.” (Footnote 3 attributes it to Fischer Black, “Interest Rates as Options”, 1995.)

Two rates now coexist:

|  | Shadow rate | Observed rate |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | Rate in the original tree | Rate in the adjusted tree, max(shadow, 0) |
| Economic source | Aggregate savings, investment and consumption decisions | Constrained by the option to hold cash |
| Can be negative? | Yes, “may very well be negative” | No |

Because the shadow rate keeps evolving underneath, “when the observed rate hits zero, it can remain there for a while until the shadow rate crosses back to a positive rate.” And GARP is explicit that the edit changes the distribution: “the probability distribution of the observed interest rate is not the same as that of the originally postulated shadow rate. The change, however, is localised around zero and negative rates.”

**Applying it to this question**

I: true (GARP’s definitions). II: true (persistence at zero). III: names the wrong rate; it is the observed rate that is constrained because investors can hold cash, while the shadow rate may be negative. False. IV: GARP says the distributions are not the same. False. Correct set: I and II.

**Fragile fact.** Observed rate = constrained by cash, never negative. Shadow rate = savings, investment and consumption, may be negative. The two distributions differ only near zero.

**Reference**

LO 14.c (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 14, §14.1 and footnote 3. Schweser Reading 14, LO 14.c (“force” negative rates to zero). Difference: the terms shadow and observed rate, the persistence at zero and the savings-investment justification are GARP-only; Schweser describes only the floor itself. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 c, where it is Q5 of 10.

a.reason: **I only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement. A candidate who pictures the floor as a one-off reset, after which the rate moves freely from zero, rejects II. A would be correct if the tree were rebuilt from the floored node (see Q6, option B).

b.reason: I and II restate GARP §14.1; III and IV each contradict a specific sentence of the same paragraph.

c.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: role misassignment (shadow and observed swapped). GARP: “the observed interest rate should be constrained to be positive only because investors have the alternative of investing in cash. But the shadow rate . . . may very well be negative.” III would be correct with “observed” in place of “shadow”.

d.reason: **I, II and IV.** Error type: absolute-claim trap. Relabelling negative values as zero piles probability at zero, so the distributions differ, though only locally. IV would be correct if it said the distributions agree away from zero.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a German savings bank builds a Model 1 tree for EUR short rates and then applies the shadow-rate approach: the tree is built as specified and every negative rate in it is set to zero. The inputs are:

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Current short rate, $r_{0}$ | 0.40% |
| Annual basis-point volatility, $\sigma$ | 120 bp |
| Time step, $dt$ | 0.25 year |
| Probability of an up move and of a down move | 0.5 each |
| Current 10-year EUR par swap rate | 2.30% |

Which of the following is closest to the expected observed short rate at date 2 (six months from today)?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, “Model 1” is the short-rate process $dr$ = $\sigma dw$ with normally distributed rates and no drift, where $\sigma$ is the annual basis-point volatility and $dw$ is normal with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$.
questions.solution:
**Expected observed rate in a zero-floored tree**

Stem in one line: EUR Model 1 tree, $r_{0}$ = 0.40%, $\sigma$ = 120 bp, $dt$ = 0.25; set negative rates to zero; expected observed rate at date 2.

**Concept and theory**

In the shadow-rate approach the tree is built exactly as the model specifies (here Model 1), giving the shadow rates. Each node’s observed rate is then

$r^{\text{obs}}$ = max $(r^{\text{shadow}},$ 0$)$

The shadow tree is not rebuilt from the floored values: the shadow rate carries on evolving and the observed rate stays at zero “until the shadow rate crosses back to a positive rate” (GARP). In Model 1 each step moves the rate by $\pm\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ each, where $\sigma$ is the annual basis-point volatility and $dt$ the step length in years. After two steps the terminal nodes are $r_{0}$ + 2$\sigma\sqrt{dt}$, $r_{0}$ and $r_{0} -$ 2$\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ with probabilities $\frac{1}{4}$ , $\frac{1}{2}$ and $\frac{1}{4}$ .

**Applying it to this question**

$\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ = 1.20% $\times\sqrt{0.25}$ = 0.60%

Date 1 shadow : 0.40% ± 0.60% = 1.00% and − 0.20% (observed 0%)

Date 2 shadow : 1.60%, 0.40%, −0.80%

Date 2 observed : 1.60%, 0.40%, 0%

$E \left[r^{\text{obs}}_{2}\right]$ = 0.25(1.60%) + 0.50(0.40%) + 0.25(0%) = 0.40% + 0.20% + 0 = 0.60%

| State | Date 0 | Date 1 | Date 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Up-up |  |  | 1.60% |
| Up |  | 1.00% |  |
| Middle | 0.40% |  | 0.40% |
| Down |  | −0.20% → 0% |  |
| Down-down |  |  | −0.80% → 0% |

Meaning: the floor raises the expected short rate from the shadow mean of 0.40% to 0.60%. Note that the down-up path returns to the shadow rate of 0.40%, even though its date-1 observed rate was zero. The 10-year swap rate is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Floor the nodes, not the process: the shadow tree is built first and left intact, and only the reported (observed) rates are set to zero.

**Reference**

LO 14.c (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 14, §14.1 (“construct rate trees with whatever distribution is desired . . . and then simply set all negative rates to zero”; shadow rate persistence). Tree layout from GARP §14.1 (LO 14.a content used only as an input step). Schweser Reading 14, LO 14.c. Difference: the shadow-rate mechanics are GARP-only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 c, where it is Q6 of 10.

a.reason: Error type: scope or condition error (truncation instead of censoring). Deleting the negative node and renormalising: (0.25 × 1.60% + 0.50 × 0.40%)/0.75 = 0.60%/0.75 = 0.80%. The floor replaces negative rates with zero; it does not remove their probability. Correct only for the expected rate conditional on the shadow rate being non-negative.

b.reason: Error type: wrong state variable (the tree is restarted from the floored node). Resetting the date-1 down node to 0% and branching from it gives 0.60% and −0.60% → 0%; the four paths are 1.60%, 0.40%, 0.60%, 0% with average 2.60%/4 = 0.65%. This contradicts GARP’s point that the observed rate stays at zero until the shadow rate turns positive. Correct only for a reflecting barrier at zero, which the source does not describe.

c.reason: Applying max(shadow, 0) node by node to an unchanged Model 1 tree, as GARP §14.1 prescribes, gives 0.60%.

d.reason: Error type: dropped term (the floor ignored). This is the shadow mean, $r_{0}$, because Model 1 has no drift. Correct if the question asked for the expected shadow rate.

questions.question:
A risk consultant advising a Canadian pension plan is comparing two ways of removing negative rates from its CAD short-rate model: changing the probability distribution of rates, or building the tree with the desired distribution and setting all negative rates to zero. Which of the following statements is NOT correct?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, “Model 1” is the short-rate process $dr$ = $\sigma dw$ with normally distributed rates and no drift, where $\sigma$ is the annual basis-point volatility and $dw$ is normal with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$.

options.text: Changing the form of the probability distribution, for example to a lognormal one, changes the dynamics of rates only in the neighbourhood of zero and negative rates.
Setting negative rates to zero makes the observed rate’s distribution differ from the shadow rate’s distribution, but the change is localised around zero and negative rates.
Setting negative rates to zero can be applied to a rate tree built with whatever distribution is desired, including a tree built with normally distributed rates.
Both methods remove negative rates: lognormally distributed rates cannot become negative, and the observed rate in a floored tree cannot fall below zero.

questions.solution:
**Comparing the two methods**

Stem in one line: which statement comparing distribution change and the zero floor is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

The two methods differ in where they change the model. GARP closes the discussion with the comparison: for the floor, “the change, however, is localised around zero and negative rates. By contrast, changing the form of the probability distribution changes dynamics across the entire range of rates.” Schweser draws the practical conclusion: the floor “may be preferred over the first method because it forces a change in the original distribution only in a very low interest rate environment, whereas changing the entire distribution will impact a much wider range of rates.”

Both methods do remove negative rates: lognormal rates “cannot become negative”, and the floored observed rate is by construction never below zero. The floor is also distribution-agnostic: it is applied to trees built “with whatever distribution is desired, as done in this section”, that is, the normal Model 1 tree.

**Applying it to this question**

This is a NOT-correct question, so three options are true source statements and one is corrupted. A attaches the floor’s “localised” property to the distribution change. B, C and D each restate GARP §14.1.

**Fragile fact.** Floor = local change (near zero). Distribution change = global change (entire range). Swapping these is the classic trap.

**Reference**

LO 14.c (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 14, §14.1, final paragraph on negative rates. Schweser Reading 14, LO 14.c (“may be preferred over the first method”). No conflict; Schweser states the preference that GARP’s comparison implies.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 c, where it is Q7 of 10.

a.reason: A is the false statement. GARP: changing the form of the distribution “changes dynamics across the entire range of rates”, not only near zero.

b.reason: True. GARP: the observed distribution “is not the same as that of the originally postulated shadow rate. The change, however, is localised around zero and negative rates.” It would be the answer only if it claimed the two distributions were identical.

c.reason: True. GARP: construct the tree “with whatever distribution is desired, as done in this section” (a normal tree), then set negative rates to zero. It would be the answer if it said the floor works only with a lognormal tree.

d.reason:
True. Both remedies rule out negative rates; they differ in side effects, not in that outcome. It would be the answer if it claimed either method only made negative rates less likely.

Corruption operator in A: sibling swap (the floor’s localised property given to the distribution change).

questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee at a UK life insurer is reviewing the GBP asset-liability model. It is a normal short-rate tree whose volatility of 90 basis points per year was validated against market implied volatilities for rates between 3% and 8%. The current short rate is 0.60% and the 10-year gilt yield is 3.90%. The committee wants negative rates removed while keeping the validated dynamics for rates well above zero. Which recommendation is most consistent with this objective?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, “Model 1” is the short-rate process $dr$ = $\sigma dw$ with normally distributed rates and no drift, where $\sigma$ is the annual basis-point volatility and $dw$ is normal with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$.

options.text: Replace the normal distribution with a lognormal one, because it rules out negative rates while leaving the validated volatilities unchanged at every rate level.
Increase the number of time steps in the tree, because a finer tree approximates the normal distribution more closely and so removes the negative nodes.
Keep the unadjusted normal tree, because with the short rate as low as 0.60% the possibility of negative rates is less of a concern for the model.
Keep the normal tree as a shadow-rate tree and set every negative rate to zero, because the change to the distribution is localised around zero and negative rates.

questions.solution:
**Choosing a method that preserves dynamics away from zero**

Stem in one line: GBP insurer, short rate 0.60%, wants negative rates gone but validated dynamics for rates of 3% to 8% kept; best recommendation?

**Concept and theory**

The choice of remedy depends on which part of the rate distribution the user needs to protect. If the model’s behaviour away from zero has been validated (for example its volatility, here matched to implied volatilities between 3% and 8%), a method that changes dynamics everywhere destroys that validation; a method that changes only the region near zero preserves it. GARP: with the floor, “the change . . . is localised around zero and negative rates”, whereas changing the distribution “changes dynamics across the entire range of rates” and “may result in volatilities that are unacceptable for the purpose at hand.” Neither leaving the model alone nor refining the tree solves the problem: the problem is “much more acute” at low rates, and a finer tree only converges more closely to the normal distribution that causes it.

**Applying it to this question**

Objective 1: no negative rates. Objective 2: keep validated dynamics well above zero. The current short rate of 0.60% makes objective 1 urgent. Only the floor meets both. The 10-year gilt yield is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Low current rates make the problem worse; to protect dynamics away from zero, use the local remedy (floor).

**Reference**

LO 14.c (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 14, §14.1. Schweser Reading 14, LO 14.c (“This method may be preferred over the first method”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 c, where it is Q8 of 10.

a.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. Lognormal rates do rule out negative rates, but GARP warns the resulting volatilities may be unacceptable; “unchanged at every rate level” is the opposite of what a global change of distribution does. A would be correct if the committee did not care about the validated volatility behaviour.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (tree convergence offered as a remedy). More steps make the tree approximate the normal distribution more closely, and the normal distribution always has a negative tail. B would be correct as a statement about approximation accuracy, not about negative rates.

c.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the level effect. GARP: the challenge is “much more acute . . . when the current level of rates is low.” C would be correct if the short rate were high, say 6%, and the horizon short.

d.reason: Setting negative rates to zero on the existing normal (shadow) tree removes negative observed rates while altering the distribution only near zero (GARP §14.1; Schweser: changes the distribution “only in a very low interest rate environment”).

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Japanese asset manager must decide whether a normally distributed short-rate model is still usable for two JPY books in a low-rate environment: a book of plain fixed-coupon government bonds and a book of bond options that are asymmetrically sensitive to the probability of low interest rates. Which of the following is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, “Model 1” is the short-rate process $dr$ = $\sigma dw$ with normally distributed rates and no drift, where $\sigma$ is the annual basis-point volatility and $dw$ is normal with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$.

options.text: The normal model is unusable for both books, because any positive probability of negative rates distorts the value of every fixed income security.
The normal model may remain usable for the coupon bond book, whose value depends mostly on the average path of rates, but could be dangerous for the option book.
The normal model may remain usable for the option book, whose value depends mostly on the average path of rates, but could be dangerous for the coupon bond book.
The normal model is usable for both books, because negative rates affect only the nodes near zero, which carry too little probability to change any price.

questions.solution:
**Application dependence: coupon bonds versus asymmetric securities**

Stem in one line: JPY coupon bond book and bond option book; is a normal model still usable for each?

**Concept and theory**

Whether negative rates disqualify a model depends on what is being valued. GARP: “The extent to which the possibility of negative rates makes a model unusable depends on the application. For securities whose value depends mostly on the average path of the interest rate, like coupon bonds, the possibility of negative rates typically does not rule out an otherwise desirable model. For securities that are asymmetrically sensitive to the probability of low interest rates, however, using a normal model could be dangerous.”

Intuition: a coupon bond discounts along the whole path, so a few negative-rate paths are averaged with many positive ones and the price barely moves. An option whose payoff lives in the low-rate tail is priced almost entirely by those paths, so overweighting them distorts the price. Schweser: for coupon bonds “the possible effect of negative interest rates (small probability of occurring or staying negative for long) is less important”, while option models “that have asymmetric payoffs will be more affected”.

**Applying it to this question**

The bond book depends on the average path; the option book is asymmetrically sensitive to low rates. The normal model may survive for the first but could be dangerous for the second.

**Fragile fact.** Coupon bonds depend on the average path (negative rates usually tolerable); securities asymmetrically sensitive to low rates (options) are where a normal model is dangerous.

**Reference**

LO 14.c (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 14, §14.1. Schweser Reading 14, LO 14.c (“it is ultimately up to the user to decide on the appropriateness of the model”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 c, where it is Q9 of 10.

a.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. GARP says the possibility of negative rates “typically does not rule out an otherwise desirable model” for coupon bonds. A would be correct if both books held only low-rate options.

b.reason: B is GARP §14.1’s application rule applied to the two books.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap (the two security types exchanged). The average-path property belongs to coupon bonds, the asymmetric sensitivity to options. C would be correct with the two books’ labels swapped.

d.reason: Error type: scope or condition error. For securities whose value is concentrated in the low-rate region, the probability on those nodes is exactly what drives the price. D would be correct if the stem contained only the coupon bond book.

An internal auditor at a US bank is reviewing the valuation of a 7-year European option, written to a client, to buy a long-term USD coupon bond at a price corresponding to a yield of 0%. The desk values it with a normally distributed short-rate model with no adjustment for negative rates. The current short rate is 1.10%. Which of the following best describes the likely valuation error and its cause?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, “Model 1” is the short-rate process $dr$ = $\sigma dw$ with normally distributed rates and no drift, where $\sigma$ is the annual basis-point volatility and $dw$ is normal with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$.

options.text: The option is overvalued, because the model assigns too much probability to negative rates.
The option is undervalued, because the model assigns too much probability to negative rates.
The option is roughly fairly valued, because its value depends mostly on the average path of rates.
The option is overvalued, but the error is small, because low current rates leave less room for negative rates.

questions.solution:
**A normal model and an option struck at a 0% yield**

Stem in one line: 7-year option to buy a long-term USD bond at a 0% yield, valued in an unadjusted normal model with the short rate at 1.10%; valuation error?

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s extreme example: “Consider . . . a 10-year call option to buy a long-term coupon bond at a yield of 0%. The model of this section would assign that option much too high a value because the model assigns too much probability to negative rates.” The option to buy at a 0% yield has value only in states where yields fall below zero. A normal model puts real probability on those states; economically they should carry little or none, because cash earns zero. The result is an overvaluation, made worse by a long horizon (the terminal standard deviation grows with $\sqrt{T}$) and by a low starting rate (“much more acute . . . when the current level of rates is low”).

**Applying it to this question**

The security is asymmetrically sensitive to very low rates, the horizon is long (7 years) and the current short rate is low (1.10%). Every factor points to a material overvaluation. For the bank, which has written the option, this overstates the liability.

**Fragile fact.** Normal model plus option struck at a 0% yield gives overvaluation; low current rates make it worse.

**Reference**

LO 14.c (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 14, §14.1 (10-year call option at a 0% yield). Schweser Reading 14, LO 14.c (option valuation models with asymmetric payoffs “more affected”). Difference: the 0% yield option example and the overvaluation direction are GARP-only. No conflict.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Japanese megabank is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts on the Ho-Lee model, $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$. The draft slide contains four statements:

I. The drift may change from date to date; for example, it might be an annualized −20 basis points over the first month and +20 basis points over the second month.

II. The drift over each period represents some combination of the risk premium and of the expected change in the short-term rate over that period.

III. Like the drift, the basis-point volatility $\sigma$ is set separately for each date, which is what allows the tree to match the market term structure of volatility.

IV. The drift must be positive and must increase from date to date, because it compensates investors for bearing risk over longer horizons.

Which of the statements are accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are annualized, trees are binomial with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ on each branch, and $dt$ is measured in years.

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
I and II only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
**What the Ho-Lee drift is, and what it is not**

Stem in one line: which of four slide statements about the Ho-Lee drift and volatility are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

The chapter builds short-rate models by changing one ingredient at a time, the drift. Model 1 has no drift, $dr$ = $\sigma dw$. Model 2 adds a constant drift, $dr$ = $\lambda dt$ + $\sigma dw$. The Ho-Lee model lets the drift depend on time:

$dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$

where $dr$ is the change in the short rate over a small interval $dt$ (in years), $\lambda$($t$) is the annualized drift that applies over the period beginning at date $t$, $\sigma$ is the annual basis-point volatility of rate changes, and $dw$ is a normal random variable with mean 0 and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$.

| Model | Drift | Volatility |
|---|---|---|
| Model 1 | 0 | constant $\sigma$ |
| Model 2 | constant $\lambda$ | constant $\sigma$ |
| Ho-Lee | $\lambda$($t$), one value per period | constant $\sigma$ |

Why allow the drift to vary? Model 2 has only two free parameters for the curve ($r_{0}$ and $\lambda$) and cannot match many market rates. Giving each period its own drift gives one free parameter per period, so the tree can match the price of one more fixed-cash-flow security at each date. GARP: the drift “might be an annualized drift of −20 basis points over the first month, of 20 basis points over the second month, and so on.” Schweser: each drift “does not have to increase and can even be negative.”

What the drift means. As in Model 2, the drift is a risk-neutral drift: GARP says the time-dependent drift over each period “represents some combination of the risk premium and of expected changes in the short-term rate.”

**Applying it to this question**

I restates GARP’s own example: drift changes sign from month 1 to month 2. True. II is GARP’s interpretation of the drift. True. III makes $\sigma$ time-dependent; in Ho-Lee only the drift depends on time, and GARP states that the time-dependent drift does not change the term structure of volatility. False. IV requires a positive and rising drift; GARP’s example has a negative first-month drift and Schweser says the drift can be negative. False. So I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Only the drift is time-dependent in Ho-Lee; $\sigma$ stays constant. The drift can be negative.

**Reference**

LO 14.d (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 14, §14.3 The Ho-Lee Model: Time-Dependent Drift. Schweser Reading 14, “Ho-Lee Model”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 d, where it is Q1 of 11.

a.reason: **I and III only.** Error type: sibling swap. It drops the true statement II and accepts III, which gives Ho-Lee the time-dependent volatility of a different model family (Reading 15). A would be correct only if the stem described a model with time-dependent volatility and a drift that is not interpreted as expectations plus risk premium.

b.reason: **I, II and III only.** Error type: sibling swap on statement III. The candidate carries the “varies by date” property from the drift over to $\sigma$. B would be correct if the process were $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma$($t$) $dw$.

c.reason: GARP §14.3: “the drift of the process may change from date to date” and it “represents some combination of the risk premium and of expected changes in the short-term rate”; the process has a single constant $\sigma$.

d.reason: **I, II and IV only.** Error type: absolute claim (“must be positive and must increase”). It treats the drift as a risk premium alone, which always compensates for longer horizons. D would be correct if IV said “the drift may be positive or negative and need not increase”.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at an Indian bank is building a monthly Ho-Lee tree ($dt$ = 1/12) for the INR short-term rate using the following inputs:

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Current short-term rate, $r_{0}$ | 6.40% |
| Annual basis-point volatility, $\sigma$ | 150 bps |
| Annualized drift, month 1, $\lambda_{1}$ | +0.90% |
| Annualized drift, month 2, $\lambda_{2}$ | −0.60% |

Which of the following gives the up-state and down-state short-term rates on date 1 (after one month)?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are annualized, trees are binomial with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ on each branch, and $dt$ is measured in years.
questions.solution:
**Building the date-1 nodes**

Stem in one line: INR monthly Ho-Lee tree, $r_{0}$ = 6.40%, $\sigma$ = 150 bps, $\lambda_{1}$ = 0.90%, $\lambda_{2}$ = −0.60%; find the date-1 up and down rates.

**Concept and theory**

A tree approximates the process by replacing the normal shock with two outcomes of equal probability. Over the period from date $k -$ 1 to date $k$, each node moves by the drift $\lambda_{k} dt$ plus or minus one volatility step $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$. With dates in columns and states in rows, the two-date Ho-Lee tree is:

| State | Date 0 | Date 1 | Date 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Up-up |  |  | $r_{0}$ + ($\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$)$dt$ + 2$\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ |
| Up |  | $r_{0}$ + $\lambda_{1}dt$ + $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ |  |
| Centre | $r_{0}$ |  | $r_{0}$ + ($\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$)$dt$ |
| Down |  | $r_{0}$ + $\lambda_{1}dt - \sigma\sqrt{dt}$ |  |
| Down-down |  |  | $r_{0}$ + ($\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$)$dt -$ 2$\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ |

Every branch has probability $\frac{1}{2}$ . The drift is added on both the up and the down branch, so it shifts the whole column; the volatility step is what separates the up and down states. The drift of the tree from date 0 to date 1 is $\frac{1}{2}$ ($\lambda_{1}dt$ + $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$) + $\frac{1}{2}$ ($\lambda_{1}dt - \sigma\sqrt{dt}$) = $\lambda_{1}dt$ and its standard deviation is $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$, matching the process.

**Applying it to this question**

Only $\lambda_{1}$ matters for date 1; $\lambda_{2}$ governs the move from date 1 to date 2.

$\lambda_{1} dt$ = 0.90% $\times\frac{1}{12}$ = 0.0750%

$\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ = 1.50% $\times\sqrt{1/12}$ = 1.50% × 0.288675 = 0.4330%

$r_{u}$ = 6.40% + 0.0750% + 0.4330% = 6.908%

$r_{d}$ = 6.40% + 0.0750% − 0.4330% = 6.042%

Meaning: after one month the INR short rate is 6.908% or 6.042%, each with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ ; their average, 6.475%, is $r_{0}$ + $\lambda_{1}dt$.

**Fragile fact.** Drift scales with $dt$; volatility scales with $\sqrt{dt}$. Date 1 uses $\lambda_{1}$ only.

**Reference**

LO 14.d (Schweser). GARP Ch. 14, §14.3 (tree), with the date-1 mechanics of §14.1 (equations 14.3 and 14.4). Schweser Reading 14, “Ho-Lee Model” (Figure 14.4, not reproduced in the extract). Notation confirmed from question bank Q671 and Q672 worked solutions. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 d, where it is Q2 of 11.

a.reason: It applies GARP’s date-1 Ho-Lee nodes $r_{0}$ +$\lambda_{1}dt\pm\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ with the month-1 drift and the $\sqrt{dt}$ scaling of volatility.

b.reason: Error type: wrong input twin. It uses $\lambda_{2}$: 6.40% − 0.60%/12 = 6.35%, then ±0.4330%. Correct if the stem had asked for the step from date 1 to date 2 starting at 6.40%, or if $\lambda_{1}$ were −0.60%.

c.reason: Error type: time-conversion slip. The annualized drift is added without multiplying by $dt$: 6.40% + 0.90% ± 0.4330%. Correct only if 0.90% were the drift for the month rather than an annual rate.

d.reason: Error type: square-root-of-time slip. Volatility is scaled by $dt$ instead of $\sqrt{dt}$: 1.50%/12 = 0.125%, so 6.475% ± 0.125%. Correct if 0.125% were the given monthly standard deviation.

questions.question:
A regulator reviewing a UK bank’s GBP interest rate risk model asks for the highest short-term rate on date 2 of the bank’s monthly Ho-Lee tree ($dt$ = 1/12). The bank’s inputs are:

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Current short-term rate, $r_{0}$ | 4.25% |
| Annual basis-point volatility, $\sigma$ | 120 bps |
| Annualized drift, month 1, $\lambda_{1}$ | 0.48% |
| Annualized drift, month 2, $\lambda_{2}$ | 1.32% |
| Market three-month GBP spot rate | 4.31% |

Which of the following is closest to the rate at the highest node on date 2?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are annualized, trees are binomial with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ on each branch, and $dt$ is measured in years.
questions.solution:
**The highest node on date 2**

Stem in one line: GBP monthly Ho-Lee tree, $r_{0}$ = 4.25%, $\sigma$ = 120 bps, $\lambda_{1}$ = 0.48%, $\lambda_{2}$ = 1.32%; find the up-up node.

**Concept and theory**

From date 1 to date 2 each date-1 node moves by $\lambda_{2} dt \pm\sigma\sqrt{dt}$. The up-up node therefore collects both drifts and two up steps:

$r_{uu}$ = $r_{0}$ + ($\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$) $dt$ + 2$\sigma\sqrt{dt}$

In Model 2 the corresponding node is $r_{0}$ + 2$\lambda dt$ + 2$\sigma\sqrt{dt}$; Ho-Lee simply replaces 2$\lambda$ with the sum of the period drifts. Because the same drift is added to every node on a date, the up-down and down-up paths meet at $r_{0}$ + ($\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$)$dt$: the tree recombines.

**Applying it to this question**

($\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$) $dt$ = (0.48% + 1.32%)/12 = 1.80%/12 = 0.1500%

$\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ = 1.20% × 0.288675 = 0.3464%

$r_{uu}$ = 4.25% + 0.1500% + 2 × 0.3464% = 4.25% + 0.1500% + 0.6928% = 5.093%

The three-month spot rate is irrelevant: it would be used to calibrate $\lambda_{2}$, which is already given. Meaning: after two consecutive up moves the GBP short rate is 5.093%, with probability $\frac{1}{4}$ .

**Fragile fact.** On date 2 the drift is cumulative, ($\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$)$dt$, and the extreme nodes sit 2$\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ from the centre.

**Reference**

LO 14.d (Schweser). GARP Ch. 14, §14.3 (tree garbled in the OCR beyond date 1); Schweser Reading 14, key concept LO 14.d. Extreme-node formula confirmed from question bank Q671 and Q672 worked solutions. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 d, where it is Q3 of 11.

a.reason: Error type: dropped term (one volatility step instead of two): 4.25% + 0.15% + 0.3464%. Correct only if the question had asked for the rate one volatility step above the date-2 centre node, which is not a node of the tree.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap with Model 2. It applies the month-1 drift twice, 2$\lambda_{1}dt$ = 0.08%: 4.25% + 0.08% + 0.6928%. Correct if the model had a constant drift of 0.48% (Model 2).

c.reason: Error type: dropped term (the first-period drift): 4.25% + 1.32%/12 + 0.6928% = 4.25% + 0.11% + 0.6928%. Correct if $\lambda_{1}$ were zero.

d.reason: It applies the recombining Ho-Lee date-2 node: cumulative drift ($\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$)$dt$ plus two volatility steps (GARP §14.3; Schweser key concept for the middle node; bank Q671 for the extreme nodes).

questions.question:
A model validator at a Swiss bank is reviewing documentation that compares the CHF Ho-Lee tree with the simpler short-rate models in the same model library. The documentation contains four statements:

I. If the drifts for every period are equal, $\lambda_{1}$ = $\lambda_{2}$ = · · · , the Ho-Lee tree is the same as the Model 2 (constant drift) tree.

II. Model 1 (no drift) is also a special case of the Ho-Lee model, obtained by setting every period’s drift to zero.

III. Because the drift differs from date to date, the Ho-Lee tree does not recombine: the up-down and down-up paths lead to different rates on date 2.

IV. Because the drift differs from date to date, the up and down probabilities of the Ho-Lee tree must be recalibrated away from 50% at each date.

Which of the statements are correct?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are annualized, trees are binomial with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ on each branch, and $dt$ is measured in years.

options.text: I only
I and II only
I, II and III only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
**Ho-Lee versus Model 1, Model 2 and the recombining property**

Stem in one line: which statements about special cases, recombination and probabilities of the Ho-Lee tree are correct?

**Concept and theory**

Ho-Lee generalizes the drift, so the simpler models are nested inside it:

| Restriction on Ho-Lee drifts | Resulting model | Date-2 centre node |
|---|---|---|
| none | Ho-Lee | $r_{0}$ + ($\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$)$dt$ |
| $\lambda_{1}$ = $\lambda_{2}$ = $\lambda$ | Model 2 | $r_{0}$ + 2$\lambda dt$ |
| $\lambda_{1}$ = $\lambda_{2}$ = 0 | Model 1 | $r_{0}$ |

Schweser: “if $\lambda_{1}$ = $\lambda_{2}$, then the Ho-Lee model reduces to Model 2”; its quiz answer adds that “the no drift and constant drift models are special cases of the Ho-Lee model”.

Why the tree recombines with 50/50 probabilities. The drift $\lambda_{k}dt$ depends only on the date, not on the level of the rate, so every node on a date shifts by the same amount. Up-then-down gives $r_{0}$ + $\lambda_{1}dt$ + $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ + $\lambda_{2}dt - \sigma\sqrt{dt}$, and down-then-up gives the same. Contrast Vasicek (LO 14.f), whose drift $k$($\theta- r$)$dt$ depends on the rate level: there the tree does not recombine, and one way to force recombination changes the probabilities away from 50%.

**Applying it to this question**

I: equal drifts reproduce Model 2. True. II: zero drifts reproduce Model 1. True. III: the tree recombines because the drift is common to all nodes on a date. False. IV: probabilities stay at $\frac{1}{2}$ ; probability recalibration belongs to the Vasicek recombining method. False. So I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Time-dependent drift: tree recombines, probabilities $\frac{1}{2}$ . Level-dependent drift (Vasicek): tree does not recombine naturally.

**Reference**

LO 14.d (Schweser). GARP Ch. 14, §14.3; Vasicek contrast from §14.5 (distractor only). Schweser Reading 14, “Ho-Lee Model”, key concepts LO 14.d, Module Quiz 14.2 Q3 answer. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 d, where it is Q4 of 11.

a.reason: **I only.** Error type: scope error, rejecting a true statement. A candidate who thinks Ho-Lee generalizes only Model 2 misses that zero drifts give Model 1. Correct if II had said “Model 1 cannot be obtained from Ho-Lee”.

b.reason: Schweser LO 14.d and Module Quiz 14.2 Q3 answer (special cases); Schweser key concept “the recombined middle node at Time 2 = $r_{0}$ + ($\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$)$dt$”; GARP §14.3 tree with probabilities $\frac{1}{2}$ .

c.reason: **I, II and III only.** Error type: sibling swap with Vasicek. Non-recombination arises when the drift depends on the rate level (mean reversion), not when it depends on time. Correct if the stem described the Vasicek tree.

d.reason: **I, II and IV only.** Error type: sibling swap with the Vasicek recombining procedure, where GARP solves for $p$ and $q$ to keep the tree recombining. Correct if IV were about recombining a mean-reverting tree.

The treasurer of a Singapore bank is reviewing the SGD Ho-Lee tree calibrated by the bank’s rates desk (monthly steps, $dt$ = 1/12). The calibrated parameters are:

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| Annualized drift, month 1, $\lambda_{1}$ | +0.36% |
| Annualized drift, month 2, $\lambda_{2}$ | +0.12% |
| Annualized drift, month 3, $\lambda_{3}$ | −0.84% |
| Annual basis-point volatility, $\sigma$ | 110 bps |

The bank’s economist estimates that the risk premium embedded in the month-3 drift is +1.5 basis points for that month. What change in the short-term rate during month 3 does the market expect, according to this decomposition?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are annualized, trees are binomial with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ on each branch, and $dt$ is measured in years.

options.text: −8.5 basis points
−5.5 basis points
−85.5 basis points
−7.0 basis points

questions.solution:
**Decomposing one period’s drift**

Stem in one line: SGD tree with $\lambda_{3}$ = −0.84%; risk premium in month 3 is +1.5 bps; what expected rate change does that imply?

**Concept and theory**

The tree is built under the risk-neutral process, so its drift is not a pure forecast. GARP explains with the Model 2 example: a drift of 1.9 bps a month “may arise because the market expects the short-term rate to increase by 1.9 basis points a month, because the short-term rate is expected to increase by one basis point with a risk premium of .9 basis points, or because the short-term rate is expected to fall by .1 basis points with a risk premium of two basis points.” In every case

$\underbrace{\lambda_{k} dt}_{\text{drift for period } k} = \underbrace{E[\Delta r_{k}]}_{\text{expected change}} + \underbrace{\text{RP}_{k}}_{\text{risk premium}}$

GARP §14.3 applies the same reading to Ho-Lee: the time-dependent drift over each period represents a combination of the two, and now the split can differ from period to period. Market prices alone cannot separate the two pieces; a split needs an outside assumption, here the economist’s risk premium.

**Applying it to this question**

$\lambda_{3} dt$ = −0.84% $\times\frac{1}{12}$ = −0.07% = −7.0 bps for month 3

$E$\[∆$r_{3}$\] = $\lambda_{3} dt - \text{RP}_{3}$ = −7.0 − 1.5 = −8.5 bps

$\lambda_{1}$, $\lambda_{2}$ and $\sigma$ are irrelevant. Meaning: with a positive risk premium, the market expects the short rate to fall by more than the drift alone shows.

**Fragile fact.** Drift = expected change + risk premium, so expected change = drift − risk premium. A positive premium makes the expected change lower than the drift.

**Reference**

LO 14.d (Schweser: “the drift is a combination of the risk premium over the period and the expected rate change”). GARP Ch. 14, §14.3, using the decomposition example from §14.2 Model 2: Drift and Risk Premium. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 d, where it is Q5 of 11.

a.reason: It converts the annualized drift to the month (multiply by $dt$) and removes the risk premium, consistent with GARP’s additive decomposition.

b.reason: **(−5.5 bps).** Error type: sign error. It adds the premium: −7.0 + 1.5. Correct if the economist’s estimate were a risk premium of −1.5 bps.

c.reason: **(−85.5 bps).** Error type: time-conversion slip. It treats −0.84% (−84 bps) as the monthly drift: −84 − 1.5. Correct only if $\lambda_{3}$ were quoted per month, not annualized.

d.reason: **(−7.0 bps).** Error type: intermediate result. It stops at the drift and ignores the risk premium. Correct if the risk premium for month 3 were zero.

A portfolio manager at an Australian superannuation fund simulates one path of the AUD short-term rate from the Ho-Lee process $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$ with monthly steps ($dt$ = 1/12). Here $dw$ is normally distributed with a mean of zero and a standard deviation of $\sqrt{dt}$, and the values below are the realized values of $dw$ itself, not standard normal draws.

|  | Month 1 | Month 2 |
|---|---|---|
| Annualized drift, $\lambda$($t$) | 0.60% | 1.08% |
| Realized $dw$ | −0.20 | +0.35 |

The current short-term rate is 3.60% and the annual basis-point volatility is 96 bps. What is the simulated short-term rate after two months?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are annualized, trees are binomial with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ on each branch, and $dt$ is measured in years.
questions.solution:
**A simulated path of the Ho-Lee process**

Stem in one line: AUD path, $r_{0}$ = 3.60%, $\sigma$ = 96 bps, drifts 0.60% and 1.08%, realized $dw$ of −0.20 and +0.35; find the rate after two months.

**Concept and theory**

The tree is an approximation of the continuous process; the process itself can take any value. GARP §14.1: “the random variable in the process, having a normal distribution, can take on any value while a single step in the tree leads to only two possible values.” In GARP’s convention $dw$ already carries the time scaling: it is normal with mean 0 and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$ (0.2887 for one month), and the change in rate is $\sigma$ times the realized $dw$ (GARP: $dr$ = 1.13% × .15 = .17%). For Ho-Lee, each month adds its own drift:

$r_{2}$ = $r_{0}$ + ($\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$) $dt$ + $\sigma$ ($dw_{1}$ + $dw_{2}$)

**Applying it to this question**

($\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$) $dt$ = (0.60% + 1.08%)/12 = 0.1400%

$dw_{1}$ + $dw_{2}$ = −0.20 + 0.35 = 0.15

$\sigma$ ($dw_{1}$ + $dw_{2}$) = 0.96% × 0.15 = 0.1440%

$r_{2}$ = 3.60% + 0.1400% + 0.1440% = 3.884%

Meaning: the simulated rate is not one of the tree’s date-2 nodes; it is one draw from the normal distribution that the tree approximates.

**Fragile fact.** In GARP’s notation $dw$ already has standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$; multiply by $\sqrt{dt}$ only when you are given a standard normal $z$.

**Reference**

LO 14.d (Schweser). GARP Ch. 14, §14.3 equation (14.7), with the $dw$ convention of §14.1 (equation 14.2). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 d, where it is Q6 of 11.

a.reason: Error type: dropped term (both drifts omitted): 3.60%+0.1440%. Correct for Model 1 with the same shocks.

b.reason: Error type: square-root-of-time slip (double scaling). It treats the $dw$ values as standard normal draws and multiplies by $\sqrt{dt}$ again: 0.96% × 0.15 × 0.288675 = 0.0416%, so 3.60% + 0.14% + 0.0416%. Correct if the stem had given standard normal draws $z$ with $dw$ = $z\sqrt{dt}$.

c.reason: It uses the Ho-Lee process $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$)$dt$ + $\sigma dw$ (GARP equation 14.7) with each month’s own drift and the realized $dw$ values as given.

d.reason: Error type: dropped term (first shock omitted): 3.60% + 0.14% + 0.96% × 0.35 = 3.60% + 0.14% + 0.336%. Correct if month 1 had a zero shock.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is explaining to a Brazilian bank’s ALCO how its monthly Ho-Lee tree ($dt$ = 1/12) is fitted to the BRL zero curve. Which of the following best describes the calibration procedure?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are annualized, trees are binomial with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ on each branch, and $dt$ is measured in years.

options.text: Set $r_{0}$ equal to the two-month rate, find $\lambda_{1}$ so that the model three-month spot rate equals the market rate, then find $\lambda_{2}$ from the four-month rate, and continue to the end of the tree.

Set $r_{0}$ equal to the one-month rate, find $\lambda_{1}$ so that the model two-month spot rate equals the market rate, then find $\lambda_{2}$ from the three-month rate, and continue to the end of the tree.
Set $r_{0}$ equal to the one-month rate, then choose a single drift $\lambda$ that fits the two-year and ten-year par rates jointly, and set $\sigma$ to the average of their implied volatilities.

Set $r_{0}$ equal to the one-month rate, then choose $\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}, . . .$ and a separate $\sigma$ for each date so that the tree matches both spot rates and implied volatilities at every maturity.

questions.solution:
**How the Ho-Lee drifts are calibrated**

Stem in one line: best description of how a monthly Ho-Lee tree is fitted to the BRL zero curve.

**Concept and theory**

The drifts $\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}, . . .$ are free parameters chosen so that the tree prices fixed-cash-flow securities at market. Calibration is a bootstrap: each new maturity adds one unknown drift. GARP §14.3: “With $dt$ = 1/12, set $r_{0}$ equal to the one-month rate. Then find $\lambda_{1}$ such that the model produces a two-month spot rate equal to that in the market. Then find $\lambda_{2}$ such that the model produces a three-month spot rate equal to that in the market. Continue in this fashion until the tree ends.”

| Step | Unknown | Market input matched |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | $r_{0}$ | one-month rate |
| 1 | $\lambda_{1}$ (given $r_{0}$) | two-month spot rate |
| 2 | $\lambda_{2}$ (given $r_{0}$, $\lambda_{1}$) | three-month spot rate |
| $k$ | $\lambda_{k}$ (given all earlier) | ($k$ + 1)-month spot rate |

The logic of the index: $\lambda_{1}$ governs rates on date 1, which first affect the discounting of a two-month cash flow. Because it matches market prices by construction, Ho-Lee is an arbitrage-free model, whereas Models 1 and 2 are equilibrium models. $\sigma$ is a single input and is not fitted date by date.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are the starting point ($r_{0}$ = one-month rate) and the one-maturity-ahead indexing ($\lambda_{1}$ to the two-month rate). Only B has both.

**Fragile fact.** $r_{0}$ = one-month rate; $\lambda_{1}$ is pinned by the two-month rate, $\lambda_{2}$ by the three-month rate. The index of $\lambda$ is one less than the maturity in months.

**Reference**

LO 14.d (Schweser). GARP Ch. 14, §14.3; Model 2 calibration from §14.2 (distractor). Schweser Reading 14, “Ho-Lee Model”. Difference: Schweser says $\lambda_{1}$ matches the “two-period market rate”; GARP specifies the two-month spot rate with monthly steps. Same substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 d, where it is Q7 of 11.

a.reason: Error type: role misassignment (each parameter matched to the next maturity up). $r_{0}$ is the date-0 rate for the first month, so it is the one-month rate, not the two-month rate. Correct if the tree’s first step were two months long.

b.reason: It reproduces GARP’s procedure; Schweser agrees: “$r_{0}$ is the observed one-period spot rate. $\lambda_{1}$ could then be estimated so that the model rate equals the observed two-period market rate. $\lambda_{2}$ could be calibrated from using $r_{0}$ and $\lambda_{1}$ and the observed market rate for a three-period security.”

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap with Model 2. GARP calibrates Model 2’s $r_{0}$ and single $\lambda$ to the 2- and 10-year par swap rates and sets $\sigma$ to their average implied volatility. Correct if the stem described the Model 2 example.

d.reason: Error type: scope error (overextended). Ho-Lee fits a drift per date to spot rates; $\sigma$ is one constant and the model does not fit implied volatilities at every maturity. Correct only for a model with time-dependent volatility, which is not Ho-Lee.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Canadian bank is checking the CAD Ho-Lee tree used by the bank’s rates desk (monthly steps, $dt$ = 1/12). The desk’s screen shows the following tree and the market two-month CAD spot rate of 2.765%.

| State | Date 0 | Date 1 | Date 2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Up-up |  |  | 3.440% |
| Up |  | 3.130% |  |
| Centre | 2.750% |  | 2.740% |
| Down |  | 2.430% |  |
| Down-down |  |  | 2.040% |

Which of the following is the annualized drift for the second month, $\lambda_{2}$, implied by the tree?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are annualized, trees are binomial with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ on each branch, and $dt$ is measured in years.
questions.solution:
**Reading $\lambda_{2}$ off a published tree**

Stem in one line: CAD tree 2.750%; 3.130%/2.430%; 3.440%/2.740%/2.040%; find the month-2 drift $\lambda_{2}$.

**Concept and theory**

Because each branch has probability $\frac{1}{2}$ and the volatility steps cancel on average, the midpoint of each column of a Ho-Lee tree shows the cumulative drift:

$\frac{1}{2}$ ($r_{u}$ + $r_{d}$) = $r_{0}$ + $\lambda_{1} dt$

$r_{ud}$ = $r_{0}$ + ($\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$) $dt$

So $\lambda_{1}dt$ is the step from $r_{0}$ to the date-1 midpoint, $\lambda_{2}dt$ is the step from the date-1 midpoint to the date-2 centre node, and $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ is half the date-1 spread. This is the tree construction run backwards.

**Applying it to this question**

date-1 midpoint = $\frac{1}{2}$ (3.130% + 2.430%) = 2.780% $\Rightarrow\lambda_{1} dt$ = 0.030%$, \lambda_{1}$ = 0.36%

$\lambda_{2} dt$ = $r_{ud} -$ midpoint = 2.740% − 2.780% = −0.040%

$\lambda_{2}$ = −0.040% × 12 = −0.48%

Check: $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ (3.130% − 2.430%) = 0.350%, and 2.740% ± 2 × 0.350% = 3.440%, 2.040%, as shown. The two-month spot rate is irrelevant. Meaning: the drift turns negative in month 2 even though it was positive in month 1, which Ho-Lee allows.

**Fragile fact.** The centre node on date 2 measures $\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$ from $r_{0}$; to get $\lambda_{2}$ alone, measure from the date-1 midpoint.

**Reference**

LO 14.d (Schweser). GARP Ch. 14, §14.3; Schweser Reading 14, key concept LO 14.d. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 d, where it is Q8 of 11.

a.reason: It isolates the month-2 drift as the change in the column midpoint from date 1 to date 2, annualized by dividing by $dt$ (GARP §14.3 tree; Schweser key concept for the centre node).

b.reason: **(+0.48%).** Error type: sign error. It computes (2.780% − 2.740%) × 12, midpoint minus centre. Correct if the date-2 centre node were 2.820%.

c.reason: **(−0.12%).** Error type: intermediate result (cumulative drift). (2.740% − 2.750%) × 12 = −0.12% = $\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$. Correct if the question had asked for $\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$, or if $\lambda_{1}$ were zero.

d.reason: **(−0.04%).** Error type: time-conversion slip. It reports $\lambda_{2}dt$, the drift for the month, without annualizing. Correct if the question had asked for the month-2 drift in percent per month.

questions.question:
A member of a French bank’s board risk committee asks what is gained by replacing the bank’s EUR Model 2 (constant drift) tree with a Ho-Lee tree whose drifts are fitted date by date to the market term structure. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are annualized, trees are binomial with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ on each branch, and $dt$ is measured in years.

options.text: The Ho-Lee tree produces a term structure of volatility that declines with maturity, because the fitted drifts damp the effect of shocks on longer-term rates.
The Ho-Lee tree reproduces the humped term structure of volatility observed in the market, because each date’s drift is fitted to market rates.
The Ho-Lee tree matches all the rates input into the model, but its term structure of volatility and its parallel-shift nature are unchanged.
The Ho-Lee tree matches all the rates input into the model, so it necessarily gives fair values and accurate hedges for derivatives on those rates.

questions.solution:
**What fitting a time-dependent drift does and does not change**

Stem in one line: most accurate statement of what moving from Model 2 to a fitted Ho-Lee tree achieves.

**Concept and theory**

The drift moves the level of expected rates through time; it does not change how rates respond to shocks. GARP §14.3: “The rate curves resulting from this model match all the rates that are input into the model. Just as adding a constant drift to Model 1 to obtain Model 2 does not affect the shape of the term structure of volatility nor the parallel-shift characteristic of the model, adding a time-dependent drift does not change these features either.”

| Feature | Model 1 | Model 2 | Ho-Lee |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fits market rates | no | roughly (2 points) | all input rates |
| Term structure of volatility | flat | flat | flat |
| Shape of factor (response to a shock) | parallel | parallel | parallel |

A volatility structure that slopes downward comes from mean reversion (Vasicek, LO 14.h), not from drift that depends on time.

**Applying it to this question**

The committee member gets an exact fit to the input rates and nothing else: the volatility structure and the parallel-shift behaviour are unchanged. C says exactly that.

**Fragile fact.** Time-dependent drift buys fit to rates only. Volatility structure stays flat and shocks stay parallel.

**Reference**

LO 14.d (Schweser). GARP Ch. 14, §14.3 (last paragraph); distractor sources §14.4 Desirability of Fitting to the Term Structure (LO 14.e) and §14.5 (Vasicek). Schweser Reading 14, “Ho-Lee Model” (fit), “Model 1 Effectiveness”. Note: Schweser’s LO 14.d section does not state the unchanged volatility structure; that point is GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 d, where it is Q9 of 11.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap with Vasicek. A volatility structure that declines with maturity and damped long-rate responses are effects of mean reversion. Correct if the stem replaced Model 2 with a Vasicek model.

b.reason: Error type: scope error. The drifts are fitted to rates (prices of fixed-cash-flow securities), not to volatilities, so the volatility structure remains flat and cannot be humped. Correct only for a model whose volatility parameters are fitted to implied volatilities.

c.reason: It is the GARP §14.3 statement quoted above.

d.reason: Error type: absolute claim, borrowed from LO 14.e. GARP: “That a model matches market prices does not necessarily imply that it provides fair values and accurate hedges for derivative securities.” Correct if “necessarily gives” read “is commonly used to price”.

questions.question:
The CRO of a Chinese bank asks a validator to summarize the distribution of the CNY short-term rate on date 2 of the bank’s monthly Ho-Lee tree ($dt$ = 1/12). The inputs are:

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Current short-term rate, $r_{0}$ | 2.10% |
| Annual basis-point volatility, $\sigma$ | 90 bps |
| Annualized drift, month 1, $\lambda_{1}$ | 0.30% |
| Annualized drift, month 2, $\lambda_{2}$ | 0.66% |
| Annualized drift, month 3, $\lambda_{3}$ | 0.84% |

Which of the following gives the probability-weighted expected short-term rate on date 2 and the standard deviation of the date-2 short-term rate implied by the tree?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are annualized, trees are binomial with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ on each branch, and $dt$ is measured in years.

options.text: Expected rate 2.150%; standard deviation 0.367%
Expected rate 2.180%; standard deviation 0.260%
Expected rate 2.180%; standard deviation 0.520%
Expected rate 2.180%; standard deviation 0.367%

questions.solution:
**Mean and standard deviation of the date-2 rate**

Stem in one line: CNY tree, $r_{0}$ = 2.10%, $\sigma$ = 90 bps, $\lambda_{1}$ = 0.30%, $\lambda_{2}$ = 0.66%; find the date-2 expected rate and standard deviation.

**Concept and theory**

With probability $\frac{1}{2}$ on each branch, the three date-2 nodes have probabilities $\frac{1}{4}$ (up-up), $\frac{1}{2}$ (centre, reached by two paths) and $\frac{1}{4}$ (down-down). Write $m$ = $r_{0}$ + ($\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$)$dt$ and $s$ = $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$; the nodes are $m$ + 2$s$, $m$, $m -$ 2$s$.

$E$\[$r_{2}$\] = $\frac{1}{4}$ ($m$ + 2$s$) + $\frac{1}{2} m$ + $\frac{1}{4}$ ($m -$ 2$s$) = $m$

$V$ \[$r_{2}$\] = $\frac{1}{4}$ (2$s$)$^{2}$ + $\frac{1}{2}$ $\text{(0)}^{2}$ + $\frac{1}{4}$ (2$s$)$^{2}$ = 2$s^{2}$

SD\[$r_{2}$\] = $s\sqrt{2}$ = $\sigma\sqrt{2 dt}$

This is the tree version of GARP’s result for Models 1 and 2 that the terminal standard deviation after $T$ years is $\sigma\sqrt{T}$ (“1.10% $\times\sqrt{10}$”). The deterministic drift moves the mean but does not change the dispersion, so Ho-Lee behaves the same way.

**Applying it to this question**

$E$\[$r_{2}$\] = 2.10% + (0.30% + 0.66%)/12 = 2.10% + 0.080% = 2.180%

$\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ = 0.90% × 0.288675 = 0.2598%

SD\[$r_{2}$\] = 0.90% $\times\sqrt{2/12}$ = 0.90% × 0.408248 = 0.367%

$\lambda_{3}$ is irrelevant to date 2. Meaning: two months out, the CNY short rate is centred on 2.180% with a standard deviation of about 37 bps.

**Fragile fact.** Date-2 standard deviation is $\sigma\sqrt{2dt}$, not 2$\sigma\sqrt{dt}$: variances add over periods, standard deviations do not.

**Reference**

LO 14.d (Schweser). GARP Ch. 14, §14.3 tree, with the tree-matches-process argument of §14.1 (equations 14.3 and 14.4) and the terminal-distribution statement of §14.2. The Ho-Lee date-2 standard deviation is derived from the tree here; GARP states $\sigma\sqrt{T}$ explicitly only for Models 1 and 2. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 d, where it is Q10 of 11.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap with Model 2. The mean uses the first drift twice, 2.10% + 2 × 0.30%/12 = 2.150%. Correct if the drift were constant at 0.30%.

b.reason: Error type: intermediate result. The standard deviation is the one-step value $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$. Correct for the date-1 rate.

c.reason: Error type: square-root-of-time slip. The one-step standard deviation is scaled by the number of steps, 2, instead of by $\sqrt{2}$: 2$\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ = 0.520%, which is the distance from the centre to an extreme node, not a standard deviation. Correct if the question asked for the gap between the centre node and the up-up node.

d.reason: The probability-weighted mean is the centre node $r_{0}$ + ($\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$)$dt$ and the standard deviation grows with the square root of elapsed time, $\sigma\sqrt{2dt}$.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Japanese trust bank is calibrating a monthly Ho-Lee tree ($dt$ = 1/12) to the JPY zero curve. All rates are continuously compounded. The value of a security at any node is $\frac{1}{2}$ ($V_{\text{up}}$ + $V_{\text{down}}$) $e^{-r dt}$, where $r$ is the short-term rate at that node, and a $t$-month zero-coupon bond has a market price of $e^{-s_{t}\times t/12}$.

| Market input | Value |
|---|---|
| One-month rate (taken as $r_{0}$) | 0.60% |
| Two-month spot rate, $s_{2}$ | 0.65% |
| Three-month spot rate, $s_{3}$ | 0.72% |
| Annual basis-point volatility, $\sigma$ | 40 bps |

Which of the following is closest to the annualized drifts $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$ that fit the tree to the two- and three-month spot rates?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are annualized, trees are binomial with probability $\frac{1}{2}$ on each branch, and $dt$ is measured in years.
questions.solution:
**Calibrating $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$ to the JPY spot curve**

Stem in one line: $r_{0}$ = 0.60%, $s_{2}$ = 0.65%, $s_{3}$ = 0.72% (continuous), $\sigma$ = 40 bps; find the $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$ that fit the tree.

**Concept and theory**

GARP §14.3: set $r_{0}$ to the one-month rate, find $\lambda_{1}$ so the model two-month spot rate equals the market, then $\lambda_{2}$ so the model three-month spot rate equals the market. To do this, price the zeros on the tree by expected discounted value. A two-month zero pays 1 on date 2; on date 1 it is worth $e^{-r_{u}dt}$ or $e^{-r_{d}dt}$; on date 0

$P_{2}$ = $e^{-r_{0}dt} \cdot\frac{1}{2} (e^{-r_{u}dt}$ + $e^{-r_{d}dt}) , r_{u,d}$ = $r_{0}$ + $\lambda_{1}dt \pm\sigma\sqrt{dt}$

The volatility terms enter only through $\frac{1}{2}$ ($e^{-\sigma}\sqrt{dt}^{dt}$ + $e^{\text{+}\sigma}\sqrt{dt}^{dt}$), which differs from 1 by about $\frac{1}{2} \sigma^{2}dt^{3}$; this is the (tiny, at a one-month step) convexity effect. Ignoring it, matching $P_{2}$ = $e^{-s_{2}\cdot2dt}$ gives

2$s_{2}$ = $r_{0}$ + ($r_{0}$ + $\lambda_{1}dt$)

and similarly for the three-month zero, whose date-2 rates are centred on $r_{0}$ + ($\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$)$dt$:

3$s_{3}$ = $r_{0}$ + ($r_{0}$ + $\lambda_{1}dt$) + ($r_{0}$ + ($\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$)$dt$)

In words: ignoring the tiny convexity term, the expected short rate on each date must equal the one-month forward rate implied by the spot curve. Note that $\lambda_{1}$ appears twice in the three-month equation, because the month-1 drift is still in the rate on date 2.

**Applying it to this question**

$\lambda_{1} dt$ = 2$s_{2} -$ 2$r_{0}$ = 1.30% − 1.20% = 0.10%

$\lambda_{1}$ = 0.10% × 12 = 1.20%

$\lambda_{2} dt$ = 3$s_{3} -$ 3$r_{0} -$ 2$\lambda_{1}dt$ = 2.16% − 1.80% − 0.20% = 0.16%

$\lambda_{2}$ = 0.16% × 12 = 1.92%

Solving the exact tree-pricing equations numerically (calc.py) gives $\lambda_{1}$ = 1.2001% and $\lambda_{2}$ = 1.9202%, so the convexity term is negligible and $\sigma$ hardly matters here. Meaning: the tree’s expected short rate is 0.70% on date 1 and 0.86% on date 2, the one-month forwards implied by the JPY curve.

**Fragile fact.** Calibrate to forwards, not to spot differences; $\lambda_{1}$ stays in the date-2 rate, so it enters the three-month equation twice.

**Reference**

LO 14.d (Schweser). GARP Ch. 14, §14.3 (calibration procedure). The expected-discounted-value pricing used in the stem is the risk-neutral pricing of GARP Ch. 12, §12.3; the continuous-compounding discount convention is stated in the stem because GARP §14.3 does not give a discounting formula. Schweser Reading 14, “Ho-Lee Model”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 d, where it is Q11 of 11.

a.reason: Error type: dropped term. $\lambda_{1}dt$ is subtracted only once in the second step: $\lambda_{2}dt$ = 2.16% − 1.80% − 0.10% = 0.26%, so $\lambda_{2}$ = 3.12%. This equals $\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$, the cumulative drift to date 2. Correct if the question asked for $\lambda_{1}$ + $\lambda_{2}$.

b.reason: It follows GARP’s sequential calibration, carrying $\lambda_{1}$ into the second equation, and annualizes each drift.

c.reason: Error type: wrong input twin (spot rate changes used in place of forward rate changes). $\lambda_{1}dt$ = $s_{2} - r_{0}$ = 0.05% and $\lambda_{2}dt$ = $s_{3} - s_{2}$ = 0.07%. Spot rates are averages of the short rates along the curve, so the short rate must move by more than the spot rate. Correct only if the tree’s expected short rates were the spot rates themselves.

d.reason: Error type: time-conversion slip. These are the monthly drifts $\lambda_{1}dt$ and $\lambda_{2}dt$, not annualized. Correct if the question asked for drift per month.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Singapore bank is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts on how the short-rate models in the reading are classified. The draft slide contains four statements:

I. Model 1 (no drift) and Model 2 (constant drift) are called equilibrium models because no effort is made to match the initial term structure closely.

II. The Ho-Lee model belongs to the class of arbitrage-free models because its time-dependent drift parameters can be chosen so that the model matches the prices of securities with fixed cash flows.

III. Model 2 becomes an arbitrage-free model once its initial rate and constant drift are calibrated to match the 2-year and 10-year par swap rates.

IV. The desirability of matching market prices is the central issue in choosing between the two classes, and the choice depends on the purpose for which the model is built.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and IV only
II, III and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
**Classifying short-rate models**

Stem in one line: which slide statements on equilibrium vs arbitrage-free classification are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

The reading builds short-rate models by adding drift specifications to a basic normal model, and it sorts them into two classes by one question: is the model made to match today’s term structure?

|  | Equilibrium model | Arbitrage-free model |
|---|---|---|
| Examples in the reading | Model 1 (no drift), Model 2 (constant drift), Vasicek | Ho-Lee (time-dependent drift) |
| Relation to market prices | No effort to match the initial term structure closely; a few parameters may be set to a couple of rates | Free drift parameters ($\lambda_{1}, \lambda_{2}, . . .$ ) chosen so model prices equal market prices |
| Output | Values that may disagree with the market | Values that agree with the fitted prices by construction |

In Ho-Lee, $dr$ = $\lambda_{t} dt$ + $\sigma dw$, where $dr$ is the change in the short rate over interval $dt$, $\lambda_{t}$ the drift for period $t$, $\sigma$ the annual basis-point volatility and $dw$ a normal shock with mean 0 and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$. Because there is one $\lambda_{t}$ per period, each can be solved so that the model reproduces the next market spot rate. GARP opens §14.4 by saying that whether to match market prices is the central issue in choosing between the classes, and that the answer depends on what the model is for.

**Applying it to this question**

I: GARP, end of §14.2, labels Models 1 and 2 equilibrium models for exactly this reason. True. II: GARP §14.3 says the free parameters $\lambda_{1}$ and $\lambda_{2}$ may be used to match the prices of securities with fixed cash flows and calls Ho-Lee a generalization of Model 2 in the arbitrage-free class. True. III: GARP calibrates Model 2’s $r_{0}$ and $\lambda$ to the 2- and 10-year par swap rates and still calls it an equilibrium model; two parameters cannot match the whole curve (the model overshoots the 30-year par rate by about 25 bp). False. IV: the opening of §14.4. True. Hence I, II and IV only.

**Fragile fact.** Fitting two rates is not fitting the term structure: calibrated Model 2 is still equilibrium. Ho-Lee is arbitrage-free because it has a drift parameter per period.

**Reference**

LO 14.e (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 14, end of §14.2 Model 2: Drift and Risk Premium; §14.3 The Ho-Lee Model: Time-Dependent Drift; opening of §14.4 Desirability of Fitting to the Term Structure. Schweser Reading 14, LO 14.e (“the key factor in choosing between these two models is based on the need to match market prices”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 e, where it is Q1 of 14.

a.reason: **I and II only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement (polarity flip on IV). A candidate who believes the choice is decided by goodness of fit rather than by purpose rejects IV. A would be correct if IV said the choice depends only on which model fits the curve best.

b.reason: Statements I, II and IV restate GARP §14.2 (end), §14.3 and §14.4 (opening); III contradicts GARP’s own labelling of the calibrated Model 2.

c.reason: **II, III and IV only.** Error type: scope error on “matching the term structure”. It accepts that calibrating two parameters to two rates makes a model arbitrage-free, and so rejects I. Would be correct only if matching any two prices were enough to call a model arbitrage-free, which GARP’s own Model 2 example rules out.

d.reason: **All four.** Error type: the same scope error as C, while keeping I. It is internally inconsistent: if calibrated Model 2 were arbitrage-free, I would be false. Correct only if III read “Model 2 remains an equilibrium model even after its initial rate and drift are calibrated to the 2- and 10-year rates”.
