questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Japanese life insurer is reviewing a vendor’s Vasicek model used to value the JPY swaption hedges of the insurer’s long-dated liabilities. The vendor chose $k$ and $\sigma$ so that the model’s par-rate volatilities equal the market implied volatilities of the 10-year and 30-year par rates. The calibrated long-run value is $\theta$ = 3.10%. Market implied par-rate volatilities are:

| Term (years) | 2 | 5 | 10 | 30 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Market implied volatility (bp per year) | 95 | 103 | 108 | 99 |

Which of the following best describes the model’s par-rate volatilities relative to the market?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation throughout: the risk-neutral Vasicek model is $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$, where $k$ is the speed of mean reversion, $\theta$ the long-run value of the short rate and $\sigma$ the annual basis-point volatility. Model 1 is $dr$ = $\sigma dw$ (normal, no drift).

options.text: They match the market at 10 and 30 years and understate it at 2 and 5 years, because mean reversion dampens volatility most at short terms.
They match the market at all four terms, because a declining volatility structure can be calibrated to fit any humped market structure.
They match the market at 10 and 30 years and are flat at about 108 bp at 2 and 5 years, because the short end behaves as in Model 1.
They match the market at 10 and 30 years and overstate it at 2 and 5 years, because the model’s volatility declines with term everywhere.

questions.solution:
**Where the Vasicek volatility structure misses the market**

Stem in one line: $k$ and $\sigma$ fitted to 10- and 30-year implied volatilities; market is 95, 103, 108, 99 bp at 2, 5, 10, 30 years; how do model volatilities compare?

**Concept and theory**

Two facts from GARP §14.5 decide this question:

1. The Vasicek term structure of par-rate volatility slopes downward at every term.
2. In GARP’s example, $k$ and $\sigma$ are chosen to fit the implied 10- and 30-year volatilities, so the model matches the market at those two terms but overstates the volatility at shorter terms.

The logic is geometric. Pin a downward-sloping curve to two points on the long end of a humped curve. To the left of the 10-year point the model curve must keep rising as term shortens, while the market curve falls as term shortens. The model therefore sits above the market at short terms.

**Applying it to this question**

Model at 10 and 30 years = 108 and 99 bp (by calibration)

Model at 5 years > model at 10 years = 108 > 103 = market at 5 years

Model at 2 years > model at 5 years > 108 > 95 = market at 2 years

So the model overstates volatility at 2 and 5 years. The value of $\theta$ is irrelevant: it sets the level of rates, not the shape of the volatility structure.

**Fragile fact.** Calibrated at the long end, the Vasicek model overstates short-term volatility. The direction of the miss depends on where it was calibrated; the slope (downward everywhere) does not.

**Reference**

LO 14.h (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 14, §14.5 (Figure 14.7 discussion) and §14.1 (Figure 14.3, humped market structure). Schweser Reading 14, LO 14.h. Difference: Schweser states that short-term volatility is overstated and long-term volatility understated; GARP says the model matches the 10- and 30-year volatilities to which it is calibrated. GARP used; the Schweser phrase looks like a compression of the figure rather than a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 h, where it is Q3 of 11.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip. Mean reversion dampens volatility at long terms, not short terms, so the model lies above, not below, the market at the short end. A would be correct if the model were calibrated to the 2- and 5-year volatilities and the question asked about the long end.

b.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. A two-parameter declining curve cannot pass through four points that first rise and then fall. B would be correct only if the market structure were itself declining and of exactly the model’s shape.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap. A flat volatility structure belongs to Model 1; the Vasicek structure has no flat segment. C would be correct for Model 1 calibrated to a 108 bp volatility (and then it would also miss the 30-year point).

d.reason: It matches GARP’s description of Figure 14.7: the model matches the market at the two calibration terms but overstates the volatility for shorter terms, because mean reversion produces a structure that slopes downward everywhere.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a UK building society is comparing two models of the GBP curve: Model N, normal with no drift and $\sigma$ = 100 bp per year, and Model V, a Vasicek model with $\sigma$ = 112 bp per year and a slow speed of mean reversion, $k$ = 0.03. The vendor reports the convexity effect on par rates, defined as the model par rate minus the par rate in the same model with zero volatility (hypothetical output):

| Term (years) | 2 | 5 | 10 | 30 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model N convexity effect (bp) | −0.6 | −4.0 | −14.7 | −106.0 |
| Model V convexity effect (bp) | −0.7 | −4.5 | −14.9 | −54.0 |

Which of the following statements about the table is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation throughout: the risk-neutral Vasicek model is $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$, where $k$ is the speed of mean reversion, $\theta$ the long-run value of the short rate and $\sigma$ the annual basis-point volatility. Model 1 is $dr$ = $\sigma dw$ (normal, no drift).

options.text: Because Model V’s convexity effects exceed Model N’s up to 10 years, mean reversion must increase the convexity effect on short- and medium-term par rates.
Mean reversion lowers the volatility of longer-term par rates and so their convexity effect, while up to 10 years Model V’s higher $\sigma$ dominates because mean reversion is slow.
The much smaller 30-year effect in Model V arises because mean reversion pulls the expected short rate toward $\theta$, so the drift offsets the convexity effect.
If Model V used $\sigma$ = 100 bp per year, its convexity effects would equal Model N’s at every term, because the convexity effect depends only on $\sigma$.

questions.solution:
**Mean reversion and the convexity effect**

Stem in one line: convexity effects of Model N ($\sigma$ = 100 bp, no drift) and Model V (Vasicek, $\sigma$ = 112 bp, $k$ = 0.03) at 2, 5, 10, 30 years; which explanation is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Convexity effect. GARP footnote 4 defines it as the par yield in the model with its assumed volatility minus the par yield in the same model with zero volatility. Bond prices are convex in rates, so volatility raises expected prices and lowers yields: the effect is negative and grows with term. Its size depends on how volatile rates of that maturity are.

Mean reversion. Because mean reversion lowers the volatility of longer-term par rates (Q2), GARP concludes that it “must also lower the impact of convexity” on those rates. GARP’s numbers (Table 14.1: Model 1, 113 bp; Table 14.2: Vasicek, 126 bp, $k$ = 0.025):

| Term (years) | 2 | 5 | 10 | 30 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model 1, 113 bp (bp) | −0.8 | −5.1 | −18.8 | −135.3 |
| Vasicek, 126 bp, $k$ = 0.025 (bp) | −1.0 | −5.8 | −19.1 | −74.7 |

Two forces act. The higher $\sigma$ raises convexity at every term. Slow mean reversion barely dampens volatility at short terms but dampens it strongly at 30 years. So the Vasicek effects are slightly larger up to 10 years and much smaller at 30 years.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem’s hypothetical table has the same pattern. The ratio of variances is $\text{(112/100)}^{2}$ = 1.254. Up to 10 years the Model V/Model N ratios are 1.17, 1.13 and 1.01: slightly larger, because the higher $\sigma$ outweighs slow mean reversion. At 30 years the ratio is 54.0/106.0 = 0.51: mean reversion has cut long-term volatility enough to roughly halve the effect despite the higher $\sigma$.

**Fragile fact.** Mean reversion lowers convexity (via lower long-term volatility). In GARP’s tables the Vasicek effect is larger up to 10 years only because its $\sigma$ is higher (126 versus 113 bp).

**Reference**

LO 14.h (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 14, §14.5 (Table 14.2 discussion), §14.1 (Table 14.1) and footnote 4. GARP-only: Schweser LO 14.h does not discuss convexity. The table in the stem is hypothetical and built to follow GARP’s pattern.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 h, where it is Q4 of 11.

a.reason: Error type: role misassignment. It credits mean reversion with an effect caused by the higher $\sigma$. Mean reversion can only lower volatility and hence convexity; the larger short-term figures come from $\sigma$ = 112 versus 100 bp. A would be correct if both models had the same $\sigma$ and Model V’s figures were still larger, which mean reversion cannot produce.

b.reason: It names both forces in the right places, exactly as GARP explains the difference between Tables 14.1 and 14.2.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap (drift confused with volatility). By definition the convexity effect compares the model with itself at zero volatility, so the drift toward $\theta$ is present in both terms and cancels. The 30-year reduction comes from lower long-term volatility. C would be correct as a description of why the level of the 30-year par rate differs between the models, not its convexity effect.

d.reason: Error type: scope error (mean reversion dropped). With equal $\sigma$, Model V would have smaller convexity effects at every term, sharply so at 30 years, because mean reversion lowers longer-term volatility. D would be correct only with $k$ = 0.

questions.question:
The chief risk officer of an Australian superannuation fund is reviewing a proposal to hedge an AUD government bond portfolio using a one-factor Vasicek model. The portfolio manager who wrote the proposal argues: “Like Model 1, the Vasicek model has a single factor, the short-term rate, so it must also be a parallel-shift model.” Which of the following responses is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation throughout: the risk-neutral Vasicek model is $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$, where $k$ is the speed of mean reversion, $\theta$ the long-run value of the short rate and $\sigma$ the annual basis-point volatility. Model 1 is $dr$ = $\sigma dw$ (normal, no drift).

options.text: The argument is wrong: with mean reversion a shock to the short rate is expected to dissipate toward $\theta$, so it moves longer-term rates by less than short-term rates.
The argument is right: in any one-factor model in which only the short rate is random, a shock to the short rate moves rates of all maturities by the same amount.
The argument is wrong: the Vasicek tree does not recombine, and its unequal middle nodes are what make longer-term rates move by less than short-term rates.
The argument is wrong: the model treats $\theta$ as a second random factor, which moves longer-term rates independently of the short-term rate.

questions.solution:
**One factor does not mean parallel shifts**

Stem in one line: a portfolio manager claims that the one-factor Vasicek model, like Model 1, must be a parallel-shift model.

**Concept and theory**

The factor structure of a model is how the whole spot curve moves when its factor moves. Model 1, Model 2, Ho-Lee and Vasicek are all one-factor models: the short rate is the only source of randomness. They differ in how a move in that factor spreads along the curve.

| Model | Response of the curve to a 10 bp rise in the short rate |
|---|---|
| Model 1, Model 2, Ho-Lee | every rate rises by 10 bp: parallel shift |
| Vasicek | short-term rates rise by about 10 bp; longer-term rates rise by less (GARP: 30-year spot only 7 bp) |

Why: under mean reversion the expected future short rate is pulled back toward $\theta$, so a shock today is expected to dissipate. Long-term rates reflect expected short rates over many years, most of which lie after the shock has partly decayed. GARP: “a model with mean reversion is not a parallel shift model.”

**Applying it to this question**

The manager’s error is the inference “one factor, therefore parallel”. The number of factors limits how many independent shapes of move the curve can make; it says nothing about what the single shape is.

**Fragile fact.** Vasicek is one-factor and non-parallel. Shock to the short rate: short end moves about 1 for 1, long end less.

**Reference**

LO 14.h (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 14, §14.5 (Figure 14.8), §14.1 to §14.3 (parallel shifts in Model 1, Model 2 and Ho-Lee). Schweser Reading 14, LO 14.h. No conflict; the 7 bp figure is GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 h, where it is Q5 of 11.

a.reason: GARP §14.5 (Figure 14.8): short-term rates rise by about 10 bp, longer-term rates less, because mean reversion implies the shock dissipates. Schweser LO 14.h: the Vasicek model “does not imply parallel shifts”.

b.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap (“any one-factor model”). The claim holds for Model 1, Model 2 and Ho-Lee but fails once the drift depends on the level of the rate. B would be correct if restricted to one-factor models with no mean reversion.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap with LO 14.f. Non-recombination is a feature of the most obvious tree approximation (the drift from a low node is larger than from a high node), and GARP shows how to make the tree recombine. The factor shape belongs to the model, not its tree. C would be correct as an explanation of why the up-down and down-up nodes differ.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap (multi-factor property given to Vasicek). In Vasicek $\theta$ is a constant parameter, not a random factor. D would be correct for a two-factor model with a stochastic long-run rate.

questions.question:
A risk consultant advising a Brazilian bank compares three one-factor normal short-rate models of the BRL curve, each with $\sigma$ = 120 bp per year. She raises the short-rate factor by 10 bp in each model and records the change in spot rates:

| Change in spot rate (bp) | 1-year | 5-year | 10-year | 30-year |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Model P | 10.0 | 10.0 | 10.0 | 10.0 |
| Model Q | 9.9 | 9.5 | 8.9 | 7.2 |
| Model R | 9.6 | 7.9 | 6.2 | 3.0 |

Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation throughout: the risk-neutral Vasicek model is $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$, where $k$ is the speed of mean reversion, $\theta$ the long-run value of the short rate and $\sigma$ the annual basis-point volatility. Model 1 is $dr$ = $\sigma dw$ (normal, no drift).

options.text: Model P has the highest mean reversion parameter of the three, because the shock is transmitted in full to every maturity.
Model R treats short-rate news as longer-lived than Model Q does, because its longer-term spot rates respond by less.
Model R has a higher mean reversion parameter and a shorter half-life than Model Q, so it treats short-rate news as shorter-lived.
Model P must be a Vasicek model with a low mean reversion parameter, because a low parameter makes all rates respond equally.

questions.solution:
**Reading the factor shape: which model reverts fastest?**

Stem in one line: spot-rate responses to a 10 bp factor shock for Models P (flat 10.0), Q (9.9 to 7.2) and R (9.6 to 3.0); which conclusion is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

In a one-factor normal model the response of the spot curve to a shock in the short rate shows how long the shock is expected to persist:

- No mean reversion ($k$ = 0): the shock is permanent in expectation; every rate moves by the full amount (parallel shift).
- Low $k$, long half-life ($\tau$ = ln 2$/k$): the shock decays slowly; long rates still move by most of the shock. In GARP, $k$ = 0.025 ($\tau$ = 27.73 years) and the 30-year spot rises 7 of 10 bp.
- High $k$, short half-life: the shock decays fast; long rates move by little.

GARP links this to the lifespan of news: a very low $k$ (very long half-life) means news is long-lived; a very high $k$ (very short half-life) means news is short-lived.

**Applying it to this question**

Model P: 10.0 at all terms ⇒ parallel shift $\Rightarrow k$ = 0 (no mean reversion)

Model Q: 30-year response = 7.2 bp = 72% of the shock ⇒ low $k$

Model R: 30-year response = 3.0 bp = 30% of the shock ⇒ higher $k$

R’s responses fall away faster with maturity, so R has the larger $k$, the shorter half-life and the shorter-lived news. The common $\sigma$ = 120 bp is irrelevant: volatility does not determine the shape of the factor.

**Fragile fact.** Steeper decline of the factor with maturity ⇒ higher $k \Rightarrow$ shorter half-life ⇒ shorter-lived news. Exactly flat factor $\Rightarrow k$ = 0.

**Reference**

LO 14.h (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 14, §14.5 (Figure 14.8 and the news paragraph; half-life equation 14.25). Schweser Reading 14, LO 14.h. No conflict. The table in the stem is hypothetical.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 h, where it is Q6 of 11.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip. Full transmission to every maturity means the shock never decays: $k$ = 0, the lowest possible mean reversion. A would be correct if the question asked which model has the lowest mean reversion parameter.

b.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the news interpretation. Smaller long-term responses mean the shock dies out sooner, i.e. shorter-lived news. B would be correct with “longer-lived” replaced by “shorter-lived”.

c.reason: Faster decay of the response with maturity means faster mean reversion; GARP equates a high $k$ (short half-life) with short-lived news.

d.reason: Error type: scope error (“low $k$” stretched to “$k$ = 0”). Any positive $k$, however small, makes long rates move by less than the short rate (GARP’s $k$ = 0.025 still gives 7 bp at 30 years). An exactly parallel response requires no mean reversion: Model 1, Model 2 or Ho-Lee. D would be correct with “must be a model without mean reversion”.

questions.question:
The treasurer of an Indian private-sector bank is briefing the ALCO on how a mean-reverting short-rate model of the INR curve treats two pieces of economic news: (1) a monsoon disruption expected to depress farm output for one quarter only; (2) a nationwide digital payments reform expected to raise productivity for many years. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation throughout: the risk-neutral Vasicek model is $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$, where $k$ is the speed of mean reversion, $\theta$ the long-run value of the short rate and $\sigma$ the annual basis-point volatility. Model 1 is $dr$ = $\sigma dw$ (normal, no drift).

options.text: The monsoon news is long-lived, because it changes the market’s view of the economy in the near future, when its effect on rates is largest.
The reform news is best represented by a very short half-life, because a short half-life means that a shock affects the short rate for many years.
A single Vasicek model can represent the monsoon news with a high $k$ and the reform news with a low $k$ at the same time, since $k$ adapts to each shock.
The reform news is long-lived and is best represented by a very low mean reversion parameter, so that it affects the short rate for many years to come.

questions.solution:
**Long-lived and short-lived economic news**

Stem in one line: monsoon disruption for one quarter versus a productivity-raising reform for many years; how does a mean-reverting model treat them?

**Concept and theory**

GARP reinterprets mean reversion as a statement about economic news. Short rates move because of news or shocks; mean reversion says the effect of any shock eventually dissipates, since the short rate is assumed to reach the same long-term goal $\theta$ whatever happens. In this interpretation, mean reversion measures the length of economic news in the model.

|  | Long-lived news | Short-lived news |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | changes the market’s view of the economy many years in the future | changes the view in the near but not the far future |
| GARP example | technological innovation that raises productivity | retail sales below expectations due to cold holiday weather |
| Mean reversion parameter | very low $k$ | very high $k$ |
| Half-life (ln 2$/k$) | very long | very short |
| Effect on short rate | for many years to come | for a relatively short period |

**Applying it to this question**

The reform raises productivity for many years: it changes the view of the economy far in the future, so it is long-lived, matching GARP’s technology example. A model representing it needs a very low $k$, i.e. a very long half-life. The monsoon disruption lasts one quarter: short-lived, high $k$.

**Fragile fact.** Long-lived news ↔ low $k \leftrightarrow$ long half-life. The adjective on news and on half-life match; the one on $k$ is the opposite.

**Reference**

LO 14.h (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 14, §14.5 (paragraph on long-lived and short-lived news). Schweser Reading 14, LO 14.h. Difference: Schweser says news is “assimilated into security prices” faster with a larger $k$; GARP frames it as how long news affects the short rate. Same direction; GARP used. Multi-factor remark GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 h, where it is Q7 of 11.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip of the definitions. News that changes the view only in the near future is short-lived by definition. A would be correct with “long-lived” replaced by “short-lived”.

b.reason: Error type: polarity flip on half-life. A short half-life means the shock halves quickly, so its effect is short-lived. B would be correct for the monsoon news, with “affects the short rate for a relatively short period”.

c.reason: Error type: scope error. A one-factor Vasicek model has a single constant $k$, so it gives all news the same lifespan. GARP notes that in reality some news is short-lived and some long-lived, “a feature captured by the multi-factor Gauss+ model”. C would be correct for a multi-factor model with fast- and slow-reverting factors.

d.reason: GARP §14.5: a very low mean reversion parameter (very long half-life) implies that news is long-lived and will affect the short rate for many years to come.

questions.question:
A risk analyst at a Swiss private bank is choosing between two Vasicek calibrations of the CHF short rate. The rates desk wants a model in which news affecting the short rate is long-lived. Use the Vasicek expectation of the short rate $T$ years ahead, with continuous exponential decay.

| Parameter | Calibration X | Calibration Y |
|---|---|---|
| Speed of mean reversion, $k$ | 0.035 | 0.28 |
| Volatility, $\sigma$ (bp per year) | 95 | 95 |
| Long-run value, $\theta$ | 2.40% | 2.40% |
| Current short rate, $r_{0}$ | 0.90% | 0.90% |

Which calibration meets the desk’s requirement, and by about how much does an immediate 20 bp increase in today’s short rate raise the expected short rate five years ahead under that calibration?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation throughout: the risk-neutral Vasicek model is $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$, where $k$ is the speed of mean reversion, $\theta$ the long-run value of the short rate and $\sigma$ the annual basis-point volatility. Model 1 is $dr$ = $\sigma dw$ (normal, no drift).

options.text: Calibration X (half-life 19.8 years); about 14.1 bp
Calibration X (half-life 19.8 years); about 16.8 bp
Calibration Y (half-life 2.5 years); about 4.9 bp
Calibration X (half-life 19.8 years); about 3.2 bp

questions.solution:
**Half-life and the persistence of a short-rate shock**

Stem in one line: $k$ = 0.035 (X) or 0.28 (Y); desk wants long-lived news; effect of a 20 bp rise in $r_{0}$ on the expected rate in 5 years.

**Concept and theory**

GARP shows that the distance between the current value of the factor and its goal $\theta$ decays exponentially at the rate $k$. The expectation of the short rate after $T$ years is

$E$\[$r_{T}$ \] = $r_{0} e^{-kT}$ + $\theta($1 $- e^{-kT} )$

a weighted average of today’s rate $r_{0}$ and the long-run value $\theta$, with weight $e^{-kT}$ on $r_{0}$. The half-life, the time for the factor to cover half the distance to $\theta$, solves $e^{-k\tau}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ :

$\tau$ = $\frac{\text{ln 2}}{k}$

A shock ∆$r_{0}$ to today’s rate changes the expectation by ∆$E$\[$r_{T}$ \] = $e^{-kT}$ ∆$r_{0}$, because $\theta$ is unchanged. A low $k$ keeps $e^{-kT}$ close to 1: the shock persists, which is what long-lived news means.

**Applying it to this question**

$\tau_{X}$ = $\frac{\text{ln 2}}{0.035}$ = $\frac{0.69315}{0.035}$ = 19.80 years

$\tau_{Y}$ = $\frac{\text{ln 2}}{0.28}$ = 2.48 years

Long-lived news ⇒ low $k,$ long half-life ⇒ Calibration X

$e^{-k}X^{T}$ = $e^{-0.035\times5}$ = $e^{-0.175}$ = 0.83946

∆$E$\[$r_{5}$\] = 0.83946 × 20 bp = 16.79 bp

Meaning: under X, about 84% of today’s 20 bp shock is still expected to be present in the short rate five years ahead, so the news is long-lived. The values of $\sigma$, $\theta$ and $r_{0}$ are not needed: $\sigma$ does not affect expectations, and $\theta$ and $r_{0}$ affect the level of $E$\[$r_{5}$\] but not its sensitivity to the shock.

**Fragile fact.** Weight $e^{-kT}$ goes on $r_{0}$ (and on any shock to it); 1 $- e^{-kT}$ goes on $\theta$. Long-lived news needs low $k$.

**Reference**

LO 14.h (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 14, §14.5 (news paragraph; exponential decay, equation 14.22; half-life, equations 14.24 and 14.25). questions.question:
A member of the risk committee of a German Landesbank asks the head of market risk why the Vasicek model of the EUR curve, unlike Model 1, produces both a downward-sloping term structure of volatility and a downward-sloping factor structure. Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation throughout: the risk-neutral Vasicek model is $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$, where $k$ is the speed of mean reversion, $\theta$ the long-run value of the short rate and $\sigma$ the annual basis-point volatility. Model 1 is $dr$ = $\sigma dw$ (normal, no drift).

options.text: Long-term rates are determined mostly by current economic conditions, as measured by the short rate, so they respond by less than short-term rates to shocks.
The drift is fitted date by date to market prices, as in the Ho-Lee model, so longer-term rates absorb a smaller share of each shock to the short rate.
Rates of every term combine current conditions, measured by the short rate, and long-term conditions, measured by $\theta$; longer terms depend mostly on the latter.
Rates of every term are determined exclusively by current economic conditions, so shocks to the short rate fade at longer terms only through convexity.

questions.solution:
**Why mean reversion makes both structures slope downward**

Stem in one line: why does Vasicek, unlike Model 1, give a downward-sloping volatility structure and a downward-sloping factor?

**Concept and theory**

GARP closes the chapter with one explanation that covers both features. Rates of every term are combinations of:

- current economic conditions, measured by the short rate $r$; and
- long-term economic conditions, measured by the long-run value of the short rate, $\theta$.

|  | No mean reversion (Model 1) | Mean reversion (Vasicek) |
|---|---|---|
| What determines rates | exclusively current conditions | short terms: mostly current; long terms: mostly long-term |
| Effect of a short-rate shock | all rates equally | short-term rates more than long-term rates |
| Result | parallel shifts; flat volatility | downward-sloping factor; downward-sloping volatility |

A shock to the short rate changes current conditions but not $\theta$, so it moves the rates that depend on current conditions (the short end) the most.

**Applying it to this question**

The committee member asks for the reason behind both shapes. The deciding fact is the split of attribution: short terms are driven mostly by $r$, long terms mostly by $\theta$. Only C states it.

**Fragile fact.** Short-term rates ↔ current conditions ($r$); long-term rates ↔ long-term conditions ($\theta$). No mean reversion ⇒ everything from current conditions.

**Reference**

LO 14.h (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 14, §14.5 (closing paragraph). GARP-only: Schweser LO 14.h states the result without this explanation.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 h, where it is Q9 of 11.

a.reason: Error type: role misassignment. It assigns current conditions to long-term rates; GARP assigns current conditions mostly to short-term rates and long-term conditions to long-term rates. A would be correct with “long-term rates” replaced by “short-term rates” and the conclusion reversed.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap with Ho-Lee (LO 14.d). A time-dependent drift fitted to market prices leaves the volatility structure and the parallel-shift nature of Model 1 unchanged. B would be correct as a description of how Ho-Lee matches the curve, not of why Vasicek shocks fade.

c.reason: It paraphrases GARP’s closing paragraph of §14.5 directly.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap with Model 1. “Exclusively current conditions” is GARP’s description of the model without mean reversion, where shocks affect all rates equally. Convexity explains the downward slope of Model 1’s rate curve, not the factor shape. D would be correct only as half a statement about Model 1.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a Chinese bank is reviewing the CNY model inventory. Each of the following models starts from Model 1 ($dr$ = $\sigma dw$) and changes only the drift:

I. A constant drift, $dr$ = $\lambda dt$ + $\sigma dw$ (Model 2).

II. A time-dependent drift fitted to market prices, $dr$ = $\lambda_{t} dt$ + $\sigma dw$ (Ho-Lee).

III. A mean-reverting drift, $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$ (Vasicek).

Relative to Model 1, which of these changes qualitatively alter both the term structure of volatility and the parallel-shift nature of the model?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation throughout: the risk-neutral Vasicek model is $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$, where $k$ is the speed of mean reversion, $\theta$ the long-run value of the short rate and $\sigma$ the annual basis-point volatility. Model 1 is $dr$ = $\sigma dw$ (normal, no drift).

options.text: III only
II and III only
I, II and III
None of I, II or III

questions.solution:
**Which drift specifications change Model 1’s behaviour?**

Stem in one line: constant drift, time-dependent drift, mean-reverting drift; which alter both the volatility structure and the parallel-shift nature of Model 1?

**Concept and theory**

The chapter builds models by changing one block at a time, the drift, and records what each change does:

| Model | Drift | Volatility structure | Factor structure |
|---|---|---|---|
| Model 1 | 0 | flat | parallel |
| Model 2 | $\lambda$ (constant) | flat (“does not qualitatively change”) | parallel |
| Ho-Lee | $\lambda_{t}$ (depends on $t$) | flat (“does not change these features”) | parallel |
| Vasicek | $k$($\theta- r$) (depends on $r$) | declining everywhere | declining (not parallel) |

The key is whether the drift depends on the level of the rate. A constant or time-dependent drift adds the same amount to every path, so it shifts expectations but leaves the dispersion of rates, and their response to a shock, unchanged. A mean-reverting drift is larger when the rate is further from $\theta$, so it partly undoes shocks over time.

**Applying it to this question**

I (Model 2): GARP says moving from Model 1 to Model 2 does not qualitatively change the volatility structure, the convexity effects or the parallel-shift nature. Not included. II (Ho-Lee): adding a time-dependent drift does not change these features either. Not included. III (Vasicek): declining volatility, non-parallel shifts. Included. Answer: III only.

**Fragile fact.** Constant drift: no change. Time-dependent drift: no change (better fit only). Mean reversion: both structures slope down.

**Reference**

LO 14.h (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 14, §14.2 (closing paragraph), §14.3 (paragraph after the Ho-Lee calibration), §14.4 (first warning on fitting), §14.5. Schweser Reading 14, LO 14.h and Module Quiz 14.2 Q3 answer. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 h, where it is Q10 of 11.

a.reason: GARP §14.2 and §14.3 (closing sentences) exclude I and II; §14.5 includes III.

b.reason: **II and III.** Error type: sibling swap (fitting confused with improving the model). Ho-Lee matches all input rates, but GARP warns that adding a time-dependent drift to a parallel-shift model to match market prices does not make it more suitable if the parallel-shift assumption is inadequate (LO 14.e). B would be correct if the question asked which models improve the fit to the rate curve relative to Model 2.

c.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: absolute-claim trap (“any drift changes the dynamics”). Two of the three drifts leave the volatility and factor structures flat. C would be correct if the question asked which changes alter the expected path of the short rate.

d.reason: **None.** Error type: scope error. “A drift does not affect volatility” is true for drifts independent of the rate level but false for a mean-reverting drift, which damps shocks over time. D would be correct if III were removed.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is drafting a memo for the board risk committee of a US regional bank on the limitations of a one-factor Vasicek model of the USD curve. The draft contains four statements:

I. A single mean reversion parameter gives all economic news the same lifespan, whereas in reality some news is short-lived and some long-lived, a feature that a multi-factor model can capture.

II. Mean reversion is a strong assumption: long rate histories from stable markets may display it partly because no catastrophe, such as hyperinflation, occurred during the sample.

III. The model’s term structure of volatility slopes downward at every term, so it cannot reproduce a market volatility structure that first rises and then declines with term.

IV. Because the short rate is always pulled back toward $\theta$, the Vasicek model rules out negative short-term rates, unlike Model 1.

Which of the statements should the consultant present as correct?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation throughout: the risk-neutral Vasicek model is $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$, where $k$ is the speed of mean reversion, $\theta$ the long-run value of the short rate and $\sigma$ the annual basis-point volatility. Model 1 is $dr$ = $\sigma dw$ (normal, no drift).

options.text: I and II only
I and III only
I, II, III and IV
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
**Limitations of the one-factor Vasicek model**

Stem in one line: which of four draft memo statements on the limitations of a one-factor Vasicek model are correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP credits mean reversion with capturing several features of term structure behaviour in an economically intuitive way: a declining volatility structure, lower long-term convexity and a nonparallel factor. It also records the limits:

1. One speed for all news. A single $k$ fixes one lifespan for every shock. In reality some news is short-lived and some long-lived, a feature captured by the multi-factor Gauss+ model.
2. A strong assumption. Footnote 5: long series from relatively stable markets may show mean reversion because no catastrophe occurred over the sample; hyperinflation is inconsistent with mean reversion and destroys the currency. Critics say rates “mean revert until they don’t”.
3. Volatility shape. The structure slopes downward everywhere, so the humped market structure is out of reach, and the model overstates short-term volatility when fitted at the long end (Q3).
4. Curve fit. As calibrated, probably not flexible enough for the range of observed term structures (Q1).

Mean reversion does not remove the normal-model problem of negative rates: the Vasicek terminal distribution is normal (GARP: the short rate in 10 years “is normally distributed”), so negative rates keep a positive probability.

**Applying it to this question**

I: GARP’s multi-factor remark. True. II: footnote 5. True. III: downward everywhere, no hump. True. IV: the short rate is normally distributed in the Vasicek model, so it can become negative; mean reversion damps long-horizon dispersion but does not bound the distribution at zero. False. Answer: I, II and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Vasicek is still a normal (Gaussian) model: mean reversion damps dispersion but does not prevent negative rates. One $k$ means one lifespan for all news.

**Reference**

LO 14.h (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 14, §14.5 (opening paragraph, footnote 5, Figure 14.7 discussion, news paragraph, terminal distribution) and §14.1 (negative rates in normal models). GARP-only: Schweser LO 14.h omits the multi-factor remark, footnote 5 and the hump. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-14 h, where it is Q11 of 11.

a.reason: **I and II only.** Error type: scope error on III (“improves on flat” read as “fits the market shape”). Rejecting III means believing the Vasicek structure can rise and then fall. A would be correct if III claimed that the model cannot produce any non-flat volatility structure.

b.reason: **I and III only.** Error type: absolute-claim trap in reverse: treating mean reversion as an established fact and so rejecting II. GARP calls mean reversion reasonable but strong. B would be correct if II claimed that mean reversion is never observed in historical data.

c.reason: **I, II, III and IV.** Error type: absolute-claim trap (“rules out”), borrowing from LO 14.c the property of non-negative distributions such as the lognormal. It accepts IV. C would be correct only for a model whose rate distribution rules out negative values, which a normal model does not.

d.reason: I, II and III each restate a limitation given in GARP §14.5 or its footnote 5; IV contradicts the normality of the Vasicek terminal distribution.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at an Indian bank is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts on the short-rate process

$dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma$($t$) $dw.$

The draft slide contains four statements:

I. Because $dw$ has a mean of zero, the expected change in the short rate over a short interval $dt$ is $\lambda$($t$) $dt$.

II. Because $\sigma$($t$) is a deterministic function of time, the volatility the model assigns to the short rate at each future date is fixed when the model is set up.

III. Because $\sigma$($t$) changes with time, the basis-point volatility of the short rate at a given date rises with the level of the short rate on that date.

IV. The term $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ carries the random part of the change in the short rate, while the term $\sigma$($t$) $dw$ sets its expected value.

Which of the statements are accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the continuously compounded short-term rate, $t$ is measured in years, and $dw$ is the random shock of the process.

options.text: I only
I and III only
I and II only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
**Anatomy of $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma$($t$) $dw$**

Stem in one line: which of four slide statements about the drift and volatility terms are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

The models of the previous reading let the drift change over time (Ho-Lee) but held the volatility of the short rate constant. GARP §15.1 opens by extending the same idea to volatility: just as a time-dependent drift can be used to fit many bond or swap rates, a time-dependent volatility function can be used to fit many option prices. The resulting process is

$dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma$($t$) $dw$ (GARP Eq. 15.1)

where $dr$ is the change in the short rate over the interval $dt$; $\lambda$($t$) is the drift, a deterministic function of calendar time $t$; $\sigma$($t$) is the volatility of the short rate, also a deterministic function of $t$; and $dw$ is the random shock, normal with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$.

| Term | Random? | Depends on | Role |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ | No | Time only | Sets the expected change, since $E$\[$dw$\] = 0 |
| $\sigma$($t$) $dw$ | Yes, through $dw$ | Time only (via $\sigma$($t$)) | Sets the dispersion of the change |

GARP calls $\lambda$($t$) and $\sigma$($t$) “deterministic functions”: they are chosen when the model is calibrated and do not react to the rates the model later produces. GARP §15.2 adds that the models presented up to that point, (15.1) included, have basis-point volatility independent of the level of the short rate.

**Applying it to this question**

Statement I: taking expectations, $E$\[$dr$\] = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma$($t$) $E$\[$dw$\] = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$. True. Statement II: a deterministic $\sigma$($t$) is a fixed schedule of volatilities by date. True. Statement III: time dependence is not rate dependence; $\sigma$($t$) contains no $r$. False. Statement IV: the roles are reversed; the drift term is non-random and the shock term has mean zero. False. So I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** “Time-dependent” means a function of the calendar date, fixed in advance; it never means “depends on the level of $r$”.

**Reference**

LO 15.a (Schweser, verbatim): “Describe the short-term rate process under a model with time-dependent volatility.” GARP Ch. 15, §15.1 Time-Dependent Volatility: Model 3 (Eq. 15.1 and “Deterministic volatility functions”); §15.2 opening paragraph. Schweser Reading 15, Module 15.1, LO 15.a. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 a, where it is Q1 of 9.

a.reason: **I only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement (scope error on “deterministic”). A candidate who thinks a time-varying volatility must be uncertain rejects II. A would be correct if the model’s volatility were itself random, which (15.1) does not allow.

b.reason: **I and III only.** Error type: sibling swap. III attributes to (15.1) the property of the CIR model ($\sigma\sqrt{r}$) and the lognormal model ($\sigma r$) of LO 15.d, in which basis-point volatility rises with the rate. B would be correct for a process such as $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma\sqrt{r} dw$, with II reworded accordingly.

c.reason: GARP §15.1 describes $\lambda$($t$) and $\sigma$($t$) as deterministic functions of time, and Schweser LO 15.a states that $dw$ has mean zero; hence I and II hold and III and IV do not.

d.reason: **I, II and IV only.** Error type: role misassignment. IV gives the randomness to the drift and the expected value to the shock. It would be correct only with the labels exchanged: “$\sigma$($t$) $dw$ carries the random part and $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ sets the expected value.”

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at an Australian bank is reading the calibration output of an AUD short-rate model of the form $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma$($t$) $dw$. The current short rate is 4.10%. The calibrated volatility function is:

| Date $t$ (years) | 0.5 | 1 | 2 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\sigma$($t$) | 1.45% | 1.38% | 1.22% | 1.30% |

Which of the following statements about this output is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the continuously compounded short-term rate, $t$ is measured in years, and $dw$ is the random shock of the process.

options.text: The volatility of the short rate in two years is 122 basis points per year, below the 138 basis points per year that applies to the short rate in one year.
The standard deviation of the short rate two years from now is 1.22%, because $\sigma$(2) summarizes the volatility of the rate over the whole two-year horizon.
The volatility of the short rate in two years is 122 basis points per month, below the 138 basis points per month that applies to the short rate in one year.
The short rate is expected to move by 122 basis points over the year that starts in two years, because $\sigma$(2) sets the size of the expected rate change.

questions.solution:
**Reading a calibrated $\sigma$($t$) schedule**

Stem in one line: AUD model with $\sigma$(0.5) = 1.45%, $\sigma$(1) = 1.38%, $\sigma$(2) = 1.22%, $\sigma$(5) = 1.30%; which reading is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

$\sigma$($t$) is the annualized volatility of the short rate at date $t$. GARP’s own example: if $\sigma$(1) = 1.26% and $\sigma$(2) = 1.20%, then the volatility of the short rate in one year is 126 basis points per year, and the volatility of the short rate in two years is 120 basis points per year. Two points matter:

- Units. $\sigma$($t$) is quoted per year, in rate units (basis points). It is the annualized standard deviation of $dr$ at that date, not a per-month or per-step figure.
- Instantaneous, not cumulative. $\sigma$(2) describes how volatile the rate is at year 2. The standard deviation of the short rate’s terminal distribution at a horizon builds up from the shocks at every date before it, so it is a different object: GARP Figure 15.1 shows it rising with horizon in Model 3 even though that model’s $\sigma$($t$) falls over time.

**Applying it to this question**

Convert each entry: 1.38% = 138 bp per year at $t$ = 1; 1.22% = 122 bp per year at $t$ = 2. Since 122 \< 138, volatility is lower at year 2 than at year 1. The current short rate of 4.10% is irrelevant: in this model volatility does not depend on the rate level. The rise to 1.30% at $t$ = 5 is also legitimate, because (15.1) imposes no shape (Q7).

**Fragile fact.** $\sigma$($t$): per year, at date $t$, in basis points. Not per month, not cumulative, not a forecast of the rate’s direction.

**Reference**

LO 15.a (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 15, §15.1 Time-Dependent Volatility: Model 3 (the $\sigma$(1), $\sigma$(2) example and Figure 15.1). Schweser Reading 15, LO 15.b opening (220 bp and 260 bp illustration). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 a, where it is Q2 of 9.

a.reason: It reads $\sigma$($t$) exactly as GARP §15.1 does: the value at date $t$ is the volatility of the short rate at that date, in basis points per year.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (instantaneous volatility read as the terminal standard deviation, an LO 15.b object). The two-year terminal standard deviation accumulates the shocks from $t$ = 0 to $t$ = 2, when $\sigma$ was between 1.45% and 1.22%, so it is not 1.22%. B would be correct if the stem asked for the volatility of the short rate at year 2 rather than the standard deviation of the rate two years from now.

c.reason: Error type: time-conversion slip (per year read as per month). The figures are annualized. The standard deviation of a one-month change at $t$ = 2 would be 1.22%$\times\sqrt{1/12}$ = 0.352%, about 35 bp, not 122 bp. C would be correct only if $\sigma$($t$) were stated per month, which the model’s convention excludes.

d.reason: Error type: role misassignment (volatility given the drift’s job). The expected change comes from $\lambda$($t$) $dt$; $\sigma$($t$) sizes the dispersion around it. D would be correct if 1.22% were the value of $\lambda$($t$) over that year.

questions.question:
A model validator at a Swiss private bank is reviewing the documentation of a CHF short-rate model, $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma$($t$) $dw$, which is simulated in monthly steps ($dt$ = 1/12 year). Which of the following statements in the documentation correctly describes the shock $dw$ and its effect on one monthly step?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the continuously compounded short-term rate, $t$ is measured in years, and $dw$ is the random shock of the process.

options.text: $dw$ is normal with mean zero and standard deviation $dt$, so the standard deviation of $dr$ over one step is $\sigma$($t$) $dt$ = $\sigma$($t$)/12.
$dw$ is normal with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$, so the standard deviation of $dr$ over one step is $\sigma$($t$)$\sqrt{r dt}$.
$dw$ is normal with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$, so the standard deviation of $dr$ over one step is $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma$($t$)$\sqrt{dt}$.
$dw$ is normal with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$, so the standard deviation of $dr$ over one step is $\sigma$($t$)$\sqrt{dt}$ = $\sigma$($t$)$/\sqrt{12}$.

questions.solution:
**The shock $dw$ in a monthly simulation**

Stem in one line: CHF model simulated with $dt$ = 1/12; which statement correctly describes $dw$ and the standard deviation of one step?

**Concept and theory**

Schweser LO 15.a: as in the earlier models, $dw$ is normally distributed with mean 0 and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$. GARP §15.2 uses the same fact when it explains basis-point volatility: since the drift term is not a random variable and the standard deviation of $dw$ equals $\sqrt{dt}$ by definition, the annualized standard deviation of $dr$ is the coefficient on $dw$. Applied to (15.1):

Var($dr$) = $\sigma$($t$)$^{2}$ Var($dw$) = $\sigma$($t$)$^{2} dt$

SD($dr$) = $\sigma$($t$)$\sqrt{dt}$

annualized SD of $dr$ = $\frac{\sigma\text{(}t\text{)}\sqrt{dt}}{\sqrt{dt}}$ = $\sigma$($t$)

where Var and SD are the variance and standard deviation over one step. The drift $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ shifts the mean of $dr$ but adds nothing to its dispersion. Variance scales with $dt$; standard deviation scales with $\sqrt{dt}$.

**Applying it to this question**

With $dt$ = 1/12, $\sqrt{dt}$ = 1$/\sqrt{12}$ = 0.28868. So the standard deviation of a monthly change is $\sigma$($t$) × 0.28868 = $\sigma$($t$)$/\sqrt{12}$, and the annualized volatility remains $\sigma$($t$). No value of $\sigma$($t$) is needed to identify the right description.

**Fragile fact.** $dw$: mean 0, standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$, variance $dt$. Drift moves the mean; only $\sigma$($t$) sets the spread.

**Reference**

LO 15.a (Schweser, verbatim above). Schweser Reading 15, LO 15.a ($dw$ normal with mean 0; the $\sqrt{dt}$ symbol is dropped in the extract). GARP Ch. 15, §15.2 (standard deviation of $dw$ equals $\sqrt{dt}$, OCR “Vdt”). Gap: symbol missing in Schweser, garbled in GARP; confirmed from question bank Q708 (Reading 15). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 a, where it is Q3 of 9.

a.reason: Error type: time-conversion slip (standard deviation of $dw$ taken as $dt$ instead of $\sqrt{dt}$). This scales volatility with time rather than with the square root of time and gives $\sigma$($t$)/12, which understates the monthly standard deviation by a factor of $\sqrt{12} \approx$ 3.46. A would be correct for the variance of $dw$, which does equal $dt$.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (CIR form). $\sigma\sqrt{r}\sqrt{dt}$ is the step standard deviation of the CIR model, $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma\sqrt{r} dw$ (LO 15.d). The coefficient on $dw$ in (15.1) contains no $r$. B would be correct if the diffusion term were $\sigma\sqrt{r} dw$.

c.reason: Error type: role misassignment (the deterministic drift treated as a source of dispersion). $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ is not random, so it moves the mean of $dr$, not its standard deviation. C would be correct as a description of a one-standard-deviation up-move, $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma$($t$)$\sqrt{dt}$, not of the standard deviation itself.

d.reason: It states the distribution of $dw$ exactly as Schweser LO 15.a does and draws the consequence GARP §15.2 draws: the only random term is $\sigma$($t$) $dw$, whose standard deviation is $\sigma$($t$)$\sqrt{dt}$.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is explaining to the ALM team of a Canadian pension fund how the CAD short-rate model $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma$($t$) $dw$ relates to simpler models of the short rate. The consultant’s notes contain three statements:

I. Setting $\sigma$($t$) equal to a constant $\sigma$ at all dates, while leaving $\lambda$($t$) free, gives the Ho-Lee model.

II. Setting $\lambda$($t$) = 0 and $\sigma$($t$) equal to a constant $\sigma$ at all dates gives Model 1.

III. Setting $\lambda$($t$) = 0 at all dates, while leaving $\sigma$($t$) time-dependent, gives the Ho-Lee model.

Which of the statements are correct?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the continuously compounded short-term rate, $t$ is measured in years, and $dw$ is the random shock of the process.

options.text: I only
I and II only
II and III only
I, II and III

questions.solution:
**Which restrictions recover Ho-Lee and Model 1**

Stem in one line: which restrictions on $\lambda$($t$) and $\sigma$($t$) give Ho-Lee and Model 1?

**Concept and theory**

Schweser LO 15.a describes (15.1) as an augmentation of two earlier models:

| Model | Process | What (15.1) adds |
|---|---|---|
| Model 1 | $dr$ = $\sigma dw$ | Time-dependent drift and time-dependent volatility |
| Ho-Lee | $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$ | Non-constant (time-dependent) volatility |
| Time-dependent volatility | $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma$($t$) $dw$ |  |

Read the other way, each earlier model is a restriction of (15.1). Ho-Lee keeps a free drift and freezes volatility: $\sigma$($t$) = $\sigma$. Model 1 freezes both: no drift, constant volatility. Schweser’s Key Concepts state that the special cases of (15.1) include Model 1 and the Ho-Lee model. GARP §15.1 makes the same contrast from the other side: unlike the models of the previous chapter, the volatility in (15.1) depends on time.

**Applying it to this question**

I: $\sigma$($t$) = $\sigma$, $\lambda$($t$) free gives $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$, the Ho-Lee model. True. II: $\lambda$($t$) = 0, $\sigma$($t$) = $\sigma$ gives $dr$ = $\sigma dw$, Model 1. True. III: $\lambda$($t$) = 0 with $\sigma$($t$) free gives $dr$ = $\sigma$($t$) $dw$, which has no drift and a time-varying volatility. Ho-Lee has the opposite pattern (time-varying drift, constant volatility). False. So I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Ho-Lee: drift varies with time, volatility constant. Model 1: no drift, volatility constant. Only (15.1) lets volatility vary with time.

**Reference**

LO 15.a (Schweser, verbatim above). Schweser Reading 15, LO 15.a and Key Concepts LO 15.a (Schweser-only for the Model 1 and Ho-Lee equations within this reading). GARP Ch. 15, §15.1 Time-Dependent Volatility: Model 3 (“Unlike the models presented in Chapter 14”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 a, where it is Q4 of 9.

a.reason: **I only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement (scope error). Model 1 is reached by switching off both the drift and the time variation in volatility; a candidate who thinks only one restriction can be imposed at a time drops II. A would be correct if Model 1 contained a drift term.

b.reason: Schweser LO 15.a and Key Concepts: Model 1 ($dr$ = $\sigma dw$) and Ho-Lee ($dr$ = $\lambda$($t$)$dt$ + $\sigma dw$) are special cases of $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$)$dt$ + $\sigma$($t$)$dw$.

c.reason: **II and III only.** Error type: sibling swap (Ho-Lee’s time-dependent component moved from the drift to the volatility), with I rejected as a result. C would be correct if Ho-Lee were defined as $dr$ = $\sigma$($t$) $dw$.

d.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: sibling swap in III, accepted alongside the true statements. I and III cannot both describe Ho-Lee, since they impose opposite restrictions. D would be correct only if III read “setting $\sigma$($t$) = $\sigma$ while leaving $\lambda$($t$) free”.

questions.question:
The CRO of a Singapore bank is reviewing a proposal to move the bank’s SGD term structure model from a time-dependent drift with constant volatility to $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma$($t$) $dw$. Which of the following best describes what each deterministic function in the proposed model is designed to do?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the continuously compounded short-term rate, $t$ is measured in years, and $dw$ is the random shock of the process.

options.text: $\lambda$($t$) is used to fit many option prices, and $\sigma$($t$) is used to fit many bond or swap rates; such functions are popular with market makers in interest rate options.
$\lambda$($t$) and $\sigma$($t$) are both used to fit many bond or swap rates, with option prices produced as outputs; such functions are popular with market makers in interest rate options.
$\lambda$($t$) is used to fit many bond or swap rates, and $\sigma$($t$) is used to fit many option prices; such functions are popular with market makers in interest rate options.
$\lambda$($t$) is used to fit many bond or swap rates, and $\sigma$($t$) is used to fit many option prices; such functions are popular with investors who value and hedge bond portfolios.

questions.solution:
**What $\lambda$($t$) and $\sigma$($t$) are each fitted to**

Stem in one line: SGD model moving to $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$)$dt$ + $\sigma$($t$)$dw$; what is each deterministic function designed to do?

**Concept and theory**

GARP §15.1 motivates (15.1) by a division of labour between the two free functions:

| Function | Controls | Fitted to |
|---|---|---|
| $\lambda$($t$) (time-dependent drift) | Expected path of the short rate | Many bond or swap rates |
| $\sigma$($t$) (time-dependent volatility) | Dispersion of the short rate at each date | Many option prices |

Bond and swap prices depend mainly on where rates are expected to go, so the drift is the natural tool for matching them (as in Ho-Lee). Option prices depend on how widely rates may be spread at each expiry, so a volatility that varies by date is the tool for matching options of many expiries. GARP adds that deterministic volatility functions are popular, particularly among market makers in interest rate options.

**Applying it to this question**

All four options are built on the same skeleton; the discrimination sits in two slots: which function is fitted to which prices, and who favours such models. Only C has drift to bond or swap rates, volatility to option prices, and market makers in interest rate options.

**Fragile fact.** Drift fits bond and swap rates; volatility fits option prices. Market makers in rate options are the users GARP names.

**Reference**

LO 15.a (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 15, §15.1 Time-Dependent Volatility: Model 3, opening sentence and “Deterministic volatility functions are popular” (GARP-only; Schweser’s LO 15.a section does not state this division of roles, and its LO 15.c section covers the related caps and floors argument). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 a, where it is Q5 of 9.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip (the two fitting roles exchanged). The drift cannot set the dispersion that option prices depend on. A would be correct with $\lambda$($t$) and $\sigma$($t$) swapped back.

b.reason: Error type: scope error (the option-fitting role of $\sigma$($t$) dropped). If both functions served only bond and swap rates there would be no reason to make volatility time-dependent. B would describe a calibration in which options are priced off a curve fit alone, which is not the purpose GARP gives for $\sigma$($t$).

c.reason: GARP §15.1: a time-dependent drift may be used to fit many bond or swap rates, and a time-dependent volatility function may be used to fit many option prices; deterministic volatility functions are popular among market makers in interest rate options.

d.reason: Error type: role misassignment (right feature, wrong user). GARP names market makers in interest rate options; for valuing and hedging fixed income securities it notes that a mean-reverting model might be preferred (an LO 15.c argument). D would be correct if it named market makers in interest rate options.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a UK building society is testing a GBP simulation engine built on $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma$($t$) $dw$, with $\sigma$(2) = 1.10%. Two simulated paths are inspected at $t$ = 2 years:

| Path | Route taken from $t$ = 0 to $t$ = 2 | Short rate at $t$ = 2 |
|---|---|---|
| X | Falling steadily | 1.50% |
| Y | Rising steadily | 6.00% |

Which of the following best describes the annualized volatility of the short rate that the engine should apply at $t$ = 2 on each path?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the continuously compounded short-term rate, $t$ is measured in years, and $dw$ is the random shock of the process.

options.text: 110 basis points per year on both paths, because $\sigma$(2) depends on the date alone and not on the rate level or the route taken.
110 basis points per year on path X and more on path Y, because the volatility of the short rate rises with the level of the rate.
110 basis points per year on both paths only if $\lambda$($t$) is zero from $t$ = 0 to $t$ = 2; with a non-zero drift the two paths differ.
110 basis points per year as a starting value, but different on the two paths because $\sigma$($t$) is re-estimated from each realized route.

questions.solution:
**Volatility on two simulated paths**

Stem in one line: GBP engine with $\sigma$(2) = 1.10%; paths at 1.50% and 6.00% at $t$ = 2; which volatility applies on each?

**Concept and theory**

In (15.1) the coefficient on $dw$ is $\sigma$($t$), a deterministic function of the calendar date. Three things it does not depend on:

| Possible driver | In (15.1)? | Model where it does matter |
|---|---|---|
| Calendar date $t$ | Yes | (15.1), Model 3 |
| Level of $r$ at that date | No | CIR ($\sigma\sqrt{r}$), lognormal ($\sigma r$) |
| Route taken to reach that date | No | Not a feature of any model in this reading |

GARP §15.2: the models presented so far assume that the basis-point volatility of the short rate is independent of the level of the short rate. Because $\sigma$($t$) is fixed in advance, every path that reaches date $t$ faces the same volatility.

**Applying it to this question**

Both paths are at $t$ = 2, so both use $\sigma$(2) = 1.10% = 110 bp per year. The rate levels (1.50% and 6.00%) and the routes (falling, rising) are irrelevant inputs. The drift $\lambda$($t$) affects where each path ends up, not the volatility applied there.

**Fragile fact.** Same date, same volatility, whatever the rate level or route. The dependence is on $t$, never on $r$.

**Reference**

LO 15.a (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 15, §15.1 Time-Dependent Volatility: Model 3 (Eq. 15.1, deterministic functions); §15.2 opening paragraph (basis-point volatility independent of the level in the models presented so far). Schweser Reading 15, LO 15.a. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 a, where it is Q6 of 9.

a.reason: $\sigma$($t$) is a deterministic function of time only (GARP §15.1, Eq. 15.1), and basis-point volatility in this model is independent of the rate level (GARP §15.2).

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (the lognormal or CIR rule imported). In those models basis-point volatility is $\sigma r$ or $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ and would be higher on path Y. B would be correct if the engine used $dr$ = . . . + $\sigma r dw$ (LO 15.d).

c.reason: Error type: scope error (an invented condition). Drift and volatility are separate functions; a non-zero $\lambda$($t$) changes where the paths go but not $\sigma$(2). The drift would matter only in a model whose volatility depends on the rate level (LO 15.d), because there the drift moves the rate and so the volatility; even then the “only if $\lambda$($t$) is zero” condition would not follow.

d.reason: Error type: scope error on “deterministic”. Nothing in (15.1) re-estimates $\sigma$($t$) from realized rates; the schedule is set at calibration. D would describe a volatility that responds to the simulated path, which (15.1) does not have.

questions.question:
A member of the risk committee of a Chinese bank is reviewing the documentation of a CNY short-rate model of the form $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma$($t$) $dw$. Which of the following statements about the shape the function $\sigma$($t$) may take is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the continuously compounded short-term rate, $t$ is measured in years, and $dw$ is the random shock of the process.

options.text: $\sigma$($t$) must decline exponentially to zero, because the market cannot forecast the volatility of the short rate in the distant future.
$\sigma$($t$) must rise with $t$, because the standard deviation of the terminal distribution of the short rate rises with the horizon.
$\sigma$($t$) may take any shape over time, but $\lambda$($t$) must then be held constant so that the drift does not offset the volatility.
$\sigma$($t$) may rise, fall or do both over different horizons; very many shapes are possible, and an exponential decline is only one special case.

questions.solution:
**What shapes $\sigma$($t$) may take**

Stem in one line: CNY model documentation; which statement about the admissible shape of $\sigma$($t$) is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

(15.1) leaves $\sigma$($t$) completely general. GARP §15.1: the shape of the Model 3 standard deviation curve depends on the volatility function chosen, but very many shapes are possible with the more general specification in (15.1). Schweser makes the same point: the relationships between volatility in each period could take an almost limitless number of combinations, for example $\sigma$(1) = 220 bp with $\sigma$(2) = 260 bp, or $\sigma$(1) = 220 bp with $\sigma$(2) = 160 bp. Model 3, $\sigma$($t$) = $\sigma e^{-\alpha t}$, is one special case that GARP chooses for teaching; it starts at $\sigma$ and declines exponentially to zero, and GARP notes it could equally have been built to decline to another constant.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding fact is that (15.1) imposes no monotonicity and no link to $\lambda$($t$). Only D says so.

**Fragile fact.** General $\sigma$($t$): any shape. Model 3: exponential decay to zero. Do not carry Model 3’s shape back into (15.1).

**Reference**

LO 15.a (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 15, §15.1 Time-Dependent Volatility: Model 3 (“very many shapes are possible”; Model 3 introduced as a special case; Figure 15.1). Schweser Reading 15, LO 15.b opening paragraph and Key Concepts LO 15.b. Boundary note: Schweser places the “limitless combinations” sentence under LO 15.b; GARP states it about the general specification (15.1), which is the LO 15.a process. No content conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 a, where it is Q7 of 9.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap (the Model 3 parameterization of LO 15.b treated as a requirement, justified by an LO 15.c criticism). The exponential decline is a teaching choice, and the objection that the market has no forecast of distant volatility leads GARP to a volatility that settles at a constant, not one that must reach zero. A would be correct for the question “how does volatility behave in Model 3?”

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (instantaneous volatility confused with the terminal standard deviation). In Model 3 the terminal standard deviation rises with horizon while $\sigma$($t$) falls (GARP Figure 15.1), so a rising terminal standard deviation does not require a rising $\sigma$($t$). B would be correct as a statement about the terminal standard deviation in Model 3, not about $\sigma$($t$).

c.reason: Error type: scope error (a restriction that the source does not impose). $\lambda$($t$) and $\sigma$($t$) are both free deterministic functions; GARP notes that their flexibility may be used to match market prices. C would be correct if the stem asked which restriction produces a model with a constant drift and a time-dependent volatility.

d.reason: GARP §15.1 (“very many shapes are possible”) and Schweser LO 15.b opening (“almost limitless number of combinations”), with Model 3 introduced as a special case of (15.1).

questions.question:
A banking supervisor at a euro area national authority is reviewing a bank’s EUR short-rate model, $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma$($t$) $dw$, at a time when the short rate is 0.25%. The bank’s model owner states: “Because our $\sigma$($t$) declines steadily over time, the model cannot produce negative short rates.” Which of the following is the most accurate assessment of this claim?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the continuously compounded short-term rate, $t$ is measured in years, and $dw$ is the random shock of the process.

options.text: The claim holds, because a volatility function that declines over time keeps the basis-point volatility of the short rate small enough to bound the rate at zero.
The claim fails, because the basis-point volatility $\sigma$($t$) does not fall as the rate approaches zero, so a negative rate remains possible whenever $\sigma$($t$) > 0.
The claim fails, because negative rates arise only when $\lambda$($t$) is negative; with $\lambda$($t$) ≥ 0 at all dates the short rate could not fall below zero.
The claim holds, provided that the drift is positive when the rate is zero, since a positive drift at a zero rate prevents the short rate from becoming negative.

questions.solution:
**Can a declining $\sigma$($t$) rule out negative rates?**

Stem in one line: EUR short rate at 0.25%; model owner claims a declining $\sigma$($t$) prevents negative rates; assess the claim.

**Concept and theory**

Two facts about (15.1) settle the question.

- The shock is normal and its size does not depend on the rate. $dw$ is normal with mean zero (Schweser LO 15.a), and $\sigma$($t$) contains no $r$. GARP §15.2: the models presented so far assume basis-point volatility independent of the level of the short rate. At $r$ = 0.25% the model applies exactly the same $\sigma$($t$) as at $r$ = 5%.
- What it takes to rule out negative rates. GARP §15.2: the property that basis-point volatility equals zero when the short rate is zero, combined with a positive drift when the rate is zero, guarantees that the short rate cannot become negative. GARP calls this an improvement over models with basis-point volatility that does not depend on the rate, which allow rates to become negative.

| Condition for non-negative rates (GARP §15.2) | CIR ($k\theta>$ 0) | (15.1) |
|---|---|---|
| Basis-point volatility is zero at $r$ = 0 | Yes | No |
| Drift is positive at $r$ = 0 | Yes | Not by construction |

A volatility that declines over time is still the same at every rate level, so it never shrinks to zero as $r$ approaches zero.

**Applying it to this question**

At any date with $\sigma$($t$) > 0, the change $dr$ is normal with a positive standard deviation $\sigma$($t$)$\sqrt{dt}$, so there is a positive probability that the rate falls from 0.25% to below zero. The declining schedule makes such moves smaller at later dates, but does not remove them. The claim fails the first of GARP’s two conditions.

**Fragile fact.** Time-dependent is not level-dependent. Non-negativity needs zero volatility at zero and positive drift at zero; (15.1) lacks the first.

**Reference**

LO 15.a (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 15, §15.2 The Cox-Ingersoll-Ross and Lognormal Models: Volatility as a Function of the Short Rate (opening paragraph and the non-negativity paragraph). Schweser Reading 15, LO 15.a ($dw$ normal with mean 0) and LO 15.d (normal distribution implies a positive probability of negative rates). Note: GARP phrases the contrast as “models with constant basis-point volatility”; for (15.1) the basis-point volatility varies over time but is constant across rate levels, which is the sense that matters here. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 a, where it is Q8 of 9.

a.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. A smaller volatility makes negative rates less likely, not impossible; no time profile of $\sigma$($t$) creates a barrier at zero. A would be correct only if $\sigma$($t$) were zero, which removes all randomness.

b.reason: It identifies the missing property: in (15.1) basis-point volatility does not fall as the rate approaches zero (GARP §15.2), so the zero-volatility-at-zero condition that protects the CIR model is absent.

c.reason: Error type: scope error (the source of negative rates misplaced). Even with $\lambda$($t$) ≥ 0, a large enough negative shock $\sigma$($t$) $dw$ takes the rate below zero. C would be correct for a model with no random term, $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$.

d.reason: Error type: scope error (one of GARP’s two joint conditions dropped; the CIR argument borrowed). A positive drift at zero guarantees non-negative rates only together with basis-point volatility that is zero at zero. D would be correct for the CIR model, $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma\sqrt{r} dw$ with $k\theta>$ 0 (LO 15.d).

questions.question:
The head of a JPY rates desk at a Japanese trust bank currently prices with a Ho-Lee model calibrated to the JGB curve. A quantitative analyst proposes replacing the model’s constant volatility $\sigma$ with a function $\sigma$($t$), keeping everything else unchanged. Which of the following best describes the proposed model relative to the current one?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the continuously compounded short-term rate, $t$ is measured in years, and $dw$ is the random shock of the process.

options.text: The drift becomes a constant and the volatility becomes a function of time, so the Ho-Lee model is no longer a special case of the new model.
The drift remains a function of time and the volatility becomes a function of the rate level, so basis-point volatility now rises with the short rate.
The drift remains a function of time and the volatility becomes a function of time, so the Ho-Lee model is the special case of a constant $\sigma$($t$).
The drift remains a function of time and the volatility becomes a function of time, so the new model is the special case of Ho-Lee with $\sigma$($t$) = $\sigma$.

questions.solution:
**From Ho-Lee to time-dependent volatility**

Stem in one line: JPY desk replaces Ho-Lee’s constant $\sigma$ with $\sigma$($t$); how does the new model relate to the old one?

**Concept and theory**

Schweser LO 15.a: the Ho-Lee model, $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$, now includes non-constant volatility. Writing the change as one substitution:

$\underbrace{dr = \lambda(t)\,dt + \sigma\,dw}_{\text{Ho-Lee}} \;\xrightarrow{\;\sigma \to \sigma(t)\;}\; \underbrace{dr = \lambda(t)\,dt + \sigma(t)\,dw}_{\text{time-dependent volatility}}$

The drift is untouched (still a function of time, still used to fit the curve). Volatility becomes a function of time, not of the rate. The direction of nesting follows from generality: the new model contains Ho-Lee as the case in which $\sigma$($t$) happens to be the same at every date, so Ho-Lee is the special case, and the new model is the general one.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem fixes “everything else unchanged”, so $\lambda$($t$) remains time-dependent. Replacing $\sigma$ by $\sigma$($t$) makes volatility time-dependent. Setting $\sigma$($t$) = $\sigma$ recovers the desk’s current model. C states all three.

**Fragile fact.** The general model is (15.1); Ho-Lee and Model 1 sit inside it. Ho-Lee keeps $\lambda$($t$); the new model adds $\sigma$($t$).

**Reference**

LO 15.a (Schweser, verbatim above). Schweser Reading 15, LO 15.a and Key Concepts LO 15.a (Schweser-only for the Ho-Lee equation within this reading). GARP Ch. 15, §15.1 Time-Dependent Volatility: Model 3 (“Unlike the models presented in Chapter 14, the volatility . . . depends on time”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 a, where it is Q9 of 9.

a.reason: Error type: scope error (“everything else unchanged” ignored; the drift loses its time dependence). Ho-Lee’s time-dependent drift is kept. A would be correct if the proposal also replaced $\lambda$($t$) by a constant $\lambda$, in which case a Ho-Lee model with a non-constant drift could no longer be recovered.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (time dependence read as rate dependence, the CIR or lognormal feature of LO 15.d). B would be correct if $\sigma$ were replaced by $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ or $\sigma r$ instead of $\sigma$($t$).

c.reason: Schweser LO 15.a and Key Concepts: Ho-Lee is a special case of $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma$($t$) $dw$; the generalization is the non-constant volatility.

d.reason: Error type: polarity flip (direction of nesting reversed). A constant is a special case of a function, not the other way round. D would be correct with the two model names exchanged: “Ho-Lee is the special case of the new model with $\sigma$($t$) = $\sigma$.”
