questions.question:
An internal auditor at an Indian bank is reviewing a model-selection memo for the INR rates book. The memo argues: “Our Vasicek model misprices several INR caplets and does not capture rate behaviour well enough for hedging. Model 3, calibrated to match every caplet price exactly, is therefore the better model for valuing and hedging our bond and swaption book.” Which assessment of the memo is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, $dw$ is normally distributed with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$, volatilities are annualized basis-point volatilities, and “Model 3” denotes $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma e^{-\alpha t} dw$.

options.text: The argument is weak: if the Vasicek model is not good enough for the hedging purpose, a parallel shift model calibrated to match caplet prices is unlikely to be better suited to it.
The argument is sound: a model that matches the caplet prices by construction necessarily provides fair values and accurate hedges for the bond and swaption book as well.
The argument is weak: Model 3 cannot match caplet prices at many expiries, because its volatility is a single constant that does not change with the horizon of the caplet.
The argument is sound: since Model 3 can be made to give the same terminal standard deviations as the Vasicek model, its hedges will be at least as accurate as Vasicek hedges.

questions.solution:
**Calibration cannot rescue a parallel shift model**

Stem in one line: memo says Model 3 fitted to every INR caplet beats Vasicek for valuing and hedging bonds and swaptions; assess.

**Concept and theory**

GARP gives two reasons why mean reversion may be preferred for valuing and hedging. The second ends with a direct answer to this memo: “the downward-sloping factor structure and term structure of volatility in mean-reverting models capture the behavior of interest rate movements better than parallel shifts and a flat term structure of volatility. It may very well be that the Vasicek model does not capture the behavior of interest rates sufficiently well to be used for a particular valuation or hedging purpose. But in that case it is unlikely that a parallel shift model calibrated to match caplet prices will be better suited for that purpose.”

This echoes Reading 14’s warning on fitting: “a mediocre or bad model cannot be rescued by calibrating it to match market prices” and “That a model matches market prices does not necessarily imply that it provides fair values and accurate hedges.” Calibration fixes levels (prices); it does not change the model’s dynamics (how rates of different maturities move together), which is what hedging relies on.

**Applying it to this question**

The memo’s premise (Vasicek is not good enough for hedging) is allowed. Its conclusion (so a caplet-calibrated Model 3 is better) is exactly the inference GARP rejects, because Model 3 is still a parallel shift model with a flat volatility term structure.

**Fragile fact.** Calibration matches prices, not dynamics: a parallel shift model fitted to caplets is still a parallel shift model.

**Reference**

LO 15.c (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 15, §15.1 (final paragraph of the section). GARP Ch. 14, §14.4 Desirability of Fitting to the Term Structure. Schweser Reading 15, “Model 3 Effectiveness”. GARP-only: the “calibrated to match caplet prices” sentence is not in Schweser.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 c, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: It paraphrases GARP’s closing sentences of §15.1.

b.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. “Necessarily provides fair values and accurate hedges” is contradicted by GARP Ch. 14, §14.4. Would be correct only as the weaker claim “matches the caplet prices it was fitted to”.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap. A single constant volatility is Model 1 or Ho-Lee; Model 3’s volatility decays with time, and the general $\sigma$($t$) can fit caplets at many expiries. The memo is weak for a different reason. Would be correct if the memo had proposed the Ho-Lee model.

d.reason: Error type: scope error. Matching terminal standard deviations (Q4) does not match factor structure, so hedges differ. Would be correct only for a claim about the dispersion of the short rate at a single future date.

questions.solution:
**The parallel between time-dependent drift and time-dependent volatility**

Stem in one line: documentation says arguments for and against $\sigma$($t$) resemble those for $\lambda$($t$); what is the parallel?

**Concept and theory**

GARP §15.1 opens: “Just as a time-dependent drift may be used to fit many bond or swap rates, a time-dependent volatility function may be used to fit many option prices.” Later: “The arguments for and against using time-dependent volatility resemble those for and against using a time-dependent drift.”

|  | Time-dependent drift $\lambda$($t$) | Time-dependent volatility $\sigma$($t$) |
|---|---|---|
| Fits | many bond or swap rates | many option prices |
| Use | interpolate odd-maturity swap rates | interpolate unobservable option prices |
| After fitting | still parallel shift, flat vol | still parallel shift, flat vol |
| Limitation | cannot rescue a poor model | cannot rescue a poor model |

Reading 14: “adding a time-dependent drift does not change” the shape of the term structure of volatility or “the parallel-shift characteristic”; GARP §15.1: Model 3 is a parallel shift model with a flat term structure of volatility.

**Applying it to this question**

Two slots decide the answer: what each function fits (drift: bond or swap rates; volatility: option prices) and what the fit leaves unchanged (parallel shifts). Only C gets both slots right.

**Fragile fact.** Drift fits bond and swap rates; volatility fits option prices; neither changes the parallel-shift nature of the model.

**Reference**

LO 15.c (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 15, §15.1 (opening sentence and “The arguments for and against. . . ”). GARP Ch. 14, §14.3 and §14.4. Schweser Reading 15, “Model 3 Effectiveness”. GARP-only: the explicit drift analogy. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 c, where it is Q10 of 13.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap (the two fitting targets exchanged). Drift moves the mean and fits bond and swap rates; volatility sets dispersion and fits option prices. Would be correct with “option prices” and “bond or swap rates” swapped back.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (properties of mean reversion attributed to the time-dependent functions). Neither $\lambda$($t$) nor $\sigma$($t$) creates mean reversion or a downward-sloping term structure of volatility. Would be correct as a description of what adding mean reversion (Vasicek) does.

c.reason: First half: GARP §15.1, opening sentence. Second half: GARP Ch. 14, §14.3 and Ch. 15, §15.1 (both models remain parallel shift models).

d.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. A fit to market prices does not guarantee accurate hedges (GARP Ch. 14, §14.4). Would be correct with “guarantees” replaced by “allows interpolation from known to unknown prices”.

Which of the following is least likely to be one of the reasons given by Tuckman?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, $dw$ is normally distributed with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$, volatilities are annualized basis-point volatilities, and “Model 3” denotes $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma e^{-\alpha t} dw$.

options.text: Mean reversion rests on economic intuition about how short rates behave over time.
Mean reversion keeps the short rate non-negative, unlike time-dependent volatility.
Time-dependent volatility relies on a market forecast of volatility in the distant future.
Mean-reverting models have a downward-sloping factor structure and volatility term structure.

questions.solution:
**Tuckman’s two reasons for preferring mean reversion**

Stem in one line: which is least likely one of Tuckman’s reasons for preferring mean reversion to time-dependent volatility when valuing and hedging?

**Concept and theory**

GARP §15.1 gives exactly two reasons, both relevant only when the purpose is to value and hedge:

| Reason | GARP wording |
|---|---|
| 1 | “while mean reversion is based on the economic intuitions outlined earlier, time-dependent volatility relies on the difficult argument that the market has a forecast of short-term volatility in the distant future.” |
| 2 | “the downward-sloping factor structure and term structure of volatility in mean-reverting models capture the behavior of interest rate movements better than parallel shifts and a flat term structure of volatility.” |

Non-negativity of rates is a separate issue, addressed in §15.2 by the CIR and lognormal models (and in Reading 14 by shadow rates and other devices). The Vasicek model is a normal model, so its short rate can become negative; mean reversion only pulls rates toward $\theta$.

**Applying it to this question**

A and C are the two halves of reason 1; D is reason 2. B is not a reason at all and is factually wrong for Vasicek.

**Fragile fact.** Mean reversion does not stop rates going negative; non-negativity belongs to CIR and lognormal models.

**Reference**

LO 15.c (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 15, §15.1 (“First, while mean reversion. . . ” and “Second, the downward-sloping. . . ”). GARP Ch. 15, §15.2 (non-negativity under CIR and lognormal). Schweser Reading 15, “Model 3 Effectiveness”. Difference: Schweser lists the distant-forecast criticism and the downward-sloping volatility term structure but omits “economic intuition” and “factor structure”; GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 c, where it is Q11 of 13.

a.reason: Not the answer: a true reason, stated without corruption. It is the first half of reason 1. It would be the answer only if the stem asked for a reason for preferring time-dependent volatility.

b.reason: Non-negativity is neither among GARP’s two reasons nor a property of the normal, mean-reverting Vasicek model.

c.reason: Not the answer: a true reason, stated without corruption. Second half of reason 1, the criticism of time-dependent volatility. It would be the answer if the stem asked for a feature that favours Model 3.

d.reason: Not the answer: a true reason, stated without corruption. Reason 2, a point in favour of mean reversion (Schweser: “A point in favor of the mean reversion models is the downward-sloping volatility term structure”). It would be the answer if the stem asked which property Model 3 shares with Vasicek.

The bank’s model risk committee objects that a time-dependent volatility specification relies on the difficult argument that the market has a forecast of short-term volatility in the distant future. The consultant considers four replacement specifications. Which one best addresses the committee’s objection?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, $dw$ is normally distributed with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$, volatilities are annualized basis-point volatilities, and “Model 3” denotes $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma e^{-\alpha t} dw$.

options.text: $\sigma$($t$) = 1.60%$\times e^{\text{+0}.15t}$ for all $t$, so that volatility rises with the horizon to reflect greater long-run uncertainty.
$\sigma$($t$) fitted separately to caplet prices at every annual expiry from 1 to 30 years, and re-estimated every month.
$\lambda$($t$) fitted to bond prices out to 5 years and then held constant, with $\sigma$($t$) = 1.60% $\times e^{-0.15t}$ unchanged.
$\sigma$($t$) fitted to caplet prices out to 5 years, and then held constant at 0.90% per year for all later dates.

questions.solution:
**Fixing the distant-future volatility forecast problem**

Stem in one line: EUR Model 3 ($\sigma$ = 1.60%, $\alpha$ = 0.15); which replacement volatility specification answers the “market forecasts distant volatility” objection?

**Concept and theory**

A time-dependent $\sigma$($t$) fitted to option prices implicitly claims that today’s market knows what short-rate volatility will be at every future date, however distant. GARP calls this “the difficult argument that the market has a forecast of short-term volatility in the distant future” and gives the fix: “A modification of the model that addresses this objection, by the way, is to assume that volatility depends on time in the near future and then settles at a constant.” GARP also notes that Model 3’s volatility “could have easily been designed to decline to another constant instead of zero”. The fix keeps the useful part (fitting near-term option prices where the market really does have information) and drops the implausible part (a detailed long-run volatility path).

**Applying it to this question**

Check each candidate against two tests: (1) is volatility time-dependent only in the near term? (2) does it settle at a constant? Only D passes both: fitted to caplets out to 5 years, then constant at 0.90%. The current $\sigma$ and $\alpha$ values are context only.

**Fragile fact.** The fix acts on volatility: time-dependent in the near term, then a constant.

**Reference**

LO 15.c (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 15, §15.1 (“A modification of the model that addresses this objection. . . ” and “Volatility could have easily been designed to decline to another constant instead of zero”). Schweser Reading 15, “Model 3 Effectiveness”. Difference: Schweser describes the compromise as “forecast volatility approaching a constant value (in Model 3, the volatility approaches 0)”, which can be read as saying Model 3 already embodies the compromise; GARP presents it as a modification of the model. GARP wording used; no option relies on the disputed reading.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 c, where it is Q12 of 13.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip (decay turned into growth). Volatility still depends on time at every horizon, so a distant-future forecast is still embedded, and it never settles. Would be correct for nothing in the reading; it is simply Model 3 with the sign of $\alpha$ reversed.

b.reason: Error type: scope error (time dependence extended rather than limited). Fitting $\sigma$($t$) annually out to 30 years maximizes reliance on distant-future forecasts; re-estimation frequency is irrelevant to the objection. Would be correct as a description of the most flexible fit to caplet prices, which is the market maker’s use, not the fix.

c.reason: Error type: role misassignment (drift adjusted instead of volatility). The objection is about forecasting volatility; changing $\lambda$($t$) leaves $\sigma e^{-0.15t}$, and its implied long-run path, untouched. Would be correct if the objection were about a forecast of the distant-future level of rates.

d.reason: It is a direct implementation of GARP’s modification: “volatility depends on time in the near future and then settles at a constant”.

An ALM manager at a Canadian bank reviews two years of CAD market data before choosing between Model 3 and a mean-reverting model for valuing and hedging the bank’s bond portfolio. She observes:

- across the 5-year to 30-year range, implied volatilities of CAD rates decline with term;
- on days when the short rate rose by about 12 bp, the 25-year CAD spot rate typically rose by about 6 bp.

Which conclusion is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, $dw$ is normally distributed with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$, volatilities are annualized basis-point volatilities, and “Model 3” denotes $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma e^{-\alpha t} dw$.

options.text: The evidence favours Model 3, because its exponentially decaying volatility gives longer-term rates lower volatility than short-term rates.
The evidence favours a mean-reverting model, whose downward-sloping factor structure and term structure of volatility fit it better than Model 3.
The evidence favours Model 3 once $\lambda$($t$) is fitted to CAD bond prices, because fitting to market prices gives it a downward-sloping factor structure.
The evidence favours a mean-reverting model, but it is irrelevant for hedging, since hedges depend only on terminal distributions, which both can share.

questions.solution:
**Reading market evidence on factor structure**

Stem in one line: CAD implied volatilities decline with term and a 12 bp short-rate rise moves the 25-year rate about 6 bp; which model does this favour?

**Concept and theory**

The second reason GARP gives for preferring mean reversion when valuing and hedging is empirical: “the downward-sloping factor structure and term structure of volatility in mean-reverting models capture the behavior of interest rate movements better than parallel shifts and a flat term structure of volatility.” Two observable fingerprints separate the models:

| Observation | Model 3 predicts | Mean reversion predicts |
|---|---|---|
| Response of long rate to short-rate move | same size (parallel shift) | smaller (downward-sloping) |
| Volatility across maturities at a date | flat | downward-sloping |

Reading 14 explains the mean-reversion pattern: short-term rates depend mostly on current conditions and long-term rates mostly on long-term conditions ($\theta$), so shocks to the short rate affect short-term rates more than long-term rates.

**Applying it to this question**

A 12 bp short-rate rise moving the 25-year rate only about 6 bp is a downward-sloping factor structure, which Model 3 cannot produce (it would predict about 12 bp). Volatility falling with term over 5 to 30 years is a downward-sloping term structure of volatility, which Model 3 also cannot produce (it is flat). Both observations favour mean reversion, and both matter for hedging.

**Fragile fact.** Smaller long-rate moves and volatility falling with maturity are signatures of mean reversion; Model 3’s decay is over time and leaves both curves flat.

**Reference**

LO 15.c (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 15, §15.1 (“Second, the downward-sloping factor structure. . . ”). GARP Ch. 14, §14.5 The Vasicek Model (interpretation of the downward-sloping factor structure). Schweser Reading 15, “Model 3 Effectiveness” (“A point in favor of the mean reversion models is the downward-sloping volatility term structure”). GARP-only: factor structure. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 c, where it is Q13 of 13.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap (decline over time confused with decline over maturity). Model 3’s volatility decays with the calendar date, but at any date it is the same for all maturities. Would be correct only if the evidence were that all rates were becoming less volatile over the calendar years.

b.reason: It is GARP’s second reason applied to data: mean-reverting models’ downward-sloping factor structure and term structure of volatility capture rate behaviour better than Model 3’s parallel shifts and flat term structure of volatility.

c.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap (calibration as a cure). Fitting $\lambda$($t$) to bond prices does not change the parallel-shift characteristic (GARP Ch. 14, §14.3). Would be correct if “gives it a downward-sloping factor structure” read “matches the CAD bond prices it was fitted to”.

d.reason: Error type: scope error. Hedges depend on how rates of different maturities move together, which terminal distributions of the short rate do not capture (Q6). Would be correct for a single caplet on the short rate, whose value depends only on the short-rate distribution at expiry.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at an Indian private-sector bank is drafting an ALCO paper arguing that the bank’s INR short-rate model should no longer assume that the basis-point volatility of the short rate is independent of the level of the rate. The draft contains four statements:

I. The assumption that basis-point volatility is independent of the level of the short rate is almost certainly not true at extreme levels of the short rate.

II. Periods of high inflation and high short-term rates are inherently unstable, so the basis-point volatility of the short rate tends to be high in such periods.

III. When the short rate is very low, its basis-point volatility tends to be high, because a rate close to zero can move sharply in either direction.

IV. Arguments of this kind have led modellers to specify the basis-point volatility of the short rate as a function of calendar time rather than of the rate.

Which of the statements are consistent with the reasoning in the reading?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the short-term rate, $dt$ the time step, $dw$ a normally distributed shock with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$, and “basis-point volatility” the annualized standard deviation of $dr$.

options.text: II only
I and II only
I, II and III only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
**Why basis-point volatility should depend on the rate level**

Stem in one line: which ALCO-paper statements on the motivation for rate-dependent basis-point volatility match the reading?

**Concept and theory**

Every model in Reading 14 and in Model 3 of this reading has a random term that does not depend on $r$: $\sigma dw$ or $\sigma$($t$) $dw$. The basis-point volatility (the annualized standard deviation of $dr$) is therefore the same whether the rate is 0.5% or 15%. GARP §15.2 says this “is almost certainly not true at extreme levels of the short rate”, for two reasons that point the same way:

| Regime | What happens | Implication for basis-point vol |
|---|---|---|
| High inflation, high rates | Periods that are “inherently unstable” | Tends to be high |
| Very low rates | Rates “cannot decline much below zero”; Schweser: zero acts as a downside barrier that dampens volatility | Limited, i.e. low |

High at high rates and low at low rates means basis-point volatility should increase with the level of the rate. GARP: “Economic arguments of this sort have led to specifying the basis-point volatility of the short rate as an increasing function of the short rate.” The CIR and lognormal models are the two specifications that follow.

**Applying it to this question**

I restates GARP’s opening judgement. True. II is GARP’s high-inflation argument. True. III reverses the low-rate argument: near zero, volatility is limited by the floor, not amplified. False. IV attaches the conclusion to calendar time; the conclusion is a function of the rate. False. Hence I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: high rates go with high basis-point volatility; rates near zero go with limited basis-point volatility. The fix is a function of the rate, not of time.

**Reference**

LO 15.d: “Describe the short-term rate process under the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) and lognormal models.” GARP Ch. 15, §15.2 The Cox-Ingersoll-Ross and Lognormal Models: Volatility as a Function of the Short Rate (opening paragraphs). Schweser Reading 15, Module 15.2 (opening). Difference: Schweser adds that rates “should be bounded below by zero or should be at most small, negative rates” and calls zero a “downside barrier”; GARP says rates “cannot decline much below zero”. Same substance; GARP wording used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 d, where it is Q1 of 10.

a.reason: **II only.** Error type: absolute-claim trap misread. A candidate who rejects I usually reads it as “never true” and objects. The source qualifies it: not true at extreme levels. A would be right if I claimed independence fails at all rate levels.

b.reason: GARP §15.2: the independence assumption “is almost certainly not true at extreme levels”; high-inflation periods are “inherently unstable and, as a result, the basis-point volatility of the short rate tends to be high”; these arguments lead to basis-point volatility as “an increasing function of the short rate”.

c.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: polarity flip. III turns “limited” into “high” at low rates. It would be right only if the reading argued that the zero bound amplifies volatility, which is the opposite of the barrier argument.

d.reason: **I, II and IV.** Error type: sibling swap. A volatility that is a function of calendar time is Model 3 (LO 15.a), whose motivation is fitting option prices at many expiries, not the level of rates. IV would be right for a statement about why Model 3 uses $\sigma$($t$).

questions.question:
A model validator at an Australian superannuation fund is reviewing vendor documentation for an AUD short-rate engine. The documentation states that the engine uses the risk-neutral dynamics of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) model, with speed of mean reversion $k$, long-run level $\theta$ and volatility parameter $\sigma$. Which description of the process should the validator accept as most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the short-term rate, $dt$ the time step, $dw$ a normally distributed shock with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$, and “basis-point volatility” the annualized standard deviation of $dr$.

options.text: The drift pulls the rate toward $\theta$ at speed $k$; $\sigma$ declines exponentially with calendar time, so the random shocks shrink as time passes.
The drift pushes the rate away from $\theta$ at speed $k$; $\sigma$ is constant, and the random shocks are scaled by the square root of the rate.
The drift is a time-dependent function $\lambda$($t$) fitted to the curve; $\sigma$ is constant, and the random shocks are scaled by the square root of the rate.
The drift pulls the rate toward $\theta$ at speed $k$; $\sigma$ is constant, and the random shocks are scaled by the square root of the rate.

questions.solution:
**The CIR short-rate process**

Stem in one line: which description of the CIR risk-neutral dynamics should the validator accept?

**Concept and theory**

GARP gives the risk-neutral dynamics of the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model as

$dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma\sqrt{r} dw$ (15.3)

where $r$ is the short rate, $k$ the speed of mean reversion, $\theta$ the long-run level toward which the rate is pulled, $\sigma$ a constant volatility parameter, $dt$ the time step and $dw$ a normal shock with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$. Read it in two pieces:

| Term | What it is | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ | Drift, not random | Positive when $r < \theta$, negative when $r > \theta$: pulls $r$ toward $\theta$ (same as Vasicek) |
| $\sigma\sqrt{r} dw$ | Random term | $\sigma$ is constant; the shock is scaled by $\sqrt{r}$, so its size depends on the level of the rate |

GARP: “in the CIR model the parameter $\sigma$ is constant, but basis-point volatility is not”. How basis-point volatility then behaves as $r$ rises is LO 15.e; here the point is only what the random term depends on.

**Applying it to this question**

Three attributes must all be right: the direction of the drift (toward $\theta$), the nature of $\sigma$ (constant) and the scaling of the shock ($\sqrt{r}$). Only D has all three.

**Fragile fact.** In CIR, $\sigma$ is the constant; the shock varies because it is multiplied by $\sqrt{r}$. Time plays no role in the volatility.

**Reference**

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Swiss private bank is labelling the short-rate processes in the bank’s CHF model library. In the table, $\lambda$($t$) is a deterministic function of time and $a$, $k$, $\theta$, $\alpha$ are positive parameters.

| Process | Dynamics |
|---|---|
| P | $dr$ = $ar dt$ + $\sigma r dw$ |
| Q | $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma r dw$ |
| R | $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma\sqrt{r} dw$ |
| S | $dr$ = $\lambda$($t$) $dt$ + $\sigma e^{-\alpha t} dw$ |

Which of the following statements is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the short-term rate, $dt$ the time step, $dw$ a normally distributed shock with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$, and “basis-point volatility” the annualized standard deviation of $dr$.

options.text: P is the simplest lognormal model (Model 4): its drift and its random shocks are both proportional to the rate, and $\sigma$ is a constant yield volatility.
Q is the simplest lognormal model (Model 4): its drift reverts toward $\theta$, its random shocks are proportional to the rate, and $\sigma$ is a constant yield volatility.
R is the simplest lognormal model (Model 4): its drift reverts toward $\theta$, its random shocks are proportional to the rate, and $\sigma$ is a constant yield volatility.
P is the simplest lognormal model (Model 4): its drift and its random shocks are both proportional to the rate, and $\sigma$ is a yield volatility that decays over time.

questions.solution:
**Identifying the simplest lognormal process (Model 4)**

Stem in one line: which label correctly identifies Model 4 among four candidate processes?

**Concept and theory**

After CIR, GARP describes a second way to tie volatility to the rate: make basis-point volatility proportional to the rate. Then $\sigma$ is “often called yield volatility” because it is a percentage of the rate. GARP gives two examples:

Courtadon: $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma r dw$ (15.4)

Model 4 (simplest lognormal): $dr$ = $ar dt$ + $\sigma r dw$ (15.5)

where $a$ is a constant drift rate (the drift is $a$ times the rate), $\sigma$ the constant yield volatility, and the other symbols are as before. “In these two specifications, yield volatility is constant”. The two differ only in the drift: Courtadon mean reverts toward $\theta$; Model 4’s drift is proportional to the rate and has no long-run level. GARP adds that a variation of Model 4 is developed in the next section (LO 15.f).

| Process | Drift | Random term | Name |
|---|---|---|---|
| P | $ar$ (proportional) | $\sigma r$ | Model 4, simplest lognormal |
| Q | $k$($\theta- r$) (mean reverting) | $\sigma r$ | Courtadon |
| R | $k$($\theta- r$) (mean reverting) | $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ | CIR |
| S | $\lambda$($t$) (time dependent) | $\sigma e^{-\alpha t}$ | Model 3 |

**Applying it to this question**

Find the process whose drift is $ar$ and whose random term is $\sigma r$ with constant $\sigma$: that is P. Then check the attribute list: drift proportional, shocks proportional, $\sigma$ constant. A matches all three.

**Fragile fact.** Model 4 has no $\theta$: its drift is $ar$. The mean-reverting process with $\sigma r$ is Courtadon, not Model 4.

**Reference**

LO 15.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 15, §15.2, eqs. (15.4) and (15.5). Schweser Reading 15, Module 15.2 (“lognormal model (Model 4)”). GARP-only: the Courtadon model (used only as a distractor). Notation: Schweser drops the Model 4 formula; $dr$ = $ar dt$ + $\sigma r dw$ read from GARP (15.5) and confirmed by the question bank’s worked solution (Q730). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 d, where it is Q3 of 10.

a.reason: GARP §15.2, eq. (15.5): the simplest lognormal model, Model 4, is $dr$ = $ar dt$ + $\sigma r dw$, with $\sigma$ a constant yield volatility.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap. Q has the proportional random term but a mean-reverting drift: it is the Courtadon model, GARP’s other example of constant yield volatility. B would be right if the question asked which process has proportional volatility and mean reversion.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap. R is CIR: its random term is $\sigma\sqrt{r}$, so “proportional to the rate” is false for R. C would be right with “CIR” in place of “Model 4” and “square root of the rate” in place of “proportional to the rate”.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap of the volatility attribute. P is correctly identified, but $\sigma$ in Model 4 is constant; decaying volatility belongs to S (Model 3). Correct only for a statement about S’s volatility.

questions.question:
In a training session for newly hired analysts at a Singapore bank, a junior risk analyst states: “The CIR short rate cannot become negative because its drift is mean reverting toward a positive long-run level.” A senior colleague corrects the statement. Which correction is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the short-term rate, $dt$ the time step, $dw$ a normally distributed shock with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$, and “basis-point volatility” the annualized standard deviation of $dr$.

options.text: No correction is needed: mean reversion toward a positive long-run level is on its own sufficient to keep the short rate from becoming negative.
Basis-point volatility of zero at a zero rate is on its own sufficient to keep the short rate from becoming negative, whatever the sign of the drift at zero.
Basis-point volatility of zero at a zero rate, combined with a positive drift at a zero rate, is what keeps the short rate from becoming negative.
A value of $\sigma$ small enough that a one-standard-deviation shock cannot carry the rate from its current level to below zero is what keeps it non-negative.

questions.solution:
**What keeps the CIR rate from becoming negative**

Stem in one line: correct the claim that CIR rates stay non-negative because of mean reversion.

**Concept and theory**

A short rate can cross below zero only if, when it is at or near zero, something pushes it down. Two forces act at $r$ = 0: the drift and the random shock. GARP: “The property that basis-point volatility equals zero when the short rate is zero, combined with the condition that the drift is positive when the rate is zero, guarantees that the short rate cannot become negative.”

| Condition at $r$ = 0 | Why it is needed | In CIR |
|---|---|---|
| Basis-point volatility is zero | No random shock can push the rate below zero | $\sigma\sqrt{0}$ = 0 |
| Drift is positive | The deterministic part pushes the rate back up, not down | $k$($\theta-$ 0) = $k\theta>$ 0 |

Both are needed. Vasicek has the same mean-reverting drift as CIR, yet its random term $\sigma dw$ does not vanish at zero, so it allows negative rates; GARP calls CIR and lognormal non-negativity “an improvement over models with constant basis-point volatility that allow interest rates to become negative.”

**Applying it to this question**

The junior analyst credits the drift alone. Mean reversion supplies only the positive drift at zero. Without the vanishing shock it is not enough (Vasicek is the counterexample). The correction must name both conditions together.

**Fragile fact.** Two conditions, both evaluated at a zero rate: zero basis-point volatility and positive drift.

**Reference**

LO 15.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 15, §15.2 (paragraph after Figure 15.2). Schweser Reading 15, Module 15.2. Difference: Schweser states “as long as the short-term rate is not negative, then a positive drift implies that the short-term rate cannot become negative”, leaving the zero-volatility-at-zero condition implicit; GARP states both conditions. GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 d, where it is Q4 of 10.

a.reason: Error type: scope or condition error (the volatility condition dropped). Vasicek mean reverts toward a positive $\theta$ and still allows negative rates. A would be right only for a model whose shocks already vanish at zero.

b.reason: Error type: scope or condition error (the drift condition dropped). If volatility is zero at zero but the drift there is negative, the deterministic part alone carries the rate below zero. B would be right with “provided the drift at zero is positive” added.

c.reason: It restates GARP’s two-part condition exactly: zero basis-point volatility at a zero rate combined with a positive drift at a zero rate.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap with a calibration argument. GARP’s guarantee is a structural property of the process at $r$ = 0 (what the drift and the shock are when the rate is zero), not a statement about the size of $\sigma$ relative to the current rate. A small $\sigma$ makes negative rates less likely in a constant volatility model but, by GARP’s argument, does not rule them out. D would be right for a question about reducing, not excluding, the probability of negative rates.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a Japanese life insurer is choosing a model to value a book of long-dated JPY caps and floors whose strikes lie far from the expected future short rate. Three models have been calibrated so that their ten-year terminal distributions of the short rate share the same mean and standard deviation:

| Model | Mean | Std. dev. | Prob. rate \< 0 | Run time per valuation (s) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Normal | 3.00% | 1.60% | 3.0% | 0.4 |
| CIR | 3.00% | 1.60% | 0.0% | 2.1 |
| Lognormal | 3.00% | 1.60% | 0.0% | 1.8 |

The manager concludes: “Because the first two moments match, the out-of-the-money option values will be close across the three models, so the choice of model is immaterial.” Which assessment of this conclusion is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the short-term rate, $dt$ the time step, $dw$ a normally distributed shock with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$, and “basis-point volatility” the annualized standard deviation of $dr$.

options.text: It holds, because option values depend only on the mean and the standard deviation of the terminal distribution of the short rate.
It holds for the CIR and lognormal models, because both are non-negative, but not for the normal model, which places mass below zero.
It fails only for options struck below zero, because the three distributions differ only in the region of negative rates.
It fails, because the probabilities of outcomes away from the mean differ enough across the three shapes to give significantly different values.

questions.solution:
**Matched moments do not give matched option values**

Stem in one line: three models with the same ten-year mean and standard deviation; is the out-of-the-money option value the same across them?

**Concept and theory**

GARP Figure 15.3 compares the ten-year terminal distributions of the short rate under the CIR, normal and lognormal models. To isolate shape, the parameters are chosen so that all three have an expected value of 5% and a standard deviation of 2.32%. Two conclusions are drawn:

1. The CIR and lognormal models have the advantage of not allowing negative rates; the normal does.
2. “Out-of-the-money option prices could differ significantly under the three models.” Even with the same mean and volatility, “the probability of outcomes away from the means are different enough to generate significantly different options prices.”

The mechanism: an out-of-the-money option pays only in a tail of the distribution. Two distributions can share a mean and a standard deviation while putting very different mass in each tail (one symmetric with mass below zero, two non-negative with a longer right tail). GARP generalizes: “the shape of the distribution used in an interest rate model is an important determinant of that model’s performance.” Schweser’s key concept adds that “the non-normality of the distributions can lead to derivative mispricings.”

**Applying it to this question**

The strikes lie far from the expected rate, so these are out-of-the-money options whose values depend on tail probabilities. Matching the first two moments does not match the tails. The table’s 3.0% negative-rate probability for the normal model (Φ(−3.00/1.60) = Φ(−1.875) ≈ 3.0%, consistent with the stated moments) is one visible difference in the left tail, but the shapes also differ elsewhere, including between CIR and lognormal. The run-time column is irrelevant to the question asked.

**Fragile fact.** Same mean and same standard deviation, different shape, different out-of-the-money prices. The difference is between all three, not just normal versus the rest.

**Reference**

LO 15.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 15, §15.2 and Figure 15.3 (Terminal distributions of the short rate after ten years in CIR, normal, and lognormal models). Schweser Reading 15, Module 15.2 (Figure 15.1 discussion) and Key Concepts LO 15.d. Difference: Schweser frames distribution differences as potential “derivative mispricings” and, in Module Quiz 15.2 Q2, as a disadvantage of CIR; GARP presents them neutrally as differences in option prices driven by distribution shape. GARP framing used. The numbers in the stem are original, not GARP’s.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 d, where it is Q5 of 10.

a.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. Option values depend on the whole distribution, not just two moments. A would be right only if all three distributions had the same shape (for example, all normal).

b.reason: Error type: scope or condition error. Non-negativity is a shared property of CIR and lognormal, but GARP says prices can differ “under the three models”, so CIR and lognormal can still disagree with each other. B would be right if the question asked which models rule out negative rates.

c.reason: Error type: scope or condition error. The shapes differ throughout, including in the right tail where high-strike caplets pay; the difference is not confined to negative rates. C would be right if the distributions were identical above zero, which they are not.

d.reason: It is GARP’s own conclusion from Figure 15.3: equal mean and volatility, yet outcome probabilities away from the mean differ enough to produce significantly different option prices.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is reviewing the model choice of an interest rate options trader at a Canadian dealer. The trader prices her CAD book with a constant basis-point volatility model. She holds three beliefs: (1) the assumption of constant volatility is best in the current economic environment; (2) the possibility of negative rates has a small impact on the prices of the securities she trades; (3) the computational simplicity of constant volatility models has great value. Which conclusion should the consultant reach?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the short-term rate, $dt$ the time step, $dw$ a normally distributed shock with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$, and “basis-point volatility” the annualized standard deviation of $dr$.

options.text: The choice is inappropriate, because a model that assigns any probability to negative rates should not be used to price interest rate options.
The choice may well be appropriate, because model choice depends on the purpose at hand and her beliefs limit the value of CIR or lognormal non-negativity.
The choice may well be appropriate, because constant basis-point volatility models also rule out negative rates whenever the drift is positive at a zero rate.
The choice is inappropriate, because the CIR model is computationally simpler than constant volatility models and also rules out negative rates.

questions.solution:
**When a model allowing negative rates is acceptable**

Stem in one line: trader with three stated beliefs uses a constant basis-point volatility model; is the choice defensible?

**Concept and theory**

CIR and lognormal models rule out negative rates. GARP calls this “in some respects” an improvement, then immediately qualifies it: “choosing a model depends on the purpose at hand.” It offers a trader who believes three things:

1. the assumption of constant volatility is best in the current economic environment;
2. the possibility of negative rates has a small impact on the pricing of the securities under consideration;
3. the computational simplicity of constant volatility models has great value.

“This trader might very well opt for a model that allows some probability of negative rates.” The logic: non-negativity is worth paying for (in complexity and in a possibly worse volatility fit) only if negative-rate probability actually moves prices.

**Applying it to this question**

The trader’s beliefs are exactly GARP’s three. The consultant should conclude that the constant volatility model may well be appropriate, because the purpose (pricing this book) does not benefit much from non-negativity.

**Fragile fact.** Computational simplicity belongs to constant volatility models. Non-negativity is an advantage only when negative rates matter for the prices at hand.

**Reference**

LO 15.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 15, §15.2 (trader paragraph). Schweser Reading 15, Module 15.2. Difference: Schweser’s version has a market maker who “feels that interest rates will be fairly flat” and chooses the simpler constant volatility model over CIR; GARP’s three beliefs are about constant volatility being the best assumption, the small pricing impact of negative rates and computational simplicity. Schweser’s “rates fairly flat” compresses GARP’s first belief; GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 d, where it is Q6 of 10.

a.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. GARP explicitly allows such a model. A would be right only if the reading required non-negativity in every application.

b.reason: GARP §15.2: model choice depends on the purpose at hand; a trader with these three beliefs “might very well opt for a model that allows some probability of negative rates”.

c.reason: Error type: scope or condition error. A positive drift at zero is only half the condition; with constant basis-point volatility the shock does not vanish at zero, so negative rates remain possible (GARP: models with constant basis-point volatility “allow interest rates to become negative”). C would be right for a model whose basis-point volatility is zero at a zero rate.

d.reason: Error type: polarity flip. GARP credits the constant volatility model with computational simplicity, not CIR. D would be right with the two models’ simplicity reversed, which the source does not support.

questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee at a German bank asks the model risk team which features are shared by the two EUR short-rate models under review: the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) model and the simplest lognormal model (Model 4). The team drafts four statements:

I. In both models the random term is scaled by a function of the level of the short rate that equals zero when the rate is zero.

II. In both models the drift pulls the short rate toward a long-run level $\theta$.

III. In both models the parameter $\sigma$ multiplying the random term is a constant.

IV. In the reading’s comparison of ten-year terminal distributions, neither model places any probability on negative rates.

Which statements correctly describe both models?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the short-term rate, $dt$ the time step, $dw$ a normally distributed shock with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$, and “basis-point volatility” the annualized standard deviation of $dr$.

options.text: I and III only
I, II, III and IV
I, III and IV only
III and IV only

questions.solution:
**CIR and Model 4 compared as processes**

Stem in one line: which statements describe both CIR and the simplest lognormal model?

**Concept and theory**

Put the two equations side by side:

| Feature | CIR: $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$)$dt$ + $\sigma\sqrt{r} dw$ | Model 4: $dr$ = $ar dt$ + $\sigma r dw$ |
|---|---|---|
| Drift | Mean reverting toward $\theta$ | Proportional to $r$; no long-run level |
| Random term scaled by | $\sqrt{r}$ (zero at $r$ = 0) | $r$ (zero at $r$ = 0) |
| Parameter $\sigma$ | Constant | Constant (“yield volatility”) |
| Negative rates | Not allowed | Not allowed |
| (Fig. 15.3) |  |  |

GARP: “Both models have the basis-point volatility equal to zero at a rate of zero”, and the ten-year comparison “illustrates the advantage of the CIR and lognormal models with respect to not allowing negative rates.”

**Applying it to this question**

I: $\sqrt{0}$ = 0 and 0 $\cdot\sigma$ = 0, so both random terms vanish at zero. True for both. II: Model 4’s drift is $ar$; it has no $\theta$. False for Model 4. III: $\sigma$ is constant in both. True. IV: GARP Figure 15.3 and its text. True. Hence I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Model 4 has no $\theta$. Only CIR (of these two) mean reverts.

**Reference**

LO 15.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 15, §15.2, eqs. (15.3), (15.5), Figures 15.2 and 15.3. Schweser Reading 15, Module 15.2. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 d, where it is Q7 of 10.

a.reason: **I and III only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement (sibling confusion with the normal model). Rejecting IV means believing one of these models can produce negative rates, which is a property of the normal model. A would be right if one of the two models were normal.

b.reason: **I, II, III and IV.** Error type: sibling swap. Accepting II gives Model 4 the CIR (or Courtadon) mean-reverting drift. B would be right only if Model 4’s drift were mean reverting, as in the Courtadon model $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$)$dt$ + $\sigma r dw$.

c.reason: GARP §15.2, eqs. (15.3) and (15.5) and the Figure 15.3 discussion support I, III and IV; II fails for Model 4.

d.reason: **III and IV only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement (role misassignment of the scaling). Rejecting I usually comes from thinking the lognormal random term does not depend on the rate. It does: $\sigma r dw$. D would be right if Model 4’s random term were $\sigma dw$.

The report contains a chart of the ten-year terminal distributions of the short rate under a normal model, the CIR model and a lognormal model, calibrated to the same mean and standard deviation. The auditor must choose which statement to keep in the report’s commentary. Which statement is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the short-term rate, $dt$ the time step, $dw$ a normally distributed shock with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$, and “basis-point volatility” the annualized standard deviation of $dr$.

options.text: The CIR and lognormal distributions are non-negative and skewed right, while the normal distribution assigns positive probability to negative rates.
The CIR and lognormal distributions are non-negative and skewed left, while the normal distribution assigns positive probability to negative rates.
Because all three are calibrated to the same mean and standard deviation, all three assign the same probability to rates below zero.

questions.solution:
**Shape of the terminal distributions**

Stem in one line: which commentary on the ten-year normal, CIR and lognormal terminal distributions is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

A normal model’s terminal distribution is symmetric and unbounded, so it always gives some probability to negative rates. Schweser: “the normal distribution will always imply a positive probability of negative interest rates. In addition, the longer the forecast horizon, the greater the likelihood of negative rates occurring.” The CIR and lognormal processes cannot cross zero (Q4), so their terminal distributions sit entirely on non-negative rates. Schweser: “the lognormal and CIR terminal distributions are always non-negative and skewed right.”

| Distribution | Negative rates | Shape |
|---|---|---|
| Normal | Positive probability | Symmetric |
| CIR | None | Skewed right |
| Lognormal | None | Skewed right |

**Applying it to this question**

The auditor needs a statement that gets both the sign property and the skew direction right for all three models. Only A does.

**Fragile fact.** Non-negative goes with right skew. The normal’s negative-rate probability rises with the horizon (Schweser).

**Reference**

LO 15.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 15, §15.2, Figure 15.3. Schweser Reading 15, Module 15.2, Figure 15.1 discussion. Schweser-only (condensed source): the words “skewed right” and the horizon effect on negative-rate probability; GARP’s text states non-negativity and shape differences but its figure, which shows the skew, is not legible in the OCR extract. No conflict in substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 d, where it is Q8 of 10.

a.reason: Schweser Module 15.2 (Figure 15.1 discussion) and GARP §15.2 (Figure 15.3): CIR and lognormal do not allow negative rates and are right-skewed; the normal assigns positive probability to negative rates.

b.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the skew. Schweser describes both non-negative distributions as skewed right. B would be right only for a distribution with its long tail toward low rates, which the source does not describe for either model.

c.reason: Error type: scope or condition error. Matching two moments does not match shapes; the CIR and lognormal assign zero probability below zero while the normal does not. C would be right only if all three were normal.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap. It gives CIR the normal model’s property. Mean reversion pulls toward $\theta>$ 0, and the CIR shock vanishes at zero, so CIR cannot cross zero. D would be right with “normal” in place of “CIR”.

Applying the condition stated in the reading that guarantees the short rate cannot become negative, for which specification(s) is a non-negative short rate guaranteed?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the short-term rate, $dt$ the time step, $dw$ a normally distributed shock with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$, and “basis-point volatility” the annualized standard deviation of $dr$.

questions.solution:
**Applying the non-negativity condition**

Stem in one line: four BRL specifications; for which is a non-negative short rate guaranteed?

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s condition (Q4): the short rate cannot become negative if, at $r$ = 0, (1) basis-point volatility is zero and (2) the drift is positive. The test is mechanical: set $r$ = 0 in the drift and in the coefficient of $dw$, and check both. Neither the current rate nor how well the model fits caps enters the condition. R: drift = 0.25(−0.5% − 0) = −0.125%; coefficient of $dw$ = 6.0%$\sqrt{0}$ = 0 ⇒ fails (2)

S: drift = +0.30%; coefficient of $dw$ = 2.5% $e^{-0.15t} >$ 0 for all $t \Rightarrow$ fails (1)

Only Q meets both conditions. The current rate of 10.50% and the cap-fit errors are irrelevant inputs (S has the best cap fit, which is what Model 3 is designed for, but that says nothing about negative rates).

**Fragile fact.** Evaluate both terms at $r$ = 0. A volatility that decays over time is not zero at a zero rate.

questions.question:
The CRO of a US bank runs a Vasicek model, $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$, and a CIR model for USD rates, calibrated with the same speed of mean reversion $k$ and the same long-run level $\theta$. A risk committee member asks how the two short-rate processes differ. Which answer is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the short-term rate, $dt$ the time step, $dw$ a normally distributed shock with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$, and “basis-point volatility” the annualized standard deviation of $dr$.

options.text: They share the drift $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$; they differ in the random term, which in CIR is $\sigma\sqrt{r} dw$ rather than $\sigma dw$, so its size depends on the rate level.
They share the random term $\sigma dw$; they differ in the drift, which in CIR is multiplied by $\sqrt{r}$, so the pull toward $\theta$ vanishes at a zero rate.
They share the drift $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$; they differ in the random term, but with equal $k$ and $\theta$ their terminal distributions and negative-rate probabilities coincide.
They share the drift $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$; they differ in the random term, whose parameter $\sigma$ in CIR declines exponentially with calendar time rather than staying constant.

questions.solution:
**CIR versus Vasicek: same drift, different random term**

Stem in one line: Vasicek and CIR with the same $k$ and $\theta$; how do the two processes differ?

**Concept and theory**

Vasicek: $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$

CIR: $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma\sqrt{r} dw$

The drift terms are identical: both pull the rate toward $\theta$ at speed $k$. The only change CIR makes is in the random term, which is multiplied by $\sqrt{r}$. GARP motivates exactly this: the models before §15.2 “assume that the basis-point volatility of the short rate is independent of the level of the short rate”, and CIR replaces that assumption. Consequences: the CIR shock vanishes at $r$ = 0, so with a positive drift there ($k\theta>$ 0) the CIR rate cannot become negative, while Vasicek’s normal distribution always gives some probability to negative rates. Their terminal distributions therefore differ in shape even when $k$ and $\theta$ match.

**Applying it to this question**

Ask which term changes. The drift is the same; the random term differs by the $\sqrt{r}$ factor, which makes the shock size depend on the rate level. A says exactly this.

**Fragile fact.** The $\sqrt{r}$ multiplies the random term, not the drift. CIR and Vasicek share the drift.

**Reference**

LO 15.d (verbatim above). GARP Ch. 15, §15.2, eq. (15.3); Vasicek dynamics from GARP Ch. 14 used for comparison only. Schweser Reading 15, Module 15.2. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 d, where it is Q10 of 10.

a.reason: GARP eq. (15.3) versus the Vasicek dynamics: same $k$($\theta- r$)$dt$, random term $\sigma\sqrt{r} dw$ instead of $\sigma dw$; “in the CIR model the parameter $\sigma$ is constant, but basis-point volatility is not”.

b.reason: Error type: role misassignment. The $\sqrt{r}$ factor is placed on the drift instead of the random term. B would be right for a hypothetical model $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$)$\sqrt{r} dt$ + $\sigma dw$, which is not CIR.

c.reason: Error type: scope or condition error. Equal drift parameters do not make the distributions equal, because the random terms differ; Vasicek allows negative rates and CIR does not. C would be right only if the random terms were also identical.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap with Model 3. In CIR $\sigma$ is constant; exponentially declining $\sigma$ is the Model 3 specification. D would be right for a comparison of Vasicek with Model 3’s volatility.

questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee at a Japanese bank notes that JPY short rates have spent years close to zero and asks why the term structure models in the bank’s model inventory, such as the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) and lognormal models, make the basis-point volatility of the short rate an increasing function of the level of the short rate rather than a constant. Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the short rate (continuously compounded, annualized), $dt$ is measured in years, and $dw$ has mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$ unless a question states that $dw$ is already scaled.

options.text: Mean reversion pulls the short rate toward its long-run level faster when the rate is far from that level, so the basis-point volatility of the short rate must rise with the level of the rate.
Very low short rates are inherently unstable and so carry high basis-point volatility, while at high rate levels the basis-point volatility is limited by the long-run level of rates.
Periods of high inflation and high short rates are inherently unstable, so basis-point volatility tends to be high, while at very low rates it is limited because rates cannot fall much below zero.
Basis-point volatility is observed to be exactly proportional to the level of the short rate at every rate level, so any model with a different volatility function is misspecified.

questions.solution:
**Why basis-point volatility rises with the short rate**

Stem in one line: why do CIR and lognormal models make basis-point volatility increase with the level of the short rate?

**Concept and theory**

Basis-point volatility is the annualized standard deviation of $dr$, in rate units (for example 100 bp per year). In Model 1, Model 2, Ho-Lee, Vasicek and Model 3 the coefficient on $dw$ contains no $r$, so basis-point volatility does not depend on the rate level. GARP §15.2 challenges this: the assumption that basis-point volatility is independent of the rate level “is almost certainly not true at extreme levels of the short rate.” Two economic arguments are given:

| Regime | Argument in GARP |
|---|---|
| High rates | Periods of high inflation and high short rates are inherently unstable, so the basis-point volatility of the short rate tends to be high. |
| Very low rates | Basis-point volatility is limited because rates cannot decline much below zero; the zero area acts as a floor that dampens moves. |

These arguments “have led to specifying the basis-point volatility of the short rate as an increasing function of the short rate.” CIR uses $\sigma\sqrt{r}$; the lognormal (proportional) specification uses $\sigma r$.

**Applying it to this question**

The JPY experience is the low-rate case: near zero, rates have little room to fall, so basis-point volatility is small. The deciding fact is the pair of directions (high rates, high basis-point volatility; low rates, limited basis-point volatility). Only C states both directions and both reasons.

**Fragile fact.** High rates, high basis-point volatility; low rates, low basis-point volatility. Mean reversion is a drift feature.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 15, §15.2, opening paragraphs. Schweser Reading 15, Module 15.2 opening. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 e, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap (a drift property attributed to volatility). Mean reversion, $k$($\theta- r$), controls the drift, not the coefficient on $dw$; Vasicek has mean reversion and constant basis-point volatility. A would be right if the stem asked why the expected change in the rate is larger when the rate is far from its long-run level.

b.reason: Error type: polarity flip. It reverses both regimes: GARP says low rates limit basis-point volatility and high-rate periods are the unstable ones. B would be right only if the stem described a world where shocks grow as rates approach zero, which is the opposite of the reading.

c.reason: C reproduces GARP’s two arguments; Schweser makes the same two points (hyperinflation; zero as a downside barrier that dampens volatility).

d.reason: Error type: absolute claim. GARP says only that constant basis-point volatility is “almost certainly not true at extreme levels”; it presents two different increasing forms (square root and proportional), not one exact law. D would be right only if “exactly proportional at every level” read “tends to rise with the level, especially at extremes”.

A treasury analyst at a Singapore bank simulates SGD short rates with the CIR model, $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma\sqrt{r} dw$, using a monthly step ($dt$ = 1/12). The inputs are:

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Current short rate, $r_{0}$ | 3.20% |
| Long-run level, $\theta$ | 4.80% |
| Speed of mean reversion, $k$ | 0.35 |
| CIR volatility parameter, $\sigma$ | 0.045 |
| Yield volatility used by the bank’s lognormal desk model | 16% |
| Realized $dw$ for the month (already scaled for the time step) | +0.25 |

Which of the following is closest to the short rate after one month?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the short rate (continuously compounded, annualized), $dt$ is measured in years, and $dw$ has mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$ unless a question states that $dw$ is already scaled.
questions.solution:
**CIR one-month rate change with $r$ below $\theta$**

Stem in one line: CIR, monthly step, $r_{0}$ = 3.20%, $\theta$ = 4.80%, $k$ = 0.35, $\sigma$ = 0.045, scaled $dw$ = +0.25; find $r$ after one month.

**Concept and theory**

The CIR risk-neutral dynamics (GARP Eq. 15.3) are

$dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma\sqrt{r} dw$

where $r$ is the current short rate, $\theta$ the long-run level to which it reverts, $k$ the speed of mean reversion (per year), $\sigma$ the constant CIR volatility parameter, $dt$ the time step in years and $dw$ a normal shock with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$. The drift is positive when $r < \theta$ and negative when $r > \theta$; the shock is scaled by $\sqrt{r}$. The new rate is $r_{0}$ +$dr$. Schweser’s worked example uses these two pieces with an already-scaled $dw$.

**Applying it to this question**

Here $dw$ = 0.25 is already scaled, so it is used as given (no further $\sqrt{dt}$).

Drift = $k$($\theta- r_{0}$) $dt$ = 0.35 × (0.0480 − 0.0320) $\times\frac{1}{12}$ = 0.35 × 0.0160/12 = 0.000467 (0.0467%)

$\sqrt{r_{0}}$ = $\sqrt{0.0320}$ = 0.178885

Shock = $\sigma\sqrt{r_{0}} dw$ = 0.045 × 0.178885 × 0.25 = 0.002012 (0.2012%)

$dr$ = 0.0467% + 0.2012% = 0.2479%

$r_{1/12}$ = 3.20% + 0.2479% = 3.4479%

The rate rises for two reasons: it sits below $\theta$ (positive drift of about 5 bp) and the shock is positive (about 20 bp). The 16% lognormal yield volatility belongs to a different model and is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Drift is scaled by $dt$; the shock by $\sqrt{r}$ and (if not already done) by $\sqrt{dt}$. Read whether $dw$ is already scaled before multiplying by $\sqrt{dt}$ again.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 15, §15.2, Eq. 15.3. Schweser Reading 15, LO 15.e, CIR worked example (formula image missing in Schweser; structure confirmed by the bank’s worked CIR solutions for this LO). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 e, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: It applies Eq. 15.3 with the drift scaled by $dt$ and the shock scaled by $\sqrt{r}$, exactly as in Schweser’s CIR example.

b.reason: Error type: dropped term. The $-r$ inside ($\theta- r$) is omitted, giving a drift of $k\theta dt$ = 0.35 × 0.048/12 = 0.14%; then 3.20% + 0.14% + 0.2012% = 3.5412%. Correct only if the model’s drift were $k\theta dt$, with no dependence on the current rate.

c.reason: Error type: time-conversion slip. The drift is not multiplied by $dt$: 0.35 × 1.60% = 0.56%, so 3.20% + 0.56% + 0.2012% = 3.9612%. Correct if the step were one year with the same scaled $dw$.

d.reason: Error type: dropped term (the $\sqrt{r}$ factor), treating CIR like Vasicek: shock = 0.045 × 0.25 = 1.125%, so 3.20% + 0.0467% + 1.125% = 4.3717%. Correct if the model were $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$)$dt$ + $\sigma dw$ with $\sigma$ = 4.5% basis-point volatility.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a German bank is reviewing the EUR model documentation for a CIR short-rate model, $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma\sqrt{r} dw$. The volatility section contains four statements:

I. The parameter $\sigma$ is constant, but the annualized basis-point volatility of the short rate, $\sigma\sqrt{r}$, rises with the level of the short rate.

II. The annualized standard deviation of $dr$ equals $\sigma\sqrt{r}$, because the drift term is not a random variable and the standard deviation of $dw$ is $\sqrt{dt}$.

III. Because basis-point volatility is proportional to the square root of the rate, a doubling of the short rate doubles the basis-point volatility.

IV. Basis-point volatility increases with the level of the short rate at an increasing rate.

Which of the statements are accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the short rate (continuously compounded, annualized), $dt$ is measured in years, and $dw$ has mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$ unless a question states that $dw$ is already scaled.

options.text: I only
I and III only
II and IV only
I and II only

questions.solution:
**Basis-point volatility in the CIR model**

Stem in one line: which of four documentation statements on CIR volatility are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Only the second term of $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma\sqrt{r} dw$ is random. GARP: “Since the first term on the right-hand side of (15.3) is not a random variable and since the standard deviation of $dw$ equals $\sqrt{dt}$ by definition, the annualized standard deviation of $dr$ (i.e., the basis-point volatility) is proportional to the square root of the rate.” Formally,

sd($dr$) = $\sigma\sqrt{r} \sqrt{dt}$ $\Rightarrow\sigma^{\text{CIR}}_{bp}$ = $\frac{\text{sd(}dr\text{)}}{\sqrt{dt}}$ = $\sigma\sqrt{r}.$

So the parameter $\sigma$ is constant but basis-point volatility is not. Because $\sqrt{r}$ is concave, basis-point volatility rises with $r$ at a decreasing rate (Schweser Key Concepts; GARP Figure 15.2). Scaling property: multiplying $r$ by $m$ multiplies $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ by $\sqrt{m}$.

| Short rate | $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ with $\sigma$ = 0.05 | Ratio to 2% level |
|---|---|---|
| 2% | 70.7 bp | 1.00 |
| 4% | 100.0 bp | 1.41 |
| 8% | 141.4 bp | 2.00 |

**Applying it to this question**

I matches GARP: constant $\sigma$, basis-point volatility $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ rising with the rate. True. II restates GARP’s derivation. True. III: doubling $r$ multiplies basis-point volatility by $\sqrt{2}$ = 1.414, not 2. False. IV: the increase is at a decreasing rate. False. Hence I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** CIR: $\sigma$ constant; basis-point volatility $\sigma\sqrt{r}$; doubling $r$ raises it by a factor of 1.414; it rises at a decreasing rate.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 15, §15.2, paragraph after Eq. 15.3 and Figure 15.2. Schweser Reading 15, LO 15.e and Key Concepts (“basis point volatility that increases at a decreasing rate”). Difference: Schweser’s text loosely says “$dr$ increases at a decreasing rate”; GARP attaches the property to basis-point volatility. GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 e, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: **I only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement (scope error on what makes $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ the standard deviation). A candidate who thinks the drift adds to the standard deviation of $dr$ rejects II; the drift is deterministic and adds nothing to the variance. A would be right if II claimed the drift term were random.

b.reason: **I and III only.** Error type: sibling swap. Doubling basis-point volatility when the rate doubles is the proportional (lognormal) specification, $\sigma r$. B would be right if the model were $dr$ = $ar dt$ + $\sigma r dw$.

c.reason: **II and IV only.** Error type: polarity flip in IV (“increasing” for “decreasing” rate of increase), plus rejection of the true statement I. IV would be right for a convex function of $r$; the square root is concave.

d.reason: I and II are GARP’s own description; III and IV each corrupt one property.

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Current short rate, $r_{0}$ | 11.25% |
| Drift parameter, $a$ | 0.02 |
| Yield volatility, $\sigma$ | 18% |
| Current 10-year swap rate | 12.10% |
| Standard normal draw for the month | −0.90 |

Which of the following is closest to the short rate after one month?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the short rate (continuously compounded, annualized), $dt$ is measured in years, and $dw$ has mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$ unless a question states that $dw$ is already scaled.
questions.solution:
**Lognormal (Model 4) one-month rate change**

Stem in one line: Model 4, monthly, $r_{0}$ = 11.25%, $a$ = 0.02, $\sigma$ = 18%, standard normal draw −0.90; find $r$ after one month.

**Concept and theory**

GARP’s simplest lognormal model, Model 4 (Eq. 15.5), is

$dr$ = $ar dt$ + $\sigma r dw$

where $a$ is a drift parameter (per year) that scales the current rate, $\sigma$ is the yield volatility (a constant percentage of the rate), $r$ the current short rate, $dt$ the step in years and $dw$ a normal shock with standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$. Both the drift and the shock are proportional to $r$: the model works in percentage moves of the rate. The basis-point volatility is $\sigma r$. If the shock is supplied as a standard normal draw $z$, then $dw$ = $z\sqrt{dt}$.

**Applying it to this question**

$dw$ = $z\sqrt{dt}$ = −0.90 $\times\sqrt{1/12}$ = −0.90 × 0.288675 = −0.259808

Drift = $ar_{0} dt$ = 0.02 × 0.1125/12 = 0.000188 (0.0188%)

Shock = $\sigma r_{0} dw$ = 0.18 × 0.1125 × (−0.259808) = −0.005261 (−0.5261%)

$dr$ = 0.0188% − 0.5261% = −0.5074%

$r_{1/12}$ = 11.25% − 0.5074% = 10.7426%

The annualized basis-point volatility today is $\sigma r_{0}$ = 0.18 × 11.25% = 2.025% (202.5 bp); a −0.9 standard-deviation month moves the rate down about 53 bp. The 10-year swap rate is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** In Model 4 the shock is $\sigma\times r \times z\sqrt{dt}$: multiply by the rate (not $\sqrt{r}$, not 1) and by $\sqrt{dt}$ when given a standard normal draw.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 15, §15.2, Eq. 15.5 (OCR reads “ardt + crrdw”; reconstructed as $ar dt$+$\sigma r dw$, confirmed from the question bank’s worked solution to Schweser Module Quiz 15.2 Q1 for this LO). Schweser Reading 15, LO 15.e (“basis point volatility is equal to $\sigma r$”; formula image missing). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 e, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: time-conversion slip (the draw is not scaled by $\sqrt{dt}$): shock = 0.18 × 0.1125 × (−0.90) = −1.8225%, so 11.25% + 0.0188% − 1.8225% = 9.4462%. Correct if −0.90 were the already-scaled $dw$.

b.reason: It scales the standard normal draw by $\sqrt{dt}$, the drift by $dt$, and both terms by the current rate, exactly as Eq. 15.5 requires.

c.reason: Error type: time-conversion slip on the drift (not multiplied by $dt$): drift = 0.02 × 11.25% = 0.225%, so 11.25% + 0.225% − 0.5261% = 10.9489%. Correct only if $a$ = 0.02 were a monthly drift rate.

d.reason: Error type: sign error on the shock: 11.25% + 0.0188% + 0.5261% = 11.7949%. Correct if the draw were +0.90.

A supervisor at the UK regulator is reviewing a GBP rates desk that values options with the lognormal model $dr$ = $ar dt$ + $\sigma r dw$, where $\sigma$ = 15%. The desk’s model note must describe how the model’s volatility behaves when the short rate moves from 3% to 6%. Which of the following descriptions is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, $r$ is the short rate (continuously compounded, annualized), $dt$ is measured in years, and $dw$ has mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$ unless a question states that $dw$ is already scaled.

options.text: Yield volatility stays constant at 15%, while basis-point volatility equals $\sigma r$ and rises in proportion to the rate, from 45 bp to 90 bp per year.
Yield volatility stays constant at 15%, while basis-point volatility equals $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ and rises less than proportionally, from 260 bp to 367 bp per year.
Basis-point volatility stays constant at $\sigma$, while yield volatility falls as the rate rises, because yield volatility equals basis-point volatility divided by the rate.
Basis-point volatility equals $\sigma r$ and rises from 45 bp to 90 bp per year, and yield volatility rises in the same proportion, from 15% to 30%.

questions.solution:
**Yield volatility and basis-point volatility in the lognormal model**

Stem in one line: lognormal model with $\sigma$ = 15%; describe the volatility as $r$ moves from 3% to 6%.

**Concept and theory**

GARP §15.2: “Another popular specification is that the basis-point volatility is proportional to rate. In this case the parameter $\sigma$ is often called yield volatility.” Examples are the Courtadon model, $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$)$dt$ + $\sigma r dw$, and Model 4, $dr$ = $ar dt$ + $\sigma r dw$. “In these two specifications, yield volatility is constant but basis-point volatility equals $\sigma r$ and increases with the level of the rate.”

| Model | On $dw$ | Yield volatility | Basis-point volatility |
|---|---|---|---|
| Normal (Vasicek, Ho-Lee) | $\sigma$ | falls as $r$ rises | constant, $\sigma$ |
| CIR | $\sigma\sqrt{r}$ | not constant | $\sigma\sqrt{r}$, less than proportional |
| Lognormal (Model 4) | $\sigma r$ | constant, $\sigma$ | $\sigma r$, in proportion to $r$ |

**Applying it to this question**

$\sigma_{bp}$(3%) = $\sigma r$ = 0.15 × 0.03 = 0.0045 = 45 bp per year

$\sigma_{bp}$(6%) = 0.15 × 0.06 = 0.0090 = 90 bp per year

Doubling the rate doubles the basis-point volatility, and yield volatility stays at 15%. That is option A.

**Fragile fact.** Lognormal: the yield volatility is the constant; the basis-point volatility moves one-for-one in proportion with the rate.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 15, §15.2, Eq. 15.4 and 15.5 and the following paragraph. Schweser Reading 15, LO 15.e (“the yield volatility, $\sigma$, is constant, but basis point volatility increases with the level of the short-term rate”). Courtadon model is GARP-only. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 e, where it is Q5 of 12.

questions.solution:
**Calibrating CIR and lognormal parameters to a basis-point volatility**

Stem in one line: match 75 bp per year at $r$ = 2.50% with CIR and proportional specifications; find $\sigma_{\text{CIR}}$ and $\sigma_{Y}$ .

**Concept and theory**

GARP compares the three specifications by choosing each parameter so that basis-point volatility is identical at one reference rate (100 bp at 8% in GARP Eq. 15.6 to 15.8):

$\sigma_{bp}$ = target basis-point volatility (constant model)

$\sigma_{\text{CIR}}\sqrt{r^{*}}$ = $\sigma_{bp} \Rightarrow\sigma_{\text{CIR}}$ = $\sigma_{bp}/\sqrt{r^{*}}$

$\sigma_{Y} r^{*}$ = $\sigma_{bp} \Rightarrow\sigma_{Y}$ = $\sigma_{bp}/r^{*}$

where $r^{*}$ is the reference rate, written as a decimal. GARP’s own numbers: $\sigma_{\text{CIR}}$ = 0.01$/\sqrt{0.08}$ = 0.0354 and $\sigma_{Y}$ = 0.01/0.08 = 12.5%. GARP notes the units differ: basis-point volatility is in rate units, yield volatility is a percentage of the rate.

**Applying it to this question**

$\sigma_{bp}$ = 75 bp = 0.0075$, r^{*}$ = 0.025$, \sqrt{r^{*}}$ = 0.158114

$\sigma_{\text{CIR}}$ = 0.0075/0.158114 = 0.0474

$\sigma_{Y}$ = 0.0075/0.025 = 0.30 = 30.0%

Check: 0.0474 × 0.158114 = 0.0075 and 0.30 × 0.025 = 0.0075. At low rates a large yield volatility is needed to produce a modest basis-point volatility, because the rate it multiplies is small.

**Fragile fact.** Divide by $\sqrt{r}$ for CIR and by $r$ for the proportional model, with $r$ as a decimal; the yield volatility comes out as a percentage of the rate.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 15, §15.2, Eq. 15.6 to 15.8 and the units paragraph. GARP-only (Schweser omits the calibration example). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-15 e, where it is Q6 of 12.
