questions.question:
A model validator at an Australian bank is reviewing a candidate Gauss+ calibration on the AUD curve. Treat the half-life of a factor as the time for half of its gap to its target to decay, with the target held fixed. The candidate parameters are:

| Parameter | Estimate | Parameter | Estimate |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\alpha_{r}$ | 0.45 | $\sigma_{m}$ | 112 bps |
| $\alpha_{m}$ | 1.20 | $\sigma_{l}$ | 88 bps |
| $\alpha_{l}$ | 0.025 | $\rho$ | 0.25 |

Which of the following conclusions about the calibration is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, the Gauss+ model is written in the cascade form $dr_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt$, $dm_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{m}$($m_{t} - l_{t}$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{m}(\rho dW^{1}_{t}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}_{t})$, $dl_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{l}$($l_{t} - \mu$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}_{t}$, with $E$\[$dW^{1}_{t} dW^{2}_{t}$\] = 0.

options.text: Consistent with the model’s economic interpretation, because the long-term factor has by far the longest half-life, about 27.7 years.
Inconsistent, because the short-term rate’s half-life, about 1.54 years, exceeds the medium-term factor’s half-life, about 0.58 years.
Inconsistent, because the short-term rate’s half-life, about 2.22 years, exceeds the medium-term factor’s half-life, about 0.83 years.
Inconsistent, because the long-term factor should revert fastest of the three factors, yet its half-life is about 27.7 years.

questions.solution:
**Ordering of reversion speeds and half-lives**

Stem in one line: AUD calibration $\alpha_{r}$ = 0.45, $\alpha_{m}$ = 1.20, $\alpha_{l}$ = 0.025; is it consistent with the model’s interpretation?

**Concept and theory**

GARP: “The mean reversion parameters are expected to be consistent with these economic interpretations; that is, the short-term rate reverts quickly to the medium-term factor; the medium-term factor reverts more slowly to the long-term factor; and the long-term factor reverts slowest of all to its target.” So the structure requires

$\alpha_{r} > \alpha_{m} > \alpha_{l}.$

Speeds are often quoted as half-lives. If a gap $g$ to a fixed target decays as $g e^{-\alpha t}$, half of it is gone when $e^{-\alpha h}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ , so

$h$ = $\frac{\text{ln 2}}{\alpha}$

where $h$ is the half-life in years and $\alpha$ the speed per year (GARP Eq (16.8)). A larger speed means a shorter half-life, so the required ordering is $h_{r} < h_{m} < h_{l}$. In GARP’s estimated model the half-lives are about eight months for $r$, 13 months for $m$ and 42 years for $l$.

**Applying it to this question**

$h_{r}$ = ln 2/0.45 = 0.6931/0.45 = 1.540 years

$h_{m}$ = ln 2/1.20 = 0.6931/1.20 = 0.578 years

$h_{l}$ = ln 2/0.025 = 0.6931/0.025 = 27.73 years

The long factor is slowest, as required, but $h_{r} > h_{m}$: the short rate would close half its gap to $m$ almost three times more slowly than $m$ closes half its gap to $l$, contradicting a policy rate that reacts quickly to business-cycle conditions. The volatility parameters and $\rho$ are irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Fastest $r$, then $m$, slowest $l$: $\alpha_{r} > \alpha_{m} > \alpha_{l}$, so $h_{r} < h_{m} < h_{l}$, with $h$ = ln 2$/\alpha$, not 1$/\alpha$.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.2 The Gauss+ Model (speed ordering); §16.1 Eq (16.8) (half-life); Table 16.1 half-life column (0.66, 1.09, 42.01 years) as a check. Schweser Reading 16, “Gauss+ Model” (“the long-term factor shifts the slowest”). Parameters are hypothetical; estimating them is LO 16.d. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 a, where it is Q7 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: scope error (only one link checked). $h_{l}$ = 27.7 years is correctly computed and is the longest, but the ordering condition has two links, and the $r$ to $m$ link fails. A would be correct if $\alpha_{r}$ exceeded 1.20, for example $\alpha_{r}$ = 1.50.

b.reason: It identifies the violated link ($\alpha_{r} < \alpha_{m}$) and states the correct half-lives from $h$ = ln 2$/\alpha$.

c.reason: Error type: time-conversion slip (mean reversion time scale 1$/\alpha$ used for the half-life). 1/0.45 = 2.22 and 1/1.20 = 0.83 years. The conclusion is right but the numbers are not half-lives; they would be correct if the stem asked for 1$/\alpha$.

d.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the ordering. The long-term factor should revert slowest, so a 27.7-year half-life is exactly what the structure expects. D would be correct only if the cascade ran the other way.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a UK building society is reviewing a GBP model note on how the Gauss+ model reproduces the term structure of volatility. The note contains four statements:

I. In a model whose factors are all mean reverting, the term structure of volatility tends to slope downward with term.

II. Empirical and implied term structures of volatility tend to be hump-shaped, largely because of the behaviour of central banks.

III. In Gauss+, the absence of a random shock in the dynamics of $r_{t}$ keeps short-term rate volatility low, allowing the model to match the hump.

IV. In Gauss+, the hump arises because the long-term factor has both the largest volatility parameter and the fastest mean reversion of the factors.

Which of the statements are accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, the Gauss+ model is written in the cascade form $dr_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt$, $dm_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{m}$($m_{t} - l_{t}$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{m}(\rho dW^{1}_{t}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}_{t})$, $dl_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{l}$($l_{t} - \mu$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}_{t}$, with $E$\[$dW^{1}_{t} dW^{2}_{t}$\] = 0.

options.text: I and II only
II and III only
I, III and IV only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
**Mean reversion, a shock-free short rate and the hump**

Stem in one line: which of four statements on how Gauss+ reproduces the volatility term structure are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

A shock to a mean-reverting factor is expected to decay, so it moves near-term expectations a lot and far-term ones little: forward-rate volatility falls with term (in Vasicek, $\sigma e^{-kt}$). GARP: “mean-reverting factors generate a downward-sloping term structure of volatility.”

Now look at the data. GARP: “Largely because of central banks, however, empirical and implied term structures of volatility tend to have a hump; that is, volatility is low for very short-term rates before increasing to a peak at intermediate-term or longer rates.”

How does Gauss+ reconcile the two? By leaving the shock out of $dr_{t}$. GARP: “In the Gauss+ model, the lack of a random shock in the dynamics of $r$ keeps short-term rate volatility low. In this way, the Gauss+ model can match empirically observed hump-shaped term structures of volatility.”

| Curve segment | Observed volatility | Structural reason in Gauss+ |
|---|---|---|
| Very short end | Low | $r_{t}$ has no shock; it only follows $m_{t}$ |
| Intermediate | Peak | Shocks to $m_{t}$ and $l_{t}$ feed through |
| Long end | Declining | Mean reversion of the factors |

**Applying it to this question**

I: GARP’s general statement about mean-reverting factors. True. II: GARP’s empirical statement, including the actor (central banks). True. III: GARP’s mechanism. True. IV: In GARP’s estimates $\sigma_{l}$ = 96.4 bps is smaller than $\sigma_{m}$ = 109.2 bps, and $\alpha_{l}$ is the slowest speed by design; the hump is attributed to the shock-free short rate, not to $l$. False. So I, II and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Mean reversion alone slopes volatility down; the low short end comes from the absence of a shock in $r$; the actor behind the hump is the central bank.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.2 The Gauss+ Model (paragraph beginning “The lack of a volatility term in Equation (16.9)”); §16.1 on the Vasicek volatility term structure for the mean-reversion intuition. Schweser “Gauss+ Model”. Difference: Schweser states the hump without the shock-free mechanism; GARP gives it and is used. $\sigma_{m}$, $\sigma_{l}$ are from Table 16.1 (LO 16.d), cited only to refute IV.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 a, where it is Q8 of 15.

a.reason: **I and II only.** Error type: rejecting the true mechanism (hump credited to the volatility parameters alone, so III is dropped). Correct if III had said “a large shock in the dynamics of $r_{t}$”.

b.reason: **II and III only.** Error type: polarity flip on mean reversion (rejecting I means believing it makes volatility rise with term). Correct if I read “slope upward”.

c.reason: **I, III and IV.** Error type: accepts the sibling swap in IV (largest volatility and fastest reversion given to $l$, the slowest factor) and rejects II. Correct only for a fast, highly volatile long factor and a monotone empirical volatility curve.

d.reason: Statements I to III are each a GARP §16.2 sentence; IV contradicts both the stated mechanism and the speed ordering.

questions.question:
A bank supervisor reviewing a US bank’s Gauss+ implementation notes that the Federal Reserve changes its target rate in discrete steps on scheduled meeting dates, while the model’s short-term rate moves continuously. Which of the following best describes how the model’s structure treats this?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, the Gauss+ model is written in the cascade form $dr_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt$, $dm_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{m}$($m_{t} - l_{t}$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{m}(\rho dW^{1}_{t}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}_{t})$, $dl_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{l}$($l_{t} - \mu$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}_{t}$, with $E$\[$dW^{1}_{t} dW^{2}_{t}$\] = 0.

options.text: The model approximates the future outcomes of discrete policy decisions with a continuous process starting at today’s short rate; $m$ and $l$ move continuously because expectations move smoothly.
The model lets the short-term rate jump on meeting dates while $m$ and $l$ move continuously, because expectations of future short-term rates move smoothly over time.
The model lets $m$ and $l$ jump on meeting dates while the short-term rate moves continuously, because policy decisions change expectations of future short-term rates.
The model treats the discrete policy moves as the second source of risk, $dW^{2}_{t}$, which shocks the short-term rate directly on the scheduled meeting dates.

questions.solution:
**Continuous approximation of discrete policy moves**

Stem in one line: the Fed moves in discrete steps on meeting dates but model $r$ is continuous; how does the structure treat this?

**Concept and theory**

Different factors are meant to capture different kinds of movement.

- $m_{t}$ and $l_{t}$ move expectations of the short rate at future dates. GARP: “Because these expectations move smoothly over time, the medium- and long-term factors are assumed to move in a continuous fashion.”
- The real short rate is different. GARP: “The short-term rate, by contrast, changes in the real world by discrete amounts, on a set of fixed dates, according to central bank policy decisions. The model approximates the future outcomes of this process, however, by a continuous process starting at today’s short-term rate.”

So the model knowingly trades realism at the very short end for tractability: it does not model meeting-date jumps, it approximates them with a smooth, shock-free drift from today’s observed rate toward $m_{t}$.

**Applying it to this question**

The deciding facts are (i) the model does not put jumps in anywhere, (ii) $r$ is a continuous approximation starting from today’s rate, (iii) $m$ and $l$ are continuous because expectations are smooth. Only A has all three.

**Fragile fact.** Real world: $r$ discrete, on fixed dates. Model: $r$ continuous from today’s rate, no shock; $m$ and $l$ continuous because expectations are smooth.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.2 The Gauss+ Model (paragraph beginning “The medium- and long-term factors move expectations”). GARP-only; Schweser does not discuss the discrete versus continuous point.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 a, where it is Q9 of 15.

a.reason: It paraphrases the GARP §16.2 passage directly.

b.reason: Error type: scope error (real-world condition imported into the model). The real short rate jumps; the model’s $r$ does not. B would be correct for a jump-diffusion extension of the model.

c.reason: Error type: role misassignment (discreteness moved to the factors). $m$ and $l$ are explicitly continuous because expectations move smoothly. C would be correct only if expectations themselves jumped on meeting dates in the model.

d.reason: Error type: role misassignment of a risk source. $dW^{2}_{t}$ shocks only $m_{t}$ (through the $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}$ loading); nothing shocks $r_{t}$ directly. D would be correct only if $dr_{t}$ contained a $dW^{2}_{t}$ term.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a US macro hedge fund extracts Gauss+ factors from daily USD market data. During a period when the policy rate was close to zero, the extracted medium-term factor $m_{t}$ fell deeply negative; when rates were high it closely tracked the two-year forward rate. Which interpretation is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, the Gauss+ model is written in the cascade form $dr_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt$, $dm_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{m}$($m_{t} - l_{t}$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{m}(\rho dW^{1}_{t}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}_{t})$, $dl_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{l}$($l_{t} - \mu$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}_{t}$, with $E$\[$dW^{1}_{t} dW^{2}_{t}$\] = 0.

options.text: The extraction has failed, because $m_{t}$ is by construction the model’s two-year forward rate and so cannot fall far below the level of the policy rate.
$m_{t}$ is a shadow rate in the sense of the level the short-term rate would have today if it were not bounded, so the model’s current short-term rate is negative.
$m_{t}$ acts as a forward shadow rate that reflects expectations of the future short-term rate, so it can fall deeply negative near the zero lower bound.
Negative values of $m_{t}$ reflect a negative risk premium, because in the model’s application the medium-term factor is the factor that earns the risk premium.

questions.solution:
**The medium-term factor as a forward shadow rate**

Stem in one line: extracted $m_{t}$ tracks the two-year forward when rates are high but goes deeply negative near zero; interpretation?

**Concept and theory**

GARP: the factors “can be thought of as rates,” but “$m$ and $l$ are in no way those forward rates themselves, in the way that $r$ equals the fed funds rate.”

When factors are extracted from market data (GARP Figure 16.8): “When rates are high, this factor closely tracks the two-year forward rate, confirming that the medium-term factor loosely corresponds to where the market expects the short-term rate to be in two years. When rates are low, however, near the zero lower bound, the medium-term factor can fall into deeply negative territory. In this sense, the medium-term factor is a ‘forward shadow rate’ that reflects future expectations of the short-term rate.” GARP also contrasts this with the more common meaning: “This interpretation differs from models in which the ‘shadow rate’ is what the short-term rate would be now if it were not bounded above zero.”

|  | Gauss+ forward shadow rate ($m_{t}$) | Conventional shadow rate |  |
|---|---|---|---|
| Refers to | Expected short rate in the future (about two years) | Today’s short rate if bounded | un- |
| Negative near zero bound | Yes, deeply | Yes |  |
| Today’s model $r$ negative | No; $r$ is the policy rate | Yes, by definition |  |

**Applying it to this question**

The stem’s pattern is exactly what GARP reports, so the forward shadow rate reading, C, applies.

**Fragile fact.** Gauss+ “forward shadow rate” is about the future short rate; the conventional shadow rate is about the short rate now.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.2 (“can be thought of as rates”; risk premium earned only by the long-term factor) and §16.3 (time-series properties, Figure 16.8). GARP-only; Schweser says only that $m$ and $l$ are not tied to particular forward rates (placed under its LO 16.c). Boundary call: used here because it interprets a structural factor.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 a, where it is Q10 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: scope error (“loosely corresponds” turned into identity). $m$ tracks the two-year forward only when rates are high. Correct if $m$ were defined as that forward rate.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (conventional shadow-rate definition), which GARP explicitly distinguishes; the model’s $r$ is the policy rate, not negative. Correct for a shadow-rate model of the current short rate.

c.reason: GARP §16.3: $m$ is “a ‘forward shadow rate’ that reflects future expectations of the short-term rate” and “can fall into deeply negative territory” near the zero lower bound.

d.reason: Error type: role misassignment of the risk premium. In GARP’s application, “only the long-term factor earns a risk premium”. D would be correct only if the medium-term factor were the one assumed to carry the premium.

questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee of a Chinese bank sees that a CNY Gauss+ calibration gives $\mu$ = 9.8% while the policy rate is about 2%, and asks whether the model therefore forecasts a policy rate near 9.8%. Which response is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, the Gauss+ model is written in the cascade form $dr_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt$, $dm_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{m}$($m_{t} - l_{t}$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{m}(\rho dW^{1}_{t}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}_{t})$, $dl_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{l}$($l_{t} - \mu$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}_{t}$, with $E$\[$dW^{1}_{t} dW^{2}_{t}$\] = 0.

options.text: Yes: $\mu$ is the real-world long-run expectation of the policy rate, so the calibration implies the market expects the central bank to set a rate near 9.8% eventually.
No: the equations are risk-neutral dynamics, so $\mu$ can be thought of as including both a long-term expectation of the short rate and a risk premium, and $l$ reverts to it very slowly.
No: $\mu$ is the direct target of the short-term rate, so the short-term rate is pulled straight toward 9.8% and gets halfway there within one short-rate half-life.
No: $\mu$ is purely a risk premium, because the long-term expectations of inflation and the real interest rate are carried entirely by the medium-term factor $m_{t}$.

questions.solution:
**Risk-neutral dynamics and the meaning of $\mu$**

Stem in one line: CNY calibration gives $\mu$ = 9.8% with a 2% policy rate; does the model forecast a 9.8% policy rate?

**Concept and theory**

Bond prices reflect both expectations of future rates and a premium for bearing rate risk, and prices alone cannot separate the two. In the Vasicek section GARP shows that a risk premium $\lambda$ is “indistinguishable from a drift”, so the risk-neutral long-run value $\theta$ combines the real-world long-run rate and the premium: $\theta$ = $r_{\infty}$ + $\lambda/k$.

Gauss+ inherits this. GARP: the long-term factor “reverts to a constant, $\mu$, which, as in the Vasicek model, can be thought of as including both a long-term expectation of the short-term rate and a risk premium.” And: “Equations (16.9) through (16.12) are the risk-neutral dynamics of the model. Additional assumptions allow for the identification of an implicit risk premium,” with GARP’s application “assuming that only the long-term factor earns a risk premium.” On GARP’s own estimate of over 10%: it “might seem high . . . but the long-term factor reverts very slowly to this target, and that target includes a risk premium.”

**Applying it to this question**

A high $\mu$ is not a policy-rate forecast. Two reasons, both structural: $\mu$ is a risk-neutral constant containing a risk premium, and only $l$ reverts to it, very slowly. B states both.

**Fragile fact.** $\mu$ = long-run expectation plus risk premium; only $l$ (the slowest factor) reverts to it.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.2 The Gauss+ Model (“as in the Vasicek model, can be thought of as including both” and “risk-neutral dynamics”); §16.1 Eq (16.3) for the Vasicek analogue; §16.3 for the comment on $\mu$ above 10%. GARP-only for the risk-premium content; Schweser states only that $\mu$ is fixed. The 9.8% figure is hypothetical.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 a, where it is Q11 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: scope error (risk premium dropped; risk-neutral read as real-world). A would be correct only if the risk premium were zero, so that risk-neutral and true dynamics coincided.

b.reason: It combines the GARP statements that the dynamics are risk-neutral, that $\mu$ includes a risk premium, and that $l$ reverts to $\mu$ very slowly.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap with Vasicek, where $r$ reverts directly to $\theta$. In Gauss+ $r$ reverts to $m$, and only $l$ reverts to $\mu$, with a half-life of decades in GARP’s estimates. C would be correct in a one-factor model with $\theta$ = 9.8%.

d.reason: Error type: role misassignment twice: long-run inflation and real-rate expectations are carried by $l$, not $m$, and $\mu$ contains an expectation component as well as the premium. D would be correct only if $\mu$ were defined as a pure premium.

questions.question:
The treasurer of a German insurer hedges EUR liabilities with a Gauss+ model. A recalibration raises $\alpha_{m}$ materially while leaving $\alpha_{r}$, $\alpha_{l}$ and all volatility parameters unchanged. Which consequence for the model’s term structure is most likely?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, the Gauss+ model is written in the cascade form $dr_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt$, $dm_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{m}$($m_{t} - l_{t}$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{m}(\rho dW^{1}_{t}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}_{t})$, $dl_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{l}$($l_{t} - \mu$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}_{t}$, with $E$\[$dW^{1}_{t} dW^{2}_{t}$\] = 0.

options.text: The medium-term factor would converge more slowly to $l_{t}$, so its influence on forward rates would extend further out along the curve.
The long-term factor’s effect on longer-term yields would become less parallel, because $l_{t}$ would converge to $\mu$ more quickly.
Changes in the factors $m_{t}$ and $l_{t}$ would make their way into the term structure of rates more slowly than before the recalibration.
The medium-term factor would converge more quickly to $l_{t}$, so changes in $m_{t}$ would have less effect on longer-term yields.

questions.solution:
**How reversion speeds shape where factors act on the curve**

Stem in one line: $\alpha_{m}$ is raised, all else fixed; most likely effect on the term structure?

**Concept and theory**

The structure of the cascade determines how a move in a factor spreads along the curve. GARP states the three comparative statics:

- “the larger $\alpha_{r}$, the faster changes to the factors $m$ and $l$ make their way into the term structure of rates.”
- “The larger $\alpha_{m}$, the faster $m$ converges to $l$, and the less $m$ affects longer-term yields.”
- “the smaller $\alpha_{l}$, the slower $l$ converges to $\mu$, and the more similar or parallel is the effect of $l$ on all longer-term yields.”

Intuition: a shock to $m$ is a temporary deviation of $m$ from $l$. The faster $m$ is pulled back to $l$, the sooner the shock dies, so it shows up only in nearer forward rates. In GARP’s estimated model (Figure 16.7) the short factor affects only the very short end, the medium factor drives the two- to three-year part, and the long factor has its biggest impact at six to eight years and is the sole driver beyond ten years.

**Applying it to this question**

Only $\alpha_{m}$ changes, and it rises. The $\alpha_{m}$ rule applies: $m$ converges faster to $l$, and $m$’s footprint retreats toward the shorter end. That is D.

**Fragile fact.** Larger $\alpha_{m}$: $m$ matters less for long yields. Smaller $\alpha_{l}$: $l$ is more parallel. Larger $\alpha_{r}$: factors pass into the curve faster.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.3 A Practical Estimation Method (paragraph beginning “Although the model ultimately fits the two- and 10-year forward rates”) and Figure 16.7 discussion. GARP-only; Schweser has no counterpart. Boundary call: this sits in GARP’s estimation section but describes an implication of the structure, so it is used here; the estimation procedure itself (LO 16.d) is not tested.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 a, where it is Q12 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip. A larger $\alpha_{m}$ means faster convergence and a shorter reach. A would be correct if $\alpha_{m}$ were lowered.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap ($\alpha_{l}$ rule applied to $\alpha_{m}$). The parallelism of $l$’s effect depends on $\alpha_{l}$, which is unchanged. B would be correct if $\alpha_{l}$ were raised.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap ($\alpha_{r}$ rule) with a polarity twist. The speed at which $m$ and $l$ feed into the curve depends on $\alpha_{r}$, which is unchanged. C would be correct if $\alpha_{r}$ were lowered.

d.reason: It is GARP’s $\alpha_{m}$ statement applied to an increase.

questions.question:
A risk consultant presenting to newly hired analysts at a Brazilian bank shows four statements about the random structure of the Gauss+ model used on the BRL curve:

I. The model has three state variables: the short-term rate, the medium-term factor and the long-term factor.

II. The model has two sources of risk, $dW^{1}_{t}$ and $dW^{2}_{t}$, which are uncorrelated with each other.

III. The long-term factor is shocked by both $dW^{1}_{t}$ and $dW^{2}_{t}$, which is why its changes are correlated with those of the medium-term factor.

IV. The correlation between changes in $m_{t}$ and changes in $l_{t}$ equals $\rho$, whatever the values of $\sigma_{m}$ and $\sigma_{l}$.

Which of the statements are accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, the Gauss+ model is written in the cascade form $dr_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt$, $dm_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{m}$($m_{t} - l_{t}$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{m}(\rho dW^{1}_{t}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}_{t})$, $dl_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{l}$($l_{t} - \mu$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}_{t}$, with $E$\[$dW^{1}_{t} dW^{2}_{t}$\] = 0.

options.text: I, II and IV only
I and II only
I, II and III only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
**State variables, sources of risk and the correlation $\rho$**

Stem in one line: which of four statements on the random structure of Gauss+ are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Write the shocks explicitly:

shock to $m_{t}$ : $\sigma_{m}(\rho dW^{1}_{t}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}_{t}),$ shock to $l_{t}$ : $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}_{t}, E$\[$dW^{1}_{t} dW^{2}_{t}$\] = 0.

$dW^{1}_{t}$ is common to both factors; $dW^{2}_{t}$ is private to $m_{t}$. Then (GARP Eqs (16.13) to (16.15)):

SD($dm_{t}$) = $\sigma_{m}\sqrt{\rho\text{2 + (1} - \rho\text{2)}} \sqrt{dt}$ = $\sigma_{m}\sqrt{dt}$

Cov($dm_{t}, dl_{t}$) = $\sigma_{m}\rho\sigma_{l}$ Var($dW^{1}_{t}$) = $\rho\sigma_{m}\sigma_{l} dt$

Corr($dm_{t}, dl_{t}$) = $\frac{\rho\sigma_{m}\sigma_{l} dt}{\sigma_{m}\sqrt{dt} \times\sigma_{l}\sqrt{dt}}$ = $\rho$

The odd-looking weights simply guarantee that $m$’s shock has volatility $\sigma_{m}\sqrt{dt}$ and correlation $\rho$ with $l$’s shock. Three state variables ($r$, $m$, $l$), two sources of risk ($dW^{1}$, $dW^{2}$).

**Applying it to this question**

I: true (GARP: “three state variables . . . $r$, $m$, and $l$”). II: true (Eq (16.12): zero correlation). III: false; $l$ loads only on $dW^{1}_{t}$; the correlation arises because $m$ also loads on $dW^{1}_{t}$. IV: true; the volatilities cancel in the correlation. So I, II and IV only.

**Fragile fact.** $l$ gets $dW^{1}$ only; $m$ gets both. Correlation is $\rho$; covariance is $\rho\sigma_{m}\sigma_{l} dt$.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.2 The Gauss+ Model, Eqs (16.10) to (16.15) and the “three factors, but only two sources of risk” paragraph. Eqs (16.10) and (16.13) are garbled in the GARP extract; the $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}$ loading was confirmed from the question bank’s worked solutions (Q739, Q759) and is consistent with GARP Eq (16.14). Schweser: “the changes in $m_{t}$ and $l_{t}$ are related through the parameter $\rho$”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 a, where it is Q13 of 15.

a.reason: It accepts exactly the three GARP statements and rejects the misplaced loading.

b.reason: **I and II only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement. A candidate who thinks the correlation must depend on $\sigma_{m}$ and $\sigma_{l}$ (confusing covariance with correlation) rejects IV. B would be correct if IV said “the covariance equals $\rho$”.

c.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: role misassignment accepted in III (the private shock $dW^{2}_{t}$ attributed to $l$) and the true IV rejected. C would be correct if $l$ loaded on both shocks and $m$ on one.

d.reason: **II, III and IV.** Error type: rejecting the state-variable count in I and accepting the misloading in III. Rejecting I usually comes from equating “factor” with “source of risk”. D would be correct only for a model with two state variables in which $l$ carried both shocks.

questions.question:
A quantitative risk analyst at a UK bank is checking the factor-shock module of a GBP Gauss+ engine. Use a daily step $dt$ = 1/250 year. The inputs are:

| Input | Value | Input | Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\sigma_{m}$ | 120 bps per year | $\alpha_{m}$ | 0.64 |
| $\sigma_{l}$ | 85 bps per year | $m_{t} - l_{t}$ | 0.50% |
| $\rho$ | 0.30 |  |  |

What is the covariance of the daily changes $dm_{t}$ and $dl_{t}$, in basis points squared?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, the Gauss+ model is written in the cascade form $dr_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt$, $dm_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{m}$($m_{t} - l_{t}$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{m}(\rho dW^{1}_{t}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}_{t})$, $dl_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{l}$($l_{t} - \mu$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}_{t}$, with $E$\[$dW^{1}_{t} dW^{2}_{t}$\] = 0.
questions.solution:
**Covariance of the factor shocks**

Stem in one line: $\sigma_{m}$ = 120 bps, $\sigma_{l}$ = 85 bps, $\rho$ = 0.30, $dt$ = 1/250; covariance of daily $dm_{t}$ and $dl_{t} \text{in bp}^{2}$.

**Concept and theory**

Over a short step the drifts are deterministic, so they add nothing to variances or covariances; only the shock terms matter. With $m$’s shock $\sigma_{m}$($\rho dW^{1}_{t}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}_{t}$) and $l$’s shock $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}_{t}$, only the common $dW^{1}_{t}$ part covaries, and Var($dW^{1}_{t}$) = $dt$ (not $\sqrt{dt}$, which is the standard deviation). GARP Eq (16.14):

Cov($dm_{t}, dl_{t}$) = $\rho\sigma_{m} \sigma_{l} dt$

where $\rho$ is the correlation parameter, $\sigma_{m}, \sigma_{l}$ are annual volatility parameters and $dt$ is the step in years.

**Applying it to this question**

$\sigma_{m}\sigma_{l}$ = 120 × 85 = 10,200 $\text{bp}^{2}$ per year

$\rho\sigma_{m}\sigma_{l}$ = 0.30 × 10,200 = 3,060 $\text{bp}^{2}$ per year

Cov($dm_{t}, dl_{t}$) = 3,060 $\times\frac{1}{250}$ = 12.24 $\text{bp}^{2}$

Cross-check: SD($dm_{t}$) = 120$\sqrt{1/250}$ = 7.59 bps, SD($dl_{t}$) = 85$\sqrt{1/250}$ = 5.38 bps, and 12.24/(7.59× 5.38) = 0.30 = $\rho$. The inputs $\alpha_{m}$ = 0.64 and $m_{t} - l_{t}$ = 0.50% are irrelevant: they set the deterministic drift of $m$ (about −0.13 bp per day) and do not affect the covariance. The number means that on a typical day the medium- and long-term factors move together only weakly, with correlation 0.30.

**Fragile fact.** Covariance scales with $dt$, standard deviation with $\sqrt{dt}$; only the $dW^{1}$ component of $m$ covaries with $l$.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.2 The Gauss+ Model, Eqs (16.10), (16.11), (16.14) and (16.15). Eq (16.10)’s $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}$ loading is garbled in the GARP extract and was confirmed from the question bank’s worked solutions (Q739, Q759); Eq (16.14) itself is legible: Cov\[$\sigma_{m}$($\rho dW^{1}$ +$\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}dW^{2}$)$, \sigma_{l}dW^{1}$\] = $\rho\sigma_{m}\sigma_{l} dt$. Schweser omits the formula. All options computed in calc.py.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 a, where it is Q14 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: correlation misuse ($\rho^{2}$ for $\rho$). 0.09 × 10,200/250 = 3.672. $\rho^{2}$ is the share of $m$’s variance that comes from the common shock, not the covariance weight. Correct only if the stem asked for $\rho^{2}\sigma_{m}\sigma_{l} dt$.

b.reason: Error type: wrong input twin (the private-shock loading $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}$ = 0.954 used instead of $\rho$). 0.954 × 10,200/250 = 38.92. Correct only if $l$ loaded on $dW^{2}_{t}$ rather than $dW^{1}_{t}$.

d.reason: Error type: time-conversion slip ($\sqrt{dt}$ instead of $dt$). 3,060 $\times\sqrt{1/250}$ = 3,060 × 0.06325 = 193.53. Each shock has standard deviation scaling with $\sqrt{dt}$, so the product of two scales with $dt$. Correct only if the stem asked for $\rho\sigma_{m}\sigma_{l}\sqrt{dt}$, which is not a covariance.

questions.question:
A senior model validator at a Japanese bank receives a proposal to add an independent shock to the short-term rate, so that $dr_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{r} dW^{3}_{t}$, with the equations for $m_{t}$ and $l_{t}$ unchanged. Which consequence of this change is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Throughout, the Gauss+ model is written in the cascade form $dr_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt$, $dm_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{m}$($m_{t} - l_{t}$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{m}(\rho dW^{1}_{t}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}_{t})$, $dl_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{l}$($l_{t} - \mu$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}_{t}$, with $E$\[$dW^{1}_{t} dW^{2}_{t}$\] = 0.

options.text: Short-term rate volatility would fall further, sharpening the hump in the volatility term structure, while the model would keep three factors and two sources of risk.
The feature that keeps short-term rate volatility low would be lost, weakening the hump fit, and with three sources of risk for three factors the “+” would no longer apply.
The model would reduce to a Vasicek model, because the short-term rate would once again carry its own shock and revert to a single fixed long-run target.
The volatility term structure would be unaffected because it depends only on $\sigma_{m}$, $\sigma_{l}$ and $\rho$, and the “+” would still apply because $r_{t}$ remains a state variable.

questions.solution:
**Adding a shock to the short-term rate**

Stem in one line: a proposal adds $\sigma_{r} dW^{3}_{t}$ to $dr_{t}$; most accurate consequence?

**Concept and theory**

Run the LO in reverse: remove a structural feature and predict what the model can no longer do. Two features of Gauss+ depend on the absence of a shock in $dr_{t}$:

| Feature | Gauss+ as specified | With $\sigma_{r} dW^{3}_{t}$ added |
|---|---|---|
| Short-end volatility | Kept low: “the lack of a random shock in the dynamics of $r$ keeps short-term rate volatility low” | Driven directly by $\sigma_{r}$; no longer held low by construction |
| Hump fit | Matches hump-shaped empirical volatility | Mechanism for the low short end removed; hump harder to match |
| State variables vs risks | 3 factors, 2 sources of risk | 3 factors, 3 sources of risk |
| The “+” | “a factor or state variable that is not also a source of risk” | No such factor; the “+” no longer applies |
| Economic reading of $r$ | Pegged policy rate over $dt$ | Randomly shocked over $dt$ |

Mean reversion still slopes the long end down; the low short end came from the shock-free $r$.

**Applying it to this question**

Both consequences are needed: loss of the low-short-end mechanism and loss of the “+”. Only B has both.

**Fragile fact.** The shock-free short rate does two jobs: it keeps short-end volatility low (hump) and it is the reason for the “+”.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.2 The Gauss+ Model (paragraphs on the lack of a volatility term in Equation (16.9) and on the name). Schweser Reading 16, “Gauss+ Model” (hump-shaped volatility). GARP-only for the mechanism and the name; the modified model is hypothetical.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 a, where it is Q15 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip. Adding a shock raises short-term volatility; and with a third shock the model would no longer have only two sources of risk. A would be correct only if the proposal removed a shock.

b.reason: GARP §16.2 ties the hump fit and the “+” to the shock-free $r$; adding $dW^{3}_{t}$ removes both.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap with Vasicek (one factor, fixed $\theta$). The modified model keeps $m$ and $l$, and $r$ still reverts to the moving $m$. Correct only if $m$ and $l$ were deleted and $r$ reverted to a constant.

d.reason: Error type: scope error plus absolute claim. The short end depends directly on whether $r$ is shocked, and the “+” requires a state variable that is not a risk source, not merely that $r$ is a state variable. D would be correct for a change to $m$ or $l$ that left $dr_{t}$ shock-free.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at a Canadian pension plan is presenting to newly hired analysts on how the two short-rate models move rates when no shock occurs. Both models have been fitted to the same CAD curve, and today’s state is:

| Model | Quantity | Value |
|---|---|---|
| Vasicek | Short rate $r$ | 4.00% |
| Vasicek | Long-run level $\theta$ | 3.00% |
| Vasicek | Volatility $\sigma$ | 1.10% |
| Gauss+ | Short rate $r_{t}$ | 4.00% |
| Gauss+ | Medium-term factor $m_{t}$ | 5.00% |
| Gauss+ | Long-term factor $l_{t}$ | 3.50% |
| Gauss+ | Long-run constant $\mu$ | 3.00% |

Which of the following best describes the direction of the short rate’s instantaneous drift today in each model?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are continuously compounded and annualized, time is measured in years, and “Gauss+” refers to the cascade form of the model in the reading.

options.text: The short rate is expected to fall in the Vasicek model and to fall in the Gauss+ model, because in each model it is pulled toward the fixed level of 3.00%.
The short rate is expected to fall in the Vasicek model and to rise in the Gauss+ model, because in the Gauss+ model it is pulled toward the medium-term factor.
The short rate is expected to fall in the Vasicek model and to stay unchanged in the Gauss+ model, because in the Gauss+ model it carries no shock term.
The short rate is expected to fall in the Vasicek model and to fall in the Gauss+ model, because in the Gauss+ model it is pulled toward the long-term factor.

questions.solution:
**Where each model pulls the short rate**

Stem in one line: $r$ = 4.00% in both models; Vasicek $\theta$ = 3.00%; Gauss+ $m_{t}$ = 5.00%, $l_{t}$ = 3.50%, $\mu$ = 3.00%; direction of the short rate’s drift in each model.

**Concept and theory**

Both models are mean reverting, but they disagree on what the short rate reverts to.

Vasicek. The risk-neutral dynamics are

$dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$

where $r$ is the short rate, $k$ the mean reversion parameter, $\theta$ the long-run value of the short rate (a constant), $\sigma$ the volatility parameter and $dw$ a normal shock with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$. GARP: “When below its long-term value, the short-term rate is expected to increase; when above its long-term value, the short-term rate is expected to decrease.” The target never moves.

Gauss+. The cascade form is

$dr_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt$

$dm_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{m}$($m_{t} - l_{t}$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{m} (\rho dW^{1}_{t}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}_{t})$

$dl_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{l}$($l_{t} - \mu$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}_{t}$

where $m_{t}$ and $l_{t}$ are the medium- and long-term factors, $\alpha_{r}, \alpha_{m}, \alpha_{l}$ the mean reversion parameters, $\sigma_{m}, \sigma_{l}$ the factor volatilities, $\rho$ their correlation and $\mu$ a constant. The short rate chases $m_{t}$, which chases $l_{t}$, which chases $\mu$. Schweser: “the only fixed parameter here is $\mu$, while the other factors are dynamically moving targets.”

|  | Vasicek | Gauss+ |
|---|---|---|
| Short rate reverts to | Fixed $\theta$ | Moving $m_{t}$ |
| Fixed anchor | $\theta$ | $\mu$ (reached only via $l_{t}$) |
| Sign of short-rate drift set by | $\theta- r$ | $m_{t} - r_{t}$ |

**Applying it to this question**

Vasicek: $\theta- r$ = 3.00% − 4.00% = −1.00%, so the drift $k$($\theta- r$) is negative: the short rate is expected to fall.

Gauss+: $r_{t} - m_{t}$ = 4.00% − 5.00% = −1.00%, so the drift $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$) is positive: the short rate is expected to rise toward $m_{t}$. That $m_{t}$ is itself drifting down toward $l_{t}$ = 3.50%, and $l_{t}$ toward $\mu$ = 3.00%, does not change the sign of the short rate’s drift today. The Vasicek $\sigma$ = 1.10% is irrelevant to a drift question.

**Fragile fact.** In Gauss+ the short rate’s drift has the sign of $m_{t} - r_{t}$, not $\mu- r_{t}$. A Gauss+ short rate can be expected to rise while sitting above the long-run constant.

**Reference**

LO 16.b (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 16, §16.1 The Vasicek Model (eq. 16.1) and §16.2 The Gauss+ Model (eqs. 16.9 to 16.12). Schweser Reading 16, “Vasicek Model” and “Gauss+ Model”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 b, where it is Q1 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap. It imports Vasicek’s fixed-target logic into Gauss+, as if $r_{t}$ reverted directly to $\mu$. It would be correct if the question asked about the long-term factor $l_{t}$ = 3.50%, which does revert to the fixed $\mu$ = 3.00% and so drifts down.

b.reason: GARP §16.2: the short rate “is pushed gradually . . . toward the medium-term factor, $m$, which in turn reverts to the long factor, $l$”; Vasicek reverts to the fixed $\theta$ (§16.1). With $r$ above $\theta$ but below $m_{t}$, the two models give opposite drifts.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap, “no shock” confused with “no drift”. The Gauss+ short rate has no random term, but it still has the drift $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$). It would be correct only if $r_{t}$ = $m_{t}$, the equilibrium case in which the short rate does not change.

d.reason: Error type: role misassignment. It gives the short rate the medium-term factor’s target. It would be correct if the question asked about $m_{t}$: with $m_{t}$ = 5.00% $> l_{t}$ = 3.50%, the medium-term factor drifts down toward $l_{t}$.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Swiss bank is contrasting the one-month behaviour of the short rate in a Vasicek model with that in a Gauss+ model. The risk-neutral Vasicek process is $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$, where $dw$ is normal with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$. Use $dt$ = 1/12.

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Current short rate $r_{0}$ | 1.20% |
| Long-run level $\theta$ | 4.40% |
| Mean reversion parameter $k$ | 0.30 |
| Volatility $\sigma$ | 0.80% |
| 10-year CHF swap rate | 2.35% |

Which of the following correctly gives the expected change in the Vasicek short rate over the month and the standard deviation of its shock over the month?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are continuously compounded and annualized, time is measured in years, and “Gauss+” refers to the cascade form of the model in the reading.

options.text: Expected change +96.0 bp; shock standard deviation 23.1 bp
Expected change +8.0 bp; shock standard deviation 6.7 bp
Expected change −8.0 bp; shock standard deviation 23.1 bp
Expected change +8.0 bp; shock standard deviation 23.1 bp

questions.solution:
**Vasicek drift and shock over one month**

Stem in one line: $r_{0}$ = 1.20%, $\theta$ = 4.40%, $k$ = 0.30, $\sigma$ = 0.80%, $dt$ = 1/12; expected monthly change and monthly shock standard deviation.

**Concept and theory**

In the Vasicek model “the instantaneous change in the short-term rate, $dr$, is determined by a trend or drift plus a random fluctuation or shock” (GARP §16.1).

- Drift per year: $k$($\theta- r$). Because all variables are annualized, “the $dt$ factor adjusts for the actual passage of time”, so the expected change over $dt$ is $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$.
- Shock: $\sigma dw$, where $dw$ is normal with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$. The shock over $dt$ therefore has standard deviation $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$: volatility scales with the square root of time, the drift with time itself.

GARP’s own illustration: $r$ = 2%, $k$ = 0.0165, $\theta$ = 11% give a drift of 14.85 bp per year, about 1.2 bp per month; $\sigma$ = 0.95% gives a monthly shock volatility of 95 $\times\sqrt{1/12}$ = 27.4 bp. In the Gauss+ model the corresponding short-rate shock is zero: $r_{t}$ moves only through its drift toward $m_{t}$.

**Applying it to this question**

Annual drift = $k$($\theta- r_{0}$) = 0.30 × (4.40% − 1.20%)

= 0.30 × 3.20% = 0.96% = 96.0 bp per year

Expected change over the month = 96.0 $\times\frac{1}{12}$ = +8.0 bp

$\sqrt{dt}$ = $\sqrt{1/12}$ = 0.288675

Shock sd over the month = $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ = 80 bp × 0.288675 = 23.09 bp ≈ 23.1 bp

Meaning: the short rate is expected to rise by 8 bp in the month because it sits below $\theta$, but a one-standard-deviation shock is almost three times as large as the drift. The 10-year swap rate is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Drift scales with $dt$; volatility scales with $\sqrt{dt}$. The sign of the drift follows $\theta- r$.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.1 The Vasicek Model (eq. 16.1 and the worked drift and shock example). Schweser Reading 16, “Modeling Interest Rates” and “Vasicek Model” (equation images missing in the Schweser extract). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 b, where it is Q2 of 15.

a.reason: **(+96.0 bp; 23.1 bp).** Error type: time-conversion slip. The annual drift 0.30 × 3.20% = 96 bp was not multiplied by $dt$ = 1/12. Correct if the question asked for the expected change per year (a one-year horizon with the drift held at today’s value).

b.reason: **(+8.0 bp; 6.7 bp).** Error type: time-conversion slip on volatility. 80 × 1/12 = 6.67 bp scales volatility by $dt$ instead of $\sqrt{dt}$. Correct only for a deterministic quantity of 80 bp per year spread evenly over the month, as with the drift; a random shock whose $dw$ has standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$ scales with $\sqrt{dt}$.

c.reason: **(−8.0 bp; 23.1 bp).** Error type: sign error. Using $k$($r_{0} - \theta$) pushes the rate away from $\theta$. Correct if the short rate sat 3.20% above $\theta$ ($r_{0}$ = 7.60%), so that the pull were downward.

d.reason: Drift scaled by $dt$ and shock scaled by $\sqrt{dt}$, exactly as in GARP §16.1: +8.0 bp and 23.1 bp.

questions.question:
A model validator at an Indian bank is reviewing an INR model-documentation note that compares the sources of randomness in the Vasicek and Gauss+ models. The note contains four statements:

I. In the Vasicek model, the shock to the short rate over an interval $dt$ is normally distributed with mean zero and standard deviation $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$.

II. In the Gauss+ model, the short rate receives its own shock, scaled by a volatility parameter $\sigma_{r}$, in addition to being pulled toward the medium-term factor.

III. The Vasicek model has one state variable and one source of risk, whereas the Gauss+ model has three state variables but only two sources of risk.

IV. In the Vasicek model, because the short rate mean reverts, the standard deviation of the short rate at a future date $t$ equals $\sigma\sqrt{t}$.

Which of the statements are accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are continuously compounded and annualized, time is measured in years, and “Gauss+” refers to the cascade form of the model in the reading.

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
I, III and IV only
II and IV only

questions.solution:
**Sources of randomness in the two models**

Stem in one line: audit four statements on shocks, state variables and the dispersion of the short rate.

**Concept and theory**

|  | Vasicek | Gauss+ |
|---|---|---|
| Shock on the short rate | $\sigma dw$, sd $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ | None: $dr_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt$ |
| Shocks elsewhere | None (one factor) | $dW^{1}$ on $l_{t}$; $dW^{1}$ and $dW^{2}$ on $m_{t}$ |
| State variables | 1 ($r$) | 3 ($r_{t}, m_{t}, l_{t}$) |
| Sources of risk | 1 ($dw$) | 2 ($dW^{1}, dW^{2}$) |

Why no shock on the Gauss+ short rate? GARP: the equation “is meant to reflect how central banks conduct rate policy”: the policy rate is pegged at a target over a very short interval and moved over time. The model’s parameters are $\alpha_{r}, \alpha_{m}, \alpha_{l}, \sigma_{m}, \sigma_{l}, \rho$ and $\mu$: there is no $\sigma_{r}$. GARP: the Gauss+ model “strictly speaking, has three factors, but only two sources of risk”.

Dispersion in Vasicek. The variance of the short rate at time $t$ is $V$ \[$r_{t}$\] = $\sigma^{2}$(1$-e^{-2kt}$)/(2$k$). GARP: “Without mean reversion, the standard deviation of the short-term rate is greater, at $\sigma\sqrt{t}$. Put another way, the pull of the short-term rate to the constant value $\theta$ reduces the standard deviation of the short-term rate as of any future date.”

**Applying it to this question**

I: true (GARP §16.1). II: false; Gauss+ has no shock and no volatility parameter on $r_{t}$. III: true. IV: false; $\sigma\sqrt{t}$ is the no-mean-reversion standard deviation, and mean reversion makes it smaller. Accurate: I and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Gauss+: three state variables, two sources of risk, and the short rate is the one without a shock. Vasicek: mean reversion narrows the dispersion below $\sigma\sqrt{t}$.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.1 (shock $\sigma dw$; eq. 16.5; dispersion discussion) and §16.2 (eq. 16.9 discussion; “three factors, but only two sources of risk”). Eq. 16.5 is garbled in the GARP OCR; the form above is reconstructed from its visible fragments ($\sigma^{2}$, 1 $- e^{-2kt}$, 2$k$), and the statement tested rests on GARP’s clean text on $\sigma\sqrt{t}$. Schweser Reading 16, “Gauss+ Model”. No conflict. (The “two sources of risk” point is GARP-only.)

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 b, where it is Q3 of 15.

a.reason: Statements I and III match GARP §16.1 and §16.2 directly; II and IV each contain one error.

b.reason: **I, II and III.** Accepts II. Error type in II: sibling swap, giving the Gauss+ short rate the Vasicek feature of its own shock. II would be true of a Vasicek short rate (or of a generic three-factor model with three sources of risk).

c.reason: **I, III and IV.** Accepts IV. Error type in IV: scope or condition error; the $\sigma\sqrt{t}$ result needs $k$ = 0, and the statement attaches it to the mean-reverting case. IV would be true if it read “without mean reversion”.

d.reason: **II and IV.** Accepts both false statements and rejects both true ones. It would be correct only if Gauss+ shocked the short rate and Vasicek dispersion ignored mean reversion.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Japanese life insurer is explaining to the risk committee why the JPY options desk prefers the Gauss+ model to the Vasicek model. The desk observes implied volatilities that are low for very short-term rates, peak at intermediate terms, and decline for long terms. Which of the following explanations is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are continuously compounded and annualized, time is measured in years, and “Gauss+” refers to the cascade form of the model in the reading.

options.text: In the Vasicek model, forward-rate volatility rises with term toward $\sigma$; the Gauss+ model matches the observed hump because its short rate carries no shock term.
In the Vasicek model, forward-rate volatility declines with term from $\sigma$; the Gauss+ model matches the observed hump because its factors have stochastic volatility.
In the Vasicek model, forward-rate volatility declines with term from $\sigma$; the Gauss+ model matches the observed hump because its short rate carries no shock term.
In the Vasicek model, forward-rate volatility declines with term from $\sigma$; the Gauss+ model matches the observed hump because its long-term factor carries no shock term.

questions.solution:
**Term structure of volatility: decline versus hump**

Stem in one line: implied volatility is low at the very short end, peaks at intermediate terms and declines; why Gauss+ and not Vasicek.

**Concept and theory**

Vasicek. The only volatility in the model is the volatility of the short rate, so the volatility of the forward rate of term $t$ is

vol\[$f$ ($t$)\] = $\sigma e^{-kt}$

with $\sigma$ the volatility parameter and $k$ the mean reversion parameter. At $t$ = 0 it equals $\sigma$; for $k >$ 0 it falls with term. GARP: mean reversion “captures the empirical regularity that, for longer terms, the term structure of volatility is downward sloping”.

The data. GARP: “Largely because of central banks, however, empirical and implied term structures of volatility tend to have a hump; that is, volatility is low for very short-term rates before increasing to a peak at intermediate-term or longer rates.” Central banks peg the short rate, which keeps its volatility low.

Gauss+. “In the Gauss+ model, the lack of a random shock in the dynamics of $r$ keeps short-term rate volatility low. In this way, the Gauss+ model can match empirically observed hump-shaped term structures of volatility.” Mean reversion of $m_{t}$ and $l_{t}$ then delivers the decline at long terms. Schweser: low volatility on the short end, higher in the middle, declining on the long end, which also lets Gauss+ price caps and floors consistently.

**Applying it to this question**

Two facts must both be right: the Vasicek shape (declining from $\sigma$) and the Gauss+ mechanism (no shock on $r_{t}$). Only C has both.

**Fragile fact.** Vasicek: highest volatility at the shortest term, then down. Gauss+: lowest at the shortest term, because the short rate has no shock (central bank peg).

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.1 (Figure 16.3 discussion) and §16.2 (“The lack of a volatility term in Equation (16.9) is an important feature”). Schweser Reading 16, LO 16.a “Gauss+ Model” and LO 16.b “Vasicek Model vs. Gauss+ Model”. Difference: Schweser’s quiz calls Vasicek volatility “constant”; GARP shows the parameter $\sigma$ is constant but forward-rate volatility $\sigma e^{-kt}$ declines with term. GARP used; a compression, not a version difference.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 b, where it is Q4 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the Vasicek shape. $\sigma e^{-kt}$ falls with term; it never rises toward $\sigma$. Correct only if the Vasicek half read “declines with term from $\sigma$”.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (stochastic volatility). Gauss+ is a Gaussian model with constant parameters $\sigma_{m}$ and $\sigma_{l}$; the hump comes from structure, not from random volatility. Correct only for a stochastic-volatility model, which is outside this reading.

c.reason: GARP §16.1 (vol of $f$ ($t$) is $\sigma e^{-kt}$, downward sloping) and §16.2 (no shock in $dr_{t}$ keeps short-rate volatility low, matching the hump).

d.reason: Error type: role misassignment. It is the short rate, not the long-term factor, that has no shock; $l_{t}$ carries $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}$. Correct if “long-term factor” read “short rate”.

questions.question:
A risk consultant reviewing an Australian bank’s AUD rates models finds that the Vasicek volatility parameter $\sigma$ was set so that the model’s volatility of the instantaneous forward rate of term 10 years matches the market’s. She then checks what the model implies at the short end.

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean reversion parameter $k$ | 0.08 |
| Market volatility of the 10-year forward rate | 72 bp per year |
| Market volatility of the 1-year forward rate | 38 bp per year |
| Current 2-year spot rate | 3.85% |

Which of the following is closest to the Vasicek model’s volatility of the instantaneous forward rate of term 1 year?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are continuously compounded and annualized, time is measured in years, and “Gauss+” refers to the cascade form of the model in the reading.

options.text: 147.9 bp per year
160.2 bp per year
66.5 bp per year
35.0 bp per year

questions.solution:
**Vasicek fitted at one point: what it implies elsewhere**

Stem in one line: $k$ = 0.08; $\sigma$ set so the 10-year forward volatility is 72 bp; find the model’s 1-year forward volatility.

**Concept and theory**

With one volatility parameter, Vasicek can match market volatility at one term only. GARP: “The parameter $\sigma$ can be used to approximate an implied option volatility at one point of the term structure.” Every other term is then dictated by

vol\[$f$ ($t$)\] = $\sigma e^{-kt}$

where $t$ is the term of the forward rate in years. Schweser: Vasicek “only has one volatility parameter; therefore, volatility is only calibrated to be consistent with one point on the interest rate curve.”

**Applying it to this question**

Calibration at $t$ = 10 : $\sigma e^{-0.08\times10}$ = 72 bp

$e^{-0.8}$ = 0.449329

$\sigma$ = 72/0.449329 = 160.24 bp per year

Model at $t$ = 1 : $\sigma e^{-0.08\times1}$ = 160.24 × 0.923116 = 147.92 bp per year

Meaning: the model says the 1-year forward rate is about 148 bp volatile while the market says 38 bp, a factor of 147.92/38 = 3.9. Calibrating to the 10-year point forces a short end that is far too volatile, because Vasicek’s volatility is highest at the short end while the market’s is low there. The 2-year spot rate is irrelevant, and the 38 bp is used only to interpret the result.

**Fragile fact.** In Vasicek, shorter terms are always more volatile ($\sigma e^{-kt}$ falls with $t$). Fitting $\sigma$ at a long term inflates the short end.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.1 (forward-rate volatility $\sigma e^{-kt}$; $\sigma$ approximates implied volatility at one point). Schweser Reading 16, “Vasicek Model vs. Gauss+ Model”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 b, where it is Q5 of 15.

a.reason: $\sigma$ is backed out at $t$ = 10 and then carried to $t$ = 1 through $e^{-kt}$: 147.9 bp.

b.reason: Error type: intermediate result. This is $\sigma$, the volatility of the instantaneous short rate ($t$ = 0), before applying $e^{-0.08}$. Correct if the question asked for the model’s short-rate volatility.

c.reason: Error type: wrong input twin. The market 10-year forward volatility was used as $\sigma$: 72 $\times e^{-0.08}$ = 66.46. Correct if $\sigma$ itself had been set to 72 bp.

d.reason: Error type: sign error in the exponent. Scaling down from the 10-year point, 72 $\times e^{-0.08\times9}$ = 35.05, treats the shorter term as less volatile. The correct move from $t$ = 10 to $t$ = 1 multiplies by $e^{\text{+0}.72}$. Its closeness to the market’s 38 bp is exactly the trap: a Vasicek model cannot produce a short end below its long end.

questions.question:
A portfolio manager at a UK liability-driven investment fund compares how long a shock to today’s GBP short rate persists in two fitted models, using half-life = ln 2/(mean reversion speed).

| Model | Parameter | Estimate |
|---|---|---|
| Vasicek | $k$ | 0.0231 |
| Gauss+ | $\alpha_{r}$ | 0.924 |
| Gauss+ | $\alpha_{m}$ | 0.462 |
| Gauss+ | $\alpha_{l}$ | 0.0231 |

Which of the following comparisons is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are continuously compounded and annualized, time is measured in years, and “Gauss+” refers to the cascade form of the model in the reading.

options.text: The Vasicek short rate has a half-life of 30.0 years; the Gauss+ short rate has a half-life of 1.50 years toward the medium-term factor.
The Vasicek short rate has a half-life of 30.0 years; the Gauss+ short rate has a half-life of 0.75 years toward the medium-term factor.
The Vasicek short rate has a half-life of 43.3 years; the Gauss+ short rate has a half-life of 1.08 years toward the medium-term factor.
The Vasicek short rate has a half-life of 30.0 years; the Gauss+ short rate has a half-life of 30.0 years toward the long-run constant $\mu$.

questions.solution:
**Persistence of a short-rate shock: half-lives**

Stem in one line: Vasicek $k$ = 0.0231; Gauss+ $\alpha_{r}$ = 0.924, $\alpha_{m}$ = 0.462, $\alpha_{l}$ = 0.0231; compare short-rate half-lives.

**Concept and theory**

A mean reversion speed can be quoted as a half-life $h$, the time for half of a deviation from the target to decay. In Vasicek a shock to $r_{0}$ decays by the factor $e^{-kt}$, so

$e^{-kh}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow h$ = $\frac{\text{ln 2}}{k}$

GARP’s example: $k$ = 0.0165 gives $h$ over 42 years, “which means that any shock to $r$ affects rate expectations over a very long period of time.”

The contrast with Gauss+ is where the slow speed sits. In Vasicek there is one speed, and it governs the short rate itself. In Gauss+ the speeds are ordered $\alpha_{r} > \alpha_{m} > \alpha_{l}$: “the short-term rate reverts quickly to the medium-term factor; the medium-term factor reverts more slowly to the long-term factor; and the long-term factor reverts slowest of all to its target.” Long persistence lives in $l_{t}$, not in $r_{t}$. (In GARP’s estimates $\alpha_{l}$ = 0.0165, the same speed as GARP’s Vasicek example, with half-lives of 0.66 years for $r$ and 42.01 years for $l$.)

**Applying it to this question**

Vasicek: $h$ = ln 2/0.0231 = 0.693147/0.0231 = 30.0 years

Gauss+ short rate: $h_{r}$ = ln 2/0.924 = 0.75 years (toward $m_{t}$)

Gauss+ medium factor: $h_{m}$ = ln 2/0.462 = 1.50 years (toward $l_{t}$)

Gauss+ long factor: $h_{l}$ = ln 2/0.0231 = 30.0 years (toward $\mu$)

Meaning: a Vasicek short-rate shock is only half gone after 30 years; in Gauss+ the short rate closes half its gap to $m_{t}$ in nine months, and the 30-year persistence belongs to the long-term factor.

**Fragile fact.** $h$ = ln 2$/\alpha$, not 1$/\alpha$. In Gauss+ the slow speed belongs to $l_{t}$; the short rate is the fastest factor.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.1 (eq. 16.8, $h$ = ln(2)$/k$) and §16.2 (ordering of the mean reversion speeds); §16.3 Table 16.1 for the cited GARP estimates (context only). Schweser Reading 16, LO 16.a “Gauss+ Model” (“the short-term rate reacts quickly . . . the long-term factor shifts the slowest”). No conflict. The half-life formula is GARP-only.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 b, where it is Q6 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: wrong input twin. $\alpha_{m}$ = 0.462 was used for the short rate; 1.50 years is the medium-term factor’s half-life toward $l_{t}$. Correct if the question asked about $m_{t}$.

b.reason: It applies ln 2$/k$ to the right parameter in each model: $k$ for Vasicek and $\alpha_{r}$ for the Gauss+ short rate.

c.reason: Error type: time-conversion slip, 1$/\alpha$ instead of ln 2$/\alpha$: 1/0.0231 = 43.29, 1/0.924 = 1.08. Correct if the question asked for the mean reversion time scale 1$/\alpha$ rather than the half-life.

d.reason: Error type: role misassignment. The Gauss+ short rate does not revert to $\mu$; only $l_{t}$ does, at $\alpha_{l}$. Correct if the question asked for the long-term factor’s half-life.

questions.question:
The CRO of a Singapore bank asks a risk analyst how much of the Vasicek model’s long-run level reflects expectations. The model was calibrated to SGD bond prices under risk-neutral dynamics. The analyst assumes that the short rate’s long-run value under true probabilities is $r_{\infty}$ and that a constant risk premium of $\lambda$ per year adds to the true drift, so that the risk-neutral drift is $k$($r_{\infty} - r$) + $\lambda$.

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Risk-neutral long-run level $\theta$ | 5.40% |
| Mean reversion parameter $k$ | 0.04 |
| Assumed risk premium $\lambda$ | 0.12% per year |
| Current short rate $r_{0}$ | 2.10% |
| Volatility $\sigma$ | 1.00% |

Which of the following is closest to the implied true long-run value of the short rate, $r_{\infty}$?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are continuously compounded and annualized, time is measured in years, and “Gauss+” refers to the cascade form of the model in the reading.
questions.solution:
**Splitting the Vasicek long-run level: $\theta$ = $r_{\infty}$ + $\lambda/k$**

Stem in one line: $\theta$ = 5.40%, $k$ = 0.04, assumed $\lambda$ = 0.12% per year; find the true long-run value $r_{\infty}$.

**Concept and theory**

Bond prices are set under the risk-neutral process $dr$ = $k$($\theta- r$) $dt$ + $\sigma dw$. Prices may contain a risk premium that is “indistinguishable from a drift in the evolution of the short-term rate” (GARP §16.1). Suppose the true (real-world) long-run value is $r_{\infty}$ and investors earn a constant risk premium of $\lambda$ per year. Then the risk-neutral drift is the true drift plus $\lambda$:

$dr$ = $k$($r_{\infty} - r$) $dt$ + $\lambda dt$ + $\sigma dw$

= $k ([r_{\infty}$ + $\frac{\lambda}{k} ] - r) dt$ + $\sigma dw$

$\theta$ = $r_{\infty}$ + $\frac{\lambda}{k}$

where $k$ is the mean reversion parameter, $r_{\infty}$ the long-run value under true probabilities, $\lambda$ the risk premium per year and $\theta$ the risk-neutral long-run level. A small $\lambda$ becomes a large wedge when divided by a small $k$. GARP’s example: $\theta$ = 11%, $\lambda$ = 0.125%, $k$ = 0.0165 give $r_{\infty}$ = 11% − 0.125%/0.0165 = 3.424%.

**Applying it to this question**

$\frac{\lambda}{k}$ = $\frac{0.\text{12\%}}{0.04}$ = 3.00%

$r_{\infty}$ = $\theta- \frac{\lambda}{k}$ = 5.40% − 3.00% = 2.40%

Meaning: of the 5.40% long-run level priced into SGD bonds, 3.00 percentage points are risk premium and only 2.40% is the expected long-run short rate, given the assumed $\lambda$. Prices alone cannot confirm that split. $r_{0}$ = 2.10% and $\sigma$ = 1.00% are irrelevant to the long-run level.

**Fragile fact.** $\theta$ is the risk-neutral level and is larger than $r_{\infty}$ when $\lambda>$ 0; the wedge is $\lambda/k$, not $\lambda$.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.1 (eqs. 16.2 and 16.3 and Figure 16.4 parameters). The equations are garbled in the GARP OCR; the form above is reconstructed from the visible fragments and checked against GARP’s own numbers ($r_{\infty}$ = 3.424% from $\theta$ = 11%, $\lambda$ = 0.125%, $k$ = 0.0165). GARP-only: Schweser does not cover the risk-premium split.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 b, where it is Q7 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: dropped term (the division by $k$). 5.40% − 0.12% = 5.28% subtracts one year of premium instead of the capitalized premium $\lambda/k$. Correct only if $k$ = 1.

b.reason: Error type: sign error. 5.40% + 3.00% = 8.40% adds the premium to $\theta$. Correct if the question gave $r_{\infty}$ = 5.40% and asked for the risk-neutral $\theta$.

c.reason: Error type: wrong input twin, half-life used for 1$/k$. $\lambda\times$ ln 2$/k$ = 0.12% × 17.33 = 2.08%, so 5.40% − 2.08% = 3.32%. Correct only if the formula used the half-life ln 2$/k$, which it does not.

d.reason: GARP eq. 16.3, $\theta$ = $r_{\infty}$ + $\lambda/k$, rearranged: $r_{\infty}$ = 2.40%.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a German bank is reviewing a EUR rates desk memo that compares how the long-run level in each model relates to expectations and risk premium. Which of the following statements in the memo is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are continuously compounded and annualized, time is measured in years, and “Gauss+” refers to the cascade form of the model in the reading.

options.text: In the Vasicek model, $\theta$ can be split into $r_{\infty}$ and $\lambda$ by observing bond prices; in the Gauss+ model, $\mu$ also combines a long-run expectation and a risk premium.
In the Vasicek model, $\theta$ combines $r_{\infty}$ and $\lambda$ and cannot be split from prices alone; in the Gauss+ model, $\mu$ is a pure long-run expectation with no risk premium.
In the Vasicek model, $\theta$ combines $r_{\infty}$ and $\lambda$ and cannot be split from prices alone; in the Gauss+ model, $\mu$ also combines both, and splitting them requires added assumptions.
In the Vasicek model, $\theta$ combines $r_{\infty}$ and $\lambda$ and cannot be split from prices alone; in the Gauss+ model, the split assumes that only the medium-term factor earns a risk premium.

questions.solution:
**Long-run level, expectations and risk premium in both models**

Stem in one line: which memo statement correctly compares what $\theta$ (Vasicek) and $\mu$ (Gauss+) contain?

**Concept and theory**

Vasicek. Equation 16.3, $\theta$ = $r_{\infty}$ + $\lambda/k$, “neatly emphasizes the inability to distinguish expectations from risk premium by observing security prices: an infinite number of combinations of $r_{\infty}$ and $\lambda$ give the same $\theta$ and, therefore, the same risk-neutral price process” (GARP §16.1).

Gauss+. The long-term factor reverts to $\mu$, “which, as in the Vasicek model, can be thought of as including both a long-term expectation of the short-term rate and a risk premium” (GARP §16.2). GARP’s estimate of $\mu$ is over 10%, which “might seem high”, because it includes a risk premium. The equations are risk-neutral dynamics; “additional assumptions allow for the identification of an implicit risk premium”, and GARP’s application assumes “that only the long-term factor earns a risk premium”. For the macro decomposition of forward rates, the key assumption is that expectations of future short-term rates do not change past some point in the future (§16.4).

|  | Vasicek | Gauss+ |
|---|---|---|
| Long-run level | $\theta$ | $\mu$ |
| Contains risk premium? | Yes ($\lambda/k$) | Yes |
| Separable from prices alone? | No | No; needs added assumptions |
| Premium earned by (GARP application) | The single factor | Long-term factor only |

**Applying it to this question**

All options except A agree on the Vasicek half. The Gauss+ half decides it: $\mu$ also contains a risk premium (rules out B), the split needs additional assumptions (C), and in GARP’s application only the long-term factor earns the premium (rules out D).

**Fragile fact.** Both long-run levels are risk-neutral and contain a risk premium. In GARP’s Gauss+ application the premium is attached to the long-term factor.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.1 (eq. 16.3), §16.2 (“As a final comment on the structure of the model”) and §16.4. GARP-only: Schweser does not discuss the risk premium in $\theta$ or $\mu$.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 b, where it is Q8 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip. Prices identify only $\theta$; infinitely many ($r_{\infty}, \lambda$) pairs give the same prices. Correct if it read “cannot be split by observing bond prices”.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap. It treats $\mu$ as a pure expectation, the property of $r_{\infty}$, not of a risk-neutral level. Correct if the question asked about the true long-run value $r_{\infty}$ in the Vasicek decomposition.

c.reason: GARP §16.1 (eq. 16.3 and the “infinite number of combinations” sentence) and §16.2 (“as in the Vasicek model”, “additional assumptions”).

d.reason: Error type: role misassignment. GARP’s application assumes that only the long-term factor earns a risk premium. Correct if “medium-term” read “long-term”.

A portfolio manager at a US life insurer is deciding where a Vasicek model, fitted to USD Treasury data, could reasonably be used. Which of the following tasks is most consistent with the reading’s description of appropriate Vasicek applications?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are continuously compounded and annualized, time is measured in years, and “Gauss+” refers to the cascade form of the model in the reading.

options.text: Pricing a book of caps and floors with expiries from 1 to 10 years, consistently with the market’s humped implied volatility curve.
Hedging a portfolio of 2-year notes with 10-year bonds, relying on the model’s single-factor sensitivities across the curve.
Pricing short-dated options on 1-year rates, with the volatility parameter set to match the implied volatility of 10-year rates.
Valuing and hedging 25-year bonds first callable in 10 years, with the model fitted to 10- to 30-year noncallable bond prices and 10-year rate volatility.

questions.solution:
**Where the Vasicek model can reasonably be used**

Stem in one line: which task fits the reading’s description of reasonable Vasicek applications?

**Concept and theory**

GARP gives Vasicek “some limited uses for practitioners”, all resting on two strengths: simplicity (“most rates and prices from the model can be expressed through simple formulae”) and the fact that “a single factor can explain a large fraction of term structure variability, particular across longer maturities.”

- $r_{0}$, $k$ and $\theta$ are calibrated jointly to approximate the shape of the term structure and the shape of rate sensitivities to the factor; $\sigma$ approximates the implied option volatility at one point.
- The model “can reasonably be used . . . to price, compare values, and hedge long-term bonds that are first callable after some intermediate number of years. The model is flexible enough to match the prices of noncallable bonds from 10 to 30 years, and also to match the most relevant volatility, namely, the volatility of 10-year rates.”

The pattern: every input sits in one region of the curve (10 to 30 years), and the one volatility needed is the one $\sigma$ can match. Schweser’s condensed version: Vasicek suits simple applications such as pricing zero-coupon bonds and basic hedging, while Gauss+ suits proprietary trading and complex analysis.

**Applying it to this question**

D is GARP’s own example. A, B and C each require something Vasicek cannot do: match a volatility hump, hedge across segments with one factor, or rely on $\sigma$ away from its calibration point.

**Fragile fact.** Vasicek works when everything sits in the long end: long callable bonds, 10- to 30-year noncallables, 10-year volatility.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.1 (paragraphs beginning “The Vasicek model has some limited uses” and “The Vasicek model is not very widely used”). Schweser Reading 16, “Vasicek Model”. Difference: Schweser names zero-coupon pricing and basic hedging; GARP names callable long bonds and 10-to 30-year bonds. Compatible; GARP is more specific and is used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 b, where it is Q9 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: scope error. Vasicek “cannot simultaneously handle options or other volatility-sensitive products that are spread out across the term structure”, because it cannot produce a hump. Correct if the model were Gauss+.

b.reason: Error type: scope error. “More than one factor is needed to hedge intermediate- and shorter-term bonds”, and Vasicek cannot “reliably hedge bonds most sensitive to one segment of the term structure with bonds most sensitive to another segment.” Correct for a hedge of 25-year bonds with 30-year bonds, within one segment.

c.reason: Error type: scope or condition error. $\sigma$ approximates volatility at its calibration point only; the model then implies a short end that is too volatile (Q5). Correct if the options were on 10-year rates, the point $\sigma$ was fitted to.

d.reason: GARP §16.1, quoted above: callable long bonds, 10- to 30-year noncallables, 10-year volatility.
