A treasury analyst at a Chinese bank is documenting how CNY bond hedge ratios are produced with a Vasicek model. The fitted parameters are $k$ = 0.10, $\theta$ = 4.50% and $\sigma$ = 1.20%, and the analyst shifts the short rate $r_{0}$ by 10 bp. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are continuously compounded and annualized, time is measured in years, and “Gauss+” refers to the cascade form of the model in the reading.

options.text: Sensitivities come from shifting $r_{0}$ and repricing; the 10-year forward rate moves by about 3.68 bp, and hedge effectiveness depends on how reliable this sensitivity shape is.
Sensitivities come from shifting $r_{0}$ and repricing; the 10-year forward rate moves by about 27.18 bp, and hedge effectiveness depends on how reliable this sensitivity shape is.
Sensitivities come from shifting $r_{0}$ and repricing; the 10-year forward rate moves by 10.00 bp, and hedge effectiveness depends on how reliable this sensitivity shape is.
Sensitivities come from shifting $r_{0}$ and repricing; the 10-year forward rate moves by about 3.68 bp, and with one factor driving all rates, hedges between any two maturities are fully effective.

questions.solution:
**How Vasicek hedge ratios are produced**

Stem in one line: $k$ = 0.10, 10 bp shift in $r_{0}$; how much does the 10-year forward move, and what does hedge effectiveness depend on?

**Concept and theory**

In Vasicek, “bond sensitivities to changes in interest rates, defined in the model as changes in $r$, can be computed by shifting $r_{0}$, recomputing prices, and computing DV01s or durations” (GARP §16.1). Why $e^{-kt}$? The expected short rate at time $t$ is

$E$\[$r_{t}$\] = $\theta$ + ($r_{0} - \theta$)$e^{-kt}$

so “a shock to $r_{0}$ decays according to the factor $e^{-kt}$” (GARP §16.1). A change in today’s short rate therefore moves expectations of the short rate $t$ years ahead, and the forward rate of term $t$, by $e^{-kt}$ times the change:

∆$f$ ($t$) = $e^{-kt}$ ∆$r_{0}$

GARP: “the sensitivity of each forward rate to changes in the short-term rate is $e^{-kt}$”, and hedge effectiveness depends “on the reliability of the shape”.

**Applying it to this question**

$e^{-kt}$ = $e^{-0.10\times10}$ = $e^{-1}$ = 0.367879

∆$f$ (10) = 10 bp × 0.367879 = 3.68 bp

Meaning: the model assumes the 10-year forward moves about 37% as much as the short rate; if the market’s co-movement differs, hedges fail. $\theta$ and $\sigma$ are irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Vasicek sensitivity of $f$ ($t$) to $r_{0}$ is $e^{-kt}$: below one and falling with term. Hedge quality is only as good as that shape.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.1 (eqs. 16.4 and 16.6 discussion and the paragraphs on hedging long-term bonds). Eq. 16.4 is missing from the GARP OCR; its form is confirmed from the question bank’s worked solution for this LO. The tested result, $e^{-kt}$, is in GARP’s clean text. GARP-only: Schweser does not give the sensitivity.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 b, where it is Q10 of 15.

a.reason: Correct mechanics (shift $r_{0}$, reprice), correct number (3.68 bp) and correct caveat (hedge effectiveness depends on the reliability of the $e^{-kt}$ shape), all from GARP §16.1.

b.reason: Error type: sign error in the exponent, 10 $\times e^{\text{+1}}$ = 27.18, so long forwards appear more sensitive than the short rate. Correct only for a model with $k$ = −0.10, which is explosive, not mean reverting.

c.reason: Error type: scope or condition error (mean reversion dropped). A one-for-one move holds only if $k$ = 0. Correct for a model without mean reversion.

d.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. The number is right, but one factor does not make all hedges fully effective; GARP says effectiveness depends on the reliability of the sensitivity shape and that Vasicek cannot reliably hedge one segment with another. Correct if “fully effective” read “only as effective as the $e^{-kt}$ shape is reliable”.

questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee at a Brazilian bank receives a BRL model-governance paper explaining why the bank is replacing its Vasicek model. The paper contains four statements about the Vasicek model:

I. Calibrating the model to match one point on the term structure relies too heavily on the model to approximate all other points.

II. A single factor explains a large fraction of term structure variability, particularly across shorter maturities, so one factor suffices to hedge intermediate- and shorter-term bonds.

III. The model cannot capture the empirical regularity that the term structure of volatility rises quickly with term and then flattens or declines, so it cannot simultaneously handle options spread across the term structure.

IV. The single volatility parameter can be used to approximate an implied option volatility at one point of the term structure.

Which of the statements are accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are continuously compounded and annualized, time is measured in years, and “Gauss+” refers to the cascade form of the model in the reading.

options.text: I and III only
I, II and III only
I, III and IV only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
**Vasicek limitations**

Stem in one line: audit four statements on why the bank is replacing its Vasicek model.

**Concept and theory**

GARP gives three reasons the Vasicek model “is not very widely used”:

1. Inflexible shape: “calibrating the model to match one point on the term structure relies too heavily on the model to approximate all other points.”
2. One factor is not enough: “while one factor does explain a lot of term structure variability, a second factor can capture significantly more variability. More than one factor is needed to hedge intermediate- and shorter-term bonds.”
3. No volatility hump: it “cannot capture the empirical regularity . . . that the term structure of volatilities . . . typically rises quickly with term and then flattens or declines”, so it cannot “simultaneously handle options or other volatility-sensitive products that are spread out across the term structure”.

Schweser compresses the same points: one volatility parameter, little flexibility in curve shape, and no ability to capture derivative pricing. The Gauss+ model mitigates each.

**Applying it to this question**

I: true (reason 1). II: false; one factor explains much variability “particular across longer maturities”, and more than one factor is needed for intermediate and shorter bonds. III: true (reason 3). IV: true; GARP says $\sigma$ “can be used to approximate an implied option volatility at one point of the term structure.” Accurate: I, III and IV.

**Fragile fact.** One factor explains most variability at the long end; the short and intermediate end needs more factors.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.1 (paragraph beginning “The Vasicek model is not very widely used”). Schweser Reading 16, “Vasicek Model vs. Gauss+ Model”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 b, where it is Q11 of 15.

a.reason: **I and III only.** Rejects IV, a true feature. A candidate who reads the stem as “limitations only” drops IV; but the question asks which statements are accurate. Correct if IV read “can match implied volatility at every point”.

b.reason: **I, II and III.** Accepts II. Error type in II: polarity flip (shorter for longer), which also reverses GARP’s conclusion on hedging. Correct if II read “longer maturities” and “does not suffice”.

c.reason: Statements I, III and IV are GARP §16.1 almost verbatim; II reverses the maturity range.

d.reason: **II, III and IV.** Accepts II and rejects I. Correct only if Vasicek’s one-point calibration reliably fixed all other points, which GARP denies.

questions.question:
The treasurer of a Canadian credit union hedged a CAD 250 million long position in 3-year notes by selling 10-year government bonds, using DV01 ratios from a Vasicek model fitted to the curve. Over a quarter in which markets repriced expected central bank policy, 2- to 3-year yields rose 45 bp while 10-year yields rose 8 bp, and the hedged position lost heavily. Which of the following best explains the failure and the remedy?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are continuously compounded and annualized, time is measured in years, and “Gauss+” refers to the cascade form of the model in the reading.

options.text: $\sigma$ was calibrated to the 10-year point; recalibrating $\sigma$ to the 3-year implied volatility would make the single-factor hedge ratio reliable.
One factor cannot reliably hedge bonds sensitive to one curve segment with bonds sensitive to another; intermediate and shorter bonds need a multifactor model such as Gauss+.
The Vasicek model has no mean reversion, so it assumed that the 10-year bond would move one-for-one with the 3-year note; adding mean reversion fixes the ratio.
One factor cannot reliably hedge bonds sensitive to one curve segment with bonds sensitive to another; Gauss+ fixes this by adding a random shock to the short rate.

questions.solution:
**Case: a single-factor hedge across curve segments**

Stem in one line: 3-year notes hedged with 10-year bonds on Vasicek DV01s; 2 to 3-year yields up 45 bp, 10-year up 8 bp; why it failed.

**Concept and theory**

A one-factor model has one sensitivity shape, $e^{-kt}$, linking every rate to every other. A hedge between two maturities works only if the market moves them in that fixed ratio. When the curve moves in a way that is not a multiple of $e^{-kt}$ (for example, the 2- to 3-year sector reprices on central bank expectations while the 10-year stays put), the hedge breaks. GARP: Vasicek cannot “reliably hedge bonds most sensitive to one segment of the term structure with bonds most sensitive to another segment”, and “more than one factor is needed to hedge intermediate- and shorter-term bonds.” Gauss+ has three factors, and a medium-term factor that reflects business cycles and monetary policy, so exposures to different segments can be hedged separately.

**Applying it to this question**

The loss came from a non-parallel, segment-specific move that a single-factor DV01 ratio cannot represent. The CAD 250 million size and the exact basis points only describe the damage. The remedy is more factors, not a different $\sigma$.

**Fragile fact.** Single-factor hedges fail across segments; fixing $\sigma$ does not help because hedge ratios depend on $k$.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.1 (limitations) and §16.2 (factor interpretation). Schweser Reading 16, “Vasicek Model vs. Gauss+ Model” (“does not offer much flexibility on the shape of the curve, which affects the ability to accurately match rates to the degree necessary to enable effective hedging”). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 b, where it is Q12 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap ($\sigma$ for $k$). Vasicek hedge ratios come from $e^{-kt}$, which does not involve $\sigma$; recalibrating $\sigma$ leaves the ratio unchanged. Correct if the problem were pricing an option at the 3-year point, where $\sigma$ matters.

b.reason: GARP §16.1, second and third reasons Vasicek is not widely used.

c.reason: Error type: polarity flip. Mean reversion is the Vasicek model’s defining feature, and it makes the 10-year respond less than the short rate. Correct for a model with $k$ = 0.

d.reason: Error type: role misassignment. Gauss+ has no shock on the short rate; its randomness enters through $m_{t}$ and $l_{t}$. Correct if it said the remedy is extra factors with their own shocks (the medium-and long-term factors).

A risk consultant at a US asset manager is building a USD factor-exposure report and compares how forward rates of different terms respond to a change in each model’s factor or factors, using the estimated Gauss+ model described in the reading. Which of the following comparisons is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are continuously compounded and annualized, time is measured in years, and “Gauss+” refers to the cascade form of the model in the reading.

options.text: Vasicek forward rates respond with sensitivity $e^{-kt}$; in Gauss+, the medium-term factor dominates forward rates beyond 10 years, and the long-term factor drives mainly the 2- to 3-year part of the curve.
Vasicek forward rates respond with sensitivity $e^{-kt}$; in Gauss+, the long-term factor has its largest impact at the very short end, and its effect fades steadily beyond 10 years.

Vasicek forward rates respond with sensitivity $e^{-kt}$; in Gauss+, the short-term factor affects only the very short end, the medium-term factor drives mainly the 2- to 3-year part, and the long-term factor alone drives terms beyond 10 years.

Vasicek forward rates respond with sensitivity $e^{-kt}$; in Gauss+, the short-term factor, being the policy rate, moves forward rates of all terms by similar amounts, while $m_{t}$ and $l_{t}$ add only small corrections.

questions.solution:
**Forward-rate sensitivities to the factors**

Stem in one line: which statement correctly contrasts how forward rates respond to the factor(s) in each model?

**Concept and theory**

Vasicek: one factor, one shape. The sensitivity of $f$ ($t$) to $r$ is $e^{-kt}$, declining smoothly with term (GARP §16.1).

Gauss+: each factor has its own footprint on the curve. From GARP’s description of Figure 16.7 (estimated model):

| Factor | Effect on forward rates |
|---|---|
| Short-term rate $r_{t}$ | Affects only the very short end of the curve |
| Medium-term factor $m_{t}$ | Drives the 2- to 3-year part; captures where the market believes the short rate will be in two to three years (monetary policy) |
| Long-term factor $l_{t}$ | Biggest impact at 6 to 8 years; beyond 10 years, the sole factor driving forward rate changes and volatilities |

GARP also explains the mechanism: the larger $\alpha_{r}$, the faster changes in $m$ and $l$ reach the curve; the larger $\alpha_{m}$, the faster $m$ converges to $l$ and the less $m$ affects longer yields; the smaller $\alpha_{l}$, the more parallel the effect of $l$ on all longer yields.

**Applying it to this question**

All four options give Vasicek correctly; the discrimination is the segment assigned to each Gauss+ factor. Only C matches Figure 16.7.

**Fragile fact.** Gauss+: short factor = very short end; medium = 2 to 3 years; long = peak at 6 to 8 years and sole driver beyond 10 years.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.1 (sensitivity $e^{-kt}$) and §16.3 (Figure 16.7 discussion; figure image not legible in the OCR, text used). GARP-only: Schweser does not give the factor-sensitivity profile.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 b, where it is Q13 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: role misassignment ($m_{t}$ and $l_{t}$ swapped). Correct if the labels were exchanged.

b.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the long-term factor’s profile. Its effect grows with term and dominates beyond 10 years. The described profile (largest at the short end, fading with term) is closer to the short-rate factor’s.

c.reason: GARP §16.3, text on Figure 16.7, quoted in the table.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap with the Vasicek mental model, in which the short rate drives every term. In Gauss+ the short-rate factor affects only the very short end. Correct for a Vasicek model with very small $k$.

A risk consultant at a Japanese bank compares two JPY relative value set-ups proposed by the trading desk, one built on the Vasicek model and one on the Gauss+ model. Which of the following descriptions is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are continuously compounded and annualized, time is measured in years, and “Gauss+” refers to the cascade form of the model in the reading.

options.text: Vasicek: $r_{0}$ is reset daily so the model 10-year rate matches the market; Gauss+: factors are set daily so the short rate equals the policy rate and the 1-year rates 2 and 10 years forward are fair, and trades are structured to minimize factor exposure.

Vasicek: $\theta$ is reset daily so the model 10-year rate matches the market; Gauss+: factors are set daily so the short rate equals the policy rate and the 1-year rates 2 and 10 years forward are fair, and trades are structured to minimize factor exposure.

Vasicek: $r_{0}$ is reset daily so the model 10-year rate matches the market; Gauss+: $m_{t}$ and $l_{t}$ are set equal to the 1-year rates 2 and 10 years forward themselves, and trades are structured to minimize factor exposure.

Vasicek: $r_{0}$ is reset daily so the model 10-year rate matches the market; Gauss+: factors are set daily so the short rate equals the policy rate and the 1-year rates 2 and 10 years forward are fair, and trades take outright views on the factors.

questions.solution:
**Relative value set-ups in the two models**

Stem in one line: compare a Vasicek and a Gauss+ relative value framework.

**Concept and theory**

Vasicek relative value. “The value of $r_{0}$ might be set each day so that the model 10-year rate matches the market 10-year rate. Deviations of calculated prices of longer-term bonds from model predictions might then be taken as signals of relative value” (GARP §16.1). Success depends on how well the model captures the steady-state shape of the term structure, and hedging on the reliability of the sensitivity shape.

Gauss+ relative value. The short rate is taken each day as the fed funds target rate, and the factors are chosen to fit the one-year rates two and 10 years forward. “With these two- and 10-year forward rates fair by construction, the model becomes a tool for trading value in other parts of the curve.” The factors $m$ and $l$ “are in no way those forward rates themselves”. A relative value trade “is one that is not exposed to or hedged against changes in the factors”: the trader receives where forwards are high relative to the model, pays where they are low, and “structures trades to minimize factor exposures”.

|  | Vasicek | Gauss+ |
|---|---|---|
| Reset daily | $r_{0}$ | $r_{t}$, $m_{t}$, $l_{t}$ |
| Fair by construction | 10-year rate | Policy rate; 1-year rates 2 and 10 years forward |
| Trades | Long bonds versus model | Fitting errors elsewhere, factor-hedged |

**Applying it to this question**

Check three slots: what is reset in Vasicek ($r_{0}$), what $m_{t}$ and $l_{t}$ are (factors fitted so the forwards are fair, not the forwards themselves), and the nature of a relative value trade (factor-hedged). Only A has all three.

**Fragile fact.** Vasicek: one point fair ($r_{0}$ to the 10-year rate). Gauss+: three points fair; $r$ equals the policy rate but $m$ and $l$ are not the forwards they are fitted to.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.1, §16.3 and §16.4. GARP-only: Schweser mentions proprietary trading but not these set-ups.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 b, where it is Q14 of 15.

a.reason: GARP §16.1 (Vasicek $r_{0}$ reset), §16.3 (fitted points) and §16.4 (definition of a relative value trade).

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap ($\theta$ for $r_{0}$). GARP resets the short rate $r_{0}$ daily; $\theta$ is a calibrated parameter. Correct if “$\theta$” read “$r_{0}$”.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap (factor equated to the fitted rate). GARP: the factors are “in no way those forward rates themselves, in the way that $r$ equals the fed funds rate.” Correct only for the short rate, which does equal the policy rate.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap (macro for relative value). Outright views on the factors define macro trading; relative value minimizes factor exposure. Correct if the question asked about macro-style trading.

questions.question:
The head of rates strategy at a UK asset manager proposes a GBP strategy. Using a fitted Gauss+ model, the team will estimate the market-implied long-run expectation of the short rate as the 10-year forward rate minus a term-appropriate risk premium plus a term-appropriate convexity, compare it with an economist’s fundamental estimate of the long-run rate, and buy or sell long-dated bonds outright on the gap. Which of the following statements about the proposal is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless stated otherwise, rates are continuously compounded and annualized, time is measured in years, and “Gauss+” refers to the cascade form of the model in the reading.

options.text: It is a relative value trade, because the position is structured to be hedged against changes in the medium- and long-term factors.
It is a macro trade, and the Gauss+ model separates expectations from risk premium using observed bond prices alone, with no extra assumption.
It is a macro trade, and when rates fall and the curve steepens, the model interprets the steepening as a fall in the risk premium.
It is a macro trade, and separating expectations from risk premium relies on assuming that short-rate expectations stop changing beyond some future date.

questions.solution:
**Case: a macro trade on the long-run rate**

Stem in one line: estimate the market-implied long-run short rate with Gauss+, compare it with an economist’s view, and trade long bonds outright on the gap.

**Concept and theory**

GARP distinguishes two uses of Gauss+ for proprietary trading:

- Relative value: find value “in the absence of factor exposure”.
- Macro trading: “takes direct or indirect views on the factors”. A more complex example is “trying to trade the long-run level of the short-term rate”.

Long-term forward rates combine expectations, risk premium and convexity; convexity is easy to compute, but separating expectations from risk premium is hard (in Vasicek, impossible from prices, Q8). GARP’s method “relies on one key assumption: expectations of future short-term rates do not change past some point in the future”. The long-run expectation is then the 10-year forward rate minus the term-appropriate risk premium plus the term-appropriate convexity. The gap to an exogenous fundamental view (GARP uses the Cleveland Fed) “can be used as a basis for taking outright long or short positions in bonds.” “The risk premium often moves in the opposite direction of rates. As rates decline, the term structure typically steepens, which the model interprets as an increase in risk premium.”

**Applying it to this question**

Outright positions on a view about the long-run rate are macro trades (rules out A). The separation needs the key assumption (rules out B). Falling rates with steepening are read as a rise in risk premium (rules out C). D states the assumption correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Macro = outright views on factors; relative value = factor-hedged. Falling rates with steepening: risk premium up.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 16, §16.4 Relative Value and Macro-Style Trading with the Gauss+ Model (Figures 16.10 and 16.11 discussion). GARP-only: Schweser mentions only that Gauss+ is beneficial for proprietary trading.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 b, where it is Q15 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap (relative value for macro). The proposal takes outright long or short positions, the opposite of factor-hedged relative value. Correct for a pay-9-year, receive-5-year fitting-error trade.

b.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. Prices alone cannot separate expectations from risk premium, in Gauss+ as in Vasicek. Correct only for the convexity component, which the model computes directly.

c.reason: Error type: polarity flip. The model interprets the steepening as an increase in risk premium. Correct if “fall” read “increase”.

d.reason: GARP §16.4: the decomposition “relies on one key assumption: expectations of future short-term rates do not change past some point in the future.”

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at an Australian bank is simulating one quarterly step ($dt$ = 0.25) of an AUD rate path with a Gauss+ model. The current state, the parameters and the standard normal draw for the step are:

| Input | Value | Input | Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Short-term rate $r_{t}$ | 3.60% | Reversion speed $\alpha_{r}$ | 0.90 |
| Medium-term factor $m_{t}$ | 4.40% | Reversion speed $\alpha_{m}$ | 0.55 |
| Long-term factor $l_{t}$ | 4.10% | Volatility $\sigma_{m}$ (per year) | 105 bp |
| Long-run target $\mu$ | 5.00% | Volatility $\sigma_{l}$ (per year) | 90 bp |
|  |  | Draw $Z_{1}$ for the step | −1.20 |

Which of the following is the change in the short-term rate over the quarter on this path?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question says otherwise, the Gauss+ model is in its cascade form, time is in years, one step of length $dt$ is taken by applying each factor’s equation once, and each random term is $dW^{i}$ = $Z_{i}\sqrt{dt}$, where $Z_{1}$ and $Z_{2}$ are independent standard normal draws.
questions.solution:
**Short-rate change over a quarter**

Stem in one line: AUD Gauss+, $r_{t}$ = 3.60%, $m_{t}$ = 4.40%, $\alpha_{r}$ = 0.90, $dt$ = 0.25; find the change in $r$ (several inputs irrelevant).

**Concept and theory**

The Gauss+ model describes the term structure with three state variables: the short-term rate $r$, a medium-term factor $m$ and a long-term factor $l$. They are linked in a cascade: each factor is pulled toward the next one, and only the last target, $\mu$, is a fixed constant. GARP gives the risk-neutral dynamics as

$dr_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{r}$ ($r_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt$ (16.9)

$dm_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{m}$ ($m_{t} - l_{t}$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{m} (\rho dW^{1}_{t}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}_{t})$ (16.10)

$dl_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{l}$ ($l_{t} - \mu$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}_{t}$ (16.11)

$E\left[dW^{1}_{t} dW^{2}_{t}\right]$ = 0 (16.12)

where $\alpha_{r}, \alpha_{m}, \alpha_{l}$ are the mean reversion speeds (per year), $\sigma_{m}, \sigma_{l}$ the annual volatility parameters of $m$ and $l$, $\rho$ the correlation parameter, $\mu$ the constant long-run target, $dt$ the time step in years and $dW^{1}, dW^{2}$ independent normal shocks with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$.

Why the short rate has no shock. GARP explains that Equation (16.9) mirrors central bank practice: the policy rate is pegged over a very short interval, “in the sense that there is no random variable shocking the dynamics of $r$”, but the target is moved over time toward where the business cycle points, which is $m$. So the one-step change in $r$ is pure drift: speed times gap to $m$ times the length of the step.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula: ∆$r$ = $-\alpha_{r}$ ($r_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt$.

Gap to target: $r_{t} - m_{t}$ = 3.60% − 4.40% = −0.80%

Annual drift: $- \alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$) = −0.90 × (−0.80%) = +0.72% per year

Change over the quarter: ∆$r$ = +0.72% × 0.25 = +0.18% = +18.00 bp

The short rate is below the medium-term factor, so it moves up toward it by 18 bp this quarter. $l_{t}$, $\mu$, $\alpha_{m}$, $\sigma_{m}$, $\sigma_{l}$ and $Z_{1}$ are all irrelevant to this step: none of them appears in Equation (16.9).

**Fragile fact.** Short rate: target is $m$ (not $l$, not $\mu$), the sign is $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$), and there is no shock term, so the draws are irrelevant to $r$ over one step.

**Reference**

LO 16.c (Schweser, verbatim above). GARP Ch. 16, §16.2 The Gauss+ Model, Eq. (16.9) and following text. Schweser Reading 16, “Applying the Gauss+ Model”, Steps 2 to 3. Formula notation confirmed from question bank Q761 (Eq. (16.9) is garbled in the GARP extract and missing in Schweser). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 c, where it is Q1 of 12.

a.reason: **(−18.00 bp).** Error type: sign error. Computing $-\alpha_{r}$($m_{t} - r_{t}$) $dt$ = −0.90 × 0.80% × 0.25 = −0.18% pushes $r$ away from its target. A would be correct if $r_{t}$ were 4.40% and $m_{t}$ 3.60%.

b.reason: **(+11.25 bp).** Error type: wrong input twin (long-term factor used as the target). −0.90 × (3.60% − 4.10%) × 0.25 = +0.1125%. This treats $r$ as reverting to $l$, skipping a level of the cascade. B would be correct only if the stem’s medium-term factor were 4.10%.

c.reason: GARP 16.2: “The rate, $r$, is pushed gradually . . . toward the medium-term factor, $m$” with no random term. Schweser LO 16.c, Step 2 plugs the state into the three equations; for $r$ only $\alpha_{r}$, $r_{t}$, $m_{t}$ and $dt$ enter.

d.reason: **(+72.00 bp).** Error type: time-conversion slip ($dt$ omitted). −0.90 × (−0.80%) = +0.72% is the annual drift rate, not the change over a quarter. D would be correct for a one-year step ($dt$ = 1) in a single Euler step.

questions.question:
A risk analyst at an Indian bank is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts on how the sign of each factor’s change is determined in a one-step Gauss+ simulation of INR rates with all random shocks set to zero. The draft slide contains four statements:

I. If $r_{t} < m_{t}$, the change in the short-term rate over the step is positive, whatever the levels of $l_{t}$ and $\mu$.

II. If $m_{t} > l_{t}$, the change in the medium-term factor over the step is negative, even when $l_{t}$ is below $\mu$.

III. If $l_{t} > \mu$, the change in the long-term factor over the step is positive, because the long-term factor is the slowest to revert.

IV. If $r_{t} > m_{t}$ but $r_{t} < \mu$, the change in the short-term rate over the step is positive, because the short-term rate ultimately reverts to $\mu$.

Which of the statements are accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question says otherwise, the Gauss+ model is in its cascade form, time is in years, one step of length $dt$ is taken by applying each factor’s equation once, and each random term is $dW^{i}$ = $Z_{i}\sqrt{dt}$, where $Z_{1}$ and $Z_{2}$ are independent standard normal draws.

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
I and IV only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
**Sign of each factor’s drift**

Stem in one line: which statements about the sign of each factor’s one-step change (shocks set to zero) are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

With the shocks at zero, each factor’s change is its drift only:

∆$r$ = $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt,$ ∆$m$ = $-\alpha_{m}$($m_{t} - l_{t}$) $dt,$ ∆$l$ = $-\alpha_{l}$($l_{t} - \mu$) $dt.$

Each $\alpha$ is positive, so the sign of each change is the sign of that factor’s own gap to its own target, reversed: a factor above its target falls, a factor below its target rises. The targets are, in order, $m$ for $r$, $l$ for $m$ and $\mu$ for $l$. Schweser: “rt is seeking to converge to mt, which is trying to converge to lt, which is trying to converge to $\mu$. Note that the only fixed parameter here is $\mu$, while the other factors are dynamically moving targets.”

| Factor | Target | Speed | Shock in its own equation |
|---|---|---|---|
| $r$ | $m$ | $\alpha_{r}$ (fastest) | none |
| $m$ | $l$ | $\alpha_{m}$ | $\sigma_{m}$($\rho dW^{1}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}$) |
| $l$ | $\mu$ (fixed) | $\alpha_{l}$ (slowest) | $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}$ |

The speed only scales the size of the move; it never changes its sign.

**Applying it to this question**

I: $r_{t} < m_{t} \Rightarrow r_{t} - m_{t} <$ 0 ⇒ ∆$r >$ 0. $l_{t}$ and $\mu$ are not in Equation (16.9). True.

II: $m_{t} > l_{t} \Rightarrow$ ∆$m <$ 0. Where $l$ sits relative to $\mu$ affects $l$’s own change, not $m$’s change over this step. True.

III: $l_{t} > \mu\Rightarrow-\alpha_{l}$($l_{t} - \mu$) \< 0, so the change is negative, however slow $\alpha_{l}$ is. False.

IV: $r_{t} > m_{t} \Rightarrow$ ∆$r <$ 0. The short rate’s target is $m$; $\mu$ does not appear in its equation. False.

Accurate: I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Each factor looks only one level down the cascade: $r \to m$, $m \to l$, $l \to\mu$. Above target means a negative change, whatever the speed.

**Reference**

LO 16.c. GARP Ch. 16, §16.2 The Gauss+ Model, Eqs. (16.9) to (16.11). Schweser Reading 16, “Gauss+ Model” (cascade of convergence) and “Applying the Gauss+ Model”. Statements III and IV use LO 16.a and LO 16.b ideas only as distractors. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 c, where it is Q2 of 12.

a.reason: GARP 16.2: the short-term rate reverts to the medium-term factor, the medium-term factor to the long-term factor, and the long-term factor “reverts to a constant, $\mu$”. Signs follow directly from Equations (16.9) to (16.11).

b.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: polarity flip in III. Being slow ($\alpha_{l}$ = 0.0165 in GARP’s estimates) makes the move small, not positive. III would be right if it read “If $l_{t} < \mu$”.

c.reason: **I and IV.** Error type: sibling swap in IV (Vasicek-style reversion to a fixed long-run level grafted onto $r$) and rejection of the true II. IV would be right in a one-factor Vasicek model where $r$ reverts to the fixed $\theta$; in Gauss+ the short rate only “sees” $m$.

d.reason: **II, III and IV.** Error type: rejects the true I and accepts the polarity flip in III and the sibling swap in IV. It would need $r$ to revert to $\mu$ and $l$ to move away from $\mu$, neither of which the equations allow.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Japanese bank is checking one monthly step ($dt$ = 1/12) of a JPY Gauss+ simulation. The draws for the month are $Z_{1}$ = +0.80 (driving $dW^{1}$) and $Z_{2}$ = −1.40 (driving $dW^{2}$). The relevant inputs are:

| Input | Value |
|---|---|
| Medium-term factor $m_{t}$ | 1.20% |
| Long-term factor $l_{t}$ | 1.65% |
| Reversion speed $\alpha_{m}$ | 0.64 |
| Volatility $\sigma_{m}$ (per year) | 110 bp |
| Correlation parameter $\rho$ | 0.25 |

Which of the following is closest to the change in the medium-term factor over the month?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question says otherwise, the Gauss+ model is in its cascade form, time is in years, one step of length $dt$ is taken by applying each factor’s equation once, and each random term is $dW^{i}$ = $Z_{i}\sqrt{dt}$, where $Z_{1}$ and $Z_{2}$ are independent standard normal draws.
questions.solution:
**Medium-term factor change over a month**

Stem in one line: JPY, $m_{t}$ = 1.20%, $l_{t}$ = 1.65%, $\alpha_{m}$ = 0.64, $\sigma_{m}$ = 110 bp, $\rho$ = 0.25, $Z_{1}$ = +0.80, $Z_{2}$ = −1.40, $dt$ = 1/12; find ∆$m$.

**Concept and theory**

The medium-term factor has two parts to its change, a trend and a fluctuation (GARP: the factors “trend as described . . . they also fluctuate around these trends”):

$\Delta m = \underbrace{-\alpha_{m}(m_{t} - l_{t})\,dt}_{\text{drift toward } l} + \underbrace{\sigma_{m}\left(\rho\,dW^{1} + \sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}\,dW^{2}\right)}_{\text{shock}}.$

The shock mixes the two independent random terms. The weight $\rho$ sits on $dW^{1}$, the same term that drives the long-term factor, which is how the model makes the fluctuations of $m$ and $l$ correlated. The weight $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}$ sits on $dW^{2}$, the shock unique to $m$. Each random term is a standard normal draw scaled to the step: $dW^{i}$ = $Z_{i}\sqrt{dt}$ (Schweser Step 1: “random draws from a standard normal distribution multiplied by the square root of the time”).

**Applying it to this question**

$\sqrt{dt}$ = $\sqrt{1/12}$ = 0.288675

$dW^{1}$ = 0.80 × 0.288675 = 0.230940

$dW^{2}$ = −1.40 × 0.288675 = −0.404145

$\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}$ = $\sqrt{1 - 0.0625}$ = 0.968246

Drift = −0.64 × (1.20% − 1.65%) $\times\frac{1}{12}$ = +0.0240% = +2.40 bp

Mixed shock = 0.25(0.230940) + 0.968246(−0.404145) = 0.057735 − 0.391312 = −0.333577

Shock = 110 bp × (−0.333577) = −36.69 bp

∆$m$ = +2.40 − 36.69 = −34.29 bp

The trend pulls $m$ up toward $l$ by 2.4 bp, but the month’s negative $dW^{2}$ draw dominates, so $m$ falls about 34 bp on this path.

**Fragile fact.** In the $m$ equation, $\rho$ multiplies $dW^{1}$ (the shared shock) and $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}$ multiplies $dW^{2}$ (the shock unique to $m$). Scale the draws by $\sqrt{dt}$, not $dt$.

**Reference**

LO 16.c. GARP Ch. 16, §16.2 The Gauss+ Model, Eqs. (16.10) and (16.12) and the discussion of the random terms. Schweser Reading 16, “Applying the Gauss+ Model”, Steps 1 to 3. Weights confirmed from question bank Q739 and Q759 (GARP extract garbled; Schweser formula missing). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 c, where it is Q3 of 12.

a.reason: **(−36.69 bp).** Error type: dropped term (an intermediate result). It is the shock alone; the drift of +2.40 bp is left out. A would be correct if $m_{t}$ equalled $l_{t}$, so that the drift were zero.

b.reason: It is GARP Equation (16.10) evaluated for one step with both terms, the random terms built as in Schweser Step 1.

c.reason: **(−39.09 bp).** Error type: sign error on the drift. Using $-\alpha_{m}$($l_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt$ = −2.40 bp gives −2.40 − 36.69 = −39.09 bp. C would be correct if $m_{t}$ were 0.45% above $l_{t}$ rather than below it.

d.reason: **(+15.88 bp).** Error type: wrong input twin (weights swapped). 110 × (0.968246 × 0.230940 + 0.25 × (−0.404145)) = 110 × 0.122571 = +13.48 bp, plus 2.40 bp drift = +15.88 bp. D would be correct if the stem’s correlation parameter were about 0.968 (so that $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}$ = 0.25).

An internal auditor at a UK insurer is reviewing a GBP scenario report produced with a Gauss+ model. For a single monthly step, the report shows, for each of the three factors, the expected change (both random terms set to their mean of zero) next to the realized change on one simulated path on which the draws for $dW^{1}$ and $dW^{2}$ were both non-zero. Which of the following statements in the report is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question says otherwise, the Gauss+ model is in its cascade form, time is in years, one step of length $dt$ is taken by applying each factor’s equation once, and each random term is $dW^{i}$ = $Z_{i}\sqrt{dt}$, where $Z_{1}$ and $Z_{2}$ are independent standard normal draws.

options.text: The realized change equals the expected change for all three factors, because $dW^{1}$ and $dW^{2}$ each have a mean of zero.

The realized change in the short-term rate differs from its expected change by $\sigma_{m}$($\rho dW^{1}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}$), because the short-term rate reverts to the medium-term factor.
The realized change in the short-term rate equals its expected change, while the realized changes in the medium-term and long-term factors differ from their expected changes by their shock terms.
The realized change in the long-term factor equals its expected change, because it reverts so slowly, while the short-term rate and medium-term factor differ by their shock terms.

questions.solution:
**Expected versus realized one-step change**

Stem in one line: GBP report compares, for each factor, the expected one-month change with the realized change on a path with non-zero draws; which statement is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Every factor’s change over a step is “drift plus shock”. The shocks $dW^{1}$ and $dW^{2}$ are normal with mean zero, so the expected change is the drift alone. The realized change on a particular path is the drift plus whatever the shocks happened to be. The difference between them is therefore exactly the shock term of each factor’s own equation:

| Factor | Expected one-step change | Realized minus expected |
|---|---|---|
| $r$ | $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt$ | 0 (no shock in Eq. 16.9) |
| $m$ | $-\alpha_{m}$($m_{t} - l_{t}$) $dt$ | $\sigma_{m}$($\rho dW^{1}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}$) |
| $l$ | $-\alpha_{l}$($l_{t} - \mu$) $dt$ | $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}$ |

GARP: the short-term rate is “fixed over the very short time interval, $dt$, in the sense that there is no random variable shocking the dynamics of $r$”. Randomness reaches $r$ only later, through the shocked value of $m$ that becomes its next target.

**Applying it to this question**

Over one step, $r$’s change uses $m_{t}$, the value at the start of the step, which is known. So on any path the realized change in $r$ equals the expected change. For $m$ and $l$, the draws were non-zero, so their realized changes differ from expectations by their own shock terms. That is statement C.

**Fragile fact.** Of the three factors, only the short-term rate has a one-step change that is known before the draws are made.

**Reference**

LO 16.c. GARP Ch. 16, §16.2 The Gauss+ Model, Eqs. (16.9) to (16.12) and the paragraph on the evolution of the short-term rate. Schweser Reading 16, “Applying the Gauss+ Model”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 c, where it is Q4 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: scope error (“mean zero” stretched to “zero on every path”). A zero mean says the shocks cancel on average across paths, not that a single realized draw is zero. A would be correct if the stem compared the expected change with the average realized change across many paths.

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap. It attaches the medium-term factor’s shock term to the short-term rate. Reverting to $m$ means $r$’s drift depends on $m_{t}$, not that $r$ inherits $m$’s shock within the step. B would describe the realized minus expected change of $m$, not of $r$.

c.reason: GARP Equations (16.9) to (16.11): only $m$ and $l$ carry random terms, and the random terms have mean zero (GARP: “$dW^{1}$ is normally distributed with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$”).

d.reason: Error type: role misassignment. The “no shock” property belongs to $r$, not to $l$; a slow reversion speed makes $l$’s drift small but leaves $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}$ in place. D would be correct if “long-term factor” read “short-term rate” and the shocked pair were $m$ and $l$.

A portfolio manager at a Swiss pension fund simulates CHF rates weekly with a Gauss+ model, using $dt$ = 1/52. For the current week the inputs are:

| Long-term factor $l_{t}$ | 0.95% | Medium-term factor $m_{t}$ | 1.40% |
| Long-run target $\mu$ | 3.20% | Reversion speed $\alpha_{m}$ | 0.70 |
| Reversion speed $\alpha_{l}$ | 0.018 | Draw $Z_{1}$ (drives $dW^{1}$) | −1.10 |
| Volatility $\sigma_{l}$ (per year) | 92 bp | Draw $Z_{2}$ (drives $dW^{2}$) | +1.75 |

Which of the following is closest to the change in the long-term factor over the week?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question says otherwise, the Gauss+ model is in its cascade form, time is in years, one step of length $dt$ is taken by applying each factor’s equation once, and each random term is $dW^{i}$ = $Z_{i}\sqrt{dt}$, where $Z_{1}$ and $Z_{2}$ are independent standard normal draws.
questions.solution:
**Long-term factor change over a week**

Stem in one line: CHF, $l_{t}$ = 0.95%, $\mu$ = 3.20%, $\alpha_{l}$ = 0.018, $\sigma_{l}$ = 92 bp, $Z_{1}$ = −1.10, $Z_{2}$ = +1.75, $dt$ = 1/52; find ∆$l$.

**Concept and theory**

The long-term factor is the bottom of the cascade:

∆$l$ = $-\alpha_{l}$ ($l_{t} - \mu$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}, dW^{1}$ = $Z_{1}\sqrt{dt}.$

Three features matter for the calculation. (1) Its target $\mu$ is a fixed constant, the only one in the model. (2) Its reversion speed is tiny (GARP’s estimate $\alpha_{l}$ = 0.0165, a half-life of about 42 years), so over a short step its drift is almost nothing; the change is dominated by the shock. (3) It is driven by $dW^{1}$ only. $dW^{2}$ appears only in the medium-term factor’s equation. GARP: “the fluctuation over a short time $dt$ is $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}$ . . . the instantaneous fluctuation of the long-term factor around its trend has mean zero and volatility $\sigma_{l}\sqrt{dt}$.”

**Applying it to this question**

$\sqrt{dt}$ = $\sqrt{1/52}$ = 0.138675

Drift = −0.018 × (0.95% − 3.20%) $\times\frac{1}{52}$ = +0.000779% = +0.08 bp

$dW^{1}$ = −1.10 × 0.138675 = −0.152543

Shock = 92 bp × (−0.152543) = −14.03 bp

∆$l$ = +0.08 − 14.03 = −13.96 bp

Even with $l$ 225 bp below its target, a week of drift adds less than a tenth of a basis point; the weekly change is essentially the $dW^{1}$ shock. $m_{t}$, $\alpha_{m}$ and $Z_{2}$ are irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** $l$ takes $dW^{1}$, never $dW^{2}$; shocks scale with $\sqrt{dt}$, drifts with $dt$.

**Reference**

LO 16.c. GARP Ch. 16, §16.2 The Gauss+ Model, Eq. (16.11) and following text; §16.3, Table 16.1 (half-life of $l$ of 42 years, for context). Schweser Reading 16, “Applying the Gauss+ Model”, Step

1. Notation confirmed from question bank Q739. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 c, where it is Q5 of 12.

a.reason: GARP Equation (16.11) for one weekly step, with $dW^{1}$ scaled by $\sqrt{dt}$ as in Schweser Step 1.

b.reason: **(+22.40 bp).** Error type: wrong input twin ($Z_{2}$ used for $l$). 92 × 1.75 × 0.138675 = +22.33 bp, plus 0.08 bp drift = +22.40 bp. B would be correct if the long-term factor were the one driven by the second draw, which it is not in GARP’s Equation (16.11).

c.reason: **(−1.87 bp).** Error type: time-conversion slip ($dt$ instead of $\sqrt{dt}$ on the shock). 92×(−1.10)$\times\frac{1}{52}$ = −1.95 bp, plus 0.08 = −1.87 bp. Shocks scale with the square root of time; drifts scale with time. C would be correct only for the drift-like quantity $\sigma_{l}Z_{1} dt$, which is not part of the model.

d.reason: **(−101.12 bp).** Error type: time-conversion slip (no scaling of the shock). 92×(−1.10) = −101.20 bp is an annual-size shock; adding the weekly drift gives −101.12 bp. D would be closer to correct for a one-year step (and even then the drift would be 4.05 bp, not 0.08 bp).

Starting from one fixed state ($r_{t}, m_{t}, l_{t}$), the engine generates 10,000 one-month steps with independent draws. The validator finds that the one-month changes in the short-term rate across these 10,000 paths have a standard deviation of 3.1 bp. Which implementation error is most consistent with this output?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question says otherwise, the Gauss+ model is in its cascade form, time is in years, one step of length $dt$ is taken by applying each factor’s equation once, and each random term is $dW^{i}$ = $Z_{i}\sqrt{dt}$, where $Z_{1}$ and $Z_{2}$ are independent standard normal draws.

options.text: The weights $\rho$ and $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}$ on $dW^{1}$ and $dW^{2}$ have been swapped in the medium-term factor equation.
The long-term factor equation is driven by $dW^{2}$ instead of $dW^{1}$.
The drift of the short-term rate is computed with $dt$ = 1 instead of $dt$ = 1/12.
A random shock term has been added to the short-term rate equation.

questions.solution:
**Validator: dispersion in one-step short-rate changes**

Stem in one line: from one fixed state, 10,000 one-month steps give one-month changes in $r$ with a standard deviation of 3.1 bp; which bug explains it?

**Concept and theory**

Start from Equation (16.9): ∆$r$ = $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt$. From a fixed starting state, every input on the right-hand side ($\alpha_{r}$, $r_{t}$, $m_{t}$, $dt$) is the same on every path. So all 10,000 one-step changes in $r$ must be identical, and their standard deviation must be exactly zero. This is the feature that GARP says gives the model its name and its realism: “The lack of a volatility term in Equation (16.9) is an important feature of the Gauss+ model”, keeping short-term rate volatility low, as with a central-bank-pegged rate. (The “+” signals a factor, $r$, that is a state variable but not a source of risk.)

Randomness reaches $r$ only from the second step onward, because $m$ is shocked and becomes the next target.

**Applying it to this question**

A non-zero dispersion across paths in the first step of $r$ can only come from a random term inside the $r$ update itself. Errors in how $m$ or $l$ are shocked would change those factors’ first-step distributions, and $r$’s later steps, but not $r$’s first step. An error in the drift’s $dt$ would change the size of every $r$ change by the same amount on every path, leaving the dispersion at zero.

**Fragile fact.** From a fixed state, the one-step change in $r$ is a single known number. Dispersion in $r$ appears only from the second step, through the shocked $m$.

**Reference**

LO 16.c. GARP Ch. 16, §16.2 The Gauss+ Model, Eq. (16.9) and the paragraphs on the lack of a volatility term and on the model’s name (the naming is LO 16.a context, used here only to motivate). Schweser Reading 16, “Applying the Gauss+ Model”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 c, where it is Q6 of 12.

The CRO of a Canadian bank is reviewing a vendor’s CAD Gauss+ calibration. The vendor reports each reversion parameter as a half-life, in years: the time for a factor to close half of the gap to its target. The current state and the reported values are:

| Input | Value | Input | Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| Short-term rate $r_{t}$ | 2.25% | Half-life of $r$ | 0.75 years |
| Medium-term factor $m_{t}$ | 3.05% | Half-life of $m$ | 1.25 years |
| Long-term factor $l_{t}$ | 3.40% | Half-life of $l$ | 38 years |
| Long-run target $\mu$ | 5.00% |  |  |

With all random shocks set to zero and $dt$ = 1/12, which of the following gives the one-month changes in the short-term rate and in the medium-term factor?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question says otherwise, the Gauss+ model is in its cascade form, time is in years, one step of length $dt$ is taken by applying each factor’s equation once, and each random term is $dW^{i}$ = $Z_{i}\sqrt{dt}$, where $Z_{1}$ and $Z_{2}$ are independent standard normal draws.

options.text: Short-term rate +5.00 bp; medium-term factor +3.65 bp
Short-term rate +8.89 bp; medium-term factor +2.33 bp
Short-term rate +6.16 bp; medium-term factor +1.62 bp
Short-term rate +6.16 bp; medium-term factor +9.01 bp

questions.solution:
**Reversion speeds from half-lives**

Stem in one line: CAD vendor reports half-lives 0.75 years ($r$) and 1.25 years ($m$); $r_{t}$ = 2.25%, $m_{t}$ = 3.05%, $l_{t}$ = 3.40%; find the one-month drifts of $r$ and $m$.

**Concept and theory**

A reversion speed $\alpha$ is a rate per year; a half-life $h$ is the time for half of a gap to close. With exponential decay of the gap at rate $\alpha$, half of a shock is gone when

$e^{-\alpha h}$ = $\frac{1}{2}$ $\Rightarrow h$ = $\frac{\text{ln 2}}{\alpha} \Leftarrow\Rightarrow\alpha$ = $\frac{\text{ln 2}}{h} .$ (16.8)

GARP reports the Gauss+ estimates in both forms (Table 16.1: $\alpha_{r}$ = 1.0547 with half-life 0.66 years; $\alpha_{m}$ = 0.6358 with 1.09 years; $\alpha_{l}$ = 0.0165 with 42.01 years). The change equations need $\alpha$, so a vendor’s half-lives must be converted first. A longer half-life means a smaller $\alpha$ and a slower move.

**Applying it to this question**

$\alpha_{r}$ = ln 2/0.75 = 0.693147/0.75 = 0.924196

$\alpha_{m}$ = ln 2/1.25 = 0.693147/1.25 = 0.554518

∆$r$ = −0.924196 × (2.25% − 3.05%) $\times\frac{1}{12}$ = 0.924196 × 0.80%/12 = +0.0616% = +6.16 bp

∆$m$ = −0.554518 × (3.05% − 3.40%) $\times\frac{1}{12}$ = 0.554518 × 0.35%/12 = +0.0162% = +1.62 bp

Both factors are below their targets, so both drift up; $r$ moves more because its gap is larger and its speed faster. The half-life of $l$ (38 years) and $\mu$ are not needed for these two changes.

**Fragile fact.** $\alpha$ = ln 2$/h$: longer half-life, smaller speed. Then $m$’s target is $l$, not $\mu$.

**Reference**

LO 16.c. GARP Ch. 16, §16.3 A Practical Estimation Method, Table 16.1 (“Half-Life Is in Years”); §16.1, Eq. (16.8) for the half-life relation; §16.2, Eqs. (16.9) to (16.10). Schweser does not give the half-life relation for Gauss+ (GARP-only). Boundary call: converting a reported half-life is treated as preparing an input to the LO 16.c calculation, not as LO 16.d estimation.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 c, where it is Q7 of 12.

a.reason: **(+5.00, +3.65).** Error type: wrong input twin (half-life used as the speed). 0.75 × 0.80%/12 = 5.00 bp and 1.25 × 0.35%/12 = 3.65 bp. Note the giveaway: it makes $m$, with the longer half-life, revert faster. A would be correct if the vendor’s numbers were speeds $\alpha_{r}$ = 0.75 and $\alpha_{m}$ = 1.25.

b.reason: **(+8.89, +2.33).** Error type: dropped term (ln 2 omitted, $\alpha$ = 1$/h$). 1.3333 × 0.80%/12 = 8.89 bp; 0.80 × 0.35%/12 = 2.33 bp. 1$/\alpha$ is the mean reversion time scale, not the half-life. B would be correct if the reported figures were 1$/\alpha$ rather than half-lives.

c.reason: Speeds converted with GARP’s half-life relationship (Eq. (16.8), the same relation that produces Table 16.1’s half-life column), then GARP Equations (16.9) and (16.10) with zero shocks.

d.reason: **(+6.16, +9.01).** Error type: sibling swap (medium-term factor reverting to $\mu$, skipping $l$). 0.554518 × (5.00% − 3.05%)/12 = 9.01 bp. D would be correct only if $m$ were the bottom of the cascade, which is $l$’s role.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is reviewing the documentation of a Chinese bank’s CNY Gauss+ simulation engine, which takes two independent standard normal draws per step. The documentation contains four statements:

I. Over a step of length $dt$, each of $dW^{1}$ and $dW^{2}$ is normally distributed with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$.

II. The same random term $dW^{1}$ enters both the medium-term factor equation and the long-term factor equation.

III. The random term $dW^{2}$ enters the long-term factor equation with weight $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}$.

IV. The one-step change in the short-term rate contains no random term.

Which of the statements are correct?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question says otherwise, the Gauss+ model is in its cascade form, time is in years, one step of length $dt$ is taken by applying each factor’s equation once, and each random term is $dW^{i}$ = $Z_{i}\sqrt{dt}$, where $Z_{1}$ and $Z_{2}$ are independent standard normal draws.

options.text: I and II only
I, III and IV only
II and IV only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
**How the random terms are built and where they enter**

Stem in one line: which documentation statements about $dW^{1}$, $dW^{2}$ and the short-rate equation are correct?

**Concept and theory**

The Gauss+ model has three factors but only two sources of risk. GARP: “There are only two sources of risk, however, namely, $dW^{1}$ and $dW^{2}$.” Each is normal with mean zero and standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$, and they are uncorrelated, $E$\[$dW^{1}dW^{2}$\] = 0 (Eq. 16.12). In a simulation each is built as $Z_{i}\sqrt{dt}$ from a standard normal draw (Schweser Step 1).

Where they enter:

| Equation | weight on $dW^{1}$ | weight on $dW^{2}$ | scale |
|---|---|---|---|
| $r$ (16.9) | 0 | 0 | none |
| $m$ (16.10) | $\rho$ | $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}$ | $\sigma_{m}$ |
| $l$ (16.11) | 1 | 0 | $\sigma_{l}$ |

Because $\rho^{2}$ + (1 $- \rho^{2}$) = 1, the weights in the $m$ equation leave $m$’s shock with standard deviation $\sigma_{m}\sqrt{dt}$ (Eq. 16.13) while giving it a correlation $\rho$ with $l$’s shock, which loads fully on $dW^{1}$.

**Applying it to this question**

I matches GARP’s description of $dW^{1}$ and $dW^{2}$. True.

II: $dW^{1}$ appears in both Equation (16.10) and Equation (16.11). True.

III: $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}$ is the weight on $dW^{2}$ in the medium-term equation; the long-term equation contains no $dW^{2}$ at all. False.

IV: Equation (16.9) has no random term. True.

Correct: I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** $dW^{1}$: shared by $m$ (weight $\rho$) and $l$ (weight 1). $dW^{2}$: $m$ only (weight $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}$). $r$: neither.

**Reference**

LO 16.c. GARP Ch. 16, §16.2 The Gauss+ Model, Eqs. (16.9) to (16.13) and text. Schweser Reading 16, “Applying the Gauss+ Model”, Step 1. Equation weights confirmed from question bank Q739 and Q759. The “two sources of risk” remark is LO 16.a context. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 c, where it is Q8 of 12.

a.reason: **I and II only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement (scope error on IV). It omits the defining feature that $r$ has no random term. A would be correct for a model in which the short rate also had its own volatility parameter.

b.reason: **I, III and IV.** Error type: role misassignment in III ($m$’s idiosyncratic shock assigned to $l$), plus rejection of the true II. B would be correct only if $l$ were the factor that mixes the two shocks, which is $m$’s role.

c.reason: **II and IV only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement (I). A candidate who thinks $dW$ has standard deviation $dt$, or 1, rejects I. With $dW^{i}$ = $Z_{i}\sqrt{dt}$ the standard deviation is $\sqrt{dt}$. C would be correct if I said “standard deviation $dt$”.

d.reason: GARP 16.2, Eqs. (16.9) to (16.13) and the accompanying text, as quoted above.

Which of the following gives the expected one-month change in the medium-term factor and the standard deviation of that change?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question says otherwise, the Gauss+ model is in its cascade form, time is in years, one step of length $dt$ is taken by applying each factor’s equation once, and each random term is $dW^{i}$ = $Z_{i}\sqrt{dt}$, where $Z_{1}$ and $Z_{2}$ are independent standard normal draws.

Expected change +1.59 bp; standard deviation 31.52 bp
Expected change −1.59 bp; standard deviation 31.52 bp

**Expected change and standard deviation of the change in $m$**

Stem in one line: GARP estimates $\alpha_{m}$ = 0.6358, $\sigma_{m}$ = 109.2 bp, $\rho$ = 0.212; $m_{t}$ = 2.80%, $l_{t}$ = 3.10%, $dt$ = 1/12; expected change and standard deviation of ∆$m$.

**Concept and theory**

Over one step, ∆$m$ = $-\alpha_{m}$($m_{t} - l_{t}$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{m}$($\rho dW^{1}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}$). Its two moments come from the two parts:

$E$\[∆$m$\] = $-\alpha_{m}$($m_{t} - l_{t}$) $dt$ (shocks have mean zero)

Var\[∆$m$\] = $\sigma^{2}_{m} (\rho^{2} dt$ + (1 $- \rho^{2}$) $dt)$ = $\sigma^{2}_{m} dt$ (independent shocks: variances add)

SD\[∆$m$\] = $\sigma_{m}\sqrt{dt}$ (16.13)

GARP: the random terms “simply ensure that the instantaneous fluctuation of the medium-term factor around its trend has a volatility of $\sigma_{m}\sqrt{dt}$ and a correlation of $\rho$ with the fluctuation of the long-term factor around its trend.” So $\rho$ shapes the correlation, not the size, of $m$’s shock.

**Applying it to this question**

$E$\[∆$m$\] = −0.6358 × (2.80% − 3.10%) $\times\frac{1}{12}$ = 0.6358 × 0.30%/12 = +0.0159% = +1.59 bp

$\sqrt{dt}$ = 0.288675

SD\[∆$m$\] = 109.2 bp × 0.288675 = 31.52 bp

Interpretation: $m$ is expected to edge up 1.6 bp toward $l$ this month, but a one-standard-deviation month moves it about 31.5 bp either way. The month’s change is dominated by noise; $\rho$ is an irrelevant input for both numbers.

**Fragile fact.** The standard deviation of $m$’s one-step change is $\sigma_{m}\sqrt{dt}$ whatever $\rho$ is; $\rho$ only sets how much of that shock is shared with $l$.

**Reference**

LO 16.c. GARP Ch. 16, §16.2 The Gauss+ Model, Eqs. (16.10), (16.12) and (16.13) and text; §16.3, Table 16.1 (parameter values). The correlation result (Eqs. 16.14 to 16.15) is LO 16.a and is used only to explain distractor A. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 c, where it is Q9 of 12.

c.reason: **(−1.59; 31.52).** Error type: sign error on the drift. $m$ is below $l$, so it rises. C would be correct if $m_{t}$ were 3.10% and $l_{t}$ 2.80%.

d.reason: Error type: time-conversion slip ($dt$ in place of $\sqrt{dt}$). 109.2/12 = 9.10 bp. Standard deviations scale with the square root of time (compare GARP’s Vasicek example: 95 bp $\times\sqrt{1/12}$ = 27.4 bp a month). D would be correct only for a quantity that scales linearly in time, such as the drift.

A member of the board risk committee at a Singapore insurer is reviewing a two-month expected path for SGD rates, generated with a Gauss+ model in monthly steps ($dt$ = 1/12) with every random term set to its mean of zero. Which of the following changes to the starting inputs would alter the change in the short-term rate over the second month but leave its change over the first month unchanged?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question says otherwise, the Gauss+ model is in its cascade form, time is in years, one step of length $dt$ is taken by applying each factor’s equation once, and each random term is $dW^{i}$ = $Z_{i}\sqrt{dt}$, where $Z_{1}$ and $Z_{2}$ are independent standard normal draws.

options.text: A higher starting long-term factor $l_{t}$.
A higher starting medium-term factor $m_{t}$.
A higher volatility parameter $\sigma_{m}$ for the medium-term factor.
A higher reversion speed $\alpha_{r}$ for the short-term rate.

questions.solution:
**Propagation along the cascade over two steps**

Stem in one line: two-month expected SGD path (shocks at mean zero, $dt$ = 1/12); which input change alters $r$’s second-month change but not its first-month change?

**Concept and theory**

Simulating a path means applying the equations step after step, each time starting from the factor values produced by the previous step (Schweser: start with $r_{0}$, simulate $r_{1}$, “and continue until there is one complete interest rate path”). Because of the cascade, information flows down one level per step:

Month 1: ∆$r_{1}$ = $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{0} - m_{0}$) $dt$ uses $\alpha_{r}, r_{0}, m_{0}$

$m_{1}$ = $m_{0} - \alpha_{m}$($m_{0} - l_{0}$) $dt$ uses $\alpha_{m}, m_{0}, l_{0}$

Month 2: ∆$r_{2}$ = $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{1} - m_{1}$) $dt$ uses $\alpha_{r}, r_{1}, m_{1}$

The starting long-term factor $l_{0}$ cannot touch $r$ in the first step, but it moves $m_{1}$, which is $r$’s target in the second step.

**Applying it to this question**

Test each option against the two lines:

| Higher input | Changes ∆$r_{1}$? | Changes ∆$r_{2}$ (expected)? |
|---|---|---|
| $l_{0}$ | no | yes, via $m_{1}$ |
| $m_{0}$ | yes | yes |
| $\sigma_{m}$ | no | no (shocks set to mean zero) |
| $\alpha_{r}$ | yes | yes |

Illustration with $r_{0}$ = 10.50%, $m_{0}$ = 11.70%, $\alpha_{r}$ = 1.10, $\alpha_{m}$ = 0.60: with $l_{0}$ = 11.00% the two monthly changes are +11.00 bp and +9.67 bp; with $l_{0}$ = 11.50% they are +11.00 bp and +9.90 bp. Only the second month moves.

**Fragile fact.** A shock or a level change at the bottom of the cascade reaches $r$ one step at a time: $l$ affects $r$ only from the second step, through $m$.

**Reference**

LO 16.c. GARP Ch. 16, §16.2 The Gauss+ Model, Eqs. (16.9) to (16.11) and text. Schweser Reading 16, “Modeling Interest Rates” (path simulation) and “Applying the Gauss+ Model”, Steps 1 to 3. Numerical illustration from calc.py. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 c, where it is Q10 of 12.

**One-month update of $m$ and $l$ with the reading’s estimates**

Schweser’s procedure for one step: Step 1, draw the random terms ($dW^{i}$ = $Z_{i}\sqrt{dt}$); Step 2, plug them into the three equations; Step 3, add each change to the starting level to get the new factor values. The parameters here are GARP’s Table 16.1 estimates from US Treasury zero-coupon yields, January 2014 to January 2022:

| Parameter | Estimate | Half-life (years) |
|---|---|---|
| $\alpha_{r}$ | 1.0547 | 0.66 |
| $\alpha_{m}$ | 0.6358 | 1.09 |
| $\alpha_{l}$ | 0.0165 | 42.01 |
| $\sigma_{m}$ | 109.2 bp |  |
| $\sigma_{l}$ | 96.4 bp |  |
| $\rho$ | 0.212 |  |
| $\mu$ | 10.555% |  |

$\sqrt{dt}$ = 0.288675

$dW^{1}$ = −0.70 × 0.288675 = −0.202073$, dW^{2}$ = 1.20 × 0.288675 = 0.346410

$\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}$ = $\sqrt{1 - 0.044944}$ = 0.977270

$m$ drift = −0.6358 × (4.60% − 3.80%) $\times\frac{1}{12}$ = −0.0424% = −4.24 bp

$m$ shock = 109.2 × (0.212(−0.202073) + 0.977270(0.346410)) = 109.2 × 0.295699 = +32.29 bp

$m_{t\text{+1}}$ = 4.60% − 0.0424% + 0.3229% = 4.881%

$l$ drift = −0.0165 × (3.80% − 10.555%) $\times\frac{1}{12}$ = +0.0093% = +0.93 bp

$l$ shock = 96.4 × (−0.202073) = −19.48 bp

$l_{t\text{+1}}$ = 3.80% + 0.0093% − 0.1948% = 3.614%

| $l_{0}$ | 11.00% | $\alpha_{l}$ | 0.02 |
| $\mu$ | 12.00% | $\sigma_{m}$, $\sigma_{l}$ (per year) | 150 bp, 100 bp |
| Month 1 draws $Z_{1}$, $Z_{2}$ Month 2 draws $Z_{1}$, $Z_{2}$ | +0.90, −2.10 +0.40, +1.30 | $\rho$ | 0.20 |

Which of the following is closest to the short-term rate at the end of month 2?

*Conventions for this paper:* Unless a question says otherwise, the Gauss+ model is in its cascade form, time is in years, one step of length $dt$ is taken by applying each factor’s equation once, and each random term is $dW^{i}$ = $Z_{i}\sqrt{dt}$, where $Z_{1}$ and $Z_{2}$ are independent standard normal draws.
questions.solution:
**Two-step short-rate path**

Stem in one line: BRL, $r_{0}$ = 10.50%, $m_{0}$ = 11.70%, $l_{0}$ = 11.00%, month 1 draws +0.90, −2.10, $dt$ = 1/12; find $r$ at the end of month 2.

**Concept and theory**

Over one step $r$ moves deterministically toward $m$. Over two steps the second move uses the updated target $m_{1}$, which already contains month 1’s shock. So randomness reaches the short rate with a one-step lag:

$r_{1}$ = $r_{0} - \alpha_{r}$($r_{0} - m_{0}$) $dt$

$m_{1}$ = $m_{0} - \alpha_{m}$($m_{0} - l_{0}$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{m} (\rho Z_{1}\sqrt{dt}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} Z_{2}\sqrt{dt})$

$r_{2}$ = $r_{1} - \alpha_{r}$($r_{1} - m_{1}$) $dt$

Month 2’s draws only produce $m_{2}$ and $l_{2}$; they would affect $r_{3}$, not $r_{2}$. $l_{0}$, $\alpha_{l}$, $\sigma_{l}$ and $\mu$ do not enter $r_{2}$ at all ($l_{0}$ would reach $r$ through $m_{1}$’s drift, which is included).

**Applying it to this question**

∆$r_{1}$ = −1.10 × (10.50% − 11.70%) $\times\frac{1}{12}$ = +0.1100%$, r_{1}$ = 10.610%

$m$ drift = −0.60 × (11.70% − 11.00%) $\times\frac{1}{12}$ = −0.0350%

$\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}}$ = 0.979796$, \sqrt{dt}$ = 0.288675

Mixed draw = 0.20 × 0.90 + 0.979796 × (−2.10) = 0.18 − 2.057571 = −1.877571

$m$ shock = 1.50% × 0.288675 × (−1.877571) = −0.8130%

$m_{1}$ = 11.70% − 0.0350% − 0.8130% = 10.852%

∆$r_{2}$ = −1.10 × (10.610% − 10.852%) $\times\frac{1}{12}$ = +0.0222%

$r_{2}$ = 10.610% + 0.0222% = 10.632%

Month 1’s large negative $dW^{2}$ draw pulled $m$ down by about 85 bp, nearly closing the gap to $r$. So in month 2 the short rate rises only 2.2 bp, against 11 bp in month 1.

**Fragile fact.** The short rate’s second-step change uses the shocked $m_{1}$; month 2’s own draws do not affect $r_{2}$.

**Reference**

LO 16.c. GARP Ch. 16, §16.2 The Gauss+ Model, Eqs. (16.9) to (16.10) and the paragraph on the short-term rate being pushed toward $m$. Schweser Reading 16, “Modeling Interest Rates” (simulating $r_{1}$ from $r_{0}$ and continuing along the path) and “Applying the Gauss+ Model”, Steps 1 to 3. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 c, where it is Q12 of 12.

a.reason: Error type: intermediate result. This is $r_{1}$, the end of month 1. A would be correct if the question asked for the rate after one month.

b.reason: Schweser Steps 1 to 3 applied twice, each step starting from the previous step’s factors, with GARP Equations (16.9) and (16.10).

c.reason: Error type: dropped term (stale target, $m_{0}$ reused in month 2). 10.610 − 1.10 × (10.610 − 11.70)/12 = 10.610 + 0.0999 = 10.710%. This ignores that $m$ moved in month 1. C would be correct if the medium-term factor were held constant at 11.70%, for example with $\sigma_{m}$ = 0 and $m_{0}$ = $l_{0}$.

d.reason: Error type: time-conversion slip (no $\sqrt{dt}$ on month 1’s $m$ shock). $m_{1}$ = 11.665% + 1.50% × (−1.877571) = 8.849%, then $r_{2}$ = 10.610 − 1.10 × (10.610 − 8.849)/12 = 10.449%. D would be correct only for an annual-size shock to $m$, which is not consistent with a monthly step.

questions.question:
A junior quantitative analyst at a Canadian asset manager is replicating the reading’s estimation of the Gauss+ model on daily US Treasury zero-coupon data. Her manager suggests replacing the fed funds target rate with the overnight general collateral (GC) repo rate as the short-term rate input. Which of the following responses is most consistent with the reading?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation throughout: $r$, $m$ and $l$ are the short-term rate, the medium-term factor and the long-term factor; $\alpha_{r}$, $\alpha_{m}$, $\alpha_{l}$ are their mean reversion parameters; $\sigma_{m}$, $\sigma_{l}$ are the volatility parameters of $m$ and $l$; $\rho$ is the correlation between the shocks to $m$ and $l$; $\mu$ is the constant to which $l$ reverts.

options.text: Switch to GC repo: it is theoretically more consistent with a Treasury term structure, and its occasional idiosyncratic jumps average out in daily data.

Keep the fed funds target: GC repo is theoretically more consistent with a Treasury term structure, but its occasional idiosyncratic jumps complicate the estimation without significant offsetting advantages.
Keep the fed funds target: GC repo is theoretically less consistent with a Treasury term structure than the policy rate, so it would bias the regression stage of the estimation.
Use neither: the short-term rate is not taken from an observed rate but is backed out each day so that the model matches the market two-year forward rate.

questions.solution:
**Choosing the short-term rate proxy**

Stem in one line: should the GC repo rate replace the fed funds target as the short-term rate input in the reading’s estimation?

**Concept and theory**

The Gauss+ model has three factors: the short-term rate $r$, a medium-term factor $m$ and a long-term factor $l$. Its risk-neutral dynamics (GARP equations 16.9 to 16.12) are

$dr_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{r}$($r_{t} - m_{t}$) $dt$

$dm_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{m}$($m_{t} - l_{t}$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{m} (\rho dW^{1}_{t}$ + $\sqrt{1 - \rho^{2}} dW^{2}_{t})$

$dl_{t}$ = $-\alpha_{l}$($l_{t} - \mu$) $dt$ + $\sigma_{l} dW^{1}_{t}, E \left[dW^{1}_{t} dW^{2}_{t}\right]$ = 0

where $\alpha_{r}, \alpha_{m}, \alpha_{l}$ are mean reversion speeds, $\sigma_{m}, \sigma_{l}$ volatility parameters, $\rho$ the correlation of the $m$ and $l$ shocks, $\mu$ the constant to which $l$ reverts, and $dW^{1}, dW^{2}$ independent normal shocks with standard deviation $\sqrt{dt}$.

To estimate the parameters from data, the model needs an observable series for $r$. Of the three factors, only $r$ is meant to equal a market rate: it represents the central bank’s policy rate. GARP therefore takes $r$ each day as equal to the fed funds target rate. GARP accepts that the alternative, a GC repo rate, is theoretically more consistent with a term structure of Treasury rates, but rejects it on practical grounds: repo rates show occasional idiosyncratic jumps that complicate the estimation, without significant offsetting advantages.

|  | Fed funds target | GC repo |
|---|---|---|
| Theory | Policy rate the model’s $r$ is designed to mimic | More consistent with a Treasury term structure |
| Practice | Changes by discrete amounts on policy dates (GARP 16.2) | Occasional idiosyncratic jumps |
| GARP choice | Used | Rejected: complicates estimation, no offsetting advantage |

**Applying it to this question**

The manager’s suggestion has a valid theoretical premise (repo is more consistent with Treasuries), so the right answer must concede the theory but keep the fed funds target for the practical reason. Only B does both.

**Fragile fact.** Repo: theoretically better, practically worse. Fed funds target is used because of repo’s jumps, not because repo is theoretically wrong.

**Reference**

LO 16.d (Schweser, verbatim in Source note). GARP Ch. 16, §16.3 A Practical Estimation Method. Schweser Reading 16, “Estimating Gauss+ Model Parameters”, Step 1. Difference: Schweser names fed funds only as an example and omits the repo discussion (GARP-only detail). Model equations: GARP 16.9 to 16.12, square root confirmed from question bank LO 16.a/16.c worked solutions.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 d, where it is Q1 of 14.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the practical verdict. It keeps the correct theory but claims the jumps “average out”; GARP says they complicate the estimation. Correct only for a repo series without idiosyncratic jumps.

b.reason: GARP 16.3: “the short-term rate, $r$, is taken each day as equal to the fed funds target rate on that day. While a general collateral repo rate is theoretically more consistent with a term structure of Treasury interest rates, repo rates exhibit occasional idiosyncratic jumps that complicate the estimation without significant offsetting advantages.” Schweser Step 1 agrees: select a proxy for the short-term rate (e.g., fed funds).

c.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the theory. GARP says repo is theoretically more consistent with a Treasury term structure. Correct only if the stem asked about a rate that is genuinely inconsistent with Treasuries, which repo is not.

d.reason: Error type: role misassignment. Backing a factor out of a forward rate is what is done to $m$ and $l$ (fitted jointly to the two- and 10-year forwards) after estimation; $r$ is the one factor read directly from an observed rate. Correct if “short-term rate” read “medium- and long-term factors”, and even then they are fitted jointly, not one to one.

questions.question:
A senior risk analyst at a Singapore bank is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts on the reading’s practical method for estimating the Gauss+ model. The draft contains four statements:

I. The estimation proceeds in stages, with each stage estimating a subset of the model’s parameters.

II. The staged approach is significantly easier to implement than the maximum likelihood methods that are standard in the term structure literature.

III. Staging is possible because the model’s term structure of volatilities depends only on the volatility parameters and not on the mean reversion parameters.

IV. The procedure is presented as the industry-standard approach, since estimation methodologies across the industry are broadly uniform.

Which of the statements are accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation throughout: $r$, $m$ and $l$ are the short-term rate, the medium-term factor and the long-term factor; $\alpha_{r}$, $\alpha_{m}$, $\alpha_{l}$ are their mean reversion parameters; $\sigma_{m}$, $\sigma_{l}$ are the volatility parameters of $m$ and $l$; $\rho$ is the correlation between the shocks to $m$ and $l$; $\mu$ is the constant to which $l$ reverts.

options.text: I, II and IV only
I, II and III only
II and III only
I and II only

questions.solution:
**Why the estimation is done in stages**

Stem in one line: which of four slide statements about the staged estimation method are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

A Gauss+ model has seven parameters: $\alpha_{r}, \alpha_{m}, \alpha_{l}, \sigma_{m}, \sigma_{l}, \rho, \mu$. Schweser notes that these parameters “can be estimated using maximum likelihood techniques”, which GARP describes as the standard in the term structure literature: all parameters estimated jointly.

GARP proposes a practical alternative that “proceeds in stages, with each stage estimating a subset of the model’s parameters”. Footnote 4: “This approach is significantly easier to implement than the maximum likelihood methods that are standard in the term structure literature.” The staging works because each subset can be matched to a feature of the data that is driven mainly by that subset:

| Stage | Parameters | Data feature matched |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | $\alpha_{r}, \alpha_{m}, \alpha_{l}$ | Regression coefficients of yield changes on 2y and 10y yield changes |
| 2 | $\sigma_{m}, \sigma_{l}, \rho$ | Term structure of yield volatilities |
| 3 | $\mu$ | Yield levels (least squares across the whole sample) |

The key independence is that the model-implied regression coefficients depend only on the mean reversion parameters. GARP also explains why it bothers to present a detailed procedure: “methodologies across the industry vary widely.”

**Applying it to this question**

I: GARP’s own description. True. II: footnote 4. True. III: states an independence, but the wrong one. The independence that makes staging possible is that the regression coefficients do not depend on the volatility parameters; nothing says the volatility term structure is free of the mean reversion parameters (indeed GARP says mean reversion is why $\sigma_{m}$, $\sigma_{l}$ translate into lower yield volatilities). False. IV: GARP says methodologies vary widely. False. So I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Direction of independence: coefficients do not depend on volatilities. Not the reverse.

**Reference**

LO 16.d. GARP Ch. 16, §16.2 (introductory paragraph: methodologies “vary widely”), §16.3 and footnote 4. Schweser Reading 16, “Estimating Gauss+ Model Parameters”. Difference: Schweser adds that the simplified procedure “is possible when random components are not used to determine mean reversion speeds” (Schweser-only wording, consistent with GARP’s independence statement).

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-16 d, where it is Q2 of 14.

a.reason: **I, II and IV.** Error type: polarity flip in IV (“vary widely” becomes “broadly uniform”). Correct if IV said methodologies across the industry vary widely, which is GARP’s reason for presenting a detailed procedure.

b.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: sibling swap in III. The independence property belongs to the regression coefficients (stage 1 output), not to the volatility term structure (stage 2 target). Correct if III read “the model regression coefficients depend only on the mean reversion parameters, not on the volatility parameters”.

c.reason: **II and III.** Error type: rejecting a true statement plus the sibling swap in III. Rejecting I denies the defining feature of the method. Correct only if the estimation were a single joint optimization, which is maximum likelihood, the method GARP avoids.

d.reason: I and II restate GARP 16.3 and its footnote 4; Schweser also notes that the parameters “can be estimated using maximum likelihood techniques” and offers a “simplified approach”.
