I. Investment-grade sovereign credit spreads have a 20-day horizon, the shortest of any credit spread risk factor.

II. Investment-grade corporate credit spreads and non-investment-grade sovereign credit spreads share the same 40-day horizon.

III. Non-investment-grade corporate credit spreads have a 120-day horizon, the same as credit spread volatility.

IV. Credit spread volatility has a 60-day horizon, half the horizon of the “other” credit spread category.

Which of the statements are accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation: “category $j$” ($j$ = 1 to 5) is the FRTB liquidity-horizon category $j$, and $\text{ES}_{j}$ is the $j$th nested 97.5% stressed ES of the internal models cascade, each estimated from 10-day changes in the risk factors.

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
II and IV only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
**Credit spread liquidity horizons**

Stem in one line: which statements on credit spread liquidity horizons are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Under the FRTB every risk factor is assigned a liquidity horizon. GARP Table 18.1 gives the allocation (reconstructed from the two-column extract):

| Risk factor | Days | Risk factor | Days |
|---|---|---|---|
| Interest rate (dependent on currency) | 10 to 60 | Equity price: small cap volatility | 60 |
| Interest rate volatility | 60 | Equity: other | 60 |
| Credit spread: sovereign, IG | 20 | FX rate (dependent on currency) | 10 to 40 |
| Credit spread: sovereign, non-IG | 40 | FX volatility | 40 |
| Credit spread: corporate, IG | 40 | Energy price | 20 |
| Credit spread: corporate, non-IG | 60 | Precious metal price | 20 |
| Credit spread: other | 120 | Other commodities price | 60 |
| Credit spread volatility | 120 | Energy price volatility | 60 |
| Equity price: large cap | 10 | Precious metal volatility | 60 |
| Equity price: small cap | 20 | Other commodities price volatility | 120 |
| Equity price: large cap volatility | 20 | Commodity (other) | 120 |

For credit spreads the ladder is: sovereign IG 20 \< sovereign non-IG 40 = corporate IG 40 \< corporate non-IG 60 \< other 120 = credit spread volatility 120. Read across the ladder, weaker credit and corporate rather than sovereign names carry longer horizons, which fits the definition: the harder an exposure is to extinguish in stressed markets, the longer its horizon. GARP §18.3.3 summarises: “the liquidity horizon for credit spread varies from 20 to 120 days and the liquidity horizon for a credit spread volatility is 120 days.”

**Applying it to this question**

I: sovereign IG is 20 days and no credit spread factor is lower. True. II: corporate IG and sovereign non-IG are both 40 days. True. III: corporate non-IG is 60 days, not 120. False. IV: credit spread volatility is 120 days, not 60. False. Answer: I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Corporate IG (40) equals sovereign non-IG (40), not sovereign IG (20). Credit spread volatility is 120, the maximum.

**Reference**

LO 18.b. GARP Ch. 18, Table 18.1 and §18.3.3 Credit Risk. Schweser Reading 18, “Liquidity Horizons” (Figure 18.2 missing from the extract; the two textual examples agree with GARP). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 b, where it is Q2 of 15.

a.reason: GARP Table 18.1 and §18.3.3. Schweser’s text gives the same two anchor points: “investment-grade sovereign credit spreads are assigned a 20-day horizon, while non-investment-grade corporate credit spreads are assigned a 60-day horizon.”

b.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: sibling swap in III. The 120-day horizon belongs to the neighbouring “credit spread: other” row and to credit spread volatility; corporate non-IG is 60. III would be correct if it read “Credit spreads in the ‘other’ category have a 120-day horizon, the same as credit spread volatility.”

c.reason: **II and IV.** Error type: wrong number in IV, plus rejecting a true statement I. 60 days is the horizon of non-IG corporate spreads and of several volatility factors (interest rate, small-cap equity, energy, precious metal), not of credit spread volatility. IV would be correct for interest rate volatility (60 days).

d.reason: **I, II and IV.** Error type: wrong number in IV, as in C. Correct only if credit spread volatility were 60 days.

options.text: Small-cap equity prices and large-cap equity price volatility both have a 10-day liquidity horizon.
Energy prices and energy price volatility both have a 20-day liquidity horizon.

questions.solution:
**Equity and commodity liquidity horizons**

Stem in one line: which comparison of equity and commodity liquidity horizons is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

From GARP Table 18.1 (full table in the Q2 solution), the equity and commodity rows pair a price with its volatility:

| Underlying | Price (days) | Volatility (days) |
|---|---|---|
| Equity, large cap | 10 | 20 |
| Equity, small cap | 20 | 60 |
| Energy | 20 | 60 |
| Precious metal | 20 | 60 |
| Other commodities | 60 | 120 |

“Equity: other” is 60 days and “Commodity (other)” is 120 days. Two patterns: (1) the volatility of an underlying always has a longer horizon than the underlying itself; (2) within equities and commodities the short end is occupied by large-cap equity, energy and precious metals.

**Applying it to this question**

A: both are 20 days, not 10. B: energy price is 20 but energy volatility is 60. C: precious metal (20) is shorter than other commodities (60). D: small-cap volatility 60 and precious metal volatility 60. True.

**Fragile fact.** Volatility horizon > price horizon for every pair. Large cap: 10 and 20; small cap, energy and precious metal: 20 and 60; other commodities: 60 and 120.

**Reference**

LO 18.b. GARP Ch. 18, Table 18.1 (GARP-only in full; Schweser figure missing, text mentions only large-cap equity as a 10-day risk factor). No conflict.

a.reason: Error type: wrong number. The pairing is genuine (both share a horizon) but the shared horizon is 20 days; 10 days is large-cap equity price. A would be correct if it read “both have a 20-day horizon.”

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (price horizon given to its volatility). Energy price volatility is 60 days. B would be correct for “energy prices and precious metal prices” (both 20).

d.reason: GARP Table 18.1 lists “Equity price: small cap volatility 60” and “Precious metal volatility 60”.

questions.solution:
**Mapping interest rate, FX and volatility factors to categories**

Stem in one line: which entry in a risk-factor-to-category mapping file is correct?

**Concept and theory**

For the internal models approach, GARP §18.3 defines categories by horizon: Category 1 = 10 days, 2 = 20, 3 = 40, 4 = 60, 5 = 120. Each risk factor goes to the category of its Table 18.1 horizon. The interest rate and FX rows are unusual: their horizons are ranges “dependent on currency” (interest rate 10 to 60; FX rate 10 to 40), so the category is not the same for every currency. Their volatilities have single horizons: interest rate volatility 60, FX volatility 40.

b.reason: GARP Table 18.1: “Interest rate volatility 60”; GARP §18.3: “Category 4 Risk Factors: Risk factors with a time horizon of 60 days.”

options.text: For each equity and commodity price in the FRTB table that has a matching volatility risk factor, the volatility has the longer liquidity horizon.

The shortest liquidity horizon, 10 days, applies only to large-cap equity prices; every interest rate and FX rate risk factor has at least 20 days.

questions.solution:
**Comparing horizons across asset classes**

Stem in one line: which board-paper statement about cross-asset liquidity horizons is NOT correct?

**Concept and theory**

Comparing the rows of Table 18.1 (Q2 solution) gives four reliable cross-asset regularities:

| Regularity | Evidence in Table 18.1 |
|---|---|
| Shortest (10 days) | Large-cap equity price; interest rates and FX rates for some currencies (ranges 10 to 60 and 10 to 40) |
| Longest (120 days) | Credit spread other, credit spread volatility, other commodities volatility, commodity (other) |
| Volatility vs level | Volatility horizon exceeds price horizon for every equity and commodity pair |
| Currency dependence | Only interest rate and FX rate horizons are stated as “dependent on currency” |

Liquidity horizons also matter outside the internal models approach. GARP §18.2: under the standardized approach the risk weights are “set equal to multiples of the stressed daily volatility to reflect the liquidity horizon and the confidence level”; the risk-weight calculation itself is LO 18.a.

**Applying it to this question**

A, B and D are true. C claims 10 days applies only to large-cap equity and that every interest rate and FX factor has at least 20 days. Both interest rate (10 to 60) and FX (10 to 40) ranges start at 10 days, so C is not correct.

**Fragile fact.** Ten days is not unique to large-cap equity: interest rates and FX rates can be 10 days depending on the currency.

**Reference**

LO 18.b. GARP Ch. 18, Table 18.1; §18.2 Standardized Approach (risk weights reflect the liquidity horizon; GARP-only, boundary with LO 18.a). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 b, where it is Q5 of 15.

a.reason: True: large cap 10/20, small cap 20/60, energy 20/60, precious metal 20/60, other commodities 60/120. It would become false with “the price has the longer horizon” (polarity flip).

b.reason: True: credit spread volatility and other commodities price volatility are both 120 days. It would become false if it named, for example, FX volatility (40) as a 120-day factor.

c.reason: GARP Table 18.1 lists interest rates (dependent on currency) at 10 to 60 days and foreign exchange rates (dependent on currency) at 10 to 40 days. C is an absolute-claim corruption of the true statement “the shortest horizon, 10 days, applies to large-cap equity prices and, for some currencies, to interest rates and FX rates.”

d.reason: True: the standardized approach builds the horizon into Basel-set risk weights, while the cascade is an internal models construct. It would become false if it said the standardized approach uses the cascade, or that banks set the risk weights (role misassignment).

options.text: Each risk factor’s stressed change was measured over overlapping periods equal to its own horizon (Day 0 to 10 and Day 0 to 60, then Day 1 to 11 and Day 1 to 61, and so on); it was replaced by five categories to reduce implementation costs.

Each risk factor’s stressed change was measured over overlapping periods equal to its own horizon (Day 0 to 10 and Day 0 to 60, then Day 1 to 11 and Day 1 to 61, and so on); it was replaced by five categories to make successive trials independent.

Each risk factor’s one-day stressed change was scaled to its own horizon by the square root of the horizon in days (by $\sqrt{10}$ and $\sqrt{60}$); it was replaced by five categories to reduce implementation costs.

Each risk factor’s stressed change was measured over non-overlapping periods equal to its own horizon (Day 0 to 10 and Day 0 to 60, then Day 10 to 20 and Day 60 to 120, and so on); it was replaced by five categories to reduce implementation costs.

questions.solution:
**The original proposal and the December 2014 revision**

Stem in one line: what was the Basel Committee’s original liquidity-horizon idea, and why was it revised?

**Concept and theory**

Schweser describes how the treatment evolved. The original idea used overlapping periods, with each risk factor’s change measured over its own horizon. For a portfolio with a 10-day factor (large-cap equity) and a 60-day factor (non-IG corporate spread):

| Trial | Large-cap equity (10-day) | Non-IG corporate spread (60-day) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Day 0 to Day 10 | Day 0 to Day 60 |
| 2 | Day 1 to Day 11 | Day 1 to Day 61 |
| .. . | .. . | .. . |
| Last | Day 249 to Day 259 | Day 249 to Day 309 |

The ES was then the average loss in the worst 2.5% of the trials. After comments, the proposal was revised in December 2014 to five categories (10, 20, 40, 60, 120 days); Schweser: “The rationale was to reduce implementation costs.” The revised method, the one GARP describes, applies 10-day changes in nested shocks and combines them in the cascade.

**Applying it to this question**

Two slots decide it: the mechanics (overlapping, each factor over its own horizon) and the reason (implementation cost). Only A has both.

**Fragile fact.** Original idea: each factor over its own horizon, overlapping, rolling one day at a time. Revision: five categories, for cost.

**Reference**

LO 18.b. Schweser Reading 18, “Liquidity Horizons” (Schweser-only, condensed source). GARP does not describe the pre-2014 proposal; it describes the final January 2019 rules (§18.3). No content conflict; the difference is one of version history.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 b, where it is Q6 of 15.

a.reason: Schweser LO 18.b, “Liquidity Horizons”: the first trial measures Day 0 to 10 for the equity and Day 0 to 60 for the spread, the next Day 1 to 11 and Day 1 to 61; the December 2014 revision to five categories was made “to reduce implementation costs.”

b.reason: Error type: sibling swap (the overlap critique given as the reason). The revised method still uses overlapping 10-day periods (GARP §18.3), so successive trials are still not independent. B would be correct if the stem asked for the econometricians’ reason to prefer non-overlapping periods.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap with Basel I and Basel II.5 practice. Scaling one-day changes by the square root of time is the old $\sqrt{10}$ rule, not the original FRTB proposal. C would be correct as a description of how Basel I banks deduced 10-day VaR.

d.reason: Error type: polarity flip (overlapping becomes non-overlapping). Non-overlapping periods of 60 days would leave very few observations in a stressed period. D would be correct only if “non-overlapping” read “overlapping” with one-day steps.

questions.question:
A market risk analyst at a Canadian bank builds the historical simulation for FRTB stressed ES. The first trial applies to today’s portfolio the changes in all risk factors between Day 0 and Day 10 of the 250-day stressed period, the second trial the changes between Day 1 and Day 11, and so on. A model validator notes that successive trials are therefore not independent. Which of the following conclusions is most accurate?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation: “category $j$” ($j$ = 1 to 5) is the FRTB liquidity-horizon category $j$, and $\text{ES}_{j}$ is the $j$th nested 97.5% stressed ES of the internal models cascade, each estimated from 10-day changes in the risk factors.

options.text: The ES estimate is biased upward, because the same extreme daily moves are counted in several overlapping trials.
The ES estimate is unbiased, and because every trial has a different start date the effective sample size equals the number of trials.
The bank should switch to non-overlapping 10-day periods, which the FRTB permits whenever 250 days of stressed data are available.
The ES estimate is not biased, but the effective sample size is reduced, so the result is noisier than the number of trials suggests.

questions.solution:
**Overlapping 10-day trials: bias versus noise**

Stem in one line: successive overlapping trials are not independent; what does that do to the ES estimate?

**Concept and theory**

FRTB requires 10-day changes observed in a stressed period, not one-day changes scaled up. GARP §18.3: “Econometricians naturally prefer that non-overlapping periods be used when VaR or ES is being estimated using historical simulation, because they want observations on the losses to be independent. However, this is not feasible when 10-day changes are considered, because it would require a very long historical period. FRTB requires banks to base their estimates on overlapping 10-day periods.”

Trial 1 uses Day 0 to Day 10, trial 2 Day 1 to Day 11, and so on, so adjacent trials share most of their underlying daily moves. The consequence, in GARP’s words: “This does not bias the results, but it reduces the effective sample size, making results more noisy than they would otherwise be.”

| Property | Overlapping 10-day trials | Non-overlapping 10-day periods |
|---|---|---|
| Independent observations | No | Yes |
| Bias in ES | None | None |
| Effective sample size | Smaller than number of trials | Equal to number of periods |
| Feasible with available history | Yes | No (very long history needed) |

**Applying it to this question**

The validator’s observation is about dependence. Dependence affects precision (noise), not the centre of the estimate (bias). The answer must therefore say “no bias” and “reduced effective sample size”. Only D does.

**Fragile fact.** Overlap costs precision, not accuracy: no bias, smaller effective sample, noisier ES.

**Reference**

LO 18.b. GARP Ch. 18, §18.3 Internal Models Approach (GARP-only; also GARP Practice Question 18.3). Schweser mentions overlapping trials only for the original proposal. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 b, where it is Q7 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the consequence (noise read as bias). Each extreme day appearing in several trials adds dependence, not a systematic tilt. A would be correct if the stem asked about a method that over-weighted stressed days relative to their frequency, which overlapping does not.

b.reason: Error type: dropped term (the effective-sample consequence omitted). Distinct start dates do not make trials independent when they share most of their daily moves. B would be correct for non-overlapping periods.

c.reason: Error type: scope or condition error. The FRTB requires overlapping periods; non-overlapping 10-day periods are infeasible because they would need a very long history, not because of a 250-day threshold. C would be correct if the stem described econometricians’ preference rather than FRTB rules.

d.reason: GARP §18.3, quoted above, states both halves: no bias; smaller effective sample, noisier results.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a UK bank is reviewing the GBP market risk methodology document for the FRTB internal models approach. The section on the historical simulation contains four statements:

I. The first simulation trial assumes that the percentage changes in all risk factors over the next 10 days equal their changes between Day 0 and Day 10 of the stressed period; the second uses Day 1 to Day 11.

II. Econometricians prefer non-overlapping periods because they give independent observations, but non-overlapping 10-day periods would require a very long historical period.

III. A measure built from 10-day changes can be more relevant than one built from one-day changes if successive daily changes are not independent while successive 10-day changes can reasonably be assumed independent.

IV. Because overlapping trials are not independent, the FRTB lets a bank instead use one-day stressed changes scaled up by $\sqrt{10}$.

Which of the statements are correct?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation: “category $j$” ($j$ = 1 to 5) is the FRTB liquidity-horizon category $j$, and $\text{ES}_{j}$ is the $j$th nested 97.5% stressed ES of the internal models cascade, each estimated from 10-day changes in the risk factors.

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
II and III only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
**Building the trials and why 10-day changes are used**

Stem in one line: which methodology statements on the overlapping 10-day historical simulation are correct?

**Concept and theory**

GARP §18.3 sets out the construction: “The first simulation trial assumes that the percentage changes in all risk factors over the next 10 days will be the same as their changes between Day 0 and Day 10 of the stressed period; the second simulation trial assumes that the percentage changes in all risk factors over the next 10 days will be the same as their changes between Day 1 and Day 11 of the stressed period; and so on.”

Why accept dependent observations? GARP: “Presumably the Basel Committee has decided that, in spite of the lack of independence of observations, a measure calculated from 10-day changes provides more relevant information than a measure calculated from one-day changes. This could be the case if changes on successive days are not independent, but changes in successive 10-day periods can reasonably be assumed to be independent.” The $\sqrt{10}$ multiplier assumes independent daily changes; if daily changes are dependent, it misstates 10-day risk, whereas directly observed 10-day changes do not rely on that assumption.

**Applying it to this question**

I: the construction, verbatim in substance. True. II: the econometric preference and its infeasibility. True. III: GARP’s stated rationale for 10-day changes. True. IV: the $\sqrt{10}$ multiplier was allowed under Basel I and Basel II.5 and is what FRTB moves away from. False. Answer: I, II and III only.

**Fragile fact.** Roll forward one day per trial (Day 0 to 10, Day 1 to 11). No $\sqrt{10}$ scaling of one-day changes under the FRTB.

**Reference**

LO 18.b. GARP Ch. 18, §18.3 Internal Models Approach (GARP-only). Schweser Reading 18, “Liquidity Horizons” (base horizon of 10 days). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 b, where it is Q8 of 15.

a.reason: **I and II only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement (polarity misread of III). A candidate who thinks the Basel Committee assumed daily changes are independent rejects III. A would be correct if III said “if successive daily changes are independent”.

b.reason: GARP §18.3, both passages quoted above; GARP: “In Basel I and Basel II.5, banks are allowed to deduce the impact of 10-day changes from the impact of one-day changes using a $\sqrt{10}$ multiplier. In FRTB, banks are required to consider changes over periods of 10 days that occurred during a stressed period in the past.”

c.reason: **II and III only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement (I). A candidate who thinks each trial uses a fresh, non-overlapping block rejects I. C would be correct if I said the second trial uses Day 10 to Day 20.

d.reason: **All four.** Error type: sibling swap in IV (Basel I / II.5 scaling carried into the FRTB). D would be correct if IV described Basel II.5 rather than the FRTB.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Japanese bank is setting up the FRTB internal models calculation for a desk whose stressed ES depends on five risk factors:

| Risk factor | Position (JPY billion) |
|---|---|
| Large-cap Japanese equity prices | 42 |
| Gold price (precious metal) | 18 |
| Investment-grade corporate credit spreads | 65 |
| Small-cap equity price volatility | 7 |
| Credit spread volatility | 11 |

In the calculation of $\text{ES}_{3}$, which risk factors are given their stressed 10-day changes?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation: “category $j$” ($j$ = 1 to 5) is the FRTB liquidity-horizon category $j$, and $\text{ES}_{j}$ is the $j$th nested 97.5% stressed ES of the internal models cascade, each estimated from 10-day changes in the risk factors.

options.text: Investment-grade corporate credit spreads, small-cap equity price volatility and credit spread volatility; large-cap equity and gold prices are held constant.
Investment-grade corporate credit spreads only; the other four risk factors are held constant.
Large-cap equity prices, gold prices and investment-grade corporate credit spreads; the two volatility risk factors are held constant.
Gold prices, investment-grade corporate credit spreads and both volatility risk factors; large-cap equity prices are held constant.

questions.solution:
**Which risk factors move in $\text{ES}_{3}$**

Stem in one line: for a five-factor desk, which risk factors receive stressed 10-day changes in $\text{ES}_{3}$?

**Concept and theory**

The cascade is built from five nested ES calculations, each using 10-day changes. GARP §18.3 and Schweser LO 18.b agree:

| Measure | Categories shocked (10-day changes) | Categories held constant |
|---|---|---|
| $\text{ES}_{1}$ | 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 | none |
| $\text{ES}_{2}$ | 2, 3, 4, 5 | 1 |
| $\text{ES}_{3}$ | 3, 4, 5 | 1, 2 |
| $\text{ES}_{4}$ | 4, 5 | 1, 2, 3 |
| $\text{ES}_{5}$ | 5 | 1, 2, 3, 4 |

The sets are nested from the top: each step drops the shortest remaining category. A risk factor in category $k$ is therefore shocked in $\text{ES}_{1} \text{to ES}_{k}$.

**Applying it to this question**

Map each factor with Table 18.1:

| Risk factor | Horizon (days) | Category |
|---|---|---|
| Large-cap equity prices | 10 | 1 |
| Gold (precious metal) price | 20 | 2 |
| IG corporate credit spreads | 40 | 3 |
| Small-cap equity price volatility | 60 | 4 |
| Credit spread volatility | 120 | 5 |

$\text{ES}_{3}$ shocks categories 3, 4 and 5: IG corporate spreads, small-cap volatility and credit spread volatility, with large-cap equity and gold held constant. The JPY positions are irrelevant to which factors are shocked.

**Fragile fact.** $\text{ES}_{j}$ shocks categories $j$ and above; shorter categories are frozen. IG corporate spreads are 40 days (category 3), not 20.

**Reference**

LO 18.b. GARP Ch. 18, §18.3 Internal Models Approach and Table 18.1. Schweser Reading 18, “Liquidity Horizons” (same nested scheme). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 b, where it is Q9 of 15.

a.reason: GARP §18.3: $\text{ES}_{3}$ is the ES when “10-day changes are made to all risk factors in categories 3, 4, and 5 with risk factors in categories 1 and 2 being kept constant”; the mapping is from Table 18.1.

b.reason: Error type: scope error (nested sets read as exclusive buckets). $\text{ES}_{3}$ is not “category 3 only”; only $\text{ES}_{5}$ is a single-category shock. B would be correct if each $\text{ES}_{j}$ shocked only category $j$, a bucket-by-bucket scheme the FRTB does not use.

c.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the nesting direction (shortest categories kept instead of dropped). C would be correct if the cascade shocked categories 1 to $j$ and held the longer ones constant.

d.reason: Error type: intermediate result (off by one category). Shocking everything except large-cap equity is $\text{ES}_{2}$. D would be correct if the stem asked about $\text{ES}_{2}$, or if gold were misclassified as a 40-day factor.

questions.question:
A member of the board risk committee of a US bank asks the CRO to explain one step in the FRTB cascade. For a portfolio whose risk factors are all in categories 1, 2 and 3, the liquidity-adjusted ES is

$\sqrt{\text{ES}^{2}_{1} \text{+ ES}^{2}_{2} \text{+ 2 ES}^{2}_{3}}.$

Which of the following correctly explains the factor 2 on $\text{ES}^{2}_{3}$?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation: “category $j$” ($j$ = 1 to 5) is the FRTB liquidity-horizon category $j$, and $\text{ES}_{j}$ is the $j$th nested 97.5% stressed ES of the internal models cascade, each estimated from 10-day changes in the risk factors.

options.text: Category 3 risk factors have a 40-day horizon, twice the 20-day horizon of category 2, and this ratio of the two horizons, 2, multiplies $\text{ES}^{2}_{3}$.
Category 3 shocks are assumed perfectly correlated with category 2 shocks over the first 20 days, which doubles the variance that is attributed to $\text{ES}_{3}$.

$\text{ES}_{1} \text{and ES}_{2}$ cover the first 20 days; category 3 risk factors need a further 20 days, assumed independent of earlier behavior, with their 20-day ES taken as $\sqrt{2} \text{times ES}_{3}$.

$\text{ES}_{1} \text{and ES}_{2}$ cover the first 20 days; category 3 risk factors need a further 20 days, assumed independent of earlier behavior, with their 20-day ES taken as 2 times $\text{ES}_{3}$.

questions.solution:
**Why $\text{ES}^{2}_{3}$ carries a factor of 2**

Stem in one line: for categories 1 to 3, explain the factor 2 in $\sqrt{\text{ES}^{2}_{1} \text{+ ES}^{2}_{2} \text{+ 2 ES}^{2}_{3}}$.

**Concept and theory**

GARP derives the cascade step by step from two assumptions: independence of behaviour over successive periods, and the square-root rule for extending a horizon.

Step 1, categories 1 and 2 only. All risk factors move over the first 10 days $\text{(ES}_{1}$). Category 2 factors need a further 10 days, captured by $\text{ES}_{2}$. GARP: “It is assumed that the behavior of all risk factors during a 10-day period is independent of the behavior of category 2 risk factors during a further 10-day period. An extension of the square root rule then leads to” $\sqrt{\text{ES}^{2}_{1} \text{+ ES}^{2}_{2}}$. Independent pieces add like variances: square, add, take the root.

Step 2, add category 3 (40 days). After 20 days, category 3 factors still need a further 40 − 20 = 20 days. GARP: “We assume that the behavior of the category 3 risk factors over an additional 20 days is independent of the behavior of all the risk factors over the periods already considered. We also assume that the ES for the category 3 risk factors over 20 days is $\sqrt{2}$ times their ES over 10 days.” So the extra term is ($\sqrt{2} \text{ES}_{3}$)$^{2}$ = 2 $\text{ES}^{2}_{3}$.

General form (GARP equation 18.2):

$\text{ES} = \sqrt{\text{ES}_{1}^{2} + \sum_{j=2}^{5}\left(\text{ES}_{j}\sqrt{\frac{LH_{j} - LH_{j-1}}{10}}\right)^{2}}$

where $\text{ES}_{j}$ is the $j$th nested 10-day ES and $LH_{j}$ the horizon of category $j$ ($LH_{1}, . . . , LH_{5}$ = 10, 20, 40, 60, 120). The squared scale factors are 1, 2, 2, 6 for $j$ = 2, . . . , 5.

**Applying it to this question**

The factor 2 is ($LH_{3} - LH_{2}$)/10 = (40 − 20)/10, the additional horizon in 10-day units, under independence and $\sqrt{\text{time}}$ scaling of ES. Option C says exactly this.

**Fragile fact.** Scale by the square root of the additional horizon over 10 days, $\sqrt{\text{(}LH_{j} - LH_{j-1}\text{)}/10}$, never by the full horizon or a ratio of horizons.

**Reference**

LO 18.b. GARP Ch. 18, §18.3 Internal Models Approach, equation (18.2) and its derivation. Schweser Reading 18, “Liquidity Horizons” (“scaled to the square root of the difference in the horizon lengths of the nested risk factors”; formula image missing). Equation (18.2) is garbled in the GARP extract; notation confirmed from the question bank’s worked solutions (Q864, Q867). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 b, where it is Q10 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: wrong formula input (ratio of horizons used instead of their difference). Here 40/20 = 2 happens to equal (40 − 20)/10, which is the trap. The reasoning fails elsewhere: for category 4 the ratio is 60/40 = 1.5 but the weight is 2, and for category 5 the ratio is 120/60 = 2 but the weight is 6. A would be correct only if the cascade scaled by $LH_{j} /LH_{j-1}$, which it does not.

b.reason: Error type: polarity flip on the dependence assumption. The cascade assumes independence; perfect correlation would add ES figures linearly, not in quadrature. B would be correct for a simple-sum aggregation that assumes perfectly correlated shocks.

c.reason: It restates GARP’s two assumptions for the category 3 step: an additional 20 days, independent of earlier periods, with 20-day ES = $\sqrt{2}\times$ 10-day ES, giving 2 $\text{ES}^{2}_{3}$.

d.reason: Error type: square-root-of-time slip. Scaling ES linearly with time would make the term (2 $\text{ES}_{3}$)$^{2}$ = 4 $\text{ES}^{2}_{3}$, contradicting the formula in the stem. D would be correct only if ES grew in proportion to the horizon.

**Correcting a horizon mapping: effect on the nested shocks**

Stem in one line: a non-IG sovereign spread was mapped as IG sovereign; what changes when the mapping is corrected?

**Concept and theory**

Two facts combine. (1) Table 18.1: sovereign IG spreads are 20 days (category 2); sovereign non-IG spreads are 40 days (category 3). (2) Nesting (Q9 solution): a category $k$ factor is shocked in $\text{ES}_{1}$ to $\text{ES}_{k}$. Moving a factor up one category adds it to one more nested calculation, and that calculation carries the squared weight ($LH_{k} - LH_{k-1}$)/10 in the cascade.

**Applying it to this question**

Before: category 2, shocked in $\text{ES}_{1} \text{and ES}_{2}$. After: category 3, shocked in $\text{ES}_{1}$, $\text{ES}_{2} \text{and ES}_{3}$. The weight on $\text{ES}^{2}_{3}$ is (40 − 20)/10 = 2. The factor’s shocks now also enter a term that represents a further 20 days of exposure.

**Fragile fact.** Category $k \Rightarrow$ shocked in $\text{ES}_{1} \text{to ES}_{k}$. Sovereign non-IG is 40 days, the same as corporate IG.

**Reference**

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 b, where it is Q11 of 15.

a.reason: GARP §18.3 (nested definitions; weight from equation 18.2) and Table 18.1 (20 versus 40 days).

b.reason: Error type: scope error (nested sets read as exclusive buckets). The factor is still shocked in $\text{ES}_{1}$ and $\text{ES}_{2}$; $\text{ES}_{1}$ shocks every risk factor. B would be correct if each $\text{ES}_{j}$ shocked only category $j$.

c.reason: Error type: counting error (number of 10-day periods confused with the category number). A 40-day horizon is category 3; $\text{ES}_{4}$ shocks only categories 4 and 5. C would be correct for a 60-day factor such as a non-IG corporate spread.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap with LO 18.c. The restriction on moving positions applies to transfers between the trading book and the banking book. A risk factor’s liquidity horizon follows its type in Table 18.1. D would be correct for a question about reclassifying an instrument from the banking book to the trading book.

A market risk manager at a German bank has run the five nested stressed ES calculations for the bank’s rates and credit desk under the FRTB internal models approach (EUR million):

| $j$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Liquidity horizon (days) | 10 | 20 | 40 | 60 | 120 |
| $\text{ES}_{j}$ | 42.0 | 30.0 | 18.0 | 11.0 | 5.0 |

The desk’s 99% one-day VaR is EUR 14.5 million. Which of the following is closest to the desk’s liquidity-adjusted ES?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation: “category $j$” ($j$ = 1 to 5) is the FRTB liquidity-horizon category $j$, and $\text{ES}_{j}$ is the $j$th nested 97.5% stressed ES of the internal models cascade, each estimated from 10-day changes in the risk factors.

options.text: EUR 76.72 million
EUR 73.10 million
EUR 67.20 million
EUR 60.86 million

questions.solution:
**Liquidity-adjusted ES: full five-category cascade**

Stem in one line: given $\text{ES}_{1} \text{to ES}_{5}$ of 42, 30, 18, 11 and 5 (EUR million), find the liquidity-adjusted ES.

**Concept and theory**

GARP equation (18.2), derived in the Q10 solution:

$\text{ES} = \sqrt{\text{ES}_{1}^{2} + \sum_{j=2}^{5}\left(\text{ES}_{j}\sqrt{\frac{LH_{j} - LH_{j-1}}{10}}\right)^{2}}$

$\text{ES}_{j}$ : 97.5% stressed ES from 10-day shocks to categories $j$ to 5; $LH_{j}$ : horizon of category $j$ in days. The bracketed term converts the 10-day $\text{ES}_{j}$ to the additional horizon that category $j$ needs beyond category $j -$ 1; squaring and adding reflects independence between those periods.

**Applying it to this question**

Squared scale factors $w_{j}$ = ($LH_{j} - LH_{j-1}$)/10, with $w_{1}$ = 1:

$w_{2}$ = (20 − 10)/10 = 1$, w_{3}$ = (40 − 20)/10 = 2

$w_{4}$ = (60 − 40)/10 = 2$, w_{5}$ = (120 − 60)/10 = 6

$\text{ES}^{2}_{1}$ = $\text{42.0}^{2}$ = 1,764

$w_{2} \text{ES}^{2}_{2}$ = 1 × $\text{30.0}^{2}$ = 900

$w_{3} \text{ES}^{2}_{3}$ = 2 × $\text{18.0}^{2}$ = 648

$w_{4} \text{ES}^{2}_{4}$ = 2 × $\text{11.0}^{2}$ = 242

$w_{5} \text{ES}^{2}_{5}$ = 6 × $\text{5.0}^{2}$ = 150

Sum = 1,764 + 900 + 648 + 242 + 150 = 3,704

ES = $\sqrt{3{,}704}$ = 60.86

A junior risk analyst at a Chinese bank is computing the liquidity-adjusted ES for a desk whose risk factors all fall in categories 1, 2 and 4; the desk has no category 3 or category 5 risk factors. She has run the following calculations (CNY million) and has left the cells for $\text{ES}_{3} \text{and ES}_{5}$ blank:

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| $\text{ES}_{1}$ | 80.0 |
| $\text{ES}_{2}$ | 52.0 |
| $\text{ES}_{4}$ | 30.0 |
| Number of trading desks at the bank | 6 |

Which of the following is closest to the desk’s liquidity-adjusted ES?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation: “category $j$” ($j$ = 1 to 5) is the FRTB liquidity-horizon category $j$, and $\text{ES}_{j}$ is the $j$th nested 97.5% stressed ES of the internal models cascade, each estimated from 10-day changes in the risk factors.

options.text: CNY 104.42 million
CNY 112.71 million
CNY 120.43 million
CNY 144.25 million

questions.solution:
**Cascade with empty categories**

Stem in one line: a desk has only category 1, 2 and 4 risk factors; with $\text{ES}_{1}$ = 80, $\text{ES}_{2}$ = 52, $\text{ES}_{4}$ = 30 (CNY million), find the liquidity-adjusted ES.

**Concept and theory**

The cascade formula (Q10 and Q12 solutions) always uses the five fixed horizons, $LH_{1}$ to $LH_{5}$ equal to 10, 20, 40, 60 and 120 days. What changes when a category is empty is the value of the nested ES terms, because each $\text{ES}_{j}$ is defined by which categories are shocked:

- $\text{ES}_{3}$ shocks categories 3, 4 and 5 with categories 1 and 2 held constant. With no category 3 or 5 factors, that is a shock to the category 4 factors alone, which is exactly what $\text{ES}_{4}$ measures. So $\text{ES}_{3}$ = $\text{ES}_{4}$.
- $\text{ES}_{5}$ shocks category 5 only. With no category 5 factors nothing moves, so $\text{ES}_{5}$ = 0.

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{ES}_{3}$ = $\text{ES}_{4}$ = 30.0$, \text{ES}_{5}$ = 0

$\text{ES}^{2}_{1}$ = $\text{80.0}^{2}$ = 6,400

1 $\times\text{ES}^{2}_{2}$ = $\text{52.0}^{2}$ = 2,704

2 $\times\text{ES}^{2}_{3}$ = 2 × $\text{30.0}^{2}$ = 1,800

2 $\times\text{ES}^{2}_{4}$ = 2 × $\text{30.0}^{2}$ = 1,800

6 $\times\text{ES}^{2}_{5}$ = 0

ES = $\sqrt{6,\text{400 + 2},\text{704 + 1},\text{800 + 1},800}$ = $\sqrt{12{,}704}$ = 112.71

Cross-check: category 4 factors need 60 − 20 = 40 days beyond the 20 days covered by $\text{ES}_{1}$ and $\text{ES}_{2}$, a squared weight of 40/10 = 4; 6,400 + 2,704 + 4 × 900 = 12,704, the same result. Meaning: the 60-day factors get credit for their full extra 40 days of exposure, split across the $\text{ES}_{3} \text{and ES}_{4}$ terms. The number of desks is irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** An empty category does not make its $\text{ES}_{j}$ zero: $\text{ES}_{j}$ shocks categories $j$ and above, so $\text{ES}_{3}$ picks up the category 4 factors.

**Reference**

LO 18.b. GARP Ch. 18, §18.3 Internal Models Approach, nested definitions and equation (18.2). The treatment of empty categories is a direct application of those definitions, not a separate rule in either source. Notation confirmed from question bank Q864. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 b, where it is Q13 of 15.

questions.question:
An internal auditor at a US bank is checking a desk’s FRTB internal models output. The desk reports a liquidity-adjusted ES of USD 60.0 million, computed with the cascade approach, and the following nested ES values (USD million); the value of $\text{ES}_{5}$ is missing from the report.

| $j$ | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\text{ES}_{j}$ | 40.0 | 28.0 | 20.0 | 10.0 |

The desk’s stressed period is the 250 days ending 31 March 2009. Which of the following is closest to the $\text{ES}_{5}$ implied by the reported figures?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation: “category $j$” ($j$ = 1 to 5) is the FRTB liquidity-horizon category $j$, and $\text{ES}_{j}$ is the $j$th nested 97.5% stressed ES of the internal models cascade, each estimated from 10-day changes in the risk factors.

options.text: USD 4.24 million
USD 4.43 million
USD 6.00 million
USD 14.70 million

questions.solution:
**Implied $\text{ES}_{5}$ from a reported cascade**

Stem in one line: reported liquidity-adjusted ES is 60.0 with $\text{ES}_{1} \text{to ES}_{4}$ of 40, 28, 20 and 10 (USD million); find the implied $\text{ES}_{5}$.

**Concept and theory**

Equation (18.2) can be inverted for any one missing term. Squaring both sides:

$\text{ES}^{2}$ = $\text{ES}^{2}_{1}$ + 1 $\cdot\text{ES}^{2}_{2}$ + 2 $\text{ES}^{2}_{3}$ + 2 $\text{ES}^{2}_{4}$ + 6 $\text{ES}^{2}_{5}$

The weight on $\text{ES}^{2}_{5}$ is ($LH_{5} - LH_{4}$)/10 = (120 − 60)/10 = 6: category 5 factors need a further 60 days beyond the 60 days already covered.

**Applying it to this question**

$\text{ES}^{2}$ = $\text{60.0}^{2}$ = 3,600

Known terms = $\text{40.0}^{2}$ + $\text{28.0}^{2}$ + $\text{2(20.0}^{2}$) + $\text{2(10.0}^{2}$) = 1,600 + 784 + 800 + 200 = 3,384

6 $\text{ES}^{2}_{5}$ = 3,600 − 3,384 = 216

$\text{ES}^{2}_{5}$ = 216/6 = 36

$\text{ES}_{5}$ = $\sqrt{36}$ = 6.00

Meaning: a 10-day stressed shock to the 120-day risk factors alone produces an ES of USD 6.0 million; scaled by $\sqrt{6}$ it contributes 6 × 36 = 216 to the squared total. The stressed-period dates are irrelevant.

**Fragile fact.** Category 5 weight is 6, not 12 and not 11: (120 − 60)/10.

**Reference**

LO 18.b. GARP Ch. 18, §18.3 Internal Models Approach, equation (18.2). Notation confirmed from question bank Q864. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 b, where it is Q14 of 15.

a.reason: Error type: wrong formula input (full horizon $LH_{5}/$10 = 12). $\sqrt{216/12}$ = $\sqrt{18}$ = 4.24. Correct only if the category 5 term had to cover all 120 days by itself.

b.reason: Error type: wrong formula input (horizon measured from the 10-day base, (120−10)/10 = 11). $\sqrt{216/11}$ = $\sqrt{19.64}$ = 4.43. Correct only if the extra horizon were counted from Day 10 rather than from the category 4 horizon.

c.reason: It inverts equation (18.2) using the incremental weight 6 for category 5.

d.reason: Error type: intermediate result (the weight of 6 never divided out). $\sqrt{216}$ = 14.70 is $\sqrt{6} \text{ES}_{5}$, the scaled term, not $\text{ES}_{5}$ itself: an intermediate result. Correct if the question asked for the scaled category 5 contribution $\text{ES}_{5}\sqrt{6}$.

questions.question:
A risk consultant is validating the methodology note on the FRTB cascade approach at an Australian bank with six trading desks. The note states:

I. The cascade assumes that the behavior of risk factors over each additional period is independent of their behavior over the periods already considered.

II. With five nested ES calculations per desk, the internal models approach as described requires 30 ES calculations across the six desks.

III. The FRTB prescribes historical simulation as the method banks must use to estimate the nested stressed ES measures.

IV. The cascade approach can be used to calculate a liquidity-adjusted VaR as well as a liquidity-adjusted ES.

Which of the statements are correct?

*Conventions for this paper:* Notation: “category $j$” ($j$ = 1 to 5) is the FRTB liquidity-horizon category $j$, and $\text{ES}_{j}$ is the $j$th nested 97.5% stressed ES of the internal models cascade, each estimated from 10-day changes in the risk factors.

options.text: I and II only
I, II and IV only
I, III and IV only
II, III and IV only

questions.solution:
**Cascade assumptions and mechanics**

Stem in one line: which methodology-note statements on the cascade approach are correct?

**Concept and theory**

Four facts from GARP §18.3 define how a bank actually runs the cascade:

| Feature | GARP §18.3 |
|---|---|
| Independence | Behaviour over each additional period is assumed independent of behaviour over the periods already considered. |
| Method | “FRTB does not prescribe a particular method for doing this. Typically the historical simulation approach is likely to be used.” |
| Scope | The cascade “can be used for VaR as well”. |
| Workload | “Calculations are carried out for each desk. If there are six desks, this means the internal models approach, as we have described it so far, requires 5 × 6 = 30 ES calculations.” |

Schweser adds that the categorical process “attempts to account for the fact that risk factor shocks might not be correlated across liquidity horizons”, which is the same independence idea.

**Applying it to this question**

I: true. II: 5 × 6 = 30, true. III: the FRTB does not prescribe the method; historical simulation is only the typical choice. False. IV: true. Answer: I, II and IV only.

**Fragile fact.** Method not prescribed (historical simulation is typical). 30 ES calculations for six desks before the stressed-period subset adjustment, which belongs to LO 18.a.

**Reference**

LO 18.b. GARP Ch. 18, §18.3 Internal Models Approach (GARP-only for method, VaR use and count). Schweser Reading 18, “Liquidity Horizons” (independence phrasing). No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 b, where it is Q15 of 15.

a.reason: **I and II only.** Error type: rejecting a true statement (IV). The cascade is a horizon-combination rule and works for VaR as well as ES. A would be correct if IV claimed the cascade could be used only for VaR.

b.reason: All four facts are in GARP §18.3 as quoted above.

c.reason: **I, III and IV.** Error type: absolute claim accepted in III, and a true statement II rejected. “Prescribes” turns “typically likely to be used” into a requirement. C would be correct if III said historical simulation is the method typically used and II gave a different count.

d.reason: **II, III and IV.** Error type: absolute claim accepted in III, and the independence assumption I rejected. D would be correct only if the FRTB mandated historical simulation and the cascade assumed dependence, neither of which GARP states.

questions.question:
A junior risk analyst at an Indian private-sector bank is preparing a slide for newly hired analysts on why the FRTB revisited the boundary between the trading book and the banking book. The draft slide contains four statements:

I. Roughly speaking, the trading book consists of instruments the bank intends to trade, and these instruments are subject to market risk capital.

II. The banking book consists of instruments expected to be held to maturity, and these are subject to credit risk capital, which is calculated in quite a different way.

III. Before the FRTB, banks often chose to hold credit-dependent instruments in the banking book, because there they attracted less regulatory capital than in the trading book.

IV. Even before the FRTB, the incremental risk charge introduced in Basel II.5 had made allocating instruments between the books so as to minimize capital less attractive.

Which of the statements are accurate?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and III only
I, II and IV only
I, II, III and IV

questions.solution:
**Why the FRTB revisited the trading book and banking book boundary**

Stem in one line: which slide statements about the two books and pre-FRTB regulatory arbitrage are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Basel capital rules treat a bank’s balance sheet as two regulatory books, and each book has its own capital regime.

|  | Trading book | Banking book |
|---|---|---|
| What it holds | Instruments the bank intends to trade | Instruments expected to be held to maturity |
| Valuation (Schweser) | Periodically marked to market | Held at cost |
| Capital regime | Market risk capital | Credit risk capital |

GARP 18.4: “The two sorts of capital are calculated in quite different ways. This has in the past given rise to regulatory arbitrage. For example, banks have often chosen to hold credit-dependent instruments in the trading book because they are then subject to less regulatory capital than they would be if they had been placed in the banking book.” The direction matters: credit-dependent instruments were cheaper in the trading book, so that is where banks put them. Schweser says the same thing in other words: banking book assets “are subject to more stringent credit risk capital rules”.

The regulators’ response came in two steps. First, Basel II.5 introduced the incremental risk charge (IRC), a charge on credit-dependent trading book positions; GARP 18.1: “In Basel II.5, the incremental risk charge made this less attractive.” Second, the FRTB “counteracts regulatory arbitrage by defining more clearly than previously the differences between the two books.”

**Applying it to this question**

I: GARP’s own “roughly speaking” definition of the trading book, with market risk capital. True. II: banking book held to maturity, credit risk capital, calculated in quite different ways. True.

III: says banks parked credit-dependent instruments in the banking book because it was cheaper. GARP says the opposite: they held them in the trading book. False.

IV: the Basel II.5 IRC made the arbitrage less attractive before the FRTB tightened the boundary. True (GARP 18.1).

So I, II and IV only.

**Fragile fact.** Direction: credit-dependent instruments were cheaper in the trading book, so arbitrage moved them into the trading book. The banking book’s credit risk rules were the more stringent.

**Reference**

LO 18.c (Schweser, verbatim on the answer key page). GARP Ch. 18, §18.1 Background (last paragraph) and §18.4 Trading Book vs. Banking Book. Schweser Reading 18, “Trading Book vs. Banking Book”. Difference: the at-cost versus marked-to-market wording and “more stringent” are Schweser-only; GARP does not mention the IRC point in §18.4 but does in §18.1. No conflict of substance.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 c, where it is Q1 of 13.

a.reason: **I and II only.** Error type: scope error (a true statement rejected). Choosing A means believing that nothing before the FRTB addressed book-shopping, treating the FRTB as the first response. GARP explicitly credits the Basel II.5 IRC with making the arbitrage less attractive. A would be correct if IV instead said the IRC increased the attraction of the arbitrage.

b.reason: **I, II and III only.** Error type: polarity flip, applied consistently. A candidate who believes the banking book was the cheaper home accepts III, and then rejects IV, because a charge that made credit-dependent positions in the trading book more expensive would then seem to push even more assets into the banking book rather than curb arbitrage. Both choices come from the one reversed direction. B would be correct only in a world where the banking book carried the lighter capital for credit-dependent instruments.

c.reason: Statements I, II and IV restate GARP 18.4 and the closing paragraph of GARP 18.1. Statement III reverses the direction of the arbitrage described in GARP 18.4.

d.reason: **I, II, III and IV.** Error type: polarity flip on III alone. The candidate recognizes the IRC point but does not notice that III points the arbitrage the wrong way. D would be correct if III read “in the trading book, because there they attracted less regulatory capital than in the banking book.”

questions.question: A risk consultant advising a Swiss bank is reviewing the CHF trading division’s draft policy on when a position may be allocated to the trading book under the FRTB. Which of the following policy wordings is most accurate?

options.text: The bank must be able to trade the instrument and manage its underlying risks on a trading desk, and day-to-day changes in its value should affect equity and pose risks to solvency.
A documented intent to trade, approved by the head of the trading desk, is sufficient, provided that day-to-day changes in the instrument’s value affect equity and pose risks to solvency.
The bank must be able to trade the instrument and manage its underlying risks on a trading desk, and the instrument must be expected to be held to maturity and carried at cost.
The bank must be able to trade the instrument, its underlying risks may be managed by any function such as treasury ALM, and day-to-day changes in its value should affect equity.

questions.solution:
**The FRTB criteria for the trading book**

Stem in one line: which draft policy wording for trading-book allocation is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Before the FRTB, the trading book boundary rested on intent: an instrument was in the trading book if the bank said it intended to trade it. Intent is unobservable and easy to assert, which is exactly why it allowed the arbitrage in Q1. The FRTB replaces intent with testable conditions. GARP 18.4: “To be in the trading book, it will no longer be sufficient for a bank to have an ‘intent to trade.’ It must be able to trade and manage the underlying risks on a trading desk. The day-today changes in value should affect equity and pose risks to solvency. The FRTB provides rules for determining for different types of instruments whether they should be placed in the trading book or the banking book.”

So there are three ingredients:

| Ingredient | What it rules out |
|---|---|
| Ability to trade | Assets with no market the bank can actually trade in |
| Risks managed on a trading desk | Assets whose risks sit with another function (for example ALM) |
| Value changes affect equity and solvency | Assets whose value moves do not hit the bank’s capital |

Schweser calls the first two “dual criteria” (able to trade; risks managed on the trading desk) and adds that “the day-to-day price fluctuations must also affect the bank’s equity position and pose a risk to bank solvency.”

**Applying it to this question**

Only A contains all three ingredients without adding anything false. B brings intent back as sufficient. C adds a banking book feature. D removes the desk condition.

**Fragile fact.** Intent is necessary in spirit but not sufficient: the bank must be able to trade, the risks must sit on a trading desk, and value changes must hit equity and solvency.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 18, §18.4 Trading Book vs. Banking Book. Schweser Reading 18, “Trading Book vs. Banking Book”. No conflict (Schweser labels the first two conditions “dual criteria”; GARP lists the same three ingredients).

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 c, where it is Q2 of 13.

a.reason: It reproduces GARP 18.4 (able to trade and manage the underlying risks on a trading desk; day-to-day changes in value affect equity and pose risks to solvency).

b.reason: Error type: scope error (the condition the FRTB removed is reinstated). “Intent to trade” is the pre-FRTB test; GARP says it “will no longer be sufficient”. Approval by the desk head adds nothing objective. B would be correct as a description of the pre-FRTB boundary.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap. “Held to maturity” and “carried at cost” are banking book attributes (GARP 18.4; Schweser). Requiring them for the trading book contradicts the definition of the trading book. C would be correct if its last clause described a banking book position.

d.reason: Error type: role misassignment. The underlying risks must be managed on a trading desk; treasury ALM is the wrong actor. D would be correct if “any function such as treasury ALM” read “a trading desk”.

questions.question:
A model validator at a Canadian bank is drafting a validation report on the CAD trading desks’ FRTB back-testing framework and must choose which statements to include. The draft lists:

I. The stressed 97.5% ES used to calculate capital under the internal models approach is not back-tested, partly because ES is more difficult to back-test than VaR.

II. A stressed measure cannot be back-tested at all, because the extreme data on which it is based are not expected to be observed with the same frequency in the future.

III. Regulators may require additional back-tests, such as computing the $p$-value of each day’s profit or loss, which should be uniformly distributed if the model is working perfectly.

IV. A desk that exceeds a back-testing exception limit must use the standardized approach permanently, and its internal models approval cannot be regained.

Which of the statements should be included as accurate?

options.text: I and II only
I, II and IV only
II, III and IV only
I, II and III only

questions.solution:
**What the FRTB back-tests, and what it does not**

Stem in one line: which validation report statements about FRTB back-testing are accurate?

**Concept and theory**

Back-testing compares a risk model’s forecasts with what actually happened. Under the FRTB, capital under the internal models approach (IMA) is based on a stressed 97.5% ES. GARP 18.3.1 gives two reasons why that measure is not back-tested:

1. “it is more difficult to back-test ES than VaR.” A VaR exception is a simple yes or no event that can be counted; ES is an average of tail losses, so there is no single exception to count.
2. “it is not possible to back-test a stressed measure at all. The stressed data upon which a stressed measure is based are extreme data that statistically speaking are not expected to be observed with the same frequency in the future as they were during the stressed period.”

Instead each trading desk back-tests a one-day VaR on the most recent 12 months of data at 99% and at 97.5% (Q8). If there are more than 12 exceptions at 99% or more than 30 at 97.5%, “the trading desk is required to calculate capital using the standardized approach until neither of these two conditions continues to exist.”

GARP adds: “Banks may be asked by regulators to carry out other back-tests. Some of these could involve calculating the $p$-value of the profit or loss on each day.” The $p$-value is the probability of observing a profit less than the actual profit or a loss greater than the actual loss. “If the model is working perfectly, the $p$-values obtained should be uniformly distributed.” The intuition: a correct model should place realized P&L at a random point of its own forecast distribution each day, so no region of the 0 to 1 range should be over- or under-populated.

**Applying it to this question**

I: reason 1. True. II: reason 2, almost verbatim. True. III: the $p$-value test and its uniform distribution. True (GARP-only). IV: “permanently” and “cannot be regained” contradict GARP’s “until neither of these two conditions continues to exist”. False. Answer: I, II and III only.

**Fragile fact.** ES is harder to back-test than VaR, and a stressed measure cannot be back-tested at all. The switch to the standardized approach lasts until neither condition continues to exist.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 18, §18.3.1 Back-Testing. Schweser Reading 18, “Backtesting”. GARP-only: the $p$-value test and the “until neither condition” duration. No conflict on statements I and II.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 c, where it is Q3 of 13.

a.reason: **I and II only.** Error type: scope error (a true statement rejected). The candidate assumes the exception count is the only back-test, or expects $p$-values to cluster rather than be uniform. GARP explicitly allows regulators to ask for $p$-value tests. A would be correct if III said the $p$-values should be concentrated near 0.5.

b.reason: **I, II and IV only.** Error type: absolute-claim trap on IV. The switch to the standardized approach lasts only while an exception condition persists. B would be correct if IV read “until neither exception condition continues to exist” and III were false.

c.reason: **II, III and IV only.** Error type: polarity flip on I plus the absolute claim in IV. Rejecting I means believing ES is easier to back-test than VaR. C would be correct only if VaR were the harder measure to back-test and the switch were permanent, neither of which GARP supports.

d.reason: Statements I to III restate GARP 18.3.1. Statement IV turns a conditional, temporary switch into a permanent one.

questions.question:
A treasury analyst at a Japanese bank is running the FRTB profit and loss attribution test for a JPY rates desk over the most recent assessment window. $U$ is the daily actual P&L minus the daily model-predicted P&L, and $V$ is the daily actual P&L. Summary statistics (JPY million):

| Statistic | Value |
|---|---|
| Mean of $V$ | 1.5 |
| Standard deviation of $V$ | 10.0 |
| Mean of $U$ | −0.9 |
| Standard deviation of $U$ | 4.2 |
| Desk’s 97.5% stressed ES | 210.0 |

Which of the following correctly states the two attribution measures and the conclusion for this window?

options.text: −9.0% and 42.0%; the second measure is outside its limit
−9.0% and 17.6%; both measures are within their limits
−21.4% and 17.6%; the first measure is outside its limit
−0.9% and 17.6%; both measures are within their limits

questions.solution:
**Computing the two P&L attribution measures**

Stem in one line: JPY rates desk, mean $U$ = −0.9, SD $U$ = 4.2, SD $V$ = 10.0; compute both measures and the conclusion.

**Concept and theory**

Back-testing asks whether the VaR model forecasts the size of losses. P&L attribution asks a different question: does the bank’s risk model explain the desk’s actual daily P&L? If the model’s pricing and risk factors are incomplete, model P&L and actual P&L will drift apart, even if the VaR count looks fine. GARP 18.3.2: “Banks are required to compare the actual profit or loss in a day with that predicted by their models. Two measures must be calculated”:

Measure 1 = $\frac{\text{Mean of} U}{\text{Standard deviation of} V} ,$ Measure 2 = $\frac{\text{Variance of} U}{\text{Variance of} V}$

where $U$ is the difference between the actual and the model P&L on a day and $V$ is the actual P&L on a day. “Regulators expect the first measure to be between −10% and +10% and the second measure to be less than 20%.”

| Measure | Detects | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| Mean($U$ )/SD($V$ ) | Systematic bias of the model P&L | −10% to +10% |
| Var($U$ )/Var($V$ ) | Noise: how much daily P&L the model fails to explain | Below 20% |

Note that both measures scale by the actual P&L ($V$ ), and the second uses variances (squared standard deviations), not standard deviations.

**Applying it to this question**

Formula first, then one step per line (JPY million):

Measure 1 = $\frac{\text{Mean(}U \text{)}}{\text{SD(}V \text{)}}$ = $\frac{-0.9}{10.0}$ = −0.090 = −9.0%

Var($U$ ) = $\text{4.2}^{2}$ = 17.64

Var($V$ ) = $\text{10.0}^{2}$ = 100.00

Measure 2 = $\frac{17.64}{100.00}$ = 0.1764 = 17.6%

Check against limits: −9.0% lies inside −10% to +10%; 17.6% \< 20%. Both pass, so this window does not count as an occasion outside the ranges. The mean of $V$ (1.5) and the stressed ES (210.0) are not inputs to either measure.

Meaning: the model has a small negative bias (it slightly overstates P&L on average) and leaves about 17.6% of the variance of actual P&L unexplained; both are within tolerance.

**Fragile fact.** Measure 1 uses SD($V$ ); measure 2 uses variances of both. The scale is always the actual P&L $V$ . A negative first measure inside −10% is a pass.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 18, §18.3.2 Profit and Loss Attribution. Schweser Reading 18, “Profit/Loss Attribution”. Notation: GARP uses $U$ and $V$ ; Schweser uses $D$ (difference) and $A$ (actual) and its formula images are missing from the extract. The GARP OCR of the two ratios is legible; the notation was also confirmed from the question bank’s worked solution to Q879 for this LO. No conflict on the limits.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 c, where it is Q4 of 13.

a.reason: **(−9.0% and 42.0%).** Error type: dropped term (the square). It divides standard deviations, 4.2/10.0 = 42.0%, instead of variances. Because the ratio is below 1, squaring it makes it smaller, so this error manufactures a false failure. A would be correct if the second measure were defined as SD($U$ )/SD($V$ ) with the same 20% limit.

b.reason: It applies GARP 18.3.2’s two ratios exactly: mean of $U$ over SD of $V$ , and variance of $U$ over variance of $V$ .

c.reason: **(−21.4% and 17.6%).** Error type: wrong input twin. It divides the mean of $U$ by the SD of $U$ : −0.9/4.2 = −21.4%. The scale must be the actual P&L, $V$ . C would be correct if the first measure were a $t$-type statistic on $U$ itself.

d.reason: **(−0.9% and 17.6%).** Error type: wrong input twin. It divides by the variance of $V$ : −0.9/100 = −0.9%. The verdict happens to be the same, but the first measure is misstated by a factor of 10. D would be correct only if the first measure used Var($V$ ) in its denominator.

questions.question: A portfolio manager at a German bank holds EUR corporate bonds on a credit trading desk that is approved for the FRTB internal models approach. She asks how the two types of credit risk exposure to an issuer are capitalized. Which of the following is most accurate?

options.text: Credit spread risk is charged through a VaR with a one-year horizon and 99.9% confidence; jump-to-default risk is captured in stressed ES with 20 to 120 day liquidity horizons.
Credit spread risk and jump-to-default risk are both captured in the stressed 97.5% ES, with jump-to-default risk allocated to the 120-day liquidity horizon.
Credit spread risk is handled like other market risks in the stressed ES, with 20 to 120 day liquidity horizons; jump-to-default risk is charged through a one-year 99.9% VaR.
Credit spread risk is handled like other market risks in the stressed ES, with 20 to 120 day liquidity horizons; jump-to-default risk is charged as exposure times LGD times a risk weight.

questions.solution:
**The two credit risks under the internal models approach**

Stem in one line: how are credit spread risk and jump-to-default risk capitalized for an IMA-approved credit desk?

**Concept and theory**

A corporate bond carries two distinct credit risks. GARP 18.3.3:

1. “Credit spread risk is the risk that the company’s credit spread will change, causing the mark-to-market value of the instrument to change.”
2. “Jump-to-default risk is the risk that there will be a default by the company.”

The two behave very differently. Spread risk is a continuous price risk, like any other market variable. Default is a sudden, discrete, rare event that a 97.5% stressed ES on 10-day changes is poorly suited to capture. The FRTB therefore treats them separately:

|  | Credit spread risk | Jump-to-default risk |
|---|---|---|
| Treated like | Other market risks | Default risks in the banking book |
| IMA measure | Stressed 97.5% ES | VaR, one-year horizon, 99.9% confidence |
| Horizon | Liquidity horizons 20 to 120 days (spread volatility 120 days) | One year |

GARP: “Under the internal models approach, the credit spread risk is handled in a similar way to market risks . . . The jump-to-default risk is handled in the same way as default risks in the banking book. In the internal models approach, the capital charge is based on a VaR calculation with a one-year time horizon and a 99.9% confidence level.”

**Applying it to this question**

The desk is IMA-approved, so the IMA treatment applies. Spread risk goes into stressed ES with horizons of 20 to 120 days; jump-to-default goes into a one-year 99.9% VaR. Only C pairs them correctly.

**Fragile fact.** Spread risk: ES, 20 to 120 days. Default: VaR, one year, **99.9%** (not 99%, not 97.5%). Under the standardized approach the default charge is LGD times risk weight instead.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 18, §18.3.3 Credit Risk. Schweser Reading 18, “Credit Risk”. Difference: Schweser attributes the split into the two risks to the Basel II.5 incremental risk charge and names the default charge the incremental default risk (IDR) charge; GARP says the FRTB distinguishes the two risks and does not use the IDR label. The numbers (99.9%, one year) agree.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 c, where it is Q5 of 13.

a.reason: Error type: sibling swap (the two treatments exchanged). The 99.9% one-year VaR belongs to jump-to-default, not to spread risk. A would be correct with “credit spread” and “jump-to-default” interchanged.

b.reason: Error type: scope error (the separate default charge dropped). Jump-to-default risk is not folded into the ES. A 120-day horizon is the longest liquidity horizon and applies to credit spread volatility and “credit spread: other”, not to default. B would be correct only if FRTB had no separate default charge.

c.reason: It matches GARP 18.3.3 on both risks.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap with LO 18.a. “Exposure times LGD times a risk weight” is the default risk charge of the standardized approach, with LGD and risk weight both specified by the Basel Committee (GARP 18.2.3). The stem’s desk is on the IMA. D would be correct if the desk calculated capital under the standardized approach.

questions.question: A regulator in Singapore is reviewing a bank that holds SGD asset-backed securities and CDO tranches in its trading book. Under Basel II.5 the bank, with supervisory approval, used its own model for the comprehensive risk measure (CRM). An industry benchmarking exercise gave several banks the same securitization portfolio and found that their CRM capital charges for it differed widely. Which of the following best describes the FRTB response?

options.text: Securitizations must use the standardized approach, because CRM internal models produced too much variation in the capital charged by different banks for the same portfolio.
Securitizations may stay under the CRM with supervisory approval, because CRM internal models are recalibrated to a stressed 97.5% ES under the FRTB.
Securitizations move to the internal models approach stressed ES, because CRM internal models were too insensitive to tail risk in securitized products.
Securitizations must use the standardized approach, because CRM internal models produced capital that was systematically too low at every bank for the same portfolio.

questions.solution:
**Securitizations: from the CRM to the standardized approach**

Stem in one line: SGD ABS and CDO tranches under a bank’s own CRM model; benchmarking shows wide dispersion across banks; FRTB response?

**Concept and theory**

Securitized products such as asset-backed securities (ABSs) and collateralized debt obligations (CDOs) are hard to model: tranche losses depend on default correlation and on the structure of the deal. Basel II.5 introduced the comprehensive risk measure (CRM) charge for them. GARP 18.3.4: “The CRM rules allow a bank (with regulatory approval) to use its own models. The Basel Committee has concluded that this is unsatisfactory because there is too much variation in the capital charges calculated by different banks for the same portfolio. It has therefore decided that under FRTB the standardized approach must be used for securitizations.”

The logic is about consistency, not about the level of capital: if two banks holding identical portfolios can hold very different capital, internal models are not producing a reliable regulatory number. This fits the broader post-2008 trend of relying less on internal models.

**Applying it to this question**

The benchmarking exercise in the stem is exactly the evidence GARP cites: the same portfolio, very different charges. The FRTB answer is that securitizations must use the standardized approach.

**Fragile fact.** The problem with the CRM was variation across banks for the same portfolio. The FRTB fix is the standardized approach, not stressed ES.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 18, §18.3.4 Securitizations. Schweser Reading 18, “Securitizations”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 c, where it is Q6 of 13.

a.reason: It gives both the rule (standardized approach) and the reason (too much variation across banks for the same portfolio) as stated in GARP 18.3.4 and Schweser.

b.reason: Error type: scope error (the CRM is kept). Under the FRTB the CRM’s own-model route is withdrawn for securitizations; supervisory approval does not revive it. B would describe Basel II.5, where own models were allowed with approval.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap (the IMA substituted for the standardized approach). Securitizations do not move to stressed ES under internal models; the problem was model variability, and the IMA is another internal model. C would be correct for an ordinary market risk factor on an approved desk.

d.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap on the motivation. The source says the charges varied across banks, not that every bank’s charge was too low. D would be correct only if the benchmark had shown a uniform understatement.

questions.question: The treasurer of an Australian bank reports that the bank is closing its AUD credit trading desk. The desk’s corporate bond positions, assigned to the trading book when they were initiated, will be transferred to the banking book, where the bank estimates they would attract AUD 18 million less capital. Which of the following best describes the FRTB treatment?

options.text: The transfer is not permitted, because instruments can never move between the books once they have been assigned at initiation.
The transfer is permitted, and the lower banking book capital applies from the date of transfer because the desk closure is genuine.
The transfer is not permitted, because only a change in accounting standards on fair value recognition qualifies as extraordinary.
The transfer is permitted, because the closing of a trading desk is an extraordinary circumstance, but any capital benefit is disallowed.

questions.solution:
**Reclassification when a trading desk is closed**

Stem in one line: AUD credit desk closing; trading book bonds to move to the banking book, saving AUD 18 million of capital; treatment?

**Concept and theory**

Clear criteria for each book would be undermined if banks could later move positions whenever the other book was cheaper. GARP 18.4: “instruments are assigned to the banking book or the trading book when they are initiated and there are strict rules preventing them from being subsequently moved between the two books. Transfers from one book to another can happen only in extraordinary circumstances. (Examples given of extraordinary circumstances are the closing of trading desks and a change in accounting standards with regard to the recognition of fair value.) Any capital benefit as a result of moving items between the books will be disallowed.”

Two separate controls work together:

| Control | Effect |
|---|---|
| Gate | A transfer happens only in extraordinary circumstances |
| Capital neutrality | Even a permitted transfer cannot reduce capital |

The gate stops casual switching; capital neutrality removes the incentive to switch at all.

**Applying it to this question**

The closing of a trading desk is one of GARP’s named examples, so the gate is passed and the transfer can happen. The AUD 18 million saving is a capital benefit from moving the items and is disallowed.

**Fragile fact.** Two examples (GARP): closing of trading desks and a change in accounting standards on fair value. Transfer allowed in those cases; capital benefit never allowed.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 18, §18.4 Trading Book vs. Banking Book. Schweser Reading 18, “Trading Book vs. Banking Book”. Difference: Schweser gives one example (a firm-wide change in accounting practices) and says the original capital is retained; GARP gives two examples. GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 c, where it is Q7 of 13.

a.reason: Error type: absolute-claim trap. Transfers are strictly limited, not banned; they “can happen only in extraordinary circumstances”. A would be correct if the FRTB allowed no exceptions at all.

b.reason: Error type: scope error (the capital-neutrality condition dropped). The transfer is permitted, but the benefit is not recognized. B would be correct for a regime that had a gate but no capital-neutrality rule.

c.reason: Error type: scope error (the list of examples narrowed to one). A change in accounting standards is one example; the closing of trading desks is another. A candidate who learned only Schweser’s single example (a change in accounting practices) may pick C. C would be correct if accounting changes were the only permitted circumstance.

d.reason: Both halves match GARP 18.4: desk closure is an extraordinary circumstance, and the capital benefit is disallowed.
