questions.question:
The head of market risk at a Brazilian bank reviews the FRTB back-testing results of four BRL trading desks, each approved for the internal models approach. Each desk back-tested a one-day VaR on the most recent 12 months of data.

| Desk | Exceptions, 99% VaR | Exceptions, 97.5% VaR | 97.5% stressed ES (BRL million) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Rates | 12 | 29 | 84.0 |
| FX | 9 | 31 | 41.0 |
| Equity | 13 | 27 | 66.0 |
| Credit | 11 | 30 | 102.0 |

Which desks are required to calculate capital using the standardized approach?

options.text: Equity only
FX and Equity only
Rates, FX and Equity only
FX, Equity and Credit only

questions.solution:
**Applying the back-testing exception limits**

Stem in one line: four BRL desks’ one-day VaR exceptions at 99% and 97.5% over 12 months; which must use the standardized approach?

**Concept and theory**

GARP 18.3.1: “FRTB back-tests a bank’s models by asking each trading desk to back-test a VaR measure calculated over a one-day horizon and the most recent 12 months of data. Both 99% and 97.5% confidence levels are to be used. If there are more than 12 exceptions for the 99% VaR or more than 30 exceptions for the 97.5% VaR, the trading desk is required to calculate capital using the standardized approach until neither of these two conditions continues to exist.”

Three features decide every exam question on this rule:

1. The test is per desk, so one desk can fail while others pass.
2. Two levels are tested, and failing either is enough (“or”).
3. The limits are strict: “more than 12” means 13 or more fails; exactly 12 passes. “More than 30” means 31 or more fails; exactly 30 passes.

**Applying it to this question**

Fail if $E_{99} >$ 12 or $E_{97.5} >$ 30:

| Desk | $E_{99}$ | $E_{97.5}$ | $E_{99} >$ 12? | $E_{97.5} >$ 30? | Result |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rates | 12 | 29 | No | No | Pass |
| FX | 9 | 31 | No | Yes | Standardized |
| Equity | 13 | 27 | Yes | No | Standardized |
| Credit | 11 | 30 | No | No | Pass |

FX and Equity must use the standardized approach. The stressed ES column is irrelevant: the stressed measure is not back-tested and plays no part in the exception rule.

**Fragile fact.** More than 12 at 99%, more than 30 at 97.5%, one-day VaR, 12 months, per desk, either level triggers.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 18, §18.3.1 Back-Testing. Schweser Reading 18, “Backtesting”. Difference: Schweser says “either” level can be applied; GARP says both are to be used, with failure at either triggering the standardized approach. GARP used; this looks like condensed wording in Schweser.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 c, where it is Q8 of 13.

a.reason: **Equity only.** Error type: scope error (one confidence level dropped). Only the 99% count is checked, so FX’s 31 exceptions at 97.5% are missed. Schweser says “Either a 99% or 97.5% confidence level can be applied”, which can encourage this; GARP requires both. A would be correct if only the 99% level were tested.

b.reason: FX fails only at 97.5% (31 > 30) and Equity only at 99% (13 > 12); either failure is sufficient (GARP 18.3.1).

c.reason: **Rates, FX and Equity.** Error type: condition error at the boundary (“12 or more” instead of “more than 12”). Rates’ 12 exceptions are counted as a failure. C would be correct if the 99% limit were “12 or more”.

d.reason: **FX, Equity and Credit.** Error type: condition error at the boundary (“30 or more” instead of “more than 30”). Credit’s 30 exceptions are counted as a failure. D would be correct if the 97.5% limit were “30 or more”.

questions.question: An internal auditor at a UK bank is reviewing the GBP trading division’s documentation of the FRTB profit and loss attribution test. Which of the following statements in the documentation is most accurate?

options.text: The “actual” P&L used in the test should be the P&L that would occur if there had been no trading in the day, sometimes called the hypothetical P&L.
The first measure divides the mean of the difference between actual and model P&L by the standard deviation of the model-predicted P&L.
The second measure divides the standard deviation of the difference between actual and model P&L by the standard deviation of actual P&L.
A desk must use the standardized approach after a single occasion in a 12-month period on which either ratio falls outside its range.

questions.solution:
**Definitions inside the P&L attribution test**

Stem in one line: which documentation statement about the P&L attribution test is most accurate?

**Concept and theory**

The attribution test compares two daily P&L series (Q4): the model-predicted P&L, and the actual P&L $V$ , with $U$ = actual minus model. A subtle point is what “actual” means. If the desk trades during the day, the realized P&L includes fees, intraday trading gains and new positions that the start-of-day model never saw. That would penalize the model for things it was never meant to explain. GARP footnote 9 resolves this: “The ‘actual’ profit/loss should be the profit and loss that would occur if there had been no trading in a day. This is sometimes referred to as the hypothetical profit and loss.”

The decision rule (GARP 18.3.2): “When there are four or more situations in a 12-month period where the ratios are outside these ranges, the desk must use the standardized approach for determining capital.”

**Applying it to this question**

A restates footnote 9. B swaps the denominator to the model P&L. C uses standard deviations in the second measure. D replaces “four or more” with “a single occasion”. Only A is accurate.

**Fragile fact.** Actual P&L in this test means hypothetical P&L (no trading in the day). The trigger is four or more occasions in 12 months.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 18, §18.3.2 Profit and Loss Attribution, including footnote 9. Schweser Reading 18, “Profit/Loss Attribution”. GARP-only: the hypothetical P&L definition. Schweser uses $D$ and $A$ for GARP’s $U$ and $V$ . No conflict on the rule.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 c, where it is Q9 of 13.

a.reason: GARP §18.3.2, footnote 9, quoted above.

b.reason: Error type: wrong input twin. The denominator of the first measure is the standard deviation of the actual P&L $V$ , not of the model P&L. B would be correct if $V$ were defined as the model-predicted P&L.

c.reason: Error type: sibling swap between the two measures. Standard deviation belongs to the denominator of the first measure; the second measure is a ratio of variances. C would be correct if the second measure were defined on standard deviations (and Q4 shows how much this changes the number).

d.reason: Error type: scope or condition error. The trigger is four or more occasions in a 12-month period, not one. D would be correct if the threshold were one occasion.

questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a Chinese bank is explaining to new analysts how the treatment of credit spread risk changes between the Basel II.5 incremental risk charge (IRC) and the FRTB. The desk holds a BBB-rated CNY corporate bond with a three-month liquidity horizon, and the bond suffers a credit-related loss during that horizon. Which of the following best describes the change?

options.text: Under the IRC the bond is assumed to be held without replacement for a one-year horizon, and the FRTB replaces this with a constant level of risk assumption.
Under the IRC the bond is assumed to be replaced at the end of its liquidity horizon by another BBB-rated bond, and the FRTB retains this constant level of risk.
Under the IRC the bond is assumed to be replaced at the end of its liquidity horizon by another BBB-rated bond, and the FRTB instead marks to market incrementally without replacement.
Under the IRC the bond is assumed to be replaced at the end of its liquidity horizon by another BBB-rated bond, and the FRTB replaces this with a one-year 99.9% VaR on the spread.

questions.solution:
**From the IRC’s constant level of risk to incremental marking to market**

Stem in one line: BBB-rated CNY bond with a three-month liquidity horizon suffers a credit loss; how does the treatment change from the IRC to the FRTB?

**Concept and theory**

This solution draws on Schweser-only content (condensed source); GARP’s Chapter 18 does not describe the constant level of risk assumption.

Schweser: “Basel II.5 introduced the incremental risk charge (IRC), which recognizes two different types of risk created by credit-dependent risk assets: credit spread risk and jump-to-default risk.” For credit spread risk, “The IRC process allows banks to assume a constant level of risk. This means that it is assumed that positions that deteriorate are replaced with other risk assets.” In Schweser’s illustration, a bank holding an A-rated bond with a three-month liquidity horizon that suffers a credit-related loss is assumed to replace it with another A-rated bond at the end of the three months. Schweser calls this “clearly a simplifying assumption, which is being replaced with incremental marking to market without assuming replacement under the FRTB proposals.”

|  | Basel II.5 IRC | FRTB |
|---|---|---|
| After a credit loss | Position assumed replaced by one of the same rating at the end of the liquidity horizon | No replacement assumed |
| Name | Constant level of risk | Incremental marking to market |

Why it matters: assuming replacement resets the portfolio’s credit quality every horizon, so a deteriorating name cannot keep deteriorating in the model. Removing the assumption lets losses from deterioration accumulate as they would in reality.

**Applying it to this question**

The BBB bond with a three-month horizon is the Schweser mechanism with a different rating: under the IRC it is assumed replaced by another BBB bond at the end of three months; the FRTB drops that assumption and marks the position to market incrementally without replacement.

**Fragile fact.** Constant level of risk = IRC (Basel II.5), replacement assumed. FRTB = incremental marking to market, no replacement.

**Reference**

Schweser Reading 18, “Credit Risk”. Schweser-only (condensed source). GARP Ch. 18, §18.1 mentions the IRC only as making book arbitrage less attractive, and §18.3.3 covers the spread and default split without the constant level of risk; no contradiction with Schweser.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 c, where it is Q10 of 13.

a.reason: Error type: polarity flip (direction of the change reversed). It puts “no replacement” in the IRC and “constant level of risk” in the FRTB. A would be correct with the two regimes swapped.

b.reason: Error type: scope error (the change denied). The FRTB does not retain the constant level of risk; Schweser says it is “being replaced”. B would be correct only as a description of Basel II.5 alone.

c.reason: It states both the IRC’s constant level of risk and the FRTB’s replacement of it by incremental marking to market without replacement (Schweser, “Credit Risk”).

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap. The one-year 99.9% VaR is the treatment of jump-to-default risk (GARP 18.3.3), not of credit spread risk, which is handled like other market risks. D would be correct if the stem asked how jump-to-default risk is charged under the IMA.

questions.question:
The CRO of a US bank is reviewing three USD positions that the head of trading says the bank intends to trade and wants allocated to the trading book under the FRTB:

| Position | Facts |
|---|---|
| X | Bilateral loan participations with no market in which the bank is able to trade them; risks managed on the credit trading desk; value changes affect equity. |
| Y | Liquid corporate bonds the bank is able to trade; risks managed by the treasury ALM function, not a trading desk; value changes affect equity. |
| Z | Listed equities the bank is able to trade; risks managed on the equity trading desk; day-to-day value changes affect equity and pose risks to solvency. |

Which of the positions may be allocated to the trading book?

options.text: X and Z only
Y and Z only
X, Y and Z
Z only

questions.solution:
**Applying the trading-book criteria to three positions**

Stem in one line: three USD positions the bank intends to trade; which meet the FRTB trading-book criteria?

**Concept and theory**

From Q2, every trading book position must pass all three FRTB conditions (GARP 18.4): the bank must be able to trade it; its underlying risks must be managed on a trading desk; and day-to-day value changes should affect equity and pose risks to solvency. Intent to trade is “no longer sufficient”. The conditions are cumulative, so failing any one sends the position to the banking book.

**Applying it to this question**

| Position | Able to trade | Risks on a trading desk | Equity and solvency | Trading book? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| X | No | Yes | Yes (equity) | No |
| Y | Yes | No (ALM) | Yes (equity) | No |
| Z | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |

The stated intent to trade, common to all three, decides nothing. Only Z qualifies.

**Fragile fact.** All conditions are needed together; the actor managing the risks must be a trading desk.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 18, §18.4 Trading Book vs. Banking Book. Schweser Reading 18, “Trading Book vs. Banking Book”. No conflict.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 c, where it is Q11 of 13.

a.reason: **X and Z.** Error type: scope error (“able to trade” replaced by intent). X has intent and desk management but no market the bank can trade in. A would be correct if the bank could trade X.

b.reason: **Y and Z.** Error type: role misassignment. Y’s risks are managed by treasury ALM, not a trading desk. B would be correct if Y’s risks were managed on a trading desk.

c.reason: **X, Y and Z.** Error type: scope error (the pre-FRTB intent test applied). All three have a stated intent to trade; under the pre-FRTB boundary that was effectively enough. C would be correct before the FRTB.

d.reason: Z is the only position meeting every GARP 18.4 condition.

questions.question:
The chief compliance officer of a French bank is drafting the EUR banking group’s policy on moving instruments between the regulatory books under the FRTB. Which of the following draft statements are consistent with the FRTB?

I. Instruments are assigned to the banking book or the trading book when they are initiated.

II. A change in accounting standards with regard to the recognition of fair value is an example of an extraordinary circumstance in which a transfer between the books can happen.

III. Transfers between the books may be made at any quarter-end, provided the asset and liability committee approves them and documents the reason.

IV. A position may be transferred when the desk’s intent to trade it changes, because intent is the test of membership of the trading book.

options.text: I only
I and II only
I, II and III only
I, II and IV only

questions.solution:
**Drafting a reclassification policy**

Stem in one line: which statements in a EUR group’s book-transfer policy are consistent with the FRTB?

**Concept and theory**

Recall the reclassification regime (Q7). GARP 18.4: instruments “are assigned to the banking book or the trading book when they are initiated and there are strict rules preventing them from being subsequently moved”. Transfers “can happen only in extraordinary circumstances”, with the closing of trading desks and “a change in accounting standards with regard to the recognition of fair value” as examples. Any capital benefit is disallowed. Schweser explains the purpose: the roadblock “has been established to minimize the act of switching between categories at will, based on how capital requirements are calculated.”

Two ideas are worth separating: when membership is fixed (at initiation) and what can change it (only extraordinary, firm-level events, not routine governance and not a change of mind about intent).

**Applying it to this question**

I: assignment at initiation. True. II: change in accounting standards on fair value is a GARP example. True. III: routine quarter-end transfers with committee approval are the “switching at will” the rule is meant to stop. False. IV: a change of trading intent is not an extraordinary circumstance, and intent is no longer the test of trading book membership (Q2). False. Answer: I and II only.

**Fragile fact.** Assigned at initiation. Moves only in extraordinary circumstances (desk closure; change in accounting standards on fair value). Intent changes and committee approval do not count.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 18, §18.4 Trading Book vs. Banking Book. Schweser Reading 18, “Trading Book vs. Banking Book”. Difference: Schweser’s example is a change in the bank’s accounting practices (“a firm-wide shift”); GARP’s is a change in accounting standards on the recognition of fair value. GARP used.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 c, where it is Q12 of 13.

a.reason: **I only.** Error type: scope error (a true example rejected). The candidate believes only desk closures, or nothing at all, qualify. A would be correct if accounting changes were not among the extraordinary circumstances.

b.reason: I and II restate GARP 18.4; III and IV contradict it.

c.reason: **I, II and III.** Error type: scope error (the “extraordinary circumstances” condition dropped). Committee approval at quarter-end is routine, not extraordinary. C would be correct under a regime that allowed transfers at the bank’s discretion.

d.reason: **I, II and IV.** Error type: sibling swap with the pre-FRTB definition. It treats intent as the test of membership, which the FRTB explicitly abandoned. D would be correct as a description of the pre-FRTB boundary.

questions.question:
A risk analyst at an Indian bank reviews the FRTB profit and loss attribution results of the INR FX desk over the past 12 months. The ratios are calculated monthly. The limits are −10% to +10% for the first measure, Mean($U$ )/SD($V$ ), and below 20% for the second, Var($U$ )/Var($V$ ). Over the same period the desk had 8 exceptions in its 99% one-day VaR back-test.

| Month | Jan | Feb | Mar | Apr | May | Jun | Jul | Aug | Sep | Oct | Nov | Dec |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Mean($U$ )/SD($V$ ), % | 4.0 | −11.5 | 6.0 | 8.0 | −3.0 | 12.0 | 2.0 | −9.5 | 5.0 | −7.0 | 3.0 | −2.0 |
| Var($U$ )/Var($V$ ), % | 12.0 | 14.0 | 19.5 | 23.0 | 9.0 | 15.0 | 16.0 | 18.0 | 11.0 | 26.0 | 12.0 | 17.0 |

Which of the following correctly states the number of occasions on which the ratios were outside the requirements and the consequence for the desk?

options.text: 3 occasions; the desk continues to use the internal models approach
4 occasions; the desk continues to use the internal models approach
4 occasions; the desk must use the standardized approach
11 occasions; the desk must use the standardized approach

questions.solution:
**Counting P&L attribution failures over 12 months**

Stem in one line: twelve monthly pairs of attribution ratios for an INR FX desk; count occasions outside the limits and state the consequence.

**Concept and theory**

The two ratios from Q4 have different limits (GARP 18.3.2): the first, Mean($U$ )/SD($V$ ), must lie between −10% and +10%, a two-sided band, because a model can be biased in either direction; the second, Var($U$ )/Var($V$ ), must be below 20%, a one-sided limit, because a variance ratio cannot be negative. An occasion counts as outside the requirements if either ratio is outside its range. “When there are four or more situations in a 12-month period where the ratios are outside these ranges, the desk must use the standardized approach for determining capital.”

**Applying it to this question**

Test each month: fail if Mean ratio \< −10% or > +10%, or if Var ratio ≥ 20%.

| Month | Mean($U$ )/SD($V$ ) | Var($U$ )/Var($V$ ) | Outside? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Feb | −11.5% | 14.0% | Yes (below −10%) |
| Apr | 8.0% | 23.0% | Yes (variance ratio above 20%) |
| Jun | 12.0% | 15.0% | Yes (above +10%) |
| Oct | −7.0% | 26.0% | Yes (variance ratio above 20%) |
| Other 8 months | within band | below 20% | No |

The near misses pass: Mar’s variance ratio of 19.5% is below 20%, and Aug’s −9.5% is inside the band. No month breaches both ratios, so there is no question of double counting.

Count = 4. Since 4 ≥ 4, the desk must use the standardized approach. The 8 back-testing exceptions at 99% are irrelevant (they are below the 12-exception limit and belong to a different test).

**Fragile fact.** Mean ratio: two-sided ±10%, so negative breaches count. Variance ratio: below 20%. Trigger: four or more occasions in 12 months.

**Reference**

GARP Ch. 18, §18.3.2 Profit and Loss Attribution. Schweser Reading 18, “Profit/Loss Attribution”. No conflict. Monthly calculation is a stem convention; neither source fixes the frequency.

**Source:** High quality question set, Market Risk: the paper for MR-18 c, where it is Q13 of 13.

a.reason: Error type: sign error. Treating only positive values above +10% as breaches ignores Feb’s −11.5%, leaving Apr, Jun and Oct. A would be correct if Feb’s figure were −8.5%, say.

b.reason: Error type: condition error on the trigger (“more than four” instead of “four or more”). The count is right but the threshold is misread. B would be correct if the rule required five or more occasions.

c.reason: Four occasions outside the ranges in a 12-month period meets GARP’s “four or more” trigger.

d.reason: Error type: sibling swap of the limits. Applying the ±10% band to the variance ratio as well flags every month except May (variance ratio 9.0%, mean ratio −3.0%). The conclusion happens to be the same, but the count is wrong. D would be correct if both ratios had the ±10% limit.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Estimate VaR using a historical simulation approach.
questions.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.topic: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.source: GARP past 10-year papers book, Q1.3
questions.question:
You are assigned to calculate the daily VaR for the stock of Fooda Inc. You are provided with the following data for the ten worst returns of the stock during the last 100 days:

−1.2%, −0.7%, −3.2%, −2.6%, −2.4%, −2.0%, −1.9%, −1.7%, −1.5%, −1.5%

Which of the following is closest to the monthly VaR for Fooda Inc. using a confidence level of 95%? (Assume there are 20 trading days in a month.)
questions.solution:
**Concept**

Historical-simulation VaR is read straight off the ordered losses. With $n$ observations, the VaR at confidence $c$ is the $[(1 - c)n + 1]^{\text{th}}$ worst observation, so that exactly $(1 - c)n$ losses lie beyond it. A 1-day figure is then scaled to a longer horizon with the square-root-of-time rule (valid for i.i.d. returns).

**Working**

**Step 1: order the losses, worst first.** −3.2, −2.6, −2.4, −2.0, −1.9, −1.7, −1.5, −1.5, −1.2, −0.7 (all in %).

**Step 2: locate the cut-off.** (1 − 0.95) × 100 + 1 = 6, so the 1-day 95% VaR is the 6th worst return, −1.7%. Five losses (5% of 100) are worse than it.

**Step 3: scale to one month.**

$\text{VaR}_{20\text{-day}} = \text{VaR}_{1\text{-day}} \times\sqrt{20} = -1.7\% \times4.472 = -7.6\%$

**Exam trap.** Two things go wrong here: reading the data in the order given instead of sorting it, and stopping at the daily number. The 5th worst (−1.9%) is the other common convention, but it is not offered, which confirms the 6th-worst convention.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q1.3 (All past year questions, Question 1).

a.reason: Correct. The 6th worst daily return, −1.7%, scaled by $\sqrt{20}$.

b.reason: −3.2% is the single worst daily return. It is neither the 95% quantile nor a monthly figure.

c.reason: −1.2% is the 9th worst daily return, read from the wrong position in the ranking and left unscaled.

d.reason: −1.4% is not the 6th worst return and has not been scaled to 20 days.

questions.loText: Estimate VaR using a parametric approach for both normal and lognormal asset price distributions.
questions.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.topic: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.question:
A risk manager at an investment bank is estimating the market risk of a portfolio both under the assumption of normally distributed arithmetic returns and normally distributed geometric returns. The manager gathers the following data on the portfolio’s daily returns:

- Annualized average of arithmetic returns: 16%
- Annualized standard deviation of arithmetic returns: 27%
- Annualized average of geometric returns: 13%
- Annualized standard deviation of geometric returns: 29%
- Current portfolio value: EUR 5,200,000
- Trading days in a year: 252

Assuming both daily arithmetic returns and daily geometric returns are serially independent, which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: The 1-day 95% normal VaR is 1.63% and the 1-day 95% lognormal VaR is 1.76%.
The 1-day 95% normal VaR is 2.69% and the 1-day 95% lognormal VaR is 2.88%.
The 1-day 95% normal VaR is 2.74% and the 1-day 95% lognormal VaR is 2.92%.
The 1-day 95% normal VaR is 3.26% and the 1-day 95% lognormal VaR is 3.48%.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Arithmetic returns that are normal give normal VaR, $-(\mu-z\sigma)$. Geometric returns that are normal give lognormal VaR, $1 - e^{\mu-z\sigma}$. Each formula uses its own mean and volatility. With serially independent returns, annual figures scale to one day as $\mu/252$ and $\sigma/\sqrt{252}$. At 95%, $z = 1.645$.

**Working**

**Normal VaR (arithmetic inputs 16%, 27%):**

VaR $= - [ \frac{0.16}{252} - 1.645 \times\frac{0.27}{\sqrt{252}} ] = - [0.000635 - 0.027979] = 2.74\%$

**Lognormal VaR (geometric inputs 13%, 29%):**

VaR $= 1 - \text{exp}[ \frac{0.13}{252} - 1.645 \times\frac{0.29}{\sqrt{252}} ] = 1 - e^{-0.029535} = 2.92\%$

In currency terms these are about EUR 142,000 and EUR 152,000 on the EUR 5.2 million portfolio.

**Exam trap.** VaR is one-tailed, so 95% means 1.645, not 1.96. And do not cross the inputs: the arithmetic pair goes into the normal formula, the geometric pair into the lognormal formula.

**Source:** 2026 PE1 Q2 (All past year questions, Question 2).

a.reason: 1.63% and 1.76% are roughly one daily standard deviation each (a multiplier near 1.0 instead of 1.645).

b.reason: 2.69% and 2.88% are slightly low for both; they do not come from $z = 1.645$ with the stated inputs.

c.reason: Correct.

d.reason: 3.26% and 3.48% use $z = 1.96$ (a two-tailed 95% multiplier) instead of the one-tailed 1.645.

questions.loText: Estimate VaR using a parametric approach for both normal and lognormal asset price distributions.

questions.question:
An analyst has gathered the following information about a portfolio which has normally distributed geometric returns:

|  |  |
|---|---|
| Mean | 12% |
| Standard deviation | 32% |
| Portfolio value | \$85 million |

What is the 95% lognormal VaR for this portfolio?

options.text: \$33.40 million
\$27.20 million
\$56.61 million
\$28.39 million

questions.solution:
**Concept**

If geometric returns are normal, prices are lognormal and VaR is $P (1 - e^{\mu-\sigma z_{\alpha}} )$. The loss can never exceed the portfolio value, which is why lognormal VaR is always below normal VaR, $P(-\mu+ \sigma z_{\alpha})$, for the same inputs.

**Working**

**Step 1: exponent.** $\mu- \sigma z_{0.95} = 0.12 - 0.32 \times1.645 = 0.12 - 0.5264 = -0.4064$

**Step 2: fraction of value retained in the bad state.** $e^{-0.4064} = 0.6660$

**Step 3: fraction lost.** 1 − 0.6660 = 0.3340

**Step 4: VaR in dollars.** $\$85 \text{million} \times0.3340 = \$28.39$ million

**Exam trap.** Option C is the intermediate-result trap: $e^{\mu-\sigma z}$ is the surviving fraction, and VaR is one minus it. The normal-VaR answer would be 85 × (−0.12 + 0.5264) = \$34.5 million, larger than the lognormal figure.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q1.4 (All past year questions, Question 3).

a.reason: \$33.40 million reads the 33.40% loss fraction as if it were the dollar answer.

b.reason: \$27.20 million is 85 × 0.32, the portfolio value times volatility alone, with no mean, no $z$ and no exponential.

c.reason: \$56.61 million is 85 × 0.6660, the value that remains in the bad state (an intermediate result), not the loss.

questions.question: A risk analyst wishes to establish the VaR of a portfolio under his management. At present, the portfolio has a value of £10 million. The annual mean and volatility of the portfolio are 15% and 30%, respectively. Evaluate how the 1-year 99% VaR, calculated using the normal distribution assumption (normal VaR), compares with the 1-year VaR calculated on the basis of the lognormal distribution (lognormal VaR).
questions.solution:
**Concept**

Normal VaR (arithmetic returns normal) is $-\mu+ \sigma z_{\alpha}$ per unit of value. Lognormal VaR (geometric returns normal) is $1 - e^{\mu-\sigma z_{\alpha}}$ . The question asks for the gap between the two in currency terms.

**Working**

At 99%, $z_{\alpha} = 2.326$, so $\sigma z_{\alpha} = 0.30 \times2.326 = 0.6978$.

**Normal VaR:** −0.15 + 0.6978 = 0.5478, i.e. £5,478,000.

**Lognormal VaR:** $1 - e^{0.15-0.6978} = 1 - e^{-0.5478} = 1 - 0.5782 = 0.4218$, i.e. £4,218,000.

**Difference:** 0.5478 − 0.4218 = 0.1260, so £10,000,000 × 0.1260 = £1,260,000.

**Exam trap.** The gap between normal and lognormal VaR is tiny over one day and large over one year, because the exponential only bites when $\sigma z$ is big. A long horizon with high volatility is exactly where the choice of distribution matters.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q1.6 (All past year questions, Question 4).

a.reason: £1,000,000 is not the gap between the two VaRs. It is 10% of the portfolio, with no link to the calculation.

b.reason: £500,000 is likewise not produced by either formula.

c.reason: £527,834 does not equal the difference of £1.26 million; it is far too small for a 1-year 99% horizon with 30% volatility.

d.reason: Correct. Normal VaR exceeds lognormal VaR by 12.6% of the portfolio, £1.26 million.

questions.topic: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview

questions.question:
A risk manager at a mid-sized bank wishes to estimate the market risk of a portfolio by employing both the normal and the lognormal distribution assumptions. The manager has gathered the following data on the portfolio:

- Daily mean: 0.00079365
- Daily volatility: 0.025198
- Trading days in a year: 252
- Current portfolio value: \$5,000,000

Which of the following statements is true?

options.text: Normal 95% VaR is greater than Lognormal 95% VaR at the 1-day holding period by 1.5%.
Normal 95% VaR is greater than Lognormal 95% VaR at the 1-year holding period by 11%.
Normal 99% VaR is greater than Lognormal 99% VaR at the 1-day holding period by 0.16%.
Normal 99% VaR is greater than Lognormal 99% VaR at the 1-year holding period by 11.21%.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Normal VaR is $-\mu+ z\sigma$ and lognormal VaR is $1 - e^{\mu-z\sigma}$, with $\mu$ and $\sigma$ stated for the holding period. Daily parameters annualise as $\mu\times252$ and $\sigma\times\sqrt{252}$. Each option names a horizon, a confidence level and a gap, so all four gaps have to be computed.

**Working**

Annual mean = 0.00079365 × 252 = 0.20. Annual volatility $= 0.025198 \times\sqrt{252} = 0.40$.

| Case | Normal VaR | Lognormal VaR | Gap |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1-day, 95% | −0.00079 + 1.645(0.025198) = 4.07% | $1 - e^{-0.04066} = 3.98\%$ | 0.08% |
| 1-year, 95% | −0.20 + 1.645(0.40) = 45.80% | $1 - e^{-0.458} = 36.75\%$ | 9.05% |
| 1-day, 99% | −0.00079 + 2.326(0.025198) = 5.78% | $1 - e^{-0.05782} = 5.62\%$ | 0.16% |
| 1-year, 99% | −0.20 + 2.326(0.40) = 73.04% | $1 - e^{-0.7304} = 51.83\%$ | 21.21% |

**Exam trap.** Normal VaR is above lognormal VaR in every row, so the direction never discriminates. Only the size does, and it grows with both horizon and confidence level.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q1.7 (All past year questions, Question 5).

a.reason: The 1-day 95% gap is about 0.08%, not 1.5%.

b.reason: The 1-year 95% gap is 9.05%, not 11%.

d.reason: The 1-year 99% gap is 21.21%, not 11.21%.

questions.question:
A risk manager is estimating the market risk of a portfolio using both the arithmetic returns with normal distribution assumptions and the geometric returns with lognormal distribution assumptions. The manager gathers the following data on the portfolio:

|  |  |
|---|---|
| Annualized average of arithmetic returns | 12% |
| Annualized standard deviation of arithmetic returns | 30% |
| Annualized average of geometric returns | 11% |
| Annualized standard deviation of geometric returns | 41% |
| Current portfolio value | EUR 5,200,000 |
| Trading days in a year | 252 |

Assuming both daily arithmetic returns and daily geometric returns are serially independent, which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: 1-day normal 95% VaR = 3.06% and 1-day lognormal 95% VaR = 4.12%
1-day normal 95% VaR = 3.57% and 1-day lognormal 95% VaR = 4.41%
1-day normal 95% VaR = 4.12% and 1-day lognormal 95% VaR = 3.57%
1-day normal 95% VaR = 4.46% and 1-day lognormal 95% VaR = 4.49%

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Arithmetic returns that are normal give normal VaR, $-(\mu- z\sigma)$. Geometric returns that are normal give lognormal VaR, $1 - e^{\mu-z\sigma}$. Each formula takes its own mean and volatility. Annual figures scale to one day as $\mu/252$ and $\sigma/\sqrt{252}$ when returns are serially independent.

**Working**

**Normal (arithmetic inputs 12%, 30%):**

VaR $= - [ \frac{0.12}{252} - 1.645 \times\frac{0.30}{\sqrt{252}} ] = - [0.000476 - 0.031087] = 3.06\%$

**Lognormal (geometric inputs 11%, 41%):**

VaR $= 1 - \text{exp}[ \frac{0.11}{252} - 1.645 \times\frac{0.41}{\sqrt{252}} ] = 1 - e^{-0.042050} = 4.12\%$

**Exam trap.** Lognormal VaR is normally the smaller of the two for the same inputs. Here the inputs differ, so the lognormal figure is larger. Compute both; do not rank them from memory.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q1.9 (All past year questions, Question 6).

a.reason: Correct. 3.06% and 4.12%.

b.reason: 3.57% and 4.41% are not produced by the two formulas with the correct inputs and $z = 1.645$.

c.reason: These are close to the right magnitudes but attached to the wrong labels: the larger figure belongs to the lognormal VaR here, because the geometric volatility (41%) is much higher than the arithmetic one (30%).

d.reason: 4.46% and 4.49% overstate both; they do not come from the 95% inputs.
