questions.loText: Estimate the expected shortfall given profit and loss (P&L) or return data.
questions.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.topic: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.question:
A wealth management firm has JPY 72 billion in assets under management. A portfolio manager at the firm estimates the daily VaR at various confidence levels as follows:

|  |  |
|---|---|
| Confidence |  |
| Level | VaR (JPY) |
| 95.0% | 332,760,000 |
| 95.5% | 336,292,500 |
| 96.0% | 340,095,000 |
| 96.5% | 350,332,500 |
| 97.0% | 359,107,500 |
| 97.5% | 367,882,500 |
| 98.0% | 378,412,500 |
| 98.5% | 392,452,500 |
| 99.0% | 410,880,000 |
| 99.5% | 439,252,500 |

What is the closest estimate of the daily ES at the 97.5% confidence level?

options.text: JPY 398 million
JPY 400 million
JPY 405 million
JPY 497 million

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Expected shortfall at confidence $c$ is the average loss beyond the $c$ quantile. From a table of VaRs it is estimated as the average of the VaRs at confidence levels strictly above $c$.

**Working**

Levels above 97.5%: 98.0, 98.5, 99.0 and 99.5%.

$\text{ES}_{97.5\%} = \frac{378{,}412{,}500 + 392{,}452{,}500 + 410{,}880{,}000 + 439{,}252{,}500}{4}$

$$= \frac{1{,}620{,}997{,}500}{4} = \text{JPY} 405{,}249{,}375$$

**Exam trap.** Exclude the VaR at the stated confidence level. ES must lie above the 97.5% VaR (367.9 million) and below the largest tail VaR (439.3 million), which removes option D at once.

**Source:** 2026 PE1 Q52 (All past year questions, Question 7).

a.reason: JPY 398 million wrongly includes the 97.5% VaR itself: (1,620,997,500 + 367,882,500)/5 = 397.8 million.

b.reason: JPY 400 million is not the average of the four tail VaRs.

c.reason: Correct. About JPY 405 million.

d.reason: JPY 497 million is larger than every VaR in the table, so it cannot be an average of them.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Estimate the expected shortfall given profit and loss (P&L) or return data.
questions.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.topic: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.question:
A wealth management firm has JPY 86 billion in assets under management. The portfolio manager computes the daily VaR at various confidence levels as follows:

|  |  |
|---|---|
| Confidence |  |
| Level | VaR (JPY) |
| 95.0% | 397,463,000 |
| 95.5% | 401,682,500 |
| 96.0% | 406,224,500 |
| 96.5% | 418,453,000 |
| 97.0% | 428,934,000 |
| 97.5% | 439,415,500 |
| 98.0% | 451,993,000 |
| 98.5% | 468,763,000 |
| 99.0% | 490,773,000 |
| 99.5% | 524,663,000 |

What is the closest estimate of the daily ES at the 97.5% confidence level?

options.text: JPY 398 million
JPY 400 million
JPY 484 million
JPY 497 million

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Same template as the previous question with new numbers. ES at 97.5% is the average of the VaRs at confidence levels strictly above 97.5%.

**Working**

$\text{ES}_{97.5\%} = \frac{451{,}993{,}000 + 468{,}763{,}000 + 490{,}773{,}000 + 524{,}663{,}000}{4}$

$$= \frac{1{,}936{,}192{,}000}{4} = \text{JPY} 484{,}048{,}000$$

**Exam trap.** GARP recycles this template and leaves old answers in as distractors. Bound the answer first: it must lie between the 97.5% VaR and the 99.5% VaR.

**Source:** 2026 PE2 Q21 (All past year questions, Question 8).

a.reason: JPY 398 million is below the 97.5% VaR of 439.4 million. ES can never be below the VaR at the same confidence level. (It is the answer to the sibling question.)

b.reason: JPY 400 million is also below the 97.5% VaR.

c.reason: Correct. About JPY 484 million.

d.reason: JPY 497 million is not the average of the four tail VaRs; it sits above the 99.0% VaR.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Estimate the expected shortfall given profit and loss (P&L) or return data.
questions.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.topic: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.source: GARP past 10-year papers book, Q1.8
questions.question:
An investment bank has USD 42 billion in assets. The bank’s CRO computes the daily VaR at various levels of confidence as follows:

| Confidence level | VaR (USD) |
|---|---|
| 90.0% | 125,555,000 |
| 95.0% | 180,250,500 |
| 95.5% | 185,000,500 |
| 96.0% | 195,500,000 |
| 96.5% | 203,205,500 |
| 97.0% | 211,425,000 |
| 97.5% | 222,233,500 |
| 98.0% | 233,562,500 |
| 98.5% | 241,523,000 |
| 99.0% | 256,300,000 |
| 99.5% | 280,500,000 |

Determine the closest estimate of the daily ES at the 96.5% confidence level:
questions.solution:
**Concept**

Expected shortfall at confidence $c$ is the average loss in the tail beyond the $c$ quantile. Given a table of VaRs, it is estimated as the average of the VaRs at the confidence levels strictly above $c$.

**Working**

Levels above 96.5%: 97.0, 97.5, 98.0, 98.5, 99.0 and 99.5% (six values).

$\text{ES}_{96.5\%} = \frac{211{,}425{,}000 + 222{,}233{,}500 + 233{,}562{,}500 + 241{,}523{,}000 + 256{,}300{,}000 + 280{,}500{,}000}{6}$

$$= \frac{1{,}445{,}544{,}000}{6} = \text{USD} 240{,}924{,}000$$

**Exam trap.** The boundary value is excluded. Including the VaR at the stated confidence level (option D) is the built-in distractor in this template, which GARP reuses with new numbers.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q1.8 (All past year questions, Question 9).

a.reason: USD 203,205,500 is the 96.5% VaR itself. ES must exceed the VaR at the same confidence level.

b.reason: Correct. The average of the six VaRs above 96.5%.

c.reason: USD 280,500,000 is the 99.5% VaR, the largest value in the table, not an average of the tail.

d.reason: USD 235,535,643 averages seven values because it wrongly includes the 96.5% VaR: 1,648,749,500/7.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Estimate risk measures by estimating quantiles.
questions.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.topic: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.question: A risk analyst at an investment bank is examining how quantile estimators can be incorporated into the bank’s risk measures. The analyst focuses on how estimators are constructed and how their precision and usefulness are determined. Which of the following statements about quantile estimators is correct?

options.text: Each quantile in the loss distribution must have an equal weight when used to create a coherent risk measure.
The data and processes involved in estimating quantiles are different from those used to estimate coherent risk measures.
QQ plots are a useful tool to evaluate the precision of a quantile estimator.
Both the halving error and the standard error of a quantile estimator decrease as the number of quantiles used in the estimation process increases.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

A coherent risk measure can be estimated as a weighted average of quantiles: slice the tail into $n$ pieces, take the quantile for each slice and weight it. The more slices, the more accurate the estimate. The halving error (the change when $n$ is doubled) and the standard error of the estimator both shrink as $n$ grows.

**Exam trap.** Sibling swap in option C. QQ plots diagnose which distribution fits the data. Standard errors, not QQ plots, measure the precision of a quantile estimator.

**Source:** 2026 PE2 Q61 (All past year questions, Question 10).

a.reason: Coherent risk measures can be created using sophisticated weighting functions and do not need to be equally weighted.

b.reason: The building blocks of quantile estimation are essentially the same needed to estimate coherent risk measures.

c.reason: QQ plots are a useful diagnostic tool when considering what kind of distribution might fit the profit and loss data. QQ plots are not used to analyze or evaluate quantile estimators.

d.reason: The halving error and the standard error of a quantile estimator will both decrease as the number of slices, n, or quantiles, used in the process of estimating the risk measure increases.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Interpret quantile-quantile (QQ) plots to identify the characteristics of a distribution.
questions.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.topic: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.question: A risk analyst is studying a series of graphs plotting the empirical distribution of a portfolio’s profit and loss quantiles against the quantiles of different specified reference distributions. The analyst plans to use these QQ plots to gain insights into the properties of the empirical distribution of the portfolio’s profits and losses. Which of the following statements is correct regarding QQ plots?

options.text: The tails of the empirical distribution are heavier than those of the reference distribution if the QQ plot has a steeper slope at its tails.
QQ plots are used to smooth the empirical distribution by removing outliers through the use of quantiles.
A distribution is considered a good reference distribution if data drawn from it produces a QQ plot that is non-linear in the central mass of the distribution.
The primary purpose of a QQ plot is to measure the skewness and kurtosis of the empirical data.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

A QQ plot sets empirical quantiles against those of a reference distribution. A straight line means the reference fits. Steeper slopes at the two ends mean the empirical data have heavier tails than the reference; flatter slopes mean lighter tails.

**Exam trap.** A QQ plot identifies the reference distribution and reveals skew and kurtosis by eye, but it does not measure them. “Primary purpose is to measure” is the overreach.

**Source:** 2026 PE2 Q43 (All past year questions, Question 11).

a.reason: If the empirical distribution has heavier tails than the reference distribution, the QQ plot will have steeper slopes at its tails. Conversely, if the empirical distribution has lighter tails than the reference distribution, the QQ plot will have flatter slopes at its tails.

b.reason: Outliers are easily identified on QQ plots due to the nature of the plotting, and this is one of the ways QQ plots are useful.

c.reason: Reference distributions that produce non-linear QQ plots can be dismissed from consideration as a good representative of the empirical data since data drawn from the reference distribution should produce a linear QQ plot.

d.reason: The primary purpose of a QQ plot is to determine the proper reference distribution. One can see if there is skewness and kurtosis although it cannot be measured with a QQ plot.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Interpret quantile-quantile (QQ) plots to identify the characteristics of a distribution.
questions.reading: MR-1: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.topic: Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
questions.source: GARP past 10-year papers book, Q1.5
questions.question:
Richard Wayne, FRM, is examining a sample of return data. He constructs a QQ plot of the data as shown below:

![QQ plot: sample quantiles against theoretical quantiles](/figures/past-paper-q12-qq-plot.png)

Based on your examination of the QQ plot above, which of the following statements is most likely correct?

options.text: The returns are normally distributed.
The return has fat tails relative to the normal distribution.
The return distribution is negatively skewed relative to the normal distribution.
The return distribution isn’t normal, but normality would be a reasonable estimation.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

A QQ plot sets the empirical quantiles against the quantiles of a reference distribution (here the normal). Points on a straight line mean the two distributions have the same shape. Fat tails show up as an S-shape: the ends bend away from the line in opposite directions, steeper than the middle. Skew shows up as curvature on one side only.

**Exam trap.** Read the middle and the ends of a QQ plot separately. A straight middle with small deviations at the ends is “approximately normal”; pronounced bending at both ends is fat tails.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q1.5 (All past year questions, Question 12).

a.reason: Too strong. The extreme observations sit slightly off the line, so exact normality cannot be claimed.

b.reason: Fat tails would make both ends of the plot bend sharply away from the line (steeper slope at the extremes). The plot does not show that.

c.reason: Negative skew would show a long left tail, with the left end falling well below the line. The plot is close to symmetric and, if anything, hints at a slightly shorter left tail.

d.reason: Correct. The central mass lies very close to a straight line and only the extremes drift slightly, so the data are not exactly normal but normality is a reasonable approximation.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Apply the bootstrap historical simulation approach to estimate coherent risk measures.
questions.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
questions.topic: Non-Parametric Approaches
questions.source: GARP past 10-year papers book, Q6.3
questions.question: A risk analyst at an investment bank has been asked to evaluate the bank’s risk measurement process. The bank currently uses VaR as its primary risk measure, but the analyst believes ES may be a better measure during periods of market turmoil. When comparing VaR and ES, which of the following statements is correct?

options.text: When estimating ES and VaR at the same confidence level, ES will always be greater than VaR.
If a VaR model backtest at a specified confidence level accepts the model, then the corresponding ES model will also be accepted.
While VaR ensures that the estimate of portfolio risk is less than or equal to the sum of the risks of that portfolio’s positions, ES does not.
While ES is more difficult to estimate than VaR, it is easier to backtest than VaR.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

VaR is a quantile: the smallest loss in the worst $(1 - \alpha)$ of outcomes. Expected shortfall is the average loss in that same tail, $\text{ES}_{\alpha} = \mathbb{E}[L \mid L \ge\text{VaR}_{\alpha}]$. An average of values that are all at least VaR cannot be below VaR. ES is also a coherent risk measure (it is subadditive); VaR is not.

**Exam trap.** Options C and D are sibling swaps: each states a true property and gives it to the wrong measure. ES: coherent, tail-sensitive, hard to backtest. VaR: not subadditive, blind beyond the quantile, easy to backtest.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q6.3 (All past year questions, Question 13).

a.reason: Correct. ES averages the losses beyond VaR, so at the same confidence level it is at least as large as VaR and exceeds it whenever the tail has any spread.

b.reason: A VaR backtest only counts exceptions. It says nothing about how large the losses beyond VaR are, which is what ES measures, so passing one does not validate the other.

c.reason: This reverses the two measures. Subadditivity (portfolio risk ≤ sum of the parts) holds for ES and can fail for VaR.

d.reason: ES is harder to backtest than VaR, because the test has to judge the size of tail losses and not just their frequency.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Compare and contrast the age-weighted, the volatility-weighted, the correlation-weighted, and the filtered historical simulation approaches.
questions.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
questions.topic: Non-Parametric Approaches
questions.question: A junior risk analyst is asked to prepare a report comparing the various weighted historical simulation (HS) approaches. The analyst focuses on the ways the different HS approaches adjust the returns observed in the data set. Which of the following statements is correct for the analyst to make?

options.text: The correlation-weighted HS approach adjusts the return observations by multiplying each return by the current correlation divided by the historical correlation.
The filtered HS approach accommodates volatility clustering and allows positive and negative returns to impact volatility differently.
The volatility-weighted HS approach adjusts returns upward when the current volatility is below the long-term average volatility.
The age-weighted HS approach assumes that the value of the information contained in a return observation declines in a linear manner starting from the date it is first observed.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Four refinements of historical simulation. Age-weighted (BRW): exponentially decaying weights on older observations. Volatility-weighted (HW): each return is rescaled by current volatility over historical volatility. Correlation-weighted: returns are adjusted with the current covariance matrix. Filtered HS: bootstrap of standardised residuals from a GARCH-type model, so it captures volatility clustering and asymmetric responses.

**Exam trap.** Polarity in option C: returns are scaled up when current volatility is above the historical level. And age weights decay exponentially, not linearly.

**Source:** 2026 PE1 Q33 (All past year questions, Question 14).

a.reason: The correlation-weighted historical simulation approach uses a variance-covariance matrix to adjust the returns in the data set. This is more complex than the volatility-weighted approach, which simply multiplies each return by the current volatility estimate divided by the historical volatility estimate.

b.reason: Filtered historical simulation accommodates conditionally changing volatility, volatility clustering, and allows for the “leverage effect”, a phenomenon where positive and negative returns have differing impacts on volatility.

c.reason: Volatility-weighted HS increases (decreases) a historical return observation if the current forecast of volatility is greater (less) than the historical forecast of volatility corresponding with the historical return observation.

d.reason: Age-weighted HS allows the risk management practitioner to choose a value of lambda that represents the exponential rate of decay in the weight given to an observation as it ages. This approach does not assume that the decay is linear.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Identify advantages and disadvantages of non-parametric estimation methods.
questions.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
questions.topic: Non-Parametric Approaches
questions.question: A risk analyst at an investment bank is evaluating the historical simulation approach to estimating ES. The analyst researches the assumptions, inputs, process, and output related to the historical simulation approach and compiles a report detailing its advantages and disadvantages. Which of the following statements accurately describes an advantage of the historical simulation approach to estimating ES?

options.text: Since the data reflect actual historical events, an ES estimate derived from this data is more accurate than an estimate derived from using parametric methods.
The precision of ES estimates and their responsiveness to new market observations can typically be enhanced by increasing the length of the sample period.
Major shifts in markets, their structure, or the factors that influence them can be ignored since any effects of these shifts will be included in historical datasets.
Features such as fat tails and skewness are easily accommodated without making assumptions about the distribution.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Non-parametric (historical simulation) methods assume no distribution, so fat tails and skewness come through automatically. The price is complete dependence on the sample period, a trade-off between sample length and responsiveness, and slow reaction to structural shifts.

**Exam trap.** Option B hides a trade-off as a free lunch: a longer window improves precision but reduces responsiveness to new observations.

**Source:** 2026 PE1 Q53 (All past year questions, Question 16).

a.reason: A major potential weakness of a historical simulation approach is that its results are very dependent on the historical data set. If the period these data were taken from was unusually quiet or unusually volatile (or is otherwise not reflective of likely future events), the ES estimate could fail to accurately represent the risk we are actually facing, and a well-specified parametric estimation method could be more accurate.

b.reason: There is a tradeoff between these two objectives when choosing the length of the sample window for a historical simulation. A reasonably long window is needed for the sample size to be large enough to get risk estimates of acceptable precision; however, the longer the window, the more the news in current market observations is likely to be drowned out by older observations.

c.reason: A historical simulation approach can have difficulty handling shifts that take place during the sample period. It can be slow to reflect permanent shifts in a market’s risk profile or episodic changes in risk resulting from major events.

d.reason: Since historical simulation requires no parametric assumptions about a distribution of P/L, it can easily accommodate fat tails and skewness.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Identify advantages and disadvantages of non-parametric estimation methods.
questions.reading: MR-2: Non-Parametric Approaches
questions.topic: Non-Parametric Approaches
questions.source: GARP past 10-year papers book, Q2.2
questions.question:
During a brainstorming session by two FRM Part II Exam candidates, the pair delves into the use of parametric and non-parametric approaches for calculating VaR. One of the candidates outlines the following conditions as being suitable for non-parametric approaches:

I. Unusually low volatility during the data period

II. Unusually high volatility during the data period

III. Data is highly skewed, i.e., fat-tailed

IV. Scarcity of high-magnitude loss events

Is the candidate correct?

options.text: Only I and II are correct
Only II and IV are correct
Only III is correct
Yes: all of the above conditions are appropriate

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Non-parametric methods let the data speak and assume no distribution, so they cope well with fat tails and skewness. Their weakness is total dependence on the sample: a quiet sample understates risk, a turbulent one overstates it, and a sample with few large losses gives unreliable tail estimates.

**Exam trap.** The four statements mix one strength with three weaknesses. Ask of each: “does this make the historical sample unrepresentative?” If yes, it argues against the non-parametric approach.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q2.2 (All past year questions, Question 17).

a.reason: I and II are the opposite of suitable: an unusually calm or unusually volatile data period makes historical-simulation VaR and ES too low or too high.

b.reason: II and IV are both weaknesses of the non-parametric approach, not conditions that favour it.

c.reason: Correct. Only III (fat-tailed, skewed data) is a condition under which non-parametric methods are preferred, because parametric assumptions such as normality break down.

d.reason: I, II and IV are exactly the situations where dependence on the historical sample hurts.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe extreme value theory (EVT) and its use in risk management.
questions.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
questions.topic: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
questions.question: The CRO of a regional bank expresses concern in a meeting of the risk team that the bank’s internal risk models are not adequately assessing potential random extreme losses. A risk analyst asks if implementing a model based on extreme value theory (EVT) would address the CRO’s concern. Which of the following is correct when applying EVT and examining distributions of losses exceeding a threshold value?

options.text: As the threshold value is increased, the distribution of losses over a fixed threshold value converges to a generalized Pareto distribution.
If the tail parameter value of the generalized extreme-value (GEV) distribution goes to infinity, then the GEV essentially becomes a normal distribution.
To apply EVT, the underlying loss distribution must be either normal or lognormal.
The number of exceedances decreases as the threshold value decreases, which causes the reliability of the parameter estimates to increase.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Extreme value theory describes the tail without assuming a shape for the whole distribution. The GPBdH theorem says that, as the threshold rises, the distribution of losses in excess of the threshold converges to a generalized Pareto distribution, whatever the parent distribution. This is the basis of the peaks-over-threshold approach.

**Exam trap.** Two polarity traps. The tail index going to zero (not infinity) gives the light-tailed Gumbel case. And lowering the threshold increases the number of exceedances.

**Source:** 2026 PE1 Q57 (All past year questions, Question 18).

a.reason: A key foundation of EVT is that as the threshold value is increased, the distribution of loss exceedances converges to a generalized Pareto distribution. Assuming the threshold is high enough, excess losses can be modeled using the generalized Pareto distribution. It is known as the Gnedenko– Pickands–Balkema– deHaan (GPBdH) theorem and is heavily used in the peaks-over-threshold (POT) approach.

b.reason: If the tail parameter value of the generalized extreme-value (GEV) distribution goes to zero, and not infinity, then the distribution of the original data (not the GEV) could be a light-tail distribution such as normal or log-normal. In other words, the corresponding GEV distribution is a Gumbel distribution.

c.reason: To apply EVT, the underlying loss distribution can be any of the commonly used distributions: normal, lognormal, t, etc.

d.reason: As the threshold value is decreased, the number of exceedances increases.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe extreme value theory (EVT) and its use in risk management.
questions.reading: MR-3: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
questions.topic: Parametric Approaches (II): Extreme Value
questions.question: A risk analyst at an investment bank is evaluating the bank’s application of extreme value theory (EVT) in managing financial risks. The analyst compares different methods of estimating extreme value (EV) parameters for the bank’s operational loss distribution and examines the mechanics of each method, as well as their advantages and disadvantages. Which of the following statements regarding a method used for estimating EV parameters is correct?

options.text: The regression method uses an ordered sample of losses to obtain least squares estimates of the EV parameters.
The maximum-likelihood method uses the average of a random number of the most extreme observations to estimate EV parameters.
The main challenge associated with the moment-based method is choosing the number of observations that minimizes the mean-squared-error loss function.
A drawback of the semi-parametric estimation method is that the Hill estimator is neither consistent nor asymptotically normal.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Three ways to estimate extreme-value parameters. Maximum likelihood: the standard method, with good properties but needing numerical optimisation. Regression: order the extremes and fit by least squares, the easiest to apply. Semi-parametric: the Hill estimator, which uses an arbitrary number of the most extreme observations and is consistent and asymptotically normal.

**Exam trap.** Option B describes the Hill estimator (semi-parametric) and labels it maximum likelihood; option C gives the semi-parametric method’s main difficulty to the moment-based method. Both are sibling swaps.

**Source:** 2026 PE2 Q66 (All past year questions, Question 19).

a.reason: The regression method is the easiest method to apply, and the recovery of least squares estimates of the EV parameters from a regression is straightforward. The first step in applying the regression method is to order the sample of extreme values from lowest to highest.

b.reason: The use of an arbitrary (not random) number would correctly describe the Hill estimator, which is used in semi-parametric estimation method. However, this would still be an incorrect answer to this specific question.

c.reason: The main challenge with the semi-parametric method (not the moment-based method) is choosing the number of observations to include in the tail, as the parameter estimates can be sensitive to this number.

d.reason: The most popular semi-parametric estimation method is the Hill estimator, which is known to be consistent and asymptotically normal.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe backtesting and exceptions and explain the importance of backtesting VaR models.
questions.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
questions.topic: Backtesting VaR
questions.question: An analyst at bank LKS has been asked to validate the bank’s VaR model through backtesting. The analyst uses two sets of returns data to generate results of predicted and actual losses that can be compared in the validation process. Which of the following correctly describes the two most appropriate sets of returns data to use in backtesting?

options.text: The cleaned returns, which are the actual returns minus any profit and loss from intraday trades, and the actual returns, which correspond to the total returns on the bank’s trading portfolio

The actual returns, which correspond to the total return on the bank’s trading portfolio, and the hypothetical returns, which represent the returns obtained from freezing the starting positions in the bank’s trading portfolio

The hypothetical returns, which represent the returns obtained from freezing the starting positions in the bank’s trading portfolio, and the cleaned returns, which are the actual returns minus any profit and loss from intraday trades

The trading returns, which are the actual returns minus any fees and commissions, and the hypothetical returns, which represent the actual returns obtained from freezing the starting positions in the bank’s trading portfolio

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Backtesting compares VaR with realized results, and the choice of return series matters. Actual returns include intraday trading, fees and commissions. Hypothetical returns freeze the start-of-day portfolio and revalue it at end-of-day prices, which is what the VaR model really forecasts. Using both isolates the source of a failure.

**Exam trap.** If the model passes on hypothetical returns but fails on actual returns, the problem is intraday trading, not the model. Cleaned returns (actual minus fees, commissions and net interest) are only an approximation to hypothetical returns.

**Source:** 2026 PE1 Q31 (All past year questions, Question 21).

a.reason: The descriptions of the cleaned returns are not correct, and these are not the correct two sets of returns that the analyst should use. Cleaned returns will also subtract any fees, commissions, net interest margin from actual returns. The correct definition of cleaned returns can sometimes be used as an approximation of hypothetical returns, but not the incorrectly defined returns stated here.

b.reason: Ideally, the analyst will use both the actual and hypothetical returns for backtesting since both yield informative comparisons. If the model passes backtesting with hypothetical but not actual returns, the problem in the model lies with intraday trading. If the model does not pass backtesting with hypothetical returns, the modelling methodology should be re-examined.

c.reason: These are not the correct two sets of returns that the analyst should use, and the description of cleaned returns is incorrect.

d.reason: There is not a return set that is called trading returns.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe backtesting and exceptions and explain the importance of backtesting VaR models.
questions.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
questions.topic: Backtesting VaR
questions.question: An analyst at a bank is asked to evaluate the efficacy of the VaR model that the bank used over the last year. While evaluating the model, the analyst finds that the bank experienced more VaR exceptions than were forecast by the bank’s VaR model and examines both the reason this occurred and its potential impact on the bank. Which of the following is correct regarding the analyst’s examination of the situation?

options.text: The confidence level of the backtest performed on the VaR model was set too low.
The model is most likely overestimating the market risk faced by the bank.
The risk-taking units of the bank will likely be allocated less capital than they should be.
The bank’s regulator will impose a financial penalty on the bank.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

An exception is a day on which the loss exceeds VaR. Too many exceptions mean VaR is too low: the model understates risk, and capital allocated on the basis of that VaR is too small.

**Exam trap.** Polarity: too many exceptions ⇒ risk underestimated ⇒ too little capital. Regulatory penalties are not automatic; exceptions caused by bad luck may not be penalised.

**Source:** 2025 PE2 Q49 (All past year questions, Question 22).

a.reason: Observing too many or too few exceptions is not a related to the confidence level of the model.

b.reason: A model that produces too many exceptions is underestimating the market risk the bank faces.

c.reason: A model that produces too many exceptions may cause too little capital to be allocated to risk-taking units.

d.reason: The bank’s VaR model may see too many exceptions due to a poorly designed model, deliberately underestimating risk, or bad luck. The regulator may impose penalties to prevent the first two reasons, but the regulator may not impose penalties if the exceedances are the result of bad luck, or intraday trading.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
questions.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
questions.topic: Backtesting VaR
questions.source: GARP past 10-year papers book, Q4.4
questions.question: Michael Roy, a risk analyst at a large multinational bank, is backtesting the VaR model of the bank. The model being tested is a daily, 98% VaR model. If the backtest is conducted for one year at a 95% confidence level, and assuming 252 days in a year, what is the number of daily losses that will lead Roy to conclude that the model is not calibrated correctly?

options.text: All three choices

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Under a correct model the number of exceptions $x$ in $T$ days is binomial with mean $pT$ and variance $p(1 - p)T$, where $p = 1 - c$ is the VaR tail probability. The model is rejected when $z = \frac{x - pT}{\sqrt{p(1 - p)T}}$ exceeds the cut-off for the test confidence level (1.96 at 95%). Keep the two confidence levels apart: 98% belongs to the VaR, 95% to the test.

**Working**

$p = 0.02$, $T = 252$, cut-off = 1.96.

**Mean:** $pT = 0.02 \times252 = 5.04$

**Standard deviation:** $\sqrt{0.02 \times0.98 \times252} = \sqrt{4.9392} = 2.222$

**Largest acceptable count:** $x < 5.04 + 1.96 \times2.222 = 9.40$

Nine exceptions are still acceptable. Ten is the first count that rejects the model.

**Exam trap.** Using $p = 0.05$ (the test level) instead of $p = 0.02$ (the VaR tail) is the standard slip. The test level only chooses the 1.96.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q4.4 (All past year questions, Question 23).

a.reason: 8 exceptions give $z = (8 - 5.04)/2.222 = 1.33$, inside the non-rejection region.

b.reason: 9 exceptions give $z = 1.78$, still below 1.96.

c.reason: Correct. 10 exceptions give $z = 2.23 > 1.96$, so the model is rejected.

d.reason: Only 10 leads to rejection; 8 and 9 do not.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
questions.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
questions.topic: Backtesting VaR
questions.source: GARP past 10-year papers book, Q4.8
questions.question: Paul Ferguson, FRM, works as an analyst at a U.S.-based bank. He wishes to test the bank’s 1-day 99.5% VaR model over a 1-year horizon at a 99% confidence level. Assuming 252 days in a year, determine the maximum number of daily losses exceeding the 1-day 99.5% VaR that is acceptable to conclude that the model is well calibrated.
questions.solution:
**Concept**

Same failure-rate test, solved for the largest number of exceptions that keeps $z$ inside the cut-off. At a 99% test confidence level (two-tailed) the cut-off is 2.576.

**Working**

$p = 0.005$, $T = 252$.

**Mean:** $pT = 0.005 \times252 = 1.26$

**Standard deviation:** $\sqrt{0.005 \times0.995 \times252} = \sqrt{1.2537} = 1.1197$

**Largest acceptable count:** $x = 1.26 + 2.576 \times1.1197 = 1.26 + 2.884 = 4.14$

So up to 4 exceptions are acceptable.

**Exam trap.** Round down: the question asks for the maximum acceptable count, and 4.14 means the fifth exception crosses the line. Also check the test level: 1.96 would give 3.45, i.e. 3 (option B).

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q4.8 (All past year questions, Question 24).

a.reason: 2 is well inside the acceptable range but is not the maximum.

b.reason: 3 is acceptable but is not the maximum.

c.reason: Correct. 4 is the largest whole number below 4.14.

d.reason: 5 exceeds 4.14, so five exceptions would reject the model.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
questions.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
questions.topic: Backtesting VaR
questions.source: GARP past 10-year papers book, Q4.9
questions.question: A large investment firm has a trading book whose size changes depending on the perceived trading opportunities among traders. According to the firm’s chief risk analyst, the one-day VaR, at the 95% confidence level, is GBP 110 million. Suppose you were asked to evaluate how good a job the analyst is doing in estimating the one-day VaR. Assuming that losses are i.i.d., which of the following would serve as convincing evidence that the manager is performing poorly?

options.text: Over the past 250 days, there is no exception
Over the past 250 days, the mean loss is GBP 132 million
Over the past 250 days, the largest loss is GBP 1.1 billion
Over the past 250 days, there are seven exceptions

questions.solution:
**Concept**

A VaR model can fail in either direction. Too many exceptions means risk is understated. Too few means VaR is set too high, which is also a calibration failure. The evidence is the exception count compared with its binomial expectation, not the size of individual losses.

**Working**

Expected exceptions = (1 − 0.95) × 250 = 12.5, with standard deviation $\sqrt{250 \times0.05 \times0.95} = 3.45$. **Zero exceptions:** probability $0.95^{250} \approx2.7 \times10^{-6}$. Essentially impossible under a correct model. **Seven exceptions:** $z = (7 - 12.5)/3.45 = -1.60$, inside ±1.96, so it is consistent with chance.

**Exam trap.** “Performing poorly” does not mean “too many losses”. An over-conservative VaR fails the backtest too. With a changing trading book, loss sizes are even less comparable from day to day, so only the exception count is usable.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q4.9 (All past year questions, Question 25).

a.reason: Correct. No exceptions in 250 days when 12.5 are expected is overwhelming evidence that the VaR estimate is far too high.

b.reason: A mean loss figure says nothing about how often the 95% quantile is breached.

c.reason: One very large loss is uninformative without the rest of the P&L distribution; a fat tail can produce it even when the 95% VaR is right.

d.reason: Seven exceptions is within sampling error of 12.5.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the accuracy of a VaR model based on exceptions or failure rates by using a model verification test.
questions.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
questions.topic: Backtesting VaR
questions.source: GARP past 10-year papers book, Q4.11
questions.question: A risk manager is backtesting a company’s 1-day 99.5% VaR model over a 10-year horizon at the 95% confidence level. Assuming 250 trading days in a year and that daily returns are i.i.d., which of the following is closest to the maximum number of daily losses exceeding the 1-day 99.5% VaR in 10 years that is acceptable to conclude that the model is calibrated correctly?
questions.solution:
**Concept**

Failure-rate test again, now with a long sample. More days means more expected exceptions and a tighter test.

**Working**

$p = 0.005$, $T = 250 \times10 = 2{,}500$, cut-off = 1.96.

**Mean:** $pT = 0.005 \times2{,}500 = 12.5$

**Standard deviation:** $\sqrt{0.005 \times0.995 \times2{,}500} = \sqrt{12.4375} = 3.527$

**Largest acceptable count:** 12.5 + 1.96 × 3.527 = 12.5 + 6.91 = 19.4, so 19.

**Exam trap.** $T$ is the number of days (2,500), not the number of years. Using $T = 250$ gives 3.4 and no matching option.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q4.11 (All past year questions, Question 26).

a.reason: Correct. 19 is the largest whole number below 19.4.

b.reason: 25 would require $z = (25 - 12.5)/3.527 = 3.54$, far beyond 1.96.

c.reason: 35 is far outside the non-rejection region.

d.reason: 39 is far outside the non-rejection region.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
questions.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
questions.topic: Backtesting VaR
questions.question: A model validation team at a bank is backtesting the bank’s VaR model. In preparation for the backtest, one of the team members expresses a concern that the validation process could result in the team committing a Type I error or a Type II error and discusses the characteristics of these errors with the team. Which of the following is correct regarding Type I and Type II errors?

options.text: The probability of committing a Type II error decreases when the sample size increases and the level of significance is held constant.
A backtest is considered statistically powerful if it minimizes the probability of committing a Type II error regardless of the probability of committing a Type I error.
A Type I error is committed when an incorrectly specified model is accepted.
A Type II error is committed when a correctly specified model is rejected.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Type I error: rejecting a correct model. Type II error: failing to reject an incorrect model. The power of a test is its ability to reject a wrong model. A larger sample narrows the non-rejection region for a correct model, so a wrong model is rejected more easily and the Type II error rate falls.

**Exam trap.** Options C and D are the two definitions swapped. Option B’s “regardless of Type I” is the absolute-claim trap: a powerful test keeps both error rates low.

**Source:** 2026 PE2 Q70 (All past year questions, Question 27).

a.reason: As the sample size increases, the confidence region of the failure rate (expressed as N/T) for a correctly specified model will shrink, and an incorrectly specified model should be able to be rejected more easily.

b.reason: A test with a low type I error rate and a low type II error rate is said to be powerful. The power of a test relates to the error rates of both type I and type II errors.

c.reason: A type I error is rejecting a correctly specified model.

d.reason: A type II error is not rejecting an incorrectly specified model.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
questions.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
questions.topic: Backtesting VaR
questions.question: A newly hired risk analyst at a mid-size bank is assisting in backtesting the bank’s VaR model. Currently, the 1-day VaR is estimated at the 95% confidence level but the bank is considering a change to estimating 1-day VaR at the 99% confidence level, as recommended in the Basel framework. Which of the following statements concerning this change is correct?

options.text: The decision to accept or reject a VaR model based on the results of a backtest that uses a two-tailed 95% confidence level is less reliable when applied to a 99% VaR model than when applied to a 95% VaR model.
The 95% VaR model is less likely to be rejected by a backtest than the 99% VaR model.
When using a two-tailed 90% confidence level test in a backtest, there is a smaller probability of incorrectly rejecting a 95% VaR model than a 99% VaR model.
Using a 99% VaR model will lower the probability of committing both Type I error and Type II error.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Two confidence levels are in play. The VaR confidence level (95% or 99%) sets how many exceptions to expect. The test confidence level (here a two-tailed 95%) sets the cut-off for rejecting the model. A 95% VaR produces about five times as many expected exceptions as a 99% VaR, which gives the backtest more information and more power.

**Exam trap.** Do not confuse the VaR confidence level with the test confidence level. Higher VaR confidence sounds more rigorous but makes the backtest weaker.

**Source:** 2025 PE1 Q53 (All past year questions, Question 28).

a.reason: Correct. With a 99% VaR there are very few expected exceptions, so a good model and a bad model are hard to tell apart and the accept or reject decision is less reliable.

b.reason: The reverse is true. The backtest has more power against a 95% VaR model, so a wrong 95% model is more likely to be rejected.

c.reason: The probability of incorrectly rejecting a correct model (Type I error) is fixed by the test confidence level, about 10% here, whichever VaR confidence level is used.

d.reason: Moving to a 99% VaR lowers the power of the test, so the probability of a Type II error rises.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
questions.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
questions.topic: Backtesting VaR
questions.source: GARP past 10-year papers book, Q4.5
questions.question: A model gives a VaR value of \$5 million for a portfolio at a 99% confidence interval. A one-year backtest conducted at the 95% confidence level reveals that losses exceeded \$5 million on 8 occasions. The model is accepted as accurate. Assuming 252 days in a year, which of these statements is most likely true?

options.text: A Type I error has occurred
A Type II error has occurred
Both Type I and Type II errors have occurred
The model has been accepted correctly

questions.solution:
**Concept**

In backtesting, the null hypothesis is that the VaR model is correct. A Type I error rejects a correct model. A Type II error accepts an incorrect model. To decide which applies, first run the failure-rate test.

**Working**

$p = 0.01$, $T = 252$, $x = 8$.

$$z = \frac{x - pT}{\sqrt{p(1 - p)T}} = \frac{8 - 2.52}{\sqrt{0.01 \times0.99 \times252}} = \frac{5.48}{1.580} = 3.47$$

3.47 > 1.96, so the evidence says the model understates risk and should be rejected. It was accepted anyway.

**Exam trap.** Polarity: Type I = reject a good model, Type II = accept a bad model. Regulators worry most about Type II, because a bad model that passes leaves the bank under-capitalised.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q4.5 (All past year questions, Question 29).

a.reason: A Type I error would be rejecting a model that is actually correct. Here the model was accepted.

b.reason: Correct. An inaccurate model has been accepted, which is a Type II error.

c.reason: The two errors are mutually exclusive for a single decision.

d.reason: With 8 exceptions against 2.52 expected, the test statistic is far beyond the cut-off, so acceptance was not correct.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Identify and describe Type I and Type II errors in the context of a backtesting process.
questions.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
questions.topic: Backtesting VaR
questions.source: GARP past 10-year papers book, Q4.10
questions.question: A newly recruited intern has been tasked with backtesting a firm’s VaR model. Since inception, the firm has always calculated 1-day VaRs at the 95% level of confidence. In light of changes in required practices as dictated by the Basel framework, the intern has recommended a shift to the 99% level of confidence. What will be the implication of making this switch?

options.text: Decisions on whether to accept or reject VaR models based on backtesting will be more reliable
The power of statistical tests will increase
The 95% VaR model is less likely to be rejected using backtesting than the 99% VaR model
Decisions on whether to accept or reject VaR models based on backtesting will be less reliable

questions.solution:
**Concept**

The power of a backtest is its ability to reject a wrong model (to avoid a Type II error). Power comes from having enough exceptions to work with. A higher VaR confidence level means fewer expected exceptions in the same sample, so the test has less information and less power.

**Exam trap.** Polarity. Higher VaR confidence sounds “more rigorous” but weakens the backtest. This is why 1-day 99% backtests over 250 days are statistically feeble, and why the Basel zones were calibrated around that weakness.

**Learning objectives tested:** MR-4d, MR-4c.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q4.10 (All past year questions, Question 30).

a.reason: Moving to 99% cuts the expected exceptions from 5% to 1% of days, which makes decisions less reliable, not more.

b.reason: Power falls, because with so few expected exceptions a bad model and a good model look alike.

c.reason: This reverses the comparison. A 95% model is easier to reject when it is wrong, because the test has more power.

d.reason: Correct. Fewer exceptions means a wider relative non-rejection region and less reliable accept or reject decisions.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the Basel rules for backtesting.
questions.reading: MR-4: Backtesting VaR
questions.topic: Backtesting VaR
questions.question: A regulatory analyst at an investment bank is reviewing the Basel Committee rules for backtesting VaR models. The analyst notes that under the Basel framework, a penalty can be given to banks that have more than four exceptions to their 1-day 99% VaR over the last 250 trading days. Which of the following scenarios is most likely to result in a penalty?

options.text: A large move in interest rates occurs in conjunction with a small move in correlations.
The bank’s model calculates interest rate risk based on the median duration of the bonds in the portfolio.
A sudden market crisis in an emerging market, which leads to losses in the equity positions in that country.
A sudden devastating earthquake that causes major losses in the bank’s key area of operation.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Under the Basel backtesting rules (1-day 99% VaR, 250 days), up to four exceptions is the green zone, five to nine the yellow zone and ten or more the red zone. In the yellow zone the supervisor decides whether to apply a penalty according to the cause: basic integrity of the model or a model that could be more accurate (penalty), intraday trading (penalty should be considered), or bad luck (no penalty).

**Exam trap.** Ask whose fault the exception is. If the bank could have fixed it (model imprecision), expect a penalty. If the market did it, expect none.

**Source:** 2026 PE1 Q58 (All past year questions, Question 31).

a.reason: A large move in rates together with a move in correlations is a market event the model could not have anticipated: bad luck, no penalty.

b.reason: Correct. Measuring interest rate risk with the median duration of the portfolio is an imprecise model whose accuracy could easily have been improved, which draws a penalty.

c.reason: A sudden crisis in an emerging market is an unpredictable market move: bad luck.

d.reason: A natural disaster is outside anything a market risk model is expected to capture: bad luck.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
questions.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
questions.topic: VaR Mapping
questions.question: A senior risk analyst at a large investment bank is proposing to the CRO a plan to improve the efficiency of the bank’s risk measurement system. The analyst suggests simplifying the bank’s portfolio VaR estimation process by mapping the bank’s large number of trading positions to a smaller number of elementary risk factors. Which of the following is the most appropriate way of mapping the given position?

options.text: Mapping USD/EUR forward contracts to the USD/EUR spot exchange rate.
Mapping each position in a corporate bond portfolio to the bond with the closest maturity among a set of government bonds.
Mapping zero-coupon government bonds to government bonds paying regular coupons.
Mapping a position in a stock market index to a position in a stock within that index.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Mapping replaces each position with exposures to a small set of primitive risk factors. A good mapping simplifies the sources of uncertainty without discarding a material risk.

**Exam trap.** Mapping runs from the specific position to a simpler, more general factor. A single stock is mapped to its index, never the index to a stock. Mapping corporate bonds to government bonds drops spread risk.

**Source:** 2026 PE1 Q30 (All past year questions, Question 32).

a.reason: Mapping several USD/EUR forward contracts to USD/EUR spot exchange rate is an adequate process, because all the forward positions are exposed to a single major risk factor, which is the USD/EUR spot exchange rate. However, this is not a perfect mapping (for instance, the sensitivity of both the forward and the spot exchange rates to a specific risk factor such as changes in interest rates, may differ). While the single aggregation of exposure of this risk factor is acceptable for risk measurement, it is not adequate for pricing of the portfolio.

b.reason: Any bond must be mapped on yields that best represent its current profile and the yield differences between the corporate bonds and the government bonds disqualify this as the best mapping.

c.reason: Such procedure maps a simple single source of uncertainty (the payoff at the maturity) to multiple sources of uncertainty (coupon payments and the payoff at the maturity) which violates the first principle of mapping, simplify the source of uncertainty.

d.reason: The stock market index is a more diversified factor than a single stock. In fact, it is usually the reverse, i.e., a position of stock within an index is mapped to a position in that index.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Explain the principles underlying VaR mapping and describe the mapping process.
questions.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
questions.topic: VaR Mapping
questions.source: GARP past 10-year papers book, Q5.5
questions.question: A risk manager wishes to compute the VaR on a portfolio containing a very large number of positions. He believes he can significantly simplify the process by mapping these small positions to a smaller number of elementary risk factors. Which of the following mappings would be most appropriate?

options.text: A position in the S&P 500 index is mapped to a position in a stock included within the index
Mapping zero-coupon government bonds on other government bonds paying a regular series of coupons
Mapping each position in a corporate bond on a government bond with a similar term to maturity
Mapping EUR/USD forward contracts on the EUR/USD spot exchange rate

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Mapping replaces each position with exposures to a small set of primitive risk factors. A mapping is appropriate when the position really is driven by the chosen factor and no material risk is thrown away.

**Exam trap.** Mapping always goes from the specific position to a simpler, more general factor. Options A and B reverse that direction, and C drops a whole risk class.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q5.5 (All past year questions, Question 33).

a.reason: This runs the wrong way. An index is diversified; mapping it to a single constituent stock adds that stock’s specific risk and misstates the index’s risk.

b.reason: A zero-coupon bond has one cash flow; mapping it to a coupon bond with many cash flows introduces exposures the zero does not have.

c.reason: Mapping a corporate bond to a government bond of similar maturity keeps the interest-rate risk but discards the credit-spread risk.

d.reason: Correct. EUR/USD forwards are driven overwhelmingly by the EUR/USD spot rate, so the spot rate is an adequate risk factor (not perfect, since forwards also depend on the two interest rates).

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate among the three methods for mapping portfolios of fixed-income securities.
questions.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
questions.topic: VaR Mapping
questions.source: GARP past 10-year papers book, Q5.6
questions.question:
Study the following statements regarding risk factor mapping approaches:

I. Using more risk factors generally yields better risk measures, but on the downside, it requires the commitment of more time to the modeling and risk computation processes.

II. Under the duration mapping approach, the risk of a bond is mapped to a zero-coupon bond of a similar duration.

III. For a fixed-income portfolio, such as a series of fixed-income bonds, cash flow mapping is the least precise approach.

IV. Under the cash flow (CF) mapping approach, only the risk associated with the average maturity of a fixed-income portfolio is mapped.

Which of these statements are correct?

options.text: III and IV
I and II
I only
IV only

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Three ways to map a fixed-income portfolio. Principal mapping uses only the average maturity of the redemption payments. Duration mapping uses a zero-coupon bond with maturity equal to the portfolio’s duration. Cash-flow mapping maps every cash flow to its own vertex and is the most precise, because it uses the correlations between vertices.

**Exam trap.** Precision ranking: principal (least) $< \text{duration} <$ cash-flow (most). Statement III flips the ranking and statement IV gives cash-flow mapping the definition of principal mapping, a sibling swap.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q5.6 (All past year questions, Question 35).

a.reason: III and IV are both false.

b.reason: Correct. I is true: more risk factors give better risk measures at the cost of more modelling and computation time. II is true: duration mapping replaces the bond with a zero of the same duration.

c.reason: I is true, but II is true as well.

d.reason: IV is false: cash-flow mapping maps each cash flow, not the average maturity. Mapping the average maturity is principal mapping.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Differentiate among the three methods for mapping portfolios of fixed-income securities.
questions.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
questions.topic: VaR Mapping
questions.source: GARP past 10-year papers book, Q5.10
questions.question: A portfolio manager is mapping a fixed-income portfolio into exposures on selected risk factors. The manager is analyzing the comparable mechanics and risk measurement outputs of principal mapping, duration mapping, and cash-flow mapping. Which of the following is correct?

options.text: Cash-flow mapping groups cash flows into buckets based on their size.
Cash-flow mapping uses the average rates in each risk group as a discount factor.
Principal mapping incorporates correlations among zero-coupon bonds.
Duration mapping replaces the portfolio with a zero-coupon bond with maturity equal to the duration of the portfolio.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Principal mapping: one risk factor, the average maturity of the principal payments. Duration mapping: one risk factor, a zero-coupon bond whose maturity equals the portfolio’s duration. Cash-flow mapping: every cash flow is discounted at its own zero rate and placed in a maturity bucket, with correlations between the buckets taken into account.

**Exam trap.** Options A to C each take a true feature and attach it to the wrong method or corrupt one word (size for maturity, average for own-maturity). Fix the one-line definition of each of the three methods.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q5.10 (All past year questions, Question 36).

a.reason: Cash flows are grouped into buckets by maturity (the vertices for which volatilities are available), not by size.

b.reason: Each cash flow is discounted at the zero-coupon rate for its own maturity, not at an average rate for the group.

c.reason: Principal mapping looks only at the timing of the redemption payments. Correlations between zero-coupon bonds are used in cash-flow mapping.

d.reason: Correct. This is the definition of duration mapping.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the method of mapping forwards, forward rate agreements, interest rate swaps, and options.
questions.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
questions.topic: VaR Mapping
questions.question: A fund manager owns a portfolio of options on TUV, a non-dividend paying stock. The portfolio is made up of 5,000 deep in-the-money call options on TUV and 20,000 deep out-of-the-money call options on TUV. The portfolio also contains 10,000 forward contracts on TUV. Currently, TUV is trading at USD 52. Assuming 252 trading days in a year, the volatility of TUV is 12% per year, and that each of the option and forward contracts is on one share of TUV, which of the following amounts would be closest to the 1-day 99% VaR of the portfolio?
questions.solution:
**Concept**

Delta-normal mapping replaces each option with delta units of the underlying. A deep in-the-money call has a delta of about 1, a deep out-of-the-money call about 0, and a forward on a non-dividend-paying stock exactly 1. Then VaR $= z \times S \times\Delta_{P} \times\sigma_{\text{daily}}$.

**Working**

**Portfolio delta:** 1 × 5,000 + 0 × 20,000 + 1 × 10,000 = 15,000 share-equivalents.

**Daily volatility:** $0.12/\sqrt{252} = 0.007559$

**1-day 99% VaR:** $2.326 \times52 \times15{,}000 \times0.007559 = \text{USD} 13{,}715$

**Exam trap.** The out-of-the-money calls are the largest position and contribute nothing. Read the moneyness before the size. Option D is exactly what you get by ignoring it.

**Source:** 2026 PE1 Q59 (All past year questions, Question 37).

a.reason: USD 11,557 uses a multiplier of 1.96 instead of the one-tailed 99% value of 2.326.

b.reason: USD 12,627 is too low; it does not follow from the full delta of 15,000 at 99%.

c.reason: Correct.

d.reason: USD 32,000 counts the 20,000 out-of-the-money options as if they had a delta of 1 (35,000 share-equivalents gives USD 32,000).

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the method of mapping forwards, forward rate agreements, interest rate swaps, and options.
questions.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
questions.topic: VaR Mapping
questions.question: A risk manager at Bank QRP is examining the process of estimating the VaR of derivative contracts after mapping their risks to a set of factors. The bank holds several forward contracts in foreign currencies, commodities, and interest rates. The manager is interested in how the inputs and outputs of a mapping process differ across the different forward contracts the bank holds. Which of the following statements is correct about mapping forward contracts?

options.text: Valuing a commodity forward through mapping is simpler and more precise than valuing a financial forward, since commodity forwards generally do not make periodic cash payments.
A key factor used in valuing a forward rate agreement is the convenience yield arising from the buyer’s ability to lock in long-term borrowing rates.
When mapping the risks of a foreign currency forward contract to risk factors, volatility of the underlying spot contract is the primary source of risk.
The VaR of an interest rate forward contract increases as it approaches maturity, reflecting lower confidence in estimates of the future levels of the risk factors.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

A forward contract is mapped to its underlying risk factors: the spot price, the domestic interest rate and the foreign rate or yield. For a currency forward the volatility of the spot rate is by far the largest contributor to risk.

**Exam trap.** The VaR of an interest rate forward falls as maturity approaches, because less time remains for the rate to move. Option D flips the direction.

**Source:** 2026 PE2 Q49 (All past year questions, Question 38).

a.reason: While it is true that commodity forwards do not generally make monetary payments, the underlying commodities offer an implied benefit known as a convenience yield that is difficult to measure and highly variable, and cannot be tied to another financial variable.

b.reason: The convenience yield is a key factor in valuing commodity forwards.

c.reason: The volatility of the underlying spot contract has been shown to be the largest contributor to the risk of a forward contract.

d.reason: The VaR of interest rate forward contracts decreases with maturity.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe the method of mapping forwards, forward rate agreements, interest rate swaps, and options.
questions.reading: MR-5: VaR Mapping
questions.topic: VaR Mapping
questions.source: GARP past 10-year papers book, Q5.8
questions.question: A fund manager owns a portfolio of options on a non-dividend paying stock ABC. The portfolio consists of 16,500 deep-in-the-money call options on ABC and 88,000 deep-out-of-the-money call options on ABC. In addition, the portfolio contains 44,000 forward contracts on ABC. At present, ABC has a market price of USD 167. Assuming 250 trading days in a year and ABC volatility of 22% per year, determine the 1-day VaR of the portfolio at the 95% level of confidence.
questions.solution:
**Concept**

Under delta-normal mapping an option is replaced by delta units of the underlying. A deep in-the-money call has a delta close to 1, a deep out-of-the-money call has a delta close to 0, and a forward on a non-dividend stock has a delta of 1. Then VaR $= z \times S \times\Delta_{P} \times\sigma_{\text{daily}}$.

**Working**

**Portfolio delta:** 1 × 16,500 + 0 × 88,000 + 1 × 44,000 = 60,500 share-equivalents.

**Daily volatility:** $0.22/\sqrt{250} = 0.013914$

**VaR:** $1.645 \times167 \times60{,}500 \times0.013914 = \text{USD} 231{,}255$

**Exam trap.** The 88,000 deep out-of-the-money calls are the largest count in the question and contribute nothing. Read the moneyness, not the size of the position. Then check the day count the question specifies.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q5.8 (All past year questions, Question 39).

a.reason: USD 164,846 understates the exposure; it does not correspond to the full delta of 60,500 share-equivalents.

b.reason: Correct.

c.reason: USD 230,335 uses 252 trading days ($0.22/\sqrt{252}$) instead of the 250 given.

d.reason: USD 230,000 is a rounded figure, not the result of the calculation.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe financial correlation risk and the areas in which it appears in finance.
questions.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
questions.topic: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
questions.question: A newly hired risk analyst at a large investment bank is examining how financial correlation risk affects the bank’s portfolios. The bank holds portfolios consisting of different types of assets and enters into various hedging contracts with multiple counterparties. Which of the following statements would the analyst be correct to make?

options.text: The buyer of a CDS faces wrong-way risk when there is a positive default correlation between the reference asset and the CDS counterparty.
The risk-adjusted return of a portfolio typically increases when correlations of assets in the portfolio increase.
Dynamic correlation risk in a portfolio of pairs trades is most appropriately estimated using Gaussian copulas.
Correlation risk is highest during periods of relatively benign market movements when correlations are difficult to predict.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

Correlation risk is the risk of loss from an adverse change in the correlation between two or more variables. It appears in investments, trading, risk management, the global financial crisis and regulation. In a CDS, a positive default correlation between the reference entity and the protection seller is wrong-way risk: the protection is worth least exactly when it is needed.

**Exam trap.** Correlation risk peaks in crises, when correlations jump toward one, not in calm markets. Gaussian copulas model static default correlation (CDOs), not the dynamic correlation of pairs trades.

**Source:** 2026 PE1 Q55 (All past year questions, Question 40).

a.reason: Wrong-way risk arises when there is a positive default correlation between the reference asset and the CDS counterparty.

b.reason: The lower the correlation between the assets in a portfolio, the higher the return/risk (risk-adjusted returns) ratio.

c.reason: Gaussian copulas are used to measure the static default correlation risk of CDOs, they would not be used in a portfolio of pairs trades.

d.reason: Periods of systemic crises have the highest correlation risk as the change in correlation is often highest in these crises as correlations move closer to 1.

questions.subject: Market Risk
questions.loText: Describe financial correlation risk and the areas in which it appears in finance.
questions.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
questions.topic: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
questions.source: GARP past 10-year papers book, Q7.3
questions.question: Which of these is an example of a dynamic financial correlation?

options.text: Value at Risk
Correlation copulas for CDOs
Pairs trading
Binomial default correlation model

questions.solution:
**Concept**

A static financial correlation measures how assets move together over a fixed period. A dynamic financial correlation describes how the co-movement behaves through time. Value-at-risk, the copula models used for CDOs and the binomial default correlation model all use a static correlation. Pairs trading, deterministic correlation approaches and stochastic correlation processes are dynamic.

**Exam trap.** The question is a classification, and three of the four options belong to the same class. If three options share a property, the odd one out is the answer.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q7.3 (All past year questions, Question 41).

a.reason: VaR uses one correlation (or one correlation matrix) estimated for a given period: static.

b.reason: Copula correlations for CDOs are a single correlation input for the life of the deal: static.

c.reason: Correct. Pairs trading bets on the spread between two assets reverting over time, which depends on how the correlation behaves through time.

d.reason: The binomial default correlation model uses a fixed default correlation: static.

questions.loText: Describe the structure, uses, and payoffs of a correlation swap.
questions.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
questions.topic: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
questions.question: The manager of the equity trading desk of an investment bank is presenting to a group of newly hired analysts on complex derivatives the desk uses to take positions on equity correlations. The manager discusses characteristics and uses of rainbow options, quanto options, and correlation swaps, and demonstrates how the payoff of each product can be modeled with examples that use the Dow Jones Industrial Average as the underlying asset for each instrument. Which of the following statements could the manager correctly make during the presentation?

options.text: The payoff for each of these products is highest when the price movements of the underlying assets are uncorrelated.
Investors can take a synthetic long position in equity correlation by buying put options on an equity index and selling put options on the components of that index.
The payoff for the correlation buyer in a correlation swap is negative if the realized correlation of the underlying assets is higher than the fixed correlation in the swap.
The trader known as the London Whale created large losses by continuing to purchase index swaps even when losses from earlier positions continued to increase.

questions.solution:
**Concept**

A correlation swap pays the buyer notional times (realized correlation minus fixed correlation). Correlation can also be bought with options: buy put options on an index and sell put options on its components (a dispersion-style trade), since index volatility rises with the correlation between the components.

**Exam trap.** Polarity in option C: the correlation buyer gains when realized correlation is above the fixed rate. The London Whale sold index CDS protection and bought single-name protection.

**Source:** 2026 PE2 Q33 (All past year questions, Question 42).

a.reason: The payoff for the options is highest when the price movements of the underlying assets are completely negatively correlated. The payoff of the correlation swap will be highest when the price movements of the underlying assets are either completely positively correlated, or completely negatively correlated.

b.reason: Another way of buying correlation is to buy put options on an index and sell put options on the individual stocks in the index.

c.reason: The payoff of a correlation swap for the correlation buyer is positive if the realized correlation is higher than the fixed correlation in the swap.

d.reason: The London Whale traded correlation synthetically by selling index CDSs and purchasing CDSs on individual bonds, amassing very large positions. The index CDS position took massive losses when hedge funds executed a “short squeeze”.

questions.loText: Describe the structure, uses, and payoffs of a correlation swap.

questions.topic: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
questions.source: GARP past 10-year papers book, Q7.4
questions.question: The buyer of a correlation swap with three assets and a maturity of one year pays a fixed rate of 2.5%. The notional amount of the swap is \$1 million. If the realized pairwise correlations of the daily log returns for the three assets are $\rho_{2{,}1} = 0.2$, $\rho_{3{,}1} = 0.4$ and $\rho_{3{,}2} = 0.3$, what is the realized correlation?
questions.solution:
**Concept**

A correlation swap exchanges a fixed correlation for the realized correlation, which is the simple average of all pairwise correlations between the $n$ assets: $\rho_{\text{realized}} = \frac{2}{n^{2} - n} \sum_{i>j} \rho_{i,j}$. With $n$ assets there are $(n^{2} - n)/2$ pairs.

**Working**

$n = 3$, so there are (9 − 3)/2 = 3 pairs.

$$\rho_{\text{realized}} = \frac{2}{3^{2} - 3} (0.2 + 0.4 + 0.3) = \frac{1}{3} \times0.9 = 0.30$$

The fixed-rate payer (the buyer) would receive \$1,000,000 × (0.30 − 0.025) = \$275,000, although the question only asks for the realized correlation.

**Exam trap.** The fixed rate (2.5%) and the notional are not needed for the realized correlation. They only matter for the payoff, $N \times(\rho_{\text{realized}} - \rho_{\text{fixed}})$.

**Source:** GARP past 10-year papers book, Q7.4 (All past year questions, Question 43).

a.reason: Correct. The average of the three pairwise correlations.

b.reason: 0.20 is the lowest of the three pairwise correlations, not their average.

c.reason: 0.45 is half of the sum (0.9/2), which uses the wrong number of pairs.

d.reason: 0.16 does not correspond to the average of the pairwise correlations.

questions.question: A risk analyst at a bank is estimating the VaR of an equally weighted, two-asset portfolio as an exercise to demonstrate the impact of correlation on VaR. The volatility of the daily returns of each asset in the portfolio is 2%, the value of the portfolio is USD 20 million, and the 10-day 99% VaR of the portfolio is USD 2.33 million. If the correlation between the two assets doubles, which of the following is closest to the new estimate of the 10-day 99% portfolio VaR?

options.text: USD 1.16 million
USD 2.55 million
USD 4.66 million
USD 5.43 million

questions.solution:
**Concept**

For an equally weighted two-asset portfolio with equal volatilities, $\sigma^{2}_{P} = w^{2}_{1}\sigma^{2}_{1} + w^{2}_{2}\sigma^{2}_{2} +$ $2w_{1}w_{2}\sigma_{1}\sigma_{2}\rho= 0.0002 (1 + \rho)$, so VaR is proportional to $\sqrt{1 + \rho}$. Back out the original correlation from the given VaR, double it, and re-price.

**Working**

**Step 1: portfolio volatility in terms of** $\rho$**.** $\sigma_{P} = \sqrt{0.0002 (1 + \rho)} = 0.01414\sqrt{1 + \rho}$

**Step 2: back out** $\rho$ **from the 10-day 99% VaR.**

$$2{,}330{,}000 = \sqrt{10} \times2.326 \times20{,}000{,}000 \times0.01414\sqrt{1 + \rho} = 2{,}080{,}123\sqrt{1 + \rho}$$

$$\sqrt{1 + \rho} = 1.1201 \Rightarrow1 + \rho= 1.2547 \Rightarrow\rho= 0.2547$$

**Step 3: double the correlation.** $\rho_{\text{new}} = 0.5094$

**Step 4: new VaR.** VaR scales with $\sqrt{1 + \rho}$:

$\text{VaR}_{\text{new}} = 2.33 \times\sqrt{\frac{1.5094}{1.2547}} = 2.33 \times1.0968 = \text{USD} 2.55$ million

**Exam trap.** Doubling correlation does not double VaR. The upper bound is the undiversified VaR at $\rho= 1$ (USD 2.94 million here), which eliminates options C and D immediately.

**Source:** 2025 PE2 Q53 (All past year questions, Question 44).

a.reason: USD 1.16 million halves the VaR. A higher correlation means less diversification, so VaR must rise.

b.reason: Correct.

c.reason: USD 4.66 million doubles the VaR along with the correlation. VaR depends on $\sqrt{1 + \rho}$, not on $\rho$ itself.

d.reason: USD 5.43 million is far too large; even perfect correlation ($\rho= 1$) would only give 2.33 × $\sqrt{2/1.2547} = 2.94$ million.
